lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise causal argument with one obvious gap: the lozenge's effect must explain the recoveries rather than the illness resolving on its own.
lr.stimulus: Pediatrician: Every child in our clinic who received the new antiviral lozenge recovered from the sore throat within four days. So the lozenge must be effective at curing this type of sore throat.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the pediatrician's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The children would not have recovered within four days without taking the lozenge.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other antiviral treatment cures sore throats more quickly than the lozenge does.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lozenge has been tested in clinics other than the pediatrician's.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sore throats of this type are caused by a virus rather than by bacteria.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every child who took the lozenge followed the dosing instructions exactly.

explanations.correct: The argument credits the lozenge for the recoveries. If the children would have recovered anyway in the same timeframe, the lozenge did nothing. Negating A destroys the inference.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument claims the lozenge works, not that it is the fastest available treatment.
explanations.C: Out of scope — external replication is not a link in the pediatrician's reasoning.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — the argument is about whether the lozenge cures these sore throats, not about their underlying cause.
explanations.E: Defender disguised as strengthener — compliance would bolster the argument, but the pediatrician observed recoveries regardless of strict adherence.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise ethical argument with one clear gap linking the premise's category (promise under duress) to the conclusion's category (contract under threat).
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A promise made under duress is not morally binding. Thus, the contract Mara signed while being threatened by her employer imposes no moral obligation on her.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mara's employer will face legal consequences for threatening her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A contract signed under threatening conditions counts as a promise made under duress.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No contract is ever morally binding if one party benefits more than the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mara intended to break the contract from the moment she signed it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contracts and promises differ in the legal obligations they create.

explanations.correct: The premise speaks of promises under duress; the conclusion is about a contract signed under threat. Without the bridge that such a contract qualifies as a promise made under duress, the premise does not reach the conclusion.
explanations.A: Out of scope — the argument is about moral obligation, not legal consequences for the employer.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — introduces a sweeping rule about benefit that the argument does not need.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — Mara's intent is irrelevant to whether the contract binds her morally.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the ethicist's claim concerns moral, not legal, force.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward economic analogy argument with one evident gap — conditions responsible for the cited town's outcome must carry over.
lr.stimulus: Economist: When the neighboring town of Parrish raised its minimum wage last year, overall consumer spending in Parrish rose within six months. If our town raises its minimum wage by a similar amount, consumer spending here will also rise within six months.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the economist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Parrish's minimum-wage increase was the largest in the region that year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumer spending is the most important indicator of a town's economic health.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No economic conditions unique to Parrish were responsible for the rise in spending there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every business in our town supports raising the minimum wage.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Our town has a larger population than Parrish does.

explanations.correct: The analogy needs the Parrish result to transfer. If something peculiar to Parrish caused the rise there, the inference to our town collapses. Negating C destroys the argument.
explanations.A: Out of scope — magnitude rank does not connect Parrish's outcome to ours.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument does not claim spending is the most important indicator, only that it will rise.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — business support is not a link in the economist's causal chain.
explanations.E: Reversed direction — if anything, the argument would prefer similarity of size, not a size difference.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise legal argument with one obvious gap linking a statutory category to the specific case at issue.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The statute prohibits any commercial use of the public fountain. My client used the fountain as the backdrop for a paid photography shoot. Therefore, my client violated the statute.
lr.questionStem: The attorney's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: using the fountain as a backdrop for a paid photography shoot is a commercial use of the fountain

choices.label: B
choices.text: the statute has been enforced against other photographers in the past

choices.label: C
choices.text: the client was aware of the statute at the time of the photo shoot

choices.label: D
choices.text: no public official granted the client permission to use the fountain

choices.label: E
choices.text: the fountain is the only public landmark covered by the statute

explanations.correct: The statute prohibits commercial use; the conclusion asserts a violation. Unless the photo shoot counts as commercial use, the premise cannot reach the conclusion. Negating A breaks the argument.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Out of scope — past enforcement patterns are not part of the reasoning.
explanations.C: Shift in subject — the argument turns on what the client did, not on what the client knew.
explanations.D: Defender disguised as strengthener — permission would rebut the charge, but the argument does not need to rule it out to connect its premise to its conclusion.
explanations.E: Out of scope — coverage of other landmarks is irrelevant to whether this use violated the statute.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise causal inference with one obvious chronological alternative that must be ruled out.
lr.stimulus: Ecologist: Populations of the spotted salamander have declined sharply in ponds where a certain pesticide has been detected. So the pesticide must be responsible for the decline of the spotted salamander in those ponds.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the ecologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pesticide was present in these ponds before the salamander populations began to decline.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pesticide is more harmful to salamanders than to any other amphibian.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Salamander populations have not declined in any pond where the pesticide is absent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The pesticide will eventually cause the salamander to become extinct.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulators intend to ban the pesticide in response to the ecologist's findings.

explanations.correct: For the pesticide to be responsible, it must have been present before the decline, not after. Negate A — the pesticide arrived after the decline — and it cannot be the cause.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument only claims the pesticide is responsible in these ponds, not that it is uniquely harmful.
explanations.C: Too strong — the argument does not need declines to happen exclusively in pesticide ponds; other causes elsewhere are allowed.
explanations.D: Out of scope — extinction projections are not part of the inference.
explanations.E: Out of scope — regulatory response is unrelated to whether the pesticide caused the observed decline.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise inference from a test result to a product property, with one evident gap about what the test actually measures.
lr.stimulus: Reviewer: The new laptop ran every benchmark program we tried without slowing down once. So this laptop is powerful enough for any task our readers are likely to perform.
lr.questionStem: The reviewer's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The benchmark programs collectively demand at least as much of the laptop as any task the readers are likely to perform.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The laptop is priced within the range most readers can afford.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other laptop on the market outperformed this one on the benchmarks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Benchmark programs have improved significantly over the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most readers have previously owned a laptop from the same manufacturer.

explanations.correct: The conclusion extrapolates from benchmarks to real-world tasks. Without the assumption that the benchmarks are at least as demanding as those tasks, the benchmark success tells us nothing about readers' tasks.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Out of scope — price is not linked to the laptop's power.
explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion is about sufficiency for readers' tasks, not about ranking among competitors.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — trend data on benchmarks is not used by the argument.
explanations.E: Out of scope — prior ownership has no bearing on the laptop's capability.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise dating inference with one obvious gap: the inscription and the tablet must be contemporaneous.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: The inscription on this stone tablet is written in Old Phrygian, and every known Old Phrygian inscription dates from between the 8th and 4th centuries BCE. Therefore, this tablet dates from between the 8th and 4th centuries BCE.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the linguist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No language other than Old Phrygian used a writing system that resembled the one on the tablet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The inscription was not added to the tablet long after the tablet itself was made.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most Old Phrygian inscriptions are found on stone rather than on other materials.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tablet was discovered in a region where Old Phrygian was spoken.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Old Phrygian is closely related to the language now called Modern Phrygian.

explanations.correct: The inscription's date only dates the tablet if the two were made at the same time. Negate B — the inscription was added much later — and the tablet itself could be far older or younger than the inscription.
explanations.A: Defender disguised as strengthener — misidentification would undermine the argument, but the stimulus already stipulates the inscription is in Old Phrygian.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Out of scope — typical material of Old Phrygian inscriptions is irrelevant to this tablet's date.
explanations.D: Out of scope — where the tablet was found is not a link in the dating inference.
explanations.E: Shift in subject — a relationship to a modern language has no bearing on the dating of Old Phrygian inscriptions.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise historical inference with one obvious gap about what the document actually reports.
lr.stimulus: Historian: A letter written by General Halpern on June 3, 1794, describes his troops marching through the town of Valcour that morning. Therefore, Halpern's troops were in Valcour on June 3, 1794.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Halpern's letter accurately describes where his troops were on the day it was written.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Halpern personally marched alongside his troops as they passed through Valcour.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other general's troops were in Valcour on June 3, 1794.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Halpern wrote letters describing his troops' movements on most days of the campaign.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The town of Valcour was strategically important to both sides in the conflict.

explanations.correct: The argument treats the letter as a reliable report. If the letter misstates where the troops were that morning, the conclusion does not follow. Negating A destroys the inference.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — Halpern's personal location is not what the conclusion claims.
explanations.C: Out of scope — the argument does not require Halpern's troops to be the only ones present.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the historian needs one accurate letter, not a pattern of letter-writing.
explanations.E: Out of scope — strategic importance has nothing to do with where the troops actually were.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise policy argument with one clear gap between program goal and program adoption.
lr.stimulus: City planner: Residents have said repeatedly that their top priority is reducing traffic congestion downtown. The proposed congestion-pricing plan would reduce traffic congestion downtown. Therefore, the city should adopt the congestion-pricing plan.
lr.questionStem: The city planner's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The city should adopt any plan that advances residents' top priority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congestion pricing has successfully reduced traffic in every city that has tried it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents would be willing to pay significantly higher fees to drive downtown.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The plan would reduce congestion more effectively than any alternative the city is considering.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The planner was hired specifically to address downtown traffic congestion.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from a plan that advances residents' top priority to the conclusion that the city should adopt it. Without a principle connecting those two, the premises do not support the conclusion. Negating A blocks the inference.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument does not require universal success, only that this plan will reduce congestion.
explanations.C: Out of scope — willingness to pay is not invoked in the reasoning.
explanations.D: Too strong — the planner claims the plan should be adopted, not that it is the best available option.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the planner's hiring is not a link in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-premise attribution argument with one obvious gap linking stylistic features to authorship.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: The brushwork on this newly examined landscape displays all the distinctive features of Vermeer's known paintings. So this landscape was painted by Vermeer.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the art historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No painter other than Vermeer produces brushwork displaying all the distinctive features of Vermeer's known paintings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vermeer painted more landscapes than any other subject during his career.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The landscape was found in a location where Vermeer is known to have worked.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The canvas and pigments used in the landscape are consistent with those available in Vermeer's lifetime.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Art historians can identify any painting's creator on the basis of brushwork alone.

explanations.correct: The argument infers Vermeer's authorship from brushwork features. If another painter could produce the same distinctive features, the inference fails. Negating A destroys the argument.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Out of scope — the frequency of Vermeer's landscapes does not help link this painting's brushwork to him.
explanations.C: Defender disguised as strengthener — location would bolster attribution, but the stylistic argument does not depend on it.
explanations.D: Defender disguised as strengthener — material consistency would support the attribution, but it is not what the brushwork inference turns on.
explanations.E: Too strong — the argument claims this painting is a Vermeer, not that brushwork alone identifies every painting.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-premise medical argument. The gap is a hidden equivalence between the experimental marker (inflammation) and the clinical outcome (arthritis), and a reference-class trap is available. Negating the correct answer severs the marker-to-disease bridge.
lr.stimulus: Researcher: Patients who took the experimental compound Relvanix for six months showed significantly lower levels of joint inflammation than a comparable group who took a placebo. Since elevated joint inflammation is a precursor to osteoarthritis in older adults, we conclude that Relvanix will reduce the incidence of osteoarthritis among older adults who take it.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Relvanix produces no side effects more serious than the osteoarthritis it is intended to prevent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reducing joint inflammation through means other than Relvanix would also lower the incidence of osteoarthritis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reduction in joint inflammation produced by Relvanix is sufficient to decrease the rate at which osteoarthritis develops.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most older adults who develop osteoarthritis have previously exhibited elevated joint inflammation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No medication currently on the market reduces joint inflammation as effectively as Relvanix does.

explanations.correct: The argument leaps from 'Relvanix lowers inflammation' to 'Relvanix prevents osteoarthritis.' Inflammation being a precursor does not guarantee that any reduction in it is large enough to change disease rates. Negate C — the reduction is not sufficient — and the conclusion about osteoarthritis incidence falls apart.
explanations.A: Out of scope — side effects are not a link in the inflammation-to-arthritis inference.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — the argument concerns Relvanix specifically, not alternative means of reducing inflammation.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Reversed direction — the argument needs inflammation reduction to prevent arthritis, not that arthritis patients had inflammation.
explanations.E: Too strong and off-point — relative efficacy against other drugs is not required for the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic argument relies on a conditional about consumer behavior. The necessary assumption rules out a specific alternative explanation (stockpiling) that would otherwise undermine the causal claim.
lr.stimulus: Economist: In the month after the city imposed a new tax on sugary drinks, sales of those drinks within city limits dropped by nearly 30 percent. Clearly, the tax has succeeded in discouraging residents from consuming sugary drinks.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument depends on the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: residents did not stockpile significant quantities of sugary drinks before the tax took effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: the tax revenue collected will be used to fund public health programs

choices.label: C
choices.text: sugary drinks are the leading cause of preventable illness in the city

choices.label: D
choices.text: no other city has imposed a comparable tax on sugary drinks

choices.label: E
choices.text: the tax applies equally to all sugary drinks sold in the city

explanations.correct: The argument infers reduced consumption from reduced post-tax sales. If residents had stockpiled before the tax took effect, post-tax sales would drop even though total consumption was unchanged. Negate A and the sales drop no longer shows discouraged consumption.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Out of scope — how revenue is used has no bearing on whether the tax discouraged consumption.
explanations.C: Shift in subject — the conclusion is about this tax's effect, not about the overall health importance of sugary drinks.
explanations.D: Irrelevant comparison — other cities' taxes are not a link in the inference.
explanations.E: Out of scope — uniform application is not required for the sales drop to reflect reduced consumption.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical argument with a chronological subtlety: the coin's presence at the site only dates the settlement if the coin arrived during occupation rather than later. Several close-cousin distractors.
lr.stimulus: Archaeologist: A silver coin minted between 180 and 160 B.C.E. was unearthed last summer in a soil layer at the Helvetian hill settlement. This strongly suggests that the settlement was inhabited during the second century B.C.E.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the archaeologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coins from this mint circulated widely throughout the region during the second century B.C.E.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other artifacts at the settlement have been dated to earlier than the second century B.C.E.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The coin was not deposited in that soil layer long after the settlement was abandoned.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most inhabitants of the settlement would have handled silver coins at some point in their lives.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The coin was minted within a few years of reaching the settlement.

explanations.correct: The argument dates occupation from the coin's presence. If the coin was dropped at the site centuries after the settlement was abandoned (by a later traveler, a burial, soil disturbance), the coin tells us nothing about when the site was inhabited. Negate C and the inference collapses.
explanations.A: Too strong — wide circulation is not required for a single coin to reach the site during occupation.
explanations.B: Out of scope — other artifacts' dates are not a link in this particular inference.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — whether most inhabitants handled coins is irrelevant to dating the settlement from this coin.
explanations.E: Too strong — the coin could have reached the site decades after minting and still fall within the occupation period.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental argument pivots on a reference-class assumption: the studied wetlands must be representative of the ones the policy would protect. Strong distractors invoke related scope.
lr.stimulus: Environmental analyst: Wetlands in the Bayou Tertre region that have been fenced off from cattle over the past decade have regenerated native grasses at three times the rate of unfenced wetlands. Therefore, a statewide policy that fences cattle out of wetlands would significantly accelerate native-grass regeneration across the state.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wetlands outside the Bayou Tertre region do not differ from those within it in ways that would prevent fencing from having the same effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cattle are the most significant threat to native grasses in the state's wetlands.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No native grasses will regenerate in wetlands that remain accessible to cattle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cost of fencing cattle out of wetlands statewide will not exceed the ecological benefits.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ranchers in the Bayou Tertre region were legally required to fence their cattle out of wetlands.

explanations.correct: The argument generalizes from Bayou Tertre to the whole state. If wetlands elsewhere differ in ways that defeat the fencing effect (different grass species, different soil, other dominant pressures), the generalization fails. Negate A and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument needs only that fencing helps, not that cattle are the single leading threat.
explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion requires acceleration, not that unfenced wetlands regenerate nothing.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — cost-benefit is not part of the regeneration-rate inference.
explanations.E: Out of scope — what motivated the Bayou Tertre fencing is not a link in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal-reasoning argument with a hidden conditional: the conclusion that the ordinance is void requires not only a conflict but that state law prevail over municipal law in this area. The defender-style assumption is easy to overlook.
lr.stimulus: Legal analyst: The city's new ordinance forbids short-term rentals of residential property for fewer than thirty days. But state law grants property owners the right to rent their homes for any length of time they choose. Consequently, the city's ordinance is unenforceable.
lr.questionStem: The analyst's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most homeowners in the city would prefer to rent their property for fewer than thirty days.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The state legislature has the exclusive authority to regulate all real-estate transactions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: When a municipal ordinance conflicts with state law on this subject, state law prevails.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The city had no legitimate reason to restrict short-term rentals.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts have previously struck down similar short-term rental ordinances in other cities.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes the conflict between the ordinance and state law resolves in favor of state law — otherwise the ordinance remains enforceable despite the conflict. Negate C and the conclusion no longer follows.
explanations.A: Out of scope — homeowner preferences are not a link in the enforceability inference.
explanations.B: Too strong — the argument needs state law to prevail on this subject, not exclusive state authority over all real-estate matters.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — whether the city's reasons are legitimate is irrelevant to legal enforceability against state law.
explanations.E: Out of scope — what other courts have done is not cited as a premise in this argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology argument relies on a hidden bridge between a security metric (password strength) and the conclusion (reduced breaches). The assumption must rule out the main alternative cause of breaches.
lr.stimulus: Technology consultant: Last year our firm rolled out a password manager that generated long, randomized passwords for every employee account. Since then, the number of successful breaches of employee accounts has dropped by more than half. The password manager has clearly been the key to improving our security.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the consultant's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every employee at the firm uses the password manager for each of their accounts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other change made during the past year was largely responsible for the drop in successful breaches.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Randomized passwords are harder to crack than any passwords employees would have chosen themselves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Successful breaches of employee accounts had been increasing before the password manager was introduced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The password manager's randomized passwords cannot be recovered even by the manager's developer.

explanations.correct: The argument credits the password manager for the drop in breaches. If some other change (new firewall, staff training, phishing filter) was largely responsible, the causal claim fails. Negate B and the conclusion loses its support.
explanations.A: Too strong — the argument needs the manager to drive the drop, not universal adoption.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion needs the manager to have contributed to the drop, not that its passwords are uncrackable-relative-to-every-alternative.
explanations.D: Out of scope — a pre-existing trend is not required by the argument.
explanations.E: Out of scope — developer access is not a link in the causal claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistic argument hinges on a subtle equivalence between a writing system's age and the language's age. Several distractors mimic the correct answer's scope.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Inscriptions written in the Turvanic script have been recovered from sites dated to at least 3,200 years ago. Because the Turvanic script was used exclusively to record the Turvanic language, we conclude that the Turvanic language was spoken at least 3,200 years ago.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Turvanic script was not developed significantly earlier than it began to be used for inscriptions

choices.label: B
choices.text: the inscriptions were produced by people who were native speakers of the Turvanic language

choices.label: C
choices.text: any language used for inscriptions at a site must have been spoken at that site

choices.label: D
choices.text: the Turvanic script was the only script in use in the region 3,200 years ago

choices.label: E
choices.text: the Turvanic language was not used exclusively for ceremonial purposes at the time of the inscriptions

explanations.correct: The argument concludes that the language was spoken, based on an inscribed script. But a script can be used to record a language that was not actually spoken by the inscribers (a liturgical or imported language, as with Latin in medieval Europe). The bridge needed is that the script was being used to record a spoken language at the time. Negate B — the inscribers did not speak Turvanic — and the conclusion that Turvanic was spoken 3,200 years ago loses support.
explanations.A: Shift in subject — the conclusion is about the language, not about when the script was invented.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — the argument needs only that someone spoke Turvanic, not that every inscribed language was locally spoken.
explanations.D: Out of scope — other scripts' presence doesn't affect the Turvanic inference.
explanations.E: Reversed direction — this rules out ceremonial-only use, which is close, but the argument actually needs the stronger claim that speakers produced the inscriptions; E alone permits a script without any living speakers using it.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/aesthetics argument contains a category-bridge: a 'mastery of perspective' attribution requires ruling out that the work is a later copy. Sharp negation test.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: The recently discovered panel depicting a market square uses precise single-point perspective of a kind not developed until the 1420s. The panel is signed by Pietro di Marco, who died in 1398. Since works signed by Pietro are almost never forged, we may conclude that Pietro anticipated single-point perspective by more than two decades.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The panel was not painted by a later artist and signed with Pietro's name for commercial reasons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pietro di Marco was the most accomplished painter of his generation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No other painter working before 1420 made use of single-point perspective.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The perspective techniques developed in the 1420s were based on Pietro's work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The market square depicted on the panel was a familiar subject for painters of Pietro's era.

explanations.correct: The argument infers Pietro's authorship from the signature, then credits Pietro with anticipating perspective. If a later artist painted the panel and appended Pietro's signature (even without a forgery's typical intent to deceive collectors), Pietro didn't anticipate anything. Negate A and the conclusion collapses.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Out of scope — Pietro's overall standing isn't a link in the inference.
explanations.C: Too strong — the conclusion is about Pietro's anticipation, not a universal claim about all pre-1420 painters.
explanations.D: Reversed direction — the argument doesn't claim the 1420s techniques derived from Pietro.
explanations.E: Out of scope — subject matter is not part of the reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument moves from a program's prior effectiveness to a prediction about the current case. The necessary assumption guards against a relevant change in conditions.
lr.stimulus: Policy adviser: The tutoring program that we implemented in Millbrook's public schools five years ago improved student reading scores by an average of 12 percent within two years. Our neighboring district has demographics nearly identical to Millbrook's. If the same program is adopted there, reading scores will improve by about 12 percent within two years.
lr.questionStem: The adviser's argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The factors that made the tutoring program effective in Millbrook are still present in the neighboring district today.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No other reading-improvement initiative in the neighboring district could produce gains larger than 12 percent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Student reading scores in the neighboring district are currently lower than Millbrook's were five years ago.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every student in the neighboring district would participate in the tutoring program.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The tutoring program's costs are comparable to those of existing programs in the neighboring district.

explanations.correct: The argument predicts the same outcome from the same program. If the background conditions that made the program work in Millbrook (funded libraries, trained tutors, cooperating parents) are absent in the neighboring district today, the prediction fails. Demographics alone don't guarantee those conditions. Negate A and the conclusion no longer follows.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Shift in subject — the argument predicts this program's effect, not a comparison to other initiatives.
explanations.C: Out of scope — current baseline is not a link in the inference from program to improvement.
explanations.D: Too strong — universal participation is not part of the Millbrook precedent or the prediction.
explanations.E: Out of scope — cost comparisons are not a link in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics argument has a conditional-style gap: the conclusion that the executive acted wrongly depends on a linking principle between duties to shareholders and the specific disclosure at issue. Multiple distractors shift scope.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Corporate executives have a duty to disclose to shareholders any information that would materially affect the value of their shares. When CEO Lanier learned of the impending product recall, she waited two weeks before informing shareholders. Therefore, Lanier violated her duty to the shareholders.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any information about a product recall would materially affect the value of a company's shares.

choices.label: B
choices.text: CEOs who delay disclosing material information always do so for personal financial gain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lanier had a duty to disclose the recall before she was legally required to do so.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shareholders would have sold their shares had they been informed of the recall sooner.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two weeks is the longest an executive can reasonably delay any corporate disclosure.

explanations.correct: The premise is about materially-share-affecting information; the conclusion is about this recall. Without the bridge that the recall qualifies as such information, the duty the ethicist cited doesn't attach. Negate A — not all recall information materially affects share value — and Lanier's particular recall may fall outside the duty, so the conclusion does not follow.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — motive is not required for a duty violation.
explanations.C: Shift in subject — the argument is about ethical duty, not legal timing.
explanations.D: Shift in subject — shareholder reaction is not what 'material' means in the stated duty.
explanations.E: Too strong — a general timing rule is not needed; the ethicist only needs this delay to have violated the duty.

lr.difficultyReason: Medical argument with a hidden reference-class shift: the trial measured a surrogate biomarker in one population, but the conclusion generalizes to a clinical outcome in a broader, older population. Tempting distractors include a too-strong universal, a shift-in-subject about alternative mechanisms, and a reversed-direction trap. Negation test requires re-identifying what the researchers actually measured.
lr.stimulus: Cardiologist: In our six-week trial, adults aged 40 to 55 who took the drug Noviran had, on average, measurably lower resting blood pressure than those who took a placebo. Since sustained high blood pressure is a leading cause of stroke in older adults, physicians should prescribe Noviran to their patients over 70 to reduce those patients' risk of stroke.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the cardiologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any intervention that lowers blood pressure in middle-aged adults will lower blood pressure by a comparable margin in adults over 70.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Noviran has no side effects in older adults that outweigh its benefits for stroke prevention.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Noviran's effect on blood pressure in middle-aged adults is not attributable solely to mechanisms that cease to operate in adults over 70.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most adults over 70 who suffer strokes have had elevated blood pressure for an extended period before the stroke.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No drug currently prescribed to adults over 70 lowers blood pressure more effectively than Noviran.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'Noviran lowered blood pressure in 40-to-55-year-olds' to 'Noviran will reduce stroke risk in people over 70.' That requires the drug still to lower blood pressure in the older group. Negate C: the mechanism by which Noviran lowers blood pressure in middle-aged adults ceases to operate in people over 70. Then the trial data no longer supports any stroke-risk claim about over-70s, and the conclusion collapses. C is therefore necessary — stated defensively, ruling out the specific alternative that the drug simply doesn't work in the target population.
explanations.A: Too strong and shifted. The argument doesn't need 'any intervention' to work comparably — only Noviran. A universal claim about all blood-pressure-lowering interventions is not required.
explanations.B: Out of scope. Side-effect balance is a separate prudential question, not a link in the inflammation-to-stroke inference. Negating B (there are worse side effects) would make prescribing imprudent but would not undermine the reasoning from trial data to stroke-risk reduction.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Reversed direction. The argument needs lowering blood pressure to reduce stroke risk, not that stroke patients previously had high blood pressure. Negating D leaves the argument intact.
explanations.E: Out of scope and too strong. Relative efficacy against other drugs is not what the conclusion depends on; Noviran could be second-best and the stroke-reduction claim could still hold.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental science stimulus with a counterfactual trap. The recovery of the fish population after the pollution-control policy is being credited to the policy itself; the necessary assumption rules out a non-policy explanation (prior natural rebound already underway). Close-cousin distractors include a too-strong comparison claim and an out-of-scope observation about other species.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Five years after Lake Halberg's watershed council imposed strict limits on agricultural runoff, the lake's yellow perch population, which had declined for decades, had rebounded to near its historical average. The council's chair credits the limits with the recovery. Since nothing else changed about the lake's management in that period, the chair's explanation is almost certainly correct.
lr.questionStem: The scientist's argument depends on the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: runoff limits of comparable strictness have produced measurable fish recoveries in other lakes with similar pollution profiles

choices.label: B
choices.text: the yellow perch population would not have rebounded to near its historical average during those five years had the runoff limits not been imposed

choices.label: C
choices.text: agricultural runoff was the single largest source of pollution in Lake Halberg prior to the limits

choices.label: D
choices.text: no other species in Lake Halberg declined during the five years following the imposition of the limits

choices.label: E
choices.text: the watershed council enforced the runoff limits consistently throughout the entire five-year period

explanations.correct: To credit the limits with the recovery, the scientist must assume the recovery would not have happened without them. Negate B: the perch would have rebounded to near the historical average over those five years even without the limits (for example, a long-delayed natural cycle). Then the post-policy recovery is not evidence that the policy caused it, and the chair's explanation is undercut. B is thus the indispensable counterfactual bridge.
explanations.A: Shift in subject and too strong. Other lakes' responses are not a premise of the argument; the conclusion is about Lake Halberg specifically. Negating A leaves this lake's situation unchanged.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong. The limits could have caused the recovery even if runoff was not the single largest pollution source — only that limiting it made the difference. Negating C does not destroy the argument.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Other species' trajectories are not a link in the reasoning about perch recovery.
explanations.E: Tempting but not strictly necessary. Even inconsistent enforcement could have produced the rebound if sufficient overall; the argument needs only that the limits (however enforced) made the difference, not that enforcement was consistent throughout.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic argument with a comparative-claim subtlety. The conclusion says Brindale has a lower cost of living than Coverdale, but the evidence is that Brindale residents spend less on housing and groceries. The necessary assumption is that the non-measured categories do not make up the difference — a defensive assumption easily overlooked in favor of more aggressive-sounding distractors.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Residents of Brindale spend, on average, a smaller share of their income on housing and groceries than residents of Coverdale do. Since housing and groceries are among the largest household expenses in both cities, the overall cost of living in Brindale must be lower than that in Coverdale.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Residents of Brindale do not spend a sufficiently larger share of their income on expenses other than housing and groceries to offset the difference in housing and grocery spending.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Housing and groceries together account for more than half of an average household's spending in both Brindale and Coverdale.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents of Brindale earn, on average, the same income as residents of Coverdale.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any city in which housing and groceries consume a smaller share of income than in Coverdale has a lower overall cost of living than Coverdale.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Brindale's housing and grocery prices are lower in absolute terms than those in Coverdale.

explanations.correct: The conclusion compares overall cost of living. The premises compare only housing and groceries. Negate A: Brindale residents spend enough more on other categories to offset the housing-and-grocery savings. Then overall cost of living in Brindale is not lower, and the conclusion fails. A is necessary — a classic defensive, gap-closing assumption.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Close cousin but not required. The argument needs only that the offset not erase the difference, not any specific threshold share. The argument could hold even if housing plus groceries were less than half of total spending.
explanations.C: Shift in subject. The comparison is of shares of income, not absolute income. Equal income is not needed for the share-based inference to yield a cost-of-living conclusion.
explanations.D: Too strong. This is a general principle that would prove the conclusion rather than merely enabling it; necessary assumptions are narrower. It is a sufficient-assumption, not necessary-assumption, answer.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. The premises are about share of income, not absolute prices. Negating E (absolute prices are equal or higher in Brindale) does not block the argument, which works off share-of-income data.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal argument with a statistical-inference gap. The prosecutor infers from a matching DNA profile that the defendant was present; the necessary assumption constrains the reference class — specifically, that the profile is not shared by a substantial number of other people who could plausibly have been at the scene. Distractors include a reversed-direction assumption and a too-strong uniqueness claim.
lr.stimulus: Prosecutor: DNA extracted from a hair found at the crime scene matches the defendant's genetic profile on all thirteen markers tested. Profiles matching on all thirteen markers are extremely rare in the general population. We should therefore conclude that the hair came from the defendant, placing him at the scene.
lr.questionStem: The prosecutor's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the hair could not have been transferred to the scene by someone other than the person it came from

choices.label: B
choices.text: the thirteen markers tested are the markers least likely to coincide by chance in unrelated individuals

choices.label: C
choices.text: the population from which potential contributors to the hair would plausibly be drawn is not substantially enriched in people sharing the defendant's thirteen-marker profile

choices.label: D
choices.text: the defendant has no identical twin living within the city where the crime occurred

choices.label: E
choices.text: the matching profile alone constitutes sufficient evidence to convict the defendant of the crime

explanations.correct: The argument hinges on the rarity of a thirteen-marker match in the general population. But what matters is rarity in the reference class of people who could plausibly have contributed the hair. Negate C: that reference class is substantially enriched in matching profiles (for example, because the defendant's close relatives live nearby and were frequent visitors). Then the match is no longer strong evidence that the hair is the defendant's, and the conclusion collapses. C fills the reference-class gap.
explanations.A: Out of scope for this conclusion. The conclusion is that the hair came from the defendant, placing him at the scene; secondary transfer is a separate issue from source identification.
explanations.B: Too strong. The argument doesn't need the thirteen markers to be the best possible choice, only that a match on them be rare enough in the relevant population.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Close cousin, but narrower than necessary. The problem of enriched reference-class matches is broader than identical twins; ruling out only twins leaves other enrichment sources (close relatives, an isolated subpopulation) unaddressed.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. Whether the match suffices for conviction is a legal-standard question, not a premise of the source-identification inference.

lr.difficultyReason: History stimulus with a chronology-dependent gap. The historian dates a trade network from merchandise found in a shipwreck, but the conclusion requires that the ship sank while the merchandise was in active trade, not long after. Distractors include a too-strong claim about trade routes and a reversed-direction temporal claim.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Amphorae bearing stamps that were used only by vintners in the port city of Rhodion between 140 and 110 B.C.E. have been recovered from a shipwreck off the coast of Sicily. The amphorae still contained residues of Rhodian wine when found. We conclude that a commercial wine trade connecting Rhodion to western Mediterranean markets was active during the second half of the second century B.C.E.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rhodian vintners did not export wine to western Mediterranean markets at any time before 140 B.C.E.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ship carrying the amphorae sank no more than a few decades after the amphorae were filled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stamps used by Rhodian vintners after 110 B.C.E. differed from those used during 140 to 110 B.C.E.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No stamped Rhodian amphorae from the period in question have been recovered from sites outside the western Mediterranean.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rhodian wine was the most valuable cargo commonly shipped to western Mediterranean ports during the period in question.

explanations.correct: The dating premise is the stamps' production window, 140 to 110 B.C.E. To conclude that the wine trade was active in that window, the historian must assume the shipwreck occurred close to that window rather than long afterward. Negate B: the ship sank two centuries later, perhaps while transporting antique-filled amphorae for some unrelated purpose. Then the wreck's existence does not establish an active second-century trade, and the conclusion falls apart. B is the necessary chronological bridge — parallel to the lake-sediment bones case.
explanations.A: Shift in subject. The conclusion concerns whether the trade was active in 140 to 110 B.C.E., not whether it was uniquely active then. Earlier trade is compatible with the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Close cousin, but not required. Even if later stamps were identical, the stamps recovered could still plausibly be from the 140 to 110 B.C.E. window. The argument can work without ruling out later identical stamps, provided B holds.
explanations.D: Too strong and out of scope. Whether other amphorae surface elsewhere is independent of whether this wreck establishes the trade.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Relative cargo value is not a premise of the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology stimulus with a hidden reference-class issue: benchmark tests on a processor were run under controlled lab conditions, but the conclusion generalizes to everyday performance. The necessary assumption rules out the alternative that the lab conditions favored the tested chip in ways not replicated in typical use. Distractors include a shift-in-subject comparison and a too-strong universal.
lr.stimulus: Technology reviewer: In our laboratory benchmarks, the Aster X7 processor completed standard computational tasks, on average, 18 percent faster than the leading competitor's chip. Because these benchmarks are the accepted industry standard for gauging processor speed, consumers should expect the Aster X7 to handle their everyday computing needs noticeably more quickly than the competitor's chip handles them.
lr.questionStem: The reviewer's argument depends on the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Aster X7 is priced competitively with the leading competitor's chip

choices.label: B
choices.text: the conditions under which the laboratory benchmarks were run did not give the Aster X7 an advantage that is absent in typical everyday computing use

choices.label: C
choices.text: no other processor currently sold to consumers performs better on the industry-standard benchmarks than the Aster X7

choices.label: D
choices.text: every task that consumers commonly perform on a personal computer is included in the industry-standard benchmark suite

choices.label: E
choices.text: consumers typically choose processors on the basis of laboratory benchmark performance rather than on the basis of other considerations

explanations.correct: The argument extrapolates from controlled benchmarks to everyday performance. That extrapolation requires that the benchmark setup not have favored the Aster X7 in ways absent from normal use (for example, thermal management tuned to the benchmarks, or minimal background processes). Negate B: the lab conditions did favor the Aster X7 in ways absent from everyday use. Then the 18-percent advantage would not transfer to consumer settings, and the conclusion falls apart.
explanations.A: Out of scope. Pricing is irrelevant to whether the processor handles tasks more quickly; the conclusion is about speed, not value.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong and shifted. The conclusion compares the Aster X7 to 'the leading competitor's chip,' not to all other processors. Negating C does not block the argument.
explanations.D: Too strong. The argument needs only that benchmark performance reasonably predict everyday performance, not that every common task appear in the suite. Negating D (some tasks are missing) does not destroy the argument provided the suite is reasonably representative.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. The conclusion is a prediction about what consumers should expect, not about how consumers in fact choose. Consumer purchasing criteria are orthogonal to the speed claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics stimulus with a scope-narrowing gap. The corpus shows a vocabulary contraction, but the conclusion generalizes to speakers' actual vocabulary knowledge. The necessary assumption rules out the possibility that the corpus is unrepresentative of general usage. Trap answers include a too-strong universal and a reversed-direction claim about written versus spoken language.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: A study of text messages sent by teenagers over the past twenty years finds that the average number of distinct English words appearing in a year's worth of messages has declined by roughly 15 percent. We conclude that the working vocabulary of the average English-speaking teenager has contracted correspondingly over the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contraction in the number of distinct words appearing in teenagers' text messages does not primarily reflect shifts in what teenagers choose to write about in messages rather than in what words they know.

choices.label: B
choices.text: English-speaking teenagers today send, on average, approximately the same number of text messages per year as teenagers did twenty years ago.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every word known by a teenager has some probability of appearing in a year's worth of that teenager's text messages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Teenagers whose working vocabularies contract are also the teenagers whose text messages contain the fewest distinct words.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The vocabularies used by teenagers in text messages are a larger subset of their overall vocabularies than are the vocabularies they use in spoken conversation.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from corpus evidence (distinct words in messages) to a claim about working vocabulary. If the contraction reflects a narrowing of message topics rather than a narrowing of known words, then the corpus is not a valid proxy for working vocabulary. Negate A — the contraction does primarily reflect topic shift — and the conclusion collapses. A is the narrow, defensively phrased bridge required.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Close cousin, but not strictly necessary. Even if teenagers send fewer or more messages today, the distinct-word count per year could still track vocabulary. The argument can survive a moderate change in message volume.
explanations.C: Too strong. The argument doesn't need every word to have some chance of appearing — only that the sample be representative enough for the comparison.
explanations.D: Reversed direction. This states how vocabulary contraction correlates with corpus data, not what the argument requires to move from corpus data to vocabulary.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The argument is about text-message corpora, not a comparison between written and spoken vocabularies. Negating E does not break the inference.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics stimulus with a counterfactual gap. The ethicist concludes the sanctions policy was morally justified on the grounds that it achieved its stated aim. The necessary assumption is that the aim could not have been achieved by an alternative with less serious harm. Tempting wrong answers include a too-strong impossibility claim and a shift-in-subject about general sanctions theory.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: The economic sanctions imposed by nation A on nation B succeeded in compelling nation B's government to abandon its program of forced labor. The sanctions also caused meaningful hardship for many civilians in nation B who had no role in the program. Nevertheless, because the sanctions accomplished their stated aim, imposing them was morally justified.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the ethicist's argument relies?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No alternative measure available to nation A would have compelled nation B's government to abandon the forced-labor program while causing less hardship to uninvolved civilians.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Economic sanctions are, in general, morally justified whenever they succeed in achieving their stated aim.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The hardship caused to uninvolved civilians in nation B was not foreseeable by nation A at the time the sanctions were imposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nation B's government would not have abandoned the forced-labor program in the absence of the sanctions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The forced-labor program caused harm to nation B's civilians at least as severe as the hardship imposed by the sanctions.

explanations.correct: The ethicist must bridge 'sanctions achieved the aim' to 'sanctions were justified' given that they harmed civilians. A policy with avoidable collateral harm is hard to call justified if a less harmful alternative would have worked. Negate A: an alternative was available that would have succeeded with less civilian hardship. Then the sanctions' collateral harm was avoidable, and their justification evaporates. A is the necessary assumption.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — a universal principle about sanctions. Necessary assumptions are narrow; the argument needs only this case, not a general rule. This is a sufficient-assumption trap.
explanations.C: Close cousin, but not required. Foreseeability affects blame but not whether these sanctions were justified given the alternatives available. The argument can be defended even if the hardship was foreseeable, so long as A holds.
explanations.D: Tempting as a counterfactual but concerns effectiveness, which is already granted. The sanctions are stipulated to have succeeded; the argument does not additionally need that the program would have continued otherwise.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. A comparison of severity between forced labor and sanctions hardship is not a link in the argument as stated; the argument rests on the achievement of the aim plus justification. Negating E does not block A's reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument with a statistical-inference subtlety. The analyst infers that the tutoring program raised test scores from a year-over-year jump at participating schools; the necessary assumption rules out a confounding change that coincided with the program. Distractors include a too-strong claim about causation in general and a shift-in-subject about non-participating schools.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: After the state launched its after-school tutoring initiative, participating schools saw standardized math scores rise by an average of 9 percent in a single year — a jump far larger than any observed in the preceding decade. Since the initiative is the most salient change at these schools over that time, the initiative must be responsible for the jump.
lr.questionStem: The analyst's argument requires the assumption that

choices.label: A
choices.text: no factor other than the tutoring initiative that could plausibly have produced the jump in math scores changed at the participating schools during that year

choices.label: B
choices.text: the tutoring initiative increased math scores at every individual school that participated in it

choices.label: C
choices.text: schools that did not participate in the tutoring initiative did not see any comparable jump in math scores during the same year

choices.label: D
choices.text: standardized math scores are a reliable indicator of students' overall academic achievement

choices.label: E
choices.text: the tutoring initiative will continue to raise math scores in subsequent years if funding is maintained

explanations.correct: The argument infers causation from a coincident change, reasoning that the initiative is 'the most salient change.' That inference holds only if no other plausible cause changed too. Negate A: another plausible cause (for example, a simultaneous curriculum overhaul) did change at those schools. Then the initiative is not uniquely positioned to explain the jump, and the conclusion fails. A is the necessary alternative-cause-ruled-out assumption.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong. The conclusion concerns average improvement, not school-by-school uniformity. Some participating schools could have seen no gain while the average still rose.
explanations.C: Close cousin. It would strengthen the argument, but it is not required: the initiative could still be responsible for the participating-school jump even if other forces independently produced a comparable jump elsewhere. Necessary-assumption answers do not usually require this kind of comparison across populations.
explanations.D: Shift in subject. The conclusion is about the score jump, not about overall academic achievement. Score reliability for broader claims is not a premise here.
explanations.E: Out of scope. The conclusion is about what happened, not about what will happen in later years.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts argument with a comparative-claim gap. The critic concludes a novelist is the greatest of her generation based on literary-prize tallies over a period, but the conclusion requires that the prizes track greatness and that the comparison population is her generation. Tempting wrong answers include a reversed-direction claim and a too-strong universal about prize-giving.
lr.stimulus: Literary critic: Over the past two decades, Mira Adelaide has received more major international literary prizes than any other novelist writing in English during that period. These prizes are awarded by expert panels specifically to recognize the highest literary achievement. We can therefore conclude that Adelaide is the greatest English-language novelist of her generation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A novelist who writes in a language other than English cannot belong to Adelaide's generation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The major international literary prizes awarded over the past two decades tracked literary achievement at least as reliably among English-language novelists of Adelaide's generation as among those of other generations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adelaide's generation of English-language novelists is represented among the novelists who received major international literary prizes over the past two decades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No novelist writing in English over the past two decades who did not receive as many major international prizes as Adelaide achieved as much as she did in literary terms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The expert panels awarding the major international literary prizes over the past two decades consisted of members drawn from diverse national and cultural backgrounds.

explanations.correct: The argument needs the prize-tally lead to translate into a greatness lead over Adelaide's generation. Negate D: some other English-language novelist of the past two decades, with fewer prizes, in fact achieved more in literary terms than Adelaide. Then Adelaide is not the greatest of her generation, and the conclusion fails. D is the necessary defensive bridge — phrased as 'no one uncredited surpassed her.'
explanations.A: Shift in subject and too strong. The conclusion concerns English-language novelists, but restricting Adelaide's generation to English speakers is not required by the argument; it would alter the conclusion's scope rather than support it.
explanations.B: Close cousin but inverted. The argument does not need a cross-generational reliability comparison; it needs only that within Adelaide's generation, the prizes track greatness well enough for her tally lead to correspond to a greatness lead — which is what D establishes.
explanations.C: Necessary-sounding but vacuous: Adelaide herself is an English-language novelist of her generation who received prizes, so representation is guaranteed by the stimulus. C adds nothing the argument needs.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Panel diversity is not a link in the argument; the stimulus already asserts that the panels are expert and award for literary achievement.

lr.difficultyReason: One-step conditional gap. Stimulus places Dr. Aronson in a named category; conclusion moves her to a second category; the correct answer supplies the missing universal link between the two categories.
lr.stimulus: Every physician at Brighton Clinic is certified in emergency medicine. Dr. Aronson practices at Brighton Clinic. So Dr. Aronson is qualified to staff the county trauma ward.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone certified in emergency medicine is qualified to staff the county trauma ward.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some physicians qualified to staff the county trauma ward are certified in emergency medicine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No physician who lacks certification in emergency medicine practices at Brighton Clinic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anyone qualified to staff the county trauma ward is certified in emergency medicine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most physicians at Brighton Clinic have staffed a trauma ward at some point in their careers.

explanations.correct: The premises establish that Dr. Aronson is certified in emergency medicine. To force the conclusion that she is qualified to staff the trauma ward, we need every emergency-certified physician to be so qualified. (A) supplies exactly that universal bridge.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too weak. 'Some' qualified staffers being certified does not put Dr. Aronson in the qualified group.
explanations.C: This restates the first premise in contrapositive form. It tells us who can practice at Brighton, not who is trauma-ward qualified.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional. This says qualified → certified, but the argument needs certified → qualified.
explanations.E: 'Most' does not guarantee Dr. Aronson is among them, and past staffing is not the same as present qualification.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-step gap between 'breaks a promise' and 'acts wrongly.' The correct answer is a universal ethical principle that closes the gap directly.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Councilor Marsh pledged during her campaign to vote against the stadium subsidy, but last week she voted in favor of it. In doing so, she broke a promise she had made to her constituents. Therefore, Councilor Marsh acted wrongly.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who breaks a promise made to constituents acts wrongly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A councilor who votes for a stadium subsidy acts wrongly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most promises made during political campaigns ought to be kept.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anyone who acts wrongly has broken a promise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No councilor who keeps her campaign promises acts wrongly.

explanations.correct: The premise establishes that Marsh broke a promise to her constituents. To force the conclusion that she acted wrongly, the argument needs the universal 'breaking such a promise → acting wrongly.' (A) is that conditional.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The stimulus never claims that voting for the subsidy is itself wrong — only that breaking the promise is the wrong act.
explanations.C: 'Most' is too weak to force a conclusion about Marsh's particular promise.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional: wrong → promise-breaking, rather than promise-breaking → wrong.
explanations.E: Tells us only what follows when promises are kept; Marsh did not keep hers, so this yields no conclusion about her conduct.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct one-concept gap. Premise identifies a firm as a monopolist; conclusion attributes a consequence (raises prices above competitive levels). Correct answer is the universal linking the two.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Northgate Utilities is the sole provider of natural gas in this region and therefore operates as a monopolist. It follows that Northgate charges prices above the level that a competitive market would produce.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every monopolist charges prices above the level that a competitive market would produce.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any firm that charges prices above competitive levels is a monopolist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monopolists tend to charge higher prices than firms facing competitors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A firm that is the sole provider of a service in a region faces no meaningful substitutes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some monopolists charge prices above the level that a competitive market would produce.

explanations.correct: The argument moves from 'Northgate is a monopolist' to 'Northgate charges above competitive prices.' Forcing that inference requires every monopolist to charge above competitive prices. (A) supplies the universal link.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional. This guarantees only that above-competitive firms are monopolists, not that Northgate prices above the competitive level.
explanations.C: 'Tend to' falls short of certainty. Sufficient assumptions demand all, not a tendency.
explanations.D: Explains why Northgate counts as a monopolist but says nothing about its pricing.
explanations.E: 'Some' leaves open that Northgate belongs to the monopolists who do not price above competitive levels.

lr.difficultyReason: One-step gap between 'contract signed under duress' and 'unenforceable.' The correct answer is the universal principle linking duress to unenforceability.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The settlement agreement that Rollins signed was obtained under duress, for the opposing party threatened to publicize confidential medical records unless he signed. It follows that the settlement agreement cannot be enforced against Rollins.
lr.questionStem: The attorney's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No contract signed under duress can be enforced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any threat to publicize medical records constitutes duress.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some contracts signed under duress cannot be enforced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any contract that cannot be enforced was signed under duress.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rollins signed the settlement agreement only because of the threat.

explanations.correct: The premise places the contract in the category 'signed under duress,' and the conclusion places it in 'cannot be enforced.' A universal from the first category to the second forces the conclusion. (A) does that.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Supports that what happened counts as duress, but duress is already granted in the premise.
explanations.C: 'Some' leaves open that Rollins's contract is one of the enforceable duress-signed contracts.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional. The argument needs duress → unenforceable, not the reverse.
explanations.E: Fills in a causal detail but does not connect duress to unenforceability, which is the unbridged step.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent one-step gap. Premise: the wetland is classified as an old-growth fen. Conclusion: it merits protection under the statute. The missing universal is the bridge.
lr.stimulus: Ecologist: The Alderbrook wetland has been formally classified as an old-growth fen by the state survey. Therefore, the Alderbrook wetland merits protection under the Wetlands Heritage Act.
lr.questionStem: The ecologist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every old-growth fen merits protection under the Wetlands Heritage Act.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every wetland that merits protection under the Wetlands Heritage Act is an old-growth fen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most old-growth fens in the state have been formally classified by the state survey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No wetland can be classified as an old-growth fen unless it merits protection.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Wetlands Heritage Act protects wetlands that are rare or ecologically significant.

explanations.correct: The argument places Alderbrook in 'old-growth fen' and concludes it is in 'merits protection.' The universal 'every old-growth fen merits protection' is the missing link. (A) states precisely that.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional: meriting protection → old-growth fen. Does not put Alderbrook into the protected category.
explanations.C: Shifts the subject to classification practice; irrelevant to whether Alderbrook merits protection.
explanations.D: This would be a requirement for classification, not an entailment from classification to protection.
explanations.E: Too vague — 'rare or ecologically significant' is not stipulated of Alderbrook, and protection is not guaranteed by this general description.

lr.difficultyReason: Single transparent gap. Premise: the device uses end-to-end encryption. Conclusion: intercepted messages cannot be read by third parties. The universal that links the two is the needed assumption.
lr.stimulus: The new Larkspur messaging app uses end-to-end encryption for all communications between users. It follows that any message sent through Larkspur cannot be read by a third party who intercepts it in transit.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No message protected by end-to-end encryption can be read by a third party who intercepts it in transit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any message that cannot be read by a third party who intercepts it is protected by end-to-end encryption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most messaging apps that use end-to-end encryption also encrypt stored copies of messages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: End-to-end encryption prevents third parties from determining who sent a given message.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Messages sent through Larkspur are encrypted on the sender's device before transmission.

explanations.correct: The argument classifies Larkspur messages as end-to-end encrypted and concludes they cannot be read by intercepting third parties. The universal in (A) forces that step.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional: unreadable-if-intercepted → end-to-end encrypted. This does not place Larkspur messages in the unreadable category.
explanations.C: Shifts to stored copies; the conclusion concerns in-transit interception.
explanations.D: Introduces sender identity, a different property from message readability.
explanations.E: Provides a plausible mechanism but does not guarantee the interceptor cannot read the message.

lr.difficultyReason: One-step gap between a linguistic property (derived from Proto-Indo-European) and a classification (Indo-European language). The universal bridge supplies the inference.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Tocharian B is a language whose vocabulary and grammar descend directly from Proto-Indo-European. It follows that Tocharian B is an Indo-European language.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any language whose vocabulary and grammar descend directly from Proto-Indo-European is an Indo-European language.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every Indo-European language has a vocabulary and grammar that descend directly from Proto-Indo-European.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most languages classified as Indo-European are descended from Proto-Indo-European.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tocharian B shares vocabulary with several other Indo-European languages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No language is classified as Indo-European unless specialists agree on its ancestry.

explanations.correct: The premise places Tocharian B in the category 'descends from Proto-Indo-European.' The conclusion places it in 'Indo-European language.' (A) universalizes the move.
explanations.A: Correct.
