explanations.B: Reversed conditional. It tells us a property of every Indo-European language, not that descent from PIE suffices for that classification.
explanations.C: 'Most' leaves room for Tocharian B to be an exception.
explanations.D: Shared vocabulary is evidence, but the argument already stipulates direct descent; what is missing is the link to the classification.
explanations.E: Introduces a gatekeeping condition about specialists that the stimulus never invokes.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct one-step gap. Premise: the document was issued by the royal chancery before 1154. Conclusion: it must be written in Medieval Latin. The universal from category A to category B is the needed assumption.
lr.stimulus: Historian: The charter granting market rights to the village of Ashworth was issued by the royal chancery during the reign of Henry I, which ended in 1154. It follows that the original text of the charter was written in Medieval Latin.
lr.questionStem: The historian's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every document issued by the royal chancery before 1154 was written in Medieval Latin.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any document written in Medieval Latin was issued by the royal chancery before 1154.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most surviving charters from the reign of Henry I are written in Medieval Latin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medieval Latin was used throughout Western Europe for official documents during the twelfth century.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The charter granting market rights to Ashworth has been preserved in its original form.

explanations.correct: The argument places the charter in the class 'issued by the royal chancery before 1154' and concludes it is in 'written in Medieval Latin.' The universal in (A) forces that move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional. It tells us the provenance of every Medieval Latin document, not the language of every pre-1154 chancery document.
explanations.C: 'Most' allows the charter to be among the exceptions.
explanations.D: Even if broadly true, it does not establish that this particular charter was in Medieval Latin rather than, say, Old English or Old French.
explanations.E: Preservation status is irrelevant to the original language.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-step gap between 'raises effective tax rates on low-income households' and 'should be rejected by the council.' The universal principle linking the two closes the gap directly.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: The proposed sales-tax expansion would raise the effective tax rate on low-income households in our district. Therefore, the council should reject the proposal.
lr.questionStem: The analyst's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The council should reject any proposal that would raise the effective tax rate on low-income households.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any proposal the council rejects would have raised the effective tax rate on low-income households.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most proposals that raise taxes on low-income households also fail to raise significant revenue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The council has previously rejected tax proposals that burdened low-income households.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sales-tax expansions generally burden low-income households more than high-income households.

explanations.correct: The premise places the proposal in 'raises rates on low-income households.' The conclusion places it in 'should be rejected.' (A) is the universal that forces the jump.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional: rejected → raises rates on low-income. Does not support the council's duty to reject this one.
explanations.C: Introduces revenue, a concern the argument never raised, and uses 'most,' which is too weak.
explanations.D: Past practice does not entail what the council should do now.
explanations.E: Supports the premise's plausibility rather than bridging premise to conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: One-step conditional gap. Premise: the painting was produced by the Utrecht Caravaggisti. Conclusion: it employs tenebrist lighting. The universal bridging movement to technique is the needed assumption.
lr.stimulus: Art historian: The oil painting recently acquired by the Kessel Museum was produced by the Utrecht Caravaggisti during the 1620s. It follows that the painting employs tenebrist lighting.
lr.questionStem: The art historian's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every painting produced by the Utrecht Caravaggisti employs tenebrist lighting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every painting that employs tenebrist lighting was produced by the Utrecht Caravaggisti.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most 1620s paintings acquired by major museums employ tenebrist lighting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paintings that employ tenebrist lighting are typically more valuable than those that do not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Utrecht Caravaggisti were influenced by the Italian painter Caravaggio.

explanations.correct: The premise places the painting in the class 'produced by the Utrecht Caravaggisti'; the conclusion places it in 'employs tenebrist lighting.' The universal in (A) closes that gap.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional. It says tenebrist paintings are all Utrecht Caravaggisti works, not that every Utrecht Caravaggisti work is tenebrist.
explanations.C: 'Most' leaves the possibility that this painting is one that does not employ tenebrism.
explanations.D: Market value has no bearing on the technique used.
explanations.E: Explains influence but does not entail that every Utrecht Caravaggisti painting is tenebrist.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step conditional chain: the argument links 'approved by the review board' and 'meets safety standards,' and concludes about funding. The student must supply the missing link from 'safety standards met' to 'funding granted.' Trap (B) reverses the conditional; trap (E) is a near-restatement of a premise.
lr.stimulus: Every proposal that is approved by the hospital's research review board meets the federal safety standards. The gene-therapy proposal submitted by Dr. Okafor was approved by the review board last month. It follows that Dr. Okafor's proposal will receive federal funding.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any proposal that meets the federal safety standards will receive federal funding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any proposal that receives federal funding meets the federal safety standards.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No proposal that fails to meet federal safety standards is approved by the hospital's research review board.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most proposals that meet the federal safety standards receive federal funding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Okafor's gene-therapy proposal was approved by the hospital's research review board.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes 'approved → meets safety standards' and applies it to Okafor's proposal, giving us 'Okafor meets safety standards.' The conclusion is 'Okafor receives funding.' The missing link is 'meets safety standards → receives funding,' which (A) supplies as a universal conditional — forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional — this gives 'funding → safety,' which doesn't help derive 'funding' from 'safety.'
explanations.C: Restates the first premise in contrapositive form; adds no new bridge to the funding conclusion.
explanations.D: Too weak — 'most' does not force the conclusion that Okafor's particular proposal will receive funding.
explanations.E: Restates a premise rather than adding the missing link.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-concept gap between 'fluent in a second language by age seven' and 'capable of native-level pronunciation,' with the conclusion about a specific child. Trap (D) shifts the subject from 'native-level pronunciation' to 'accent-free speech'; trap (C) reverses the key conditional.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Every child who becomes fluent in a second language by age seven retains the capacity for native-level pronunciation in that language throughout life. Mira, who is now an adult, became fluent in Portuguese by age six. So Mira can be trained to speak Portuguese without any detectable foreign accent.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any adult who retains the capacity for native-level pronunciation in a language can be trained to speak that language without any detectable foreign accent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most adults who became fluent in a second language as children can be trained to speak that language without a foreign accent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every adult who can speak a second language without a detectable foreign accent became fluent in that language before age seven.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any adult who can be trained to speak accent-free in a language retains the capacity for native-level pronunciation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mira has, in fact, maintained regular exposure to Portuguese since childhood.

explanations.correct: The stimulus gives us 'Mira retains the capacity for native-level pronunciation in Portuguese.' The conclusion is 'Mira can be trained to speak without a detectable foreign accent.' (A) supplies the universal bridge from capacity to trainability, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too weak — 'most' does not guarantee that Mira in particular can be so trained.
explanations.C: Reversed conditional — gives 'accent-free → fluent by seven,' not the direction needed.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional — bridges from 'accent-free trainability' back to 'capacity,' not forward.
explanations.E: Adds a factual detail but no logical link between capacity and trainability.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-link chain through 'organic certification' and 'pesticide-free,' with a further jump to 'safe for pregnant consumers.' Trap (E) is a principle-wrapping distractor that sounds strong but trades in different vocabulary.
lr.stimulus: All produce sold at the Harrow Market bears organic certification. Any food that bears organic certification is free of synthetic pesticides. Clearly, then, any produce purchased at the Harrow Market is safe for pregnant consumers to eat.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any food that is free of synthetic pesticides is safe for pregnant consumers to eat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any food that is safe for pregnant consumers to eat is free of synthetic pesticides.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most foods free of synthetic pesticides are safe for pregnant consumers to eat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some produce sold at the Harrow Market is free of synthetic pesticides.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether a food is safe for pregnant consumers depends principally on the absence of chemical residues of any kind.

explanations.correct: The premises chain 'Harrow produce → organic certified → pesticide-free.' The conclusion is 'Harrow produce → safe for pregnant consumers.' (A) adds 'pesticide-free → safe,' closing the final link.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional — doesn't help derive safety from the pesticide-free premise.
explanations.C: Too weak — 'most' does not force the universal conclusion about any produce at the market.
explanations.D: Already entailed by the premises — adds no bridge to safety.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping distractor — 'principally' is too weak, and it shifts from pesticides to 'chemical residues of any kind.'

lr.difficultyReason: Counterexample refutation structure modeled on Peacock/Hacker. The critic claims 'publishing under a pseudonym = deceiving readers.' The student must supply the link that someone who cannot deceive readers cannot perform that act. Trap (B) uses 'often' and is too weak.
lr.stimulus: Book critic: Some reviewers have claimed that any novelist who publishes under a pseudonym is deceiving her readers. That is simply wrong. Consider Aleksandra Novak, who publishes her thrillers under the name 'J. R. Larsen' but who discloses her real name openly in every interview and on her publisher's website.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No one who openly discloses her real identity to the public is capable of deceiving her readers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Novelists who use pseudonyms often disclose their real identities in interviews.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any novelist who deceives her readers does so by publishing under a pseudonym.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Readers of thrillers are generally indifferent to whether the author's name is a pseudonym.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A pseudonym does not count as a deception unless it is chosen with the intent to deceive.

explanations.correct: The critic needs to show that Novak's using a pseudonym is not deceiving readers. Given that Novak openly discloses her real identity, (A) forces the conclusion: if no one who openly discloses her real identity can deceive her readers, then Novak cannot be deceiving them by using a pseudonym.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too weak — 'often' and 'disclose in interviews' do not force the conclusion about this author and this act.
explanations.C: Reversed — gives 'deceives → pseudonym,' not 'pseudonym + disclosure → not deceives.'
explanations.D: Reader indifference does not entail that the author is not deceiving them.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping; 'intent to deceive' is a new concept not anchored in the stimulus and does not connect disclosure to non-deception.

lr.difficultyReason: Economic argument with a two-step gap between 'tariff imposed' and 'consumer prices rise,' mediated by 'domestic suppliers raise prices.' Trap (C) supplies a partial bridge; trap (D) is reversed.
lr.stimulus: Whenever a tariff is imposed on an imported good, domestic suppliers of that good raise their own prices. Last month, the government imposed a 20 percent tariff on imported steel. Therefore, consumers will soon pay more for cars manufactured domestically.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whenever domestic suppliers of steel raise their prices, consumers pay more for domestically manufactured cars.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumers pay more for domestically manufactured cars whenever a tariff is imposed on any imported good.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whenever a tariff is imposed on imported steel, domestic suppliers of steel raise their prices.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whenever consumers pay more for domestically manufactured cars, domestic suppliers of steel have raised their prices.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Domestic suppliers of steel sometimes raise their prices in response to changes in tariff policy.

explanations.correct: The premises yield 'domestic steel suppliers raise prices.' The conclusion is 'consumers pay more for domestically manufactured cars.' (A) provides the universal link from steel-price increases to car-price increases, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too broad and off-target: it ranges over tariffs on 'any imported good,' not steel specifically, and it bypasses the domestic-supplier mechanism the stimulus uses. (A) supplies the exact link from the step the premises actually establish.
explanations.C: Restates the first premise as applied to steel; adds no bridge to car prices.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional — gives 'car prices up → steel prices up,' not the needed direction.
explanations.E: Too weak — 'sometimes' cannot force a definite conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental-science chain: 'reduce carbon emissions' → 'slow ocean acidification' → 'protect coral reefs.' Student must supply the missing link from acidification to coral protection. Trap (D) inverts the conditional; trap (E) is too weak.
lr.stimulus: Environmentalist: Any policy that significantly reduces global carbon emissions will slow the acidification of the oceans. Our government has just enacted the strictest emissions policy in its history. Therefore, this policy will protect the world's coral reefs from further degradation.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The government's new emissions policy significantly reduces global carbon emissions, and any policy that slows ocean acidification protects the world's coral reefs from further degradation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The government's new emissions policy will not slow ocean acidification unless it also reduces other pollutants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most policies that slow ocean acidification protect some coral reefs from further degradation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any policy that protects the world's coral reefs from further degradation significantly reduces global carbon emissions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The government's emissions policy is likely to contribute, along with other measures, to the protection of coral reefs.

explanations.correct: Two gaps exist: (i) the stimulus says the policy is strict, not that it 'significantly' reduces emissions — the trigger required by the first conditional; and (ii) there is no link from 'slows acidification' to 'protects coral reefs.' (A) supplies both, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Adds a defeater, not a bridge.
explanations.C: Too weak — 'most' and 'some' do not force a universal conclusion about 'the world's coral reefs.'
explanations.D: Reversed conditional — gives 'protects reefs → reduces emissions.'
explanations.E: Too weak — 'likely' and 'along with other measures' do not force the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal-reasoning chain from 'contract is enforceable' through 'both parties had capacity' to 'agreement is binding.' Trap (B) reverses; trap (C) supplies only a partial bridge.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: A contract is enforceable only if both parties had legal capacity at the time of signing. The agreement between Forsyth Holdings and Vellum Inc. is enforceable, since investigators have confirmed that both signatories had legal capacity. It follows that the agreement is binding on Vellum Inc.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any enforceable contract is binding on each of its parties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any contract that is binding on its parties is enforceable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any contract whose signatories had legal capacity at the time of signing is enforceable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most enforceable contracts are binding on the corporate parties involved.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vellum Inc. signed the agreement under the advice of counsel.

explanations.correct: From the premises, the attorney has established that the contract is enforceable. The conclusion jumps to 'binding on Vellum.' (A) supplies the needed universal link from 'enforceable' to 'binding on each party,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed — gives 'binding → enforceable.'
explanations.C: Restates a premise in slightly different terms; adds no link to 'binding.'
explanations.D: Too weak — 'most' does not force the conclusion about this particular party.
explanations.E: Irrelevant factual detail; does not bridge 'enforceable' to 'binding.'

lr.difficultyReason: Historical-causal structure: the author claims a period could not have been the 'origin of X' because its evidence shows Y. Student must supply the universal principle connecting 'evidence of Y' to 'not origin of X.' Trap (A) shifts the subject; trap (C) is too weak.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Some scholars claim that the early Bronze Age in the Aegean was the origin of complex state bureaucracy. This is mistaken. Recent excavations show that early-Bronze-Age Aegean societies kept no written administrative records whatsoever.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No society that lacked writing entirely could have invented any form of bureaucratic practice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No society that kept no written administrative records was the origin of complex state bureaucracy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most societies that developed complex state bureaucracy also developed extensive written administrative records.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some early-Bronze-Age Aegean societies maintained oral administrative traditions comparable in sophistication to later written ones.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any society that kept written administrative records had complex state bureaucracy.

explanations.correct: The historian establishes that early-Bronze-Age Aegean societies kept no written administrative records. The conclusion is that they were not the origin of complex state bureaucracy. (B) supplies exactly the universal link: 'no written records → not origin,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Shifts the subject from 'origin of complex state bureaucracy' to 'any bureaucratic practice,' and the stimulus did not establish the societies lacked writing entirely — only that they lacked administrative records.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too weak — 'most' leaves open that these Aegean societies were the exception.
explanations.D: Weakens the argument by suggesting bureaucracy without writing is possible.
explanations.E: Reversed conditional — gives 'written records → bureaucracy,' not the contrapositive the argument needs.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology/ethics chain: 'algorithm trained on biased data' → 'produces biased predictions' → 'should not be used in hiring.' Trap (D) reverses; trap (A) is a near-restatement of a premise.
lr.stimulus: Data ethicist: Every hiring algorithm trained on historical résumé data inherits the demographic biases present in that data. And any system that inherits demographic biases makes predictions that disadvantage underrepresented applicants. So the algorithm that OmniTrust Corp. plans to deploy in its hiring process ought to be rejected.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: OmniTrust Corp.'s algorithm was trained on historical résumé data, and any system that makes predictions disadvantaging underrepresented applicants ought to be rejected.

choices.label: B
choices.text: OmniTrust Corp.'s algorithm has been tested for demographic bias in the past and performed poorly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most algorithms that disadvantage underrepresented applicants ought to be rejected for use in hiring.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any algorithm that ought to be rejected disadvantages underrepresented applicants.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No hiring algorithm that inherits demographic biases can be corrected through post-deployment auditing.

explanations.correct: Two things are missing: a factual premise placing OmniTrust's algorithm in the class 'trained on historical résumé data,' and the normative bridge from 'disadvantages underrepresented applicants' to 'ought to be rejected.' (A) supplies both, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Adds an empirical claim about past testing, but not the categorical link needed.
explanations.C: Too weak — 'most' does not force the conclusion about this particular algorithm.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional — gives 'ought to be rejected → disadvantages applicants.'
explanations.E: Addresses correctability, not the normative step the argument actually needs.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument with a chain from 'passes committee' and 'receives mayor's signature' to 'takes effect before year's end.' Trap (C) reverses the scheduling conditional; trap (E) is a principle-wrapped distractor.
lr.stimulus: Every ordinance that passes the city's zoning committee by October is guaranteed to receive the mayor's signature. The Westbrook rezoning ordinance passed the committee in September. So the Westbrook ordinance will take effect before the end of this year.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any ordinance that receives the mayor's signature takes effect before the end of the year in which it is signed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any ordinance that takes effect before the end of a given year has received the mayor's signature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any ordinance that takes effect before the end of a given year passes the city's zoning committee by October.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most ordinances signed by the mayor take effect within a year of their signing.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A properly enacted ordinance, once signed, should ordinarily be implemented without undue delay.

explanations.correct: The premises establish that the Westbrook ordinance will receive the mayor's signature this year. The conclusion is that it will take effect before year's end. (A) provides the universal link from signing to year-end effectiveness, forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed — gives 'takes effect → signed.'
explanations.C: Reversed — gives 'takes effect → passes committee.'
explanations.D: Too weak — 'most' and 'within a year of signing' do not force that this particular ordinance takes effect before year's end.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping — 'ordinarily' and 'should' do not force the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-step chain with a buried scope shift from 'produces measurable clinical benefit' in the premises to 'warrants insurance coverage' in the conclusion. The correct answer must bridge clinical benefit to coverage-worthiness as a universal — not merely as a trend. Traps (B) and (D) reverse the conditional; (C) is too narrow; (E) is a principle-wrapping distractor that trades 'cost-effectiveness' for the stimulus's 'measurable benefit.'
lr.stimulus: Medical researcher: Any therapy approved by the federal regulatory agency has been shown in controlled trials to produce measurable clinical benefit. The newly approved monoclonal antibody infusion for early-stage Parkinson's disease was approved by that agency last spring. It follows, then, that private insurers are obligated to cover the infusion for any patient whose physician prescribes it.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Private insurers are obligated to cover any therapy that has been shown in controlled trials to produce measurable clinical benefit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any therapy that private insurers are obligated to cover has been approved by the federal regulatory agency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Private insurers are obligated to cover any therapy that has been approved by the federal regulatory agency and prescribed for early-stage Parkinson's disease.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any therapy that has been shown in controlled trials to produce measurable clinical benefit has been approved by the federal regulatory agency.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether private insurers are obligated to cover a therapy depends principally on whether that therapy is cost-effective relative to alternatives.

explanations.correct: The premises chain 'approved → shown to produce measurable clinical benefit,' applied to the infusion. The conclusion jumps to 'insurers obligated to cover.' (A) supplies the universal 'measurable clinical benefit → insurers obligated to cover,' forcing the conclusion for any prescribed patient.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional — 'covered → approved' runs the wrong direction and cannot deliver coverage from the premise that the therapy was approved.
explanations.C: Too narrow to close the gap through the stated premises — it bypasses 'measurable clinical benefit' and adds an unneeded disease-specific qualifier; it also fails to tie to the 'any patient whose physician prescribes it' claim without additional work, and more importantly, its universal quantifier isn't what the argument's stated chain requires.
explanations.D: Reversed conditional — gives 'measurable benefit → approved,' the opposite of the needed bridge.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping trap. 'Cost-effectiveness' is a different concept than 'measurable clinical benefit,' and 'depends principally' is too weak to force the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus nests two conditionals and a subject shift from 'an action' to 'a person who performs it.' The credited answer must convert action-level wrongness into person-level blameworthiness. Trap (A) substitutes 'illegal' for 'morally wrong'; (B) reverses the needed conditional; (D) is too weak ('typically'); (E) is a tempting broad principle that leaves the agency gap open.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Any action that causes harm to a sentient being without that being's consent is morally wrong. Factory-farmed meat production causes substantial harm to sentient beings without their consent. Therefore, anyone who knowingly purchases factory-farmed meat is morally blameworthy for doing so.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who knowingly purchases a product whose production is illegal is morally blameworthy for doing so.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anyone who is morally blameworthy for performing an action has knowingly contributed to an action that is morally wrong.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anyone who knowingly contributes to an action that is morally wrong is morally blameworthy for doing so.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A person who knowingly purchases a product of a morally wrong process is typically blameworthy for the wrong, unless unaware of feasible alternatives.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Consumer demand is the principal driver of the harms associated with industrial food production.

explanations.correct: The premises yield 'factory-farmed meat production is morally wrong' and 'purchaser knowingly contributes to that production.' The conclusion is 'purchaser is morally blameworthy.' (C) supplies the universal bridge from 'knowingly contributing to a morally wrong action' to 'morally blameworthy,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Connects the wrong concepts — it runs through 'illegal,' but the stimulus traffics in 'morally wrong.'
explanations.B: Reversed conditional — 'blameworthy → knowingly contributed to wrong' does not give us blameworthiness as an output.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too weak ('typically') and introduces an exception clause ('unless unaware of feasible alternatives') that would undermine the certainty the conclusion requires.
explanations.E: Strengthens the argument's causal picture but does not logically entail that any particular purchaser is blameworthy.

lr.difficultyReason: The argument links rising interest rates, declining housing starts, and rising rents through an implied but unstated intermediate about renter demand. The credited answer must universally bind 'fewer housing starts' to 'rising rents.' Trap (B) reverses the bridge; (C) is a near-restatement; (D) adds a plausible but too-weak economic hedge; (E) is a principle-wrapping distractor using different vocabulary.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Whenever the central bank raises its benchmark interest rate by more than one percentage point in a single year, new housing starts in the following year decline sharply. The central bank raised its benchmark rate by 1.75 percentage points last year. We can therefore conclude that average residential rents in the metropolitan area will rise over the next twelve months.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whenever new housing starts in a metropolitan area decline sharply in a given year, average residential rents in that area rise over the following twelve months.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whenever average residential rents rise over a twelve-month period, new housing starts have declined sharply in the preceding year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whenever the central bank raises its benchmark interest rate by more than one percentage point in a single year, average residential rents in the metropolitan area rise within twelve months.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Declines in housing starts tend, in most metropolitan areas, to exert upward pressure on residential rents in the short term.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residential rents are determined principally by the balance between the number of occupied units and the number of available dwellings.

explanations.correct: The premises chain 'rate hike > 1 pct → sharp decline in housing starts,' applied to last year, giving 'housing starts will decline sharply this year.' The conclusion is 'rents will rise over the next twelve months.' (A) supplies the universal bridge 'sharp decline in starts → rents rise,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional — bridges from rent rises back to housing-start declines rather than forward.
explanations.C: Near-restatement of the conclusion plus a premise; it asserts the chain's conclusion without supplying the missing intermediate link that the argument depends on to justify its inference.
explanations.D: Too weak — 'tend' and 'in most metropolitan areas' leave room for this area to be an exception, so the conclusion does not follow with necessity.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping distractor — names a different mechanism ('balance between occupied and available dwellings') and does not entail that rents will rise in this particular case.

lr.difficultyReason: Multi-step legal chain linking 'prior consent,' 'reasonable search,' and 'admissible evidence,' with a buried scope shift from 'searches' to 'evidence obtained.' The correct answer must universally license the inference from 'reasonable search' to 'admissibility.' Trap (B) is too narrow (a specific exception); (C) reverses the conditional; (D) is a 'most' hedge; (E) misaligns the concepts.
lr.stimulus: Legal analyst: Any search conducted with the prior written consent of the premises' owner is deemed reasonable under the Fourth Amendment. The officers who searched the storage unit where the disputed ledger was found had obtained the owner's prior written consent. It follows that the ledger should be admitted as evidence at trial.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any item of evidence obtained through a search that is deemed reasonable under the Fourth Amendment should be admitted at trial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any ledger recovered from a storage unit searched with the owner's consent should be admitted at trial as evidence of the crime charged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any item of evidence that should be admitted at trial has been obtained through a search deemed reasonable under the Fourth Amendment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most items of evidence obtained through searches deemed reasonable under the Fourth Amendment are admitted at trial.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A search is constitutionally permissible only when it respects the legitimate privacy interests of the person whose effects are examined.

explanations.correct: The premises give us 'search of the storage unit was reasonable under the Fourth Amendment' (via prior written consent) and 'the ledger was obtained through that search.' The conclusion is 'ledger should be admitted.' (A) supplies the universal 'evidence from a reasonable search → admitted,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too narrow — it speaks to ledgers-from-storage-units, a specific case, and its 'evidence of the crime charged' qualifier adds a requirement the stimulus never establishes.
explanations.C: Reversed conditional — 'admitted → reasonable search' does not let us derive admissibility from a reasonable search.
explanations.D: Too weak — 'most' does not force admissibility for this particular ledger.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping distractor — names a constitutional rationale but does not bridge 'reasonable search' to 'admissibility.'

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus establishes that a wetland contains migratory bird habitat and concludes that a development permit should be denied. The gap requires a universal from 'migratory bird habitat' to 'permit denial.' Trap (A) reverses; (C) connects different concepts ('endangered species' vs. 'migratory bird'); (D) is too weak; (E) is a principle that sounds strong but trades on different vocabulary.
lr.stimulus: Environmental scientist: Any parcel of land that lies within a state-designated coastal flyway contains habitat used by migratory bird species. The Copper Creek tract, which the DeVries Corporation has asked to develop, lies entirely within the Eastern Shore coastal flyway. Therefore, the state permit board should deny the development application.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any development application denied by the state permit board is for a parcel containing habitat used by migratory bird species.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The state permit board should deny any development application for a parcel that contains habitat used by migratory bird species.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The state permit board should deny any development application for a parcel that contains habitat used by endangered species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most development applications for parcels within a state-designated coastal flyway are denied by the state permit board.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Coastal ecosystems are most effectively protected by regulatory bodies that prioritize habitat integrity above short-term economic returns.

explanations.correct: The premises chain 'within coastal flyway → contains migratory bird habitat,' applied to Copper Creek. The conclusion is 'permit board should deny the application.' (B) supplies the universal 'contains migratory bird habitat → board should deny,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional — 'denied → contains habitat' does not let us derive denial from the presence of habitat.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Connects the wrong concepts — the stimulus establishes 'migratory bird habitat,' not 'endangered species habitat.'
explanations.D: Too weak — 'most' does not force denial of this particular application.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping distractor. 'Most effectively protected' is a claim about policy efficacy, not about what the board should do in this case.

lr.difficultyReason: Three linked conditionals about encryption, data breach liability, and statutory safe harbor. The credited answer must universally bind 'uses end-to-end encryption' to 'qualifies for the safe harbor.' Trap (B) reverses; (C) substitutes 'zero-knowledge' for 'end-to-end,' a related but distinct concept; (D) hedges with 'generally'; (E) is principle-wrapping.
lr.stimulus: Technology policy analyst: Under the new federal data-protection statute, any firm whose customer database was compromised in a breach is liable for damages unless it qualifies for the statute's safe harbor. SilverNet's customer database was compromised in last month's breach, and the firm uses end-to-end encryption on all customer data at rest. Accordingly, SilverNet will not be liable for damages under the statute.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any firm that uses end-to-end encryption on all customer data at rest qualifies for the statute's safe harbor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any firm that qualifies for the statute's safe harbor uses end-to-end encryption on all customer data at rest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any firm that uses zero-knowledge encryption on all customer data at rest qualifies for the statute's safe harbor.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Firms that encrypt their customer data at rest are generally able to qualify for the statute's safe harbor.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A firm's liability under data-protection statutes depends principally on the technical sophistication of its security practices.

explanations.correct: The premises give us 'SilverNet's database was compromised' and 'SilverNet uses end-to-end encryption on all customer data at rest.' The statute makes breached firms liable unless they qualify for the safe harbor. The conclusion is 'SilverNet will not be liable.' (A) supplies the universal 'end-to-end encryption → qualifies for safe harbor,' forcing non-liability.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional — 'safe harbor → uses end-to-end encryption' cannot deliver safe harbor from the encryption premise.
explanations.C: Connects the wrong concepts — the stimulus establishes 'end-to-end encryption,' not 'zero-knowledge encryption.'
explanations.D: Too weak — 'generally' leaves room for SilverNet not to qualify.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping distractor — does not entail that SilverNet in particular qualifies for the safe harbor.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus chains 'Indo-European origin,' 'presence of laryngeal reflexes,' and 'descent from Proto-Anatolian.' The conclusion makes a claim about one language family. The correct answer must universally bridge 'laryngeal reflexes' to 'Proto-Anatolian descent.' Trap (A) reverses; (D) is too narrow; (E) is a near-restatement of a premise; (B) shifts the concept from 'reflexes' to 'consonant clusters.'
lr.stimulus: Historical linguist: Every Indo-European language that preserves laryngeal reflexes in its oldest attested layer is descended, at least in part, from Proto-Anatolian. The earliest attested stratum of Tocharian B preserves laryngeal reflexes. Thus, the speakers of Tocharian B once lived in close contact with the Anatolian heartland.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The speakers of any language descended from Proto-Anatolian preserve laryngeal reflexes in that language's oldest attested layer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The speakers of any Indo-European language whose oldest attested layer preserves archaic consonant clusters once lived in close contact with the Anatolian heartland.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The speakers of any language descended, at least in part, from Proto-Anatolian once lived in close contact with the Anatolian heartland.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The speakers of Tocharian B, unlike most Indo-European groups, once migrated through the Anatolian heartland.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The earliest attested stratum of every Indo-European language reveals meaningful information about the geographic history of its speakers.

explanations.correct: The premises chain 'Tocharian B preserves laryngeal reflexes → descended from Proto-Anatolian.' The conclusion is 'speakers of Tocharian B once lived in close contact with the Anatolian heartland.' (C) supplies the universal 'descended from Proto-Anatolian → speakers once lived in close contact with the Anatolian heartland,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional — 'Proto-Anatolian descent → laryngeal reflexes' does not let us derive contact from descent.
explanations.B: Connects the wrong concepts — 'archaic consonant clusters' is a different feature than the premise's 'laryngeal reflexes.'
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too narrow to serve as a sufficient assumption — it restates the conclusion for this one group but does not ground it in the argument's stated premises, and it introduces a contrast ('unlike most Indo-European groups') that the argument never requires.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping restatement — says the earliest stratum is informative but does not bridge descent to geographic contact.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical argument with a subject shift from 'treaty obligations' to 'legitimate casus belli.' The correct answer must bridge 'violated by the signatory' to 'justified a declaration of war' at the universal level. Trap (A) reverses; (C) is too narrow in period; (D) is too weak; (E) is principle-wrapping.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Any treaty ratified by the great powers of Europe during the nineteenth century was considered binding under the prevailing standards of international law. The 1839 Treaty of London, ratified by all five great powers, was violated by Prussia when its armies crossed Belgian soil in August 1914. Accordingly, Britain's declaration of war on Prussia that month was a legitimate exercise of belligerent rights.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any declaration of war that is a legitimate exercise of belligerent rights responds to the violation of a binding treaty.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A declaration of war responding to the violation of any treaty considered binding under the prevailing standards of international law is a legitimate exercise of belligerent rights.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A declaration of war responding to the violation of any treaty ratified during the 1830s is a legitimate exercise of belligerent rights.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the nineteenth century, most declarations of war responding to treaty violations were considered legitimate under prevailing international law.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The legitimacy of a declaration of war depends principally on whether the declaring power has exhausted reasonable diplomatic alternatives.

explanations.correct: The premises chain 'Treaty of London ratified by great powers in the nineteenth century → considered binding.' Prussia's violation and Britain's response are established as facts. The conclusion is 'Britain's declaration was a legitimate exercise of belligerent rights.' (B) supplies the universal 'response to violation of a binding treaty → legitimate declaration of war,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Reversed conditional — 'legitimate declaration → responds to violation of a binding treaty' does not let us derive legitimacy from such a response.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — and an odd fit: the treaty was ratified in 1839, but the argument's machinery runs through 'nineteenth century' and 'binding,' not through 'ratified in the 1830s.'
explanations.D: Too weak — 'most declarations' does not force the conclusion about this particular declaration.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping distractor — names a different criterion ('exhausted diplomatic alternatives') and does not bridge treaty violation to legitimacy.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument with two linked universals — congestion pricing reduces downtown traffic; reduced downtown traffic lowers particulate emissions — and a conclusion about public-health obligations. The correct answer must universally bind 'measurable reductions in particulate emissions' to 'the city ought to adopt the measure.' Trap (C) is too narrow (one borough); (B) reverses; (D) is too weak; (E) shifts to 'carbon emissions.'
lr.stimulus: Policy advisor: Every city that has implemented congestion pricing in its central business district has seen a measurable reduction in downtown vehicular traffic, and every measurable reduction in downtown vehicular traffic in a major city produces a measurable reduction in downtown particulate emissions. The city of Harmont has not implemented congestion pricing in its central business district. Therefore, the Harmont city council ought to enact the proposed congestion-pricing ordinance this session.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion drawn above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any major city whose central business district would, upon the implementation of a measure, see a measurable reduction in particulate emissions ought to enact that measure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any major city that ought to enact a proposed ordinance has seen a measurable reduction in particulate emissions in its central business district.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The borough containing Harmont's central business district ought to enact whichever measure its council judges most likely to reduce particulate emissions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Congestion pricing usually produces meaningful reductions in downtown particulate emissions in the major cities that have adopted it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any major city whose central business district would see a measurable reduction in carbon emissions upon the implementation of a measure ought to enact that measure.

explanations.correct: The premises chain, for major cities, 'congestion pricing → reduced traffic → reduced particulate emissions.' Applied to Harmont, enacting the ordinance would produce a measurable reduction in particulate emissions. The conclusion is 'Harmont ought to enact the ordinance.' (A) supplies the universal bridge from 'measurable reduction in particulate emissions upon enactment' to 'ought to enact,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversed conditional — 'ought to enact → reduced particulates' does not give us 'ought to enact' as an output.
explanations.C: Too narrow — it speaks to a single borough and a comparative judgment that the argument never invokes.
explanations.D: Too weak — 'usually' does not force that Harmont in particular will see the reduction, or that the council ought to act.
explanations.E: Connects the wrong concepts — the premises run through 'particulate emissions,' not 'carbon emissions.'

lr.difficultyReason: The argument begins with a universal about museum provenance, applies it to a specific painting, and concludes the museum must deaccession. The credited answer must bridge 'documentary evidence of wartime confiscation from a private collector' to 'museum is obligated to return.' Trap (B) reverses; (C) is a near-premise restatement; (D) is too weak; (E) is principle-wrapping with 'moral standing' rather than 'obligation.'
lr.stimulus: Art historian: Any painting in the Harmont Museum's European collection for which there is documentary evidence that it was confiscated from a private collector during wartime should be returned to the heirs of that collector. A newly surfaced 1943 customs ledger documents that the Klee canvas now displayed in Gallery IV was confiscated from the Rosenthal family in Vienna in that year. The museum must therefore deaccession the Klee canvas.
lr.questionStem: The conclusion above follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The museum must deaccession any painting that, under the relevant standards, should be returned to the heirs of the collector from whom it was confiscated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The museum must deaccession any painting whose heirs have submitted a formal restitution request through the relevant diplomatic channels.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any painting that the museum must deaccession is a painting that should be returned to the heirs of the collector from whom it was confiscated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Museums holding works with credible wartime-confiscation provenance usually deaccession those works when heirs are identified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A museum's moral standing depends principally on the transparency with which it documents the provenance of its European holdings.

explanations.correct: The premises chain 'documentary evidence of wartime confiscation → should be returned to heirs,' applied to the Klee canvas. The conclusion is 'museum must deaccession.' (A) supplies the universal 'should be returned to heirs → must be deaccessioned,' forcing the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Connects the wrong concepts — the stimulus never mentions formal restitution requests or diplomatic channels; introducing that requirement does not help us derive deaccession here.
explanations.C: Reversed conditional — 'must deaccession → should be returned' does not let us derive deaccession from the return obligation.
explanations.D: Too weak — 'usually' does not force that the museum must deaccession this particular canvas.
explanations.E: Principle-wrapping distractor — talks about 'moral standing' and 'transparency,' not about deaccessioning obligations.

lr.difficultyReason: Textbook ad hominem in pure form. The columnist dismisses a study by attacking the researcher's character rather than engaging with the evidence. The correct answer is the only one that describes that move; trap choices point at peripheral weaknesses.
lr.stimulus: Health columnist: Dr. Reyes has just published a study claiming that daily consumption of green tea modestly reduces the risk of heart disease. But Dr. Reyes was fined two years ago for filing inaccurate expense reports at her previous university. Clearly, then, we have no reason to accept her conclusions about green tea.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the health columnist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: rejects a claim by attacking the character of the person who made it rather than addressing the evidence for the claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from a single study to a conclusion about all research on green tea

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for distrusting a researcher as also necessary for doing so

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses a claim about heart disease risk with a claim about overall health outcomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on a source whose expertise in the relevant field has not been established

explanations.correct: The columnist's only reason for rejecting the study is the researcher's past expense-report issue — a matter of personal conduct unrelated to her research on green tea. That is a textbook attack on the person rather than the argument.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The columnist never generalizes across studies; she rejects the one study she discusses.
explanations.C: No necessary/sufficient move is made; the columnist simply asserts grounds for distrust.
explanations.D: The argument stays on heart disease; no scope shift to overall health occurs.
explanations.E: The columnist doesn't question Dr. Reyes's expertise; she questions her character.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure self-contradiction: the speaker affirms a universal claim and then exempts themselves from it in the same breath. The correct answer names the contradiction; trap answers describe plausible but unrelated flaws.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: It is always wrong to judge another person's actions without first hearing their reasons for acting as they did. That is why I can say with complete confidence that the council member who voted against the new park ordinance last night — I haven't spoken with her, but I've heard enough — acted wrongly and deserves public censure.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the ethicist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific action from a general principle that was never defended

choices.label: B
choices.text: violates the very principle it asserts by judging an action without hearing the actor's reasons

choices.label: C
choices.text: confuses what is morally permissible with what is legally required

choices.label: D
choices.text: appeals to the opinions of unspecified others as if they were authoritative

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a single instance of bad judgment as evidence of a broader pattern

explanations.correct: The ethicist states a universal rule — never judge without hearing reasons — and then, without hearing the council member's reasons, judges her action as wrong. The argument's conclusion is incompatible with its own stated premise.
explanations.A: The flaw isn't that the principle is undefended; it's that the ethicist's own conduct violates it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No legal/moral distinction is drawn or conflated.
explanations.D: The hearsay ('I've heard enough') is a weakness but not the central structural flaw.
explanations.E: Only one action is judged; no pattern is alleged.

lr.difficultyReason: Textbook correlation-to-causation move. Cities that raised transit spending saw ridership rise, and the analyst concludes the spending caused the rise. Correct answer names the move; traps target peripheral weaknesses.
lr.stimulus: Transportation analyst: Cities that increased their public-transit spending by at least ten percent last year saw an average rise in ridership of seven percent. Cities that did not increase spending saw no such rise. The conclusion is clear: the additional spending is what drove ridership higher in the cities that raised their budgets.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the transportation analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a causal relationship from evidence that establishes only a correlation

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on a sample of cities that is too small to support a general conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes without warrant that ridership is the most important measure of transit success

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from the behavior of a few cities to the behavior of all cities

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a necessary condition for rising ridership as if it were sufficient

explanations.correct: The data show only that spending increases and ridership increases occurred together. The analyst leaps from that co-occurrence to the causal claim that the spending drove the ridership, without ruling out alternative explanations such as fuel prices, new employers, or population growth.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Sample size isn't raised as a problem in the stimulus and isn't the structural error.
explanations.C: The argument never ranks measures of success.
explanations.D: The conclusion is about the cities in question, not all cities.
explanations.E: No conditional move is made; the argument is causal, not conditional.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure sufficient/necessary reversal. The statute makes a warrant sufficient for a lawful search; the attorney treats it as necessary. Correct answer names the reversal; traps offer plausible-sounding but wrong flaw labels.
lr.stimulus: Defense attorney: Under our state's statute, if officers obtain a valid warrant before entering a residence, the search is lawful. The officers who entered my client's home last week did not obtain a warrant beforehand. Therefore, the search of my client's home was unlawful.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the defense attorney's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a sufficient condition for a lawful search as if it were a necessary condition

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejects a claim on the basis of the character of the person making it

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a specific case from a statistic about all cases

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes without warrant that the officers acted in bad faith

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on a legal principle that has never been tested in court

explanations.correct: The statute says that a warrant is one way to make a search lawful — a sufficient condition. Other exceptions (consent, exigent circumstances, plain view) may also render a search lawful. The attorney wrongly treats the warrant as the only path to lawfulness, converting a sufficient condition into a necessary one.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No one's character is attacked; the argument is about legal conditions.
explanations.C: No statistic is invoked.
explanations.D: Bad faith is never alleged.
explanations.E: The testing history of the principle is not at issue.

lr.difficultyReason: Classic hasty generalization. Two sampled lakes, conclusion about all lakes in the region. Correct answer names the unrepresentative-sample move; traps describe other flaws the argument does not commit.
lr.stimulus: Biologist: Researchers tested two lakes in the Fenwick watershed last summer and found elevated mercury levels in fish from both. It follows that fish from every lake throughout the entire Fenwick watershed are contaminated with elevated mercury and should not be eaten.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the biologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a sweeping conclusion about an entire region from a sample that may not be representative of it

choices.label: B
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between mercury and fish habitat for a causal relationship

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to distinguish between recreational and commercial fishing practices

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without justification that mercury is the only contaminant worth testing for

choices.label: E
choices.text: uses the ambiguous term 'elevated' in two distinct senses

explanations.correct: Two lakes cannot, without further support, stand in for every lake in a watershed. The biologist leaps from a very small sample to a sweeping claim about all lakes in the region, an unrepresentative-sample flaw.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No causal claim is being defended; the claim is simply that the fish are contaminated.
explanations.C: The argument is about fish across the watershed, not about fishing practices.
explanations.D: The argument does not claim mercury is the only contaminant; it only claims mercury is elevated.
explanations.E: 'Elevated' is used consistently throughout the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure appeal to ignorance. Because no one has proved the device fails, the CEO concludes it works. Correct answer names the absence-of-evidence move; traps target unrelated flaw types.
lr.stimulus: Tech CEO: Several independent researchers have tried, without success, to prove that our company's new encryption chip can be compromised by a remote attacker. Since no one has yet demonstrated a successful attack against the chip, we can conclude that our chip is secure against remote attacks.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the tech CEO's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence that a claim is false as if it established that the claim is true

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from the experience of a few researchers to the capabilities of all possible attackers

choices.label: C
choices.text: confuses a necessary condition for a secure chip with a sufficient one

choices.label: D
choices.text: appeals to the authority of researchers whose credentials have not been verified

choices.label: E
choices.text: uses the term 'secure' in two different senses within the same argument

explanations.correct: No one has proved the chip can be cracked, so the CEO concludes it cannot be cracked. That inference treats the lack of a successful attack as positive evidence of security, which is a classic appeal-to-ignorance move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This describes a sampling flaw the argument does not actually commit — the conclusion rests on absence of evidence, not on a sample.
explanations.C: No conditional move is made.
explanations.D: The researchers' credentials are not invoked as support.
explanations.E: 'Secure' is used in a single sense throughout.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure equivocation on the word 'argument.' Shifts between 'heated dispute' and 'reasoned case.' Correct answer names the two-senses move; traps offer flaw vocabulary that doesn't match.
lr.stimulus: Linguistics student: Professor Yates said in lecture that a good argument never raises its voice. But last week in the department seminar, Professor Yates presented an argument that the dative case is disappearing from spoken Icelandic. So, by his own standard, Professor Yates's seminar presentation was not a good argument.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the linguistics student's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses the word 'argument' in two different senses without acknowledging the shift

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejects a claim by attacking the credentials of the person who made it

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a single lecture to the professor's views across his entire career

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes without justification that raising one's voice is never appropriate

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a property of a whole as if it were necessarily a property of each of its parts

explanations.correct: Professor Yates's maxim uses 'argument' to mean a heated dispute (the kind in which one might raise one's voice). The seminar sense of 'argument' is a reasoned case for a linguistic claim. The student silently trades one sense for the other to generate the contradiction.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No credentials are attacked; only a standard is invoked.
explanations.C: Only one lecture is referenced, not career-wide views.
explanations.D: The argument never addresses whether raising one's voice is appropriate.
explanations.E: No whole/part move appears in the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: Appeal to inappropriate authority. A nutrition researcher is cited on a question of historical causation outside her expertise. Correct answer names the authority mismatch; traps describe other flaws.
lr.stimulus: History student: Dr. Langford, who won a major national prize for her research on adolescent nutrition, recently stated in a podcast interview that the principal cause of the fall of the Western Roman Empire was a collapse in agricultural trade routes. Because Dr. Langford is a celebrated researcher, we should accept her account of Rome's decline.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the history student's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on the opinion of an authority whose expertise is in a field unrelated to the claim at issue

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismisses Dr. Langford's view by pointing to her work in an unrelated field

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a sufficient condition for a historical cause as a necessary one

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a conclusion about an entire empire from information about a single region

choices.label: E
choices.text: fails to consider that Dr. Langford's statements might have been taken out of context

explanations.correct: Dr. Langford is a specialist in adolescent nutrition, not in the history of Rome. The student supports a claim about Roman decline by citing her authority in an unrelated field, a classic appeal to inappropriate authority.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument accepts, not dismisses, Dr. Langford's view.
explanations.C: No conditional move is made.
explanations.D: The claim is already about the empire, not a region.
explanations.E: Context isn't at issue; expertise is.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure ignoring-alternatives flaw in false-dichotomy form. The council member insists it is cut services or raise property taxes. Correct answer names the unconsidered alternatives; traps describe unrelated flaws.
lr.stimulus: City council member: To close next year's budget gap, we face a simple choice. Either we cut funding for the public library system, or we raise property taxes on every household in the city. Nobody on this council wants to cut library funding. Therefore, we have no option but to raise property taxes.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the council member's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presents only two options while giving no reason to think that no other options are available

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition sufficient for closing the budget gap as if it were necessary

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about future budgets based solely on the current one

choices.label: D
choices.text: uses the term 'cut funding' in two different senses

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejects tax increases on the basis of the unpopularity of those who propose them

explanations.correct: The council member frames the decision as library cuts versus property-tax hikes, but a city has many other budget levers: sales taxes, user fees, spending cuts elsewhere, reserves, new revenue sources. The argument never justifies treating those two options as exhaustive.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No conditional move is made; the argument is a disjunction, not a conditional.
explanations.C: Only the next budget is at issue; no cross-year projection is made.
explanations.D: 'Cut funding' is used in one sense throughout.
explanations.E: No one's popularity is attacked.

lr.difficultyReason: Pure whole-to-part conflation. Orchestra is excellent, therefore each member is excellent. Correct answer names the division-style flaw in LSAT vocabulary; traps misdescribe the move.
lr.stimulus: Music critic: The Brenner City Orchestra has won international acclaim for its performances, and audiences routinely describe its playing as among the finest in the world. It follows that every musician employed by the orchestra must be an exceptional performer on his or her instrument.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the music critic's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes a property of a group as a whole to be a property that must belong to each of its individual members

choices.label: B
choices.text: infers a causal relationship from evidence that establishes only a correlation

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about orchestras from a single example

choices.label: D
choices.text: uses the term 'exceptional' in two subtly different senses

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on the testimony of audiences whose musical expertise has not been established

explanations.correct: The orchestra's collective excellence can arise from strong leadership, section blend, and repertoire choices — not every individual player needs to be exceptional. The critic conflates a property of the whole with a property of every part.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No causal claim is defended.
explanations.C: The conclusion is about this orchestra's members, not orchestras generally.
explanations.D: 'Exceptional' is used consistently.
explanations.E: Audience expertise is peripheral; the flaw is the whole/part move.

lr.difficultyReason: Necessary/sufficient swap buried in a causal chain. The cardiologist cites a feature that is merely necessary for heart disease to develop and treats it as sufficient to predict the disease.
lr.stimulus: Cardiologist: Every patient who develops coronary artery disease has elevated arterial inflammation at some stage of the disease. Our clinic has begun screening patients' inflammation levels using a new blood panel. Patients whose results show elevated arterial inflammation should therefore be told that they are on track to develop coronary artery disease.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the cardiologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: relies on a screening method whose accuracy has not been independently verified

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a condition that accompanies the development of a disease as if it were enough, by itself, to indicate that the disease will develop

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about individual patients from evidence that concerns only populations

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that arterial inflammation is the underlying cause of coronary artery disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: overlooks the possibility that some patients with coronary artery disease will never be screened at the clinic

explanations.correct: The cardiologist has established only that elevated inflammation is necessary for (accompanies) coronary artery disease. That does not show it is sufficient: plenty of people may have elevated inflammation for other reasons without being on track for heart disease. (B) captures that flaw.
explanations.A: The argument's trouble is logical, not evidentiary — even a perfectly accurate panel wouldn't rescue the inference.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The evidence is already about individual patients ('every patient who develops'), so this misdescribes the stimulus.
explanations.D: A trap: the argument doesn't depend on inflammation being the cause, only on its co-occurrence. The flaw is the sufficiency leap, not an unstated causal claim.
explanations.E: Coverage of the screening program is irrelevant to whether the inference about a screened patient is sound.

lr.difficultyReason: Equivocation on 'free.' The columnist shifts between 'free' meaning 'at no monetary cost' and 'free' meaning 'unconstrained.' The trap choices describe real but adjacent flaws.
lr.stimulus: Columnist: Social-media platforms promise their users a free service, and millions sign up on that basis. But a service whose users are tracked, profiled, and targeted for advertising at every turn is not truly free — the users themselves are the product. So the millions who sign up have been deceived about what they are getting.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is flawed in that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that advertisers are the only parties who profit from social-media platforms

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on an ambiguity in the meaning of a key term to reach its conclusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: takes for granted that users who are tracked object to being tracked

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers from the fact that a service has drawbacks that it provides no benefit to its users

choices.label: E
choices.text: mistakes a correlation between advertising and tracking for a causal relationship between them

explanations.correct: 'Free' in the platform's promise means 'at no charge'; the columnist shifts to 'free' meaning 'not subject to tracking.' Because the word is used in two senses, the charge of deception doesn't follow.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't claim advertisers are the sole beneficiaries.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't require users to object — only that they were misled about what 'free' meant.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't deny the service has benefits; it accuses the platforms of misrepresentation.
explanations.E: No causal claim is made; this describes a flaw the argument doesn't commit.

lr.difficultyReason: Cross-population correlation-to-causation slide. A correlation observed in one group (retirees) is imported to explain an outcome in another (working adults). Trap (A) names causation-from-correlation in overly broad form.
lr.stimulus: Economist: In a study of retirees, those who carried high credit-card balances reported significantly higher levels of anxiety than those who were debt-free. The conclusion is obvious: for working adults, paying down credit-card debt is an effective way to reduce anxiety.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the economist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a causal relationship from a mere correlation

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from evidence about one population to a claim about a different population without justifying the move

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to specify what counts as a 'high' credit-card balance

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that anxiety is undesirable for working adults

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that retirees and working adults have the same sources of income

explanations.correct: Even granting that debt causes anxiety among retirees, the economist has not shown the same relationship holds for working adults, whose financial lives differ. The move from one population to another is unjustified.
explanations.A: Too broad — and the deeper problem is not the correlation-to-cause move in retirees (which might be fine), but importing that conclusion to a group not studied.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: A definitional quibble, not the structural error.
explanations.D: The argument assumes this, but it is common ground; the flaw lies elsewhere.
explanations.E: Too specific — income source is one of many differences, none of which the economist needed to address if the real inference were legitimate.

lr.difficultyReason: Appeal to ignorance disguised as evidence. Absence of evidence for harm is treated as evidence of safety. Trap (C) reverses the actual direction of the flaw.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The prosecution has produced no document, no witness, and no recording that shows my client was present at the warehouse on the night in question. In the face of such a complete absence of evidence, the jury can only conclude that my client was in fact elsewhere that night.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the attorney's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: attacks the prosecution's motives instead of the prosecution's evidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats the absence of evidence for a claim as if it were evidence that the claim is false

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats evidence that a claim is false as if it were evidence that the claim is true

choices.label: D
choices.text: relies on a witness whose testimony has not been corroborated

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes that any defendant lacking an alibi must be guilty

explanations.correct: The attorney moves from 'no evidence presented that the client was there' to 'the client was elsewhere.' Absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence; it is compatible with the client having been there but leaving no trace.
explanations.A: No ad hominem — the attorney critiques the evidence, not the prosecutor.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Reversed: the attorney treats absence of evidence as evidence of a claim, not evidence of falsity as evidence of truth.
explanations.D: No witness is cited.
