explanations.E: The opposite of what the attorney argues.

lr.difficultyReason: Part/whole equivocation — a property of each component is transferred to the collective, though the property is not additive. Trap (A) suggests a sample flaw that is not the move.
lr.stimulus: Architect: Each brick in our new library is, on its own, remarkably lightweight and easy to carry. Our structural engineer confirms this of every brick in the specification. Critics who complain that the library's walls will be too heavy for the old foundation are therefore simply wrong.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the architect's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion from evidence about an unrepresentative sample of bricks

choices.label: B
choices.text: takes for granted that what is true of each member of a collection must be true of the collection as a whole

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on the expertise of an engineer whose credentials are not established

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that some critics may have a financial interest in the library's cancellation

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that the foundation cannot be reinforced

explanations.correct: Each brick is lightweight, but thousands of bricks stacked together produce a weight that is exactly what worries the critics. The architect transfers an individual-level property to the whole.
explanations.A: The engineer confirmed every brick, so representativeness isn't the issue.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The engineer's authority is conceded; the problem is logical.
explanations.D: Ad hominem the architect doesn't actually use; naming it doesn't repair the argument.
explanations.E: Reinforcement could address the concern, but the architect's error is about drawing the 'not too heavy' conclusion in the first place.

lr.difficultyReason: Conditional chain with a necessary/sufficient swap at the end. The conclusion affirms the consequent. Trap (A) sounds right but reverses which direction of the flaw applies.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: If a language has a future tense, then its speakers routinely mark temporal distinctions in their grammar. And speakers who routinely mark temporal distinctions in their grammar develop a habit of precise time reference. Marisol's speakers clearly have a habit of precise time reference. We can therefore conclude that Marisol has a future tense.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the linguist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a sufficient condition for Marisol's having a future tense as if it were a necessary condition for Marisol's having one

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats a necessary condition for Marisol's having a future tense as if it were a sufficient condition for Marisol's having one

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on evidence about the habits of speakers rather than evidence about grammar

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that every language with a future tense uses that tense in the same way

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizes from a single language to a claim about all languages

explanations.correct: The chain establishes: future tense → grammatical time-marking → habit of precise time reference. That makes the habit necessary for (implied by) a future tense, not sufficient for one. The linguist nevertheless concludes the tense from the habit.
explanations.A: Reversed. The habit is established as a necessary condition of having a future tense, not a sufficient one.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The speaker habits are exactly the middle link the argument set up.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't rely on a uniformity claim about future-tense use.
explanations.E: The argument is about Marisol only; no overgeneralization.

lr.difficultyReason: Subtle scope shift between 'species endangered by warming' and 'species for which warming is the chief threat.' Trap (D) names a plausibly related flaw not actually committed.
lr.stimulus: Biologist: Most amphibian species whose habitats have warmed substantially over the past decade are now endangered. It follows that for most endangered amphibian species, habitat warming is the principal threat driving them toward extinction.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the biologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that habitat warming cannot interact with other environmental threats

choices.label: B
choices.text: shifts from a claim about amphibian species affected by warming to a claim about the causes of endangerment for amphibian species generally

choices.label: C
choices.text: draws a conclusion about the past decade from evidence that concerns only recent years

choices.label: D
choices.text: infers a causal relationship between two phenomena solely from the fact that they occur together

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that amphibians are representative of all animals threatened by habitat change

explanations.correct: The premise speaks of species whose habitats warmed and are now endangered; the conclusion speaks of endangered species generally and names warming as the chief cause. Endangered amphibian species include many whose habitats have not warmed, and among those whose habitats have warmed, warming may not be the leading threat.
explanations.A: The argument doesn't deny interactions; it just drifts in scope.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Time frame isn't the issue.
explanations.D: A tempting generic flaw, but the argument's deeper trouble is the reference-class shift; the biologist never even fully commits to the pure correlation-to-cause move this answer describes.
explanations.E: No inference from amphibians to other animals is drawn.

lr.difficultyReason: Subtle overgeneralization from 'should, all else equal' to 'should, full stop.' The argument ignores that the principle's ceteris paribus clause may not hold.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: All else being equal, a person should keep the promises she has made. Mira promised her neighbor that she would water his plants while he was away. It follows that Mira should water her neighbor's plants.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the ethicist's argument is flawed because it

choices.label: A
choices.text: takes a principle that holds only when other considerations are equal and applies it as though no other considerations could be relevant

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes about what people ought to do from a single case

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on the meaning of 'promise' without defining that term

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes that neighbors always have a right to expect help from one another

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses a description of how people act with a prescription for how they ought to act

explanations.correct: The principle is conditional on all else being equal. Mira might be hospitalized, or the plants might be toxic — conditions under which the promise's force is overridden. The ethicist drops the qualifier in reaching the categorical conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No generalization — the conclusion is about Mira alone.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't turn on the definition.
explanations.D: Not assumed — the claim is about the promise's force, not a standing right.
explanations.E: Both the premise and conclusion are prescriptive; no is/ought slide occurs.

lr.difficultyReason: Treats an average as if it held of every individual member of the group. Trap (B) names the correct family of error in terms too broad to pin the exact move.
lr.stimulus: Curator: Works by early-career painters in our permanent collection have, on average, appreciated in value more rapidly over the last decade than works by established painters. Donors considering a bequest of a single painting to the museum should therefore expect their gift to appreciate more quickly if the painter is early in her career than if she is established.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the curator's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a conclusion about a particular work from evidence about the average performance of a category of works

choices.label: B
choices.text: treats what is true of a group as if it must be true of every member of the group

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on evidence about the last decade to predict performance over a longer period

choices.label: D
choices.text: fails to consider that donors may value considerations other than appreciation

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that early-career painters will become established

explanations.correct: A higher average for early-career works does not tell a donor what to expect for any single work. A small number of breakout early-career paintings could lift the average while most individual works underperform established painters.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too broad — and not quite right. The argument doesn't say every early-career work appreciated faster; it treats the average as if it straightforwardly applied to a particular donor's single painting, which is the sharper description.
explanations.C: The argument does project forward, but the flaw is about averages-vs.-individuals, not time frame.
explanations.D: True but not a reasoning flaw — the conclusion is conditional on caring about appreciation.
explanations.E: Not assumed — the argument compares painters as they stand.

lr.difficultyReason: A self-selected sample is treated as representative. Trap (B) describes an ad hominem attack the argument doesn't make; trap (E) gestures at composition.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: A recent survey posted to the city's open-data website asked residents whether the new bicycle-lane network has improved their commutes. More than seventy percent of respondents answered yes. City council can be confident, then, that the bicycle-lane network has improved commutes for most city residents.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the policy analyst's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: draws a general conclusion about a population from a group of respondents who may not be representative of that population

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismisses the views of residents who did not answer the survey by questioning their motives

choices.label: C
choices.text: confuses a claim about how residents perceive their commutes with a claim about how commutes have actually changed

choices.label: D
choices.text: takes for granted that the city council shares the policy analyst's goals

choices.label: E
choices.text: presumes that because a policy has improved the commutes of individual residents, it has improved the city's commuting patterns overall

explanations.correct: Residents who visit the city's open-data website and fill out a survey about bicycle lanes are disproportionately likely to be cyclists, tech-comfortable, and engaged with the policy — not a cross-section of the city. Their responses don't support a claim about most residents.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No motive-impugning occurs.
explanations.C: Perception/reality is a real gap, but the conclusion is plainly about whether the network has improved commutes, not about a separate objective measure; the sampling flaw is sharper and more clearly fatal.
explanations.D: Not assumed — the conclusion is an empirical claim.
explanations.E: The argument aggregates individuals to a general claim, but the trouble is the respondents' representativeness, not a composition leap from part to whole.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the epidemiologist treats a percentage increase as if it were an increase in the absolute number of cases, and buries that move inside an appeal to her own credentials. Students who spot only the ad hominem framing or only the statistical slip miss the interaction.
lr.stimulus: Epidemiologist: As someone who has spent thirty years analyzing outbreak data, I can assure the council that the new pathogen poses a graver threat than the old one. The old pathogen's incidence rose by just 4 percent last year, whereas the new pathogen's incidence rose by 60 percent. Anyone who has not worked in the field, as I have, should hesitate to dispute these numbers.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the epidemiologist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a comparison of rates of change as if it established a comparison of total case counts, while implying that the speaker's expertise insulates that inference from challenge

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes, without providing justification, that no other pathogens pose a comparable threat to public health

choices.label: C
choices.text: infers a causal relationship between the speaker's expertise and the accuracy of the data cited

choices.label: D
choices.text: relies on statistics drawn from a sample that is too small to support a general conclusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: assumes that what is true of the new pathogen's incidence must also be true of its mortality rate

explanations.correct: A percentage rise from a small base can still leave the new pathogen's total caseload far below the old one's; the argument slides from rate-of-change to absolute threat, and wards off objections by citing the speaker's experience rather than addressing the inference.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument compares only two pathogens; it does not need to rule out others.
explanations.C: The expertise claim is used to deflect disagreement, not to explain why the data are accurate.
explanations.D: Sample size is never characterized; this is a plausible-but-absent flaw.
explanations.E: Mortality is never mentioned; the conclusion is about threat, but the scope-shift at issue is rate-to-absolute, not incidence-to-mortality.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: an appeal to authority (the Nobel laureate) is used to license a scope shift from 'effective in clinical trials' to 'effective in routine practice.' Students who name only the appeal to authority or only the scope shift miss that the authority is doing the work of papering over the shift.
lr.stimulus: Pharmacologist: The new anticoagulant should be prescribed routinely to patients at risk of stroke. Dr. Reyes, a Nobel laureate in medicine, has publicly endorsed the drug, and controlled clinical trials have shown that it reduces clot formation more reliably than the current standard. Her endorsement, together with the trial data, settles the matter.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the pharmacologist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: presumes that because controlled trial results imply routine effectiveness, a respected endorsement can substitute for evidence of such effectiveness

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that Dr. Reyes's Nobel Prize was awarded in an unrelated field

choices.label: C
choices.text: treats a necessary condition for prescribing the drug as a condition sufficient to do so

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from an unrepresentative sample of clinical trial participants

choices.label: E
choices.text: attacks Dr. Reyes's credentials rather than the substance of her endorsement

explanations.correct: Controlled-trial performance and routine-practice performance are different claims; the argument leans on the laureate's endorsement to bridge that gap instead of supplying evidence that trial results carry over. The endorsement and the scope shift work together.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The stimulus never indicates Reyes's field; assuming she is unqualified would be an unsupported gloss on the argument.
explanations.C: No conditional relationship is stated; this is an accurate description of a different, absent flaw.
explanations.D: Trial representativeness is never raised.
explanations.E: The argument defers to Reyes; it does not attack her.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the ethicist equivocates on 'natural' (naturally occurring vs. morally natural) and uses that equivocation to collapse a descriptive-to-normative gap. Students who flag only the is/ought move or only the ambiguity miss that each enables the other.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Competition among members of a species is found in every biological environment we have studied; it is entirely natural. Whatever is natural in this sense is morally natural as well, since our moral intuitions themselves evolved under selection pressures. It follows that ruthless competition among humans in the marketplace is morally above reproach.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the ethicist's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: exploits an ambiguity in the term 'natural' in order to move from a claim about what is widespread in nature to a claim about what is morally permissible

choices.label: B
choices.text: takes for granted that what is true of a species as a whole must be true of each of its members

choices.label: C
choices.text: relies on evidence drawn exclusively from non-human species

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that moral intuitions cannot be subjected to further critical scrutiny

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses a claim about the origins of moral intuitions with a claim about their content

explanations.correct: The first premise uses 'natural' descriptively (occurring in nature); the second premise silently shifts 'natural' into a normative register ('morally natural'); the conclusion then treats the second sense as if it had been established by the first. The equivocation is what makes the is-to-ought leap look licensed.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No part-whole move is in play.
explanations.C: The argument draws on biology generally, including human evolution; the evidentiary scope isn't the issue.
explanations.D: The argument assumes intuitions are trustworthy, but that isn't the structural move at fault.
explanations.E: Tempting — origins-vs-content is nearby — but the argument doesn't isolate 'origins' as its hook; the equivocation on 'natural' is the pivot.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: percentage-vs-absolute confusion hidden inside selection bias. The rise in 'share of claims' could reflect fewer good drivers being insured, not worsening driving. Students who name only the selection bias or only the percentage confusion miss the interaction.
lr.stimulus: Insurance analyst: Drivers under 25 now account for 42 percent of collision claims filed with our company, up from 34 percent five years ago. Over the same period, our company raised premiums for drivers over 50, prompting many of them to switch carriers. It is therefore clear that drivers under 25 have become considerably more dangerous on the road.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the insurance analyst's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers a change in the behavior of one group from a change in that group's share of a pool whose composition has itself been altered by the speaker's own company

choices.label: B
choices.text: generalizes from the claims experience of a single insurance company to that of the industry as a whole

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes that collision claims are a reliable proxy for collisions

choices.label: D
choices.text: assumes without warrant that drivers over 50 are safer than drivers under 25

choices.label: E
choices.text: treats a cause of an increase in premiums as if it were an effect of that increase

explanations.correct: When older drivers leave the pool, younger drivers' share of claims can rise even if their absolute claim rate is unchanged. The argument also ignores that its own company caused the compositional shift, so 'more dangerous' isn't warranted.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The scope of the conclusion is plausibly about this company's drivers; even on a broader reading, the central error is the compositional shift.
explanations.C: Plausible-but-absent; no claim-vs-collision distinction is raised.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't rank the groups' safety; it claims under-25s got worse.
explanations.E: No causal reversal is asserted.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: treats evidence about what the framers individually believed as evidence about what the Constitution as a ratified document means — a category error, combined with an appeal to the framers' authority. The trap answer describes ad hominem reversed.
lr.stimulus: Constitutional scholar: Several of the framers wrote privately that they viewed a standing peacetime army as a threat to liberty. Because the framers are the supreme interpretive authorities on the Constitution they drafted, the Constitution, properly read, prohibits the maintenance of such an army. Any judge who rules otherwise is simply ignoring what the document means.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the constitutional scholar's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats the private views of individual drafters as if they determined the meaning of a ratified legal text, and treats the drafters' authority as settling an interpretive question rather than bearing on it

choices.label: B
choices.text: attacks the character of judges who disagree rather than engaging their legal arguments

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes that a document's meaning can change over time without any formal amendment

choices.label: D
choices.text: draws a universal conclusion from the views of only a few of the framers

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses what the framers hoped the Constitution would accomplish with what it in fact accomplished

explanations.correct: Private letters are a different object from a ratified text; the scholar collapses that distinction while elevating the framers from relevant authorities to decisive ones. Both moves are needed to reach the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Tempting, because the last sentence stings — but the argument targets judges' reasoning, not their character; ad hominem is the wrong label.
explanations.C: The argument implicitly denies meaning can shift; that denial is not the structural flaw.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't quantify how many framers held the view; weakening on 'only a few' would miss the category error.
explanations.E: Hopes-vs-accomplishments isn't the distinction being conflated.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: a necessary/sufficient confusion wrapped in an ad hominem. The columnist discredits opponents to distract from the logical slip between 'without clean water, no civilization' and 'clean water suffices for civilization.'
lr.stimulus: Columnist: Without access to clean water, no ancient civilization ever flourished. Critics who dismiss modern aid programs that focus on water infrastructure are either ignorant of history or indifferent to suffering. The lesson is plain: any region that receives clean water will become a flourishing society.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a condition whose absence precludes an outcome as if its presence were enough to produce the outcome, and deflects objections by impugning the motives of those who raise them

choices.label: B
choices.text: fails to consider that ancient civilizations differed in important respects from modern societies

choices.label: C
choices.text: presumes, without giving reasons, that clean water programs are the most cost-effective form of aid

choices.label: D
choices.text: confuses a claim about what has happened with a claim about what ought to happen

choices.label: E
choices.text: relies on evidence that is consistent with the denial of the conclusion it is meant to support

explanations.correct: 'Without X, never Y' makes X necessary for Y, not sufficient. The columnist upgrades necessity to sufficiency, and uses a character attack on critics to preempt scrutiny of the upgrade.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Plausible reading, but the flaw isn't ancient-modern disanalogy; even within ancient cases, necessity wouldn't yield sufficiency.
explanations.C: Cost-effectiveness isn't the conclusion.
explanations.D: No is/ought confusion; the conclusion is predictive.
explanations.E: Too vague; the conditional slip is the specific error.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the consultant equivocates on 'efficient' (completes tasks quickly vs. delivers business value) and then generalizes from the fastest team to the organization. Students who pick the equivocation miss that generalization isn't at fault; students who pick the generalization miss the term shift.
lr.stimulus: Management consultant: Our internal analytics team is the most efficient group in the company: it closes assigned tickets faster than any other team. Because maximally efficient teams are precisely the ones whose practices generate the greatest business value, the firm should require every department to adopt the analytics team's practices wholesale.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the management consultant's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: uses 'efficient' in one sense to characterize the analytics team and in a different sense to connect efficiency with business value

choices.label: B
choices.text: draws a conclusion about every department from evidence about a single department that may not be representative of the others

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that the analytics team's practices cannot be improved upon

choices.label: D
choices.text: presumes that a correlation between speed and value establishes that speed causes value

choices.label: E
choices.text: takes for granted that practices effective within one organization will be effective within another

explanations.correct: The first premise measures efficiency by ticket-closing speed; the bridging premise implicitly treats 'efficient' as meaning 'value-generating.' Without the shift, the conclusion loses its support.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Tempting distractor, but representativeness isn't the issue — the consultant asserts a link between efficiency and value, so the trouble is the word 'efficient,' not sampling.
explanations.C: Improvability isn't claimed or denied.
explanations.D: Causation language doesn't appear; the link is conceptual (via the definition of 'efficient').
explanations.E: The argument is intra-firm, not cross-firm.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: absence-of-evidence inference folded into a scope shift between 'endangered in our surveys' and 'endangered globally.' Students who identify only the absence-of-evidence move miss that the scope shift does most of the damage.
lr.stimulus: Biologist: Our three-year survey of the central rainforest failed to locate a single specimen of the blue-throated tanager. The earlier belief that the species was endangered must therefore be mistaken: had it been endangered, some individuals would surely have appeared in our data. The species is plainly thriving in regions we did not survey.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the biologist's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: infers from a failure to detect a species in a limited area that the species must be flourishing in unsurveyed areas

choices.label: B
choices.text: relies on survey methods that are not described in sufficient detail to be evaluated

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a three-year period to a conclusion about the species' long-term status

choices.label: D
choices.text: treats the belief that the species is endangered as settled rather than as an assumption requiring support

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses being undetected with being extinct

explanations.correct: Not finding a rare species in one area can just mean the species is rare there (consistent with being endangered). The argument treats that absence as evidence of abundance and then leaps to regions it didn't study.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Methodological opacity isn't what the argument turns on.
explanations.C: Time horizon isn't the key move; the spatial leap is.
explanations.D: Reversed — the argument challenges the endangered-status belief, not assumes it.
explanations.E: Opposite of what the argument does: it concludes thriving, not extinction.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: percentage-vs-absolute confusion hidden in statistical language. Declines in 'share of listening time' don't entail declines in hours listened if the overall pie grew; the critic also slips from listening data to 'cultural significance.'
lr.stimulus: Critic: Streaming data show that classical music's share of total listening time fell from 8 percent to 5 percent over the last decade. Since listening is the primary measure of a genre's cultural significance, classical music is undeniably losing cultural significance, and arts foundations should redirect their support accordingly.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the critic's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a decline in a genre's proportion of listening time as establishing a decline in the genre's cultural significance, without ruling out that total listening hours devoted to the genre rose as the overall volume of listening grew

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that streaming data are representative of all forms of music consumption

choices.label: C
choices.text: assumes that arts foundations have a duty to fund only genres whose listenership is growing

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizes from a ten-year window to a long-term trend

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses the cause of classical music's decline with its effect

explanations.correct: Share can fall while absolute hours rise if the streaming pie grows faster. The critic converts a relative statistic to a claim about absolute cultural significance without addressing that gap.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Plausible-but-absent — representativeness is a different flaw than the stats slip.
explanations.C: The argument doesn't assign foundations a duty; it draws a policy suggestion.
explanations.D: Time window isn't the pivot.
explanations.E: No cause/effect reversal is asserted.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: part-whole (composition) error wrapped in a category confusion. 'Idiomatic' is a property of sentences within a language; the speaker treats it as a property a whole language can have. Students who pick the composition move alone miss the category piece.
lr.stimulus: Linguistics professor: Every competent speaker of English occasionally produces sentences that are idiomatic — expressions whose meanings cannot be predicted from their parts. It follows that English, as a language, is fundamentally idiomatic, and therefore that any formal grammar that assigns meaning compositionally must fail to describe it.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the linguistics professor's argument is flawed because the argument

choices.label: A
choices.text: treats a property that can characterize particular sentences within a language as if it were a property that could characterize the language itself

choices.label: B
choices.text: presumes that competent speakers are reliable reporters of their own linguistic intuitions

choices.label: C
choices.text: generalizes from a feature of English to a feature shared by all natural languages

choices.label: D
choices.text: takes for granted that formal grammars are intended to describe every sentence a speaker might produce

choices.label: E
choices.text: confuses a sufficient condition for a formal grammar's success with a necessary condition for it

explanations.correct: 'Idiomatic' describes how some sentences behave; calling the language itself idiomatic conflates a sentence-level property with a language-level one — a composition/category slip. The jump to 'compositional grammars must fail' rides on that slip.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reliability of introspection isn't the structural problem.
explanations.C: The conclusion concerns English only, not all languages.
explanations.D: The argument doesn't hinge on the scope of what grammars aim to cover; it hinges on misapplying 'idiomatic.'
explanations.E: No necessary/sufficient inversion occurs around grammar's success conditions.

lr.difficultyReason: Short two-sentence stimulus with 'therefore' marking the main conclusion directly. Distractors restate the premise about vaccination rates or overstate the scope.
lr.stimulus: Recent data show that counties offering free booster clinics have vaccination rates nearly twice those of counties without such clinics. Therefore, municipalities that want to raise their local vaccination rates should invest in free booster clinics.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Municipalities that want to raise vaccination rates ought to invest in free booster clinics.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Counties that offer free booster clinics have roughly twice the vaccination rates of counties that do not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Free booster clinics are the only effective way to raise local vaccination rates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Counties without free booster clinics have unacceptably low vaccination rates.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Investing in free booster clinics always doubles a municipality's vaccination rate.

explanations.correct: The sentence following 'therefore' is the author's recommendation, and (A) paraphrases it without altering scope or modal force.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Restates the premise (the observed correlation), not the conclusion.
explanations.C: Overstates — the argument does not claim that free clinics are the only effective method.
explanations.D: Introduces an evaluative claim ('unacceptably low') the argument never makes.
explanations.E: Overstates the predicted effect; the author recommends investment, not guarantees a doubling.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-sentence argument with 'thus' introducing the main conclusion. Trap answers restate the premise or paraphrase the intermediate factual claim.
lr.stimulus: Lying to a patient about a diagnosis, even to spare feelings, undermines the trust on which the doctor-patient relationship depends. Without that trust, patients will be less willing to disclose symptoms and follow medical advice. Thus, physicians should not lie to their patients, even with good intentions.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients who are lied to are less likely to follow their physicians' medical advice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lying to a patient undermines the trust that the doctor-patient relationship depends on.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Physicians ought not to lie to their patients, even when their intentions are good.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A doctor-patient relationship cannot survive any act of deception by the physician.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The good intentions of a physician are irrelevant to evaluating that physician's conduct.

explanations.correct: The sentence after 'thus' is the author's main claim, and (C) paraphrases it faithfully.
explanations.A: Restates a premise about downstream effects of lost trust.
explanations.B: Restates the opening premise about the effect of lying on trust.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Overstates — the argument says lying undermines trust, not that relationships cannot survive any deception.
explanations.E: Generalizes beyond what the argument says about intentions.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence argument ending with 'therefore' plus a hedged recommendation. Traps restate the premise or strip the hedge.
lr.stimulus: Small businesses that adopt cloud-based accounting software report substantially fewer bookkeeping errors than those relying on spreadsheets. Therefore, a small business seeking to reduce its bookkeeping errors should consider switching to cloud-based accounting software.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spreadsheet-based bookkeeping produces more errors than any other method.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Small businesses using cloud-based accounting software report substantially fewer bookkeeping errors than spreadsheet users.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A small business that wants to reduce bookkeeping errors should consider switching to cloud-based accounting software.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any small business that switches to cloud-based accounting software will eliminate its bookkeeping errors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cloud-based accounting software is the most affordable option for small businesses.

explanations.correct: (C) paraphrases the post-'therefore' recommendation and preserves the hedged modal ('should consider').
explanations.A: Overstates — the argument compares cloud software to spreadsheets only.
explanations.B: Restates the premise (the observed comparison), not the conclusion.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Overstates — 'should consider switching' is weaker than 'will eliminate errors'.
explanations.E: Introduces affordability, which is never mentioned in the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-sentence argument with 'hence' marking the main conclusion. Trap (B) paraphrases the premise about migration; (E) overstates scope.
lr.stimulus: Several species of songbird that historically wintered in the southern plains have shifted their ranges hundreds of miles north over the past two decades. Wildlife biologists attribute this shift to milder winter temperatures across the plains. Hence, continued warming is likely to produce further northward shifts in these songbirds' winter ranges.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several songbird species have shifted their wintering grounds hundreds of miles northward over the past two decades.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Biologists believe milder winters are the cause of recent songbird range shifts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ongoing warming is likely to push the wintering ranges of these songbirds still farther north.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Songbird populations in the southern plains will collapse if warming continues.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every bird species that winters in the plains will shift its range northward.

explanations.correct: (C) paraphrases the sentence introduced by 'hence' and preserves its hedged 'likely'.
explanations.A: Restates the opening premise about observed shifts.
explanations.B: Restates the second premise about biologists' explanation.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Introduces a collapse claim the argument never makes.
explanations.E: Overstates — the argument concerns only these songbird species.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence legal-domain argument with 'so' as the conclusion marker. Traps restate the premise and overstate scope.
lr.stimulus: A municipal ordinance that is too vague to give citizens fair notice of what it prohibits cannot be enforced consistently by the courts. So any ordinance whose language fails to give citizens fair notice of the prohibited conduct should be struck down.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ordinances whose language fails to give citizens fair notice of prohibited conduct should be struck down.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vague ordinances cannot be enforced consistently by the courts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Citizens have a legal right to fair notice of the content of every municipal ordinance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Courts that enforce ordinances inconsistently should themselves be reformed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No municipal ordinance is ever sufficiently precise to satisfy constitutional requirements.

explanations.correct: (A) paraphrases the 'so'-clause verbatim in structure, preserving scope and modal force.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Restates the opening premise, not the conclusion.
explanations.C: Introduces a rights claim that is nowhere in the argument.
explanations.D: Shifts the conclusion from the ordinance to the courts themselves.
explanations.E: Overstates — the argument targets only vague ordinances, not all of them.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence economics argument ending with 'therefore' and a policy recommendation. Traps restate the premise and one overstates.
lr.stimulus: When a central bank raises interest rates sharply, consumer borrowing slows and unemployment tends to rise within a year. Therefore, central banks that wish to avoid near-term increases in unemployment should refrain from sharp rate hikes.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central banks that want to avoid near-term increases in unemployment should refrain from sharp interest rate hikes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sharp increases in interest rates slow consumer borrowing and typically raise unemployment within a year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Central banks should never raise interest rates under any circumstances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Consumer borrowing is the primary driver of unemployment in modern economies.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Avoiding unemployment should be the overriding goal of every central bank.

explanations.correct: (A) paraphrases the recommendation after 'therefore', preserving its conditional scope.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Restates the premise about the effects of rate hikes.
explanations.C: Overstates — the argument targets only sharp rate hikes by banks with a particular goal.
explanations.D: Introduces a claim about primary causation that the argument never makes.
explanations.E: Misstates the argument as prescribing an overarching priority.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-sentence technology argument with 'consequently' marker. Traps include a premise restatement and a wrong-direction paraphrase.
lr.stimulus: A smartphone app that tracks a user's location must request specific permissions from the operating system. Users who review these permissions before installing an app are far less likely to install apps that surreptitiously share location data with third parties. Consequently, users concerned about location privacy should review app permissions before installing any new app.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Users who are concerned about location privacy should review app permissions before installing any new app.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A smartphone app cannot track a user's location without requesting permissions from the operating system.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reviewing app permissions eliminates the possibility that an app will share location data with third parties.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apps that surreptitiously share location data should be removed from app stores.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Operating systems should make app permissions easier for users to interpret.

explanations.correct: (A) paraphrases the recommendation following 'consequently' while preserving its scope.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Restates the opening premise about permissions.
explanations.C: Overstates — 'far less likely' does not equal 'eliminates'.
explanations.D: Introduces a removal recommendation the argument never makes.
explanations.E: Shifts the subject from users to operating systems.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-sentence linguistics argument with 'thus' before the main conclusion. Trap (C) paraphrases a premise; (E) overstates scope.
lr.stimulus: Children raised in households where multiple languages are regularly spoken tend to develop stronger executive-function skills than children raised in monolingual households. Executive function is associated with better academic performance in later grades. Thus, exposure to multiple languages in early childhood appears to confer long-term academic benefits.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Early-childhood exposure to multiple languages appears to yield long-term academic benefits.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Executive function is associated with stronger academic performance in later grades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children in multilingual households have stronger executive-function skills than children in monolingual households.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All children should be raised in multilingual households.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Monolingual households produce children who perform poorly in school.

explanations.correct: (A) paraphrases the post-'thus' conclusion and preserves the hedged 'appears to'.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Restates the second premise.
explanations.C: Restates the opening premise.
explanations.D: Overstates — the argument notes a benefit, not a universal prescription.
explanations.E: Wrong direction — the argument praises multilingual exposure, it does not condemn monolingual households.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence history argument ending with 'therefore'. Traps restate the premise and add a claim the argument does not make.
lr.stimulus: Many innovations credited to a single inventor, such as the telephone and the light bulb, were in fact the result of overlapping work by multiple researchers competing for the same patent. Therefore, histories of technology that focus on lone inventors give a misleading picture of how major innovations actually emerge.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Histories of technology that center on lone inventors present a misleading picture of how major innovations actually arise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many innovations attributed to individual inventors were actually the product of multiple researchers competing for the same patent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The telephone and the light bulb were invented simultaneously by several researchers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patents should not be awarded to individual inventors when multiple researchers were involved.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historians of technology are uninterested in collaborative research.

explanations.correct: (A) paraphrases the sentence following 'therefore' while preserving scope.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Restates the premise about overlapping work.
explanations.C: Too specific — the argument uses these as examples, not as the conclusion.
explanations.D: Introduces a patent-policy claim the argument never makes.
explanations.E: Introduces an attitude claim the argument never makes.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence arts argument with 'therefore' and a recommendation. Traps restate the premise and overstate the recommendation.
lr.stimulus: Community theaters that offer a free admission night each month consistently attract larger and more diverse audiences over the course of a season than theaters charging admission for every performance. Therefore, community theaters seeking to broaden their audiences should consider adopting a monthly free admission night.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Community theaters aiming to broaden their audiences should consider offering a free admission night once a month.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Community theaters with monthly free admission nights draw larger and more diverse audiences than those charging for every performance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Community theaters ought to make every performance free of charge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only community theaters with monthly free admission nights will survive financially.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Audience diversity is the most important measure of a community theater's success.

explanations.correct: (A) paraphrases the recommendation after 'therefore' and preserves its hedged 'should consider'.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Restates the premise about observed attendance patterns.
explanations.C: Overstates — the argument recommends one free night, not free admission to all performances.
explanations.D: Introduces a financial-survival claim the argument never makes.
explanations.E: Introduces an evaluative claim the argument never makes.

lr.difficultyReason: The main conclusion is unmarked and sits at the end of the stimulus, while a subsidiary conclusion in the middle is signaled by 'thus.' Test-takers who latch onto the marked 'thus' clause will pick the trap paraphrase of the intermediate step.
lr.stimulus: Hospital administrators have proposed shortening resident physicians' shifts from 24 hours to 16 hours in order to reduce medical errors. But sleep is not the only determinant of clinical performance; continuity of care is also essential, and shorter shifts mean more handoffs between doctors. Thus, shorter shifts introduce a different kind of error: information lost when one physician transfers a case to another. The administrators' proposal will not achieve what they claim for it.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shortening resident physicians' shifts will not accomplish the reduction in medical errors that administrators expect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shorter shifts introduce errors caused by information lost during handoffs between physicians.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sleep deprivation is not the only factor that affects a physician's clinical performance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hospital administrators should abandon any effort to reduce errors made by resident physicians.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Continuity of care is more important to patient outcomes than is the well-rested state of the attending physician.

explanations.correct: The final sentence is the author's main claim; every other sentence — the premise about continuity, and the intermediate conclusion that handoffs cause errors — is offered in support of it.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This is the intermediate conclusion, supported by the continuity-of-care premise and used in turn to support the final sentence. It is the classic subsidiary-conclusion trap.
explanations.C: A premise used to motivate the intermediate conclusion, not the main point.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author attacks this specific proposal, not every error-reduction effort.
explanations.E: Too strong — the author says continuity is also essential, not that it outweighs rest.

lr.difficultyReason: Opens with an opposing view and buries a subsidiary conclusion in the middle of the argument. The author's main conclusion is the last sentence and carries no 'therefore' marker.
lr.stimulus: Some ethicists argue that lying is always wrong because it treats the listener as a mere means to the liar's ends. But consider the physician who withholds a grim prognosis from a patient whose recovery depends on maintaining hope; it follows that some deceptions are performed for the listener's sake rather than the speaker's. The absolutist view mistakes a typical feature of lies for a necessary one.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim that lying is always wrong rests on a feature of lies that is common but not essential.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some deceptions are undertaken for the benefit of the person being deceived rather than the benefit of the deceiver.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A physician is justified in withholding a grim prognosis when the patient's recovery depends on hope.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lying is never wrong when it is performed for the listener's sake.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lying treats the listener as a mere means to the liar's ends.

explanations.correct: The last sentence is the author's real claim. The physician example and the intermediate conclusion that some deceptions serve the listener are the support.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This is the intermediate conclusion marked by 'it follows that' — the trap.
explanations.C: A premise/illustration, not the conclusion.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author says absolutism is mistaken, not that listener-serving lies are always permissible.
explanations.E: The opposing view the author is rebutting, not the author's own view.

lr.difficultyReason: Conclusion-first structure. The opening sentence is the main claim; a 'thus' clause in the middle marks the subsidiary conclusion and attracts the unwary.
lr.stimulus: Raising the minimum wage in our city will not, on balance, reduce employment among low-wage workers. Studies of recent wage increases in comparable cities show that businesses responded not by firing staff but by modestly raising prices and reducing turnover costs. Thus, the labor savings employers seek come from keeping workers longer, not from employing fewer of them. Any increase in unemployment predicted by simple supply-and-demand models fails to appear when the data are examined.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A higher minimum wage in the city will not, overall, decrease employment of low-wage workers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The labor savings businesses obtain from higher wages come from reduced turnover, not a smaller workforce.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Simple supply-and-demand models do not accurately predict the effects of minimum-wage increases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raising the minimum wage benefits low-wage workers without imposing any cost on employers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Businesses in comparable cities raised prices modestly after recent minimum-wage increases.

explanations.correct: The first sentence states the author's main claim, and everything after it — the study findings, the 'thus' clause about turnover, and the rebuttal of simple models — is offered as support.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The subsidiary conclusion marked by 'thus.' It supports the main claim but is not the main claim.
explanations.C: A supporting point, not the main claim.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author concedes prices and turnover costs shift.
explanations.E: A premise cited from the studies.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents a legal argument with an intermediate conclusion flagged by 'so.' The main conclusion, at the end, uses a normative verb ('should') without any conclusion marker.
lr.stimulus: Under current law, search warrants must describe with particularity the items officers intend to seize. A warrant that authorizes seizure of 'all documents relating to the defendant's business' fails this requirement, since virtually any paper in the defendant's office could be said to relate to the business. So such a warrant confers on officers the very discretion the particularity rule was meant to restrain. Warrants phrased in this sweeping way should be struck down.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Warrants that authorize seizure of all documents relating to the defendant's business ought to be invalidated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A warrant for 'all documents relating to the defendant's business' gives officers the discretion the particularity rule was designed to prevent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The particularity requirement is intended to restrain officer discretion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No search warrant that fails the particularity requirement can ever be enforced by a court.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Virtually any paper in a defendant's office could be described as relating to the business.

explanations.correct: The final sentence is the author's prescriptive claim; everything before it — the statement of the rule, the example, and the 'so' clause — supports that prescription.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The subsidiary conclusion introduced by 'so.' A trap for readers who stop at the conclusion marker.
explanations.C: A premise explaining the purpose of the rule.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author addresses sweeping business-document warrants, not every warrant that could fail particularity.
explanations.E: A supporting observation, not the main claim.

lr.difficultyReason: The author's main conclusion sits at the end with no marker, while the sentence preceding it carries the 'hence' signpost and is the subsidiary conclusion most students mistake for the main one.
lr.stimulus: Conservationists have urged governments to create more protected reserves to halt species loss. But most species extinctions in recent decades have occurred not inside reserves but along the unprotected edges where reserves meet farmland and roads. Hence the greatest threat to biodiversity is not the absence of reserves but the character of the landscape surrounding them. Expanding reserves without changing what lies outside their borders will do little to stem the decline.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creating additional reserves, without altering conditions in the adjacent landscape, will do little to prevent continued species loss.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The principal danger to biodiversity is the nature of the land surrounding reserves rather than any shortage of reserves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most recent species extinctions have taken place along the unprotected edges of reserves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conservationists are wrong to concern themselves with protected reserves at all.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Governments should devote their conservation funding primarily to the management of farmland and roads.

explanations.correct: The last sentence is the author's main claim. The edge-extinction premise and the 'hence' intermediate conclusion together support it.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The subsidiary conclusion marked by 'hence.' The most common trap.
explanations.C: A premise the 'hence' clause is drawn from.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author says more reserves alone won't help, not that reserves are worthless.
explanations.E: Too strong and too specific — the author doesn't recommend a particular funding allocation.

lr.difficultyReason: A technology stimulus in which the subsidiary conclusion is introduced by 'thus' in the middle of the argument and the main conclusion, stated at the end, challenges a popular claim without a conclusion marker.
lr.stimulus: Advocates of facial-recognition systems insist that the technology will make public spaces safer. In controlled laboratory settings, the software misidentifies suspects less than one percent of the time. But in deployed conditions — variable lighting, crowds, movement — independent audits find error rates above ten percent. Thus the accuracy figures quoted by advocates describe performance the technology does not actually deliver in the field. The case for widespread adoption rests on numbers that do not reflect how these systems will be used.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arguments for adopting facial-recognition systems rely on accuracy figures that do not correspond to actual field conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The accuracy numbers advocates cite describe performance the technology does not achieve in deployment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Facial-recognition software has error rates above ten percent when used in real-world conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Facial-recognition technology cannot make public spaces safer under any conditions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Laboratory testing of facial-recognition software should be replaced entirely by field testing.

explanations.correct: The last sentence is the author's main charge against the case for adoption; the lab/field contrast and the 'thus' clause both support it.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The intermediate conclusion flagged by 'thus.' It supports the main claim but is not it.
explanations.C: A premise from the audit evidence.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author attacks the case for adoption, not the possibility of benefit.
explanations.E: Beyond the scope — the author doesn't prescribe a testing regime.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus opens with the main conclusion; a subsidiary conclusion marked 'it follows that' sits in the middle. Test-takers drawn to the marker will select the intermediate paraphrase.
lr.stimulus: The recent decline of regional dialects in our country cannot be blamed, as some linguists have claimed, on broadcast media. Surveys show that the features of regional speech began to fade earliest in communities where residents routinely traveled to distant cities for work — long before television reached those areas. It follows that sustained face-to-face contact with speakers of other dialects, not exposure to a standardized broadcast voice, is what erodes regional speech. Whatever role television has played, it has been at most an accelerant of a process already underway.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Broadcast media cannot be held responsible for the recent decline of regional dialects in the country.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Face-to-face contact with speakers of other dialects, rather than exposure to broadcast speech, is what wears away regional speech.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regional speech features began to fade earliest in communities whose residents traveled to distant cities for work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Television has had no effect whatsoever on the decline of regional dialects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Broadcast media have slightly accelerated a process of dialect decline that was already underway.

explanations.correct: The first sentence is the author's main claim, rebutting the linguists. Everything that follows — the survey evidence, the 'it follows that' clause, and the concession about television — supports that rebuttal.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The subsidiary conclusion introduced by 'it follows that.' The prime trap.
explanations.C: A premise from the surveys.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author concedes television may have been an accelerant.
explanations.E: A concession the author makes in support of the main claim, not the main claim itself.

lr.difficultyReason: A historical stimulus where the final sentence is the main conclusion and an intermediate 'so' clause in the middle offers a competing paraphrase target.
lr.stimulus: It is often said that the invention of the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation. Yet the doctrinal disputes that drove the Reformation had circulated in manuscript form for nearly a century before Luther, and several earlier movements attracted mass followings without the aid of print. So print alone cannot explain why one set of reformist ideas succeeded where earlier ones failed. Historians who treat the press as the decisive cause are mistaking the medium for the message.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historians err when they treat the printing press as the decisive cause of the Protestant Reformation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The printing press by itself cannot account for the success of Reformation ideas over earlier reformist movements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Doctrinal disputes driving the Reformation had circulated in manuscript form for nearly a century before Luther.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The printing press played no role at all in the spread of Protestant ideas during the Reformation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The true cause of the Reformation's success was the content of its doctrines rather than the channels through which they spread.

explanations.correct: The last sentence is the author's target claim about historians; the manuscript premise and the 'so' intermediate both support it.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The intermediate conclusion marked by 'so' — the subsidiary-conclusion trap.
explanations.C: A historical premise used in support.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author denies the press was decisive, not that it mattered at all.
explanations.E: A different claim the author does not actually make; goes beyond the critique of historians.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument in which the main conclusion is the final sentence, left unmarked, and a 'thus' clause midway through yields an attractive subsidiary paraphrase.
lr.stimulus: City officials have defended their congestion-pricing plan on the grounds that it will reduce traffic. But when similar plans were introduced in other cities, downtown traffic did fall while overall regional traffic simply shifted to unpriced corridors nearby. Thus congestion pricing tends to relocate traffic rather than eliminate it. The plan, sold to residents as a remedy for the region's congestion problem, will not actually solve it.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The congestion-pricing plan will not, in fact, solve the region's congestion problem as its proponents claim.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congestion pricing typically redistributes traffic to nearby unpriced corridors rather than eliminating it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In other cities that adopted similar plans, downtown traffic fell even as overall regional traffic did not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The congestion-pricing plan will have no effect whatsoever on traffic patterns in the region.

choices.label: E
choices.text: City officials should never have proposed the congestion-pricing plan in the first place.

explanations.correct: The final sentence states the author's main claim about the plan; the experience from other cities and the 'thus' generalization both support it.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The intermediate conclusion marked by 'thus' — the subsidiary-conclusion trap.
explanations.C: A premise drawn from experience elsewhere.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author says the plan will shift traffic, not that it has no effect.
explanations.E: A prescriptive claim the author does not actually make.

lr.difficultyReason: An arts stimulus with an opposing view at the start and a 'thus' subsidiary conclusion in the middle. The author's main conclusion is the last sentence and carries no explicit marker.
lr.stimulus: Some critics claim that the value of a novel lies in the moral lessons it imparts to its readers. But great novels often portray morally repugnant characters without condemning them, and readers of such novels emerge not with neat lessons but with a richer sense of human complexity. Thus what readers take from the best fiction is something other than moral instruction. Judging novels by the lessons they teach is to measure them against a standard their authors never set out to meet.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evaluating novels by the moral lessons they offer holds them to a standard their authors did not set for themselves.

choices.label: B
choices.text: What readers gain from the best fiction is something other than moral instruction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many great novels depict morally repugnant characters without passing judgment on them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The value of a novel consists in the moral lessons it imparts to its readers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Novels that attempt to offer moral lessons cannot be considered great works of fiction.

explanations.correct: The last sentence is the author's main claim about how novels should be judged. The premise about repugnant characters and the 'thus' intermediate both support it.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The subsidiary conclusion marked by 'thus' — the primary trap.
explanations.C: A premise.
explanations.D: The opposing view the author is rebutting, not the author's own view.
explanations.E: Too strong — the author rejects moral instruction as the measure of a novel, not as compatible with greatness.

lr.difficultyReason: The main conclusion is embedded as a rebuttal to an opposing view introduced at the start, and is further qualified mid-argument. A subsidiary conclusion (about the regulators) is marked with 'thus,' setting up the classic intermediate-conclusion trap.
lr.stimulus: Some commentators have claimed that the recent decline in lake-trout populations in Lake Everest is attributable primarily to the warming of the lake's surface waters. But the decline began a full decade before any measurable warming occurred, and it has continued during years when surface temperatures have been stable. Thus, surface temperature cannot be the principal driver. The more likely culprit is nutrient runoff from surrounding farms, which regulators have so far been reluctant to address. Until that reluctance is overcome, any claim to have identified the true cause of the decline is premature at best.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surface warming is not the principal driver of the decline in lake-trout populations in Lake Everest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Until regulators are willing to confront the effects of nutrient runoff, claims to have identified the true cause of the trout decline are premature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nutrient runoff from surrounding farms is the principal driver of the decline in lake-trout populations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The decline in lake-trout populations began before any measurable warming of the lake's surface waters occurred.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Commentators who attribute the decline in lake-trout populations to surface warming are entirely mistaken about the relevant science.

explanations.correct: The final sentence states the author's overall verdict: until the regulatory reluctance is overcome, no one can justifiably claim to have identified the cause. Everything else in the argument — the rebuttal of the warming hypothesis, the alternative runoff hypothesis — is in service of that final epistemic claim, which preserves the author's hedging ('premature at best').
explanations.A: Paraphrases the subsidiary conclusion introduced with 'Thus.' It is a step in the argument, not its endpoint.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Overstates the author's claim about runoff — the author calls it 'the more likely culprit,' not the established cause.
explanations.D: Paraphrases a premise offered in support of the subsidiary conclusion.
explanations.E: Overstates the rebuttal; the author denies that warming is the principal driver, not that the commentators are wholly mistaken.

lr.difficultyReason: The main conclusion is a hedged normative claim framed as a rebuttal, cushioned by a concession to the opposing side. A subsidiary 'so' clause in the middle provides the classic trap.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Proponents of strict liability for accidental harms argue that it deters carelessness more effectively than fault-based rules. I grant that some forms of strict liability do produce that deterrent effect. But strict liability also penalizes those who could not reasonably have foreseen the harm they caused, so it fails to honor a basic moral distinction between the blameworthy and the merely unlucky. For that reason, the case for strict liability as a general principle of responsibility is less compelling than its proponents suppose — even if strict liability remains defensible in certain narrow domains.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Strict liability as a general principle of responsibility is less compelling than its proponents take it to be.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Strict liability fails to honor the moral distinction between those who are blameworthy and those who are merely unlucky.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some forms of strict liability produce a meaningful deterrent effect on careless behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Strict liability cannot be defended as a principle of responsibility in any domain whatsoever.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fault-based rules deter carelessness more effectively than strict liability does.

explanations.correct: The final sentence states the ethicist's overall judgment — that the case for strict liability 'as a general principle' is less compelling than its defenders think — and the hedging ('less compelling than,' 'even if...in certain narrow domains') is preserved. The earlier material supports this verdict.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Paraphrases the subsidiary conclusion that supports the main one.
explanations.C: Paraphrases the ethicist's concession to the opposing view.
explanations.D: Overstates the conclusion; the ethicist explicitly allows that strict liability is defensible in narrow domains.
explanations.E: Restates the opposing view the ethicist is rebutting, not the ethicist's own conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: The main conclusion opens the argument as a rebuttal, followed by two tiers of support — one of which is marked with 'therefore,' baiting readers toward the intermediate conclusion.
lr.stimulus: The prevailing claim that minimum-wage increases always reduce overall employment should be treated with skepticism. Several recent studies of regional wage hikes have found no detectable employment effect, and in sectors where demand for labor is relatively inelastic, small wage increases are typically absorbed through modest price adjustments rather than layoffs. Therefore, whatever employment losses do occur in such sectors tend to be concentrated in a narrow band of firms. Even granting that larger, sudden increases can produce sharper dislocations, the blanket claim that any wage floor above the market rate destroys jobs misstates what the evidence actually shows.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Employment losses from minimum-wage increases in inelastic-demand sectors tend to be concentrated in a narrow band of firms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim that minimum-wage increases always reduce overall employment is not well supported by the available evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larger, sudden minimum-wage increases can produce sharper labor-market dislocations than smaller ones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recent studies of regional wage hikes have found no detectable effect on employment.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any wage floor set above the prevailing market rate will destroy some number of jobs.

explanations.correct: The opening sentence — that the prevailing claim should be treated with skepticism — is the author's main conclusion, and the final sentence restates it more forcefully. The hedging ('should be treated with skepticism,' 'misstates what the evidence actually shows') is preserved.
explanations.A: Paraphrases the 'Therefore' intermediate conclusion, which supports the main point.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Paraphrases the concession the author grants before restating the main claim.
explanations.D: Restates a premise, not the conclusion.
explanations.E: Restates the prevailing claim that the author is rebutting.

lr.difficultyReason: Main conclusion is embedded between two subsidiary conclusions, each introduced by its own marker ('it follows,' 'thus'). The author's actual point is a hedged normative claim about judicial reasoning.
lr.stimulus: Legal theorist: Appellate judges frequently cite foreign precedent in domestic constitutional cases. Critics charge that this practice is improper because foreign rulings lack binding authority here. It follows that foreign precedent cannot settle a domestic constitutional question. But judges do not cite such precedent in order to settle questions; they cite it to illuminate the range of reasonable answers others have reached. Courts should therefore continue the practice, albeit with candid acknowledgment of its limited evidentiary weight. Thus, wholesale rejection of foreign precedent is unwarranted.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the legal theorist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Foreign precedent cannot, on its own, settle a domestic constitutional question.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Appellate courts should continue to cite foreign precedent, while candidly acknowledging its limited evidentiary weight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A complete rejection of the practice of citing foreign precedent is not warranted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Judges who cite foreign precedent do so to illuminate, not to settle, domestic constitutional questions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The practice of citing foreign precedent in domestic constitutional cases is improper because foreign rulings lack binding authority.

explanations.correct: The penultimate sentence — 'Courts should therefore continue the practice, albeit with candid acknowledgment of its limited evidentiary weight' — is the author's normative recommendation, with its hedging intact. The following 'Thus' sentence restates a negative corollary; the 'should continue' sentence is what everything supports.
explanations.A: Paraphrases the 'It follows' subsidiary conclusion, which the theorist grants to the critics as a setup.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Paraphrases the final 'Thus' sentence, which is a restated corollary of the main recommendation, not the recommendation itself.
explanations.D: Paraphrases a premise used to support the main recommendation.
