explanations.E: Restates the critics' position, which the theorist is rebutting.

lr.difficultyReason: The author rebuts a popular claim; the rebuttal is hedged and sandwiched between a concession and a middle subsidiary conclusion introduced with 'hence.' The opposing view is recognizable enough to trap readers.
lr.stimulus: Many observers hold that rapid advances in machine translation will soon render professional translators obsolete. It is true that current systems can produce passable renderings of routine commercial correspondence with remarkable speed. Hence, the market for low-stakes translation work has already contracted sharply. But literary, legal, and diplomatic translation require judgments about tone, register, and consequence that no present system reliably replicates. So the confident prediction that translators as a profession are on their way out looks, for the foreseeable future, to be overstated.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The market for low-stakes translation work has already contracted sharply as a result of advances in machine translation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Current machine-translation systems can produce passable renderings of routine commercial correspondence with remarkable speed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rapid advances in machine translation will soon render professional translators obsolete.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim that professional translators are on their way out appears, for the foreseeable future, to be overstated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: No machine-translation system will ever match human translators at handling tone, register, and consequence.

explanations.correct: The final sentence states the author's verdict and preserves the hedging — 'for the foreseeable future' and 'overstated.' Everything else, including the concession and the 'Hence' intermediate conclusion, supports this judgment.
explanations.A: Paraphrases the 'Hence' subsidiary conclusion.
explanations.B: Restates a premise the author concedes before making the main point.
explanations.C: Restates the view the author is rebutting.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Overstates the conclusion — the author claims the prediction is overstated 'for the foreseeable future,' not that machines will never match humans.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus presents a rebuttal of a popular linguistic claim, with the main conclusion tucked between an intermediate conclusion and a final restatement of what has been shown. Hedging ('largely,' 'on the whole') is load-bearing.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: A familiar claim holds that languages with rich case-marking systems permit freer word order than languages without them. Historical surveys, however, show that many richly inflected languages maintained rigid word orders for centuries, while some impoverished-morphology languages permit substantial reordering for discourse purposes. It follows that case-marking alone does not determine word-order flexibility. The popular claim, on the whole, conflates a statistical tendency with a grammatical necessity — and that is the error most worth correcting. The tendency itself is real enough; the necessity is not.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Case-marking alone does not determine how freely a language permits reordering of words.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The popular claim linking rich case-marking to free word order errs chiefly by treating a statistical tendency as a grammatical necessity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: There is no real statistical tendency for richly inflected languages to permit freer word order than impoverished-morphology languages.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some impoverished-morphology languages permit substantial word-order variation for discourse purposes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Historical surveys of word order provide the strongest available evidence against traditional typological claims.

explanations.correct: The fourth sentence identifies the author's real target — the conflation of tendency with necessity — and labels it 'the error most worth correcting.' The final sentence underscores the same point. The 'It follows' sentence is an intermediate step en route to this diagnosis.
explanations.A: Paraphrases the 'It follows' intermediate conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Overstates/contradicts the author, who explicitly grants the statistical tendency.
explanations.D: Restates a premise.
explanations.E: Not claimed — the linguist cites historical surveys but makes no general claim about their evidentiary primacy.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical stimulus framed as a rebuttal to a standard explanation, with a 'so' intermediate conclusion and a concession. The hedged final verdict is the main point.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Textbooks typically attribute the collapse of the late-Bronze-Age trading network to a single cause — the arrival of the so-called Sea Peoples. But archaeological records show that several of the network's major cities had already entered severe economic decline decades before any incursion. So these incursions cannot have initiated the collapse. I acknowledge that raiding may have accelerated an ongoing decay. Still, to treat the incursions as the principal cause, rather than as one among several converging pressures, is to misread the evidence.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The arrival of the Sea Peoples cannot have initiated the collapse of the late-Bronze-Age trading network.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a misreading of the evidence to treat the Sea Peoples' incursions as the principal cause of the collapse rather than as one among several converging pressures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several major cities in the late-Bronze-Age trading network had entered severe economic decline before any outside incursion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raiding by the Sea Peoples may have accelerated an ongoing decay of the late-Bronze-Age trading network.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Sea Peoples had essentially no effect on the trajectory of the late-Bronze-Age trading network.

explanations.correct: The final sentence delivers the historian's verdict, preserving the hedging that the incursions are one cause among several rather than none at all.
explanations.A: Paraphrases the 'So' intermediate conclusion, which supports but is not the main point.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Restates a premise.
explanations.D: Paraphrases the historian's concession.
explanations.E: Overstates the conclusion — the historian allows that raiding may have accelerated the decay.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy stimulus in which the main conclusion is a hedged procedural recommendation framed as a rebuttal to both sides of a debate. A 'therefore' sits mid-argument to bait readers.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: Advocates of the proposed housing tax credit insist it will make homeownership attainable for middle-income families; opponents claim it will chiefly enrich developers. The credit's actual effects will depend on market conditions that cannot be reliably forecast at this stage. Therefore, any confident prediction about who will benefit is unwarranted. What follows from this, however, is not that the credit should be rejected, but that it should be adopted only with a sunset provision requiring reevaluation within five years. A program whose effects we cannot yet forecast deserves neither enthusiastic endorsement nor outright rejection.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the policy analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Confident predictions about which group will benefit from the proposed housing tax credit are not warranted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The proposed housing tax credit should be adopted only with a sunset provision requiring reevaluation within five years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The proposed housing tax credit should be rejected until more reliable market forecasts become available.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The effects of the proposed housing tax credit cannot be reliably forecast at this stage.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Advocates of the housing tax credit have offered a more defensible position than its opponents have.

explanations.correct: The fourth sentence contains the analyst's affirmative recommendation — adopt with a sunset provision — and the final sentence underscores it. The hedging ('only with,' 'deserves neither...nor') is preserved.
explanations.A: Paraphrases the 'Therefore' intermediate conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Contradicts the analyst, who explicitly rejects outright rejection.
explanations.D: Restates a premise.
explanations.E: Not claimed — the analyst rebuts both sides' confidence, not one side's position.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts-criticism stimulus in which the main conclusion is stated at the outset as a rebuttal, qualified by concession, and then restated more narrowly. A 'thus' subsidiary conclusion creates the standard trap.
lr.stimulus: Museum curator: The recent trend of evaluating historical paintings primarily in terms of the social conditions under which they were produced yields, at best, a partial understanding of those works. Granted, such evaluations have usefully corrected earlier views that treated artworks as if they floated free of their times. Thus, the purely formalist approach of previous generations is no longer tenable. Yet reducing a painting to the circumstances of its making is no better; it simply substitutes one kind of blindness for another. A fuller account must, at the very least, weigh formal achievement alongside historical situation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the curator's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The purely formalist approach to evaluating historical paintings favored by previous generations is no longer tenable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Evaluating historical paintings primarily in terms of the social conditions of their production yields only a partial understanding of those works.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Earlier views treating artworks as if they floated free of their times have been usefully corrected by recent social-context approaches.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A fuller account of historical paintings should weigh formal achievement and historical situation equally.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Evaluating historical paintings in terms of their social conditions is no less misleading than evaluating them in purely formalist terms.

explanations.correct: The opening sentence states the curator's main conclusion with its hedging intact ('at best, a partial understanding'). The rest of the argument defends that claim through a concession, a 'Thus' subsidiary conclusion, and a proposed alternative.
explanations.A: Paraphrases the 'Thus' subsidiary conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Paraphrases the curator's concession to the social-context view.
explanations.D: Overstates the final clause — the curator says formal achievement and historical situation must 'at the very least' be weighed together, not weighed equally.
explanations.E: Overstates the comparison — the curator says reducing a painting to its making is 'no better,' meaning not an improvement over formalism, but the answer choice asserts strict equivalence across the board, a stronger claim than the argument supports.

lr.difficultyReason: Medical stimulus with two tiers of reasoning: an intermediate 'therefore' conclusion about the study's scope, and a hedged final recommendation framed as a rebuttal to enthusiastic press coverage.
lr.stimulus: Medical researcher: News coverage of our recent trial has suggested that a single daily dose of compound N substantially reduces the risk of recurrent stroke in the general population. In fact, our trial enrolled only patients who had already suffered two or more strokes within the prior year. Therefore, the results can speak, at most, to a narrow subset of high-risk patients. It would accordingly be premature — and, in light of compound N's known side effects, potentially harmful — to recommend the drug for broader preventive use before larger trials are completed.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It would be premature to recommend compound N for broad preventive use against recurrent stroke before larger trials are completed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The trial's results can speak, at most, to a narrow subset of high-risk stroke patients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: News coverage has overstated the implications of the recent trial of compound N for the general population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The trial of compound N enrolled only patients who had already suffered two or more strokes within the prior year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Compound N's known side effects make it unsuitable as a preventive treatment against recurrent stroke.

explanations.correct: The final sentence delivers the researcher's recommendation with its hedging preserved ('premature,' 'before larger trials are completed'). The earlier material, including the 'Therefore' subsidiary conclusion, supports this recommendation.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Paraphrases the 'Therefore' subsidiary conclusion, which supports the main recommendation.
explanations.C: Paraphrases the rebutted view in summary form — the researcher's point is not merely that coverage overstated things but what ought to be done in response.
explanations.D: Restates a premise.
explanations.E: Overstates the conclusion — the researcher cites side effects as one reason for caution, not as establishing unsuitability outright.

lr.difficultyReason: One clear move: the physician cites a counterexample to reject a universal claim. Only (C) names that operation; the other choices describe techniques the argument does not use.
lr.stimulus: Physician: Some commentators claim that all widely prescribed medications have been subjected to large-scale, long-term clinical trials before being approved. But this is simply not true. Acetylsalicylic acid, one of the most widely prescribed medications in the world, entered routine clinical use decades before any such trial was conducted on it.
lr.questionStem: The physician's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: appealing to an authority in order to settle a disputed empirical question

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two cases to show that they should be treated alike

choices.label: C
choices.text: offering a single instance as a counterexample to a universal claim

choices.label: D
choices.text: distinguishing between two senses of a key term used by an opposing side

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring a general pattern from a representative sample of cases

explanations.correct: The commentators claim every widely prescribed drug went through large-scale trials first. The physician cites one drug that did not, which is exactly how a counterexample refutes a universal claim.
explanations.A: No authority is cited; the physician offers a factual case, not an expert opinion.
explanations.B: Only one case is discussed; no second case is compared to it.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No term is parsed into distinct senses.
explanations.E: The physician is refuting a generalization, not building one from a sample.

lr.difficultyReason: Single move: the ethicist draws an analogy between two cases. Only (B) describes that operation.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Many people believe that it is wrong to break a promise to a friend but perfectly acceptable to break a promise to a stranger. But a promise to a stranger, like a promise to a friend, creates an expectation in the person to whom the promise is made. Since breaking a promise to a friend is wrong because it violates such an expectation, breaking a promise to a stranger must be wrong for exactly the same reason.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's reasoning proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing empirical evidence to overturn a widely held moral belief

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two cases in order to argue that they should be judged alike

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to a definition in order to show that a commonly used term is misapplied

choices.label: D
choices.text: pointing out an internal contradiction in an opposing position

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from a single instance to a broad moral principle

explanations.correct: The ethicist identifies a feature shared by both kinds of promises (creating an expectation) and uses the parallel to argue that the moral verdict must be the same. That is the structure of an argument by analogy.
explanations.A: No empirical evidence is introduced; the argument is conceptual.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No definition of any term is offered.
explanations.D: No contradiction within the opposing view is exposed.
explanations.E: The ethicist does not move from one instance to a broad principle; the principle about expectations is a premise, not a conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the economist applies a general principle to a specific case to predict an outcome. Only (D) names that operation.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Whenever a government imposes a price ceiling below the market-clearing price for a good, a shortage of that good inevitably develops. The proposed cap on rental prices in our city would set the legal maximum well below the current market rate. So we should expect a shortage of available rental units in our city to follow.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: appealing to a historical example in order to predict a future outcome

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting a policy proposal by identifying an unintended benefit

choices.label: C
choices.text: inferring a cause from an observed correlation between two variables

choices.label: D
choices.text: applying a general principle to a particular case in order to predict its consequences

choices.label: E
choices.text: distinguishing between short-term and long-term effects of a policy

explanations.correct: The first sentence states a general principle about price ceilings. The economist then shows that the proposed cap fits the description in that principle and concludes about this particular case.
explanations.A: No specific past episode is cited.
explanations.B: The argument predicts a negative effect (shortage), not a benefit.
explanations.C: No correlation is mentioned; the reasoning is principle-to-case, not statistical.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: No timeframe distinction is drawn.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the attorney appeals to the testimony of a recognized expert to support a factual claim. Only (A) describes that technique.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The opposing side claims that the fracture in the victim's wrist could have been caused by a simple fall, not by the defendant's grip. But Dr. Ayala, who has served as head of orthopedic trauma at the regional medical center for over twenty years, has testified that fractures of this precise pattern almost never result from falls and are nearly always the product of direct twisting force. So we should accept that the fracture was caused by a twisting grip rather than by a fall.
lr.questionStem: The attorney's reasoning proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing the testimony of a recognized expert to support a factual claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: offering a counterexample to a broad generalization advanced by opponents

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the present case and a previously decided one

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting an opposing claim by showing that it rests on a contradiction

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing from the absence of evidence to the truth of a positive claim

explanations.correct: The attorney's sole support for the conclusion is Dr. Ayala's credentials and testimony. That is a textbook appeal to expert authority.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No single case is cited against a universal claim; the argument relies on expert statements, not instances.
explanations.C: No previously decided case is introduced.
explanations.D: The opposing side's position is not shown to contradict itself.
explanations.E: The attorney relies on positive expert testimony, not on a gap in evidence.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the ecologist offers an alternative explanation for an observed decline. Only (E) describes that operation.
lr.stimulus: Ecologist: Some researchers have argued that the recent decline in the population of native songbirds in our region must be due to increased pesticide use on nearby farms. But there is another possibility that deserves serious consideration: over the same period, the population of feral house cats in the region has more than doubled, and feral cats are well-documented predators of songbirds.
lr.questionStem: The ecologist responds to the researchers' argument by

choices.label: A
choices.text: offering an alternative explanation for the phenomenon the researchers have identified

choices.label: B
choices.text: denying that the phenomenon the researchers describe has actually occurred

choices.label: C
choices.text: pointing out that the researchers' evidence is drawn from an unrepresentative sample

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that the researchers' conclusion contradicts another of their own claims

choices.label: E
choices.text: citing a counterexample that undermines the researchers' general principle

explanations.correct: The ecologist accepts that the songbird population has declined and that it needs explaining, but proposes cat predation as a rival cause to pesticide use. That is an alternative-explanation move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The ecologist does not dispute the decline.
explanations.C: Sample representativeness is not challenged.
explanations.D: No contradiction within the researchers' position is identified.
explanations.E: The ecologist does not refute a universal claim with a single instance; the move is to supply a competing cause.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the engineer distinguishes between two cases the critic has treated as equivalent. Only (C) names that technique.
lr.stimulus: Software engineer: Critics of our new messaging platform argue that because our earlier video-conferencing product suffered from frequent connection failures, the new platform will suffer from similar problems. But the earlier product relied on a centralized server architecture, whereas the new messaging platform uses a peer-to-peer architecture in which no single server's failure can disrupt communication. The critics' inference therefore does not go through.
lr.questionStem: The software engineer's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: rejecting a claim by showing that accepting it leads to absurd consequences

choices.label: B
choices.text: conceding a critic's premise while denying that the conclusion follows from it alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: distinguishing between two cases in order to show that a comparison between them is unwarranted

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing statistical evidence to undermine an anecdotal generalization

choices.label: E
choices.text: offering a definition that shows a key term has been misapplied

explanations.correct: The critics lump the two products together. The engineer's entire move is to identify a relevant difference in architecture that breaks the analogy the critics rely on.
explanations.A: No reductio-style absurdity is derived.
explanations.B: The engineer does not concede the critics' analogy; he rejects it outright by showing the cases differ.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No statistics are introduced.
explanations.E: No definitional move is made.

lr.difficultyReason: One clean move: the linguist appeals to a definition to argue that a term has been misapplied. Only (B) describes that technique.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Commentators in the popular press routinely describe the way young people use the word "literally" as a grammatical error. But a grammatical error is, by definition, a violation of the structural rules governing word order and inflection in a language. The pattern in question involves neither word order nor inflection; it is simply a shift in the meaning speakers attach to a particular word. So whatever else one may say about it, it is not a grammatical error.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's reasoning proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing empirical data about usage to refute a prescriptive claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: appealing to a definition in order to show that a term has been misapplied

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy to a parallel case in another language

choices.label: D
choices.text: identifying an unstated assumption in an opposing argument and rejecting it

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from several instances to a rule about a broad class of cases

explanations.correct: The linguist offers a definition of "grammatical error" and then argues that the phenomenon the commentators describe does not fall under it. That is an appeal to definition to show misapplication of a term.
explanations.A: No usage data or statistics are invoked.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No second language or parallel case appears.
explanations.D: The linguist doesn't surface a hidden assumption; she relies on the meaning of a term.
explanations.E: The argument moves from a definition to a case, not from instances to a rule.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the historian supports a general claim by generalizing from representative cases. Only (D) describes that operation.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Nearly every major technological transition in the past three centuries — the shift from water power to steam, from steam to electricity, and from electricity to electronics — was accompanied by a substantial, if temporary, rise in unemployment in the industries being displaced. Given this consistent pattern, it is reasonable to expect that major technological transitions in general will be accompanied by similar temporary unemployment.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: distinguishing between short-term effects and long-term effects of a single trend

choices.label: B
choices.text: applying a general principle to a particular case in order to predict an outcome

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting an opposing explanation by offering a competing one

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from a series of cases that exhibit a common pattern

choices.label: E
choices.text: citing an authoritative source to support a contested empirical claim

explanations.correct: The historian lists several past technological transitions, notes that each shared a feature, and on that basis extends the pattern to technological transitions as a class.
explanations.A: No long-term effect is contrasted with a short-term one; the argument is about the general pattern.
explanations.B: The move runs the other direction: from cases to a general expectation, not from a principle to a case.
explanations.C: No opposing explanation is rejected.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: No authority is cited.

lr.difficultyReason: One clear move: the policy analyst rejects a proposal by showing that the principle behind it leads to an absurd consequence. Only (E) describes that technique.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: The council has proposed requiring background checks before anyone may buy any item that could conceivably be used to harm another person. But the principle behind this proposal — that we should screen purchasers of anything that could conceivably be used to cause harm — would equally require us to screen buyers of kitchen knives, garden shears, heavy hammers, and even rolls of duct tape. Clearly, then, the proposal cannot be accepted as it stands.
lr.questionStem: The policy analyst's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: offering a counterexample that falsifies a universal empirical claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: appealing to expert testimony to cast doubt on a legislative proposal

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the proposal and a successful policy in another jurisdiction

choices.label: D
choices.text: distinguishing between two categories of items that the proposal fails to separate

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejecting a proposal by showing that the principle behind it has unacceptable consequences

explanations.correct: The analyst extracts the principle implicit in the proposal, shows that applying it consistently would require screening kitchen knives and duct tape, and treats that outcome as reason to reject the proposal. That is the structure of a reductio-style objection.
explanations.A: The claim being attacked is a policy recommendation, not a universal empirical claim.
explanations.B: No expert is cited.
explanations.C: No other jurisdiction's policy is introduced.
explanations.D: The analyst lumps items together to embarrass the proposal rather than distinguishing categories within it.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: One move: the curator draws a conclusion about an individual work from a general claim about a class it belongs to. Only (A) describes that technique.
lr.stimulus: Curator: Every painting produced by the Delft workshop during the 1660s was executed on a panel of oak imported from the Baltic region. The small landscape that has just been donated to our museum was, as our own laboratory has confirmed, produced by the Delft workshop during the 1660s. So the panel on which it was painted must be Baltic oak.
lr.questionStem: The curator's reasoning proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: applying a generalization about a class of objects to a particular member of that class

choices.label: B
choices.text: inferring a general claim about a class of objects from information about one of its members

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two objects in order to argue that they share a feature

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing expert testimony to resolve a disagreement about a historical fact

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejecting a hypothesis about an object by appealing to a counterexample

explanations.correct: The curator starts from a general statement about every painting produced by the Delft workshop in the 1660s, identifies the donated painting as a member of that class, and concludes that it must have the property the generalization ascribes to the class.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument runs in the opposite direction — from a generalization to a particular case.
explanations.C: No second object is introduced for comparison.
explanations.D: The laboratory's confirmation establishes membership in the class but is not used to resolve a dispute about a historical fact.
explanations.E: No hypothesis is being refuted; the curator is establishing, not refuting, a claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-move argument: the historian first undermines a general claim with a counterexample, then advances an alternative explanation. The correct answer must capture both moves; traps describe only one.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Many scholars maintain that the printing press was the principal cause of the Reformation's rapid spread across Europe. But the Waldensian movement spread widely across the same regions three centuries earlier, entirely by hand-copied manuscripts and itinerant preachers. A better explanation for the Reformation's reach, then, is the dense network of lay preachers already connecting parishes long before any press was built.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing a historical case that conflicts with a widely accepted explanation and then proposing a different explanation in its place

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two phenomena share a feature, they must share a cause

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting an explanation solely on the ground that its proponents have a vested interest in defending it

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that an explanation is self-contradictory and therefore cannot be true

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to expert consensus in order to settle a disputed historical question

explanations.correct: The historian invokes the Waldensian movement as a counterexample that undercuts the printing-press explanation, then offers the preacher-network as an alternative. A captures both moves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No shared-feature-to-shared-cause inference is made; the Waldensian case is used against an explanation, not to infer causal identity.
explanations.C: The historian never attacks the motives of the scholars, only their explanation.
explanations.D: The printing-press explanation is shown to be insufficient, not internally contradictory.
explanations.E: No expert consensus is cited; the historian pushes back against the prevailing view.

lr.difficultyReason: The physician both questions whether the reported data actually support a causal claim and offers a competing mechanism. Traps describe only the critique or only the alternative.
lr.stimulus:
Columnist: A recent study reports that adults who take a daily multivitamin have fewer colds per year than those who do not, and concludes that the multivitamin strengthens the immune response.
Physician: The study surveyed only people who already took multivitamins voluntarily. Such people also tend to exercise, sleep more regularly, and eat more fresh produce. The apparent benefit is more plausibly attributed to those habits than to the vitamin itself.
lr.questionStem: The physician responds to the columnist by

choices.label: A
choices.text: identifying a feature of the study's sample that undermines its causal conclusion and offering an alternative explanation for the reported correlation

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that the study's authors have falsified their data in order to promote a product

choices.label: C
choices.text: denying that any correlation between multivitamin use and cold frequency exists

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that the columnist's conclusion rests on an ambiguous definition of 'immune response'

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from personal clinical experience to reject a finding supported by quantitative research

explanations.correct: The physician points to a sampling problem (self-selection) that weakens the causal claim and then supplies a rival cause. Both moves are captured by A.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No accusation of fabrication is made.
explanations.C: The correlation itself is accepted; what is challenged is the causal reading.
explanations.D: No ambiguity in terminology is raised.
explanations.E: The physician cites patterns in the study population, not personal clinical anecdotes.

lr.difficultyReason: The ethicist uses a hypothetical variant to show that an opposing principle produces an unacceptable verdict, then endorses a rival principle. Traps isolate only the hypothetical or only the endorsement.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Some argue that any act done to produce a greater overall good is thereby justified. But suppose a surgeon could save five patients by harvesting the organs of one unwilling donor who walked into the clinic. Few would accept that the surgeon acts rightly. A more adequate principle, then, is that even acts that maximize good are impermissible when they treat a person merely as a resource.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: presenting a hypothetical case whose implications conflict with one principle and offering a revised principle that better accommodates them

choices.label: B
choices.text: defending a familiar moral principle by deducing it from more basic axioms

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between medical ethics and ordinary commercial transactions

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing statistical evidence about public attitudes toward organ donation

choices.label: E
choices.text: claiming that a principle is false because it is not universally followed

explanations.correct: The surgeon hypothetical functions as a counterexample to the maximizing-good principle; the ethicist then proposes a revised principle. A captures this combined maneuver.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: There is no deduction from more basic axioms; the argument is driven by a counterexample.
explanations.C: No analogy with commerce is drawn.
explanations.D: No statistics are invoked; the ethicist appeals to what 'few would accept,' not polling data.
explanations.E: The principle is rejected as producing wrong verdicts, not as being unfollowed in practice.

lr.difficultyReason: The economist both denies a causal inference drawn from a correlation and supplies a mechanism that fits the data equally well. Traps describe only the denial or only the alternative.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Commentators frequently claim that minimum-wage increases cause long-term unemployment among teenagers, pointing to the fact that teenage joblessness has risen in several states shortly after such increases. But teenage labor-force participation in those same states declined as school enrollment grew, which on its own would raise measured unemployment. The rise in joblessness is better explained by shifting educational patterns than by the wage policy.
lr.questionStem: The economist's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: challenges a causal claim about an observed trend by identifying a separate factor that would produce the same trend

choices.label: B
choices.text: concedes that a policy had the effects attributed to it, but argues that those effects were worth the cost

choices.label: C
choices.text: appeals to a general economic principle and applies it to a specific policy question

choices.label: D
choices.text: argues that because a policy has one beneficial effect, it must have no harmful effects

choices.label: E
choices.text: attacks a conclusion by questioning the credentials of those who proposed it

explanations.correct: The economist concedes the rise in joblessness but denies the causal link to minimum-wage policy by pointing to a confounding factor (enrollment-driven drops in participation) that would yield the same statistic. A captures this technique.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No concession about minimum-wage effects is made; the economist denies those effects.
explanations.C: No general principle is cited or applied; the argument works through a specific competing cause.
explanations.D: The economist does not argue that minimum-wage policy is wholly benign.
explanations.E: No ad hominem is offered.

lr.difficultyReason: The law professor first distinguishes two kinds of cases, then applies the distinction to defeat a proposed rule. Traps describe only the distinction or only the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Law professor: It is sometimes said that judges should never rely on unpublished decisions. But a judge may rely on an unpublished decision either as binding precedent or merely as persuasive reasoning. When treated as binding, the decision controls outcomes other courts have never had a chance to scrutinize; when treated as persuasive, it is simply one more source of argument. So the blanket prohibition is unwarranted: only reliance of the first kind raises the concerns critics actually cite.
lr.questionStem: The law professor's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing a distinction between two uses of a practice and arguing that the objection to the practice applies only to one of them

choices.label: B
choices.text: showing that a proposed rule would produce an outcome the critics themselves would condemn

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting a rule on the ground that it has never been adopted in any jurisdiction

choices.label: D
choices.text: identifying an ambiguity in a legal term and concluding that the term should be abandoned

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to an analogy between legal practice and scientific experimentation

explanations.correct: The professor separates 'binding' from 'persuasive' reliance, then argues the critics' worry applies only to the first, so a blanket ban is too broad. A captures both moves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No reductio targeting critics is developed; the professor analyzes the critics' concern rather than turning it on them.
explanations.C: Adoption history is not cited.
explanations.D: The term 'unpublished decision' is not treated as ambiguous; two ways of relying on it are distinguished.
explanations.E: No analogy to science is made.

lr.difficultyReason: The ecologist concedes a premise of the opposing view but argues it does not support the recommended conclusion, and then proposes a different policy consistent with the same evidence.
lr.stimulus: Ecologist: Conservationists urge that, since the population of the spotted salamander has fallen sharply across the region, logging in the adjacent forest should be halted. It is true that the population has fallen. But the decline tracks almost perfectly with the loss of breeding pools well away from logging sites. Limiting logging would do little for the salamander; restoring those pools would do a great deal more.
lr.questionStem: The ecologist's reasoning does which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepts the factual claim on which an argument is based but denies that it supports the recommended policy, and advances a different policy better supported by the same evidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: disputes the reliability of data cited by an opponent and proposes collecting better data before any policy is set

choices.label: C
choices.text: argues that a proposed policy, though well-intentioned, would actually accelerate the problem it aims to solve

choices.label: D
choices.text: concludes that because two policies address the same problem, both should be implemented simultaneously

choices.label: E
choices.text: derives a general principle about species decline from a single local case

explanations.correct: The ecologist grants the decline but denies that logging restrictions are warranted by it, substituting pool restoration. A captures concede-then-redirect.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The population data are accepted, not impugned.
explanations.C: There is no claim that halting logging would worsen matters.
explanations.D: The argument rejects one policy in favor of another, not both.
explanations.E: No general principle about species decline is offered; the reasoning is specific to this case.

lr.difficultyReason: The engineer rejects an analogy as misleading and replaces it with a more apt one. Traps isolate one half of the move or invert the direction.
lr.stimulus: Engineer: Critics compare self-driving cars to commercial aircraft, claiming that, since aviation autopilot has had decades to mature, self-driving systems will require equally long timelines before they are safe. But aircraft operate in sparse, highly regulated airspace, while cars share crowded roads with unpredictable human drivers. A closer comparison is to industrial robotics, where machines learned to work safely alongside people only through extensive real-world co-operation, not merely through internal refinement.
lr.questionStem: The engineer's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: rejecting a comparison on the basis of a relevant dissimilarity and substituting a different comparison that the engineer regards as more apt

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two technologies share a feature, predictions about one apply to the other

choices.label: C
choices.text: claiming that critics of self-driving cars have a financial stake in delaying their deployment

choices.label: D
choices.text: using a mathematical model of risk to establish a precise timeline

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding that self-driving cars are unsafe and arguing that they should be banned

explanations.correct: The engineer points out that aviation and driving environments differ in ways that break the analogy, then proposes industrial robotics as a better match. A captures the replace-analogy technique.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument denies that aviation and cars share the relevant features; it does not transfer predictions on that basis.
explanations.C: No ad hominem is made.
explanations.D: No quantitative model is introduced.
explanations.E: The engineer implies self-driving cars can become safe, not that they should be banned.

lr.difficultyReason: The linguist disputes a definition-based claim by producing a counterexample and then offers a refined criterion. Both moves must be captured; traps name only one.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Some grammarians define a 'pidgin' as any simplified language formed from contact between speakers of different tongues. On that definition, the contact variety used by sign-language interpreters would count as a pidgin, yet it plainly is not. What distinguishes a pidgin is not simplification but the lack of native speakers for whom it is a first language.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: offering a case that a proposed definition wrongly classifies and then introducing a different criterion that avoids the misclassification

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because a term is used loosely in everyday speech, it should not be defined at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: establishing a general claim about language change from a single example

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that two definitions of a term are logically equivalent

choices.label: E
choices.text: conceding a definition but arguing that it applies to fewer cases than its proponents claim

explanations.correct: The interpreter example is offered as a misclassified case under the simplification-based definition; the linguist then supplies the native-speaker criterion. A captures both moves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The argument does not say the term should go undefined; it offers a better definition.
explanations.C: No general claim about language change is drawn.
explanations.D: Two definitions are contrasted, not shown to be equivalent.
explanations.E: The original definition is rejected as wrong, not accepted with narrower scope.

lr.difficultyReason: The curator critiques a general aesthetic principle by showing a valued work would be excluded under it, then reformulates the principle. Traps describe only the reductio-like move or only the reformulation.
lr.stimulus: Curator: The dean argues that, because good art must reward close visual attention, the museum should collect only figurative painting. But the best works of mid-century color-field abstraction reward prolonged attention every bit as fully as figurative works, and excluding them would impoverish our collection. The dean's principle is sound in its emphasis on sustained attention, but it should be framed in terms of rewarding attention, not in terms of depicting recognizable subjects.
lr.questionStem: The curator's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: arguing that a proposed criterion would exclude works it ought to include, and then restating the criterion in a way that covers them

choices.label: B
choices.text: defending one school of painting by attacking the artistic credentials of another

choices.label: C
choices.text: showing that the dean's principle rests on a false historical claim about mid-century art

choices.label: D
choices.text: arguing that aesthetic principles cannot be formulated in general terms

choices.label: E
choices.text: deriving a new principle by combining two principles already accepted by the dean

explanations.correct: The curator shows that figurative-only collecting would wrongly exclude color-field works, then reframes the principle around sustained attention rather than recognizable subjects. A captures both moves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The curator does not attack figurative painting's credentials; it argues for a broader inclusion.
explanations.C: No historical falsehood is alleged against the dean.
explanations.D: The curator offers a revised general principle, not a rejection of general principles.
explanations.E: Only one principle is in play, not a combination of two.

lr.difficultyReason: The analyst undermines a policy recommendation by showing its premise does not fit the relevant population, and then identifies a subgroup for which a different recommendation would follow.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: The mayor proposes free citywide transit on the ground that free transit in several small towns has increased ridership and cut car use. But those towns had little car traffic to begin with; residents walked or biked for most trips. In a dense city where most commuters already drive long distances, free transit is unlikely to pull drivers out of their cars. If the aim is reducing car use, congestion pricing in the downtown core, where driving is a real choice rather than a necessity, is a better lever.
lr.questionStem: The analyst's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: arguing that evidence supporting a proposal does not transfer to the relevant setting, and advocating a different measure targeted at conditions in that setting

choices.label: B
choices.text: conceding that free transit would reduce car use, but arguing that it would cost more than the city can afford

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to the preferences of a majority of residents to reject a mayoral proposal

choices.label: D
choices.text: assuming that because a policy has worked in one large city, it will work in any large city

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that a policy should be judged solely by whether it eliminates car use entirely

explanations.correct: The analyst argues that the small-town evidence fails to apply to a dense, car-dependent city, and then advocates congestion pricing in the relevant subsetting. A captures the transferability critique plus targeted alternative.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Cost is never mentioned; transferability of effects is the issue.
explanations.C: No appeal to majority preferences is made.
explanations.D: The analyst denies a generalization across settings rather than relying on one.
explanations.E: The analyst treats 'reducing car use' as the aim, not 'eliminating' it.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-move argument with an embedded concession: the jurist grants a premise for the sake of argument, derives an unacceptable verdict from it, and then uses the contradiction to reject the premise. Traps describe only one or two of the moves, or invert the concession as a genuine endorsement.
lr.stimulus: Jurist: Defenders of mandatory minimum sentences contend that any policy which reduces average sentencing disparity across judges is thereby just. Grant, for the moment, that this standard is correct. It would then follow that a statute requiring every convicted defendant, regardless of offense, to receive the same five-year term would be a model of justice, since disparity would be eliminated entirely. But such a statute would plainly be monstrous. The defenders' standard must therefore be mistaken.
lr.questionStem: The jurist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: granting an opposing standard for the sake of argument, deriving a verdict from it that is manifestly unacceptable, and concluding on that basis that the standard is in error

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting an opposing standard by showing that its defenders are motivated by considerations other than justice

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because a standard has been applied inconsistently, it must be replaced with a more precise formulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: drawing an analogy between sentencing disparity and other forms of legal inequality in order to support an opposing standard

choices.label: E
choices.text: establishing a standard of justice by eliminating each of the rival standards in turn

explanations.correct: The jurist concedes the disparity-reduction standard arguendo, derives the uniform-five-year consequence, labels that consequence monstrous, and treats the contradiction as grounds to reject the standard. A names all three moves in order.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The jurist never impugns defenders' motives; the argument is about entailments, not interests.
explanations.C: No claim is made that the standard has been inconsistently applied; it is rejected on entailment grounds.
explanations.D: No analogy to other forms of legal inequality is drawn, and the analogy would cut the wrong way.
explanations.E: Only one rival standard is in view, and no process of elimination across multiple candidates is run.

lr.difficultyReason: The economist draws an analogy, flags a disanalogy in the next breath, and proposes a refined principle grounded in that very disanalogy. Students must track all three beats; traps stop after the analogy or treat the disanalogy as a rejection of the original comparison rather than a refinement.
lr.stimulus: Economist: A central bank's inflation target is often compared to a thermostat setting: adjust the dial, and the temperature moves toward it. The comparison is a useful first pass, since expectations and interest-rate moves do anchor prices over the long run. But a thermostat works against a simple, passive medium, whereas prices are set by agents who anticipate the bank's own future moves. A more adequate rule, therefore, would direct the bank not simply to set a target but to commit credibly to a path of future policy, since only such a commitment can shape the expectations that a passive medium lacks.
lr.questionStem: The economist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two phenomena, noting a feature that limits the analogy's force, and proposing a refined principle grounded in the feature that marks the disanalogy

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting a familiar analogy outright on the ground that analogies cannot settle empirical questions

choices.label: C
choices.text: defending a controversial policy by showing that alternatives to it have failed when tried

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring, from the fact that two systems share one feature, that they must share all of their important features

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the consensus of central bankers to resolve a theoretical dispute about inflation targeting

explanations.correct: The thermostat analogy is affirmed as a useful first pass; the passive-medium disanalogy is then flagged; the refined rule (commit to a path, not just a target) is built on the expectations feature that is the very point of disanalogy.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The analogy is not rejected outright; it is refined. And no general claim about analogies is made.
explanations.C: No alternative policy is said to have failed when tried; the argument is conceptual.
explanations.D: The economist highlights a difference between the systems, not a shared-feature inference.
explanations.E: No appeal to consensus is made.

lr.difficultyReason: A dialogue in which the second speaker accepts a premise for argument's sake, extracts a further commitment that clashes with the first speaker's own practice, and uses the clash to undercut the first speaker's stance. Traps invert the role of the concession or describe only the final accusation.
lr.stimulus:
Critic: Any musical work whose score is not fixed note-for-note is an inferior composition, since genuine compositions must be reproducible exactly.
Composer: Grant that reproducibility is the measure of genuine composition. Then the great jazz standards, whose charts leave melodic and harmonic improvisation to the performer, would have to be dismissed as inferior; so would the improvised passages built into the cadenzas of Mozart's own concertos, which you otherwise praise as paradigms of composition. Your own judgments therefore cannot survive the standard you have just endorsed.
lr.questionStem: The composer responds to the critic by

choices.label: A
choices.text: provisionally accepting the critic's standard, drawing out consequences that conflict with judgments the critic elsewhere accepts, and concluding that the critic's position is untenable as it stands

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting the critic's standard by offering a single counterexample drawn from a genre the critic has no familiarity with

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because the critic's standard is widely disputed among musicologists, it should not be accepted

choices.label: D
choices.text: claiming that the critic's standard presupposes a definition of 'composition' that the composer denies

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the authority of Mozart in order to settle a question about the nature of improvisation

explanations.correct: The composer says 'grant that reproducibility is the measure,' follows out what that would entail (dismissing jazz standards and Mozart cadenzas), and points out that the critic's own praise for those works conflicts with the entailment.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The composer does not reject the standard by an unrelated counterexample; the force comes from the critic's own judgments, not from unfamiliar genres.
explanations.C: No claim about dispute among musicologists is made.
explanations.D: No ambiguity or redefinition of 'composition' is invoked; the standard is taken as given.
explanations.E: Mozart is cited as an example the critic already praises, not as an authority to settle a theoretical question.

lr.difficultyReason: The linguist identifies a regularity, acknowledges apparent exceptions, and reframes the regularity as a statistical tendency whose exceptions actually confirm the proposed mechanism. Traps describe the exception-handling as abandonment or as a shared-feature causal inference.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Across unrelated languages, words for close kin — 'mother,' 'father,' 'baby' — tend to contain the simplest consonants infants can produce. Some point to Georgian 'deda' for mother and 'mama' for father as evidence that the pattern is accidental. But those are precisely the sounds infants produce; the Georgian data show only that which simple consonant gets mapped to which parent varies, not that simple consonants fail to dominate. The regularity, then, is best understood not as a universal law but as a statistical tendency whose very 'exceptions' still fall inside its mechanism.
lr.questionStem: The linguist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: identifying a cross-linguistic regularity, addressing data that appear to contradict it, and reformulating the regularity in a way that the seeming counterevidence in fact supports

choices.label: B
choices.text: concluding that because two languages share a surface feature they must be genealogically related

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting a statistical tendency on the ground that it admits of exceptions

choices.label: D
choices.text: defending a universal law by dismissing apparent counterexamples as defective data

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that because infants cannot produce complex consonants, no language contains complex consonants in kin terms

explanations.correct: Regularity (simple consonants for kin terms) → apparent counterevidence (Georgian 'deda'/'mama') → reformulation (statistical tendency whose mechanism accommodates the Georgian mapping). A captures the three moves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No claim of genealogical relatedness is made; the argument is typological, not historical.
explanations.C: The tendency is reformulated, not rejected; the linguist treats the Georgian case as inside the mechanism.
explanations.D: The linguist explicitly declines to treat the pattern as a universal law and does not dismiss the Georgian data as defective.
explanations.E: This overgeneralizes wildly; the linguist's claim is about kin terms, not all vocabulary.

lr.difficultyReason: Dialogue in which the respondent draws an analogy, acknowledges its limits, and proposes a refined policy grounded in the point of disanalogy. Traps collapse the argument to the analogy alone or describe only the policy recommendation.
lr.stimulus:
Minister: Critics argue that a carbon tax would be as intrusive on household budgets as a tax on bread.
Economist: The comparison illuminates one thing correctly — both taxes raise the sticker price of something households buy every week. But bread has no close substitute, while carbon-intensive energy does: households can shift to transit, insulation, or off-peak usage. A carbon tax's fairness therefore depends on a feature the bread analogy cannot reach: whether the revenue is rebated in ways that let households act on the substitutes the tax newly makes cheaper by comparison.
lr.questionStem: The economist responds to the minister by

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepting the limited force of a proposed analogy, identifying a feature on which the two cases diverge, and building a policy criterion around the feature that marks the divergence

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismissing an analogy as entirely without merit because the two items taxed are not physically similar

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because carbon taxes have been endorsed by economists, the minister's critics must be mistaken

choices.label: D
choices.text: attempting to show that a carbon tax is not really a tax at all, on the ground that its revenues can be rebated

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from the experience of a single jurisdiction to conclusions about carbon taxes in general

explanations.correct: The economist grants one thing the analogy gets right (sticker-price impact), names the substitution disanalogy, and builds the fairness criterion (rebate structure) on the substitution feature that the bread analogy lacks.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The analogy is partly credited, not dismissed wholesale; physical similarity is never the point.
explanations.C: No appeal to the endorsement of economists is made.
explanations.D: The economist never denies that a carbon tax is a tax; the rebate feature is invoked as a fairness condition, not a redefinition.
explanations.E: No single jurisdiction's experience is cited.

lr.difficultyReason: The biologist grants an inferential rule, applies it to a case where it yields an accepted verdict, and then applies the same rule to a disputed case to argue the verdict there must also hold. The three-move pattern (grant rule, test on easy case, extend to hard case) is dense; traps describe only the extension.
lr.stimulus: Biologist: Conservation policy rests, most agree, on the principle that when removing a species from an ecosystem leads to cascading collapse, that species is ecologically essential. On that principle, sea otters in North Pacific kelp forests are plainly essential: when they were hunted out, kelp beds collapsed as urchin populations exploded. The same reasoning, then, applies to beavers in continental river systems: wherever beavers have been eradicated, wetland habitat has dwindled and downstream flows have become erratic. Beavers, too, must be counted ecologically essential.
lr.questionStem: The biologist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: invoking a widely accepted principle, confirming its application in an uncontroversial case, and extending the same reasoning to a further case to establish a parallel conclusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two species share a habitat type, they must play the same ecological role

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting the principle that cascading collapse marks ecological essentiality, on the ground that the sea otter case is an outlier

choices.label: D
choices.text: defending a policy recommendation by appealing to the personal expertise of field biologists

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that since no ecosystem has remained unchanged after species loss, every species is ecologically essential

explanations.correct: Move 1: grant the cascading-collapse principle; Move 2: confirm it applies to sea otters; Move 3: extend the same application to beavers. A describes this three-step pattern.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Shared habitat type is not the basis of the inference; cascading collapse is.
explanations.C: The principle is invoked and applied, not rejected.
explanations.D: No appeal to personal expertise is made; the principle and its applications carry the argument.
explanations.E: The biologist's claim is about species whose removal triggers cascades, not about every species.

lr.difficultyReason: A dialogue in which the respondent accepts an empirical correlation, points out that it fits two rival causal structures equally well, and proposes a test designed to separate them. Traps ignore the middle move or describe the test as itself the conclusion.
lr.stimulus:
Researcher: Users of our messaging app who enable two-factor authentication report 30 percent fewer account compromises. Security advocates cite this as evidence that two-factor authentication reduces compromise rates.
Engineer: The correlation is real, but it is just as consistent with a different hypothesis: security-conscious users, who were already less likely to be compromised, are the ones most willing to turn the feature on. To choose between the two explanations, we should compare compromise rates for users who were randomly assigned to receive the feature by default versus those assigned to the opt-in flow; only that comparison isolates the feature itself from the kind of user who adopts it.
lr.questionStem: The engineer responds to the researcher by

choices.label: A
choices.text: granting the correlation at issue, noting that a rival causal hypothesis accounts for it equally well, and proposing a further comparison designed to discriminate between the two hypotheses

choices.label: B
choices.text: denying that the reported correlation exists in the underlying data at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because security-conscious users are unrepresentative, no conclusions about messaging app security are possible

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting two-factor authentication on the ground that security advocates have a financial interest in promoting it

choices.label: E
choices.text: concluding that two-factor authentication does not reduce compromises, because self-selection is a known confounder

explanations.correct: The engineer accepts the correlation, names a selection-based rival hypothesis, and proposes a randomized-assignment comparison that would separate the two. The correct description names all three beats.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The correlation is explicitly granted.
explanations.C: No general skepticism about messaging-app conclusions is advanced.
explanations.D: No claim about advocates' financial interests is made.
explanations.E: The engineer does not conclude that two-factor authentication fails; a test is proposed, not a verdict.

lr.difficultyReason: The ethicist distinguishes two readings of a principle, shows that the strong reading collapses under a variant case, and endorses the weaker reading as the one that survives. Three moves (distinction, reductio, endorsement) that traps collapse into one.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: When we say a physician ought not deceive her patient, the claim might mean either that no deception is ever permissible or that deception is impermissible absent a compelling reason. Suppose a patient, delirious and momentarily convinced that a benign reflection is an intruder, asks whether anyone else is in the room; suppose too that a truthful 'no' would only deepen the terror, while a brief reassurance would allow sedation and recovery. Few would condemn the reassurance. The strong reading therefore fails the case, and the weaker reading — deception requires a compelling reason, which is present here — is the one that survives.
lr.questionStem: The ethicist's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: distinguishing two readings of a principle, showing that the stronger reading is defeated by a test case, and endorsing the weaker reading because it accommodates that case

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because physicians enjoy public trust, any deception by them is especially blameworthy

choices.label: C
choices.text: defending the claim that deception is never permissible by dismissing alleged counterexamples as fabricated

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from the ethicist's own clinical experience to a universal rule about patient communication

choices.label: E
choices.text: appealing to the fact that deception sometimes succeeds in order to show that it is sometimes required

explanations.correct: Two readings are distinguished; the strong reading is refuted by the delirium case; the weaker reading is endorsed because it accommodates the case. A describes all three moves in order.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Physician trust is never invoked; the argument is about which reading of the principle survives.
explanations.C: The strong reading is not defended — it is rejected. And the case is not dismissed.
explanations.D: No clinical experience is cited; the case is hypothetical.
explanations.E: The argument does not infer from success to requirement; it distinguishes two readings.

lr.difficultyReason: The historian acknowledges a correlation, argues that it fails to establish causation because of a confound, and proposes a narrower claim that the evidence does support. Three moves packed tightly; traps describe the reduction as outright rejection.
lr.stimulus: Historian: It is often said that the widespread adoption of mechanized looms caused the decline of the cottage textile industry in nineteenth-century England. The timing fits — looms spread as cottage weaving contracted. But railway construction spread on the same timetable, and rail access made long-distance grain markets, not mechanized textiles, the more immediate threat to cottage wages. The available evidence supports the weaker claim that mechanized looms contributed to the decline, not the stronger claim that they caused it.
lr.questionStem: The historian's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: conceding that a correlation holds between two phenomena, identifying a confounding development that undermines a causal reading, and retreating to a weaker claim that the evidence can bear

choices.label: B
choices.text: arguing that because two developments occurred on the same timetable, they must share a common cause

choices.label: C
choices.text: denying that mechanized looms had any effect on cottage textile wages

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting a causal claim solely on the ground that its defenders have failed to provide a plausible mechanism

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing that since the railway was more consequential, the mechanized loom must have been wholly irrelevant to the cottage industry's decline

explanations.correct: Timing correlation is granted; the railway/grain-market confound is named; the claim is softened from 'caused' to 'contributed to.' All three beats are covered by A.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No shared-cause inference is drawn from shared timing.
explanations.C: The historian affirms looms contributed to the decline, not that their effect was zero.
explanations.D: The causal claim is not rejected for lack of mechanism; it is weakened because of the confound.
explanations.E: The argument ends with 'contributed to,' not with 'wholly irrelevant.'

lr.difficultyReason: Dialogue in which the respondent accepts a study's finding for argument's sake, derives a prediction that the data in fact fail to show, and concludes that the proposed mechanism cannot be what the original speaker claims. Three moves embedded in doctor's voice; traps invert the roles or attribute motives.
lr.stimulus:
Pharmacologist: A recent trial shows that patients given drug X experience 20 percent fewer migraine days per month than those given placebo. The authors infer that the drug suppresses the vascular mechanism they hypothesize to cause migraines.
Physician: Grant for the moment that the drug does suppress that vascular mechanism. If so, patients who experience migraines through that mechanism should respond robustly, while those whose migraines are known to arise from other mechanisms should not. But the trial reports a uniform effect across both subgroups. The finding is therefore not evidence for the mechanism the authors name; at most, it is evidence that the drug helps by some route the trial does not distinguish.
lr.questionStem: The physician responds to the pharmacologist by

choices.label: A
choices.text: accepting a proposed mechanism for the sake of argument, deriving a pattern the trial should have shown if the mechanism were operative, and concluding, because the pattern is absent, that the trial does not support the mechanism

choices.label: B
choices.text: denying that drug X reduces migraine days at all, on the ground that the trial's controls were inadequate

choices.label: C
choices.text: arguing that because the trial's authors stand to benefit from the drug's approval, their conclusions should be dismissed

choices.label: D
choices.text: inferring from the uniform effect across subgroups that drug X operates through the very vascular mechanism the authors describe

choices.label: E
choices.text: claiming that the trial is worthless because it used a placebo rather than an active comparator

explanations.correct: The physician grants the vascular mechanism arguendo, predicts differential subgroup response as a consequence, and notes that the uniform subgroup effect defeats the prediction — so the trial fails to support that mechanism.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The physician never denies the drug's overall effect.
explanations.C: No claim about authors' interests is made.
explanations.D: This reverses the physician's point; uniform subgroup effect is the reason the mechanism is not supported, not why it is.
explanations.E: The comparator design is never challenged; the issue is the mechanism inference.

lr.difficultyReason: Three related factual observations with one clear hedged inference. Distractors are either out-of-scope or overreach into 'all'/'only' territory.
lr.stimulus: A recent survey of primary-care physicians in Valbrook found that those who had taken a one-week course on nutrition counseling were, on average, twice as likely as their colleagues to discuss diet during routine checkups. The survey also found that patients of the course-trained physicians reported making healthier food choices more often than patients of other physicians. No other differences between the two groups of physicians were noted.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every patient whose physician took the nutrition course now eats a healthier diet than before.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least some patients make healthier food choices after their physicians discuss diet with them during checkups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Physicians who take continuing-education courses are generally more competent than those who do not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nutrition counseling is the most effective tool a primary-care physician has for improving patient health.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients in Valbrook were less healthy than patients elsewhere before the nutrition course was offered.

explanations.correct: The stimulus links two facts — course-trained physicians discuss diet more often, and their patients report healthier choices more often. The most defensible hedged inference is that at least some patients' improved choices follow from such discussions.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'every patient' is not supported; the stimulus speaks in averages.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Out of scope — the stimulus is about one specific course, not continuing education generally.
explanations.D: Too strong and out of scope — no comparison is made to other tools.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no claim is made about Valbrook patients' prior health.

lr.difficultyReason: Two observational facts about a wetland; correct answer is a modest inference. Traps are overreach and opposite-direction.
lr.stimulus: Biologists studying the Oster Marsh report that populations of the marsh wren have grown substantially in each of the past five years. Over the same period, the marsh's native cattail reeds, in which marsh wrens build their nests, have expanded to cover roughly 30 percent more of the marsh than they did before. No other major changes to the marsh's vegetation or water levels have been recorded.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The marsh wren population would not have grown at all without the expansion of cattail reeds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any marsh with expanding cattail reeds will see a rise in marsh wren populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The expansion of cattail reeds in Oster Marsh has probably contributed to the growth of its marsh wren population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marsh wrens nest only in native cattail reeds and in no other vegetation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Oster Marsh contains more marsh wrens than any comparable wetland in the region.

explanations.correct: Cattails are the wrens' nesting habitat, they have expanded substantially, and no other relevant change occurred. The hedged inference that the expansion has probably contributed to the population growth is what the facts most support.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'would not have grown at all' is not supported; the stimulus allows other causes.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus is about one marsh, not any marsh.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus says wrens build nests in cattails, not that they nest nowhere else.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no comparison with other wetlands is made.

lr.difficultyReason: Two commerce facts, one clear hedged conclusion about subgroup behavior. Traps overreach to absolutes.
