lr.stimulus: Sales data from Orlen Bookshop show that among customers who purchased a novel during last year's summer discount promotion, more than half also bought at least one full-price book during the same visit. Customers who did not purchase a discounted novel, by contrast, bought a full-price book during their visits less than a quarter of the time.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The summer discount promotion caused Orlen Bookshop's overall revenue to rise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No customer who bought a full-price book last summer would have done so without the discount promotion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Customers who purchased a discounted novel tended to spend more at Orlen Bookshop per visit than customers who did not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of Orlen Bookshop's full-price sales last year came from customers buying discounted novels.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The discount promotion will be even more successful if repeated next summer.

explanations.correct: The first group bought a discounted novel plus a full-price book over half the time; the second group bought a full-price book less than a quarter of the time and no discounted novel. The hedged comparative claim about per-visit spending is what the data most strongly support.
explanations.A: Out of scope — the stimulus compares subgroups, not overall revenue.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'no customer ... would have' goes beyond what the data show.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus gives rates per customer group, not the composition of full-price sales overall.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no prediction about future promotions is supported.

lr.difficultyReason: Two legal facts about an appellate court; correct answer applies hedged language to the pattern observed.
lr.stimulus: Of the criminal convictions appealed to the Westhaven Court of Appeals last year, those in which the defense argued that the trial judge had improperly excluded evidence were overturned roughly twice as often as those that raised other grounds for appeal. The court handled a roughly equal number of appeals of each kind.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Trial judges in Westhaven improperly exclude evidence more often than they make other kinds of errors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any appeal arguing that a trial judge improperly excluded evidence will succeed in the Westhaven Court of Appeals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least some of the convictions overturned last year by the Westhaven Court of Appeals were overturned on the ground that a trial judge had improperly excluded evidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Westhaven Court of Appeals applies a less demanding standard to evidentiary-exclusion claims than to other grounds for appeal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most convictions that are appealed in Westhaven are ultimately overturned on some ground or other.

explanations.correct: If appeals citing improper exclusion are overturned at roughly twice the rate of other appeals, and the counts are roughly equal, some overturned convictions last year rested on that ground. The hedged 'at least some' claim is directly supported.
explanations.A: Out of scope — frequency of errors is not compared, only success rates on appeal.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'any appeal ... will succeed' is not supported; only a higher success rate is reported.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the stimulus does not describe the court's standards.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no overall overturn rate is given.

lr.difficultyReason: Two archaeological facts yield one hedged historical inference. Traps are scope creep and too-strong.
lr.stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a small coastal settlement dated to roughly 1200 B.C.E. uncovered storage jars containing olive oil whose chemical signature matches oils produced on an island more than 500 kilometers away. The settlement's own soil and climate are unsuitable for olive cultivation, and no evidence of olive presses has been found at the site.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Olive oil was the most widely traded commodity in the region around 1200 B.C.E.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The settlement's inhabitants obtained at least some of their olive oil through long-distance exchange.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The inhabitants of the coastal settlement were wealthier than those of inland settlements of the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No goods other than olive oil were imported into the coastal settlement from distant sources.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The island where the matching oil was produced was the largest olive-oil exporter of its era.

explanations.correct: The oil's chemical signature matches a distant source, and the settlement could not have produced olives or pressed oil locally. The hedged inference that at least some oil reached them through long-distance exchange is what the facts best support.
explanations.A: Too strong and out of scope — the stimulus says nothing about the ranking of traded commodities.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Out of scope — no comparative wealth claim is supported.
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus only addresses olive oil.
explanations.E: Too strong — the island's ranking as an exporter is not discussed.

lr.difficultyReason: Straightforward technology observation with one hedged inference; traps include absolute generalization and opposite direction.
lr.stimulus: In a controlled test, engineers measured the fuel consumption of a fleet of delivery trucks before and after installing software that automatically adjusts engine settings based on road grade and speed. Trucks using the software consumed, on average, 8 percent less fuel per kilometer than identical trucks without the software. Driving routes and cargo loads were held constant across both groups.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Installing the software reduces fuel consumption by the same amount for every truck that uses it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any technology that adjusts engine settings automatically will lower a truck's fuel consumption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Trucks equipped with the engine-adjustment software tend to consume less fuel per kilometer than otherwise comparable trucks without it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The software reduces fuel consumption primarily by lowering engine speed on steep grades.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fleet operators who adopt the software will recoup its purchase cost within a year.

explanations.correct: Identical trucks on identical routes with identical loads differed only in whether they used the software, and the software-equipped trucks averaged 8 percent lower fuel use. The hedged comparative generalization tracks exactly what was measured.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'same amount for every truck' goes beyond an 8 percent average.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus is about one specific software package.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the mechanism behind the savings is not discussed.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no claim about purchase cost or payback period is supported.

lr.difficultyReason: Two linguistics observations yield one hedged inference about an exception to a broader pattern.
lr.stimulus: In most of the world's languages, words denoting close kin such as 'mother' and 'father' tend to be short and to use only the simplest consonants. In the Ikwe language, however, the word for 'mother' is four syllables long and contains several consonants that young children acquire only after age five. Ikwe-speaking children, linguists report, typically begin using the word for 'mother' noticeably later than children acquiring other languages do.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ikwe-speaking children are generally slower than other children to acquire language overall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A word's phonetic complexity can affect how early children acquire it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every language in which kinship terms are long and phonetically complex delays children's acquisition of those terms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ikwe speakers use a different word when addressing their mothers in everyday speech.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Short words with simple consonants are easier for adults to learn than long words with complex consonants.

explanations.correct: The stimulus presents a cross-linguistic pattern and one case where a kinship word is unusually long and complex; children in that case acquire the word later. The hedged inference that phonetic complexity can affect acquisition timing is the one most supported.
explanations.A: Out of scope — only one word's acquisition is discussed, not overall language acquisition.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — a single case does not support a universal claim.
explanations.D: Out of scope — everyday usage patterns are not discussed.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus concerns children, not adult learners.

lr.difficultyReason: Two arts facts suggest one modest inference about attendance and programming. Traps overreach or are opposite-direction.
lr.stimulus: The Mercer Civic Theater reports that performances featuring works by living local playwrights sold, on average, about 20 percent more tickets last season than performances of works by better-known historical playwrights. Ticket prices, performance dates, and marketing budgets were comparable for both kinds of program.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Works by living local playwrights are of higher artistic quality than works by historical playwrights.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mercer Civic Theater audiences last season tended to prefer works by living local playwrights over works by better-known historical playwrights.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mercer Civic Theater will stop staging works by historical playwrights in future seasons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every performance by a living local playwright at Mercer Civic Theater sold out last season.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Audiences at other theaters in the region showed similar preferences last season.

explanations.correct: With ticket prices, dates, and marketing held comparable, the difference in average ticket sales most directly supports a hedged preference claim about Mercer's audiences last season.
explanations.A: Out of scope and too strong — artistic quality is not discussed.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Out of scope — no programming decision is supported.
explanations.D: Too strong — averages do not support a sold-out claim about every performance.
explanations.E: Out of scope — other theaters are not discussed.

lr.difficultyReason: Two policy facts with a clean hedged inference about cause. Traps include absolute claims and opposite-direction alternatives.
lr.stimulus: After the town of Halbrook began offering free evening bus service along three main routes last year, average evening car traffic on those routes decreased by about 15 percent over the following six months. On comparable routes in Halbrook that received no free evening bus service, evening car traffic during the same period was essentially unchanged.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Free evening bus service was the only factor that could have reduced evening car traffic on the three routes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Residents of Halbrook generally prefer bus travel to car travel.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every Halbrook resident who took a free evening bus along one of the three routes would otherwise have driven a car.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The introduction of free evening bus service in Halbrook likely contributed to the drop in evening car traffic on the three routes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Halbrook's free evening bus service will produce similar reductions if extended to every route in town.

explanations.correct: Traffic fell on exactly the routes that received free buses and held steady on comparable routes that did not. The hedged causal inference is what the pattern most strongly supports.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'only factor' is not supported; the comparison makes the free service a likely contributor, not the sole one.
explanations.B: Too strong — a general preference is broader than what the traffic pattern shows.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'every ... would otherwise have driven' goes well beyond the data.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope — extending the program town-wide is not addressed.

lr.difficultyReason: Two ethics-survey facts yield one natural hedged inference. Traps are too-strong universals and out-of-scope predictions.
lr.stimulus: In a recent anonymous survey of accountants at large firms, more than 70 percent reported that they had at some point been asked by a supervisor to record a transaction in a way they believed misleading. Of those respondents, a clear majority said they had complied with the request at least once because they feared professional retaliation.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most accountants at large firms routinely misrepresent the financial position of the companies they audit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any accountant who complies with a supervisor's misleading request does so only out of fear of retaliation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least some accountants at large firms have recorded transactions in ways they considered misleading out of fear of professional retaliation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supervisors at large accounting firms are generally indifferent to the ethical concerns of their staff.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stronger whistleblower protections would eliminate misleading accounting at large firms.

explanations.correct: A majority of the more-than-70-percent group said they had complied at least once out of fear of retaliation. The hedged 'at least some' inference about those accountants' conduct is a direct and modest reading of the numbers.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'routinely misrepresent' goes beyond having complied at least once in some cases.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'only out of fear of retaliation' is not supported; other motives are not ruled out.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Out of scope — supervisors' general attitudes are not described.
explanations.E: Too strong and out of scope — the effect of whistleblower protections is not addressed.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires integrating the adherence statistic with the subgroup finding to infer a hedged claim about adherence, not a blanket claim about the diet's efficacy. Trap (A) overreaches on efficacy; trap (D) inverts the direction.
lr.stimulus: A recent clinical trial assigned patients with elevated cholesterol either to a plant-based diet or to a standard low-fat diet. Across the full sample, average cholesterol levels dropped by similar amounts in both groups. However, fewer than half of the patients assigned to the plant-based diet reported sticking to it for the full twelve weeks, while the overwhelming majority of patients on the standard diet reported complying. Among patients who reported full adherence, those on the plant-based diet showed markedly greater reductions than those on the standard diet.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A plant-based diet is the most effective dietary intervention available for patients with elevated cholesterol.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least some patients who would benefit substantially from a plant-based diet are unlikely to follow it long enough to do so.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients assigned to a standard low-fat diet will always report higher rates of adherence than those assigned to a plant-based diet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dietary interventions are generally less effective at reducing cholesterol than medication-based interventions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The standard low-fat diet is as effective as the plant-based diet when both are followed consistently.

explanations.correct: Two facts combine to support (B): fewer than half of plant-based patients adhered, and among those who did, reductions were markedly greater. So at least some patients who would have benefited substantially did not stick with it. The hedged 'at least some' is well within what the data support.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'most effective available' makes a superlative claim well beyond a two-arm comparison.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'will always' extrapolates a single trial's adherence pattern into an absolute rule.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the stimulus says nothing about medication.
explanations.E: Opposite direction — the adherent-subgroup data show the plant-based diet produced markedly greater reductions, not equal ones.

lr.difficultyReason: Must integrate the earnings comparison with the hours datapoint to reach a hedged productivity-per-hour claim. Trap (E) overreaches to all drivers; trap (B) confuses the direction of the earnings comparison.
lr.stimulus: A survey of rideshare drivers in several large metropolitan areas found that drivers who work primarily during weekday commuting hours earn, on average, roughly the same total weekly income as drivers who work primarily on weekend evenings. The commuting-hour drivers, however, spend on average about 25 percent more hours logged into the rideshare application per week than the weekend-evening drivers do.
lr.questionStem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most rideshare drivers prefer working weekend evenings to working weekday commuting hours.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Weekend-evening drivers earn less per week than weekday commuting-hour drivers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some rideshare drivers earn more per hour logged into the application on weekend evenings than they would during weekday commuting hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rideshare passengers tip more generously on weekend evenings than during weekday commuting hours.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any driver who switches from weekday commuting hours to weekend evenings will increase his or her total weekly income.

explanations.correct: Similar total weekly income combined with substantially fewer logged-in hours implies a higher per-hour rate, at least on average, for weekend-evening drivers. 'Some drivers earn more per hour' is a hedged claim that follows cleanly from these two facts.
explanations.A: Out of scope — preferences aren't discussed.
explanations.B: Opposite direction — total weekly incomes are described as roughly equal, not lower for weekend drivers.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Unsupported — tipping is one possible source of the earnings pattern, but the stimulus doesn't establish it.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'any driver' switching guarantees no increase in earnings; the data describe averages, not individuals.

lr.difficultyReason: Combines the restoration outcome with the species-specific exception to support a hedged claim about restoration's limits. Trap (A) overreaches; trap (D) drops the qualifier about what drainage accomplishes.
lr.stimulus: When drained wetlands in the coastal region of Ferndale were re-flooded as part of a restoration program, populations of most native waterbird species rebounded to levels comparable to those recorded before drainage. One species, the banded bittern, had nested almost exclusively in a particular type of dense reed bed that had grown up during the decades of drainage. Ten years after re-flooding, banded bittern numbers in Ferndale remain less than half their pre-drainage levels.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wetland restoration programs are generally ineffective at reviving native bird populations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The banded bittern is in greater need of conservation attention than any other waterbird in Ferndale.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Re-flooding drained wetlands is not by itself sufficient to restore every native bird species that was historically present.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Drainage of wetlands typically benefits the bird species that inhabit them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The reed beds that grew during drainage are more valuable habitat than the original wetlands were.

explanations.correct: Most species rebounded after re-flooding, but the banded bittern did not — it depended on reed beds that only emerged during drainage. This supports the hedged claim that re-flooding alone is not sufficient for every species. 'Not sufficient' is exactly the language MSS favors.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — most species rebounded, which is evidence restoration is generally effective.
explanations.B: Unsupported — relative conservation priority is not established by the stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong and opposite — 'typically benefits' overreaches from one species' dependence on reed beds to a general claim about drainage.
explanations.E: Too strong — one species' preference doesn't show the reed beds are more valuable overall.

lr.difficultyReason: Integrates the borrowing pattern with the timing observation to support a hedged inference about cultural contact. Trap (B) overreaches on causation; trap (E) scope-creeps from maritime terms to the whole lexicon.
lr.stimulus: The Kaldari language contains dozens of words for types of sails, fishing equipment, and navigational landmarks that are clearly borrowed from Old Merenni, the language of a now-vanished seafaring people who lived along a coast several hundred miles to the south. By contrast, Kaldari retains no Merenni-derived words for agriculture, food preparation, or family relations. Linguists have dated the borrowed maritime terms to a period roughly a century before the first written records of regular trade between the two peoples.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Speakers of Kaldari had some maritime contact with Merenni speakers before trade between the two peoples was formally recorded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Merenni people taught the Kaldari most of what they knew about sailing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two peoples had no significant cultural contact of any kind prior to the period of recorded trade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Kaldari speakers borrowed words only from languages of peoples they encountered through trade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most Kaldari vocabulary was shaped by contact with the Merenni.

explanations.correct: Borrowed maritime terms predating the first records of regular trade support an inference that some maritime contact existed before the recorded trade period. The hedged 'some' fits the data well.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — borrowing vocabulary is evidence of contact, not of being taught 'most' of what one knows.
explanations.C: Opposite direction — the borrowed terms are themselves evidence of some prior contact.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'only' rules out all other sources of borrowing without support.
explanations.E: Scope creep — dozens of maritime terms aren't 'most' of the vocabulary.

lr.difficultyReason: Must connect the coin-distribution pattern with the absence of a local mint to support a hedged trade-route inference. Trap (C) overreaches from 'some' contact to 'primary'; trap (D) inverts the natural inference.
lr.stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a twelfth-century settlement in the inland region of Arvath have uncovered coins minted in the distant port of Daemos, in quantities comparable to those found at sites along the well-documented Daemos–Arvath trade road. Daemos coins have also been found in smaller quantities at several sites along a mountain pass route that historians had previously assumed was used only for seasonal herding. No mint is known to have operated in Arvath itself during the twelfth century.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some of the Daemos coins found at the mountain-pass sites arrived there through commercial exchange rather than seasonal herding alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mountain pass route was used more heavily for trade than the well-documented Daemos–Arvath road was.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daemos was the primary source of currency for inland Arvath during the twelfth century.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arvath produced its own coins but did so secretly to avoid Daemos's influence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Daemos–Arvath trade road fell out of regular use during the twelfth century.

explanations.correct: Coins from a distant port turning up along a pass route previously thought to serve only herding supports a hedged inference that at least some exchange occurred along that route — consistent with coins being a standard indicator of commerce.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Opposite direction — the pass sites show smaller quantities than the road sites.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'primary source' is a superlative claim not supported by the quantities alone.
explanations.D: Directly contradicted — no mint is known to have operated in Arvath.
explanations.E: Unsupported — the road sites still show trade-road-level coin quantities.

lr.difficultyReason: Combines the reuse statistic with the breach-source data to support a hedged claim about password managers as insufficient rather than harmful. Trap (A) inverts; trap (D) overreaches on a tool's sufficiency.
lr.stimulus: A survey of corporate employees found that those who regularly used a password manager were significantly less likely to reuse the same password across multiple work accounts than those who did not. Nonetheless, a study of recent security breaches at the same companies found that employees who used password managers accounted for nearly as large a share of breached accounts as those who did not. In most of these breaches, the point of compromise was a phishing attack rather than a guessed or stolen password.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Password managers tend to make corporate accounts less secure overall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corporate employees who use password managers are no more cautious about phishing attempts than their coworkers who do not use such tools.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phishing attacks are the most common cause of password reuse in corporate settings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adopting a password manager is sufficient to protect an employee from the most common forms of account compromise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Companies would experience fewer breaches if they banned the use of password managers.

explanations.correct: If managers reduce reuse but breach rates stay comparable — and most breaches are phishing-based — then use of a manager doesn't correspond to a lower phishing-compromise rate. That supports the hedged claim that manager users are no more cautious about phishing than non-users.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — the data don't show managers make things worse; they show they don't help against phishing in particular.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Category error — phishing causes breaches in this data, not password reuse.
explanations.D: Too strong, and the stimulus supports the opposite (managers don't prevent phishing-based compromise).
explanations.E: Opposite direction — a ban would restore password reuse, which the stimulus implies managers reduce.

lr.difficultyReason: Integrates the recording constraint with the soloist behavior to support a hedged inference about early jazz conventions. Trap (B) creeps to 'any recording'; trap (E) is a plausible worldly truth not anchored in the facts.
lr.stimulus: In the early days of commercial jazz recording, a single side of a 78-rpm disc could hold only about three minutes of music, far less than the typical length of a live jazz performance. Historians have observed that recordings made in this period contain noticeably fewer and shorter instrumental solos than eyewitness accounts describe as typical of the same ensembles' live performances. Several prominent soloists of the period complained in print that the recording format forced them to omit material they considered essential to their playing.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The recording format of the era probably shaped the form in which some early jazz solos have been preserved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any recording made during this period misrepresents the ensemble that produced it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Live jazz performances of the era were always substantially longer than three minutes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most jazz soloists of the period preferred live performance to studio recording.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Technological constraints have generally done more to shape music than to preserve it.

explanations.correct: The length limit, the gap between recordings and live accounts, and the soloists' own complaints together support the hedged inference that the format shaped what was preserved. 'Probably' and 'some' fit the level of warrant.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'any recording misrepresents' overreaches from 'fewer and shorter solos' to universal misrepresentation.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'always' and 'substantially' overreach the word 'typical.'
explanations.D: Unsupported — preference between media isn't established.
explanations.E: Plausible-but-unsupported worldly generalization — the stimulus speaks only to a specific case.

lr.difficultyReason: Must combine the checkout decline with the program-use rise to support a hedged inference about library function. Trap (A) inverts; trap (C) extends from 'at least one' to 'most.'
lr.stimulus: Over the past decade, the number of books checked out from the public library system of Porthaven has fallen by more than a third. During the same period, however, the total number of people who use at least one library facility in a given month has grown substantially, and library programs that do not involve borrowing books — such as tax-preparation clinics, job-search workshops, and children's story hours — have seen sharp increases in attendance.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following inferences is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Residents of Porthaven are reading fewer books than they did a decade ago.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least some Porthaven residents now rely on the library primarily for services other than borrowing books.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most people who visit the Porthaven library no longer check out any books at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The library system would attract even more users if it stopped offering non-book programs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Public libraries in other cities are experiencing trends similar to those in Porthaven.

explanations.correct: Total monthly users have grown substantially while checkouts have fallen, and non-borrowing programs have grown sharply. That combination supports the hedged claim that at least some residents now rely on the library primarily for non-book services.
explanations.A: Unsupported — people can read books obtained from sources other than the library (bookstores, e-books, etc.).
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'most' visitors no longer checking out anything goes beyond what declining-but-still-substantial checkouts can support.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — non-book programs are correlated with rising usage.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus addresses only Porthaven.

lr.difficultyReason: Integrates the sleep recommendation, the self-report finding, and the device data to support a hedged claim about under- rather than over-estimation of sleep. Trap (D) overreaches to the clinical category; trap (A) is the opposite.
lr.stimulus: Health authorities generally recommend that adults sleep between seven and nine hours each night. In a recent large survey, a majority of respondents reported that they typically slept less than the recommended amount. A subsequent study of participants who wore sleep-tracking devices for several weeks, however, found that nearly half of those who had earlier reported getting less than seven hours of sleep were in fact averaging more than seven hours per night according to the devices.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sleep-tracking devices systematically overstate the amount of time their users spend asleep.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The number of adults who actually sleep fewer than seven hours per night may be smaller than survey results have suggested.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most adults who believe themselves to be sleep-deprived are in fact getting adequate sleep.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adult sleep deprivation is not a genuine health concern.

choices.label: E
choices.text: People who use sleep-tracking devices tend to sleep longer than people who do not.

explanations.correct: If nearly half of self-reported under-sleepers were actually averaging more than seven hours, the survey-based picture probably overstates the number of adults sleeping too little. 'May be smaller' is appropriately hedged.
explanations.A: Unsupported — the stimulus doesn't say devices overstate; it says self-report and device data diverge, with no basis to privilege self-report.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'most adults who believe themselves sleep-deprived' overreaches from 'nearly half of one subgroup.'
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus doesn't dismiss the concern, only suggests its magnitude may be overstated.
explanations.E: Unsupported — the stimulus doesn't compare device users to non-users.

lr.difficultyReason: Connects the larval-survival datapoint with the protection-status contrast to support a hedged inference about the role of reserve size. Trap (A) overreaches on reserves' general effectiveness; trap (E) is a plausible worldly claim not anchored in the stimulus.
lr.stimulus: Marine biologists studying a coral reef system have found that the abundance of several commercially valuable fish species is substantially higher inside small protected reserves than in adjacent unprotected waters. Larvae of these species, however, drift on ocean currents for weeks before settling, and genetic analyses indicate that larvae produced within the reserves are regularly carried far beyond reserve boundaries. In nearby reef systems where no reserves have been established, populations of the same species have continued to decline.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Small marine reserves are sufficient to halt the decline of commercially valuable fish species throughout any reef system in which they are established.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some populations of commercially valuable fish outside small marine reserves benefit from the existence of those reserves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larval dispersal is the main factor determining fish abundance within marine reserves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most commercial fishers prefer to fish just outside the boundaries of marine reserves.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Expanding existing marine reserves would produce proportionally greater benefits for fish populations.

explanations.correct: Reserves contain more abundant populations; larvae produced there regularly drift beyond the boundaries; and unprotected reef systems without reserves continue to decline. Together these support the hedged claim that at least some outside populations benefit from the reserves. 'Some' is the right level of warrant.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'sufficient to halt decline throughout any reef system' overreaches from localized abundance findings.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'the main factor' is a superlative not supported by the stimulus.
explanations.D: Plausible-but-unsupported — fisher behavior isn't addressed.
explanations.E: Plausible-but-unsupported — proportionality of benefits isn't established.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires chaining three facts (antibody prevalence, post-exposure infection rate, severity finding) and recognizing a tension between high exposure and mild outcomes to support a hedged claim about protective factors. Trap (B) overreaches from 'some' to 'most'; trap (D) points opposite to what the severity data imply.
lr.stimulus: In a community where a newly identified respiratory virus circulated last winter, serological testing later revealed that more than 70 percent of adult residents had been exposed to the virus at some point during the season. Yet the local clinic recorded confirmed symptomatic infections in only about a quarter of the adult population. Of the symptomatic cases that were recorded, those in residents who had received the previous season's standard influenza vaccine were, on average, markedly milder than those in unvaccinated residents, even though the new virus is not closely related to any influenza strain.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some adult residents exposed to the new virus had some immune response that either prevented symptomatic infection or reduced its severity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most adult residents of the community who were exposed to the new virus experienced no symptoms at all.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The previous season's influenza vaccine confers specific immunity against the newly identified respiratory virus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Residents who received the previous season's influenza vaccine were more likely to become symptomatically infected with the new virus than unvaccinated residents were.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The newly identified respiratory virus is less dangerous than the influenza strains targeted by the previous season's vaccine.

explanations.correct: Three facts combine: exposure was widespread (over 70%), symptomatic infection was far less common (about a quarter), and among those who were symptomatic, prior flu-vaccine recipients had milder illness. Together they support the hedged claim that at least some exposed residents had an immune response that either blocked symptoms or dampened them. 'At least some' and 'either...or' match what the data can carry.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong and slightly off-scope — the stimulus gives community-wide exposure and symptomatic rates but not the specific fraction of exposed residents who were asymptomatic; 'most' is not warranted, and the stimulus speaks to recorded symptomatic cases, not a clean asymptomatic tally.
explanations.C: Too strong — milder severity in vaccinated residents is consistent with nonspecific immune effects; 'confers specific immunity' overreaches.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — the severity finding suggests vaccinated residents fared better, not worse.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — no comparison of the new virus's overall danger to influenza strains is given.

lr.difficultyReason: Must integrate three qualifications — effort-level reporting, confidence ratings, and the subgroup reversal — to support a hedged claim about the relationship between overconfidence and actual performance. Trap (C) treats a comparative as absolute; trap (E) drops the effort qualification.
lr.stimulus: In a large study of undergraduates preparing for standardized exams, students who reported studying fewer than ten hours per week rated themselves, on average, more confident about their readiness than students who reported studying twenty or more hours per week. On the exam itself, the high-study group outperformed the low-study group by a substantial margin. However, within the low-study group, those students who had rated themselves least confident scored about as well as the average student in the high-study group.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Among students who study relatively little, those who are less confident about their readiness tend to perform better on the exam than their more confident peers in the same study-hours group.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Confidence about readiness is a more reliable predictor of exam performance than reported study hours are.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any student who studies twenty or more hours per week will score higher on the exam than any student who studies fewer than ten.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students tend to overestimate how much time they actually spend studying for standardized exams.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Students who rate themselves least confident about their readiness will score about as well as students who study twice as many hours.

explanations.correct: Within the low-study group, the least-confident subset matched the average of the high-study group, while the low-study group on the whole trailed the high-study group. That subgroup reversal supports the hedged claim that, within the low-study group, lower confidence tracks with stronger performance. 'Tend to' respects the averaging in the data.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus gives no direct comparison of predictive reliability across the two variables.
explanations.C: Absolute claim from comparative data — the stimulus reports group averages, not per-individual guarantees.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the stimulus uses reported study hours and does not address their accuracy.
explanations.E: Drops the crucial qualifier that the match holds for the least-confident students within the low-study group; the inference would be stronger and misapplied as stated.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires chaining the rainfall datum, the staple-crop yield, and the household-garden finding to support a hedged inference about crop mix. Trap (B) is the plausible-but-unsupported worldly truth; trap (D) inverts the direction by treating the overall decline as uniform.
lr.stimulus: Data from agricultural monitoring stations in the semi-arid province of Marenda show that the past decade has been, on average, the driest of any decade since record-keeping began. Overall yields of the province's main staple crop, sorghum, have declined by roughly 15 percent relative to the previous decade. However, yields from small household gardens in the same region, in which farmers typically plant a mix of drought-tolerant vegetables alongside smaller amounts of sorghum, have held roughly steady over the same period.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some agricultural plots in Marenda have been less affected by the decade's drier conditions than the province's overall sorghum yield would suggest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Household gardens are generally more productive per unit of land than commercial sorghum fields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If commercial farms in Marenda shifted entirely away from sorghum to drought-tolerant vegetables, their yields would rise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All sorghum plots in Marenda have shown comparable declines in yield over the past decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rainfall is the only agricultural factor that has changed in Marenda over the past decade.

explanations.correct: Overall sorghum yields fell by about 15 percent as conditions grew drier, yet household gardens — which mix drought-tolerant vegetables with smaller amounts of sorghum — held steady. That supports the hedged claim that some plots have been less affected than the headline sorghum figure suggests. The inference chains three facts without overreaching.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — productivity per unit of land isn't established; the stimulus compares yield changes, not absolute productivity.
explanations.C: Too strong — a full shift of commercial farms is a policy prediction the stimulus does not support.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — the household-garden finding shows not all plots declined uniformly.
explanations.E: Too strong — the stimulus notes dry conditions but does not rule out other changes.

lr.difficultyReason: Must chain the settlement statistic, the docket-composition datum, and the contingency-fee observation, recognizing the tension between case mix and outcome mix, to support a hedged claim about plaintiff representation. Trap (A) overreaches to 'more skilled'; trap (C) mis-scopes the plaintiff-defendant comparison.
lr.stimulus: A recent review of civil cases filed in the Hargreave County trial court found that cases in which the plaintiff was represented by an attorney settled before trial roughly twice as often as cases in which the plaintiff appeared without counsel. The review also found that represented plaintiffs' cases disproportionately involved claims for which attorneys are willing to work on contingency — that is, claims with a relatively high expected monetary value. Among cases that were not settled and went to trial, represented and unrepresented plaintiffs prevailed at similar rates.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attorneys who represent plaintiffs in Hargreave County are, on average, more skilled at litigation than attorneys who represent defendants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The higher settlement rate among represented plaintiffs is likely due at least in part to features of their cases other than the quality of their representation at trial.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plaintiffs without counsel in Hargreave County win at trial more often than defendants without counsel do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any plaintiff who retains an attorney in Hargreave County is more likely to receive a monetary award than one who does not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Attorneys working on contingency refuse to take cases unless a pretrial settlement is likely.

explanations.correct: Three facts: represented plaintiffs settle about twice as often; their cases disproportionately involve high-value, contingency-eligible claims; yet at trial, represented and unrepresented plaintiffs prevail at similar rates. The similar trial-win rates tug against a pure 'lawyering makes plaintiffs win' story, and the case-mix fact offers another driver. Together these support the hedged claim that the settlement gap is at least partly due to non-trial-quality features of the cases themselves.
explanations.A: Out of scope — the stimulus says nothing about defense attorneys' skill.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Mis-scoped — unrepresented defendants are not addressed.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'any' and 'more likely' extrapolate beyond averages and ignore the similar trial-win finding.
explanations.E: Too strong — contingency-fee behavior is described only as a pattern, not as a rigid refusal rule.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires integrating the subscription data, the reading-time finding, and the recall-score result to recognize a tension between volume consumed and retention. Trap (E) is a plausible worldly truth; trap (B) overreaches from 'some' to 'most'.
lr.stimulus: A survey of readers of general-interest news publications found that subscribers to a high-volume daily news service reported, on average, consuming more articles per week than subscribers to a weekly news digest. The daily-service subscribers also reported spending, on average, less time per article than the digest subscribers did. When both groups were asked a week later to recall substantive details from articles they had read during the survey period, digest subscribers scored noticeably higher than daily-service subscribers on recall of policy-oriented articles, while the two groups scored comparably on recall of articles about entertainment.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reading a larger number of news articles per week tends to improve a reader's retention of details from those articles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most daily-service subscribers would retain more policy-oriented details if they spent more time per article.

choices.label: C
choices.text: For at least some categories of news, the amount of time spent per article is more closely associated with retention than is the sheer number of articles read.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Digest subscribers are, on the whole, more interested in policy issues than daily-service subscribers are.

choices.label: E
choices.text: News services that deliver fewer but longer articles should be preferred by readers who want to stay informed.

explanations.correct: Digest subscribers read fewer articles but spent more time per article; their recall of policy articles exceeded that of daily-service subscribers, though entertainment recall was comparable. This supports a hedged, category-scoped claim: for at least some kinds of news (policy), time-per-article tracks with retention more closely than article count does. The 'at least some categories' hedge and 'more closely associated' match what the data carry.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — daily-service subscribers read more articles but recalled less in the policy category.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'most' and 'would retain more' make a counterfactual and universal claim the data do not reach.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — no interest data are reported; the stimulus gives only recall scores.
explanations.E: Normative overreach — the stimulus does not license a recommendation about which service readers 'should' prefer.

lr.difficultyReason: Must chain three ethical-practice facts — the nondisclosure rate, the patient-preference survey, and the follow-up finding — to support a hedged claim about the gap between professed preferences and realized outcomes. Trap (A) overreaches; trap (D) relies on a misreading of which group showed the follow-up effect.
lr.stimulus: In a survey of physicians practicing in a large urban hospital system, roughly a third reported that they had at some point declined to disclose a minor error to a patient when they believed the error had caused no lasting harm. A separate survey of patients of the same system found that an overwhelming majority said they would want to be told of any error affecting their care, even if the error caused no lasting harm. A follow-up study found that patients who had later learned of an undisclosed minor error expressed, on average, only modestly lower trust in their physician than patients who had been promptly informed of a comparable error.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some physicians in the hospital system are not currently meeting the disclosure preferences of the patients they treat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most patients in the hospital system have at some point been the subject of an undisclosed minor medical error.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Promptly disclosing minor errors to patients maximally preserves patients' trust in their physicians.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients who learn belatedly of an undisclosed error lose trust in their physicians as sharply as patients who are told promptly would have.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Physicians who withhold disclosure of minor errors do so primarily out of concern for preserving patient trust.

explanations.correct: A third of physicians have at some point withheld disclosure of a minor error; an overwhelming majority of patients say they would want to be told of any error. That gap supports the hedged claim that at least some physicians are not meeting their patients' stated disclosure preferences. 'At least some' fits comfortably within the reported figures.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus gives the physician side ('at some point' withheld) and a preference survey, not the share of patients who have been affected.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'maximally preserves' is a superlative the follow-up study does not establish.
explanations.D: Opposite direction — the follow-up found only modestly lower trust among those who learned belatedly.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — physicians' reasons for nondisclosure are not described.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires chaining the pricing rule, the sales pattern, and the restocking observation to infer a hedged claim about demand in a specific category. Trap (B) is stimulus-neutral plausibility; trap (E) reverses direction by assuming the pattern generalizes.
lr.stimulus: An online retailer adjusts prices on many items daily according to an automated algorithm that raises a listed item's price whenever the number of units sold in the previous 24 hours exceeds a threshold. Records show that over the past year the algorithm raised the price of a popular model of wireless headphones roughly three times as often as it raised the price of a competing model from the same manufacturer, even though the two models were initially listed at the same price. Staff also reported restocking the first model noticeably more often than the second during the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first model of wireless headphones was, over the past year, in greater demand at the retailer than the competing model was.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first model of wireless headphones is of higher quality than the competing model.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The retailer's pricing algorithm raises prices only for items whose sales exceed the threshold on several consecutive days.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first model of wireless headphones is now priced considerably higher than the competing model.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any item whose price is raised three times as often as another item's price must be restocked three times as often as well.

explanations.correct: The algorithm raises prices when daily unit sales exceed a threshold; the first model's price was raised about three times as often as the competing model's, and staff restocked it noticeably more often. Together these facts support the hedged claim that the first model was in greater demand at this retailer over the year. 'Greater demand' is scoped to this retailer and this period, matching the evidence.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Plausible but unsupported — quality is not addressed; demand could reflect branding, promotion, or other factors.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'only' and 'several consecutive days' add conditions not stated.
explanations.D: Too strong — more frequent price increases don't guarantee the current listed price is considerably higher; prices can also fall.
explanations.E: Too strong — the inference overgeneralizes the relationship between price increases and restocking frequency.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires chaining emission, air-quality, and hospitalization data while recognizing the juxtaposition between lower emissions and stable hospitalizations to support a hedged claim about non-local pollution sources. Trap (A) flips direction; trap (C) over-applies the air-quality finding.
lr.stimulus: Since the city of Polford adopted stricter emission limits on its municipal power plants a decade ago, measured emissions of fine particulate matter from those plants have declined by nearly half. Air-quality monitoring stations in residential neighborhoods near the plants have recorded only a modest improvement in average particulate levels during the same period. Hospital admissions in Polford for conditions linked to airborne particulates have remained roughly constant.
lr.questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The stricter emission limits imposed on Polford's municipal power plants have caused residential air-quality monitors to record a sharp improvement in particulate levels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sources of airborne particulates other than Polford's municipal power plants are likely contributing substantially to the particulate levels measured in Polford's residential neighborhoods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Particulate pollution is no longer a significant contributor to hospital admissions in Polford.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Emission limits similar to those adopted by Polford would fail to improve air quality in any city that adopted them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Residents of neighborhoods near Polford's power plants have become less likely to seek hospital care for airborne-particulate-related conditions.

explanations.correct: Plant emissions fell by nearly half, yet residential particulate levels improved only modestly and hospitalizations were roughly constant. The gap between a large emissions drop and a small air-quality change supports the hedged claim that other sources are likely contributing substantially to local particulate levels. 'Likely' and 'substantially' fit the data without overreaching.
explanations.A: Opposite direction — the stimulus reports only a modest improvement in monitoring stations' readings.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too strong — roughly constant admissions do not show particulates are no longer a significant contributor.
explanations.D: Too strong — a universal failure claim goes well beyond one city's experience.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — admissions rates in specific neighborhoods are not broken out.

lr.difficultyReason: Chains the playwright's output pattern, the revival-frequency data, and the critical-reception datum, with a tension between later popularity and earlier acclaim. Trap (A) misreads 'among the most' as 'the most'; trap (D) drops the revival qualifier.
lr.stimulus: A comprehensive survey of twentieth-century theater records shows that the playwright Helena Orsi produced more than forty full-length plays during her career. Of these, only eight have been professionally revived more than twice since her death, and nearly all of those eight premiered during the first decade of her career. Contemporary reviewers of Orsi's later-career plays had, on average, praised them more highly than her early-career plays, describing several as among the most formally inventive works of their decade.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The most formally inventive of Helena Orsi's plays is one of the eight that have been revived more than twice since her death.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Plays that are highly praised by contemporary reviewers tend to be revived more frequently after the playwright's death than plays that are not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frequency of posthumous professional revival and contemporary critical praise do not always track each other closely in the case of Helena Orsi's work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Helena Orsi's early-career plays have been revived more often than her later-career plays.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Critics in Helena Orsi's later career systematically overrated her work.

explanations.correct: Nearly all of Orsi's frequently revived plays premiered in her first decade, yet her later-career plays received, on average, higher critical praise, with several described as among the most formally inventive of their decade. That juxtaposition supports the hedged claim that, in Orsi's case, revival frequency and critical praise do not always track each other closely. 'Not always' and 'closely' are appropriately hedged.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'among the most formally inventive' does not single out one play, and the stimulus describes several later works that way.
explanations.B: Opposite direction — the Orsi data run the other way: more-praised later plays were revived less often.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Correct reading but extrapolated — we know nearly all of the frequently revived plays are early ones, but not the aggregate revival counts across eras; the stronger comparative may not hold.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — 'systematically overrated' imputes a critical failure the stimulus does not establish.

lr.difficultyReason: Requires integrating the bandwidth-throttling policy, the queueing observation, and the peak-hour latency figure to support a hedged claim about a bottleneck's location. Trap (B) overreaches from 'some evidence' to 'primary cause'; trap (D) misreads the throttling condition.
lr.stimulus: A regional internet service provider implemented a policy in which residential connections whose monthly traffic exceeds a threshold are throttled to a lower speed until the next billing cycle. Network engineers have observed that during peak evening hours, outbound queues at the provider's core routers fill up more quickly than at any other time, even though total traffic during peak hours is only modestly greater than at late-morning hours. Average latency measured at customer endpoints rises sharply during peak evening hours, including for customers whose connections are not being throttled.
lr.questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At least some of the peak-hour latency experienced by the provider's customers is due to conditions at the provider's core routers rather than to the throttling policy alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The throttling policy is the primary cause of the elevated latency that customers experience during peak evening hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eliminating the throttling policy would substantially reduce average peak-hour latency for the provider's customers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every customer whose monthly traffic exceeds the threshold experiences higher average latency than every customer whose traffic does not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Expanding capacity at the core routers would eliminate peak-hour latency for all of the provider's customers.

explanations.correct: Core-router outbound queues fill up fastest during peak evening hours despite only modestly higher traffic than late morning, and peak-hour latency rises sharply even for non-throttled customers. Together these support the hedged claim that at least some of the peak-hour latency comes from conditions at the core routers, not only from the throttling policy. 'At least some' and 'rather than...alone' fit the data.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'primary cause' goes beyond what the non-throttled latency rise supports; it is evidence against sole-cause attribution, not for primary attribution.
explanations.C: Too strong — a counterfactual policy prediction not established by the data.
explanations.D: Mis-scoped — the stimulus does not give a throttled-versus-non-throttled latency comparison across all customers.
explanations.E: Too strong — 'eliminate...for all' overreaches from a contributing-cause inference.

lr.difficultyReason: Two simple categorical facts with a single transitive step; the credited inference follows directly from substituting one set into the other.
lr.stimulus: All licensed pharmacists in the province are required to complete thirty hours of continuing education annually. Every employee at Harbor Drug whose nametag reads 'RPh' is a licensed pharmacist in the province.
lr.questionStem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every employee at Harbor Drug is required to complete thirty hours of continuing education annually.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every Harbor Drug employee whose nametag reads 'RPh' is required to complete thirty hours of continuing education annually.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most licensed pharmacists in the province work at Harbor Drug.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any employee who completes thirty hours of continuing education is a licensed pharmacist.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The province requires more continuing education of pharmacists than of other medical professionals.

explanations.correct: Every 'RPh' employee is a licensed pharmacist, and every licensed pharmacist must complete thirty hours of continuing education. By transitivity, every 'RPh' employee has the same requirement.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus only places the 'RPh' employees in the pharmacist category, not all Harbor Drug staff.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Not supported — the stimulus says nothing about the share of the province's pharmacists that Harbor Drug employs.
explanations.D: Reversal — completing the education is necessary for licensure, not sufficient for it.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus says nothing about requirements for other medical professionals.

lr.difficultyReason: Single conditional plus a factual assertion about one individual; the credited inference is a straightforward modus ponens.
lr.stimulus: If a cargo container at the port weighs more than eight metric tons, it must be inspected by a customs officer before release. The blue container that arrived on Tuesday's shipment weighs nine metric tons.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true if the statements above are true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No container lighter than eight metric tons is inspected by a customs officer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every container on Tuesday's shipment weighs more than eight metric tons.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The blue container must be inspected by a customs officer before it is released.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The blue container will not be released on Tuesday.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most containers at the port weigh more than eight metric tons.

explanations.correct: The conditional's antecedent is satisfied — the container weighs more than eight metric tons — so its consequent applies: it must be inspected before release.
explanations.A: Negation error — the rule says nothing about whether lighter containers are inspected.
explanations.B: Unsupported generalization — only the blue container's weight is given.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the timing of release is not addressed by the stimulus.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus gives no information about the weight distribution at the port.

lr.difficultyReason: Two facts about two overlapping groups support a single existential inference; the logical step is one application of the pigeonhole-style overlap.
lr.stimulus: Every student in Professor Halden's seminar has read Kant's Groundwork. At least one student in Professor Halden's seminar has never studied philosophy formally before.
lr.questionStem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most students who read Kant's Groundwork have studied philosophy formally before.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least one person who has read Kant's Groundwork has never studied philosophy formally before.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Professor Halden requires every student to read Kant's Groundwork.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every student who has read Kant's Groundwork has never studied philosophy formally before.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Anyone who has studied philosophy formally has read Kant's Groundwork.

explanations.correct: The philosophy-novice student in the seminar has read the Groundwork, because every student in the seminar has. That student is a person who has read the Groundwork and has not studied philosophy formally before.
explanations.A: Unsupported — the stimulus provides no information about students outside this seminar.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Causal inference beyond the text — requiring isn't stated, only that each has read it.
explanations.D: Too strong — 'every' student reads it, but only 'at least one' is a newcomer.
explanations.E: Reversal and scope shift — the stimulus concerns seminar readers, not all formal philosophy students.

lr.difficultyReason: A conditional plus the denial of its consequent invites a single-step contrapositive inference.
lr.stimulus: If the township's general fund finishes the year with a surplus, the library's evening hours will be extended in January. The township's council has just confirmed that the library's evening hours will not be extended in January.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The township's general fund did not finish the year with a surplus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The township's general fund finished the year with a deficit of a significant size.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The council opposes extending the library's evening hours under any circumstances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The library will extend its evening hours later in the year instead of in January.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any future surplus will be used to extend the library's hours.

explanations.correct: By contrapositive: if a surplus would guarantee extended hours and extended hours will not happen, then there was no surplus.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong — absence of a surplus does not entail a deficit, let alone a significant one.
explanations.C: Unsupported — the council's general stance on library hours is not stated.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the stimulus says nothing about later in the year.
explanations.E: Unsupported — no claim is made about future surpluses.

lr.difficultyReason: A short conditional chain with two links collapses into a single transitive conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Whenever the coastal radar records a squall line moving east faster than forty kilometers per hour, the harbor office issues a small-craft warning. Whenever the harbor office issues a small-craft warning, the fishing fleet at Port Alden remains in dock.
lr.questionStem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fishing fleet at Port Alden remains in dock only when a small-craft warning is in effect.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whenever the coastal radar records a squall line moving east faster than forty kilometers per hour, the fishing fleet at Port Alden remains in dock.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The coastal radar records squall lines more often in winter than in summer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whenever the fishing fleet at Port Alden is in dock, the coastal radar has recorded a fast-moving squall line.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Small-craft warnings cause squall lines to intensify.

explanations.correct: Chaining the two conditionals: fast east-moving squall line -> small-craft warning -> fleet in dock. So any fast east-moving squall line entails the fleet's being in dock.
explanations.A: Reversal — the stimulus gives a sufficient condition for the fleet's staying in dock, not a necessary one.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Out of scope — seasonal frequency is not addressed.
explanations.D: Reversal — the fleet could remain in dock for other reasons.
explanations.E: Causal overreach — the stimulus describes procedural responses, not atmospheric causation.

lr.difficultyReason: Two numerical statements about exhaustive and overlapping groups support a minimal-count inference via a pigeonhole-style argument.
lr.stimulus: Forty employees work at the Linden branch of Cresta Bank. Every employee at the Linden branch is either a teller or a loan officer, and some are both. Eighteen of the branch's employees are tellers, and twenty-nine are loan officers.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: More than half of the branch's employees are tellers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least seven employees at the branch are both tellers and loan officers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exactly three employees are only loan officers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No employee at the branch is only a teller.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The branch employs more loan officers than it would if it had fewer tellers.

explanations.correct: Eighteen plus twenty-nine equals forty-seven role-slots filled by only forty employees. Since everyone fills at least one role, the seven-slot surplus must come from employees who hold both roles. So at least seven employees are both.
explanations.A: Contradicts the stimulus — only eighteen of the forty employees are tellers, less than half.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Unsupported as exact — the count of loan-officer-only employees depends on the overlap, which need not equal three.
explanations.D: Unsupported — the stimulus permits, but does not require, the existence of teller-only employees.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus makes no counterfactual comparison.

lr.difficultyReason: A rule plus a specific labeling fact produce a one-step categorical inference.
lr.stimulus: Any package labeled 'Priority Express' by the Northern Postal Service is guaranteed delivery within two business days. The parcel that Arun mailed to Ines yesterday afternoon was labeled 'Priority Express' by the Northern Postal Service.
lr.questionStem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ines will receive Arun's parcel within two business days of yesterday afternoon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Arun's parcel is guaranteed delivery within two business days.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No parcel not labeled 'Priority Express' is delivered within two business days.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Northern Postal Service only guarantees delivery for 'Priority Express' parcels.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Arun paid more to mail the parcel as 'Priority Express' than he would have for standard service.

explanations.correct: Arun's parcel belongs to the class of 'Priority Express' items, and every such item is guaranteed delivery within two business days. Therefore his parcel carries that guarantee.
explanations.A: Shift from guarantee to actual delivery — guarantees can fail in individual cases; the stimulus only asserts the guarantee.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Negation error — the stimulus does not rule out quick delivery of other parcels.
explanations.D: Scope shift — 'only' is not supported; other services may also carry guarantees.
explanations.E: Out of scope — pricing is not mentioned.

lr.difficultyReason: A disjunction combined with the denial of one disjunct yields a one-step disjunctive syllogism.
lr.stimulus: The winning entry in this year's Veldt Short Fiction Prize was submitted either by a novelist who has previously published with Veldt or by a first-time contributor. Investigation has revealed that the winning entry was not submitted by any novelist who has previously published with Veldt.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true if the statements above are true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The winning entry was submitted by an author whose work has never appeared in any journal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The winning entry was submitted by a first-time contributor to Veldt.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most previous Veldt Prize winners were first-time contributors.

choices.label: D
choices.text: First-time contributors produce stronger short fiction than returning contributors do.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The judges preferred to award the prize to a newcomer this year.

explanations.correct: Given the either/or premise and the denial of the first disjunct, the remaining disjunct holds: the winner was a first-time contributor.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'first-time contributor to Veldt' does not entail never having published anywhere else.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Unsupported — past years are not addressed.
explanations.D: Unsupported evaluative claim — the stimulus does not compare quality.
explanations.E: Unsupported — the judges' preferences are not stated.

lr.difficultyReason: Two conditionals chain through a shared middle term to produce a one-step transitive inference about a named individual.
lr.stimulus: Every treaty ratified by the Federal Assembly takes legal effect on the first day of the following month. Every law taking legal effect in the country must be published in the Official Gazette within fourteen days of taking effect. The Saldano Trade Treaty was ratified by the Federal Assembly last week.
lr.questionStem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Saldano Trade Treaty will be published in the Official Gazette within fourteen days of the first day of next month.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No law takes legal effect without being ratified by the Federal Assembly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Saldano Trade Treaty was the only treaty ratified by the Federal Assembly last week.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Official Gazette publishes all treaties before they take legal effect.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any treaty published in the Official Gazette has been ratified by the Federal Assembly.

explanations.correct: The treaty, as a ratified treaty, takes effect on the first of next month; every law taking effect must then appear in the Gazette within fourteen days of that effective date. So publication must occur within fourteen days of the first of next month.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reversal — the stimulus doesn't exclude other paths to legal effect.
explanations.C: Unsupported — uniqueness is not stated.
