lr.stimulus: A review of cardiac surgical data from ten major hospitals found that surgeons whose published long-term survival rates were the highest also had, on average, the highest rates of serious intraoperative complications. Ordinarily one would expect surgeons with fewer complications to achieve better long-term outcomes.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The surgeons with the highest published long-term survival rates are routinely referred the most complex and high-risk cases, which carry an inherently elevated risk of intraoperative complications.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intraoperative complications are reported more consistently by surgeons who also publish long-term survival data.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Long-term survival is determined not only by surgical outcomes but also by patients' post-operative care.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surgeons with the lowest intraoperative complication rates tend to perform the highest volume of routine procedures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cardiac surgeons generally receive more specialized training than surgeons in other fields.

explanations.correct: Top surgeons' case mix is skewed toward the hardest cases, which carry higher baseline complication risk, even as their skill yields superior long-term survival. The two statistics move together not because complications cause survival but because both track case difficulty and surgeon expertise.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Might make complication data look higher for some surgeons without any real difference, but doesn't explain why the same surgeons have the best survival rates.
explanations.C: True but irrelevant — post-operative care doesn't explain the within-surgeon link between intraoperative complications and published survival.
explanations.D: Explains why low-complication surgeons have low complications but not why their long-term survival is lower.
explanations.E: Cross-specialty training comparisons are beside the point.

lr.difficultyReason: Learners who spend more time immersed score worse on grammar tests — resolved by a subpopulation contrast: more-immersed learners are the less advanced ones who were placed in immersion precisely because they needed help. Distractors target test design or motivation.
lr.stimulus: A language institute reports that its intermediate Spanish students who spend the greatest number of hours each week in conversational immersion sessions score lower on the institute's end-of-term grammar exam than students who spend fewer hours in those sessions. The institute's director is surprised, since immersion is widely credited with improving grammar.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The institute assigns students with weaker entry-level grammar skills to more hours of conversational immersion than those with stronger skills.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The end-of-term grammar exam covers material that is also practiced in immersion sessions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who enroll in the institute's intermediate program differ widely in their prior exposure to Spanish.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conversational immersion sessions at the institute are led by native speakers of Spanish.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The institute's grammar exam is generally regarded as more difficult than similar exams at comparable schools.

explanations.correct: If weaker students are routed into more immersion, they may still score lower at term's end than stronger peers even if immersion helps each of them. The hours–score correlation reflects placement by need, not a harmful effect of immersion. This is the textbook confound.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Would make the grammar exam fairer to immersion students, deepening the paradox rather than resolving it.
explanations.C: Variation in prior exposure is a generic fact that doesn't connect hours of immersion to exam performance.
explanations.D: Native instruction if anything supports immersion's value and deepens the puzzle.
explanations.E: Exam difficulty applies uniformly to all students and so doesn't explain the difference between more- and less-immersed students.

lr.difficultyReason: A bike-lane network expansion coincided with an increase in cyclist injuries — resolved by an exposure effect: the lanes drew far more people to ride, so aggregate injuries rose even as per-rider injury risk fell. Traps misattribute the rise to infrastructure flaws or deepen the paradox.
lr.stimulus: The city of Marston built 85 miles of new protected bike lanes between 2020 and 2024. Studies of other cities' bike-lane networks have consistently found that such lanes reduce a cyclist's chance of being injured in traffic. Yet during those four years in Marston, the total number of cyclists injured in traffic accidents rose by 60 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: As the protected lane network expanded, the number of residents who commuted regularly by bicycle in Marston more than tripled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The protected bike lanes in Marston are not physically separated from car traffic at intersections.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marston's traffic enforcement staff was reduced during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Studies of bike-lane safety in other cities focused on lanes used primarily for recreational rather than commuter cycling.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The injury statistics for Marston include only injuries serious enough to require medical attention.

explanations.correct: A threefold rise in cyclists absorbs a smaller per-rider risk and still yields many more total injuries. The per-rider safety benefit and the aggregate injury increase are compatible once exposure is factored in.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: If intersections are the weak link, that might partially weaken the benefit — but alone it doesn't reconcile a 60 percent rise with a well-documented safety effect from completed lane segments.
explanations.C: Reduced enforcement is a plausible confound but doesn't specifically target the cyclist injury rise tied to lane construction.
explanations.D: Undermines the applicability of prior studies but doesn't explain the injury rise by itself.
explanations.E: A consistent reporting threshold applies across years and thus doesn't explain a 60 percent change.

lr.difficultyReason: Ticket sales fell while ticket revenue rose — resolved by a price-composition shift that altered average ticket price upward. Distractors address attendance growth, marketing, or adjacent venues.
lr.stimulus: The Granville Symphony Orchestra reports that the number of tickets sold to its concerts fell by 15 percent this season compared with last season. Even so, total revenue from ticket sales rose by nearly 25 percent over the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The orchestra eliminated its least expensive ticket tier this season and added a new premium tier priced at more than three times the previous top price.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The orchestra presented several of its most popular programs this season.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ticket prices at comparable orchestras in other cities also rose this season.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The orchestra's hall underwent renovations midway through last season, reducing available seating.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Season subscribers make up a larger share of the orchestra's audience than single-ticket buyers do.

explanations.correct: Removing the cheapest seats and adding a much more expensive top tier raises the average price paid per ticket sharply, so revenue can climb even as tickets sold fall. The seating-mix shift reconciles the two figures directly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Popular programming should raise attendance, deepening the paradox that fewer tickets were sold.
explanations.C: Cross-orchestra pricing doesn't explain Granville's specific revenue-versus-attendance split.
explanations.D: A renovation last season would reduce last season's baseline attendance, which should make this season's 15 percent drop larger in context, not explain the revenue surge.
explanations.E: Subscriber share is steady across both seasons and thus doesn't account for the year-over-year change.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-fact tension: a new drug outperforms placebo in trials, patients prescribed the drug in general practice recover no faster than untreated patients, yet hospitals that adopted the drug report shorter average stays. Resolution hinges on a selection effect at the hospital level — only the sickest patients are admitted and treated, so hospital averages are driven by case mix rather than drug efficacy.
lr.stimulus: In randomized trials, patients taking the antiviral drug Reviran recovered from severe influenza two days faster than patients given a placebo. In general practice, however, patients prescribed Reviran recovered no faster than patients who received no antiviral treatment. Nonetheless, hospitals that adopted Reviran as standard care for admitted flu patients reported that average length of stay fell by nearly a full day after the drug was introduced.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: General practitioners prescribe Reviran primarily to patients whose flu symptoms are already improving, whereas hospitals administer it only to patients whose symptoms are severe enough to require admission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reviran is significantly more expensive than other antiviral drugs currently on the market.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hospitals that adopted Reviran also expanded their outpatient follow-up programs during the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The placebo used in the randomized trials was indistinguishable in appearance from Reviran tablets.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most patients who are prescribed Reviran by a general practitioner do not complete the full course of treatment.

explanations.correct: If general practitioners prescribe Reviran mainly to patients already on the mend, the 'treated' group in general practice is biased toward mild cases who would have recovered quickly regardless — wiping out the drug's apparent edge. Hospitals, by contrast, give it to severe cases for whom the trial-proven two-day shortening translates into meaningfully shorter admissions. Both patterns arise from who receives the drug, not whether it works.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Cost is irrelevant to recovery speed or length of stay.
explanations.C: Expanded follow-up could explain shorter hospital stays but says nothing about why general practice showed no benefit while trials did.
explanations.D: Blinding quality supports the trial result but doesn't reconcile it with the general-practice and hospital data.
explanations.E: Non-adherence would explain why general practice saw no benefit but would leave the hospital and trial results unreconciled — and if anything deepens the contrast.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-layer paradox: nationwide worker productivity rose, average hourly wages also rose, yet median household income fell. Resolution requires recognizing a compositional shift — high earners working more hours and low earners dropping out of the labor force — which a simple productivity-wage story cannot explain.
lr.stimulus: Over the past decade, output per hour worked in the country of Alvara rose by 22 percent, and average hourly wages, adjusted for inflation, rose by 9 percent. Despite these gains, the median household's annual income fell by 4 percent during the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cost of housing in Alvara rose faster than either wages or productivity over the decade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A substantial number of lower-wage workers left the labor force during the decade, while many higher-wage workers increased their hours; the average wage figure reflects only those still employed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Productivity gains were concentrated in export industries, whose goods were sold mostly to customers outside Alvara.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the hourly wage gains were driven by increases at the top of the wage distribution, while wages at the bottom rose more slowly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Average household size in Alvara increased slightly over the decade, spreading household income over more people.

explanations.correct: If many low-wage workers exited the labor force, their zero earnings drag median household income down even as the remaining employed workers — a wealthier slice — push the average wage up. Meanwhile, higher-wage workers working more hours raise productivity. The three statistics measure different populations, so all three can move as described simultaneously.
explanations.A: Rising housing costs don't affect income measurements.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Export concentration could explain productivity gains but doesn't explain why median household income fell despite rising wages.
explanations.D: Top-heavy wage growth raises the average, but without an exit from the labor force it cannot pull median household income below its starting point.
explanations.E: Household size affects per-person income, not household income; and the stated increase is 'slight,' insufficient for a 4 percent drop.

lr.difficultyReason: Three facts: firms that adopted the new security protocol experience the same number of successful intrusions as those that didn't, security auditors unanimously rate the protocol as stronger, and yet the average dollar loss per intrusion at adopting firms is substantially lower. Resolution requires a definitional distinction between types of intrusion events — counted attacks versus data loss.
lr.stimulus: Cybersecurity researchers report that firms that adopted the new Sentinel authentication protocol suffer, on average, the same number of successful intrusions per year as comparable firms that did not adopt it. Auditors unanimously rate Sentinel as more resistant to unauthorized access than the industry standard. Nevertheless, the average dollar loss per intrusion at adopting firms is only about one-fifth of the loss at nonadopting firms.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sentinel blocks the most sophisticated intrusion techniques but allows certain low-level intrusions — such as benign automated probes that briefly access harmless files — to be logged as 'successful' even though no sensitive data is reached.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Firms that adopt Sentinel tend to be larger and hold more valuable data than firms that do not adopt it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cost of implementing Sentinel is substantially higher than the cost of maintaining the industry-standard protocol.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Auditors who rated Sentinel were not informed of the dollar-loss data when making their assessments.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many firms that adopted Sentinel also increased their spending on employee cybersecurity training in the same year.

explanations.correct: If Sentinel lets trivial probes be recorded as 'successful intrusions' while blocking the damaging ones, adopting firms can match nonadopters in raw count while losing far less per event. The auditors' favorable rating — keyed to blocking serious breaches — is also consistent. All three facts reconcile once 'successful intrusion' is understood to cover heterogeneous severity.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Larger, more valuable targets would raise, not lower, losses per intrusion at adopters — deepening the paradox.
explanations.C: Implementation cost doesn't affect intrusion counts or per-intrusion losses.
explanations.D: Blinding of auditors addresses rating integrity but not the count-vs.-loss mismatch.
explanations.E: A confounded training effect could lower losses, but it leaves unexplained why intrusion counts didn't also fall at adopting firms.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-way tension: habitat protection expanded, documented populations of the target species rose, yet field biologists report fewer sightings in the wild than before protection. Resolution requires a temporal-methodological shift — population figures derive from new surveying techniques that count animals previously invisible to observers.
lr.stimulus: When the Mersin government declared the coastal cedar forest a protected reserve ten years ago, the goal was to aid the recovery of the Mersin loris, a small nocturnal primate. Official population estimates for the loris have since risen from roughly 1,200 to over 4,000 individuals. Yet naturalists who have walked the reserve regularly for decades report seeing the loris far less often than they did before protection began.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shortly after the reserve was created, biologists began using infrared camera traps placed deep in the forest interior, which detect lorises that human observers, restricted to trails, never encounter.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Mersin loris is more active on moonless nights than on moonlit ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cedar forest contains several other nocturnal primate species besides the Mersin loris.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Visitor access to parts of the reserve has been restricted since its creation, reducing the number of trails naturalists may walk.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mersin loris populations in unprotected neighboring forests have declined sharply over the past ten years.

explanations.correct: If new camera-trap surveys detect lorises hidden from trail-bound human observers, the official population figure can climb even as naturalists' sightings on the trails fall — perhaps because behavioral change, disturbance avoidance, or simply the trails no longer intersecting dense habitat. The apparent mismatch is an artifact of two different counting methods.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Moonlight variation is a constant factor and cannot explain a directional change.
explanations.C: Presence of other species doesn't affect loris sightings or counts of lorises specifically.
explanations.D: Restricted trail access could explain fewer sightings but doesn't on its own explain the large rise in population estimates.
explanations.E: Decline in neighboring forests explains nothing about sightings in the reserve, and a loris influx would tend to raise, not lower, on-trail encounters.

lr.difficultyReason: Three interlocking facts about a reform: arrests for fraud fell, prosecutors filed charges in a higher percentage of referred cases, yet the absolute number of fraud convictions also fell. Resolution requires spotting that the reform narrowed what qualifies as a chargeable fraud case, affecting the pipeline at the front.
lr.stimulus: Five years ago, the state legislature overhauled its fraud statutes, narrowing the definition of criminal fraud to exclude certain deceptive but non-malicious business practices. Since the overhaul, arrests for fraud have fallen by 30 percent statewide. Prosecutors, however, now file formal charges in 85 percent of cases referred to them, up from 60 percent before the overhaul. Despite this higher charging rate, the absolute number of fraud convictions has fallen by nearly 20 percent.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The statutory overhaul eliminated from fraud law a large class of minor, easily-proven offenses, so the cases that remain are fewer in number but more likely to survive a prosecutor's screen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defendants charged with fraud under the new statute are more likely to request jury trials than defendants charged under the old statute.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prosecutors' offices received a budget increase in the year following the overhaul.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many businesses responded to the overhaul by increasing their internal compliance audits.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The overhaul lengthened the average sentence for fraud convictions.

explanations.correct: If the overhaul removed a large tier of low-grade offenses from fraud law, total arrests drop and the surviving cases are concentrated in serious, well-evidenced conduct — exactly the cases prosecutors readily charge, explaining the higher charging percentage. Convictions still fall in absolute terms because the pool of chargeable conduct shrank. All three statistics reconcile through the narrowed definition.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Trial choice doesn't determine how many cases are charged or arrested.
explanations.C: A budget increase should raise, not lower, conviction counts and doesn't explain the charging-rate shift.
explanations.D: Private compliance work might reduce fraud, but it doesn't explain why prosecutors' charging rate rose.
explanations.E: Sentence length is about punishment, not conviction counts or charging decisions.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-way historical paradox: printed book production surged, documented literacy rates climbed, yet surviving personal correspondence from ordinary citizens during the period is far scarcer than from the decade preceding it. Resolution requires a differential-survival confounder: paper quality or conservation practices changed in a way that disproportionately destroyed the later correspondence.
lr.stimulus: Historians studying the kingdom of Voren note that between 1620 and 1640 the annual output of printed books in the kingdom tripled and documented literacy rates among free citizens rose from roughly 25 percent to over 50 percent. Nevertheless, the number of surviving personal letters written by ordinary Vorenian citizens during 1620–1640 is substantially smaller than the number surviving from the decade 1610–1620.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Around 1620, Vorenian papermakers began using a new wood-pulp process whose acidic output becomes brittle and disintegrates within a century, whereas the rag paper used in the preceding decade has survived intact.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Literacy rates among enslaved persons in Voren, who could not legally write letters, remained near zero throughout both periods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The printed books produced during 1620–1640 were mostly religious tracts rather than works of secular correspondence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historians have studied the decade 1610–1620 far more intensively than the subsequent two decades.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The price of paper rose sharply after 1640, making private correspondence a luxury only the wealthy could afford.

explanations.correct: A shift to acidic wood-pulp paper in 1620 would cause letters written on it to disintegrate, while earlier rag-paper letters endure. The count of 'surviving' letters is then a measure of paper chemistry, not of how many letters were written. Rising literacy and book production can coexist with a shrinking surviving corpus once differential survival is in view.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Enslaved persons' literacy is held constant, so it cannot produce the observed change between the two periods.
explanations.C: Book content doesn't affect how many personal letters survive.
explanations.D: If anything, more intensive study of the earlier period could raise the count of surviving letters from it, but it doesn't explain why the later period shows fewer surviving letters in absolute terms.
explanations.E: This concerns the period after 1640, not the period of the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-way linguistic paradox: immersion-program learners outscore classroom-only learners on grammar tests, classroom-only learners outscore immersion learners on vocabulary tests, yet in unscripted conversation native speakers rate the immersion learners as substantially more fluent. Resolution turns on a hidden confounder — the vocabulary test penalizes register-appropriate word choices that immersion learners acquire.
lr.stimulus: Researchers compared two groups of adult Vethan-language learners. On standardized grammar tests, students who had completed a six-month immersion program in Vethea outperformed students who studied only in classrooms. On standardized vocabulary tests, however, the classroom-only students outperformed the immersion students. Yet in recorded unscripted conversations, native Vethan speakers rated the immersion students as substantially more fluent than the classroom-only students.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The standardized vocabulary test rewards knowledge of formal and literary Vethan words, while native speakers in everyday conversation use — and expect — colloquial and regional words that immersion students acquire and classroom students do not.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The immersion program included more hours of instruction per week than the classroom-only program.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Students who enroll in immersion programs tend to have higher baseline language-learning aptitude than students who choose classroom programs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vethan grammar is widely considered among the most difficult features of the language to master.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Native Vethan speakers who served as raters were not informed which learners had completed immersion.

explanations.correct: If the vocabulary test rewards formal words but native speakers use — and grade for — colloquial ones, immersion students can look weaker on the test while sounding more fluent in conversation. This hidden register mismatch simultaneously explains lower test scores, higher conversational ratings, and is fully compatible with the immersion group's stronger grammar.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: More instructional hours could raise all scores but cannot explain why the immersion group does worse on vocabulary while doing better on grammar and conversation.
explanations.C: Higher aptitude predicts better performance across all three measures, deepening rather than resolving the vocabulary anomaly.
explanations.D: Grammar's difficulty doesn't reconcile the vocabulary-vs.-conversation gap.
explanations.E: Blinding supports the conversational ratings' credibility but doesn't explain the vocabulary test result.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-fact policy paradox: housing subsidies expanded, the absolute number of unsheltered residents fell, yet the rate of unsheltered homelessness per capita in the city rose. Resolution requires recognizing a migration-driven base-rate change — the population denominator fell faster than the numerator, producing a rise in rate despite falling counts.
lr.stimulus: Five years ago the city of Porthaven tripled its housing subsidy budget. Since then, the number of residents classified as unsheltered — people living on the streets or in vehicles — has fallen from 4,800 to 3,900. Despite this decline, the rate of unsheltered homelessness in Porthaven, measured as unsheltered residents per 10,000 total residents, has risen by more than 15 percent during the same five years.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the five-year period, the total population of Porthaven fell sharply as many working-age residents moved to neighboring cities with lower costs of living.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most of the new subsidies were used by residents to remain in existing housing rather than to move into previously vacant units.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Residents classified as 'sheltered homeless' — those in shelters or transitional housing — also declined over the five-year period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Porthaven's unsheltered count is conducted during a single night in January each year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several neighboring cities reduced their own housing subsidy programs during the same period.

explanations.correct: A rate is a ratio. If Porthaven's total population fell faster in percentage terms than its unsheltered count, the rate per 10,000 rises even as the numerator falls. The subsidies plausibly helped drive the numerator down, while outmigration of working-age residents shrinks the denominator faster still. All three facts are reconciled through the denominator change.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This concerns how subsidies were used and wouldn't explain a rate that rises while counts fall.
explanations.C: Parallel decline in sheltered homelessness doesn't affect the per-capita unsheltered rate's direction.
explanations.D: Counting methodology is held constant across years.
explanations.E: Neighboring cuts might push homeless populations toward Porthaven, which would raise the count — but Porthaven's count fell, so this deepens the paradox.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-fact arts paradox: ticket prices fell, the number of exhibitions offered increased, yet total paid attendance dropped. Resolution requires seeing that a new free-admission policy for the permanent collection diverted visitors who would previously have purchased tickets.
lr.stimulus: The Kellerstrom Museum of Modern Art reports that over the past three years it reduced the price of a single-day admission ticket by 20 percent and increased the number of special exhibitions it hosts each year from six to nine. Nevertheless, total paid attendance at the museum fell by nearly 25 percent during the same period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain the discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Three years ago the museum began offering free admission to its permanent collection, with tickets required only for the special exhibitions; most visitors report coming primarily to see the permanent collection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The museum's three-year operating budget has remained essentially flat in inflation-adjusted terms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attendance at other art museums in the region has also declined over the past three years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several of the museum's special exhibitions have received enthusiastic reviews in major publications.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The museum's ticket price reduction was smaller, in percentage terms, than the price reductions announced by several of its peer institutions during the same period.

explanations.correct: If admission to the permanent collection became free and most visitors come primarily for it, those visitors no longer appear in paid-attendance figures. Meanwhile, the cheaper tickets and increased exhibition count draw visitors specifically to special exhibitions. Total paid attendance drops because the mass of general visitors has been redirected to free admission — a category shift, not a falling interest in the museum.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: A flat budget doesn't explain visitor choices.
explanations.C: A regional decline could explain lower attendance but leaves unexplained why the museum's own price cut and added exhibitions failed to offset it — and the choice resolves one half only.
explanations.D: Favorable reviews would raise, not lower, paid attendance; deepens the paradox.
explanations.E: Relative price position doesn't explain a 25 percent drop on top of an absolute price cut.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-fact ethical-policy paradox: an opt-out organ donation policy produces higher registered donor rates than the prior opt-in policy, public attitude surveys show approval of donation unchanged, yet the number of transplants actually performed per year has declined. Resolution rests on a temporal-logistical confounder — the policy also inadvertently shortened the window for family consultation, causing more registered donors' organs never to be recovered.
lr.stimulus: Three years ago, the nation of Berwick replaced its opt-in organ donation policy with an opt-out policy, under which citizens are presumed donors unless they register a refusal. Since the change, the proportion of adults counted as registered donors has risen from 38 percent to 74 percent, and public opinion surveys show that popular approval of organ donation has remained essentially unchanged. Yet the number of organ transplants actually performed in Berwick each year has declined by about 10 percent since the policy took effect.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The opt-out policy was accompanied by a new hospital protocol that reduced the time families are given to consent to organ recovery after a relative's death; as a result, recovery teams now miss the narrow medical window for retrieval in many more cases than before.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A majority of Berwick citizens who became registered donors under the new policy did not learn of their registration until after the policy took effect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other nations that adopted opt-out policies have reported varying effects on transplant numbers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Berwick's population has grown slightly since the policy change.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The opt-out policy was introduced alongside a public information campaign emphasizing the benefits of organ donation.

explanations.correct: Transplants require two things: a donor on the books and a successful, timely recovery. If the opt-out reform came packaged with a protocol that shortens family consultation and medical retrieval windows, registered donor numbers can climb while recoveries — and thus transplants — fall. Popular approval stays flat because approval isn't the bottleneck. All three facts reconcile once the recovery-window change is introduced.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Late-notice registration would still produce registered donors available at death; it doesn't explain why transplants fell.
explanations.C: Reports from other nations don't explain Berwick's specific outcome.
explanations.D: Slight population growth would tend to raise, not lower, the absolute transplant count; deepens the paradox.
explanations.E: A favorable information campaign should raise donation and transplant numbers, sharpening rather than resolving the conflict.

lr.difficultyReason: Transparent correlation-to-causation flaw in a short, two-sentence stimulus. Only (C) replicates the exact move — an observed correlation treated as proof of causation. Other choices commit obviously different errors or are valid.
lr.stimulus: Students who eat breakfast every day score higher on math tests than students who skip breakfast. Therefore, eating breakfast causes students to do better in math.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Runners who wear expensive shoes tend to finish races faster than those who don't. So expensive shoes must be worth the money.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every swan I have ever seen has been white. Therefore, all swans are white.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who own dogs tend to live longer than people who do not. Therefore, owning a dog causes people to live longer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If it rains, the grass will be wet. The grass is wet, so it must have rained.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The new drug worked for my neighbor. Therefore, it should be approved for everyone.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: observed correlation (breakfast-eaters score higher) is treated as proof that breakfast causes the higher scores. (C) replicates the exact move: correlation between dog ownership and longevity is treated as proof that owning a dog causes longer life.
explanations.A: Tempting because it sounds causal, but the conclusion is evaluative ('worth the money'), not a causal claim. Different structure.
explanations.B: Unwarranted generalization from a sample, not correlation-to-causation.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent — a conditional flaw, not a causal one.
explanations.E: Generalization from a single case, not correlation-to-causation.

lr.difficultyReason: Sufficient-necessary confusion stated plainly. Only (B) reverses a conditional in the same way. Other answers are valid or commit transparently different errors.
lr.stimulus: If a plant receives sunlight, it will grow. The fern in my kitchen is growing. Therefore, it must be receiving sunlight.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a student studies hard, she will pass the exam. Dana studied hard, so Dana passed the exam.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If it snows, the schools close. The schools are closed today. Therefore, it must be snowing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most people who exercise feel healthier. Marcus exercises, so Marcus probably feels healthier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All mammals have lungs. A whale is a mammal. Therefore, a whale has lungs.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The more you practice piano, the better you get. Elena practices every day, so she is improving.

explanations.correct: Stimulus form: 'If P then Q; Q; therefore P' — affirming the consequent, a sufficient-necessary confusion. (B) runs the identical move: 'If snow then schools close; schools are closed; therefore snowing.'
explanations.A: Valid reasoning — if studying hard is sufficient, then a hard-studying student passes. No flaw.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No conditional reversal; a probabilistic inference applied straightforwardly.
explanations.D: Valid categorical syllogism. No flaw.
explanations.E: No flaw — applying a stated pattern to a case.

lr.difficultyReason: Unwarranted generalization from a tiny, unrepresentative sample. Only (D) replicates the same leap from a handful of cases to a sweeping claim.
lr.stimulus: I've read three novels by contemporary British authors, and I disliked all three. Contemporary British fiction is clearly not worth reading.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The last two movies directed by Silva flopped at the box office. Therefore, Silva's next movie will also flop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: This restaurant serves excellent pasta. Therefore, it probably serves excellent risotto as well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a painting is by Goya, it is valuable. This painting is valuable, so it must be by Goya.

choices.label: D
choices.text: I've eaten at four Vietnamese restaurants in the city, and all four had slow service. Vietnamese restaurants in this city are just slow.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Jazz venues have been closing in our city. Therefore, live music in general is dying out.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: a few personal experiences (three novels) are used to condemn an entire category (contemporary British fiction). (D) does the same: four restaurant visits used to condemn every Vietnamese restaurant in the city.
explanations.A: Predicts a future event from a pattern — different structure (forecast, not sweeping generalization about a category).
explanations.B: Compositional extension from one dish to another — not a sample-to-population move.
explanations.C: Affirming the consequent — a conditional flaw, not generalization.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Scope shift from one subcategory (jazz) to a broader category (live music), not a small-sample generalization.

lr.difficultyReason: Plain equivocation on a single word ('natural') across premise and conclusion. Only (A) shifts meaning of one term between premise and conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Everything natural is good for you. Poison ivy grows naturally in the forest. Therefore, poison ivy is good for you.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nothing is better than eternal happiness. A cold sandwich is better than nothing. Therefore, a cold sandwich is better than eternal happiness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All fruits are healthy. An apple is a fruit. Therefore, an apple is healthy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most athletes train daily. Priya is an athlete. Therefore, Priya probably trains daily.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a law is unjust, it should not be obeyed. This law is unjust. Therefore, it should not be obeyed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Exercise improves health. Marta exercises. Therefore, Marta is healthy.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: 'natural' shifts meaning from 'wholesome / good-for-you natural' (premise 1) to 'occurring in nature' (premise 2). (A) equivocates on 'nothing' — 'no thing is better' vs. 'is better than no food at all.' Same meaning-shift flaw.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Valid categorical syllogism — no equivocation, no flaw.
explanations.C: Valid probabilistic inference; no shift in meaning.
explanations.D: Valid modus ponens — no flaw.
explanations.E: Overreaches from 'improves health' to 'is healthy,' but no single word shifts meaning — different flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Correlation-to-causation in an economics setting. Only (E) treats a co-occurring trend as proof of causation. Other answers are valid or commit clearly different errors.
lr.stimulus: In countries where citizens drink more coffee, average life expectancy is higher. Drinking more coffee, therefore, must increase life expectancy.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following most closely parallels the flawed reasoning above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a country has a high GDP, it tends to have low unemployment. This country has low unemployment, so it must have a high GDP.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two of my coworkers caught colds this week. Everyone at work is going to get sick.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All European nations use the euro. Germany is a European nation. Therefore, Germany uses the euro.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stock market rose last year, and so did housing prices. The stock market rise must have caused the housing prices to climb.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A used car that looks clean is probably well-maintained. This car looks clean. So it's probably well-maintained.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: two things rise together (coffee consumption, life expectancy) and the author concludes one causes the other. (D) is the same move: stock market and housing prices both rose, so one caused the other.
explanations.A: Affirming the consequent — a conditional flaw, not correlation-to-causation.
explanations.B: Hasty generalization from two cases, not a causal leap from correlation.
explanations.C: Valid categorical reasoning. The premise is actually false, but the structure is not flawed.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Applies a general pattern to a specific case — no flaw, and not causal reasoning.

lr.difficultyReason: Classic affirming-the-consequent in a legal context. Only (B) reverses a stated conditional. The other answers present valid reasoning or different fallacies.
lr.stimulus: Any defendant who forged the signature had access to the notary's office. Ms. Lowe had access to the notary's office. Therefore, Ms. Lowe forged the signature.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anyone who wins the marathon trains daily. Ravi did not train daily. Therefore, Ravi did not win the marathon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any hiker who reached the summit carried a rope. Dana carried a rope. Therefore, Dana reached the summit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All licensed pilots have passed the medical exam. Kira is a licensed pilot. Therefore, Kira has passed the medical exam.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most violinists in the orchestra studied abroad. Tomas is a violinist in the orchestra. Therefore, Tomas probably studied abroad.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the window is open, the alarm will sound. The alarm is sounding, so the window is open — unless the sensor is broken.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: having access was necessary for forgery, not sufficient; treating it as sufficient commits sufficient-necessary confusion. (B) makes the same error: carrying a rope was necessary for reaching the summit, but the argument treats it as sufficient.
explanations.A: Valid — denying the necessary condition. No flaw.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Valid categorical reasoning — no flaw.
explanations.D: Valid probabilistic inference from 'most' — no flaw.
explanations.E: Hedges the conclusion; the 'unless' clause avoids the flaw the stimulus commits.

lr.difficultyReason: Unwarranted generalization in a technology context. Only (A) jumps from a single case to a sweeping verdict on a whole category. Other answers commit transparently different flaws.
lr.stimulus: My new tablet froze twice in the first week. Clearly, tablets from this manufacturer are unreliable.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first two chapters of this textbook contained errors. The whole textbook must be poorly edited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a phone battery is damaged, it drains quickly. This phone's battery drains quickly, so it must be damaged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most users of this software report bugs. Teo is a user, so he has probably reported a bug.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apps that go viral usually have clever marketing. This app has clever marketing. Therefore, it will go viral.

choices.label: E
choices.text: New cars with high safety ratings sell well. This car has a high safety rating, so it will sell well — if people hear about it.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: a tiny experience (two freezes in one unit) is projected onto an entire manufacturer's product line. (A) mirrors the move: defects in two chapters are projected onto the whole textbook.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Affirming the consequent — different flaw.
explanations.C: Valid probabilistic inference.
explanations.D: Sufficient-necessary confusion — treats marketing as sufficient when it's only typical.
explanations.E: Hedges the conclusion and therefore is not clearly flawed.

lr.difficultyReason: Equivocation on the word 'right' across premise and conclusion in an ethics stimulus. Only (C) matches by shifting the meaning of a single term between premises.
lr.stimulus: Every citizen has a right to free speech. Whatever a person has a right to do is the right thing to do. Therefore, whatever a citizen says is the right thing to say.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All triangles have three sides. This figure has three sides. Therefore, this figure is a triangle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People who skip meals are often tired. Lin skips meals. So Lin is often tired.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A sound investment is a safe one. Soundproof walls keep noise out. Therefore, walls that keep noise out are safe investments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most voters prefer candidate Reyes. Maria is a voter. So Maria probably prefers Reyes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: When temperatures drop, ice forms. Ice has formed. So temperatures have dropped.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: 'right' shifts from 'entitled/permitted' to 'morally correct.' (C) equivocates on 'sound': 'safe/sensible investment' vs. 'sound as in noise.' Same single-word meaning shift across premises.
explanations.A: Valid structure except that having three sides is sufficient for being a triangle — no equivocation.
explanations.B: Valid probabilistic inference. No meaning shift.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Valid reasoning from 'most' — no flaw.
explanations.E: Affirming the consequent — different flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Correlation-to-causation in an environmental-policy setting. Only (B) treats co-occurrence as causation. Others commit different errors or reason validly.
lr.stimulus: Cities that installed more bike lanes last decade saw air quality improve over the same period. Installing bike lanes, therefore, causes air quality to improve.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recent graduates who attended networking events got jobs within six months. Attending networking events must make graduates more competent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neighborhoods that planted more street trees last year reported lower crime rates. Planting street trees must cause crime to drop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any runner who finishes the race gets a medal. Oskar got a medal, so Oskar must have finished the race.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every play I've seen at this theater has been disappointing. The theater must never put on good plays.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A solar panel works when it receives light. This panel is working, so it must be receiving light.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: two trends co-occurred in the same places (more bike lanes, better air) and the author concludes causation. (B) is the same move: tree-planting and crime drops co-occurred, and the author infers causation.
explanations.A: Tempting, but the conclusion shifts topic to 'competence' rather than to getting jobs — scope shift rather than pure correlation-to-causation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Affirming the consequent — different flaw.
explanations.D: Unwarranted generalization from a sample, not correlation-to-causation.
explanations.E: Valid — requires light, has light, so it works. No flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Sufficient-necessary confusion in a linguistics context. Only (E) reverses a stated conditional. Others are valid or commit different fallacies.
lr.stimulus: Anyone fluent in Portuguese can understand some written Spanish. Carla can understand some written Spanish. Therefore, Carla is fluent in Portuguese.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every experienced translator knows at least two languages. Yuki is not an experienced translator. So Yuki doesn't know two languages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most native speakers of a language speak it without an accent. Sven is a native speaker, so Sven probably speaks without an accent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: People who read a lot have large vocabularies. Reading, therefore, causes vocabulary to grow.

choices.label: D
choices.text: My two roommates are studying German. Everyone in our building must be studying German.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Everyone who has taken the advanced class can recite the declensions. Nadia can recite the declensions. Therefore, Nadia has taken the advanced class.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: fluency in Portuguese is sufficient for understanding some written Spanish, but the argument treats it as necessary — classic sufficient-necessary reversal. (E) runs the same move: taking the advanced class is sufficient for reciting the declensions, but the argument treats it as necessary.
explanations.A: Denying a necessary condition — different structure (and valid, if one reads the conditional as stated).
explanations.B: Valid probabilistic inference from 'most.' No flaw.
explanations.C: Correlation-to-causation — different flaw.
explanations.D: Unwarranted generalization — different flaw.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: the stimulus treats a sufficient condition as though it were necessary and then generalizes from one instance to a population. Two choices match one half of the flaw but not both; the correct answer replicates both moves in a different domain.
lr.stimulus: Nutritionist: Anyone who eats a serving of oily fish each day will lower their risk of heart disease. Mira eats oily fish every day, and her cardiologist tells her that her risk of heart disease is low. It follows that lowering one's risk of heart disease requires daily consumption of oily fish, and that patients who do not eat oily fish must therefore be at elevated risk.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the nutritionist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Studying two hours a night is enough to pass the bar exam. Daniel studies two hours a night and passed the bar. So studying two hours a night is the only way to pass the bar, and anyone who studies less than that must fail.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daily meditation reduces stress in those who practice it. Since Hugo reports reduced stress, he probably meditates daily.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Regular exercise lowers blood pressure. Regular exercise also improves sleep. So anyone whose blood pressure is low probably sleeps well.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Everyone who trains at high altitude builds endurance. Anika trained at high altitude, so Anika built endurance. Therefore, high-altitude training is widely available to athletes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reading aloud to children improves their vocabulary. Most parents who read aloud to their children are well educated. So well-educated parents produce children with the best vocabularies.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: (i) flips sufficient (oily fish is enough to lower risk) into necessary (required), and (ii) generalizes from one person's case to all patients. (A) flips sufficient (two hours is enough to pass) into necessary (only way) and generalizes from Daniel's case to everyone who studies less.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Parallel topic (health habit) but a different flaw — concluding from an effect back to its cause, not a sufficient/necessary swap.
explanations.C: Different flaw — treating two separate effects of one cause as though they caused each other.
explanations.D: Has the right structural opening but the conclusion drifts to an unrelated claim about availability, so the flaw is in the wrong position rather than parallel.
explanations.E: Correlational overreach about educated parents — a different flaw dressed in similar vocabulary.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw combining a part-to-whole (compositional) error with a category shift from 'some' to 'every.' Three choices are surface-parallel; only one replicates both the composition move and the universalization.
lr.stimulus: Each player on the Riverton chess club has won at least one regional tournament. Therefore, the Riverton chess club as a whole has won every regional tournament, and any team that includes a Riverton member is assured of a regional title.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each musician in the Halden Quartet has performed at Carnegie Hall. So the Halden Quartet has performed at Carnegie Hall as an ensemble, and any group that includes a Halden musician must have performed there too.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most of the dancers in the Astoria company trained in Paris. So the company's style is probably Parisian, and dancers who leave the company will carry that style with them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Velaris law firm has won every major antitrust case it has argued. So each of its partners has personally won a major antitrust case.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each scientist on the Terra team has published in a leading journal. So at least one Terra paper has appeared in a leading journal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every runner on the Corbel track squad has finished a marathon under three hours. Therefore, the squad's average marathon time is under three hours.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: attributes an individual-member property ('won a tournament') to the collective, then extends it universally to any group containing a member. (A) attributes 'performed at Carnegie Hall' from individuals to the quartet and then to any group containing one — identical compound move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Starts from 'most,' not 'each,' and the flaw is a stylistic generalization rather than a compositional leap.
explanations.C: Reverses the direction — whole-to-part rather than part-to-whole — so the flaw is in the wrong structural position.
explanations.D: Valid inference — if each scientist has published, then at least one paper has appeared. Not flawed at all.
explanations.E: Valid inference — a universal property of members can legitimately yield a claim about the group's average. Not flawed.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: correlation-to-causation fused with a scope shift from a single country to the global economy. Trap choices replicate one move but not the other.
lr.stimulus: In Norway, as the share of electric vehicles on the road has risen, urban air quality has improved. It follows that electric vehicles cause cleaner air, and that worldwide adoption of electric vehicles is therefore the primary means by which humanity will solve global air pollution.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In Japan, as broadband speeds have risen, small-business productivity has risen. So faster broadband causes higher productivity, and expanding broadband globally will be the chief driver of worldwide economic growth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In Denmark, cycling rates have increased while obesity rates have fallen. So cycling probably causes weight loss.

choices.label: C
choices.text: In several European countries, reading scores have risen alongside increased library funding. Therefore, library funding must be the main cause of rising literacy in those particular countries.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Many nations have reduced smoking rates through taxation. Therefore, taxation of unhealthy products is the most effective public-health tool available to governments everywhere.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In Finland, school meal programs are associated with better student health. So Finland's particular meal program improves health, and its specific curriculum should be exported worldwide.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: (i) treats a within-one-country correlation as causation, then (ii) inflates a local effect into the primary global solution. (A) replicates both: a Japan-internal correlation treated as causal, then inflated to the chief driver of worldwide economic growth.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Commits only the causation-from-correlation half; no global scope shift.
explanations.C: Stays within the same set of countries and stops at the causal claim. Only half the flaw.
explanations.D: Starts from a generalization across many nations, so the scope shift isn't there; the flaw is different.
explanations.E: Has a geographic expansion but leaps to a curriculum claim the premise doesn't touch — the flaw is a substitution in the conclusion, not a compound correlation/scope error.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw combines equivocation on 'right' (legal right vs. moral entitlement) with an unwarranted move from 'some' to 'all.' Traps include a valid analog and an equivocation without the quantifier move.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: Some citizens have a right to carry firearms, in the sense that the law permits them to do so. But a right, properly understood, is a moral entitlement. Therefore, all citizens have a moral entitlement to carry firearms, and any restriction on that entitlement is unjust.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some workers have a duty to report safety violations, in the sense that company policy requires them to. But a duty, properly understood, is a binding moral obligation. Therefore, every worker has a moral obligation to report safety violations, and any worker who does not report them is acting immorally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most judges have a duty to recuse themselves when they have a personal interest in a case. A duty is a moral obligation. Therefore, judges who fail to recuse themselves in such cases act immorally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some drivers have a license to operate commercial trucks, and a license is a form of permission. So every driver has permission to operate commercial trucks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some doctors are authorized to prescribe controlled substances. Since authorization is a form of trust, these doctors are trusted by the community, and patients should therefore follow any of their recommendations.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Certain parents are permitted by law to homeschool their children. Since a legal permission is a form of choice, every parent has the choice to homeschool, and any parent who does not is failing their children.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: equivocates on 'right' (legal permission → moral entitlement) and expands 'some' to 'all,' concluding any restriction is unjust. (A) equivocates on 'duty' (policy-required → moral obligation) and expands 'some' to 'every,' concluding that non-reporters act immorally — identical compound move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Starts from 'most' and omits the equivocation — duty is already used morally in both premises. The quantifier shift is also minor.
explanations.C: Has the some-to-every move but no equivocation: 'license' and 'permission' aren't being traded on two distinct senses.
explanations.D: Accurate reasoning is disguised as flawed by the final overreach, but the core move is a chained inference about trust, not a sense-shift on a single term.
explanations.E: Equivocates on 'choice,' but the conclusion is a moral indictment that doesn't parallel 'any restriction is unjust' — the flaw lands in a different structural slot.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: absence of evidence treated as evidence of absence, combined with a shift from 'in our samples' to 'in this region.' Several answer choices nail one half but miss the other.
lr.stimulus: Field biologist: In our three summer surveys of the Dorval wetlands, we never observed the marsh wren. Our surveys covered only the eastern portion of the wetlands. Since we did not detect the marsh wren in those surveys, the species must be absent from the wetlands entirely, and conservation plans for the Dorval marsh wren should therefore be canceled.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the field biologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In three spot checks of the company's eastern warehouse, auditors found no expired inventory. Since the auditors did not find expired inventory during those checks, there must be none anywhere in the company, and the firm's expired-inventory write-off policy should be eliminated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several recent dives of the Pelos reef found no evidence of the striped grouper, though divers covered only a small area. It is therefore possible that the species is rarer than previously thought.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surveys of a small southern district failed to detect the rust moth. Since the rust moth has never been detected there, it must be rare in that district, though it may thrive elsewhere.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Audits of the eastern branch of a bank revealed no fraud. So the eastern branch is free of fraud, and the bank's other branches should adopt its procedures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Our annual inspections of the northern bridge have never uncovered structural defects. The inspections are thorough and cover the whole bridge. So the northern bridge is probably structurally sound, and scheduled inspections can continue at the current interval.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: absence-in-a-partial-survey is treated as absence everywhere, and a policy (conservation) is canceled on that basis. (A) replicates: absence in partial spot checks is treated as absence company-wide, and the write-off policy is eliminated — same compound flaw, same concluding move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Not flawed — the conclusion is properly hedged ('possible... rarer than previously thought'). Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed.
explanations.C: Half-flaw only: the conclusion is restricted to the district, not overextended, and the 'rare' claim is measured.
explanations.D: Extends a local absence to a local conclusion, then pivots to a recommendation about other branches. The recommended policy change is in the wrong structural slot — it doesn't parallel canceling plans for the very region surveyed.
explanations.E: Not flawed — premises specify thorough coverage of the whole bridge, so the conclusion is warranted.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: a category error (treating a type-level entity as if it behaved like its instances) combined with a hasty generalization. Traps either commit only the category move or only the generalization.
lr.stimulus: The novel, as a literary form, has evolved for over three centuries and continues to adapt to new readers. Since The Windward Letters is a novel, it too must be evolving and adapting to new readers. And since it has sold well this year, novels in general are clearly thriving as never before.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sonnet, as a poetic form, has developed over five centuries and continues to change. Since 'Summer's Hour' is a sonnet, it too must be changing over time. And since it has recently been widely anthologized, sonnets as a form are flourishing more than ever.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The blues, as a musical genre, has influenced many later styles. So any given blues song has influenced many later styles, and the blues is the most influential genre of the last century.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The string quartet has been a staple of chamber music since Haydn. Since the Velari Quartet is performing tonight, the genre is alive, and string quartets are the most popular chamber form today.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The essay, as a form, has reinvented itself many times. Since 'On the Terrace' is an essay, it reinvents itself. Therefore, individual essays never stay the same from one reading to the next.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The documentary film has always aimed at truth-telling. Since Rivers at Dusk is a documentary, its makers aim at truth-telling. Documentaries remain one of several important film genres.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ascribes a type-level property ('evolving over centuries') to a single instance, then leaps from one work's sales to the flourishing of the entire form. (A) mirrors both moves exactly: type-level change ascribed to one sonnet, then one anthologization used to conclude the form is flourishing.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Commits only the category error (type-level property to every instance); no sales-style leap to the form's flourishing.
explanations.C: The type-to-instance move is weaker (a performance, not a property-transfer), and the final claim is about popularity without the one-instance springboard. Parallel topic, different flaw.
explanations.D: Category error is present, but the conclusion drifts to an implausible claim about essays changing between readings — the flaw is in the wrong structural slot.
explanations.E: Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed — the 'aim at truth-telling' premise arguably does transfer, and the closing claim is measured rather than an overreach.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: confuses percentage change with absolute change, then generalizes from one company's quarter to the entire industry. Students who catch only the percentage/absolute swap will be tempted by a trap that lacks the industry leap.
lr.stimulus: Analyst: Last quarter, Corten Software's profit margin rose by 20 percent, while its rival Bylor's margin rose by only 5 percent. So Corten made far more profit than Bylor last quarter, and the software industry as a whole must be shifting decisively in Corten's favor.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Last season, the Adler Bakery's customer count rose 30 percent, while the Madrona Bakery's count rose only 4 percent. So Adler served far more customers than Madrona last season, and the city's bakery market must be turning decisively toward Adler.

choices.label: B
choices.text: This year, Ganz Motors raised prices by 8 percent while Volera raised them by 3 percent. So Ganz's cars now cost more on average than Volera's, and buyers should therefore prefer Volera.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clinic A's patient load grew by 12 percent while Clinic B's grew by 11 percent. So Clinic A now sees more patients than Clinic B, and the regional market favors Clinic A.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Last year, the Haldane School's test scores rose 15 percent, while Crossfield's rose only 5 percent. So Haldane's teachers are better than Crossfield's.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Profit margins at Orell Industries rose sharply last quarter, so Orell probably made more profit than in any previous quarter, and investors are likely to favor Orell in the year ahead.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: confuses a larger percentage rise with a larger absolute amount, then generalizes from one quarter to an industry trend. (A) replicates both: larger percentage rise conflated with larger absolute customer count, then generalized from one bakery's season to the city market.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Percentage/absolute confusion exists but the conclusion is a recommendation for buyers, not an industry trend — the generalization move is in the wrong slot.
explanations.C: The percentages are too close to drive the stimulus's lopsided inference, and the mismatch between 'grew by X%' and 'sees more patients' is different in kind.
explanations.D: Different second flaw — attributing test-score growth to teacher quality rather than generalizing from one year to an industry.
explanations.E: Commits only the generalization half; no percentage-vs-absolute comparison between rivals.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: an ad hominem-adjacent move (dismissing a speaker's argument because of the speaker's profession) combined with a leap from 'no good reason to accept X' to 'X is false.' Traps include a pure ad hominem and a pure absence-to-denial fallacy.
lr.stimulus: Critic: The economist's forecast that inflation will ease by next spring should be dismissed. She works for a bank that profits when borrowers expect low inflation, so her forecast cannot be trusted. Since we therefore have no good reason to accept her forecast, we can conclude that inflation will not ease by next spring.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lawyer's claim that the new statute is constitutional should be dismissed. He is employed by a firm that benefits when the statute is upheld, so his opinion cannot be trusted. Since we therefore have no good reason to accept his claim, we may conclude that the statute is unconstitutional.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The union leader's assertion that wages have stagnated is self-serving, so her assertion can be ignored. Since we can ignore her assertion, wages have not stagnated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pundit supports the tax increase only because his favored party proposed it. So his support is biased, and we should therefore ignore everything he says on any issue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The researcher's study of air pollution was funded by an environmental group. Because of that funding, we have reason to scrutinize the methodology, though we should not dismiss the findings outright.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Since the journalist has never lived in the region she reports on, she cannot understand it, and her accounts of the region's politics must be inaccurate, so the region's politics are not as she describes.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: dismisses a forecast on professional-interest grounds and then moves from 'no good reason to accept it' to 'its contrary is true.' (A) mirrors both: dismissal of the lawyer's claim on firm-interest grounds and a move from 'no reason to accept' to 'the statute is unconstitutional.'
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Commits the ad-hominem and absence-to-denial moves but compresses them into one step; the 'self-serving' charge isn't tied to a professional interest in the way the stimulus ties it to the bank.
explanations.C: Ad hominem with a different conclusion structure — 'ignore everything he says' broadens the flaw to all topics rather than concluding the contrary of the specific claim.
explanations.D: Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed — the conclusion is measured ('scrutinize, not dismiss'). Not parallel, because the stimulus is flawed and the correct answer must be flawed.
explanations.E: Different opening — an argument from lack of residence rather than professional interest — and the conclusion is an ad hominem-adjacent but distinct move.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: conflating a statistical average with every individual in a group, then drawing a universal policy conclusion. Traps include an average/individual confusion without the policy leap and a valid analog.
lr.stimulus: City planner: The average commute in our city is 28 minutes. Since the average is 28 minutes, every commuter in the city must spend roughly 28 minutes traveling to work each day. Therefore, any transit project that shortens commutes by even a few minutes will benefit every resident equally, and the city should fund only those projects that reduce the average.
lr.questionStem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to the flawed reasoning in the city planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: School board member: The average class size in our district is 24 students. Since the average is 24, every class in the district must have roughly 24 students. Therefore, any policy that lowers class size by even a few students will benefit every student equally, and we should fund only those policies that reduce the average.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The average rainfall in our county last year was 32 inches. Since 32 inches is the average, every part of the county received roughly that amount, and farmers in every part should expect comparable yields.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The average wage in the restaurant industry is $15 per hour. Since some workers earn less than the average, policies that raise the minimum wage will help the lowest-paid workers most.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The average patient at our clinic waits 20 minutes. Since 20 minutes is the average, some patients wait longer and some shorter; our goal should be to reduce the longest waits rather than the average.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The average house price in the neighborhood has risen by 10 percent, so every house has risen by 10 percent, and each owner's equity has risen accordingly.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: treats the average as a property of each individual and then draws a universal policy conclusion that funding should target the average. (A) replicates: the 24-student average is treated as each class's size, and the policy conclusion restricts funding to policies that reduce the average.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Commits only the average/individual confusion; no policy conclusion that restricts funding.
explanations.C: Not flawed — the reasoning correctly notes variance around an average and draws a measured policy inference.
explanations.D: Not flawed — the reasoning distinguishes average from distribution and chooses a reasonable goal.
explanations.E: Commits only the average/individual confusion about house prices with a further equity claim; the policy-funding slot from the stimulus isn't present.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound flaw: treats a speaker's inability to give reasons for a belief as grounds to reject the belief (epistemic category error), and then generalizes to reject a whole body of knowledge. Traps replicate only one of the two moves.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Native speakers of a language cannot usually articulate the grammatical rules they follow. Since those speakers cannot state the rules, they must not actually know the rules, and the very idea that native speakers possess tacit grammatical knowledge is therefore a myth.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains flawed reasoning most similar to that in the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Skilled bicyclists cannot usually articulate the principles of balance they rely on. Since they cannot state the principles, they must not actually know them, and the very idea that cyclists possess tacit motor knowledge is a myth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Young children cannot usually explain why stories move them. So stories do not really move children, and adults who claim otherwise are mistaken.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Many jazz musicians can improvise without consciously thinking about music theory. This shows that music theory is irrelevant to improvisation, and formal training in theory is a waste of time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Experienced nurses can often detect subtle changes in a patient's condition without stating how they know. Because they cannot articulate the signs, their judgments are unreliable and should not influence clinical decisions.

choices.label: E
