choices.text: Competent chess players may not be able to articulate all the heuristics they use, but their results nonetheless show that the heuristics are real, so we should study their games carefully.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: moves from 'cannot articulate the rules' to 'does not know the rules,' then rejects the whole category of tacit knowledge as a myth. (A) replicates both: cyclists who cannot state balance principles are said not to know them, and tacit motor knowledge is rejected as a myth.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Different flaw — concludes children aren't moved, not that the category of being moved is mythical. The second move is missing.
explanations.C: Starts from a premise about independence from theory, not an inability to articulate it. The resulting flaw is a different kind of overreach.
explanations.D: Commits the articulation-to-ignorance move but stops at unreliability; doesn't reject the category of tacit clinical knowledge wholesale.
explanations.E: Not flawed — the reasoning correctly separates inability to articulate from absence of knowledge. Accurate reasoning disguised as flawed.

lr.difficultyReason: The stimulus weaves three errors together: equivocation on 'natural' (uncultivated vs. chemical-free), a universal generalization from a non-representative sample of heirloom tomatoes, and a sufficient-for-necessary swap turning 'naturalness suffices for nutritional value' into 'natural crops are the only nutritious crops.' The correct answer replicates all three moves.
lr.stimulus: Heirloom tomatoes grown in the wild woods near Asheville contain none of the synthetic pesticides applied on industrial farms, so they are entirely natural. And since everything natural is nutritionally superior, we may conclude that only wild-grown heirloom tomatoes are nutritionally superior to their cultivated counterparts.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Old-growth cedar harvested from the remote Alaskan coast has no artificial preservatives, and so it is entirely pure. Since everything pure is structurally stronger than its alternatives, we may conclude that only coastal old-growth cedar is structurally stronger than kiln-dried pine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the vineyards of the Mosel Valley use no herbicides, their Rieslings contain no residues. Rieslings with no residues are widely preferred by sommeliers, so Mosel Rieslings are widely preferred by sommeliers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Raw honey from alpine meadows contains no added sugars. Therefore, since consumers prefer foods with no added sugars, consumers prefer raw alpine honey to processed honey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Handwoven rugs from rural Anatolia use no synthetic dyes, so they are entirely authentic. Because authentic rugs appreciate in value, handwoven Anatolian rugs appreciate in value more than machine-made rugs do.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wild salmon caught off the Kenai Peninsula are free of farm-pen antibiotics, and so they are purer than farmed salmon. Since purer fish are healthier, wild Kenai salmon are healthier than farmed salmon.

explanations.correct: A mirrors all three moves: it equivocates on 'pure' (free of preservatives vs. unadulterated in any sense), generalizes from a narrow example to a universal 'everything pure is stronger,' and flips a sufficient condition ('purity suffices for strength') into a necessary one ('only this cedar is stronger'). The compound flaw is identical in structure to the stimulus.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Contains a linking chain but no equivocation and no sufficient/necessary reversal — the conclusion follows validly from the premises as stated.
explanations.C: A single correlation-to-preference step; no universal claim and no 'only' reversal in the conclusion.
explanations.D: Equivocates on 'authentic' but concludes with a comparative claim, not an 'only' exclusivity claim; it is missing the sufficient/necessary flip.
explanations.E: Valid chain: free of antibiotics → purer → healthier. No equivocation, no universal overreach, no exclusivity reversal.

lr.difficultyReason: Three compounding errors: (1) composition fallacy (what is true of a part of the orchestra is ascribed to the whole); (2) ambiguity on 'balanced' (acoustic balance vs. repertoire balance); (3) the conclusion then inverts the conditional, treating 'balance implies acclaim' as 'only balanced orchestras are acclaimed.' Each answer choice replicates some but not all of these moves.
lr.stimulus: Every section of the Prague Chamber Orchestra — strings, winds, brass — produces a balanced sound on its own. So the orchestra as a whole must be balanced. Because only balanced orchestras win international acclaim, the Prague Chamber Orchestra must be among the acclaimed ensembles of its generation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each of the attorneys at Merton & Voss is persuasive in oral argument, so Merton & Voss is a persuasive firm. Because persuasive firms win most of their trials, Merton & Voss wins most of its trials.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every department at Halloran College — humanities, sciences, arts — is rigorous on its own. So the college as a whole is rigorous. And because only rigorous colleges produce Rhodes Scholars, Halloran must be among the colleges producing Rhodes Scholars.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each player on the Winfield hockey team has excellent stickhandling, so the team must have excellent stickhandling. Teams with excellent stickhandling tend to win championships, so Winfield will probably win the championship.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every chapter in Professor Lin's new book is clearly written, so her book is clearly written. Clearly written books sell well, so her book will sell well.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each division of Volterra Motors meets its quarterly targets, so Volterra meets its annual targets. Since companies that meet annual targets are admired by investors, Volterra is admired by investors.

explanations.correct: B replicates all three moves: composition (each department rigorous → college rigorous); equivocation on 'rigorous' (department-level rigor vs. institutional reputation); and the 'only rigorous colleges produce Rhodes Scholars' conditional flipped into a claim that Halloran is among the Rhodes-producing colleges. The compound flaw matches precisely.
explanations.A: Composition is present, but there is no 'only' conditional reversal; the chain is linear.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Hedged conclusion ('probably') and no equivocation on 'stickhandling'; missing two of the three moves.
explanations.D: Simple composition followed by a valid inference; no ambiguity and no reversal.
explanations.E: Contains a different compositional flaw (quarterly vs. annual) and a scope shift, but no sufficient/necessary reversal in the final step.

lr.difficultyReason: Three stacked errors: (1) correlation mistaken for causation between statin use and reduced cardiac events; (2) the causal claim is then universalized beyond the study population; (3) base-rate reversal — because most patients with low cardiac events are on statins, a patient on statins is presumed to have low cardiac event risk. The correct answer must stack all three.
lr.stimulus: A ten-year observational study in Uppsala found that patients taking statins had 30% fewer cardiac events than those not taking them. It follows that statins prevent cardiac events in any patient population. Since most low-risk cardiac patients in our clinic are on statins, any patient we place on statins will likely be a low-risk cardiac patient.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A longitudinal survey in Oslo showed that readers of literary fiction score higher on empathy tests than non-readers. Therefore, literary fiction cultivates empathy in any reader. Because most empathic professionals read literary fiction, any professional who begins reading literary fiction will likely become empathic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A city-wide study found that neighborhoods with more trees have lower asthma rates. So trees must improve respiratory health. Therefore, planting trees in any city will reduce its asthma rates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Surveys show that frequent meditators report lower stress. Since meditation calms the mind, anyone who meditates will feel less stressed. Most people who feel less stressed have stable relationships, so meditation stabilizes relationships.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A regional audit found that firms using agile methodology deliver software faster than those using waterfall. Agile therefore accelerates delivery universally. Anyone who adopts agile will deliver software faster than their waterfall competitors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A decade-long trial showed that communities consuming more olive oil had lower rates of stroke. So olive oil prevents stroke. Since most stroke-free communities consume olive oil, any community that begins consuming olive oil will be stroke-free.

explanations.correct: A matches all three moves: (1) correlation-to-causation (readers scoring higher → fiction cultivates empathy); (2) universal overreach ('in any reader'); (3) base-rate reversal — 'most empathic professionals read fiction, so any professional who reads will be empathic.' The compound is exact.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Correlation-to-causation plus universalization, but no base-rate reversal — the final step is a straightforward (if unwarranted) generalization.
explanations.C: Introduces a second causal chain (meditation → relationships) rather than a base-rate inversion; the flaw pattern diverges on the third step.
explanations.D: Two moves only — correlation-to-causation and universalization. Missing the base-rate reversal step.
explanations.E: Close, but the conclusion is 'stroke-free,' a certainty claim, while the stimulus concludes a probabilistic 'likely be low-risk.' The strength mismatch makes E off-by-one.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) ad hominem dismissal that slides into (2) a genetic fallacy generalized into a universal claim about a field, which in turn (3) inverts a conditional — from 'biased sources cannot establish truth' to 'only unbiased sources can.' The correct answer must replicate the slide from personal attack through field-level generalization to necessary-condition inversion.
lr.stimulus: The historian Ackroyd was a lifelong royalist, so his account of the Glorious Revolution cannot be trusted. Indeed, because any historian with political loyalties is biased, the entire field of political history is compromised. It follows that only accounts by politically unaffiliated historians can give us genuine historical knowledge.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following exhibits a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The critic Beaumont was a declared modernist, so his review of the new opera is biased. Because biased critics misjudge opera, Beaumont misjudged this opera, and so his review should be disregarded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The economist Halvarsson advised a sitting government, so her forecasts cannot be trusted. Since any economist advising a government is compromised, the entire discipline of macroeconomic forecasting is unreliable. Therefore, only forecasts produced by economists with no governmental ties can qualify as legitimate forecasts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The journalist Ruiz has taken corporate sponsorship, so his coverage of that corporation should be discounted. Sponsored journalism is often biased, and biased journalism misleads readers. Therefore, Ruiz's readers are likely misled about the corporation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Pelham once consulted for an industrial client, and so his published findings are suspect. Because published findings by consultants are frequently disputed, Dr. Pelham's findings will probably be disputed as well.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The statistician Okoro worked briefly for a polling firm, so she is biased. Since bias invalidates polling, her polls are invalid. The only valid polls are those she did not design.

explanations.correct: B mirrors the slide: personal attack on Halvarsson → universal claim about all economists with government ties → field-wide compromise → only unaffiliated economists produce 'legitimate' forecasts. All three moves match the stimulus structure.
explanations.A: Personal attack plus a chain, but no field-level generalization and no inversion to 'only X can produce knowledge.'
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Hedged throughout ('often,' 'likely') and stops at a reader-level conclusion; no 'only' reversal.
explanations.D: Two moves, not three — no field-wide claim.
explanations.E: Personal attack and 'only' reversal, but the scope is restricted to Okoro's own polls rather than being universalized across a field.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) hasty generalization from one startup to all startups; (2) equivocation on 'fail' (bankruptcy vs. failing to reach projections); (3) denying the antecedent — from 'poor management leads to failure' to 'without poor management, no failure.' The correct answer must compound all three.
lr.stimulus: Morrow Analytics missed its revenue projections last quarter and was labeled a failure. It follows that every startup that misses projections has failed. And since poor management is what causes startups to fail, any startup with competent management will meet its projections.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments displays a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Riverton public library closed after its budget was cut, which proves that budget cuts destroy libraries. Every library facing budget cuts is at risk of being destroyed, and since inadequate public support causes library destruction, libraries with adequate public support are safe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kessler Foods recalled a batch of soup contaminated with listeria, which shows it cut corners on inspection. Therefore, every food manufacturer that recalls a batch has cut corners on inspection. Because corner-cutting causes recalls, any manufacturer that does not cut corners will never issue a recall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The manuscript Vellum & Ink was rejected by its publisher, so it was deemed unpublishable. Every manuscript rejected by a publisher is unpublishable, and since a weak premise causes rejection, manuscripts without weak premises are never rejected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Santillan's clinic was cited by the regulator last year, meaning her clinic was compromised. Every clinic cited by regulators is compromised, and because lax protocols cause citations, any clinic with strict protocols will never be cited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The engineering firm Aldebaran lost its bid on the bridge contract, so it is uncompetitive. Since every firm that loses a major bid is uncompetitive, and uncompetitive firms have poor leadership, Aldebaran's leadership is poor.

explanations.correct: B compounds the same three moves: hasty generalization (Kessler's recall → every recall means cut corners); equivocation on 'recall' (one batch vs. manufacturer reputation); and denying the antecedent (corner-cutting causes recalls → no corner-cutting, no recalls). The strength of the conclusion ('never') matches the stimulus's universal closure.
explanations.A: Generalization and denial-of-antecedent are present, but 'destroy' and 'at risk of being destroyed' are not equivocal — the argument holds 'destruction' constant. Two of three moves.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Close, but the final step shifts the dimension: 'weak premise causes rejection' is inverted, but without the equivocation on 'rejected' vs. 'unpublishable' being fully carried through.
explanations.D: The conclusion retains the same term ('cited') throughout — no equivocation. And the final 'never' is a denial of antecedent, but only two of three moves.
explanations.E: Runs the chain forward rather than inverting the final conditional; the structure is linear rather than compound-flawed in the stimulus's way.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) percentage-vs-absolute confusion (share of workforce vs. head count); (2) universalization across a region; (3) affirming the consequent — from 'automation reduces manufacturing share' to 'because manufacturing share has declined, automation must have caused it.' The correct answer must stack all three.
lr.stimulus: In the Ruhr region, manufacturing has fallen from 40% of the workforce to 25% over two decades, meaning fewer people than ever work in manufacturing there. This pattern must therefore hold across all industrialized regions. And since automation reduces manufacturing's share of the workforce, the decline in the Ruhr must have been caused by automation.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In Kyoto, tourism has fallen from 30% of service-sector employment to 15% over a decade, so fewer residents than ever work in tourism there. The same must be true of all historic cities in Asia. And because budget airlines draw tourism away from traditional hubs, Kyoto's decline must have been caused by budget airlines.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In several European capitals, the share of cycling commuters has risen above 20%. This trend holds across all urban centers. Because bike lanes increase cycling share, the rise in these capitals must have been caused by bike lane construction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Across the Midwest, family farms now account for 10% of agricultural output, down from 25% thirty years ago. This must be true nationwide. Consolidation reduces the family farm share, and so consolidation caused the decline.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In Lombardy, the textile industry's workforce share dropped from 35% to 20%, which means fewer workers than ever are in textiles. This pattern extends across all Mediterranean economies. Since offshoring reduces textile employment share, offshoring must explain the Lombardy decline.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Coal mining in Appalachia fell from 18% of regional employment to 6%, so coal employs fewer people than ever in the region. The same must be true in every coal-producing country. And because environmental regulation reduces coal's share of employment, regulation caused the Appalachian decline.

explanations.correct: D mirrors all three moves precisely: percentage-to-absolute confusion ('35% to 20%' → 'fewer workers than ever'); universalization ('all Mediterranean economies'); and affirming the consequent (offshoring reduces textile share; share fell; therefore offshoring caused it). The compound matches the stimulus closely, and the domain is economics — distinct from the stimulus's industrial context but structurally identical.
explanations.A: Present all three moves but the causal agent named ('budget airlines') and the quantity ('service-sector employment') introduce a scope mismatch — the stimulus's causal agent is more tightly tied to the dependent variable than A's is.
explanations.B: Missing the percentage-to-absolute confusion — the rise in cycling share is stated as a share, not translated into absolute counts.
explanations.C: Lacks the 'fewer than ever' absolute-number mistranslation; the argument stays in percentage terms. Two of three moves.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Close, but 'fewer people than ever' is a stronger absolute claim and the scope ('every coal-producing country') is broader than the stimulus's 'all industrialized regions' — off-by-one in breadth.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) false dichotomy (either strict liability or no accountability); (2) this dichotomy is supported by an equivocation on 'accountability' (legal liability vs. moral responsibility); (3) the necessary condition is then flipped into a sufficient one. The correct answer must replicate all three in a new domain.
lr.stimulus: Either manufacturers are held strictly liable for defective products, or there is no product accountability at all. Strict liability is therefore the only way to ensure accountability. And since accountability is necessary for consumer trust, imposing strict liability will by itself be enough to restore consumer trust in our markets.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Either a university enforces a strict plagiarism policy, or it has no academic integrity. A strict policy is thus the only route to integrity. And because integrity is necessary for scholarly reputation, a strict plagiarism policy by itself will restore the university's scholarly reputation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Either a newspaper has a strong editorial board, or it has no standards at all. Therefore, a strong editorial board is the only way to maintain standards. Because standards are important to readers, a strong editorial board will make readers loyal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A museum either charges admission or it cannot maintain its collection. Charging admission is thus the only viable model. Since funds are necessary for maintenance, charging admission will be sufficient for maintenance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either a city has strong zoning or it has chaotic development. Zoning is the only cure for chaotic development. And because orderly development is desirable, zoning will make the city's development orderly.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either athletes are subject to random drug testing, or doping goes unchecked. Random testing is thus the only remedy. Because unchecked doping harms the sport's credibility, random testing will by itself restore the sport's credibility.

explanations.correct: A mirrors all three moves: false dichotomy (strict policy vs. no integrity); equivocation on 'integrity' (policy enforcement vs. scholarly integrity); and the necessary-to-sufficient flip (integrity necessary for reputation → strict policy sufficient for reputation). The domain shift to academia leaves the structure intact.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: False dichotomy and a chain, but the final inference is a reasonable probabilistic claim — no necessary-to-sufficient inversion of the right shape.
explanations.C: Explicitly labels the necessary-to-sufficient move, but lacks the equivocation step that makes the stimulus a three-error compound.
explanations.D: All three moves are present in broad outline but the equivocation on 'orderly' vs. 'zoning' is thin; the argument reads more like a two-step chain.
explanations.E: Very close, but shares a domain with the stimulus (legal/regulatory accountability) and keeps the word 'credibility' stable throughout — no equivocation. Two of three moves.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) appeal to authority by a non-expert (a successful poet pronouncing on neuroscience); (2) that authority claim is then generalized across a whole field; (3) circular reasoning — the conclusion ('creativity requires solitude') is smuggled in as a premise ('creative work only happens alone'). The correct answer must replicate all three in a new domain.
lr.stimulus: The celebrated poet Vernier has said that he composes only in solitude, so all neuroscience of creativity must treat solitude as essential. Indeed, creative work — being work that can only happen alone — requires solitude; and since what requires solitude cannot flourish in collaborative settings, genuine creativity cannot flourish in collaborative settings.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The renowned chef Kilbane insists that great cuisine demands only the freshest local produce, so all food science must treat freshness as the decisive variable. Great cuisine — being cuisine that only local produce can produce — requires local produce; and since what requires local produce cannot come from long supply chains, genuine cuisine cannot come from long supply chains.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The celebrated architect Nesbitt has said that great buildings require symmetry, so architectural theory must prioritize symmetry. Symmetrical buildings tend to last longer than asymmetrical ones, so the best-lasting buildings are symmetrical.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The acclaimed composer Viana claims that rhythm is the heart of music, so music theorists must agree. Since rhythm is the heart of music, a piece without rhythm is not music. Therefore a piece without rhythm cannot be called music.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The renowned physicist Hertzen has argued that quantum effects dominate at small scales, so quantum theory should focus there. Because quantum effects dominate at small scales, and what dominates at small scales must be studied there, quantum theory belongs at small scales.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The celebrated novelist Orellana has written that novels must have strong characters, so critics should weight characterization highly. Since strong characters require depth, and depth comes from solitude, novelists must work alone.

explanations.correct: A matches all three moves: non-expert authority (a chef on food science); field-wide generalization ('all food science must treat freshness as decisive'); and circular reasoning ('cuisine that only local produce can produce' smuggled in to conclude 'genuine cuisine cannot come from long supply chains'). The compound is identical.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Authority plus a causal chain, but no circularity — the conclusion 'best-lasting buildings are symmetrical' is independent of the premises.
explanations.C: Contains circularity but lacks the field-wide generalization step; the argument stays narrow.
explanations.D: The conclusion is a tautological restatement of the premise rather than a smuggled-in circular claim; the structure is flatter than the stimulus.
explanations.E: Authority and a chain, but the final inference borrows the stimulus's own vocabulary ('solitude') without replicating its three-step compound flaw.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) appeal to tradition; (2) a slippery-slope inference from one regulatory change to civilizational decline; (3) conflation of 'legal permission' with 'moral endorsement.' The correct answer must match all three.
lr.stimulus: For centuries, common law has treated inherited property as a fundamental right, and so it must remain so. Any reform that narrows inheritance will inevitably unravel the entire edifice of private property. Because the law permits inheriting property, the state clearly endorses the moral goodness of transferring wealth across generations, and any challenge to that endorsement is a challenge to civilization itself.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits flawed reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For decades, our municipal code has permitted single-family zoning, and so it must remain so. Any reform that allows multifamily housing will inevitably unravel the entire neighborhood character. Because zoning permits single-family homes, the city endorses the moral goodness of that way of life, and any challenge to it is a challenge to community itself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For generations, our university has required a Latin examination for all graduates, and so the requirement should remain. Removing Latin will weaken classical education. Because the university tests Latin, it values classical learning, and challenging the test is challenging classical learning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Our courts have long allowed juries to decide capital cases, so they must continue to do so. Removing the jury will undermine confidence in the legal system, and because juries are used, the legal system clearly endorses lay decision-making.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The constitution permits free assembly, so free assembly must be preserved. Restricting assembly would unravel democratic culture. Since the constitution permits assembly, the state approves of assembly, and assembling is therefore a civic virtue.

choices.label: E
choices.text: For a century the tax code has exempted certain charitable gifts, and so this exemption must persist. Narrowing it will slowly erode all philanthropy, and because the code permits the exemption, the government formally approves of charitable giving.

explanations.correct: A replicates all three moves: appeal to tradition (decades of single-family zoning); slippery slope (any reform unravels neighborhood character); conflation of legal permission with moral endorsement ('the city endorses the moral goodness' of single-family living). Closes with the civilizational-stakes rhetoric matching the stimulus.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Tradition and a weak consequence claim, but the slope is not 'unraveling' scale and the legal-moral conflation is weakly drawn.
explanations.C: Tradition and conflation present, but no slippery slope — the consequence claim is bounded ('confidence in the legal system').
explanations.D: Conflation and a slope, but the tradition appeal is replaced by a straight appeal to the constitution; the third move is missing its traditional framing.
explanations.E: Tradition and conflation, but the slope is described as 'erode' rather than the stimulus's systemic-unraveling frame, and the civilizational stakes are absent — off-by-one in scope.

lr.difficultyReason: Three errors: (1) survivorship bias (only surviving languages are studied); (2) the resulting pattern is generalized into a universal linguistic claim; (3) the generalization is then used to predict the future — past success becomes a guarantee of continued success. The correct answer must replicate all three.
lr.stimulus: Every surviving European language today has a written tradition going back at least five hundred years, so all European languages have always had long written traditions. Since languages with long written traditions persist, and since written tradition guarantees persistence, Basque — with its long written tradition — is guaranteed to persist for another five centuries.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every established monastery in Ireland has continuously kept a scriptorium for at least eight centuries, so all Irish monasteries have always kept scriptoria. Since monasteries with scriptoria endure, and because a scriptorium guarantees endurance, Glendalough Monastery — with its eight-century scriptorium — is guaranteed to endure another eight centuries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every skyscraper still standing in Chicago was built before 1960, so Chicago skyscrapers have always been built in that era. Because pre-1960 skyscrapers are sturdy, the Monadnock Building, which predates 1960, will continue to stand.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every bank that survived the 2008 crisis had diversified holdings, so all banks at that time had diversified holdings. Since diversified banks tend to weather downturns, Commerzbank, which is diversified, will weather any future downturn.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All surviving Etruscan bronzes show a high tin content, so Etruscan bronzes uniformly contained high tin. Because high-tin bronzes resist corrosion, the Arezzo Chimera — a high-tin Etruscan bronze — will resist corrosion for centuries to come.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every jazz standard still performed today was composed before 1970, so jazz standards have always dated to that era. Because pre-1970 standards have lasting appeal, 'Mood Indigo' will continue to be performed.

explanations.correct: A replicates all three moves: survivorship bias ('every established monastery' = those that survived); universal generalization ('all Irish monasteries have always kept scriptoria'); and the leap from 'guarantees endurance' to a future-prediction certainty ('guaranteed to endure another eight centuries'). The compound is identical and the domain shift (language to religious institutions) is clean.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Survivorship and generalization, but the conclusion is softer ('will continue to stand') and lacks the certainty language — off-by-one in strength.
explanations.C: Survivorship and generalization, but the final claim is narrowed ('any future downturn') and depends on a tendency rather than a guarantee — two of three moves.
explanations.D: Survivorship and generalization present, but the conclusion concerns a material property rather than a temporal persistence claim — the domain of the third move doesn't match.
explanations.E: Survivorship and a generalization, but the conclusion 'will continue to be performed' is a tendency-style claim, not a guarantee-level prediction; the third move is weaker than the stimulus's.

lr.difficultyReason: Textbook modus ponens at the 1-star anchor: a single conditional premise plus its antecedent yielding the consequent. Only one answer choice instantiates modus ponens; the others are modus tollens, affirming-the-consequent, or a disjunctive syllogism.
lr.stimulus: If the library's roof leaks during a heavy rain, then the rare manuscripts will be moved to the basement vault. The roof leaked during yesterday's storm. Therefore, the rare manuscripts were moved to the basement vault.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If the bakery sells out of sourdough, the baker makes a fresh batch overnight. The baker did not make a fresh batch overnight, so the bakery did not sell out of sourdough.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a patient has the flu, the patient will have a fever. This patient has a fever, so this patient has the flu.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the trail is muddy, hikers wear waterproof boots. The trail is muddy today. Therefore, hikers are wearing waterproof boots.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the concert is held indoors or it is canceled. The concert was not canceled, so it was held indoors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most lawyers who pass the bar exam on the first try studied in a formal course, so any lawyer who studied in a formal course probably passed on the first try.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A -> B; A; therefore B. That is modus ponens. (C) has the same structure: muddy trail -> waterproof boots; trail is muddy; therefore boots are being worn.
explanations.A: Modus tollens (A -> B; not B; therefore not A), not modus ponens.
explanations.B: Affirms the consequent (A -> B; B; therefore A) — an invalid form and not parallel to the valid stimulus.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Disjunctive syllogism (A or B; not B; therefore A), a different valid form.
explanations.E: Reverses a 'most' generalization; not a conditional chain at all.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple universal-to-particular instantiation. One premise is a universal statement, the second places an individual in the subject category, and the conclusion applies the predicate. Only one answer choice follows this shape.
lr.stimulus: Every member of the Montrose Chamber Orchestra has performed at Carnegie Hall. Yuki is a member of the Montrose Chamber Orchestra. Therefore, Yuki has performed at Carnegie Hall.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most professional chefs own at least one copper saucepan. Andre owns a copper saucepan, so Andre is probably a professional chef.

choices.label: B
choices.text: All licensed pharmacists have passed the national board exam. Priya is a licensed pharmacist. Therefore, Priya has passed the national board exam.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a building is on the historic register, it cannot be demolished. The Flint Theater was demolished last year, so it was not on the historic register.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No reptiles are warm-blooded. Some pets are reptiles. Therefore, some pets are not warm-blooded.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either Hassan is in Lisbon or he is in Porto. Hassan is not in Lisbon, so he is in Porto.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: All A are B; x is A; therefore x is B. (B) has the identical universal-to-particular instantiation: all licensed pharmacists have passed the board; Priya is one; therefore she has passed.
explanations.A: Uses 'most' and reverses direction, concluding an individual is probably in the category from the predicate. Different structure, and weaker modal force.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Contrapositive reasoning (A -> not B; B; therefore not A), not universal instantiation.
explanations.D: Quantified syllogism with 'some'; the stimulus has no existential premise.
explanations.E: Disjunctive syllogism — different form.

lr.difficultyReason: Clean disjunctive syllogism: two disjuncts, one eliminated, the other affirmed. Wrong answers use modus ponens, modus tollens, or content-matched lures.
lr.stimulus: The office printer is jammed because either the paper tray is empty or the toner cartridge is out of ink. The paper tray is not empty. Therefore, the toner cartridge is out of ink.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whenever the alarm sounds, the front door is unlocked. The alarm is sounding, so the front door is unlocked.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the cat is hungry, she meows at the refrigerator. The cat is not meowing, so she is not hungry.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Either the flight was delayed by weather or it was delayed by a mechanical issue. The flight was not delayed by a mechanical issue. Therefore, it was delayed by weather.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All experienced pilots know how to read weather radar. Captain Olvera is an experienced pilot, so he knows how to read weather radar.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most drivers who commute on the expressway listen to podcasts. Lila listens to podcasts, so she probably commutes on the expressway.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A or B; not A; therefore B. (C) is the same disjunctive syllogism with a different topic: weather or mechanical; not mechanical; therefore weather.
explanations.A: Modus ponens, not a disjunction.
explanations.B: Modus tollens with a single conditional.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Universal-to-particular instantiation.
explanations.E: Reversed 'most' generalization, a content lure — printers, cars, and commuting are all everyday settings but the logical form is different.

lr.difficultyReason: Basic contrapositive (modus tollens): one conditional, the denial of its consequent, and the denial of its antecedent. Only one choice exhibits modus tollens.
lr.stimulus: If Senator Rhee had supported the transit bill, the bill would have passed. The bill did not pass. Therefore, Senator Rhee did not support the transit bill.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a wine is aged in oak, it acquires a vanilla note. This wine has a vanilla note, so it was aged in oak.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the soil is properly drained, the tulips will bloom. The tulips did bloom, so the soil is properly drained.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the archivist had cataloged the letters, the exhibit would have opened on time. The exhibit did not open on time. Therefore, the archivist did not catalog the letters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every accredited program requires a capstone project. This program is accredited, so it requires a capstone project.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either the server is overloaded or the database is offline. The server is not overloaded. Therefore, the database is offline.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A -> B; not B; therefore not A. (C) has the same modus tollens structure: if cataloged -> opened; not opened; therefore not cataloged.
explanations.A: Affirms the consequent — invalid, so not parallel to the valid stimulus.
explanations.B: Affirms the consequent.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Universal instantiation (modus ponens in categorical dress).
explanations.E: Disjunctive syllogism.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-link conditional chain (hypothetical syllogism): A -> B; B -> C; therefore A -> C. Distractors include modus ponens, contrapositive, and a reversed-chain lure.
lr.stimulus: If a company adopts a four-day workweek, employee retention improves. If employee retention improves, recruiting costs decline. Therefore, if a company adopts a four-day workweek, its recruiting costs decline.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a river is dammed, downstream flooding decreases. The Kestrel River has been dammed, so downstream flooding has decreased.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a reef is bleached, fish populations decline. If fish populations decline, local fisheries lose revenue. Therefore, if a reef is bleached, local fisheries lose revenue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a statute is unconstitutional, courts will strike it down. The statute was not struck down, so it was not unconstitutional.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If interest rates fall, housing prices rise. Housing prices have risen, so interest rates must have fallen.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every software patch requires a restart. This update is a software patch, so it requires a restart.

explanations.correct: Stimulus is a hypothetical syllogism: A -> B; B -> C; therefore A -> C. (B) mirrors it exactly: bleached -> fish decline; fish decline -> revenue lost; therefore bleached -> revenue lost.
explanations.A: Modus ponens with a single conditional, not a chain.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Modus tollens.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent — invalid.
explanations.E: Universal instantiation.

lr.difficultyReason: Another textbook modus ponens in an environmental-science setting. Traps include a same-topic modus tollens (B) and an affirming-the-consequent lure (E).
lr.stimulus: If the wetland's water level drops below one meter, the resident herons will relocate to the river delta. The water level dropped below one meter last week. Therefore, the resident herons relocated to the river delta.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every licensed electrician carries liability insurance. Marcus is a licensed electrician. Therefore, Marcus carries liability insurance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the wetland's pH rises above eight, the frog population declines. The frog population has not declined. Therefore, the pH has not risen above eight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the train is on schedule, the 7:15 departure leaves from platform two. The train is on schedule today. Therefore, the 7:15 departure leaves from platform two.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the greenhouse vent is open or the temperature will exceed 90 degrees. The temperature did not exceed 90 degrees. Therefore, the vent was open.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a meadow is grazed, wildflowers become more abundant. The meadow's wildflowers are more abundant, so the meadow has been grazed.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A -> B; A; therefore B. (C) matches: on-schedule -> platform two; on schedule; therefore platform two.
explanations.A: Universal instantiation — categorical rather than propositional. While close in spirit, the stimulus is explicitly conditional; (C) is a cleaner match.
explanations.B: Same wetland topic but modus tollens, not modus ponens. Classic same-topic trap.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Disjunctive syllogism.
explanations.E: Affirms the consequent — invalid.

lr.difficultyReason: Universal instantiation in an economics setting. Distractors include a 'most' generalization and a disjunctive syllogism.
lr.stimulus: All currencies pegged to the dollar fluctuate with U.S. monetary policy. The Beltran peso is pegged to the dollar. Therefore, the Beltran peso fluctuates with U.S. monetary policy.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most countries that run trade surpluses accumulate foreign reserves. Valoria accumulates foreign reserves, so it probably runs a trade surplus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every bridge built after 1980 in this province uses prestressed concrete. The Ormond Bridge was built in 1994 in this province. Therefore, the Ormond Bridge uses prestressed concrete.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a bond is rated below investment grade, institutional funds will not buy it. This bond is rated below investment grade, so institutional funds will not buy it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the exchange rate is fixed or it is floating. The Beltran peso is not floating, so it is fixed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If consumer spending rises, GDP rises. GDP did not rise, so consumer spending did not rise.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: All A are B; x is A; therefore x is B. (B) is the same universal-to-particular instantiation with bridges: all post-1980 provincial bridges use prestressed concrete; Ormond is one; therefore it does.
explanations.A: Uses 'most' and reverses direction — weaker modal force and different shape.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Modus ponens with an explicit conditional. Close but not universal instantiation.
explanations.D: Disjunctive syllogism; same topic (Beltran peso) is the lure.
explanations.E: Modus tollens.

lr.difficultyReason: Contrapositive (modus tollens) in a historical setting. Traps include a same-topic modus ponens and an affirming-the-consequent lure.
lr.stimulus: If General Hargrove had arrived before dawn, the garrison would have surrendered without a fight. The garrison did not surrender without a fight. Therefore, General Hargrove did not arrive before dawn.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If the treaty had been ratified by both assemblies, the border would have been redrawn. The border was redrawn, so the treaty was ratified by both assemblies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a compound contains sulfur, it will tarnish silver. This compound does not tarnish silver. Therefore, this compound does not contain sulfur.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If General Hargrove marches at first light, the supply lines will hold. General Hargrove marched at first light. Therefore, the supply lines held.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every cavalry officer trained at the academy learned dead-reckoning navigation. Colonel Vance trained at the academy. Therefore, Colonel Vance learned dead-reckoning.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either the siege was broken or the city fell. The siege was broken, so the city did not fall.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A -> B; not B; therefore not A — modus tollens. (B) matches: sulfur -> tarnishes silver; does not tarnish; therefore no sulfur.
explanations.A: Same historical topic but affirms the consequent — invalid and so not parallel to the valid stimulus.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Same topic but modus ponens. A same-topic trap.
explanations.D: Universal instantiation, not conditional contrapositive.
explanations.E: Disjunctive syllogism.

lr.difficultyReason: Disjunctive syllogism in a linguistics setting. Distractors include same-topic conditionals of other forms.
lr.stimulus: A verb in Old Karnish must take either the accusative suffix or the dative suffix. The verb 'velmir' does not take the accusative suffix. Therefore, 'velmir' takes the dative suffix.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a noun in Old Karnish ends in a consonant, it is masculine. The noun 'dran' ends in a consonant, so it is masculine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every vowel in the Karnish script represents a single phoneme. The symbol 'a' is a vowel in the Karnish script. Therefore, 'a' represents a single phoneme.

choices.label: C
choices.text: On any given weekday, the Mendez family eats either fish or poultry for dinner. Last Tuesday, the Mendez family did not eat poultry. Therefore, they ate fish.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a verb is irregular, it does not follow the standard suffix rules. The verb 'velmir' is not irregular, so it follows the standard suffix rules.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most verbs in Old Karnish take the accusative suffix. 'Velmir' is an Old Karnish verb, so it probably takes the accusative suffix.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A or B; not A; therefore B. (C) is the same disjunctive syllogism in a domestic setting: fish or poultry; not poultry; therefore fish.
explanations.A: Modus ponens, not a disjunction.
explanations.B: Universal instantiation.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Modus tollens with a same-topic lure.
explanations.E: Statistical generalization with 'most' and a probabilistic conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-link conditional chain in a technology context. Only one answer choice exhibits a hypothetical syllogism; the rest are single-conditional variants or a disjunctive syllogism.
lr.stimulus: If a smartphone's battery degrades below 80 percent capacity, the operating system throttles processor speed. If the operating system throttles processor speed, app launch times become noticeably slower. Therefore, if a smartphone's battery degrades below 80 percent capacity, app launch times become noticeably slower.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a smartphone is dropped in water, its speakers will malfunction. This phone was dropped in water, so its speakers will malfunction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a bicycle chain is not lubricated, it rusts. If a bicycle chain rusts, pedaling becomes harder. Therefore, if a bicycle chain is not lubricated, pedaling becomes harder.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every laptop in the teaching lab has 16 gigabytes of memory. This machine is in the teaching lab, so it has 16 gigabytes of memory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the router is offline or the cable has been unplugged. The cable has not been unplugged, so the router is offline.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a file is encrypted, it cannot be read without the key. This file can be read without the key, so it is not encrypted.

explanations.correct: Stimulus is a hypothetical syllogism: A -> B; B -> C; therefore A -> C. (B) has the identical chain: unlubricated -> rust; rust -> harder pedaling; therefore unlubricated -> harder pedaling.
explanations.A: Modus ponens with one conditional, not a chain. Same-domain lure.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Universal instantiation.
explanations.D: Disjunctive syllogism.
explanations.E: Modus tollens.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-step conditional chain with modus ponens at the end: A→B, B→C, A, therefore C. Traps (B) and (D) share topic or conclusion type but drop a link or reverse a conditional; trap (E) runs a two-premise chain rather than three.
lr.stimulus: If the municipal bond measure passes, the library's endowment will grow. If the library's endowment grows, it will be able to hire a second archivist. The bond measure will pass. So the library will be able to hire a second archivist.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If the ice on the lake thickens, ice fishing will be permitted. If ice fishing is permitted, the bait shop will reopen. The ice on the lake will thicken. Therefore, the bait shop will reopen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the tax levy passes, the school will receive new computers. The tax levy will pass. So students will learn to code more quickly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a candidate wins the primary, she will appear on the general-election ballot. Senator Park did not win the primary. Therefore, she will not appear on the general-election ballot.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the rezoning vote succeeds, a new park will be built. If a new park is built, nearby property values will rise. Property values near the proposed park have already risen. Therefore, the rezoning vote will succeed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the referendum passes, the museum will expand. The referendum will pass. Therefore, the museum will expand.

explanations.correct: Stimulus is a three-step chain: A→B, B→C, A, ∴ C. (A) matches exactly: thickens→ice fishing, ice fishing→bait shop, thickens, ∴ bait shop reopens. Same conditional directions, same number of premises, same modus-ponens conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Matches topic (civic vote) and affirms the antecedent, but the conclusion ("students will learn to code more quickly") is an unlicensed new claim — the chain structure is broken.
explanations.C: Denies the antecedent — a two-premise modus tollens-lookalike, not a three-step affirming chain. Conclusion is negative, not positive.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent of the second conditional to reach the antecedent of the first — reverses the chain's direction. Not the same form.
explanations.E: Single conditional + modus ponens (two premises, not three). Drops the middle link.

lr.difficultyReason: Universal generalization plus particular instantiation plus conditional: "All A are B; all B require C; x is A; therefore x requires C." Mixed forms force students to track both a syllogism and a conditional step.
lr.stimulus: All amphibians are ectothermic. Every ectothermic vertebrate requires an external heat source to regulate its body temperature. The hellbender is an amphibian. Therefore, the hellbender requires an external heat source to regulate its body temperature.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All corporate bonds are debt instruments. Every debt instrument carries some default risk. The Marcor bond is a corporate bond. Therefore, the Marcor bond carries some default risk.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most songbirds migrate. Every migratory bird requires fat reserves before departure. The scarlet tanager is a songbird. Therefore, the scarlet tanager requires fat reserves before departure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All mollusks have soft bodies. The nautilus has a soft body. Therefore, the nautilus is a mollusk.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All granite is igneous. The quarry stone is igneous. Every igneous rock resists weathering. Therefore, the quarry stone resists weathering.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most sonnets have fourteen lines. Every fourteen-line poem contains a volta. "Ozymandias" is a sonnet. Therefore, "Ozymandias" probably contains a volta.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: all A are B; all B require C; x is A; ∴ x requires C — two universal premises, one particular instance, universal (non-hedged) conclusion. (A) mirrors each step: all corporate bonds are debt instruments; all debt instruments carry default risk; Marcor is a corporate bond; therefore Marcor carries default risk.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Opens with "most" instead of "all," weakening the first premise's quantifier and breaking the universal-to-particular chain.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent — having a soft body doesn't make something a mollusk. This is a two-premise flawed argument; the stimulus is valid.
explanations.D: Same premises present but in a different order that converts the middle step (quarry is igneous is asserted directly, not derived), and omits the universal "all granite is igneous" chain properly; closer structurally than B/C/E but mismatches premise order and derivation path.
explanations.E: Hedges with "most" and "probably" — conclusion strength is weakened, so it does not match the stimulus's universal conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Disjunctive syllogism plus conditional: "A or B; A→C; ¬C; ∴ B." Students must recognize that the middle step is a contrapositive application that eliminates one disjunct.
lr.stimulus: Either the manuscript was written by Beaumont or it was written by Fletcher. If Beaumont wrote the manuscript, the paper would bear a Kentish watermark. The paper does not bear a Kentish watermark. Therefore, Fletcher wrote the manuscript.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Either the diamond came from the Karowe mine or it came from the Letseng mine. If the diamond came from the Karowe mine, it would contain nitrogen inclusions. The diamond does not contain nitrogen inclusions. Therefore, the diamond came from the Letseng mine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sample is either basalt or granite. It is basalt. Therefore, it is not granite.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the package was shipped from Osaka, it would bear a customs stamp. The package bears a customs stamp. Therefore, the package was shipped from Osaka.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the violin was made by Guarneri or by Stradivari. If Guarneri made it, the f-holes would be asymmetrical. The f-holes are asymmetrical. Therefore, Guarneri made it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either the essay was written in 1640 or in 1650. If it was written in 1640, it would reference the regicide. The essay references the regicide. Therefore, the essay was written in 1640.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A∨B; A→C; ¬C; ∴ B. The middle step uses contrapositive (¬C→¬A) to eliminate a disjunct. (A) matches: Karowe∨Letseng; Karowe→nitrogen; ¬nitrogen; ∴ Letseng. Same disjunctive base, same contrapositive move, same positive conclusion about the surviving disjunct.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: A bare disjunctive syllogism with no conditional middle step — two premises, not three.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent — a classic fallacy; stimulus is valid, so this cannot be parallel.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent inside the conditional step — concludes the antecedent from the consequent, reversing the contrapositive move.
explanations.E: Same affirming-the-consequent move as D — invalid, and the stimulus is valid.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogy-plus-universal: two shared properties justify inferring a third. Conclusion strength is hedged ("likely"). Students must match both the analogical form and the modal hedge.
lr.stimulus: The economies of Varland and Neufeld share two key features: both are small open economies heavily dependent on commodity exports, and both peg their currencies to the euro. When commodity prices fell last decade, Varland experienced a sharp contraction. Neufeld is now facing a similar commodity price decline, so Neufeld will likely experience a sharp contraction as well.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The novels of Marin and Quilter share two key features: both employ unreliable first-person narrators, and both are set during wartime. Marin's novels have been widely translated. Quilter's novels share these features, so Quilter's novels will likely be widely translated as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cities of Portmouth and Callenby share two key features: both are coastal harbor towns, and both rely on fishing as their primary industry. When a red tide struck Portmouth last year, its fishing yields collapsed. Callenby is now experiencing a red tide, so Callenby's fishing yields will likely collapse as well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cities of Portmouth and Callenby are both coastal harbor towns. When a red tide struck Portmouth, its fishing yields collapsed. Therefore, Callenby's fishing yields will collapse if a red tide strikes it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several coastal cities have collapsed when hit by red tides. Callenby is a coastal city. Therefore, Callenby's fishing yields must collapse.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cities of Portmouth and Callenby share many features. Portmouth's fishing yields collapsed last year. Therefore, Callenby's fishing yields collapsed last year too.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: X and Y share properties P and Q; when condition C struck X, X suffered outcome O; C is now striking Y; ∴ Y will likely suffer O. (B) mirrors each element: Portmouth/Callenby share two features; red tide caused a collapse in Portmouth; red tide now in Callenby; ∴ Callenby will likely collapse. Hedged conclusion preserved.
explanations.A: Matches surface structure of "two shared features," but the outcome being transferred (widely translated) is not triggered by a condition currently recurring in the second case — there is no parallel to the recurring commodity price decline / red tide.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Only one shared feature named; conclusion is a conditional, not a prediction. Missing the second shared property and the present-tense recurrence.
explanations.D: Draws from a general population ("several coastal cities") rather than a pairwise analogy; conclusion uses "must" instead of "likely," mismatching modal force.
explanations.E: Vague premise ("share many features") and past-tense conclusion — stimulus concludes about a future event.

lr.difficultyReason: Contrapositive chain with three steps: A→B, B→C, ¬C, ∴ ¬A. Students must trace two contrapositive moves and match both the negative conclusion and the three-premise count.
lr.stimulus: If a painting is genuinely by Vermeer, it contains ultramarine pigment in the shadow layers. If a painting contains ultramarine pigment in the shadow layers, X-ray fluorescence analysis will detect traces of lapis lazuli. X-ray fluorescence analysis of the disputed painting did not detect traces of lapis lazuli. Therefore, the disputed painting is not genuinely by Vermeer.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a fossil is from the Cambrian period, it predates the emergence of vertebrates. If a fossil predates the emergence of vertebrates, it will contain no hollow bone fragments. The specimen from Well Ridge contains no hollow bone fragments. Therefore, the specimen is from the Cambrian period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a wine is a genuine Chablis, it comes from the Kimmeridgian limestone soils. If a wine comes from the Kimmeridgian limestone soils, it will exhibit a distinctive mineral note. The wine under review does not exhibit a distinctive mineral note. Therefore, the wine under review is not a genuine Chablis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a building is a true Gothic cathedral, it has pointed arches. The building across the square does not have pointed arches. Therefore, it is not a true Gothic cathedral.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Roman denarius, it contains a high silver content. The coin in question contains a high silver content. Therefore, it is a genuine Roman denarius.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a recording is from the 1950s, it is on magnetic tape. If a recording is on magnetic tape, it can be digitized with standard equipment. The studio recording from 1952 can be digitized with standard equipment. Therefore, the studio recording is from the 1950s.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A→B, B→C, ¬C, ∴ ¬A — three premises, chained contrapositive ending in negation of original antecedent. (B) mirrors it precisely: Chablis→Kimmeridgian, Kimmeridgian→mineral note, ¬mineral note, ∴ not Chablis.
explanations.A: Affirms the final consequent (no hollow bones) and concludes the original antecedent — that's affirming the consequent, which is invalid. The stimulus is valid.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Two-premise modus tollens, not a three-premise chain. Drops the middle conditional.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent in a two-premise argument — invalid.
explanations.E: Three conditionals but ends with affirming-the-consequent move to conclude the antecedent — invalid, and also the conclusion is positive, not negative.

lr.difficultyReason: Universal generalization + conditional + modus ponens. Three-step mixed form requires matching the universal quantifier, conditional chain, and particular conclusion — not just one of these.
lr.stimulus: Every language that distinguishes grammatical gender marks it on nouns. If a language marks gender on nouns, it also marks gender on adjectives that modify those nouns. Icelandic distinguishes grammatical gender. Therefore, Icelandic marks gender on adjectives that modify nouns.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every jurisdiction that recognizes community property divides marital assets equally at divorce. If a jurisdiction divides marital assets equally at divorce, it also applies the same rule to debts acquired during the marriage. The state of Tarmouth recognizes community property. Therefore, Tarmouth applies the equal-division rule to debts acquired during the marriage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most jurisdictions that recognize community property divide marital assets equally at divorce. If a jurisdiction divides marital assets equally, it also applies the same rule to debts. The state of Tarmouth recognizes community property. Therefore, Tarmouth probably applies the equal-division rule to debts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every jurisdiction that recognizes community property divides marital assets equally. Tarmouth divides marital assets equally. Therefore, Tarmouth recognizes community property.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a jurisdiction recognizes community property, it divides marital assets equally. Tarmouth divides marital assets equally. Therefore, Tarmouth recognizes community property.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every jurisdiction that recognizes community property divides marital assets equally at divorce. Tarmouth recognizes community property. Therefore, Tarmouth divides marital assets equally at divorce.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: all A are B; B→C; x is A; ∴ x is C — universal premise feeds an instance into a conditional chain. (A) matches: all community-property jurisdictions do X; X→Y; Tarmouth is a community-property jurisdiction; ∴ Tarmouth does Y. Same three-step mixed form with universal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Weakens the first premise's quantifier to "most" and hedges the conclusion with "probably" — strength shift.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent — reverses the universal into a biconditional improperly. Invalid.
explanations.D: Same affirming-the-consequent error, now on a conditional premise. Invalid.
explanations.E: Correct universal-to-particular step but drops the middle conditional — only two premises where the stimulus has three.

lr.difficultyReason: Disjunctive syllogism with a universal-instantiation middle step: "A or B; every A has property P; this x lacks P; ∴ x is B." Mixed disjunctive + universal forms across three premises.
lr.stimulus: The archaeological layer at Site 9 dates from either the Early Bronze Age or the Middle Bronze Age. Every Early Bronze Age layer at this region's sites contains tin-rich bronze fragments. The layer at Site 9 contains no tin-rich bronze fragments. Therefore, the layer at Site 9 dates from the Middle Bronze Age.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fabric swatch was produced in either the 18th or the 19th century. Every 18th-century swatch of this type contains handspun linen fibers. The fabric swatch contains no handspun linen fibers. Therefore, the fabric swatch was produced in the 19th century.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fabric swatch was produced in either the 18th or the 19th century. Most 18th-century swatches of this type contain handspun linen fibers. The fabric swatch contains no handspun linen fibers. Therefore, the fabric swatch was probably produced in the 19th century.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fabric swatch was produced in the 18th century. Every 18th-century swatch contains handspun linen fibers. Therefore, the fabric swatch contains handspun linen fibers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every 18th-century swatch contains handspun linen fibers. The fabric swatch contains handspun linen fibers. Therefore, the fabric swatch was produced in the 18th century.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The fabric swatch was produced in the 18th or 19th century. The fabric swatch contains no handspun linen fibers. Therefore, the fabric swatch was produced in the 19th century.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A∨B; all A have P; this x lacks P; ∴ x is B. Three premises, universal + disjunctive middle, positive conclusion about surviving disjunct. (A) matches each step: 18th∨19th; every 18th-century swatch has P; this swatch lacks P; ∴ 19th century.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: "Most" weakens the universal premise and "probably" hedges the conclusion — strength mismatch on both quantifier and modal force.
explanations.C: Categorical syllogism, not a disjunction-elimination argument. Conclusion is about the property, not about which disjunct holds.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent — invalid; the stimulus is valid.
explanations.E: Drops the universal premise about 18th-century swatches entirely, so the contrapositive move that licenses the elimination is missing.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-step conditional chain with modus tollens: A→B, B→C, ¬C, ∴ ¬A. Requires distinguishing from nearby modus ponens chains and from two-premise contrapositive shortcuts.
lr.stimulus: If a server handles peak traffic without latency spikes, it must have sufficient cache capacity. If a server has sufficient cache capacity, its disk-access logs will show low read frequencies during peak hours. The disk-access logs for server Delta show high read frequencies during peak hours. Therefore, server Delta does not handle peak traffic without latency spikes.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a chef earns a Michelin star, she must source her produce locally. If a chef sources her produce locally, her supplier invoices will show regional farm names. Chef Okafor's supplier invoices show no regional farm names. Therefore, Chef Okafor has not earned a Michelin star.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a chef earns a Michelin star, she must source her produce locally. If a chef sources her produce locally, her supplier invoices will show regional farm names. Chef Okafor's supplier invoices show regional farm names. Therefore, Chef Okafor has earned a Michelin star.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a chef earns a Michelin star, her supplier invoices show regional farm names. Chef Okafor's supplier invoices show no regional farm names. Therefore, Chef Okafor has not earned a Michelin star.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most chefs who earn a Michelin star source their produce locally. If a chef sources her produce locally, her supplier invoices will show regional farm names. Chef Okafor's supplier invoices show no regional farm names. Therefore, Chef Okafor has probably not earned a Michelin star.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a chef earns a Michelin star, she must source her produce locally. Chef Okafor sources her produce locally. Therefore, Chef Okafor has earned a Michelin star.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A→B, B→C, ¬C, ∴ ¬A — three premises, chained modus tollens. (A) mirrors each step: Michelin→local sourcing, local sourcing→regional invoices, ¬regional invoices, ∴ ¬Michelin.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Affirms the final consequent (invoices show farm names) and concludes the antecedent — invalid, and the stimulus is valid.
explanations.C: Two-premise modus tollens; drops the middle conditional. Premise count mismatch.
explanations.D: Weakens the first premise to "most" and hedges the conclusion with "probably" — strength shift on both the universal and the modal.
explanations.E: Two-premise affirming-the-consequent-style argument with a positive conclusion — invalid and oppositely directed.

lr.difficultyReason: Mixed form: universal premise about a category, instantiation to a member, and a conditional step that licenses a positive conclusion. Students must match the universal strength and the number of inferential steps.
lr.stimulus: Every virus in the Flaviviridae family replicates using an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. If a pathogen replicates using an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, it is susceptible to nucleoside analog antivirals. The dengue virus belongs to the Flaviviridae family. Therefore, the dengue virus is susceptible to nucleoside analog antivirals.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every statute enacted under the Commerce Clause regulates interstate activity. If a statute regulates interstate activity, it can preempt conflicting state laws. The Mercer Act was enacted under the Commerce Clause. Therefore, the Mercer Act can preempt conflicting state laws.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many statutes enacted under the Commerce Clause regulate interstate activity. If a statute regulates interstate activity, it can preempt conflicting state laws. The Mercer Act was enacted under the Commerce Clause. Therefore, the Mercer Act probably can preempt conflicting state laws.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every statute enacted under the Commerce Clause regulates interstate activity. The Mercer Act regulates interstate activity. Therefore, the Mercer Act was enacted under the Commerce Clause.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a statute was enacted under the Commerce Clause, it can preempt conflicting state laws. The Mercer Act can preempt conflicting state laws. Therefore, the Mercer Act was enacted under the Commerce Clause.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every statute enacted under the Commerce Clause regulates interstate activity. The Mercer Act was enacted under the Commerce Clause. Therefore, the Mercer Act regulates interstate activity.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: all A do P; P→Q; x is A; ∴ x does Q. Three premises, universal + conditional, universal-strength conclusion. (A) matches: all Commerce Clause statutes regulate interstate activity; regulation→preemption; Mercer is a Commerce Clause statute; ∴ Mercer can preempt.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: "Many" weakens the universal, and "probably" hedges the conclusion — strength shift on both premise and conclusion.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent of the universal — invalid. Stimulus is valid.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent of the conditional — invalid.
explanations.E: Valid but drops the middle conditional; two premises where the stimulus has three.

lr.difficultyReason: Disjunction with contrapositive elimination producing a negative conclusion about the other disjunct's property: A∨B; A→C; x is ¬B; ∴ x is C. Tests whether students can apply the disjunctive elimination in the opposite direction.
lr.stimulus: Every work in the exhibition is either a lithograph or an etching. If a work is a lithograph, it was printed from a flat stone surface. The work titled "Harbor at Dusk" is not an etching. Therefore, "Harbor at Dusk" was printed from a flat stone surface.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every sonata on the program is either a Classical sonata or a Romantic sonata. If a sonata is Classical, it follows strict sonata-allegro form. The "Hoffmann Sonata" is not a Romantic sonata. Therefore, the "Hoffmann Sonata" follows strict sonata-allegro form.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every sonata on the program is either Classical or Romantic. Most Classical sonatas follow strict sonata-allegro form. The "Hoffmann Sonata" is not Romantic. Therefore, the "Hoffmann Sonata" probably follows strict sonata-allegro form.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every sonata on the program is either Classical or Romantic. If a sonata is Classical, it follows strict sonata-allegro form. The "Hoffmann Sonata" is Classical. Therefore, the "Hoffmann Sonata" follows strict sonata-allegro form.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a sonata is Classical, it follows strict sonata-allegro form. The "Hoffmann Sonata" does not follow strict sonata-allegro form. Therefore, the "Hoffmann Sonata" is not Classical.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every sonata on the program is either Classical or Romantic. If a sonata is Romantic, it does not follow strict sonata-allegro form. The "Hoffmann Sonata" follows strict sonata-allegro form. Therefore, the "Hoffmann Sonata" is Classical.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A∨B; A→C; x is ¬B; ∴ x is C. The ¬B premise forces x into the A disjunct by elimination, and A→C delivers the positive conclusion. (A) matches exactly: Classical∨Romantic; Classical→strict form; ¬Romantic; ∴ strict form.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Quantifier weakened to "most," conclusion hedged with "probably" — strength shift on both.
explanations.C: Directly asserts the Classical disjunct rather than deriving it by eliminating the other — removes the disjunctive-elimination step. Only two relevant premises.
explanations.D: Pure two-premise modus tollens with no disjunctive premise — drops the disjunction entirely.
explanations.E: Different conditional (Romantic→¬strict) and reaches conclusion by affirming a property to pick the disjunct — the direction of reasoning is reversed.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step chain with a biconditional hinge and modus tollens: All A are B; every B has C; C iff D; the specimen does not have D; therefore it cannot be A.
