Students must process a universal, a universal, a biconditional, and a negated particular before concluding with necessity. Traps preserve three of the four structural features while reversing one.
lr.stimulus: Every case of bacterial meningitis involves inflammation of the meninges. Any patient with inflammation of the meninges exhibits elevated cerebrospinal protein. A patient exhibits elevated cerebrospinal protein if, and only if, a lumbar puncture yields a cloudy sample. The lumbar puncture performed on this patient yielded a clear sample. It follows that this patient cannot have bacterial meningitis.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most parallel to that in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every genuine Ming porcelain contains kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. Any object containing kaolin clay from Jingdezhen shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature. An object shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature if, and only if, its firing temperature exceeded 1300 degrees Celsius. The firing temperature of the disputed vase did not exceed 1300 degrees Celsius. It follows that the disputed vase cannot be a genuine Ming porcelain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every genuine Ming porcelain contains kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. Most objects containing kaolin clay from Jingdezhen show a distinctive thermoluminescence signature. An object shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature if, and only if, its firing temperature exceeded 1300 degrees Celsius. The disputed vase did not exceed 1300 degrees Celsius. So the disputed vase is probably not genuine Ming porcelain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every genuine Ming porcelain contains kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. Any object containing kaolin clay from Jingdezhen shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature. The disputed vase shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature. It follows that the disputed vase is a genuine Ming porcelain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every genuine Ming porcelain contains kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. Any object containing kaolin clay from Jingdezhen shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature. An object shows a distinctive thermoluminescence signature only if its firing temperature exceeded 1300 degrees Celsius. The firing temperature of the disputed vase did not exceed 1300 degrees Celsius. So the disputed vase may not be genuine.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every genuine Ming porcelain contains kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. The disputed vase does not contain kaolin clay from Jingdezhen. It follows that the disputed vase cannot be a genuine Ming porcelain.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → Bx); ∀x(Bx → Cx); ∀x(Cx ↔ Dx); ¬Dp; ∴ ¬Ap (with necessity). (A) replicates each step — two universals, a biconditional, a negated particular, and a necessity conclusion — simply reskinned in the porcelain domain.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Weakens the second premise from 'any/every' to 'most' and weakens the conclusion from necessity to probability — two quantifier/modal mismatches.
explanations.C: Only three premises, and the third step affirms the consequent rather than running modus tollens through a biconditional. Structurally reversed.
explanations.D: Replaces the biconditional with a one-way conditional ('only if') and softens the conclusion to 'may not' — both modal force and connective strength are off.
explanations.E: Two premises, not four; skips the inflammation and biconditional steps entirely.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step mixed-quantifier argument: some A are B; all B require C; C iff D; x is both A and B; therefore x probably requires D. The argument moves from existential to universal to biconditional and ends with a hedged conclusion that tracks the 'probably' licensed by instantiation from an existential base.
lr.stimulus: Some medical studies that yield statistically significant results nevertheless have low replication rates. Every study with a low replication rate requires independent pre-registration to warrant continued funding. A study requires independent pre-registration if, and only if, its effect size falls below a conventional threshold. The Harmon study yielded statistically significant results and has a low replication rate. Therefore, the Harmon study's effect size probably falls below the conventional threshold.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some charitable organizations that report high donor retention nevertheless show thin program margins. Every organization with thin program margins requires a restructuring plan to maintain its rating. An organization requires a restructuring plan if, and only if, its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund reports high donor retention and shows thin program margins. Therefore, the Ardent Fund's overhead ratio probably exceeds the conventional threshold.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most charitable organizations that report high donor retention show thin program margins. Every organization with thin program margins requires a restructuring plan. An organization requires a restructuring plan if, and only if, its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund reports high donor retention. Therefore, the Ardent Fund's overhead ratio exceeds the conventional threshold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some charitable organizations that report high donor retention nevertheless show thin program margins. Most organizations with thin program margins require a restructuring plan. An organization requires a restructuring plan only if its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund reports high donor retention. So the Ardent Fund's overhead ratio probably exceeds the conventional threshold.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some charitable organizations that report high donor retention nevertheless show thin program margins. Every organization with thin program margins requires a restructuring plan. An organization requires a restructuring plan if, and only if, its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund's overhead ratio exceeds the conventional threshold. Therefore, the Ardent Fund probably shows thin program margins.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every charitable organization that reports high donor retention shows thin program margins. Every organization with thin program margins requires a restructuring plan. An organization requires a restructuring plan if, and only if, its overhead ratio exceeds a conventional threshold. The Ardent Fund reports high donor retention and shows thin program margins. Therefore, the Ardent Fund's overhead ratio exceeds the conventional threshold.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∃x(Ax ∧ Bx); ∀x(Bx → Cx); ∀x(Cx ↔ Dx); Ah ∧ Bh; ∴ probably Dh. (A) preserves all four elements: existential opener, universal middle, biconditional hinge, instantiation of both openers, hedged conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Converts the existential to 'most' and drops the hedge, then omits the second instantiation ('shows thin program margins'). Two shifts off parallel.
explanations.C: Weakens the second premise from 'every' to 'most' and the third from biconditional to one-way conditional.
explanations.D: Same premise set, but the conclusion reverses direction — it instantiates the consequent to derive the antecedent side, which is structurally a different move.
explanations.E: Opens with 'every' instead of 'some' and drops the hedge — conclusion shifts from probable to definite.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-link contrapositive chain: A→B, B→C, C→D, ¬D, ∴ ¬A. Students must run modus tollens through three conditionals in succession. Traps shorten the chain, reverse a single step, or swap quantifier strength on one premise.
lr.stimulus: If a currency union permits unlimited capital mobility, then its members must coordinate fiscal policy. If members must coordinate fiscal policy, then each member will need to cede some budgetary sovereignty. If each member cedes some budgetary sovereignty, then a central authority will have to ratify national budgets. No central authority has the power to ratify the member states' national budgets. Therefore, this currency union does not permit unlimited capital mobility.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press, then it uses a Bembo-derived typeface. If it uses a Bembo-derived typeface, then its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar. If its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar, then its ink will contain a distinctive iron-gall residue. This manuscript's ink does not contain iron-gall residue. Therefore, this manuscript was not typeset by the Aldine press.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press, then it uses a Bembo-derived typeface. If it uses a Bembo-derived typeface, then its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar. This manuscript's lowercase 'e' does not carry a slanted crossbar. Therefore, this manuscript was not typeset by the Aldine press.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press, then it uses a Bembo-derived typeface. If it uses a Bembo-derived typeface, then its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar. Most Bembo-derived manuscripts contain iron-gall residue. This manuscript's ink does not contain iron-gall residue. Therefore, this manuscript was probably not typeset by the Aldine press.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press, then it uses a Bembo-derived typeface. If it uses a Bembo-derived typeface, then its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar. If its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar, then its ink contains iron-gall residue. This manuscript's ink contains iron-gall residue. Therefore, this manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a manuscript was typeset by the Aldine press, then it uses a Bembo-derived typeface. If it uses a Bembo-derived typeface, then its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar. If its lowercase 'e' carries a slanted crossbar, then its ink contains iron-gall residue. This manuscript was not typeset by the Aldine press. Therefore, its ink does not contain iron-gall residue.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A→B; B→C; C→D; ¬D; ∴ ¬A. (A) matches all four premises with the same conditional directions and ends with modus tollens through the full chain to deny the antecedent of the first premise.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Only three premises — the chain is shortened by one link, so the structure is three-step tollens, not four-step.
explanations.C: Replaces one premise with a 'most' quantifier and hedges the conclusion to 'probably' — two features off parallel.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent at the end — this is an invalid move, and the stimulus is valid, so the parallel fails.
explanations.E: Denies the antecedent to derive denial of the consequent — also invalid, and runs the chain in the reverse direction.

lr.difficultyReason: Universal disjunctive plus a 'most' elimination plus instantiation, ending with a hedged positive conclusion. Four components: a universal conditional into a disjunction, a most-quantified negation of one disjunct, a particular instance, and a 'likely' conclusion on the surviving disjunct.
lr.stimulus: Every contract that is unconscionable at the time of signing is either procedurally defective or substantively one-sided. Most contracts that are unconscionable at the time of signing are not procedurally defective. The Marsden agreement was unconscionable at the time of its signing. Therefore, the Marsden agreement is likely substantively one-sided.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is either crystallographically flawed or chemically contaminated. Most alloys that fracture under cyclic loading are not crystallographically flawed. The bracket from the Hargrove bridge fractured under cyclic loading. Therefore, the bracket is likely chemically contaminated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is either crystallographically flawed or chemically contaminated. Most alloys that fracture under cyclic loading are chemically contaminated. The bracket from the Hargrove bridge fractured under cyclic loading. Therefore, the bracket is chemically contaminated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most alloys that fracture under cyclic loading are either crystallographically flawed or chemically contaminated. Most such alloys are not crystallographically flawed. The bracket from the Hargrove bridge fractured under cyclic loading. Therefore, the bracket is likely chemically contaminated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is either crystallographically flawed or chemically contaminated. No alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is crystallographically flawed. The bracket from the Hargrove bridge fractured under cyclic loading. Therefore, the bracket is chemically contaminated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every alloy that fractures under cyclic loading is both crystallographically flawed and chemically contaminated. Most alloys that fracture under cyclic loading are not crystallographically flawed. The bracket from the Hargrove bridge fractured under cyclic loading. Therefore, the bracket is likely chemically contaminated.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → (Bx ∨ Cx)); most A are ¬B; a is A; ∴ a is likely C. (A) matches each piece: a universal with a disjunctive consequent, a 'most' negation of one disjunct, an instantiation, and a hedged positive conclusion on the remaining disjunct.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Runs the 'most' in the opposite direction (most A are C, not most A are ¬B) and drops the hedge.
explanations.C: Softens the first premise from 'every' to 'most', weakening the universal backbone of the argument.
explanations.D: Replaces 'most' with 'no' — a universal negative rather than a hedged majority — and strengthens the conclusion from 'likely' to categorical.
explanations.E: Turns the disjunction into a conjunction, so the second premise (most aren't B) contradicts the first rather than narrowing it.

lr.difficultyReason: Biconditional plus chain plus existential generalization: A ↔ B; B → C; some A are D; therefore some D are C. Students must combine a biconditional (treat as A → B), a conditional, and an existential subject to yield an existential conclusion — an inference type that hinges on carrying the existential through two universals.
lr.stimulus: A wetland is classified as a vernal pool if, and only if, it dries completely for part of each year. Every wetland that dries completely for part of each year supports at least one obligate indicator species. Some vernal pools in the Redclay reserve also exhibit fairy-shrimp egg banks. Therefore, some wetlands in the Redclay reserve that exhibit fairy-shrimp egg banks support at least one obligate indicator species.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most parallel to that in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A language is classified as tonal if, and only if, it uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Every language that uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning has at least one minimal tone pair. Some tonal languages in the Sahel survey also employ vowel harmony. Therefore, some languages in the Sahel survey that employ vowel harmony have at least one minimal tone pair.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A language is classified as tonal if, and only if, it uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Most languages that use pitch to distinguish lexical meaning have at least one minimal tone pair. Some tonal languages in the Sahel survey also employ vowel harmony. Therefore, most languages in the Sahel survey that employ vowel harmony have at least one minimal tone pair.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A language is classified as tonal only if it uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Every language that uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning has at least one minimal tone pair. Some tonal languages in the Sahel survey employ vowel harmony. Therefore, some languages in the Sahel survey that employ vowel harmony have at least one minimal tone pair.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A language is classified as tonal if, and only if, it uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Every language that uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning has at least one minimal tone pair. Every tonal language in the Sahel survey employs vowel harmony. Therefore, every language in the Sahel survey that employs vowel harmony has at least one minimal tone pair.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A language is classified as tonal if, and only if, it uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Every language that has at least one minimal tone pair uses pitch to distinguish lexical meaning. Some tonal languages in the Sahel survey employ vowel harmony. Therefore, some languages in the Sahel survey that employ vowel harmony are tonal.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: Ax ↔ Bx; ∀x(Bx → Cx); ∃x(Ax ∧ Dx restricted to region R); ∴ ∃x(Dx ∧ Cx in R). (A) preserves the biconditional opener, the universal second step, the existential subject, and the existential conclusion at the same scope.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Downgrades the second premise from 'every' to 'most' and the conclusion from existential to 'most', changing two features.
explanations.C: Replaces the biconditional with a one-way 'only if' conditional — the biconditional strength is lost.
explanations.D: Strengthens both the existential premise and conclusion to universals ('every'), changing quantifier type.
explanations.E: Reverses the direction of the second premise, then draws a conclusion about being tonal rather than about the minimal-tone-pair property.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step argument mixing two universal conditionals, a 'most' generalization over the chain's endpoint, an instantiation, and a hedged conclusion. Students must recognize that the conclusion's 'probably' is licensed not by 'most' alone but by chaining two universals before meeting the 'most' premise.
lr.stimulus: Any operating system that ships with the latest kernel patch supports hardware-level memory tagging. Every system that supports hardware-level memory tagging can run the new sandboxed runtime. Most systems that can run the new sandboxed runtime pass the FlexBench security audit. The server in our datacenter ships with the latest kernel patch. Therefore, the server in our datacenter will probably pass the FlexBench security audit.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any vineyard that uses biodynamic practices maintains a closed compost cycle. Every vineyard that maintains a closed compost cycle meets the Demeter soil standard. Most vineyards that meet the Demeter soil standard earn an export license. The Salin estate uses biodynamic practices. Therefore, the Salin estate will probably earn an export license.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any vineyard that uses biodynamic practices maintains a closed compost cycle. Every vineyard that maintains a closed compost cycle meets the Demeter soil standard. Every vineyard that meets the Demeter soil standard earns an export license. The Salin estate uses biodynamic practices. Therefore, the Salin estate will probably earn an export license.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most vineyards that use biodynamic practices maintain a closed compost cycle. Every vineyard that maintains a closed compost cycle meets the Demeter soil standard. Most vineyards that meet the Demeter soil standard earn an export license. The Salin estate uses biodynamic practices. Therefore, the Salin estate will earn an export license.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Any vineyard that uses biodynamic practices maintains a closed compost cycle. Every vineyard that maintains a closed compost cycle meets the Demeter soil standard. Most vineyards that meet the Demeter soil standard earn an export license. The Salin estate earns an export license. Therefore, the Salin estate probably uses biodynamic practices.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Any vineyard that uses biodynamic practices maintains a closed compost cycle. Every vineyard that maintains a closed compost cycle meets the Demeter soil standard. Most vineyards that earn an export license meet the Demeter soil standard. The Salin estate uses biodynamic practices. Therefore, the Salin estate will probably earn an export license.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → Bx); ∀x(Bx → Cx); most Cx are Dx; Aa; ∴ probably Da. (A) mirrors all four steps: two universal conditionals forming a chain, a 'most' generalization over the chain endpoint, an instantiation of A, and a hedged conclusion of D.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Strengthens the third premise from 'most' to 'every' while keeping the conclusion hedged — the 'probably' no longer matches the now-universal chain.
explanations.C: Weakens the first premise from 'any' to 'most' and promotes the conclusion from 'probably' to categorical.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent at the end of the chain — concludes about the antecedent from the endpoint, reversing direction.
explanations.E: Reverses the direction of the third premise (most D are C, not most C are D) — cannot yield the same inference.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step argument combining a universal conditional, a contrapositive observation, and a disjunctive syllogism with a particular in one of the disjuncts. The contrapositive move eliminates one disjunct and forces the positive conclusion on the other.
lr.stimulus: Every Indo-European language retains at least one trace of laryngeal consonants in its oldest strata. The language recorded on the Boglath tablets shows no trace of laryngeal consonants in any stratum. The Boglath language is either Indo-European or Pre-Hurrian. Therefore, the Boglath language is Pre-Hurrian.
lr.questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every true comet released from the Oort cloud exhibits a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at its first observed perihelion. The object designated 2031 FQ exhibited no measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at its first observed perihelion. The object is either a true comet released from the Oort cloud or a Jupiter-family interloper. Therefore, the object is a Jupiter-family interloper.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most true comets released from the Oort cloud exhibit a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at first perihelion. The object designated 2031 FQ exhibited no such velocity. The object is either a true comet released from the Oort cloud or a Jupiter-family interloper. Therefore, the object is probably a Jupiter-family interloper.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every true comet released from the Oort cloud exhibits a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at first perihelion. The object designated 2031 FQ exhibited a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at first perihelion. The object is either a true comet released from the Oort cloud or a Jupiter-family interloper. Therefore, the object is a true comet released from the Oort cloud.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every true comet released from the Oort cloud exhibits a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at first perihelion. The object designated 2031 FQ exhibited no measurable hyperbolic excess velocity. Therefore, the object is not a true comet released from the Oort cloud.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every true comet released from the Oort cloud exhibits a measurable hyperbolic excess velocity at first perihelion. The object designated 2031 FQ is a Jupiter-family interloper. The object is either a true comet released from the Oort cloud or a Jupiter-family interloper. Therefore, the object exhibited no measurable hyperbolic excess velocity.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: ∀x(Ax → Bx); ¬Ba; A∨C for a; ∴ C for a. (A) matches: a universal conditional, a negated particular consequent, a binary disjunction containing the class, and a positive conclusion on the alternative disjunct.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Weakens the first premise from 'every' to 'most' and hedges the conclusion to 'probably' — two structural features change.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent and concludes on the wrong disjunct (Indo-European analog rather than the alternative) — reverses direction.
explanations.D: Only two premises, ending at the modus tollens negation; the disjunctive-syllogism step is missing entirely.
explanations.E: Uses the disjunction with an asserted disjunct as a premise rather than deriving it, and concludes about the consequent property, not the category.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step analogical argument with an embedded universal conditional and a hedged conclusion. Two cases share two properties; a universal links those properties to a third; one case has the third property; the conclusion transfers the property to the other case with 'likely'.
lr.stimulus: The reform movements of eighteenth-century Denmark and eighteenth-century Tuscany shared two features: both were led by enlightened monarchs, and both enacted agrarian reforms before any constitutional reform. Every eighteenth-century reform movement that was led by an enlightened monarch and enacted agrarian reforms before constitutional reforms eventually produced a durable legal code. The Danish movement eventually produced a durable legal code. Therefore, the Tuscan movement likely produced a durable legal code as well.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The composition curricula of Rosedale Academy and Finch Academy shared two features: both were designed by former novelists, and both sequenced revision instruction before stylistic instruction. Every composition curriculum designed by a former novelist that sequenced revision before stylistic instruction eventually produced a signature student magazine. Rosedale's curriculum eventually produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Finch's curriculum likely produced a signature student magazine as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The composition curricula of Rosedale Academy and Finch Academy shared two features. Every composition curriculum designed by a former novelist that sequenced revision before stylistic instruction eventually produced a signature student magazine. Rosedale's curriculum eventually produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Finch's curriculum produced a signature student magazine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The composition curricula of Rosedale Academy and Finch Academy shared two features: both were designed by former novelists, and both sequenced revision instruction before stylistic instruction. Most composition curricula designed by former novelists that sequence revision before stylistic instruction eventually produce a signature student magazine. Rosedale's curriculum eventually produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Finch's curriculum produced a signature student magazine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The composition curricula of Rosedale Academy and Finch Academy shared two features: both were designed by former novelists, and both sequenced revision instruction before stylistic instruction. Every composition curriculum designed by a former novelist that sequenced revision before stylistic instruction eventually produced a signature student magazine. Finch's curriculum eventually produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Rosedale's curriculum likely produced a signature student magazine — before Finch's did.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The composition curricula of Rosedale Academy and Finch Academy share several features. Rosedale's curriculum produced a signature student magazine. Therefore, Finch's curriculum likely produced a signature student magazine as well.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: X and Y share properties P and Q; ∀z((Pz ∧ Qz) → Rz); X has R; ∴ Y likely has R. (A) mirrors the shared-property opener, the universal conditional over both properties, the single-case confirmation of R, and the hedged transfer to Y.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Drops the explicit naming of the two shared features and strips the hedge from the conclusion — two structural gaps.
explanations.C: Weakens the universal premise from 'every' to 'most' and promotes the conclusion from 'likely' to categorical.
explanations.D: Keeps all premises intact but adds an extra temporal claim ('before Finch's did') to the conclusion — an unlicensed addition.
explanations.E: Vague analogical premise ('several features') and no universal conditional — drops two of the four structural elements.

lr.difficultyReason: Nested-conditional argument: if all A are B, then C; C is false; therefore some A are not B. Four structural elements to match — a conditional whose antecedent is itself a universal, a contrapositive application, the existential generalization licensed by the negation of a universal, and the explicit 'at least one' phrasing.
lr.stimulus: If every eligible voter in Callenhurst registered by the deadline, then the preliminary turnout estimate would exceed 40,000. The preliminary turnout estimate does not exceed 40,000. Therefore, at least one eligible voter in Callenhurst did not register by the deadline.
lr.questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in the argument above is most parallel to that in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. The continuing-education log does not contain over 400 entries. Therefore, at least one licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge did not complete the refresher course.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. The continuing-education log contains over 400 entries. Therefore, every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If most licensed pharmacists at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. The continuing-education log does not contain over 400 entries. Therefore, most licensed pharmacists at Greerbridge did not complete the refresher course.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. At least one licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge did not complete the refresher course. Therefore, the continuing-education log does not contain over 400 entries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If every licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course, then the continuing-education log would contain over 400 entries. The continuing-education log does not contain over 400 entries. Therefore, no licensed pharmacist at Greerbridge completed the refresher course.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: (∀x Ax → Bx) → C; ¬C; ∴ ∃x(Ax ∧ ¬Bx). (A) replicates the nested conditional whose antecedent is a universal, runs modus tollens to deny the universal antecedent, and correctly draws the existential ('at least one ... did not') conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Affirms the consequent — concludes the universal from the numerical fact being true, an invalid move.
explanations.C: Replaces 'every' with 'most' in both antecedent and conclusion, so the negation of a 'most' claim is drawn instead of an existential.
explanations.D: Runs the conditional in the opposite direction: denies the universal to conclude the consequent's negation, reversing cause and effect.
explanations.E: Overshoots from 'at least one did not' to 'no one did' — a quantifier strength error at the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-step conjunctive-consequent plus biconditional structure: A → (B ∧ C); ¬B; B ↔ D; ∴ ¬A and ¬D. Students must derive two distinct negations — one by contrapositive of a conjunction and one through the biconditional — both with necessity.
lr.stimulus: If a symphony is genuinely by Grazia, it has both a modulation to the flat mediant in its exposition and a triple-meter trio in its scherzo. The symphony on this score does not modulate to the flat mediant in its exposition. A symphony contains a modulation to the flat mediant in its exposition if, and only if, its autograph manuscript bears a triadic cipher in the margin. It follows that the symphony on this score is not genuinely by Grazia, and its autograph manuscript does not bear a triadic cipher in the margin.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has both a quadriga on the obverse and a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection does not bear a quadriga on the obverse. A coin bears a quadriga on the obverse if, and only if, its die has a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position. It follows that the coin in this collection is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, and its die does not have a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has either a quadriga on the obverse or a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection does not bear a quadriga. A coin bears a quadriga if, and only if, its die has a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position. It follows that the coin is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, and its die does not have a microscopic anchor mark.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has both a quadriga on the obverse and a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection does not bear a quadriga on the obverse. A coin bears a quadriga on the obverse only if its die has a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position. It follows that the coin is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, and its die probably lacks the anchor mark.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has both a quadriga on the obverse and a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection does not bear a facing Arethusa on the reverse. A coin bears a facing Arethusa if, and only if, its die has a microscopic anchor mark at the seven o'clock position. It follows that the coin bears a quadriga on the obverse, and its die does not have a microscopic anchor mark.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm, it has both a quadriga on the obverse and a facing Arethusa on the reverse. The coin in this collection is not a genuine Syracusan dekadrachm. A coin bears a quadriga if, and only if, its die has a microscopic anchor mark. It follows that the coin does not bear a quadriga, and its die does not have the anchor mark.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A → (B ∧ C); ¬B; B ↔ D; ∴ ¬A ∧ ¬D. (A) preserves each step: a conditional with a conjunctive consequent, a negated conjunct, a biconditional binding that conjunct to a fourth property, and a two-part necessary conclusion negating both A and D.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Converts the conjunction in the consequent to a disjunction — denying one disjunct no longer licenses denying the conditional's antecedent on its own.
explanations.C: Replaces the biconditional with a one-way 'only if' conditional and softens one half of the conclusion to 'probably', breaking both connective strength and modal match.
explanations.D: Runs the negation on the wrong conjunct (Arethusa, not quadriga), then draws an unlicensed positive conclusion that the coin bears a quadriga — an inversion of the stimulus's moves.
explanations.E: Uses ¬A as a premise rather than deriving it, then draws ¬B as a conclusion — running the conditional in the wrong direction (denying the antecedent to derive a negated conjunct).

lr.difficultyReason: Short two-speaker dialogue with sharply opposed positions on one central claim. Martina says home cooking is healthier than restaurant food; Reggie explicitly denies this. Four distractors are off-topic or only one speaker addresses them.
lr.stimulus: Martina: People who cook most of their meals at home eat healthier food than people who eat out often. Home cooks control the amount of salt, oil, and sugar in their meals, and restaurant kitchens almost always use more of each than a home cook would. Reggie: That's a myth. Restaurants now publish nutrition information and many of them prepare meals with less salt and oil than the average home cook does. People who eat out regularly are not eating less healthily than those who cook at home.
lr.questionStem: On the basis of their statements, Martina and Reggie are committed to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: restaurants are required by law to publish nutrition information

choices.label: B
choices.text: people who cook at home eat more healthily than people who eat out often

choices.label: C
choices.text: eating too much salt is unhealthy

choices.label: D
choices.text: home cooks enjoy preparing their own meals

choices.label: E
choices.text: restaurants charge more for healthy meals than for unhealthy ones

explanations.correct: Martina asserts that home cooks eat healthier than people who eat out often; Reggie explicitly denies it. That is exactly the proposition at issue.
explanations.A: Neither speaker addresses whether the disclosure is legally required.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both would agree that excess salt is unhealthy; no disagreement there.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses enjoyment of cooking.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses menu pricing.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct disagreement about whether a specific policy should be adopted. Speakers use the same vocabulary and contradict each other on the central proposal; distractors are out-of-scope or mutual-agreement traps.
lr.stimulus: Councilor Dent: Our city should ban gasoline-powered leaf blowers. They produce more pollution per hour of use than most cars, and the noise is a nuisance to every neighbor within two blocks. Councilor Vu: A ban is the wrong response. Electric leaf blowers are already widely available, and landscapers are switching to them on their own. The city should not outlaw a tool that is already being phased out voluntarily.
lr.questionStem: Dent and Vu disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: gasoline-powered leaf blowers produce more pollution per hour than most cars

choices.label: B
choices.text: electric leaf blowers are quieter than gasoline-powered ones

choices.label: C
choices.text: the city should prohibit gasoline-powered leaf blowers

choices.label: D
choices.text: landscapers should be free to choose their own equipment

choices.label: E
choices.text: noise from leaf blowers bothers neighbors

explanations.correct: Dent says the city should ban them; Vu says a ban is the wrong response. That is a direct contradiction about the policy.
explanations.A: Dent asserts this claim; Vu does not address it, so their disagreement cannot be established.
explanations.B: Neither speaker compares the noise of electric and gas blowers directly.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a general position on landscaper autonomy.
explanations.E: Dent says neighbors are bothered; Vu does not deny this.

lr.difficultyReason: Two historians dispute a factual claim about cause. One says the invention of the printing press was the primary driver of rising literacy; the other flatly denies it and assigns primacy to schooling. Distractors are off-topic or agreed-upon.
lr.stimulus: Alenka: The rise in European literacy rates between 1500 and 1800 was driven primarily by the printing press. Once books became cheap and abundant, ordinary people had both the opportunity and the incentive to learn to read. Bertil: The printing press mattered, but it was not the primary driver. Literacy rates rose mainly because governments and churches invested in schools that taught children to read. Without that schooling, cheap books would have sat unread.
lr.questionStem: Alenka and Bertil disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: books became cheaper after the printing press was invented

choices.label: B
choices.text: the printing press had any effect on European literacy rates

choices.label: C
choices.text: the printing press was the primary cause of rising literacy in Europe from 1500 to 1800

choices.label: D
choices.text: governments funded schools during the early modern period

choices.label: E
choices.text: literacy rates in Europe rose between 1500 and 1800

explanations.correct: Alenka says the press was primarily responsible; Bertil explicitly denies that it was primary and assigns primacy to schools.
explanations.A: Both would accept that books became cheaper.
explanations.B: Bertil concedes the press 'mattered'; he doesn't deny any effect.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Bertil asserts it; Alenka does not deny it.
explanations.E: Both speakers accept that literacy rates rose.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics-domain disagreement about a single evaluative claim: whether it is morally permissible to eat animals. Speakers take opposite positions in plain language; distractors are agreement or out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: Parisa: It is morally wrong to eat animals. Animals can suffer, and we now have abundant, nutritious plant foods available. Causing suffering to a sentient creature when we have good alternatives cannot be justified. Quentin: It is not morally wrong. Humans evolved as omnivores, and raising and eating animals in humane conditions is a long-standing and legitimate practice. Causing some harm is acceptable when the practice serves a genuine human interest.
lr.questionStem: Parisa and Quentin disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: animals are capable of suffering

choices.label: B
choices.text: plant-based foods are nutritionally adequate

choices.label: C
choices.text: humans evolved as omnivores

choices.label: D
choices.text: eating animals is morally wrong

choices.label: E
choices.text: factory farming is humane

explanations.correct: Parisa says it is morally wrong; Quentin says it is not. Direct contradiction of the central claim.
explanations.A: Parisa asserts it; Quentin does not deny it — he accepts that some harm is caused.
explanations.B: Parisa asserts it; Quentin says nothing about plant nutrition.
explanations.C: Quentin asserts it; Parisa does not deny it.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses factory farming specifically.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental-science dispute where each speaker makes one explicit central claim about wind power's sufficiency. Direct contradiction; distractors are out-of-scope technical points.
lr.stimulus: Sunita: Wind power alone could supply all of our country's electricity needs. Studies estimate that the wind resources across our plains and coastlines could generate several times our current total demand if fully developed. Tomas: Wind cannot supply all of our electricity. The wind does not blow reliably everywhere at once, and without enormous advances in storage we will always need some other source to fill the gaps.
lr.questionStem: Sunita and Tomas disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the country's plains and coastlines have significant wind resources

choices.label: B
choices.text: wind power can supply all of the country's electricity needs

choices.label: C
choices.text: battery storage technology has improved in recent years

choices.label: D
choices.text: wind turbines are a form of renewable energy

choices.label: E
choices.text: electricity demand is growing in the country

explanations.correct: Sunita asserts wind alone could supply all electricity needs; Tomas explicitly denies it. Direct contradiction.
explanations.A: Sunita asserts this; Tomas does not deny it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Neither speaker addresses recent storage improvements specifically.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses the classification of wind as renewable.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses demand growth.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistics domain with a crisp prescriptive versus descriptive disagreement. Speakers contradict each other over one explicit claim about whether 'literally' should be used non-literally.
lr.stimulus: Professor Holm: Using the word 'literally' to mean 'figuratively,' as in 'I literally died laughing,' is simply incorrect. 'Literally' means 'in a literal sense,' and using it to mean the opposite undermines the distinction the word exists to mark. Professor Iyer: That use is not incorrect. Words change meaning through ordinary use, and 'literally' as an intensifier is now so widespread and well understood that it is a legitimate sense of the word.
lr.questionStem: Holm and Iyer disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the non-literal use of 'literally' is widespread

choices.label: B
choices.text: words can change meaning over time

choices.label: C
choices.text: using 'literally' to mean 'figuratively' is incorrect

choices.label: D
choices.text: 'literally' has a literal sense

choices.label: E
choices.text: listeners are usually confused by the non-literal use of 'literally'

explanations.correct: Holm says the use is simply incorrect; Iyer says it is not incorrect. Direct contradiction.
explanations.A: Iyer asserts it; Holm does not deny that it is widespread.
explanations.B: Iyer asserts it; Holm does not deny it in general.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Both speakers accept that 'literally' has a literal sense.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses listener confusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal-domain dispute with one clear evaluative claim on each side. Speakers directly contradict each other about whether jury trials produce fairer outcomes than bench trials. Distractors are mutual-agreement or off-topic.
lr.stimulus: Wren: Jury trials produce fairer outcomes than bench trials. A jury of twelve ordinary citizens brings a broader range of perspectives than any single judge and is harder for a skilled attorney to manipulate. Xavier: Jury trials are not fairer. Juries are swayed by emotional appeals and often do not understand complex evidence. A seasoned judge is more likely to reach a fair verdict in difficult cases.
lr.questionStem: Wren and Xavier disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: jury trials produce fairer outcomes than bench trials

choices.label: B
choices.text: jurors are ordinary citizens

choices.label: C
choices.text: complex evidence is sometimes presented at trial

choices.label: D
choices.text: attorneys are sometimes skilled at persuasion

choices.label: E
choices.text: judges are appointed rather than elected

explanations.correct: Wren claims jury trials are fairer than bench trials; Xavier explicitly denies that claim. Direct contradiction.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Both accept that jurors are ordinary citizens.
explanations.C: Xavier implies it; Wren does not deny it.
explanations.D: Wren asserts it; Xavier does not deny it.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses how judges are selected.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology domain. Clear disagreement on one factual claim: whether social media has, on balance, worsened teen mental health. Distractors are agreement traps or single-speaker claims.
lr.stimulus: Ori: Widespread social media use has, on balance, worsened teenage mental health over the past fifteen years. Rates of anxiety and depression among teens began climbing at precisely the time smartphones and social platforms became ubiquitous, and many clinicians report a clear link. Petra: Teen mental health has not been worsened by social media on balance. The rise in diagnoses largely reflects greater awareness and willingness to seek treatment, not a real increase in underlying problems caused by these platforms.
lr.questionStem: Ori and Petra disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: smartphones have become ubiquitous among teenagers

choices.label: B
choices.text: social media use has worsened teen mental health on balance

choices.label: C
choices.text: teens should be restricted from using social media

choices.label: D
choices.text: rates of diagnosis for anxiety and depression have risen among teens

choices.label: E
choices.text: clinicians treat teenagers for anxiety and depression

explanations.correct: Ori asserts social media has worsened teen mental health on balance; Petra explicitly denies it. Direct contradiction.
explanations.A: Both accept that smartphones became ubiquitous.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Neither speaker takes a position on restricting use.
explanations.D: Both accept diagnoses have risen; they dispute the cause, not the fact.
explanations.E: Neither speaker disputes that clinicians treat such conditions.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts-domain evaluative disagreement. Speakers make one explicit claim each about whether a museum should return a specific artifact. Direct contradiction; distractors are off-topic or agreed-upon.
lr.stimulus: Curator Ambrose: Our museum should return the bronze statue to its country of origin. It was removed during a colonial expedition without the consent of the local community, and holding onto it today perpetuates that injustice. Director Basile: We should not return it. The statue has been carefully preserved and publicly displayed here for over a century, and returning it now would mean fewer people could see and study it. Our obligation is to public access.
lr.questionStem: Ambrose and Basile disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the bronze statue was removed without local consent

choices.label: B
choices.text: the museum should return the bronze statue to its country of origin

choices.label: C
choices.text: the statue has been preserved at the museum

choices.label: D
choices.text: public access to artifacts is a consideration for museums

choices.label: E
choices.text: colonial-era acquisitions were sometimes carried out without consent

explanations.correct: Ambrose says the museum should return the statue; Basile says it should not. Direct contradiction of the central proposal.
explanations.A: Ambrose asserts this; Basile does not deny it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both accept the statue has been preserved at the museum.
explanations.D: Both treat public access as a legitimate consideration; they weigh it differently.
explanations.E: Both would accept this general point.

lr.difficultyReason: Economics domain with a straightforward disagreement about whether raising tariffs will help domestic manufacturers. Direct contradiction; distractors are out-of-scope or agreement traps.
lr.stimulus: Diego: Raising tariffs on imported steel will help our domestic steel manufacturers. With foreign steel made more expensive, buyers will turn to domestic mills, and our producers will gain customers and revenue. Elise: Raising tariffs will not help our domestic manufacturers. Most of them use imported steel as an input, and higher tariffs will raise their production costs enough to more than offset any gains from reduced foreign competition.
lr.questionStem: Diego and Elise disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: tariffs on imported steel would make foreign steel more expensive for domestic buyers

choices.label: B
choices.text: domestic manufacturers use imported steel as an input

choices.label: C
choices.text: raising tariffs on imported steel will help domestic steel manufacturers

choices.label: D
choices.text: the government has the authority to impose tariffs

choices.label: E
choices.text: consumers prefer products made from domestic steel

explanations.correct: Diego asserts the tariff will help domestic manufacturers; Elise explicitly denies it. Direct contradiction of the central claim.
explanations.A: Both accept that tariffs would make imported steel more expensive.
explanations.B: Elise asserts it; Diego does not deny it.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses the government's legal authority.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses consumer preferences.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept the premise that animal testing has produced medical benefits and both grant that alternatives are improving; the disagreement is specifically about whether the current benefits justify continuing the practice. Trap (A) is an agreement in disguise; trap (E) shifts to a claim only Farooq addresses.
lr.stimulus: Farooq: Animal testing has unquestionably delivered important medical advances, and I would not deny that. But we now have cell-culture and computational methods that approximate many of those results, and continuing to subject animals to painful trials when those alternatives exist is no longer defensible. Hollister: The alternatives you cite are promising but remain unreliable for many systemic effects. Until that changes, the medical gains from animal studies still outweigh the welfare costs, even granting that those costs are real.
lr.questionStem: Farooq and Hollister disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: animal testing has historically contributed to medical progress

choices.label: B
choices.text: the current welfare costs of animal testing are outweighed by its medical benefits

choices.label: C
choices.text: cell-culture methods will eventually supplant animal testing entirely

choices.label: D
choices.text: subjecting laboratory animals to painful procedures causes genuine harm

choices.label: E
choices.text: regulators have been too slow to approve computational alternatives

explanations.correct: Farooq says the practice is no longer defensible given that alternatives exist; Hollister says the medical gains still outweigh the welfare costs. That is a direct disagreement about the current cost-benefit balance.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Farooq explicitly grants that animal testing has delivered important advances, and Hollister presupposes the same.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Neither speaker addresses complete replacement; both only compare current reliability.
explanations.D: Both would accept that the welfare costs are real; Hollister even concedes this explicitly.
explanations.E: Only Farooq gestures toward the availability of alternatives, and neither speaker takes a position on regulatory pace.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers grant that standardized tests correlate with later outcomes and both acknowledge that the correlation is imperfect; the disagreement is specifically over whether the tests should be used as admissions gatekeepers. Trap (D) is a point only one speaker addresses.
lr.stimulus: Ramsey: Standardized admissions tests correlate with first-year college grades, but the correlation is modest and the tests also track family income closely. Given that, we should not let these scores function as gatekeepers for admission. Okafor: The correlation with grades, while imperfect, is still the best single predictor we have, and no admissions office I know of uses the scores as a sole criterion. They belong in the mix precisely because they add information that transcripts alone do not.
lr.questionStem: Ramsey and Okafor's statements most strongly support the claim that they disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: standardized admissions test scores are perfectly correlated with first-year college grades

choices.label: B
choices.text: admissions offices currently use standardized test scores as the sole basis for admission

choices.label: C
choices.text: standardized test scores should be used as a factor in college admissions decisions

choices.label: D
choices.text: transcripts alone are sufficient to predict first-year college grades

choices.label: E
choices.text: standardized test scores correlate with the family income of test-takers

explanations.correct: Ramsey denies the tests should function as gatekeepers; Okafor affirms that they belong in the admissions mix. That is a disagreement about whether the scores should be a factor in admissions.
explanations.A: Both would deny this — Ramsey calls the correlation modest and Okafor calls it imperfect.
explanations.B: Only Okafor addresses current practice; Ramsey takes no position on what offices actually do.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Only Okafor implies transcripts alone are insufficient; Ramsey says nothing about transcripts.
explanations.E: Agreement in disguise — Ramsey asserts this and Okafor does not contest it.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers grant that training data includes copyrighted work and both concede the outputs are often novel; the disagreement turns on whether the training itself constitutes infringement. Trap (A) is a factual point both accept; trap (E) shifts to a normative claim only one addresses.
lr.stimulus: Dex: AI image models are trained on vast archives of copyrighted artwork without the artists' consent. Even when the resulting images look nothing like any single source, the training itself is a use of the works, and that use is an infringement. Vera: The training process analyzes statistical features of the images, not the images themselves, and the outputs are typically novel. Reading a book to learn a writing style is not infringement; training on images to learn visual style is analogous.
lr.questionStem: Dex and Vera disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: AI image models are trained on archives that include copyrighted work

choices.label: B
choices.text: the images generated by AI models are typically copies of specific source artworks

choices.label: C
choices.text: training an AI image model on copyrighted artwork constitutes copyright infringement

choices.label: D
choices.text: reading a copyrighted book to study the author's style constitutes infringement

choices.label: E
choices.text: artists should be compensated when their work is used to train AI image models

explanations.correct: Dex says the training itself is infringement; Vera's analogy is meant to show that such training is not infringement. They take opposite positions on exactly this proposition.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers presuppose that copyrighted works are included in the training data.
explanations.B: Both would deny this — Dex says the outputs look nothing like any single source and Vera says outputs are typically novel.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Only Vera addresses the book analogy; Dex does not commit to a position on reading books.
explanations.E: Neither speaker addresses compensation; the debate is about the legal/conceptual status of training, not about remedy.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that some offset projects fail to deliver the promised carbon reductions and both accept that emissions reduction at the source is desirable. The disagreement concerns whether a well-designed offset program can meaningfully substitute for on-site reductions. Trap (B) is an agreement.
lr.stimulus: Mendez: Independent audits have repeatedly found that many forest-based carbon offset projects overstate their actual carbon reductions, sometimes by an order of magnitude. A company buying such offsets instead of cutting its own emissions is not genuinely addressing its climate impact. Halligan: Audit failures have certainly tarnished offset markets, but the problem is poor measurement, not the concept. With rigorous monitoring and verification, a well-designed offset program can achieve real reductions that firms could not practically achieve on-site.
lr.questionStem: Mendez and Halligan disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: forest-based offset projects have sometimes overstated their carbon reductions

choices.label: B
choices.text: reducing emissions at the source is, in principle, a desirable goal

choices.label: C
choices.text: a well-designed offset program can substitute for a company's on-site emissions reductions

choices.label: D
choices.text: current verification protocols are adequate to detect overstated reductions

choices.label: E
choices.text: companies have a legal obligation to purchase carbon offsets

explanations.correct: Mendez claims that buying offsets instead of cutting emissions is not genuinely addressing climate impact; Halligan claims a well-designed offset program can achieve real reductions firms cannot practically make on-site. They disagree about whether offsets can substitute for on-site cuts.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Halligan concedes that audit failures have occurred.
explanations.B: Both accept this; Mendez frames cutting one's own emissions as the genuine response, and Halligan does not deny its desirability.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Only Mendez alludes to audit findings; neither takes a position on whether current protocols are adequate in general.
explanations.E: Legal obligation is out of scope — neither speaker mentions any legal requirement.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that antibiotic resistance is rising and both accept that over-prescription contributes. The disagreement turns on where the primary responsibility for reform should fall. Trap (A) is a shared premise; trap (E) splits the speakers the wrong way.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Bae: Antibiotic resistance is rising, and over-prescription in primary care is a major driver. The most effective lever is stricter prescribing guidelines enforced at the clinical level, where individual prescribing decisions actually get made. Dr. Ilundain: Physician-level guidelines alone will not be enough. The bulk of antibiotic use is in livestock agriculture, not human medicine, and regulating agricultural use is where reform will make the biggest difference.
lr.questionStem: On the basis of their statements, Dr. Bae and Dr. Ilundain are committed to disagreeing about which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic resistance in humans is a growing problem.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Primary-care physicians sometimes prescribe antibiotics when they are not clinically warranted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The most effective target for reducing antibiotic resistance is prescribing practices in primary care.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Livestock agriculture accounts for the bulk of antibiotic use.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulation of antibiotic use by farmers would, by itself, solve the problem of antibiotic resistance.

explanations.correct: Dr. Bae says the most effective lever is clinical-level prescribing guidelines; Dr. Ilundain denies this by saying the biggest difference will come from regulating agricultural use. That is a direct disagreement about where the most effective target lies.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers take resistance as a given problem worth addressing.
explanations.B: Only Dr. Bae addresses primary-care prescribing specifically; Dr. Ilundain says nothing about whether individual prescriptions are clinically unwarranted.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Only Dr. Ilundain asserts this; Dr. Bae does not deny it and takes no position on the share.
explanations.E: This splits them the wrong way — Dr. Ilundain says agricultural regulation will make the biggest difference, not that it would solve the problem alone; Dr. Bae does not address it at all.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that rent control protects current tenants and that housing supply is strained. The disagreement is specifically about the net effect on renters overall. Trap (B) is a shared premise; trap (D) is a claim only one speaker addresses.
lr.stimulus: Navarro: Rent control protects the tenants who are already in regulated units, and I grant that. But when landlords can't adjust rents on existing stock, developers build fewer new units, and renters who are not yet in the system end up paying more for worse housing. On balance, rent control hurts renters as a group. Sung: Protecting the tenants already in place is not a minor thing — it's the whole point. Displacement is catastrophic for those affected, and a policy that prevents it benefits renters, even if supply effects are real at the margin.
lr.questionStem: Navarro and Sung disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: rent control, taken as a whole, benefits renters as a group

choices.label: B
choices.text: tenants currently living in rent-controlled units are protected by the policy

choices.label: C
choices.text: housing supply effects from rent control are entirely negligible

choices.label: D
choices.text: displacement of tenants imposes severe costs on those affected

choices.label: E
choices.text: developers should be encouraged to build more housing than they currently do

explanations.correct: Navarro concludes that on balance rent control hurts renters as a group; Sung concludes that the policy benefits renters. They take opposite positions on the net effect.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Navarro explicitly grants this and Sung affirms it.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.C: Sung calls supply effects 'real at the margin,' so neither speaker denies the effects exist.
explanations.D: Only Sung characterizes displacement as catastrophic; Navarro does not deny this — he simply doesn't address it directly.
explanations.E: Neither speaker makes recommendations about developer incentives.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that the traditional literary canon is narrow in its demographic origins and both accept that canonical works have literary merit. The disagreement is about whether the curriculum should be reorganized around broader representation. Trap (C) is an agreement; trap (E) splits them the wrong way.
lr.stimulus: Acheampong: The traditional literary canon taught in our universities is overwhelmingly drawn from a narrow slice of authors. That is a fact, and it limits students' sense of what literature can do. A curriculum organized around broader representation would serve students better. Pilsen: The canon is narrow in origin, but the works in it have earned their place through sustained literary power. Reorganizing the curriculum around representation risks replacing one criterion for inclusion with another that has little to do with how good the writing is.
lr.questionStem: Acheampong and Pilsen's statements commit them to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the works in the traditional literary canon possess any literary merit

choices.label: B
choices.text: the university literature curriculum should be reorganized to emphasize broader authorial representation

choices.label: C
choices.text: the traditional literary canon is drawn from a narrow demographic range

choices.label: D
choices.text: literary merit is a criterion that can be applied objectively

choices.label: E
choices.text: students currently have an accurate sense of what literature can do

explanations.correct: Acheampong endorses a curriculum reorganized around broader representation; Pilsen opposes reorganizing on those grounds. They take directly opposing positions on the reorganization proposal.
explanations.A: Neither speaker denies the canon has literary merit — Pilsen affirms it and Acheampong does not deny it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — both speakers grant the canon's narrow origin.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses objectivity of merit directly.
explanations.E: Only Acheampong claims students' sense is limited; Pilsen does not affirm that students currently have an accurate sense — he just doesn't address it.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers grant that juries historically have engaged in nullification and both accept that judges instruct juries to apply the law. The disagreement is about whether jurors have a legitimate right to nullify, not whether they are able to or whether it happens. Trap (A) is an agreement.
lr.stimulus: Yusuf: A jury's power to acquit against the evidence — so-called nullification — has been exercised throughout the history of common law. When a jury's conscience tells it a conviction under a particular statute would be unjust, the jury is entitled to refuse to convict, regardless of the judge's instructions. Leclerc: Jurors have the raw power to acquit against the evidence, and no one disputes that juries have done so. But a power is not a right. The law binds the juror just as it binds the judge, and exercising nullification violates the oath the juror has taken.
lr.questionStem: Yusuf and Leclerc disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: juries have historically acquitted defendants against the weight of the evidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: a juror is entitled to refuse to convict when the juror believes conviction would be unjust

choices.label: C
choices.text: judges instruct juries to apply the law as given

choices.label: D
choices.text: a juror who nullifies can be legally punished for doing so

choices.label: E
choices.text: nullification has ever produced a just outcome in a particular case

explanations.correct: Yusuf says the juror is entitled to refuse to convict when conscience so dictates; Leclerc denies this entitlement, distinguishing raw power from right. That is exactly their point of disagreement.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Leclerc concedes that no one disputes juries have done this.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both accept this as background; neither disputes it.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses punishment of nullifying jurors.
explanations.E: Neither speaker takes a position on the outcomes of particular historical cases.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that reenactments engage the public and that they involve simplification. The disagreement is specifically about whether simplification for engagement produces a net educational gain. Trap (C) is an agreement; trap (E) is a point only one speaker addresses.
lr.stimulus: Professor Okonkwo: Historical reenactments draw large audiences and generate interest in the past, and I grant that this engagement is valuable. But reenactors simplify and sanitize the events they stage, and audiences walk away with tidier versions of history than the record supports. The net educational effect is negative. Curator Holst: Reenactors do simplify — they must, to stage anything at all. But an oversimplified encounter that leaves a visitor curious enough to read further is a net gain over no encounter at all.
lr.questionStem: Professor Okonkwo and Curator Holst disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: historical reenactments tend to draw large audiences

choices.label: B
choices.text: historical reenactments, on balance, have a positive educational effect on their audiences

choices.label: C
choices.text: reenactors simplify the events they stage

choices.label: D
choices.text: the historical record of the events reenactors stage is well-documented

choices.label: E
choices.text: audiences of reenactments sometimes read further about the events afterward

explanations.correct: Okonkwo concludes that the net educational effect is negative; Holst concludes that the result is a net gain. They disagree squarely on the net educational effect.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Okonkwo asserts this and Holst does not contest it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — both speakers affirm that simplification occurs.
explanations.D: Neither speaker addresses the state of the historical record.
explanations.E: Only Holst mentions post-reenactment reading; Okonkwo does not deny it happens.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers accept that a universal basic income would relieve acute poverty and both accept that it is costly. The disagreement concerns whether the work-disincentive concern should block the policy. Trap (A) is an agreement; trap (D) splits the speakers the wrong way.
lr.stimulus: Patel: A universal basic income would dramatically reduce acute poverty, and the pilot programs we have seen bear this out. The main objection — that recipients would stop working — has not materialized in any rigorous study. We should not let an empirically unsupported worry block a policy with documented benefits. Reyna: The pilots have indeed shown little aggregate decline in work effort. I concede that. But pilots are temporary, and people behave differently when they know a benefit is permanent. The work-disincentive concern is not refuted by short-run pilots; it just hasn't been properly tested yet.
lr.questionStem: Patel and Reyna disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: universal basic income pilot programs have reduced poverty among participants

choices.label: B
choices.text: the existing evidence about pilots is sufficient to set aside the work-disincentive concern

choices.label: C
choices.text: pilot participants in universal basic income studies showed significant aggregate declines in work effort

choices.label: D
choices.text: people behave identically whether a benefit is temporary or permanent

choices.label: E
choices.text: a universal basic income would eliminate poverty entirely

explanations.correct: Patel says the empirically unsupported worry should not block the policy — i.e., current evidence suffices to set the concern aside. Reyna says the concern is not refuted by short-run pilots, meaning the evidence does not suffice. That is their exact point of disagreement.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Patel asserts poverty reduction and Reyna does not contest it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Agreement in disguise — Reyna concedes that pilots showed little aggregate decline, and Patel asserts the same.
explanations.D: This splits them the wrong way — Patel does not commit to the 'identically' claim; his point is that the empirical evidence should carry weight. Reyna rejects identity of behavior, but Patel never affirms it.
explanations.E: Neither speaker claims UBI would eliminate poverty entirely; Patel says only that it would dramatically reduce acute poverty.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that the new antibiotic reduces mortality in the trial, agree side effects are non-trivial, and agree resistance is a concern. The disagreement is implicit: Tanaka's reasoning commits her to the view that the trial's mortality benefit should govern approval now, while Ruiz's commits him to the view that it should not, because resistance risks are a current decision-input, not a future one. Trap (B) is agreement in disguise; (D) swaps 'current decision' for 'future prescribing'.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Tanaka: The phase III trial showed a thirty-percent drop in mortality from drug-resistant pneumonia, and the side effect profile, while not trivial, is manageable with monitoring. The agency should approve the drug on that record. Future resistance is a real worry, but it is a worry about what comes next, and can be handled through prescribing guidelines. Dr. Ruiz: A thirty-percent mortality reduction is significant, and I would not dispute the safety data. But broad approval will drive the very resistance we are both concerned about, and once that resistance is entrenched, no prescribing guideline will undo it. The trial result tells us the drug works today; it does not tell us we should authorize it today.
lr.questionStem: Dr. Tanaka and Dr. Ruiz are committed to disagreeing over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the risk that broad approval will accelerate resistance is a sufficient reason to withhold approval now

choices.label: B
choices.text: the drug reduced mortality from drug-resistant pneumonia in the phase III trial

choices.label: C
choices.text: prescribing guidelines can completely eliminate the risk of antibiotic resistance

choices.label: D
choices.text: physicians should restrict their prescribing of the drug once it has been approved

choices.label: E
choices.text: the drug's side effects rule out approval on safety grounds alone

explanations.correct: Tanaka treats resistance as a downstream worry handleable by guidelines, so it is not a reason to withhold approval now; Ruiz treats resistance as the decisive reason to withhold approval now. Piecing together their full statements, they are committed to opposite yes/no answers on exactly this proposition.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Agreement in disguise — Tanaka asserts it and Ruiz calls it significant.
explanations.C: Neither speaker claims complete elimination; Tanaka only says guidelines can handle it, and Ruiz denies guidelines would fix entrenched resistance, not that they aim to eliminate it.
explanations.D: The dialogue is about whether to approve, not about post-approval prescribing behavior; neither speaker takes a position on what individual physicians should do after approval.
explanations.E: Both speakers agree the safety data is acceptable; Tanaka calls side effects manageable and Ruiz says he would not dispute the safety data.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the defendant lied under oath, agree the lie was material, and agree a conviction would be legally sustainable. The disagreement is whether the prosecutor was ethically required to bring the charge, which has to be reconstructed from Lund's 'duty to pursue' reasoning and Abebe's 'discretion to decline where the social cost exceeds the marginal deterrent gain'. Trap (C) is an apparent disagreement that dissolves; (E) is a shift of subject.
lr.stimulus: Lund: The defendant lied under oath about a material fact. A prosecutor who has uncontested evidence of perjury has a duty to pursue that charge; the integrity of sworn testimony depends on people knowing such lies will be prosecuted. Whether a jury convicts is a separate question. Abebe: The evidence here was uncontested, and yes, a conviction would almost certainly have been sustained on appeal. But prosecutorial resources are finite, and when the marginal deterrent value of one more perjury case is small compared to the cases it displaces, the office is entitled to decline. That is not a failure of integrity; it is a judgment about where public harm is greatest.
lr.questionStem: Lund and Abebe's statements commit them to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: a prosecutor faced with uncontested evidence of material perjury is ethically required to bring the charge

choices.label: B
choices.text: the defendant's false statement concerned a material fact

choices.label: C
choices.text: prosecutorial offices operate under genuine resource constraints

choices.label: D
choices.text: a perjury conviction in this case would have been sustained on appeal

choices.label: E
