choices.text: declining to prosecute the case would weaken public trust in sworn testimony

explanations.correct: Lund asserts a duty to pursue perjury where the evidence is uncontested; Abebe asserts the office is entitled to decline when deterrent value is low. The two positions cannot both be held.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Both speakers grant materiality — Lund asserts it and Abebe does not contest it.
explanations.C: Only Abebe invokes resource constraints; Lund takes no position either way on whether such constraints exist, only on their relevance.
explanations.D: Agreement in disguise — Lund implies a conviction was available and Abebe concedes it would likely be sustained.
explanations.E: Lund implies integrity is served by prosecution, but does not claim declining would weaken trust; Abebe's view is that declining is not a failure of integrity. Neither speaker commits to the specific trust-erosion claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree that the Phillips curve has weakened empirically and both agree that low unemployment has coincided with low inflation in the last decade. The disagreement is implicit: Haugen treats weakened correlation as evidence the underlying mechanism is gone, while Desai treats it as evidence the mechanism is masked by favorable supply conditions that may not persist. Trap (A) is agreement in disguise; (D) is out of scope.
lr.stimulus: Haugen: For most of the past decade, unemployment has been historically low without any meaningful pickup in inflation. The Phillips curve, which predicted exactly such a pickup, has lost its predictive grip, and central banks should stop designing policy around a relationship that the data no longer bears out. Desai: I grant that the simple textbook curve has been a poor forecaster recently. But that stretch coincided with uniquely favorable supply conditions — globalization, flexible labor markets, stable commodity prices. Those conditions are fading. Writing off the underlying relationship now is exactly the wrong lesson to draw from a decade of good luck.
lr.questionStem: Haugen and Desai's statements provide the most support for the claim that they would disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Phillips curve has been a poor empirical forecaster over the past decade

choices.label: B
choices.text: the relationship between unemployment and inflation the Phillips curve describes still operates as an underlying mechanism

choices.label: C
choices.text: supply-side conditions over the past decade have been unusually favorable

choices.label: D
choices.text: central banks' current policy frameworks should place more weight on commodity prices

choices.label: E
choices.text: low unemployment has coincided with low inflation in recent years

explanations.correct: Haugen treats the weakened correlation as evidence the underlying relationship is gone; Desai explicitly resists 'writing off the underlying relationship' and attributes the weakness to temporary conditions. That is a direct disagreement about whether the mechanism still operates.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Haugen calls the curve's predictive grip lost and Desai grants the textbook curve has been a poor forecaster recently.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Only Desai takes a position on supply-side conditions; Haugen does not address them.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a position on commodity prices as a policy input; Desai only cites stable commodity prices as one favorable condition.
explanations.E: Both speakers accept this — Haugen states it outright, Desai does not dispute it.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree carbon pricing reduces emissions, both agree regressive effects on low-income households are real, and both agree dividends can be paid. The disagreement is about whether dividends fully neutralize the distributive objection — Olander treats dividends as sufficient; Ibarra treats them as insufficient because the harm is not only in aggregate income but in exposure timing. Trap (A) is agreement; (E) is out of scope.
lr.stimulus: Olander: A carbon price reduces emissions efficiently, and the revenue can be rebated as equal per-person dividends. Once you do that, the typical low-income household comes out ahead in net terms, because their direct carbon footprint is smaller than average. The distributive concern about carbon pricing is, for practical purposes, solved. Ibarra: Aggregate net-positive numbers hide a timing problem. The price rise hits heating, gas, and groceries immediately every month, while the dividend arrives quarterly or annually. A family living paycheck to paycheck is not made whole by a refund that shows up after an eviction notice.
lr.questionStem: Olander and Ibarra are committed to disagreeing over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: a carbon price reduces emissions

choices.label: B
choices.text: equal per-person dividends funded by carbon pricing revenue adequately address the policy's distributional impact on low-income households

choices.label: C
choices.text: the direct carbon footprint of low-income households is smaller than the population average

choices.label: D
choices.text: carbon pricing dividends should be paid monthly rather than less frequently

choices.label: E
choices.text: the government should expand heating subsidies independently of any carbon pricing scheme

explanations.correct: Olander concludes the distributive concern is for practical purposes solved by equal dividends; Ibarra's paycheck-to-paycheck counter is precisely that dividends do not adequately address the impact. Piecing together each speaker's full statement is required.
explanations.A: Both would agree; Olander asserts it and Ibarra does not contest it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Only Olander invokes this claim; Ibarra does not address the comparative footprint.
explanations.D: Ibarra highlights the timing mismatch but does not explicitly advocate monthly payments; Olander does not address payment frequency at all. No clear yes/no disagreement.
explanations.E: Out of scope — neither speaker takes a position on heating subsidies as a separate program.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree restoration is feasible in principle, both agree the watershed has been severely degraded, and both agree native species have declined. The implicit disagreement is whether restoration is worth doing given the baseline question: Quince treats the pre-dam ecosystem as the operative target; Reyes treats it as an arbitrary benchmark not entitled to special authority. Trap (C) is an apparent disagreement that evaporates; (D) is one-sided.
lr.stimulus: Quince: The dam has transformed the watershed, and native salmon runs are down by over ninety percent. Dam removal is engineering-feasible now, and a decade of restoration would let the river return to something close to its pre-dam condition. Given what we have lost, that outcome is clearly worth pursuing. Reyes: I agree removal is feasible, and I do not contest the decline figures. But 'pre-dam condition' is just the state the river happened to be in when someone started measuring. Restoring it favors the species that were dominant then over the species that are dominant now, and I see no reason the earlier configuration has a stronger claim on us.
lr.questionStem: Quince and Reyes disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: dam removal on this river is engineering-feasible at present

choices.label: B
choices.text: restoring the pre-dam ecosystem would succeed on ecological grounds

choices.label: C
choices.text: native salmon populations have declined by over ninety percent

choices.label: D
choices.text: the current species composition of the watershed should be preserved as it now stands

choices.label: E
choices.text: the pre-dam ecosystem is the appropriate target for restoration of this watershed

explanations.correct: Quince treats pre-dam condition as the outcome clearly worth pursuing; Reyes explicitly denies that the earlier configuration has a stronger claim on us than the current one. Each speaker's full argument has to be integrated to see this.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers grant feasibility.
explanations.B: Neither speaker questions ecological success on its own terms; the dispute is whether that target is the right one.
explanations.C: Both accept the decline — Quince asserts it and Reyes does not contest it.
explanations.D: Only Reyes implicitly defends the current configuration; Quince takes no position on preservation as an independent goal.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree recommendation algorithms shape what users see, both agree platforms make editorial-like choices, and both agree user autonomy matters. The implicit disagreement is whether users' revealed consent to opaque ranking defeats an autonomy-based objection — which requires combining Kuroda's 'consent via continued use' with Ferreira's 'consent presupposes the very transparency the system withholds'. Trap (A) is shared; (D) is shift of subject.
lr.stimulus: Kuroda: Every platform that ranks content is making editorial choices; that is unavoidable. Users know this in broad outline, and they continue to use the platforms. Continued use under roughly accurate public descriptions of how ranking works is the kind of consent that settles the autonomy objection to algorithmic curation. Ferreira: Platforms do make editorial choices, and autonomy is exactly what is at stake. But the 'broad outline' users have is a press release, not a mechanism. Meaningful consent to being ranked requires knowing what is being optimized and how, and that is precisely what users are not told. What you are calling consent is compliance.
lr.questionStem: Kuroda and Ferreira's statements most strongly support the claim that they disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: recommendation algorithms make choices analogous to editorial decisions

choices.label: B
choices.text: users' continued use of ranked platforms under current disclosure practices constitutes consent sufficient to defeat the autonomy objection

choices.label: C
choices.text: users currently know the precise optimization targets of recommendation algorithms

choices.label: D
choices.text: platforms should be legally required to publish their ranking source code

choices.label: E
choices.text: autonomy is a consideration that any evaluation of algorithmic ranking must take into account

explanations.correct: Kuroda says continued use under broad public descriptions settles the autonomy objection; Ferreira says that what Kuroda is calling consent is merely compliance and does not defeat the objection. Each speaker's position has to be assembled from multiple sentences.
explanations.A: Both agree platforms make editorial-like choices.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both would deny that users know the precise optimization — Kuroda says users have only a broad outline and Ferreira agrees that is all users have.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a position on publishing source code; the dispute is about consent, not disclosure remedies.
explanations.E: Agreement in disguise — Kuroda frames his argument around the autonomy objection and Ferreira explicitly says autonomy is at stake.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the newly discovered letters are authentic, both agree the conventional account of the treaty's origins has explanatory gaps, and both agree the letters fill some of those gaps. The implicit disagreement is whether the letters warrant overturning the conventional account: Balan treats filling gaps as sufficient; Ostrow treats it as insufficient absent corroboration from independent sources. Trap (A) is agreement; (E) is a shift.
lr.stimulus: Balan: The newly discovered Hartwell letters are authentic, and they fill the awkward gaps in the standard account of the treaty's negotiation — especially the chancellor's silence in the spring of 1827. Historians have been working around those gaps for a century; the letters supply what was missing, and the standard account should be revised accordingly. Ostrow: The letters are genuine, and yes, they plug exactly the gaps you name. But a single correspondent writing from one side of the negotiation is not enough to rewrite the record. Until the Hartwell material is corroborated by sources outside his circle, the most we should say is that a rival account is now plausible, not that the standard one is wrong.
lr.questionStem: Balan and Ostrow are committed to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the Hartwell letters are genuine documents

choices.label: B
choices.text: the conventional account of the treaty's negotiation should be revised in light of the newly discovered letters

choices.label: C
choices.text: the chancellor's silence in the spring of 1827 has gone unexplained in the standard account

choices.label: D
choices.text: corroboration from sources outside Hartwell's circle would strengthen any revised account

choices.label: E
choices.text: the treaty's terms as signed differ from those the chancellor originally favored

explanations.correct: Balan concludes the standard account should be revised accordingly; Ostrow concludes that the most we should say is that a rival account is plausible, not that the standard one is wrong — a direct denial of the revision conclusion.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers affirm authenticity.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both accept this — Balan names the gap and Ostrow says the letters 'plug exactly the gaps you name.'
explanations.D: Only Ostrow invokes corroboration as a standard; Balan does not take a position on whether further corroboration would strengthen a revision.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the debate is about whether to revise the account, not about the chancellor's preferences over terms.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree grammaticality judgments shift across speakers, both agree some shifts reflect change in progress, and both agree that 'standard' usage is partly a social artifact. The implicit disagreement is whether prescriptive judgments ever track a genuine property of the language rather than social positioning. Arriaga says yes (where a construction violates a deep pattern common to most dialects); Pell says no. Trap (C) is shared; (E) is one-sided.
lr.stimulus: Arriaga: Many prescriptive rules, I grant, are just prestige dialect dressed up as grammar. But not all of them. When a construction violates a pattern that shows up in nearly every dialect of the language — say, a word-order constraint that every speaker I have tested respects below the level of awareness — calling that construction ungrammatical is tracking something real about the language, not scoring social points. Pell: Speakers' judgments shift, and what most dialects now share was once shared by fewer. 'Respected by most speakers below awareness' is a description of current distribution, which is itself a social fact. I see no version of 'genuinely ungrammatical' that is not, in the end, a statement about whose usage currently counts.
lr.questionStem: Arriaga and Pell disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: some prescriptive rules reflect prestige dialect dressed up as grammatical rules

choices.label: B
choices.text: any classification of a construction as ungrammatical can track a property of the language rather than a social fact about whose usage counts

choices.label: C
choices.text: grammaticality judgments can shift across generations of speakers

choices.label: D
choices.text: word-order constraints are operative in every dialect of the language

choices.label: E
choices.text: speakers' current usage has the same authority as their grandparents' usage

explanations.correct: Arriaga gives a case where ungrammaticality tracks a genuine property of the language; Pell asserts he sees no version of 'genuinely ungrammatical' that is not a social fact. Resolving this requires reading across each speaker's reasoning.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Arriaga concedes it and Pell plainly endorses it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both accept this — Pell asserts judgments shift and Arriaga does not dispute it.
explanations.D: Arriaga hedges to 'nearly every dialect' and Pell does not take a position on universality; no clean yes/no disagreement.
explanations.E: Only Pell hints at this; Arriaga does not address generational authority.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the work is aesthetically accomplished, both agree the artist held views most would find odious, and both agree the views influenced the work's content. The implicit disagreement is whether aesthetic merit can be evaluated independently of the moral defects expressed in the content. Merton says yes (craft and content separate at the level of evaluation); Salazar says no. Trap (A) is shared; (D) is shift.
lr.stimulus: Merton: The novel is, on any ordinary craft measure, a major achievement — structurally daring, prose of extraordinary control. Everyone grants the author's published views were repellent, and those views do shape what the characters argue. But the quality of the book as a made thing is one judgment, and the moral content it carries is another, and we evaluate them separately. Salazar: Structural daring, prose control, yes. And the views inflect the characters' arguments, as you say. But the book's architecture is built around a sympathetic portrait of those same views. The craft is not hovering above the content; it is how the content is made persuasive. You cannot rate the craft high and the content low and call yourself done.
lr.questionStem: Merton and Salazar's statements provide the most support for the claim that they disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the author's published views are morally objectionable

choices.label: B
choices.text: the aesthetic quality of the novel can be evaluated separately from the moral content the novel expresses

choices.label: C
choices.text: the novel's prose is unusually controlled

choices.label: D
choices.text: novels whose authors hold repellent views should be removed from school curricula

choices.label: E
choices.text: the views of the author shape what the characters of the novel argue

explanations.correct: Merton treats the quality judgment as one thing and the moral content as another, evaluated separately; Salazar says you cannot rate craft high and content low and call yourself done — i.e., the two cannot be evaluated separately. That is the implicit yes/no axis.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — Merton calls the views repellent and Salazar does not contest it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both agree the prose has extraordinary control.
explanations.D: Out of scope — neither speaker takes a position on curricular inclusion.
explanations.E: Both accept this — Merton says the views shape what characters argue and Salazar agrees the views inflect the characters' arguments.

lr.difficultyReason: Both speakers agree the firm's conduct was legal, both agree it caused significant harm to a third party, and both agree the harm was foreseeable. The implicit disagreement is whether foreseeable but lawful harm to a third party triggers moral obligation to compensate — which requires combining Essien's 'legality is the limit of enforceable duty' with Yavuz's 'foreseeability plus causation grounds a moral duty even where law is silent'. Trap (C) is agreement; (D) is a shift.
lr.stimulus: Essien: The firm operated within every rule on the books, and the harm to the downstream community, while real and foreseeable, resulted from conduct no regulator had chosen to prohibit. Where the law draws the line is where enforceable duty ends; beyond that, you may disapprove, but you may not demand payment. Yavuz: I will stipulate the conduct was legal and that the harm was foreseeable — those are precisely my premises. If a firm knowingly acts in a way that predictably injures an identifiable third party, the absence of a statute does not dissolve the obligation to make that party whole. A duty is not only what a legislature has written down.
lr.questionStem: Essien and Yavuz are committed to disagreeing about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: the firm's conduct violated any statute or regulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: a firm has a moral obligation to compensate a third party for foreseeable harm caused by conduct that is not prohibited by law

choices.label: C
choices.text: the harm caused to the downstream community was foreseeable at the time the firm acted

choices.label: D
choices.text: legislatures should enact new statutes prohibiting the firm's type of conduct

choices.label: E
choices.text: regulators have been lax in not prohibiting the firm's conduct

explanations.correct: Essien holds that beyond the law's line you may not demand payment — a denial of obligation to compensate; Yavuz holds the absence of a statute does not dissolve the obligation to make the injured party whole — an affirmation. The pieces have to be assembled from each speaker's full argument.
explanations.A: Agreement in disguise — both speakers stipulate the conduct was lawful.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both accept foreseeability — Essien calls the harm real and foreseeable and Yavuz stipulates the same.
explanations.D: Neither speaker takes a position on future statutes; the debate is about obligation given the current legal landscape.
explanations.E: Only Essien implicitly defends the regulators by saying no regulator chose to prohibit; Yavuz does not take a position on regulator conduct.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-antecedent principle ('only when one has caused harm')  with a direct one-step application. Correct answer satisfies both antecedent and consequent; distractors miss one or both.
lr.stimulus: An apology is called for only when one has caused harm to another person through one's own actions.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wen need not apologize for arriving late to the meeting, even though his tardiness delayed an important decision, because traffic was heavy that morning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although Priya's email contained no errors, she should still apologize to her colleague because the colleague felt uneasy after reading it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Dmitri's careless remark embarrassed his coworker in front of clients, Dmitri ought to apologize to the coworker.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lena should apologize to her neighbor for the loud construction next door, even though a different contractor is doing the work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tomas owes no apology for the canceled flight that stranded his guests, since the airline is at fault and the guests were never harmed.

explanations.correct: Dmitri's own action (the careless remark) caused harm (embarrassment in a professional setting) to another person. The principle's antecedent is met, and the consequent (an apology is called for) is exactly what the judgment reaches.
explanations.A: Reverses the principle. The principle says an apology is called for only when one has caused harm through one's own actions, but the judgment excuses Wen on a different ground (external cause), ignoring that his tardiness still caused harm.
explanations.B: Violates the principle. No harm is identified (no errors, only unease), yet the judgment nevertheless calls for an apology.
explanations.D: Outside the principle's scope. The construction is done by a different party, so Lena did not cause the harm through her own actions.
explanations.E: Partial fit with confused reasoning. The judgment declines to require an apology, but justifies it by denying harm while also invoking a third-party cause; Tomas's own actions are not what the principle tracks here.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct conditional ('a judge must recuse if she has a personal financial stake'). One-step legal application; correct answer matches antecedent and consequent exactly.
lr.stimulus: A judge must recuse herself from any case in which she has a personal financial stake in the outcome.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Judge Ortega need not recuse herself from a contract dispute involving a company in which her adult brother owns a small number of shares.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Judge Halley, whose retirement portfolio holds substantial shares in the defendant corporation, must recuse herself from the pending securities case.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Judge Park should recuse herself from the trademark hearing because the plaintiff's attorney once clerked for her chambers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Judge Nakamura need not recuse herself from the zoning appeal, even though she lives in the neighborhood at issue, because she has no ownership interest in any affected property.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Judge Lin must recuse herself from the sentencing hearing because she publicly criticized the defendant in an interview last year.

explanations.correct: Judge Halley's personal portfolio contains substantial shares in a party to the case, so she has a personal financial stake in the outcome; the principle requires recusal, which the judgment states.
explanations.A: Sibling's holdings are not the judge's personal financial stake, so the antecedent is not met, but this does not itself match the conform question — it merely sits outside the principle.
explanations.C: Satisfies the consequent (recusal) without the principle's antecedent (no financial stake is identified).
explanations.D: Living in the neighborhood is not a financial stake; the judgment declines recusal on a different ground than the principle licenses.
explanations.E: Public criticism is not a financial stake. The judgment requires recusal on a ground the principle does not address.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-antecedent policy principle ('if a public resource is at risk of permanent depletion'). Straightforward application; correct answer has both parts, distractors miss antecedent or invert the conditional.
lr.stimulus: A local government is justified in restricting private use of a public resource if that resource is at risk of permanent depletion.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The town of Marlow is justified in banning the painting of houses in bright colors, because local historians find the tradition of muted tones aesthetically pleasing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The city of Derwent should not limit fishing in its public lake, even though overfishing would soon exhaust the remaining native trout population.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because its underground aquifer is being pumped faster than rainfall can replenish it and will be permanently drained within a decade, the county of Vellis is justified in capping private well withdrawals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The village of Ashmere is justified in regulating private garden plots because residents have complained about unsightly weeds.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The province should restrict private use of the new public beach, since tourism revenue from the beach is important to the local economy.

explanations.correct: The aquifer is a public resource and is at risk of permanent depletion (draining within a decade). The antecedent holds; the judgment (capping private withdrawals is justified) matches the consequent.
explanations.A: Antecedent not met: aesthetic preference is not permanent depletion of a public resource.
explanations.B: Violates the principle: the antecedent (risk of permanent depletion of public fish stock) is met, yet the judgment declines the restriction the principle would license.
explanations.D: Antecedent not met: complaints about weeds do not concern depletion of a public resource.
explanations.E: Antecedent not met: tourism revenue is not the same as the resource itself being at risk of permanent depletion.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple medical-ethics conditional ('a physician should disclose a side effect to the patient before prescribing if it is common and serious'). Both parts of the antecedent are obvious; one-step match.
lr.stimulus: A physician should disclose a potential side effect to a patient before prescribing a medication whenever that side effect is both common and serious.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Ahmed should disclose that a newly approved blood-pressure drug may cause a faint metallic taste, since a handful of early patients reported it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Sato need not disclose the risk of severe liver failure from a new antifungal before prescribing it, since only about one in fifty thousand patients is affected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Before prescribing the new antidepressant, Dr. Moreau should inform each patient about the drug's well-documented risk of severe allergic reaction, which occurs in roughly fifteen percent of users.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Chen should disclose a rare and mild rash associated with a new topical cream, since some patients prefer to know about any cosmetic effects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Volkov need not disclose any side effects of a new arthritis drug to a patient who asks not to hear about them.

explanations.correct: A severe allergic reaction affecting roughly fifteen percent of users is both serious and common; the principle then requires disclosure before prescribing, which matches the judgment.
explanations.A: Partial fit: the side effect may be common among early patients but is not serious (a faint metallic taste).
explanations.B: Violates the principle, but the antecedent is not fully met — liver failure is serious but rare (one in fifty thousand), so the principle does not require disclosure; the judgment's declination is on the wrong ground to conform.
explanations.D: Partial fit: rare and mild fails both parts of the antecedent, yet the judgment requires disclosure on other grounds.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope: a patient's preference not to hear about side effects is not a consideration the principle addresses.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-antecedent ethical principle ('only if one could reasonably have foreseen the consequences'). One-step application to a concrete case.
lr.stimulus: A person is morally blameworthy for a harmful outcome only if she could reasonably have foreseen that her action would cause it.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Helena is morally blameworthy for her cousin's allergic reaction to the pastry she baked, because she had been told of the cousin's nut allergy and knowingly used ground almonds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marcus is not morally blameworthy for the flood damage to his office, since he was out of town when the pipe burst.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rosa is morally blameworthy for her friend's disappointment, even though she could not have known her friend was expecting a different gift.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nadia is not morally blameworthy for the bicycle accident, because no one was seriously injured.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Idris is morally blameworthy for the failed surprise party, because he did not attend it.

explanations.correct: Helena had been told of the nut allergy and knowingly used ground almonds, so she could reasonably have foreseen the harmful outcome; the principle licenses blame, which the judgment imposes.
explanations.B: Not being present is not the same as the outcome being unforeseeable; the judgment excuses on a ground the principle does not track.
explanations.C: Violates the principle. The antecedent (foreseeability) is explicitly not met, yet the judgment assigns blame.
explanations.D: Outside scope: the severity of injury is not the principle's criterion for blame.
explanations.E: Outside scope: non-attendance is not a harmful action whose consequences were foreseeable in the relevant sense.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple economic policy principle ('a subsidy is warranted only if the market systematically underprovides a clear public benefit'). One-step match.
lr.stimulus: A government subsidy is warranted only if the market systematically underprovides some good that confers a clear public benefit.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The federal government is warranted in subsidizing a popular brand of soda, since soda is widely purchased and contributes to consumer satisfaction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because childhood vaccination reduces the spread of infectious disease across the population but private markets routinely fall short of universal coverage, the government is warranted in subsidizing childhood vaccines.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The government should subsidize luxury automobiles, given that their manufacturers employ many workers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The government is not warranted in subsidizing basic scientific research, even though the market funds too little of it and the resulting knowledge benefits the public.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The government is warranted in subsidizing home renovations because renovated homes raise property values for the owners.

explanations.correct: Childhood vaccination confers a clear public benefit (reduced disease spread) and the market systematically underprovides it. The antecedent holds, and the judgment warrants the subsidy.
explanations.A: Antecedent not met: soda is widely sold, so the market is not underproviding it, and consumer satisfaction is not a clear public benefit.
explanations.C: Antecedent not met: employment alone is not the kind of systematic market failure plus public benefit the principle names.
explanations.D: Violates the principle: the antecedent (underprovision of a good with clear public benefit) is met, yet the judgment declines the subsidy the principle would license.
explanations.E: Antecedent not met: higher property values for owners is a private, not a public, benefit.

lr.difficultyReason: Basic environmental-policy conditional ('an activity must be halted if it causes irreversible damage to a protected habitat'). Direct antecedent match; one-step application.
lr.stimulus: Any activity that is causing irreversible damage to a legally protected habitat must be halted.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Logging on private land adjacent to the national forest should be halted, because residents find the noise disruptive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The resort's beachfront expansion need not be halted, even though it is permanently destroying the legally protected sea-turtle nesting grounds beneath it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The limestone quarry operating within the designated wetland reserve, which is draining groundwater and permanently altering the reserve's ecology, must be halted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Commercial fishing in the open ocean should be halted because fish stocks vary from year to year.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The research station's temporary observation platform, which causes no measurable damage, must be halted because it is located in a protected habitat.

explanations.correct: The quarry is an activity causing irreversible damage (permanently altering ecology, draining groundwater) in a legally protected habitat (designated wetland reserve). Principle requires halting; judgment matches.
explanations.A: Antecedent not met: disruption from noise on adjacent private land is not irreversible damage to a protected habitat.
explanations.B: Violates the principle: the antecedent is met (permanent destruction of protected nesting grounds) yet the judgment declines to halt the activity.
explanations.D: Antecedent not met: yearly variation is not irreversible damage, and the open ocean is not described as a legally protected habitat.
explanations.E: Antecedent not met: the platform causes no measurable damage, let alone irreversible damage, so the principle does not require halting it.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple tech-ethics conditional about user notification. One antecedent; direct consequent. Distractors miss the antecedent or satisfy only the consequent.
lr.stimulus: A software company is obligated to notify its users promptly whenever a security breach has exposed their personal data.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because an intrusion last week exposed the stored addresses and phone numbers of its account holders, the cloud-storage firm Meridian is obligated to notify those users promptly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The social-media company Fable need not notify its users about a breach that exposed only aggregated, anonymous usage statistics.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The online retailer Breva should notify its users about its new pricing structure as soon as possible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The messaging app Larkwood need not notify its users promptly about a breach that exposed their private chat logs, since a public announcement would alarm them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gaming platform Quorum should notify users about upcoming server maintenance, since advance notice is a common courtesy.

explanations.correct: A security breach exposed users' personal data (addresses and phone numbers), so the antecedent holds; the judgment that Meridian is obligated to notify users promptly matches the consequent.
explanations.B: Antecedent not met: aggregated anonymous statistics are not personal data, so the principle is silent.
explanations.C: Outside scope: a new pricing structure is not a security breach exposing personal data.
explanations.D: Violates the principle: the antecedent (breach exposed private chat logs, which are personal data) is met, yet the judgment declines the required notification.
explanations.E: Outside scope: server maintenance is not a security breach.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple journalism-ethics principle ('an anonymous source's name should be withheld only if revealing it would place the source in serious danger'). Single antecedent; one-step match.
lr.stimulus: A journalist is justified in withholding the name of an anonymous source only when revealing the name would place the source in serious danger.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reporter Elif is justified in withholding the name of a whistleblower who would face documented retaliation, including threats against her life, from a powerful cartel if identified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reporter Kai is justified in withholding the name of a restaurant critic who simply prefers to remain anonymous for professional ease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reporter Anya should reveal the name of a source whose identification would cost her her job and expose her to credible death threats.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reporter Benno is justified in withholding the name of a local gardener because the gardener finds media attention unpleasant.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reporter Carla must reveal the name of any source whose testimony is disputed, regardless of the consequences.

explanations.correct: The whistleblower faces documented retaliation including threats against her life — serious danger — if named. The principle's antecedent holds; the judgment withholds the name, matching the consequent.
explanations.B: Antecedent not met: professional ease is not serious danger.
explanations.C: Violates the principle: the antecedent is met (credible death threats), so withholding would be justified, yet the judgment reveals the name.
explanations.D: Antecedent not met: unpleasant attention is not serious danger.
explanations.E: Outside scope: disputed testimony is not what the principle addresses; it speaks only to danger.

lr.difficultyReason: Single-antecedent legal principle ('a landlord must return the security deposit in full if the tenant has caused no damage beyond ordinary wear'). Direct, one-step application.
lr.stimulus: A landlord must return a tenant's security deposit in full at the end of the lease if the tenant has caused no damage to the premises beyond ordinary wear and tear.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because tenant Okafor left faded paint and lightly scuffed floors but caused no damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, her landlord must return her security deposit in full.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Landlord Petrov need not return the full security deposit to a tenant who caused no damage, because the apartment has been on the market for two months.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Landlord Mehta must return the full security deposit to tenant Wylan, even though Wylan punched several holes in the drywall that required substantial repair.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Landlord Quiroga should return half of the security deposit to a tenant who caused no damage, because half seems like a fair compromise.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Landlord Reyes must return the full security deposit to tenant Halim because Halim paid rent on time every month.

explanations.correct: Faded paint and lightly scuffed floors are ordinary wear and tear, and the tenant caused no damage beyond that. The principle's antecedent is met, and the judgment returns the full deposit.
explanations.B: Violates the principle: the antecedent is met (no damage), yet the judgment declines full return on an unrelated ground (market conditions).
explanations.C: Violates the principle: punched holes in drywall requiring substantial repair exceed ordinary wear and tear, so the antecedent is not met, yet the judgment requires full return.
explanations.D: Violates the principle: the antecedent is met (no damage), so the principle requires full — not half — return.
explanations.E: Antecedent not met — or at least not invoked. Timely rent payment is not the condition the principle tracks; the judgment reaches the right outcome on the wrong ground.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent with an 'unless' exception. Correct answer must satisfy both conditions and confirm the exception does not apply. Trap (A) satisfies only the first condition; trap (D) meets both conditions but triggers the exception the principle's consequent defers to.
lr.stimulus: A journalist is obligated to grant a source anonymity if (a) the source could plausibly face retaliation for speaking and (b) the information the source provides cannot be reliably obtained elsewhere, unless the source has knowingly provided false information to the journalist on a prior occasion.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Merrin, a city accountant, risks being fired if her employer learns she spoke with a reporter about questionable expenditures. Because many other accountants in the office have access to the same records, the reporter is obligated to grant her anonymity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Orson, a factory foreman, has documented evidence of unreported chemical spills that regulators have been unable to obtain through official channels. Because Orson would likely be dismissed if identified, and has never misled the reporter before, the reporter is obligated to grant him anonymity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pell, a retired engineer, has volunteered details about long-closed safety investigations. Since Pell faces no professional consequences and the information is widely documented in archives, the reporter may decline to grant anonymity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Quill, a shipping clerk, faces likely retaliation for disclosing smuggling operations that the reporter cannot corroborate through other witnesses. However, Quill once fabricated a quotation for the same reporter two years ago. The reporter is nonetheless obligated to grant him anonymity.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ravi, a lab technician, could lose his visa if identified, and has always been truthful with the reporter. The reporter grants him anonymity even though the same information has already been reported accurately by a rival newspaper.

explanations.correct: Orson satisfies both antecedent conditions — he faces plausible retaliation (dismissal) and the information is not reliably available elsewhere (regulators could not obtain it). The exception does not apply because he has never misled the reporter. The principle's consequent (obligation to grant anonymity) therefore attaches.
explanations.A: Satisfies only condition (a). The information is available through other accountants with the same records, so condition (b) fails.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Misapplies the principle by treating the antecedent's failure as though it licensed a judgment about what the journalist 'may' do; the principle only states what obligation arises when both conditions hold, not permissions when they fail.
explanations.D: Correctly identifies both conditions but then ignores the exception — Quill's prior fabrication triggers the 'unless' clause, which defeats the obligation. The judgment contradicts the principle.
explanations.E: Fails condition (b) — the information is reliably available elsewhere (already reported by a rival). Granting anonymity is not required by the principle.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound antecedent requiring three matching features. Correct answer aligns each feature to the principle's terms. Trap (B) collapses two features into one; trap (E) misreads the 'proportionate' requirement as any penalty whatsoever.
lr.stimulus: A public official may be sanctioned for accepting a gift from a regulated party only if (a) the gift's value materially exceeds customary hospitality and (b) the official had decision-making authority over a matter affecting the giver at the time the gift was accepted. Any sanction imposed must be proportionate to the value of the gift received.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Commissioner Aldin accepted a $3,000 watch from a firm whose zoning application he was then reviewing. He is suspended for six months — a sanction proportionate to the gift's value.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inspector Belan accepted a catered lunch from a vendor she had already finished auditing two years earlier. She is suspended for two weeks because the lunch exceeded customary hospitality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Director Ceylan accepted an $8,000 vacation package from a contractor, but she had no authority over any matter concerning the contractor. She is sanctioned because the gift's value was plainly excessive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Auditor Derwin accepted a modest holiday fruit basket from a company he was currently auditing. He is sanctioned because he had decision-making authority at the time.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulator Estin accepted a $500 sports ticket from a licensee whose renewal he was reviewing. He is permanently barred from public service on the ground that any gift from a regulated party is intolerable.

explanations.correct: Aldin satisfies both antecedent conditions: a $3,000 watch materially exceeds customary hospitality, and he had decision-making authority over the giver's zoning application at the time. A six-month suspension is described as proportionate to the gift's value, matching the principle's consequent requirement.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Fails condition (b). Belan had no current decision-making authority over the vendor; the audit had concluded. The principle does not license a sanction.
explanations.C: Fails condition (b). Without authority over any relevant matter, the principle does not authorize a sanction regardless of the gift's value.
explanations.D: Fails condition (a). A modest fruit basket does not materially exceed customary hospitality; authority alone is not enough.
explanations.E: Violates the proportionality requirement. A $500 ticket, even if both antecedent conditions are met, does not justify permanent bar — the sanction is not proportionate.

lr.difficultyReason: Conditional with 'unless' exception for emergencies. Correct answer shows both antecedent conditions satisfied with no exception triggered. Trap (C) confuses the exception for the main rule; trap (D) satisfies only one antecedent condition.
lr.stimulus: A physician should disclose a diagnosis to a patient's immediate family only if (a) the patient has given prior written consent to such disclosure and (b) the disclosure would facilitate care the patient is presently receiving, unless an emergency renders the patient incapable of expressing preferences.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Farrow tells Mr. Halden's daughter about Mr. Halden's diabetes because she asks and seems concerned, even though Mr. Halden has not signed any consent form and is currently alert.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Glent, caring for Ms. Ives who signed a consent form last year, informs Ms. Ives's spouse of her new hypertension diagnosis because the spouse will help administer her daily medication.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Henner, treating Mr. Jeran who is conscious and has refused to sign any consent, nonetheless informs his brother of Mr. Jeran's test results, citing the emergency exception because Mr. Jeran looks anxious.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Ionne, whose patient Ms. Kell signed a general consent form, tells Ms. Kell's cousin about a diagnosis unrelated to any current treatment because the cousin is curious about family health history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Lamas declines to share any information with Mr. Morn's family, even though Mr. Morn is unconscious after a stroke and his family needs the diagnosis to coordinate immediate care.

explanations.correct: Ms. Ives has given prior written consent, and the disclosure facilitates care she is presently receiving (her spouse will administer her medication). Both antecedent conditions hold, no exception applies, and the judgment that disclosure is appropriate tracks the principle's consequent.
explanations.A: Fails condition (a). No written consent exists, and the patient is alert, so the exception does not apply either.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Misapplies the exception. The patient is conscious and has refused consent; 'anxious' does not render him incapable of expressing preferences. The judgment treats the exception as a freestanding license.
explanations.D: Fails condition (b). The diagnosis is unrelated to care the patient is presently receiving, so disclosure to a curious cousin is not authorized.
explanations.E: Misapplies the exception — the patient is incapable of expressing preferences, the emergency exception is precisely meant to apply, and disclosure would be appropriate under the principle. Declining contradicts the principle.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part conjunctive antecedent; correct answer threads both conditions precisely. Trap (A) inverts the 'in advance' requirement; trap (E) meets one condition but not the other.
lr.stimulus: A research institution is justified in retracting a published study only if (a) the study's central empirical claim has been shown to be incorrect and (b) the error cannot be adequately addressed by publishing a correction in place of retraction.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A journal retracts a study after the authors announce in advance that they might publish revisions in the future.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A journal retracts a paper whose central finding about a drug's efficacy has been shown wrong by subsequent trials; because the error pervades the paper's data, methods, and conclusions, a correction would not suffice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A journal retracts a paper whose supplemental appendix contains typographical errors, even though the study's main finding remains well-supported.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A journal declines to retract a paper whose central claim has been conclusively refuted, on the ground that retractions are disfavored as a matter of institutional culture.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A journal retracts a study because its central finding turned out to be wrong, despite the fact that a brief erratum would clearly have corrected the single misreported figure at issue.

explanations.correct: The retraction is justified: the central empirical claim (drug efficacy) is shown to be incorrect, and the pervasive nature of the error means a correction would not adequately address it. Both antecedent conditions hold, and retraction is the matching consequent.
explanations.A: Fails both conditions. There is no showing of incorrectness and no showing that correction would be inadequate; 'announced in advance' is not a factor in the principle.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Fails condition (a). The central finding is well-supported; typographical errors in an appendix do not satisfy the antecedent.
explanations.D: Contradicts the principle's implied permissive force — when both conditions are met, retraction is justified; refusing it on cultural grounds disregards the principle.
explanations.E: Fails condition (b). Because a brief erratum would have corrected the error, retraction is not justified even though condition (a) is met.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound antecedent with an exception for substantial public benefit. Correct answer requires both conditions plus a judgment that weighs the exception. Trap (B) wrongly applies the exception; trap (D) satisfies only the first condition.
lr.stimulus: A government agency should refuse to award a contract to a bidder if (a) the bidder has previously defaulted on a similar public contract and (b) credible alternative bidders are available, unless awarding the contract to the defaulting bidder would produce a substantial public benefit unavailable from any alternative.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The transportation authority awards a bridge-maintenance contract to Verdin Ltd., which defaulted on a prior bridge contract, because Verdin's bid is the lowest by a small margin.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The water district awards a treatment contract to Stellan Co., which defaulted on a similar contract last year, reasoning that Stellan has changed its management and probably will not default again.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The housing agency refuses a rehabilitation contract to Polmer Inc., which defaulted on a similar public rehabilitation contract two years ago, because three credible alternative bidders have submitted comparable offers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The parks department refuses to award a landscaping contract to Nivan Corp., which has never defaulted on any public contract, on the ground that alternative bidders are available.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The defense office awards a specialized radar contract to Oberst GmbH, which defaulted on a similar contract, because Oberst alone possesses a patented technology essential to national air-traffic monitoring that no alternative can replicate.

explanations.correct: Polmer satisfies both antecedent conditions — prior default on a similar contract and credible alternative bidders are available. No substantial public benefit is identified that would trigger the exception, so refusal is exactly what the principle prescribes.
explanations.A: Violates the principle — Verdin meets the antecedent conditions (prior default and, implicitly, other bidders exist since a margin is mentioned), yet the authority awards rather than refuses, with no exception triggered.
explanations.B: Misapplies the exception. Management changes and hope of non-default are not 'substantial public benefit unavailable from any alternative.' The antecedent was met and refusal was required.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Fails condition (a) — Nivan has never defaulted. The principle supplies no basis for refusal.
explanations.E: Correctly invokes the exception (unique patented technology), so the award is consistent with the principle. However, E describes an exception case — the question is which conforms, and E's judgment is that the agency awards; that is permitted, but C more precisely illustrates conformance because the principle's main operative consequent is 'refuse,' and E depends entirely on the exception clause with some ambiguity about comparable alternatives.

lr.difficultyReason: Conditional principle with two joint conditions and a 'proportionate' qualifier on the consequent. Trap (C) meets both antecedent conditions but selects a disproportionate remedy; trap (A) satisfies only one.
lr.stimulus: An employer is justified in terminating an employee for a single policy violation only if (a) the violation caused substantial harm to the company or its customers and (b) the employee was on notice that the conduct was prohibited; otherwise, any discipline imposed should be proportionate to the harm caused.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rhelan fires Truso after Truso's single data-entry error caused a customer to receive a duplicate shipment costing $40; Truso had received no prior training on the data-entry protocol.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Umber fires Vail after Vail, who had signed the company's confidentiality policy, leaked a client roster that caused the company to lose its largest account worth millions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Welton fires Xeran after Xeran ignored a posted safety rule, resulting in a minor delay that cost the company roughly $200, even though Xeran had attended the mandatory safety briefing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ylarn issues a written warning to Zemi after Zemi, despite signed training records, leaked proprietary source code that caused the company millions in competitive losses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Acrell fires Boden, a new hire on his first day, after Boden posted an offhand social-media comment about the company that caused no measurable harm.

explanations.correct: Vail satisfies both conditions — the leak caused substantial harm (loss of the largest account worth millions), and he had notice of the prohibition (signed the confidentiality policy). Termination is the proportionate response to harm of that magnitude, tracking the principle's consequent.
explanations.A: Fails both conditions: $40 is not substantial harm, and Truso had no notice of the protocol. Termination is not justified.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Violates the proportionality qualifier. The harm ($200 delay) was minor; termination is disproportionate even though both antecedent conditions are met.
explanations.D: Meets both antecedent conditions with substantial harm (millions in competitive losses), so termination would be justified; a written warning is disproportionately lenient, contradicting the principle's proportionality requirement.
explanations.E: Fails both conditions — no measurable harm, and a first-day offhand comment suggests no notice of a specific prohibition. Termination is unjustified.

lr.difficultyReason: Principle with two-part antecedent and an 'unless' exception for urgency. Correct answer satisfies both conditions with no exception; trap (D) inverts the exception by treating it as a separate sufficient condition.
lr.stimulus: A legislator ought to abstain from voting on a measure if (a) the measure would financially benefit a member of the legislator's immediate family and (b) the legislator has not publicly disclosed the relationship, unless the vote cannot be postponed and the legislator's participation is necessary for a quorum.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Senator Arun, whose sister owns stock in a company that would benefit from a tax measure, abstains from the vote even though he publicly disclosed the relationship in advance and a quorum was present without him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Representative Balin, whose brother-in-law owns a firm that would profit from a contracting bill, abstains from the vote; she has never disclosed the relationship publicly and the vote could easily be rescheduled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Councilor Cordel votes on a zoning measure that would benefit his uncle's business, even though he has made no public disclosure and the vote is a routine matter that could be taken next week.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Assemblywoman Dorien, whose son would profit from a highway appropriation, abstains during an emergency session where her vote is needed for a quorum and the measure cannot be postponed, citing the urgency exception.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Delegate Eriss, whose father-in-law benefits from a subsidy bill, votes on the measure after publicly disclosing the relationship; her vote is not needed for a quorum and the bill could have waited a week.

explanations.correct: Balin's brother-in-law is an immediate family member whose firm would financially benefit, she has not disclosed the relationship, and the vote could be postponed (so the exception does not apply). Abstention is the precise consequent the principle demands.
explanations.A: Fails condition (b) — Arun has publicly disclosed the relationship, so the antecedent is not satisfied. The principle does not require abstention; abstaining is not dictated by the rule.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Contradicts the principle. Both conditions are met (undisclosed relationship, family benefit, postponable vote), but Cordel votes rather than abstaining.
explanations.D: Inverts the exception. The exception is precisely designed for this situation (unpostponable vote + quorum necessity), so Dorien should vote, not abstain. Citing the urgency exception to justify abstention reverses the rule's direction.
explanations.E: Ambiguous on condition (b) — Eriss disclosed, so the antecedent fails. The principle does not mandate abstention here. But voting on a self-benefiting measure when waiting is feasible is not addressed, and the judgment does not clearly conform to the rule's operative consequent.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound sufficient condition with an 'unless' clause. Correct answer meets both predicates; trap (C) satisfies the exception rather than the main conditions; trap (E) meets one predicate but not both.
lr.stimulus: A book reviewer is justified in giving a strongly negative review only if (a) the book fails to achieve the goals the author explicitly sets for it and (b) the reviewer has read the book in its entirety, unless the book is a revised edition whose revisions the reviewer has read alongside the prior published review.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Critic Feris writes a strongly negative review of a novel whose stated aim is to depict a coherent fictional society, arguing that the world-building is incoherent; Feris read only the first third of the book before concluding it was unsalvageable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Critic Glint writes a strongly negative review of a biography whose author announced the goal of establishing the subject's hidden role in founding a political party; Glint, having read the full book, concludes the book provides no evidence of any such role.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Critic Hanel writes a strongly negative review of a revised edition, having read only the revisions and not the original edition or any prior review of it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Critic Indri writes a strongly negative review of a cookbook whose author promised 'quick weeknight meals'; Indri, having read it cover-to-cover, concedes that the recipes do take only 20 minutes but dislikes the photography.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Critic Jorsan writes a strongly negative review of a policy book whose author explicitly aimed to defend a particular reform; Jorsan has read the book cover to cover and finds the reform defense forceful and well-documented.

explanations.correct: Glint satisfies both conditions — the book fails to meet its explicit goal (establishing the subject's hidden role), and Glint has read the entire book. The exception is irrelevant (this is not a revised edition). A strongly negative review is justified.
explanations.A: Fails condition (b) — Feris read only a third of the book. The principle does not license a strongly negative review on partial reading.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Misapplies the exception — the exception requires both the revisions and the prior published review, and Hanel has not read the prior review. The conditions for the exception are not fully satisfied.
explanations.D: Fails condition (a) — the book achieves its stated goal (quick weeknight meals); dissatisfaction with photography falls outside the stated aims.
explanations.E: Fails condition (a) — the book accomplishes its stated goal. A strongly negative review is not justified by the principle.

lr.difficultyReason: Compound antecedent with exception for the merchant's own wrongdoing. Correct answer satisfies both conditions and confirms the exception does not apply; trap (A) meets only one condition; trap (E) triggers the exception.
lr.stimulus: A consumer is entitled to a full refund on a returned product if (a) the product failed to perform as advertised within the warranty period and (b) the failure was not caused by the consumer's misuse, unless the merchant can show that the consumer had concealed a defect from the merchant at the time of purchase.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Karan is entitled to a full refund on a blender that stopped working after he used it to crush metal bolts, a use not advertised; the blender was still within its warranty.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lerin is entitled to a full refund on a laptop that failed to achieve the battery life advertised on the box; the failure occurred within the one-year warranty, resulted from a manufacturing defect, and Lerin had no defect to conceal at the time of purchase.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marsha is not entitled to a full refund on a vacuum cleaner that stopped working because she vacuumed water despite the manual's warnings, even though the failure occurred within warranty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nevers is entitled to a partial refund on a printer that failed to print at the advertised speed within warranty, even though the failure was caused by his own firmware tampering.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ollim is entitled to a full refund on a used motorcycle whose engine seized within warranty; at purchase, Ollim had inspected the engine privately and concealed from the dealer that its oil seals were already leaking.

explanations.correct: Lerin satisfies both antecedent conditions — advertised performance failure within warranty, not caused by misuse — and the exception does not apply (no concealed defect at purchase). A full refund is exactly what the principle prescribes.
explanations.A: Fails condition (b) — crushing metal bolts is misuse of a blender. The principle does not entitle Karan to a refund.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Correctly denies a refund, but the judgment is about what the consumer is not entitled to; while consistent with the principle, it describes an antecedent-failure case rather than conforming to the principle's operative consequent (entitlement).
explanations.D: Confuses the principle's consequent. The principle speaks of a full refund; condition (b) is not met (firmware tampering is misuse), so the principle does not entitle Nevers to any refund under its terms.
explanations.E: Triggers the exception — Ollim concealed a known defect from the dealer at the time of purchase. The merchant's showing defeats entitlement, and a full refund is not required.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-part antecedent with explicit scope limitation. Correct answer satisfies both conditions precisely within scope; trap (B) satisfies neither; trap (D) meets only the first condition.
lr.stimulus: A public university is justified in restricting an invited speaker's appearance on campus only if (a) the speaker's planned remarks would reasonably be expected to cause imminent disruption to ongoing instruction and (b) less restrictive measures would not adequately prevent that disruption; restrictions are never justified merely because the remarks are unpopular.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pren University bars a speaker from campus solely because a faculty committee finds her previously published arguments offensive; classes elsewhere on campus would not have been disrupted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Querst University permits a speaker to appear at its largest auditorium even though credible reports suggest that her remarks will almost certainly trigger a protest inside adjacent lecture halls, disrupting classes; campus police decline to coordinate any crowd management.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rellen University relocates a planned speech from a classroom building to an off-peak evening time in a separate venue, after credible evidence that daytime remarks would disrupt adjacent classes and after ruling out lighter measures that proved insufficient in similar prior events.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sorent University cancels a talk because its provost expects that the speaker's arguments will offend many alumni donors, though no disruption to instruction is anticipated.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Traven University restricts a speaker's use of amplified sound during a campus speech because the amplification — not the content — would disrupt adjacent classes; however, the university does so without first considering whether a smaller sound system would suffice.

explanations.correct: Rellen's relocation satisfies both antecedent conditions — credible evidence of imminent disruption to instruction, and less restrictive measures have been ruled out after prior failure. The restriction is not based on the remarks' unpopularity, honoring the scope limitation. The judgment matches the principle.
explanations.A: Violates the principle's explicit scope limitation: the restriction is based solely on offensiveness of prior arguments, not on imminent disruption to instruction.
explanations.B: Fails the principle's consequent direction — where both conditions would justify at least some restriction or coordination, Querst takes no action at all. This tests the opposite misapplication.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Violates the scope limitation and fails condition (a) — cancellation rests on offense to donors, not on disruption to instruction.
explanations.E: Fails condition (b) — the university has not determined whether less restrictive measures (a smaller sound system) would suffice before imposing the restriction.

lr.difficultyReason: Three compound antecedent conditions, an 'unless' exception whose own antecedent must be checked, and a proportionality clause. Correct answer must satisfy all three conditions, show the exception does not trigger, and confirm the punishment scales with the harm. Traps satisfy the main conditions but fall under the exception, invert the proportionality requirement, or rely on a different subsidiary principle.
lr.stimulus: A judge should impose the maximum statutory sentence on a convicted defendant only if (a) the crime caused serious and lasting harm to an identifiable victim, (b) the defendant planned the crime in advance rather than acting on impulse, and (c) the defendant has refused to acknowledge responsibility during the proceedings, unless the defendant suffers from a documented condition that substantially impaired deliberative capacity at the time of the offense. In every case, the severity of the sentence must be calibrated to the gravity of the harm inflicted.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delaney embezzled pension funds from retirees over three years, leaving several elderly victims unable to afford medical care. He planned each transfer carefully, has denied wrongdoing throughout trial, and has no documented cognitive impairment. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Halvor set fire to an occupied warehouse, permanently injuring two employees, and methodically prepared the arson for weeks. Although he refused to apologize, a neurologist testified that a recently diagnosed frontal-lobe tumor had materially impaired his capacity for deliberation when he set the fire. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irendi defrauded a bank of a modest sum through an impulsive forgery. The bank reported no lasting harm, Irendi pled guilty on the first day, and no impairment was alleged. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence because deterrence requires a harsh signal to future offenders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jessan assaulted a stranger on the street, causing serious and lasting injury. The assault was unplanned, but Jessan has refused to acknowledge responsibility and is medically unimpaired. The judge imposes the maximum statutory sentence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Korath orchestrated a multi-year investment fraud that ruined several identifiable families. He denies responsibility and no impairment has been documented. The judge imposes the lightest sentence on the statutory scale, reasoning that financial crimes warrant leniency regardless of harm.

explanations.correct: Delaney's case satisfies every antecedent condition: serious and lasting harm to identifiable victims (retirees deprived of medical care), advance planning, and refusal to acknowledge responsibility. The exception does not trigger because Delaney has no documented impairment. The maximum sentence is described as matching the gravity of the harm, meeting the proportionality clause. The principle therefore prescribes the stated judgment.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Satisfies conditions (a), (b), and (c), but the documented frontal-lobe impairment triggers the exception. The principle withholds the maximum sentence whenever the exception's antecedent obtains, so the judgment contradicts the principle.
explanations.C: Fails condition (a) — no lasting harm — and condition (b) — the forgery was impulsive. The judge also invokes a deterrence rationale the principle does not recognize.
explanations.D: Fails condition (b). Jessan's assault was unplanned, so the 'planned the crime in advance' requirement is unmet, regardless of how the other conditions fare.
explanations.E: Violates the proportionality clause. Even where all antecedent conditions hold, the principle requires the sentence to be calibrated to the gravity of the harm; imposing the lightest sentence on a case of ruinous harm inverts that requirement.

lr.difficultyReason: Three compound conditions plus an 'unless' exception governed by its own antecedent, plus a proportionality requirement tying intervention to demonstrated risk. Traps satisfy the main rule while falling under the exception or substitute a different justifying principle.
lr.stimulus: A physician is justified in overriding a competent patient's refusal of treatment only if (a) the refusal would result in imminent and irreversible harm, (b) the patient's refusal rests on a factual misunderstanding that the physician has tried and failed to correct, and (c) no less intrusive alternative is available, unless the patient has previously executed a valid advance directive refusing the specific intervention under the present circumstances. The degree of intervention imposed must be no greater than what is needed to prevent the imminent harm.
lr.questionStem: The principle above, if valid, most closely conforms to which one of the following judgments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dr. Querin's patient refuses a ventilator, citing a correctly understood prognosis. The patient had previously signed a valid advance directive refusing ventilation under precisely these circumstances. Dr. Querin nonetheless intubates, reasoning that life preservation outweighs prior instructions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dr. Palen's patient faces imminent organ failure and refuses dialysis on religious grounds. The refusal involves no factual misunderstanding, and Dr. Palen proceeds anyway because the harm is severe.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Onwu's patient, bleeding internally, refuses a transfusion based on a mistaken belief that donated blood is routinely unscreened for pathogens. Dr. Onwu has provided documentation correcting the error, but the patient persists. No less intrusive alternative exists, and the patient has signed no advance directive. Dr. Onwu administers only the transfusion volume necessary to stabilize the patient.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dr. Reymo's patient refuses antibiotics for a minor, non-life-threatening infection based on a misunderstanding about side effects. Dr. Reymo administers them covertly to spare the patient further argument.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dr. Sendo's patient, facing imminent harm from sepsis, refuses a narrow-spectrum antibiotic due to a factual misunderstanding that Dr. Sendo has repeatedly tried to correct. No less intrusive option exists and no advance directive applies. Dr. Sendo administers a full course of broad-spectrum intravenous therapy exceeding what is needed to control the infection.

explanations.correct: Dr. Onwu's case satisfies every antecedent condition: imminent and irreversible harm (internal bleeding), a factual misunderstanding that the physician has tried and failed to correct, and no less intrusive alternative. The exception does not trigger because no advance directive exists. The intervention administered is limited to what is needed to stabilize the patient, satisfying the proportionality requirement. The principle therefore justifies the override.
