choices.text: An employee who becomes aware of significant wrongdoing by her employer is entitled to disclose that wrongdoing publicly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Public disclosure of an employer's wrongdoing by an employee is warranted when the employee has direct knowledge of ongoing wrongdoing, has first pursued internal remedies without success, and the wrongdoing endangers the public.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Confidentiality agreements between employers and employees are unenforceable to the extent that they conflict with any interest of the public.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An employee who signs a confidentiality agreement must honor it in every circumstance in which the employer continues to observe its side of the agreement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Government agencies, rather than private employees, should bear primary responsibility for exposing corporate wrongdoing that endangers the public.

explanations.correct: The columnist justifies disclosure by pointing to three conditions — direct knowledge of ongoing wrongdoing, exhausted internal remedies, and public safety at stake. Principle (B) ties exactly those three into a standard of justified disclosure.
explanations.A: Too broad — would license disclosure on mere awareness, regardless of severity, internal remedies, or public impact.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too broad — renders confidentiality void for any public interest, a sweeping claim the columnist does not make.
explanations.D: Aligned with the concession rather than the conclusion — the columnist acknowledges the obligation exists but is not defending its absoluteness.
explanations.E: Shifts the subject to which entity should act, not when an employee's disclosure is justified.

lr.difficultyReason: Conclusion requires the conjunction of species endemism, credible threat of extinction, and absence of comparable ecological substitutes. Trap (B) is too broad; trap (C) is too narrow, restricting to charismatic species; trap (E) reverses the priority.
lr.stimulus: Conservation biologist: A coastal wetland slated for a shipping-terminal expansion is the sole habitat of a small fish, the marsh stickleback, which exists nowhere else. Without intervention, the planned dredging will almost certainly drive the species to extinction, and no other local fish fills its role in the food web. The government insists that economic development must take precedence. It must not: halting the expansion is warranted here.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the biologist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When a planned project would probably eliminate a species endemic to the site and no ecological substitute for that species exists in the local system, halting the project is warranted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A government may never permit a project that endangers any wildlife, regardless of the project's economic benefits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Projects that threaten charismatic species should be subjected to stricter review than projects threatening less visible species.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Economic development should be pursued only when it produces gains exceeding the monetary value of the ecosystems it displaces.

choices.label: E
choices.text: When economic development and species protection conflict, the outcome that maximizes long-term public welfare should prevail.

explanations.correct: The biologist's conclusion rests on three conditions: the stickleback is endemic to the site, extinction is likely if the project proceeds, and no ecological substitute exists. Principle (A) combines those exact three conditions and yields the conclusion that halting is warranted.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too broad — would license halting any project that endangers any wildlife, including species that are not endemic or have substitutes.
explanations.C: Too narrow — restricts the rule to charismatic species; the stickleback need not be charismatic, so the principle may fail to reach this case.
explanations.D: Tangential — introduces a monetary balancing the biologist does not employ.
explanations.E: Reversed — a welfare-maximization rule could license the expansion if its gains are sufficient, which is the opposite of what the biologist concludes.

lr.difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: data collection outside the disclosed purpose, user reliance on the disclosure, and material use of the data against users. Trap (B) omits reliance; trap (D) aligns with the concession; trap (E) is inverted.
lr.stimulus: Technology ethicist: A fitness-tracking app disclosed in its sign-up flow that heart-rate data would be used to improve training recommendations. Later reporting revealed that the company had been selling the same data to insurers, who used it to raise premiums for some users. The company points out that buried in the full terms-of-service document was a clause permitting secondary data sales. That clause does not exonerate the company: what it did was wrong.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the ethicist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any commercial transfer of personal data to third parties is impermissible unless the user has been individually compensated for the transfer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A firm that collects personal data acts wrongly when it uses the data for purposes beyond those the user was told about at sign-up, whenever any user is later disadvantaged by that use.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A firm that collects personal data acts wrongly when it uses the data in a manner outside the purpose foregrounded at sign-up, where users reasonably relied on that stated purpose and the subsequent use materially disadvantages them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Broad consent clauses in terms-of-service documents, once accepted, authorize any subsequent use of the data that falls within their literal wording.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A firm that sells user data is acting wrongly only if the sale violates an explicit statutory prohibition.

explanations.correct: The ethicist rests the judgment on three conditions: use outside the foregrounded sign-up purpose, user reliance on that purpose, and subsequent material disadvantage (higher premiums). Principle (C) ties those three together precisely.
explanations.A: Too broad — would condemn even transfers users had clearly and knowingly authorized, a conclusion the ethicist does not draw.
explanations.B: Too broad — omits the reliance condition, so it would condemn firms even when users were not misled about the primary purpose.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Aligned with the concession — the ethicist acknowledges the clause exists but denies that it exonerates.
explanations.E: Reversed — would exculpate the firm whenever no statute is violated, the opposite of the ethicist's verdict.

lr.difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: a primary source exists, a later scholar's interpretation is inconsistent with it, and the scholar had access to the source. Trap (A) is too broad. Trap (D) inverts the direction.
lr.stimulus: Historian: A recently reissued textbook claims that Empress Wu's early policy favored the aristocratic clans over the scholar-officials. But the empress's own memoranda from that period — documents long available in published archives consulted by the textbook's author — detail systematic reassignments that consistently advantaged scholar-officials at the clans' expense. The textbook's characterization is unacceptable: it cannot be allowed to stand.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the historian's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historical characterization is unacceptable whenever any historian has raised objections to it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A textbook's characterization of a historical figure should not stand when primary sources accessible to the textbook's author are inconsistent with that characterization.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Historians are obligated to give primary sources greater evidentiary weight than secondary scholarship whenever the two conflict.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historians should reserve judgment on a characterization until the relevant primary sources have been independently verified.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Characterizations of rulers based solely on their self-authored memoranda are unreliable and should be treated with skepticism.

explanations.correct: The historian rests the verdict on three conditions: a primary source (the memoranda) exists, its content is inconsistent with the textbook's characterization, and the author had access to that source. Principle (B) captures exactly those three conditions.
explanations.A: Too broad — any objection by any historian would suffice, regardless of source access or inconsistency, licensing conclusions the historian does not draw.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow on audience — speaks about what historians are obligated to do, not when a characterization should fail to stand; it also omits the access condition.
explanations.D: Reverses the direction — counsels reserving judgment rather than rejecting the characterization, whereas the historian issues a definite rejection.
explanations.E: Inverted — the historian is relying on the memoranda as authoritative, not disparaging them.

lr.difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: tax on a discretionary activity, externalized social cost, and revenue earmarked for harm mitigation. Trap (A) omits earmarking. Trap (D) is aligned with the concession about regressivity. Trap (E) is inverted.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Opponents of the city's new tax on sugary beverages argue that it falls disproportionately on low-income consumers. That regressivity is a real concern, but it does not settle the question. The tax targets a consumption choice that generates documented public-health costs borne by the broader health system, and the revenue is dedicated to clinics serving the same neighborhoods that pay the tax. Under these conditions, enacting the tax was justified.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the economist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A tax on a discretionary consumption choice that imposes demonstrable social costs is justified whenever the tax is projected to reduce the targeted consumption.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A tax targeting a discretionary consumption choice is justified when the activity imposes demonstrable costs on those outside it and the tax revenue is directed to mitigating those costs within the affected communities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any policy whose burden falls disproportionately on low-income residents should be rejected in favor of alternatives that distribute costs more evenly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A tax is justified only if the primary burden falls on those who can most easily absorb it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A government should avoid taxes whose revenues are earmarked for specific programs rather than flowing into the general treasury.

explanations.correct: The economist justifies the tax on three grounds: the activity is discretionary, imposes external costs on the health system, and the revenue is earmarked to the clinics in the affected communities. Principle (B) ties all three conditions into a justification.
explanations.A: Too broad — omits the earmarking condition the economist invokes and would justify taxes whose revenues are spent elsewhere.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Aligned with the concession — the economist acknowledges regressivity but does not endorse rejection on that ground.
explanations.D: Aligned with the concession and reversed in upshot — would counsel rejecting the tax, which the economist defends.
explanations.E: Reversed — would condemn the earmarking the economist treats as part of the justification.

lr.difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: documented displacement risk, meaningful consultation failure, and available less-harmful alternative. Trap (B) is too broad, covering any displacement. Trap (D) is too narrow on housing type. Trap (E) is aligned with the concession.
lr.stimulus: Urban planner: The commission approved a luxury tower on the east-side block last month. Supporters stress the housing shortage that motivated the approval. But the block's long-standing residents, who face documented displacement if the project proceeds, were not meaningfully consulted before the vote, and a modified design preserving most of the existing housing was on the table and would have added nearly as many units. Given this, the commission's decision was wrong.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the planner's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When a development decision poses a documented displacement risk to existing residents, those residents must be meaningfully consulted, and a less displacing alternative of comparable benefit exists, approving the decision is wrong.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any urban development project that may displace existing residents should be rejected, regardless of the project's contribution to housing supply.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Planning commissions should prioritize preserving existing housing stock over adding new housing units of any kind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Approvals of luxury residential towers must always be preceded by a formal vote among the residents of the block to be redeveloped.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Responses to housing shortages should maximize the total number of new units produced within the jurisdiction.

explanations.correct: The planner's verdict combines three stated conditions: documented displacement risk, failure of meaningful consultation, and the availability of a comparably beneficial, less-displacing alternative. Principle (A) combines exactly those three into a wrongness judgment.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too broad — condemns any displacing project, including ones with full consultation and no alternative, conclusions the planner does not draw.
explanations.C: Too broad and one-sided — would oppose adding new housing even absent displacement or alternatives, which the planner does not endorse.
explanations.D: Too narrow — limited to luxury towers and imposes a procedural rule stricter than the planner's criterion of meaningful consultation.
explanations.E: Aligned with the concession — the planner acknowledges the housing shortage but does not accept unit-maximization as dispositive.

lr.difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: work commissioned for public display, later discovery of fabricated provenance, and museum knowledge of the fabrication. Trap (B) omits the commissioning condition. Trap (D) is aligned with the concession about aesthetic value.
lr.stimulus: Curator: The Hartwell Museum's 1890 seascape, long admired for its craftsmanship, has been shown to rest on falsified provenance documents: the painting was commissioned specifically for public exhibition on the strength of a fabricated attribution to a celebrated master, and archivists have now confirmed the fabrication. Defenders of the display argue the work remains aesthetically valuable. So it does; but the museum cannot continue to exhibit it as it has.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the curator's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A museum that has come to know that a work commissioned for public display was accepted on the basis of falsified provenance must not continue to exhibit the work on the same basis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any artwork whose provenance is later shown to be falsified must be removed from public view, regardless of the circumstances of its acquisition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Museums have a duty to correct their provenance records as new archival evidence becomes available.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The aesthetic value of an artwork provides sufficient justification for its continued public display, whatever its provenance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Falsified attributions should be publicly acknowledged and then disregarded when assessing an artwork's place in a museum's collection.

explanations.correct: The curator's conclusion rests on three conditions: the painting was commissioned specifically for public exhibition, the attribution used to justify that exhibition was fabricated, and the museum now knows this. Principle (A) ties those three into a prohibition on continuing the same exhibition basis.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too broad — would mandate removal even when the fabrication was unknown or the work was not acquired for public display on that basis.
explanations.C: Too narrow — imposes only a record-correction duty, which leaves the continued display untouched, whereas the curator's conclusion is that the display cannot continue as it has.
explanations.D: Aligned with the concession — the curator accepts aesthetic value but denies it settles the question.
explanations.E: Reverses the force of the fabrication — would permit continued display after a public note, which is exactly what the curator rejects.

lr.difficultyReason: Conclusion requires three conditions: widespread adoption within a speech community, no communication barrier, and consistency with the language's existing grammatical patterns. Trap (B) is too broad. Trap (C) is too narrow on written usage. Trap (E) is inverted.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Editors at the journal have rejected submissions that use the verb 'to impact' in the sense 'to affect,' on the grounds that the usage is nonstandard. This position is untenable. The usage is now routine among fluent speakers across many dialects, it causes no confusion for readers, and it conforms to the ordinary pattern by which English converts nouns to verbs. The editors' rule should be withdrawn.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify the linguist's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A proposed usage rule that forbids a form which is widely adopted by fluent speakers, causes no communication difficulty, and follows the language's established patterns should be withdrawn.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any rule that forbids a widely adopted linguistic form should be withdrawn, regardless of whether it causes confusion or fits existing patterns.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Editorial standards governing formal writing should be based exclusively on patterns documented in written, rather than spoken, usage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Usages that originated as conversions from one part of speech to another should be treated with caution in formal writing until they have been accepted for at least a generation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The fact that a linguistic form has been widely adopted is by itself insufficient reason to revise standing usage rules about that form.

explanations.correct: The linguist's conclusion combines three conditions: the usage is widespread among fluent speakers, it causes no confusion, and it fits the established noun-to-verb pattern of English. Principle (A) combines exactly those three and licenses withdrawing the rule.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too broad — would license withdrawal on adoption alone, which could justify withdrawing rules against genuinely confusing or pattern-violating forms, conclusions the linguist does not draw.
explanations.C: Too narrow and tangential — restricts editorial standards to written usage, which would block the linguist's appeal to spoken-language facts.
explanations.D: Reversed — counsels caution against precisely the type of conversion the linguist defends.
explanations.E: Reversed — denies the very inference the linguist draws from widespread adoption together with the other conditions.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence argument with an explicit conclusion marker ("therefore"). The target claim sits before the marker and plainly provides the evidence, so only the supporting-premise answer fits.
lr.stimulus: Regular aerobic exercise has been shown in numerous clinical studies to lower resting blood pressure in adults with mild hypertension. Therefore, physicians treating patients with mild hypertension should routinely recommend aerobic exercise as part of the treatment plan.
lr.questionStem: The claim that regular aerobic exercise has been shown in numerous clinical studies to lower resting blood pressure in adults with mild hypertension plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the argument's main conclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a claim the argument is designed to discredit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a generalization that the argument's conclusion is meant to explain.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background information unrelated to the argument's reasoning.

explanations.correct: The explicit marker "therefore" introduces the recommendation to physicians as the conclusion. The claim about clinical studies is the evidence given for that recommendation, i.e., a supporting premise.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the recommendation about physicians' practice, not the claim about clinical studies.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Nothing in the argument signals disagreement with the cited studies; they are endorsed, not discredited.
explanations.D: The argument uses the studies to support, not to explain away, the recommendation.
explanations.E: The claim is load-bearing evidence, not extraneous context.

lr.difficultyReason: The conclusion marker "thus" introduces the target claim, which follows a single supporting observation. Textual position uniquely fixes the answer as main conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Every time the library has extended its weekend hours in the past, student check-outs of print books have risen by more than 20 percent within a month. Thus, if the library extends its weekend hours next semester, student check-outs of print books will very likely rise by a similar margin.
lr.questionStem: The claim that if the library extends its weekend hours next semester, student check-outs of print books will very likely rise by a similar margin plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the main conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is an assumption on which the argument's premise depends.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a counterexample meant to undermine a general claim.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a prediction cited only to be rejected.

explanations.correct: The word "thus" introduces the target claim as the point the prior sentence is offered to support. That makes the target claim the main conclusion.
explanations.A: The supporting premise is the historical pattern in the first sentence, not the target claim.
explanations.B: The claim is explicitly stated, not left unstated as an assumption.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The argument treats the target as what follows from the evidence, not as a counterexample.
explanations.E: The author endorses, rather than rejects, the prediction.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence argument with "so" signaling the conclusion. The target claim sits in the premise position and is the sole reason offered.
lr.stimulus: Critic: Most successful technology startups in the region have relied on at least one senior engineer with more than ten years of industry experience. So Beldon Software, a new regional startup currently without any senior engineer, is unlikely to succeed unless it hires one.
lr.questionStem: The claim that most successful technology startups in the region have relied on at least one senior engineer with more than ten years of industry experience plays which one of the following roles in the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the critic's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a subsidiary conclusion drawn from the claim about Beldon Software.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a premise offered to support the critic's main conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a claim the critic acknowledges but rejects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a counterexample to an earlier generalization.

explanations.correct: The critic's point — signaled by "so" — is about Beldon Software's prospects. The generalization about regional startups is the evidence offered for that point, i.e., a supporting premise.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the prediction about Beldon Software, not the generalization.
explanations.B: The generalization supports, rather than is supported by, the Beldon-specific claim.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The critic endorses the generalization; nothing signals disagreement.
explanations.E: No earlier generalization is offered for the claim to counter.

lr.difficultyReason: Clear two-sentence argument with "hence" marking the conclusion. Target claim is the conclusion; only one choice matches the textual position.
lr.stimulus: The fine for overdue municipal parking meters has not been raised in more than twenty years, and during that time the average cost of city services funded by such fines has more than doubled. Hence, the city council should increase the overdue-meter fine at its next session.
lr.questionStem: The claim that the city council should increase the overdue-meter fine at its next session plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the argument's main conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a claim the argument treats as already widely accepted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a counterproposal the argument ultimately rejects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a factual observation about current council practice.

explanations.correct: "Hence" introduces the recommendation as the point the prior observations are offered to support. That makes the recommendation the main conclusion.
explanations.A: The supporting premises are the stagnant fine and the rising costs; the recommendation is what they support.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The argument is arguing for the recommendation, not assuming it is already accepted.
explanations.D: The argument endorses the recommendation, not rejects it.
explanations.E: The recommendation is prescriptive, not a description of current practice.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence argument with "therefore" marking the conclusion. Target sits in premise position and is the only evidence cited.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Children exposed to a second language before age five consistently achieve native-like pronunciation in that language, while those who first encounter it after age twelve almost never do. Therefore, the window for acquiring native-like pronunciation in a second language closes well before adolescence.
lr.questionStem: The claim that children exposed to a second language before age five consistently achieve native-like pronunciation in that language, while those who first encounter it after age twelve almost never do plays which one of the following roles in the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the linguist's main conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the empirical finding offered in support of the linguist's main conclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an alternative view the linguist is arguing against.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a subsidiary conclusion supported by the claim about the pronunciation window.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an assumption the linguist leaves unstated.

explanations.correct: The linguist concludes, after "therefore," that the acquisition window closes before adolescence. The target claim reports the observations that drive that conclusion — a supporting premise.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the claim about when the pronunciation window closes.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The linguist endorses the empirical finding; it is not treated as an opposing view.
explanations.D: The target supports, rather than is supported by, the window claim.
explanations.E: The claim is explicitly stated, so it is not an unstated assumption.

lr.difficultyReason: Short two-sentence argument with an explicit "therefore" conclusion marker. The target claim is clearly the main conclusion.
lr.stimulus: In the three counties where a deposit was placed on beverage containers, roadside litter dropped by more than 60 percent within two years, while in neighboring counties without a deposit, roadside litter remained essentially unchanged. Therefore, container-deposit programs are an effective means of reducing roadside litter.
lr.questionStem: The claim that container-deposit programs are an effective means of reducing roadside litter plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a background observation used to introduce the topic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the argument's main conclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a hypothesis the argument is designed to refute.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a prediction that the argument does not actually defend.

explanations.correct: The word "therefore" introduces the general claim about container-deposit programs as the point the comparison between counties is offered to support. That general claim is the main conclusion.
explanations.A: Background would precede the evidence, not follow "therefore."
explanations.B: The supporting premise is the comparison among counties; the general claim is what it supports.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The argument endorses, rather than refutes, the general claim.
explanations.E: The argument explicitly offers the county comparison as support for the claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence ethics argument with explicit "thus" marker. The target claim is the premise and is the sole reason cited for the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: A person who makes a promise is obligated to keep it unless doing so would cause significant harm to others. Thus, Dr. Karimi, who promised to speak at the conference, should honor that promise, since her speaking would not cause such harm.
lr.questionStem: The claim that a person who makes a promise is obligated to keep it unless doing so would cause significant harm to others plays which one of the following roles in the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the ethicist's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a general principle offered in support of the main conclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an exception to the main conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a moral view the ethicist is arguing against.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an observation about Dr. Karimi's specific situation.

explanations.correct: The ethicist's conclusion, signaled by "thus," concerns Dr. Karimi. The general principle about promises is the reason offered for that conclusion — a supporting premise in the form of a principle.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is about Dr. Karimi specifically, not the general principle.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The principle frames the conclusion; it is not carved out as an exception.
explanations.D: The ethicist endorses the principle rather than arguing against it.
explanations.E: The principle is general, not a fact about Dr. Karimi's situation.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence environmental argument; "therefore" clearly marks the conclusion, which is the target claim.
lr.stimulus: The coastal wetlands at Marsh Point serve as the primary breeding ground for three species of shorebirds whose populations have declined sharply elsewhere in the region. Therefore, protecting Marsh Point from further development should be a priority for the state wildlife agency.
lr.questionStem: The claim that protecting Marsh Point from further development should be a priority for the state wildlife agency plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is an observation about the region's shorebirds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of a broader claim about wildlife policy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a policy the argument is designed to discredit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a claim that the argument takes to be already established.

explanations.correct: The recommendation follows "therefore" and is what the earlier ecological observation is offered to support. That makes it the main conclusion.
explanations.A: It is a prescriptive policy claim, not an observation about shorebirds.
explanations.B: The argument ends with this recommendation; no broader claim is drawn from it.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The argument endorses, rather than discredits, the recommendation.
explanations.E: The argument is arguing for the recommendation; it is not treated as already settled.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence history argument with explicit conclusion marker "so." The target claim is a supporting premise and the only evidence offered.
lr.stimulus: Historian: Every major city in the empire that survived the plague of 432 had a fortified harbor, while nearly every city without a fortified harbor was abandoned within a decade. So fortified harbors were a key factor in whether a city survived the plague years.
lr.questionStem: The claim that every major city in the empire that survived the plague of 432 had a fortified harbor, while nearly every city without a fortified harbor was abandoned within a decade plays which one of the following roles in the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the historian's main conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a claim offered as evidence for the historian's main conclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an opposing view the historian is arguing against.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a sub-conclusion derived from a claim about fortified harbors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background information unrelated to the argument's reasoning.

explanations.correct: The historian concludes, after "so," that fortified harbors were a key factor in survival. The pattern reported before "so" is the evidence — a supporting premise.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the causal claim about fortified harbors.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The historian endorses, rather than opposes, the reported pattern.
explanations.D: The pattern supports the causal claim, not the other way around.
explanations.E: The pattern is the central evidence, not extraneous background.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-sentence arts argument with explicit "therefore" conclusion marker. Target claim is the main conclusion; textual position uniquely determines the answer.
lr.stimulus: Museums that reduce admission fees on weekday evenings in cities comparable to ours have reported sustained increases in overall attendance and in revenue from gift-shop sales. Therefore, the Westlake Museum should introduce reduced weekday-evening admission fees.
lr.questionStem: The claim that the Westlake Museum should introduce reduced weekday-evening admission fees plays which one of the following roles in the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the main conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a claim the argument takes to be already widely accepted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a description of what other museums have reported.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a prediction that the argument goes on to reject.

explanations.correct: "Therefore" introduces the recommendation about the Westlake Museum as the point the first sentence is offered to support. That recommendation is the main conclusion.
explanations.A: The supporting premise is the report about comparable museums; the recommendation is what it supports.
explanations.B: The argument is arguing for the recommendation, not treating it as already accepted.
explanations.C: The description of other museums is in the first sentence; the target is about the Westlake Museum specifically.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: The argument endorses the recommendation rather than rejecting it.

lr.difficultyReason: Three-claim stimulus with a concession-rebuttal frame. The quoted claim is acknowledged by the columnist but then rejected, not endorsed. Trap (A) misreads it as the main conclusion; trap (D) misreads it as supporting that conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Columnist: Some commentators have argued that the rise of remote work will hollow out downtown business districts within a decade. Admittedly, office vacancy rates in several major cities have climbed sharply since remote work became widespread. However, those same districts have seen a surge in residential conversions and new restaurants, and foot traffic on weekends now exceeds pre-pandemic levels. Downtowns are therefore not being hollowed out; they are being transformed.
lr.questionStem: The claim that office vacancy rates in several major cities have climbed sharply since remote work became widespread plays which one of the following roles in the columnist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion that the columnist is defending.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a consideration the columnist concedes but argues does not establish what commentators take it to establish.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is offered as direct support for the conclusion that downtowns are being transformed rather than hollowed out.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the commentators' position that the columnist endorses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is cited as evidence that foot traffic has returned to pre-pandemic levels.

explanations.correct: The columnist uses 'admittedly' to acknowledge the vacancy data, then uses 'however' to rebut the inference commentators draw from it. That is a conceded consideration the columnist grants but argues is insufficient for the commentators' conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is that downtowns are being transformed, not hollowed out — signaled by 'therefore.'
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The vacancy data would, if anything, cut against the columnist's conclusion; the conversions and foot-traffic data support it.
explanations.D: The columnist explicitly rejects the commentators' conclusion rather than endorsing their supporting premise.
explanations.E: Accurate content, wrong function — it has nothing to do with foot-traffic restoration.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-claim stimulus in which the quoted phrase is a subsidiary conclusion supporting the main one. Students must distinguish it from the main conclusion and from the premises cited for it.
lr.stimulus: Historian: The standard view that the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation overstates technology's role. In the decades before Gutenberg, hand-copied tracts by reformers like Wycliffe and Hus circulated widely throughout Europe and provoked real ecclesiastical crises. So the ideas driving the Reformation were already gaining traction without mechanical reproduction. The press accelerated a process that was underway, rather than initiating one.
lr.questionStem: The claim that the ideas driving the Reformation were already gaining traction without mechanical reproduction plays which one of the following roles in the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise offered in direct support of the claim that hand-copied tracts circulated widely before Gutenberg.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is an intermediate conclusion drawn from evidence about pre-Gutenberg tracts and used to support the historian's main claim about the press's role.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a view the historian attributes to opponents in order to rebut it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background context that orients the reader before the argument begins.

explanations.correct: The claim is drawn ('so') from the evidence about Wycliffe and Hus and is then used to support the final claim that the press accelerated rather than initiated the Reformation. It is both conclusion and premise — an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the final sentence, about the press accelerating rather than initiating.
explanations.B: Reverses the support relation — the tracts claim supports the traction claim, not the other way around.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The historian endorses the claim; it is not attributed to opponents.
explanations.E: It is argumentatively load-bearing, not scene-setting.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogy-based argument where the quoted phrase is a premise of the analogy. Students must distinguish it from the main conclusion about the policy and from stand-alone background.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: Some officials insist that the city's new congestion-pricing plan will fail because drivers will simply shift to side streets. But a comparable pricing plan in Stockholm produced a durable 20 percent reduction in total vehicle miles within two years. Since Stockholm's street grid, commuter patterns, and driver demographics closely resemble ours, we should expect a similar reduction here. The officials' pessimism is therefore unfounded.
lr.questionStem: The claim that a comparable pricing plan in Stockholm produced a durable 20 percent reduction in total vehicle miles within two years plays which one of the following roles in the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion the analyst defends.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the basis for an analogy from which the analyst infers the expected effect of the city's plan.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a view the analyst attributes to officials in order to reject it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is offered as evidence that Stockholm's street grid resembles the city's.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a concession the analyst makes to critics before rebutting them.

explanations.correct: The analyst compares the city to Stockholm and uses Stockholm's observed reduction as the comparator in the analogy. The similarity premises then license projecting Stockholm's result onto the city.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is that officials' pessimism is unfounded — the final sentence.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The analyst endorses Stockholm's result rather than attributing it to officials.
explanations.D: Reverses the support relation — the grid similarity supports the projection, not the other way around.
explanations.E: The analyst isn't conceding ground; the Stockholm datum anchors the argument.

lr.difficultyReason: Concession-rebuttal structure in a medical context. The quoted phrase is a consideration the physician raises in order to reject its implications. Trap (C) misreads as endorsed support; trap (D) misreads as the conclusion itself.
lr.stimulus: Physician: Critics of the new screening guidelines argue that fewer screenings will mean more late-stage diagnoses. It is true that screening programs sometimes detect cancers at earlier stages than they would otherwise be found. Nevertheless, the new guidelines will not increase late-stage diagnoses overall, because the cancers most likely to be flagged by early screening are slow-growing types that rarely progress to serious disease in the interval between recommended screenings.
lr.questionStem: The claim that screening programs sometimes detect cancers at earlier stages than they would otherwise be found plays which one of the following roles in the physician's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the physician's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a claim whose truth the physician grants but whose critic-favored inference the physician denies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is evidence directly supporting the conclusion that late-stage diagnoses will not rise under the new guidelines.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the critics' main conclusion, which the physician argues against.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an intermediate conclusion drawn from data about slow-growing cancers.

explanations.correct: The physician uses 'it is true that ... nevertheless' to grant the factual claim while denying the critics' inference from it. That is a conceded consideration.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is that the new guidelines will not increase late-stage diagnoses.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: If anything, this claim cuts against the physician's conclusion; the slow-growing-cancer point is what supports it.
explanations.D: The critics' conclusion is that late-stage diagnoses will rise; the quoted claim is a premise for that conclusion, not the conclusion itself.
explanations.E: No evidence for this claim is supplied in the stimulus.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-level argument in linguistics. The quoted claim is an intermediate conclusion: supported by the corpus observation and used to support the main claim about adult learners.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: A recent corpus study found that young children use grammatical constructions they have never heard from caregivers. It follows that children are not learning grammar simply by imitating adult speech. If they were, their output would be bounded by the constructions available to them as input. Therefore adult language learners, who rely more heavily on explicit imitation, face a genuinely different cognitive task from children.
lr.questionStem: The claim that children are not learning grammar simply by imitating adult speech plays which one of the following roles in the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is offered as background context that does not bear on the main conclusion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a view the linguist attributes to others and rejects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a conclusion for which the corpus observation is offered as support, and which in turn is used to support the argument's main claim about adult learners.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a premise for the corpus observation that precedes it.

explanations.correct: 'It follows that' signals that this claim is concluded from the corpus observation. The final sentence, signaled by 'therefore,' uses it to support the claim about adult learners. It is therefore an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion concerns adult learners, reached in the final sentence.
explanations.B: It is load-bearing, not background.
explanations.C: The linguist endorses the claim rather than attributing it to others.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Reverses the support relation — the corpus observation supports this claim, not the other way around.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental-science argument with explicit concession signal. The quoted claim is acknowledged but rejected as decisive; distinguishing it from a supporting premise is the test.
lr.stimulus: Environmentalist: Advocates of a wetland-restoration project near our river claim that it will substantially reduce downstream flooding. Granted, wetlands in general can absorb significant volumes of floodwater during storm surges. However, the site proposed for restoration lies upstream of only a small fraction of the tributaries that contribute to our river's flood peaks. The project is therefore unlikely to produce the broad flood reduction its advocates promise.
lr.questionStem: The claim that wetlands in general can absorb significant volumes of floodwater during storm surges plays which one of the following roles in the environmentalist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is evidence offered directly in support of the conclusion that the project is unlikely to produce broad flood reduction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a claim whose truth the environmentalist grants but whose relevance to the specific project the environmentalist disputes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is an intermediate conclusion supported by evidence about the project site.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the advocates' main conclusion, which the environmentalist rejects.

explanations.correct: 'Granted ... however' marks a conceded consideration. The environmentalist accepts that wetlands generally absorb floodwater but argues that this general fact does not carry the weight the advocates want for the specific site.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is that the project is unlikely to produce broad flood reduction.
explanations.B: The absorption capability, if anything, cuts the other way; the tributary point supports the environmentalist's conclusion.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: No evidence is offered for this general claim; the environmentalist simply grants it.
explanations.E: The advocates' conclusion is about this project specifically, not about wetlands in general.

lr.difficultyReason: Ethics argument with an analogy premise. Students must distinguish a premise of the comparison from the main evaluative conclusion it supports.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: When a pharmacist mistakenly dispenses the wrong medication and a patient is harmed, we rightly hold the pharmacist morally responsible, even if the mistake was inadvertent. An autonomous vehicle's decision algorithm sorts among options and chooses actions in much the way a pharmacist sorts and selects from available drugs. Thus, when an autonomous vehicle inadvertently causes harm, the company that designed its algorithm bears genuine moral responsibility.
lr.questionStem: The claim that when a pharmacist mistakenly dispenses the wrong medication and a patient is harmed, we rightly hold the pharmacist morally responsible, even if the mistake was inadvertent, plays which one of the following roles in the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the ethicist's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is one term of an analogy, offered to support the conclusion about the company that designed the algorithm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a view the ethicist attributes to others in order to rebut it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is an intermediate conclusion drawn from the claim about autonomous vehicles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a concession to critics of algorithmic accountability.

explanations.correct: The ethicist uses the pharmacist case as the familiar term in an analogy and then, by comparing the algorithm's decision-making to the pharmacist's, draws the conclusion about the company's moral responsibility.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is about the company's moral responsibility, signaled by 'thus.'
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The ethicist endorses, not rejects, the pharmacist judgment.
explanations.D: No evidence is offered for the pharmacist claim; it is a starting premise.
explanations.E: Nothing in the stimulus presents the claim as a concession; it is affirmed.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts-criticism stimulus with a subsidiary conclusion supporting the main aesthetic claim. Trap (A) confuses the subsidiary conclusion with the main one; trap (C) describes a role not played.
lr.stimulus: Critic: Several reviewers have praised the novel's intricate nested timelines as its principal achievement. But the nested structure only works because each timeline ends on a moment of specific, quiet loss, and those losses echo one another. So it is the emotional architecture, not the temporal puzzle, that does the real work. The novel's power is therefore best understood as a triumph of sentiment, not of form.
lr.questionStem: The claim that it is the emotional architecture, not the temporal puzzle, that does the real work plays which one of the following roles in the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the critic's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a subsidiary conclusion drawn from observations about the timelines and their endings, and it in turn supports the final claim about the novel's power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a view the critic attributes to reviewers in order to reject it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is offered as direct support for the claim that several reviewers have praised the nested timelines.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a concession the critic makes before turning to the main argument.

explanations.correct: The claim is drawn ('so') from observations about the matched endings and is then used to support the final sentence's verdict about where the novel's power lies. It is a subsidiary conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the final sentence about the novel's power.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The critic endorses this claim rather than attributing it to reviewers.
explanations.D: Reverses the support relation — the timeline-endings observation supports this claim, not the other way around.
explanations.E: The critic advances, rather than concedes, this claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal-reasoning stimulus with concession structure. The quoted claim is a consideration the professor raises only to argue it does not entail the critics' conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Law professor: Critics of the new evidence rule argue that it will let juries hear too much prejudicial testimony. To be sure, the rule permits a broader range of character evidence than the previous standard allowed. But trial judges under the new rule retain the same discretion to exclude evidence whose probative value is outweighed by its prejudicial effect. Thus the critics' worry is overstated; the practical scope of admissible prejudicial testimony will not expand appreciably.
lr.questionStem: The claim that the rule permits a broader range of character evidence than the previous standard allowed plays which one of the following roles in the professor's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the professor's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a factual concession that the professor grants to critics but argues does not support the conclusion the critics draw from it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is offered as direct support for the conclusion that the practical scope of admissible prejudicial testimony will not expand appreciably.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a view the professor attributes to judges rather than to critics.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is an intermediate conclusion supported by the claim about judges' discretion.

explanations.correct: 'To be sure ... but' frames a conceded consideration. The professor grants the claim and then argues, via the discretion point, that the critics' worry does not follow from it.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is that the critics' worry is overstated.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This claim actually seems to favor the critics; the discretion claim is what supports the professor's conclusion.
explanations.D: The professor attributes the broader worry to critics, not this factual observation to judges.
explanations.E: No evidence is offered for this claim; it is simply granted.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology-policy argument whose quoted claim is a subsidiary conclusion bridging premises about outages to the main claim about regulation. Trap (D) reverses the support direction; trap (E) mislabels as a concession.
lr.stimulus: Technologist: Over the past decade, outages at large cloud providers have caused cascading failures across banks, hospitals, and transit systems. Each incident traces back to configuration errors at a single provider that simultaneously handled workloads for all the affected sectors. So the concentration of critical services in a few providers is itself a public-safety problem. Regulators should therefore require large providers to support standardized interoperability so that customers can fail over to competitors during outages.
lr.questionStem: The claim that the concentration of critical services in a few providers is itself a public-safety problem plays which one of the following roles in the technologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the technologist's argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a claim drawn from the pattern of outages described, and it is in turn used to support the call for standardized interoperability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is background context unrelated to the regulatory recommendation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a premise offered in direct support of the claim that configuration errors caused the outages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a concession the technologist makes to defenders of the current cloud market before rejecting their view.

explanations.correct: 'So' marks this claim as concluded from the outage pattern, and 'therefore' in the final sentence uses it to support the regulatory recommendation. That double role is characteristic of an intermediate conclusion.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the regulatory recommendation in the final sentence.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: It is the pivot of the argument, not peripheral context.
explanations.D: Reverses the support relation — the configuration-error observation supports this claim, not the other way around.
explanations.E: The technologist advances, rather than concedes, the claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Five-claim medical argument with a two-tier support structure. The quoted claim is a subsidiary conclusion drawn from two pieces of evidence and then used to support BOTH the main conclusion about screening policy AND another subsidiary conclusion about overdiagnosis. Trap (D) captures only the premise-function; trap (A) misidentifies the main conclusion.
lr.stimulus: Epidemiologist: Routine screening for early-stage thyroid cancer should be curtailed. A fifteen-year cohort study in one region showed that screening rates tripled while mortality from thyroid cancer remained flat. Moreover, autopsies in that region routinely uncover small thyroid tumors in people who died of unrelated causes. Together these findings indicate that most of the tumors detected by screening would never have become clinically harmful. Since the detected tumors are typically treated with surgery that carries its own risks, widespread screening is exposing many patients to harm without a corresponding mortality benefit.
lr.questionStem: The claim that most of the tumors detected by screening would never have become clinically harmful plays which one of the following roles in the epidemiologist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument, for which the cohort-study and autopsy data are offered as direct support.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a generalization inferred from the cohort-study and autopsy evidence and then used to support both the claim that widespread screening exposes patients to harm without mortality benefit and the final recommendation that screening be curtailed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the autopsy finding that small tumors are common in people who died of unrelated causes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the main conclusion, but is not itself supported by anything in the argument.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a consideration the epidemiologist concedes in order to rebut it with the claim about surgical risks.

explanations.correct: The word 'Together these findings indicate' marks the claim as drawn from prior evidence (cohort plus autopsy). It then functions as support for the harm-without-benefit claim, which in turn supports the recommendation to curtail screening. That dual role — supported below, supporting above — is the intermediate-conclusion structure, and B names both what supports it and what it supports.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the opening recommendation that screening should be curtailed, restated at the end. The tumors-would-never-harm claim is inferred midway and then deployed in support of it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Reverses the support relation — the autopsy finding is cited as evidence for the tumors-would-never-harm claim, not the other way around.
explanations.D: Partial function. The claim is indeed used as a premise above, but the answer wrongly denies that anything supports it; 'together these findings indicate' flags the support from below.
explanations.E: The epidemiologist endorses the claim and builds on it; nothing in the argument treats it as a concession to be rebutted.

lr.difficultyReason: Five-claim ethics argument in which the quoted claim is conceded to a hypothetical objector and then used as a foil for a stronger counter-argument. Students must resist reading it as the author's own premise or as pure rebuttal.
lr.stimulus: Ethicist: Critics of anonymous organ donation often object that anonymity deprives recipients of the chance to thank their donors and so impoverishes the moral relationship between them. I grant that gratitude, when possible, enriches any transfer of benefit. But the alternative to anonymity is a system in which donors can select recipients, and any such selection inevitably tracks markers like shared ethnicity, religion, or class. Since a just allocation system must be blind to those markers, anonymity is morally required — even at the cost of forgone gratitude.
lr.questionStem: The claim that gratitude, when possible, enriches any transfer of benefit plays which one of the following roles in the ethicist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion, which the rest of the argument is designed to establish.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a premise from which the ethicist directly infers that anonymity is morally required.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a consideration the ethicist grants to critics only in order to be overridden by a stronger argument from justice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a view the ethicist attributes to critics and then argues is false.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is background information that orients the reader before the main argument begins.

explanations.correct: 'I grant that' signals a concession — the ethicist acknowledges gratitude's value to critics. The subsequent 'But... since a just allocation system must be blind to those markers' supplies a stronger counter-argument from justice that overrides the conceded point without denying it. The closing phrase 'even at the cost of forgone gratitude' makes the override explicit.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is that anonymity is morally required, not the claim about gratitude.
explanations.B: The ethicist does not infer anonymity's requirement from gratitude's value; the premise driving the inference is the blindness-to-markers principle.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The ethicist grants the claim rather than denying it. The rebuttal targets critics' overall position, not this specific point.
explanations.E: Scene-setting answers fail when the claim is explicitly introduced by 'I grant that' — a marker of argumentative engagement, not orientation.

lr.difficultyReason: Four-claim economics argument with an intermediate conclusion that simultaneously supports the main conclusion and another subsidiary claim about consumer welfare. Traps (B) and (E) each capture one function.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Proposed limits on corporate mergers should be relaxed. Empirical studies of mergers in the manufacturing sector consistently find that post-merger firms lower unit costs within three years through production consolidation. Lower unit costs translate into lower retail prices where markets remain competitive. It follows that mergers in competitive industries tend to benefit consumers. Since regulatory policy should be calibrated to consumer welfare, the current blanket restrictions on such mergers are misdirected.
lr.questionStem: The claim that mergers in competitive industries tend to benefit consumers plays which one of the following roles in the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion, supported by the empirical studies of manufacturing mergers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a conclusion drawn from the cost-and-price evidence that is itself used to support the recommendation that merger restrictions be relaxed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a premise offered in direct support of the claim that post-merger firms lower unit costs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a consideration the economist concedes but ultimately rejects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a premise used to support the recommendation that merger restrictions be relaxed, but is not itself supported by any other claim in the argument.

explanations.correct: 'It follows that' marks the consumer-benefit claim as a conclusion drawn from the cost-reduction and price-transmission premises. That conclusion is then paired with the consumer-welfare principle to support the main recommendation. B captures both directions — supported from below, supporting above.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the recommendation that merger restrictions be relaxed, stated in the opening and closing sentences.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Reverses the direction of support — the cost-reduction claim supports the consumer-benefit conclusion, not the other way around.
explanations.D: The economist endorses the claim and uses it affirmatively; nothing is rejected.
explanations.E: Partial function. Correct that it supports the recommendation, but wrong that nothing supports it — 'it follows that' signals inferential support from the preceding claims.

lr.difficultyReason: Five-claim legal argument. The quoted claim is a subsidiary conclusion supporting both the main conclusion about the statute's scope and a parallel subsidiary about due-process protection. Traps pull toward partial-function and premise readings.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: The computer-fraud statute should not be extended to cover mere terms-of-service violations. When Congress drafted the statute, it identified the harms it sought to address as intrusions that compromise the security or integrity of a computer system. Routine terms-of-service violations do neither. So such violations fall outside the statute's original scope. Extending the statute beyond that scope would also criminalize conduct that ordinary users cannot reliably identify as illegal, thereby offending basic due-process norms. For both reasons, the extension should be rejected.
lr.questionStem: The claim that routine terms-of-service violations fall outside the statute's original scope plays which one of the following roles in the scholar's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion the scholar defends.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a subsidiary conclusion inferred from the account of the harms Congress identified and the fact that terms-of-service violations do not produce those harms, and it is then used to support the scholar's rejection of the proposed extension.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a premise supporting the claim that the extension would criminalize conduct ordinary users cannot identify as illegal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is an objection the scholar entertains in order to rebut it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the main conclusion, but is not itself defended by anything in the argument.

explanations.correct: 'So' marks the quoted claim as inferred from the congressional-harms account plus the premise that terms-of-service violations don't produce those harms. The final sentence ('for both reasons') uses this claim as one of two supports for the rejection. B names both halves of that dual role.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the recommendation that the extension be rejected, stated in the first and last sentences.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The two subsidiary conclusions (original-scope and due-process) run in parallel. Neither supports the other; both support the main conclusion.
explanations.D: The scholar endorses the claim; nothing in the argument treats it as an objection.
explanations.E: Partial function. It is indeed used to support the main conclusion, but it is also itself defended by the preceding scope analysis.

lr.difficultyReason: Five-claim environmental science argument. The quoted claim is a generalization that starts as a description of past evidence and then functions mid-argument as a premise licensing a projection. Trap (A) captures only the description function.
lr.stimulus: Climate researcher: Historical records show that coastal wetlands in temperate estuaries have tracked sea-level changes by migrating inland when rising seas submerged their seaward edges. This wetland mobility has been a reliable buffer against erosion for thousands of years. In the coming century, however, seawalls and hardened shorelines will block the inland migration routes for most major estuarine wetlands. Without room to retreat, the wetlands will be squeezed between the rising sea and the hardened shore. We should therefore expect widespread wetland loss along coasts where hardening is already extensive.
lr.questionStem: The claim that wetland mobility has been a reliable buffer against erosion for thousands of years plays which one of the following roles in the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is a historical observation about past wetland behavior and nothing more.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a generalization drawn from the historical record that is then used, together with the claim that migration routes will be blocked, to support the prediction of widespread wetland loss.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the main conclusion, supported by the historical record and by the claim about hardened shorelines.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a consideration the researcher concedes to opponents in order to set up a counter-argument.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a premise offered in direct support of the claim that seawalls will block inland migration routes.

explanations.correct: The claim begins as a generalization drawn from the historical-records sentence. 'Without room to retreat... we should therefore expect' uses that generalization — combined with the hardening premise — to license the prediction. B names both directions: drawn from the record, used to support the prediction.
explanations.A: Partial function. The claim is a historical observation, but within the argument it is deployed inferentially, not merely reported.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The main conclusion is the final sentence, predicting widespread wetland loss.
explanations.D: The researcher endorses the claim and builds on it; no concession structure is present.
explanations.E: Reverses the support relation. The hardened-shorelines claim is asserted independently; the mobility generalization does not support it but is joined with it.

lr.difficultyReason: Five-claim technology argument. The quoted phrase functions first as a descriptive premise about user behavior and then, via the designer's inference, as support for a subsidiary conclusion that in turn supports the main recommendation. Dual function across two conclusions.
lr.stimulus: Software designer: The app's onboarding flow should be shortened. Logs from the past year show that users who abandon the app during setup are far more likely to do so after the third screen than before it. Given that users form their initial impressions quickly, this late-stage attrition reflects growing impatience rather than confusion about any particular screen. Attempts to fix the problem by clarifying individual screens will therefore not recover those users. Only a structurally shorter flow will.
lr.questionStem: The claim that the late-stage attrition reflects growing impatience rather than confusion about any particular screen plays which one of the following roles in the designer's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is an inference drawn from the abandonment data and the premise about quick initial impressions, and it is then used to support the conclusion that clarifying individual screens will not recover the abandoning users.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a premise supporting the claim that users form their initial impressions quickly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a view the designer attributes to other observers in order to rebut it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a restatement of the main conclusion in different terms.

explanations.correct: The claim is drawn from the abandonment data combined with the quick-impressions premise ('given that'). It then underwrites the next sentence's conclusion that screen-level fixes will not recover users, which in turn supports the opening recommendation. B names both the support below and the use above.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the recommendation to shorten the onboarding flow, not the impatience diagnosis.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Reverses the support relation — the quick-impressions claim supports the impatience inference, not vice versa.
explanations.D: The designer endorses the claim; no opposing view is identified or rebutted.
explanations.E: The main conclusion is about shortening the flow; the impatience claim has different content and a different function.

lr.difficultyReason: Five-claim linguistics argument with a conceded consideration followed by a stronger counter-argument. Students must avoid reading the concession as the author's own premise and resist the trap that treats it as the view being rebutted.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Some advocates argue that endangered-language preservation programs should focus exclusively on written documentation, since written records are stable and searchable. I acknowledge that written documentation has important uses for future scholars. But a living language cannot be preserved merely by capturing a snapshot of it. Because the grammar and vocabulary of any language shift continuously in response to its speakers' needs, only sustained intergenerational use can keep a language alive. Preservation programs must therefore devote most of their resources to supporting everyday speaker communities, not to documentation alone.
lr.questionStem: The claim that written documentation has important uses for future scholars plays which one of the following roles in the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion of the argument.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a consideration the linguist acknowledges in order to be overridden by a stronger argument from the dynamic nature of languages.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the position the argument is designed to refute.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a premise from which the linguist directly infers that preservation programs must support speaker communities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is cited as evidence that grammar and vocabulary shift continuously.

explanations.correct: 'I acknowledge that' marks the claim as granted, not endorsed as one of the linguist's own premises. The subsequent 'But... because' introduces a stronger counter-consideration — language dynamism — that overrides the concession without denying its truth. The final recommendation overrides without contradicting.
explanations.A: The main conclusion is the recommendation that programs must devote most resources to speaker communities.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The linguist concedes the claim, rather than refuting it. What is refuted is the advocates' broader conclusion that programs should focus exclusively on documentation.
explanations.D: The inference to the main conclusion runs through the language-dynamism premise, not through the conceded value of documentation.
explanations.E: Accurate content is irrelevant — the claim is not functioning as evidence for the shift premise.

lr.difficultyReason: Five-claim history argument. The quoted claim is an intermediate conclusion simultaneously supported by two pieces of archival evidence and supporting both the main conclusion and a second subsidiary claim about labor organization. Multiple partial-function traps.
lr.stimulus: Historian: The standard account of the nineteenth-century textile mill town overstates the coercive power of mill owners. Surviving diaries of mill workers record frequent departures for better-paying positions whenever such positions became available elsewhere. Payroll ledgers from the period likewise show unusually rapid turnover in the workforce. These records together establish that workers exercised real exit options. Because the threat of exit is a principal source of bargaining power, mill workers were not as powerless as the standard account assumes, and informal negotiation over wages was a live feature of daily mill-town life.
lr.questionStem: The claim that workers exercised real exit options plays which one of the following roles in the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the main conclusion, which the diary and payroll evidence are cited to support.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a subsidiary conclusion drawn from the diary and payroll evidence and then used to support both the claim that workers were not as powerless as the standard account assumes and the claim that informal wage negotiation was a live feature of mill-town life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is a premise supporting the diary evidence about frequent departures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a consideration the historian concedes in order to rebut it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is a premise offered in support of the main conclusion, but is not itself supported by anything in the argument.

explanations.correct: 'These records together establish that' marks the exit-options claim as inferred from the diary and payroll evidence.
