When an earlier model without captions was tested, users who were hard of hearing abandoned it within two weeks at three times the rate of other users. Since captions directly address that group's difficulties, the Velora will probably retain hard-of-hearing users at roughly the same rate as other users.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the columnist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Users of the earlier model who remained after two weeks tended to continue using it for at least a year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Among users of the earlier model who abandoned it, those who were hard of hearing cited difficulty understanding spoken responses more often than any other reason.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Velora's captions can be disabled through a setting in the companion app.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Velora costs somewhat more than the earlier model but is sold through the same retail channels.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several competing smart speakers released this year also include on-screen captions for spoken responses.

explanations.correct: The columnist assumes the earlier model's high abandonment rate among hard-of-hearing users was caused by difficulty understanding speech — the exact problem captions fix. (B) confirms that mechanism, making it far more plausible that adding captions will close the retention gap.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — about long-term retention of users who already stayed, not about the hard-of-hearing abandonment gap.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Weakens — if users can disable captions, the mechanism may not operate for them.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant — price and distribution don't speak to whether captions solve the retention problem.
explanations.E: Irrelevant — competitor features don't bear on whether the Velora will retain hard-of-hearing users.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical-linguistic argument with a compared-scenarios structure. The correct answer rules out a non-obvious third alternative (prior exposure through trade). Trap (D) strengthens a neighboring claim about a different language family; trap (B) is opposite-direction.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Speakers of the now-extinct Kellish language used a suffix that marked the speaker's degree of certainty about a reported event. The same suffix, with nearly the same range of meanings, appears in texts written in Antoric, a language spoken a thousand kilometers away. Since the two languages had no known common ancestor, the simplest explanation is that Antoric borrowed the suffix from Kellish during a period of contact between the two communities.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the linguist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antoric texts that use the suffix were composed at least two centuries after the earliest surviving Kellish texts that use it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several other Kellish grammatical features appear in the earliest Antoric texts that use the suffix.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most languages spoken in the broader region used some system for marking speaker certainty about reported events.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Languages descended from a common ancestor of Antoric, spoken far to the north, also use suffixes to mark speaker certainty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trade goods of Kellish origin have been found in Antoric archaeological sites but not the other way around.

explanations.correct: If Antoric independently happened to develop a similar certainty suffix, that would undercut the borrowing claim. (B) rules that alternative out: the clustering of multiple Kellish features in the earliest Antoric texts that use the suffix is far more consistent with borrowing than with coincidence.
explanations.A: Weakly supportive but does not rule out independent development — chronology alone doesn't distinguish borrowing from coincidence.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Weakens — regional ubiquity makes independent development of such a suffix in Antoric more plausible.
explanations.D: Strengthens a different conclusion — about the Antoric family's inherited tendencies, which would actually undermine the borrowing explanation.
explanations.E: Consistent with contact but doesn't establish the linguistic borrowing specifically; it's at best weak background support.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical causal argument with compared scenarios. The correct answer addresses a subtle reverse-causation threat. Trap (A) strengthens a sister claim about a different period; trap (D) introduces an unwarranted comparison.
lr.stimulus: Historian: In the two decades after the introduction of mechanical printing in Delsar, the number of pamphlets published per capita rose fivefold, and the number of literate adults in the city's trade guilds roughly doubled. In neighboring Trelford, which did not adopt mechanical printing until much later, literacy rates in comparable guilds remained flat. Mechanical printing therefore probably caused the rise in guild literacy in Delsar.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the historian's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the two decades before printing was introduced in Delsar, literacy rates in Delsar's trade guilds had been essentially constant.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several Trelford printers traveled to Delsar to learn the new technology before returning home to set up their own presses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pamphlets published in Delsar during the period in question dealt largely with matters of commercial practice relevant to guild members.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cities elsewhere in the region that adopted mechanical printing at roughly the same time as Delsar did not experience comparable literacy gains.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Many Delsar guild members began sending their children to informal schools during the period in question.

explanations.correct: A natural reverse-causation worry is that guilds were already becoming more literate — and that rising demand, not the press, caused the surge in pamphlets. (A) rules out that alternative by showing pre-printing literacy was flat, so the post-printing rise is more plausibly caused by the press.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Tangential — printer mobility doesn't speak to whether printing caused the literacy rise in Delsar.
explanations.C: Tempting, but content relevance alone doesn't rule out that literate guild members demanded the pamphlets rather than the press causing the literacy.
explanations.D: Weakens — if comparable cities with printing did not see the gains, the press is unlikely to be sufficient, undermining the causal attribution.
explanations.E: Introduces an alternative cause (informal schooling) that would weaken rather than strengthen the press attribution.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument with a nested causal chain (program feature → behavioral change → outcome). Correct answer confirms the middle link. Trap (B) is accurate but irrelevant; trap (C) strengthens a misreading of the argument.
lr.stimulus: City planner: When Harford adopted evening parking meters on its main commercial street, foot traffic at nearby restaurants during dinner hours rose by 18 percent within six months. The meters discourage long-term parking by commuters, freeing spaces for diners. The meters are therefore probably responsible for the increase in dinner-hour foot traffic.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the city planner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The revenue from the evening meters has been earmarked for maintenance of the commercial street's sidewalks and lighting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hourly meter rate during evening hours is the same as the rate during business hours.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Restaurants near the commercial street that offer private parking lots reported similar increases in dinner-hour foot traffic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: After the meters were installed, the average length of time parked cars remained on the commercial street during dinner hours fell sharply.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several new restaurants opened on the commercial street during the six months following the meters' installation.

explanations.correct: The planner's causal chain has two links: meters shorten parking durations, and shorter durations free spaces for diners. (D) directly confirms the first link with observed data, making the full chain substantially more plausible.
explanations.A: Accurate but irrelevant — how the revenue is spent has no bearing on the mechanism.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant — uniform pricing doesn't speak to whether the meters changed parking behavior.
explanations.C: Weakens — if restaurants with private lots saw similar gains, the meters are unlikely to be the cause.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Weakens — new restaurants supply an alternative cause for the traffic increase.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts/statistical argument where the correct answer rules out a subtle self-selection threat. Trap (E) is a plausible strengthener for a misreading about all students; trap (A) strengthens a sister conclusion about adult learners.
lr.stimulus: Music instructor: Among children at the Arris conservatory, those who begin piano lessons before age seven tend, on average, to achieve higher scores on sight-reading exams at age twelve than children who begin later. The earlier start therefore probably causes the stronger sight-reading performance.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the instructor's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adult students who begin piano lessons after age thirty tend to achieve lower sight-reading scores than those who began earlier in adulthood.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sight-reading exam at Arris is administered using the same format and difficulty level to all twelve-year-old students.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Among Arris children, age of starting piano lessons is not correlated with parental income or with prior exposure to other musical instruments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Teachers at Arris observe that early-starting students generally seem more confident during lessons than later-starting students.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Students at Arris who practice more hours per week tend to score higher on sight-reading exams than students who practice less.

explanations.correct: The natural alternative is that early-starting students are systematically different — wealthier families, more musical households — and that those factors, not the early start, drive sight-reading scores. (C) rules out both confounders, making the causal attribution to age-of-start more plausible.
explanations.A: Strengthens a sister conclusion about adult learners and doesn't bear on the causal claim about children.
explanations.B: Rules out a measurement concern but does nothing to address the underlying self-selection threat.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Accurate but tangential — confidence during lessons doesn't establish that the early start caused the exam-score gap.
explanations.E: Plausible strengthener for a misreading that practice hours explain the effect; it actually introduces an alternative cause.

lr.difficultyReason: Medical argument with a nested causal claim relying on timing. The correct answer rules out a reverse-causation alternative. Trap (A) strengthens a different conclusion; trap (D) is accurate but irrelevant.
lr.stimulus: Researcher: A large study of adults over age sixty has found that those who walk briskly for at least thirty minutes a day are significantly less likely to show early markers of cognitive decline than those who are less active. Brisk walking probably helps prevent early cognitive decline in older adults.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Older adults who engage in strenuous cardiovascular exercise other than walking also show fewer early markers of cognitive decline than less active peers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Study participants who began walking briskly only after enrolling in the study showed fewer cognitive-decline markers five years later than those who remained inactive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Among study participants, the difference in cognitive-decline markers between brisk walkers and less active adults grew larger with each year of follow-up.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Brisk walking has been shown to improve cardiovascular health in adults of all ages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Study participants who reported the most enjoyment of their daily activities were slightly more likely to walk briskly than those who reported less enjoyment.

explanations.correct: The central threat is reverse causation: people whose cognition is already declining may simply walk less. (B) addresses this by showing that adults who took up brisk walking after enrolling — and so could not have selected into walking on the basis of prior cognitive health — still showed fewer decline markers, strongly supporting the causal direction the researcher claims.
explanations.A: Strengthens a different conclusion — that cardiovascular exercise broadly helps cognition — rather than the specific brisk-walking claim, and doesn't rule out reverse causation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Consistent with the conclusion but equally consistent with cognitive decline making people progressively less active; does not rule out reverse causation.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant to cognitive decline specifically.
explanations.E: Weakens — introduces mood or life satisfaction as an alternative cause of both walking and better cognition.

lr.difficultyReason: Single causal claim with one obvious confounder. The stimulus jumps from a correlation (new medication, fewer headaches) to a causal conclusion, and the correct answer supplies an alternative cause that arose at the same time. Matches the 1★ anchor: one clear weakener, one opposite-direction strengthener, and three distractors that are irrelevant, too narrow, or shift the subject.
lr.stimulus: Dr. Halvorsen: Six weeks after I started prescribing a new migraine medication to my regular patients, the number of headache complaints they reported at follow-up visits had fallen by nearly a third. The medication is therefore responsible for the decline in their headaches.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens Dr. Halvorsen's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the same six-week period, the clinic replaced the fluorescent lighting in its waiting area with fixtures that many patients had previously said triggered their headaches.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients who received the new medication reported fewer side effects than patients who had received the previously prescribed medication.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dr. Halvorsen has been treating migraine patients for more than twenty years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The new medication is more expensive than the medication it replaced at Dr. Halvorsen's clinic.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some patients at a neighboring clinic who were not prescribed the new medication also reported a drop in tension headaches during the same period.

explanations.correct: If the trigger lighting was removed during the very same period the medication was introduced, there is a plausible alternative cause for the drop in headache complaints. That alternative explanation directly undercuts the doctor's leap from correlation to causation.
explanations.A: Correct. Supplies an obvious confounding cause that operated over the same six weeks.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — patients who tolerate a medication better are likelier to take it, making the medication a more credible cause of the decline.
explanations.C: Irrelevant. The doctor's experience says nothing about whether this particular medication caused this particular drop.
explanations.D: Cost is accurate-but-irrelevant: it has no bearing on whether the medication reduces headaches.
explanations.E: Shift in subject. The doctor's conclusion is about her migraine patients; a drop in tension headaches at another clinic is a neighboring claim, not the argument itself.

lr.difficultyReason: Direct 1★ pattern: a single causal claim about an ethics policy. The correct answer denies the premise's load-bearing fact by showing the reported decrease reflects reporting behavior rather than actual conduct. Distractors include a strengthener, an out-of-scope comparison, and a subject-shift.
lr.stimulus: Ethics officer: Last year our firm replaced its annual ethics workshop with a monthly online refresher course. In the twelve months that followed, the number of internal complaints about employee misconduct fell by half. Clearly, the monthly refresher is a more effective deterrent to misconduct than the annual workshop was.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the ethics officer's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shortly before the monthly course was introduced, the firm quietly eliminated the anonymous hotline that employees had previously used to file most of their misconduct complaints.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The monthly refresher course takes, in total, less of each employee's time than the annual workshop did.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Employees at a competing firm that also uses monthly refresher courses report high satisfaction with them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the complaints filed in previous years concerned conduct by senior managers rather than by junior employees.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The monthly refresher course includes a short quiz that employees had generally rated as useful.

explanations.correct: If the main reporting channel was removed, a drop in recorded complaints tells us little about actual misconduct. The argument's premise — that fewer complaints mean less misconduct — is no longer reliable, so the causal conclusion loses its footing.
explanations.A: Correct. Undermines the load-bearing premise that complaint counts reflect misconduct.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. Total time says nothing about deterrent effectiveness.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Satisfaction at another firm doesn't bear on whether the new course deters misconduct here.
explanations.D: Describes who filed past complaints; doesn't address the move from complaint counts to misconduct levels.
explanations.E: Strengthens, if anything — a useful quiz is some evidence the course is engaging.

lr.difficultyReason: Textbook 1★: a single causal leap from a price change to a sales change, with a clear confounder (competitor closure) available. Traps include the strengthener, an unwarranted comparison, and an accurate-but-irrelevant fact about pricing policy.
lr.stimulus: Store owner: In March, we dropped the price of our store-brand coffee by fifteen percent. Over the following two months, sales of that coffee rose by more than twenty percent compared with the two months before the price cut. The price reduction must be what drove the additional sales.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the store owner's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Store-brand tea, whose price was not reduced, sold slightly fewer units over the same period than in the preceding two months.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A competing grocery chain closed its two nearest locations at the beginning of March, and customers from those stores began shopping at the owner's store.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The store's national-brand coffee is still more expensive, per ounce, than its store-brand coffee.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Customers who bought the store-brand coffee said, in surveys, that they appreciated the lower price.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The store owner has reduced prices on several other products in the past year.

explanations.correct: The arrival of customers displaced from closed competitor stores is an obvious alternative cause of the sales increase that operated over the same period. With that confounder in play, the price cut no longer has to do the explaining.
explanations.A: A neighboring data point; doesn't address whether the price cut, rather than something else, drove coffee sales.
explanations.B: Correct. Introduces an independent cause of the increase.
explanations.C: Unwarranted comparison — the argument isn't about the national brand.
explanations.D: Strengthens, if anything — customer appreciation of the lower price supports the owner's causal story.
explanations.E: Accurate but irrelevant. The owner's pricing history doesn't speak to this particular cause.

lr.difficultyReason: Generalizing-from-a-sample stimulus at the 1★ level: a public defender concludes a program reduces reoffending, and the correct answer reveals a selection effect that makes the sample unrepresentative. Distractors include an opposite-direction strengthener and two irrelevancies.
lr.stimulus: Public defender: Of the defendants whom our county routed through the new restorative-justice program last year, only ten percent were arrested again within six months. Among defendants in similar cases who went through standard sentencing, the six-month rearrest rate was almost thirty percent. These figures show that the restorative-justice program is substantially better than standard sentencing at preventing reoffending.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the public defender's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Judges referred defendants to the restorative-justice program only if the prosecutor, the defense, and the victim all agreed the defendant was unlikely to reoffend.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Standard sentencing in the county typically involves a fine, probation, or a short jail term.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The restorative-justice program has been used in several neighboring counties for more than a decade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Defendants who completed the restorative-justice program reported that they felt better understood by the court.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A defendant's six-month rearrest rate is one of the most commonly cited measures of reoffending.

explanations.correct: If only defendants already judged unlikely to reoffend were admitted to the program, the low rearrest rate reflects who was picked, not what the program did. The comparison with standard-sentencing defendants is no longer apples-to-apples, which undermines the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Exposes a selection effect that supplies an alternative explanation for the lower rearrest rate.
explanations.B: Background about the comparison group; doesn't threaten the causal inference.
explanations.C: History of use elsewhere is accurate but irrelevant.
explanations.D: Strengthens, if anything — a sense of being understood is often linked to compliance.
explanations.E: Endorses the metric; doesn't weaken the conclusion.

lr.difficultyReason: Simple 1★ causal argument in environmental science: a single causal claim (cleanup caused fish recovery) paired with an available confounder (a stocking program). Wrong answers include a strengthener and two accurate-but-irrelevant facts.
lr.stimulus: Park ranger: Since our team finished removing the old tire dump from the banks of Miller Creek three years ago, the creek's native trout population has nearly doubled. The removal of the dump is clearly what allowed the trout to rebound.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the park ranger's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In the same year the dump was removed, the state began releasing thousands of young native trout into Miller Creek every spring.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Samples taken before the cleanup showed that leachate from the tire dump contained compounds toxic to aquatic life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Miller Creek is popular with recreational anglers, several of whom have praised the cleanup.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tires removed from the dump were recycled rather than sent to a landfill.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Native trout have also rebounded in a nearby creek that has never had a tire dump nearby.

explanations.correct: A hatchery-stocking program begun at the same time supplies an independent cause of the population increase. The cleanup no longer needs to be the reason, so the ranger's causal conclusion is undercut.
explanations.A: Correct. Provides an alternative cause that coincides with the cleanup.
explanations.B: Strengthens — it reinforces the premise that the dump was harming the fish.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Praise from anglers doesn't address the fish population's cause.
explanations.D: Accurate but irrelevant. What happened to the tires after removal doesn't bear on the trout.
explanations.E: Shift in subject; reports a neighboring trend rather than challenging this creek's causal story.

lr.difficultyReason: 1★ causal argument in technology: the IT manager attributes reduced help-desk tickets to a new training video. The correct answer supplies a competing cause (a simultaneous software update) that operated over the same window. Wrong answers include a strengthener and two accurate-but-irrelevant facts.
lr.stimulus: IT manager: After we required all employees to watch a short training video on the new email system, the number of help-desk tickets about email problems dropped by forty percent in the following month. The training video must be responsible for the drop.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the IT manager's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the same month, the vendor pushed an automatic update that fixed several of the bugs that had generated most of the previous month's email tickets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Employees rated the training video as clearer than the written instructions they had previously been given.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The training video is longer than most other training videos the company has produced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Help-desk tickets about unrelated software have remained at roughly their usual level for several months.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A few employees in another department had already watched an earlier version of the training video.

explanations.correct: If the vendor fixed the very bugs driving most of last month's tickets, the ticket drop has a plausible alternative cause. The training video no longer has to explain the change, so the causal conclusion is weakened.
explanations.A: Correct. Provides a competing cause that operated in the same month.
explanations.B: Strengthens — perceived clarity is evidence the video could help.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Video length doesn't bear on effectiveness here.
explanations.D: Steady levels elsewhere don't challenge the causal story for email tickets.
explanations.E: Too narrow — a small early-exposure group doesn't explain a forty-percent drop.

lr.difficultyReason: 1★ causal argument in linguistics: a teacher concludes a new drill caused higher exam scores. The correct answer presents a clean confounder (an easier exam form). Distractors include a strengthener and a subject-shift.
lr.stimulus: Language teacher: This semester I replaced our weekly vocabulary quiz with a short speaking drill on Fridays. My students' average score on the end-of-semester exam rose by twelve points compared with last semester's class. The speaking drill was clearly what produced the higher exam scores.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the language teacher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: This semester's end-of-semester exam used a different form that the department's testing office had previously rated as substantially easier than last semester's form.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Students this semester said they enjoyed the speaking drill more than last semester's students had enjoyed the vocabulary quiz.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The speaking drill covered vocabulary in addition to pronunciation and grammar.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Students in a different section of the course, who did not do the speaking drill, scored about the same this semester as last semester.

choices.label: E
choices.text: End-of-semester exam scores in the teacher's other courses have stayed roughly constant for several years.

explanations.correct: If this semester's exam was simply easier, higher average scores would be expected no matter what happened in class. That undermines the leap from the score increase to the drill as cause.
explanations.A: Correct. Provides an alternative explanation for the higher scores.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — enjoyment tends to support engagement with the drill.
explanations.C: Too narrow — coverage overlap doesn't by itself explain the twelve-point jump.
explanations.D: Neighboring claim. Relevant to the drill's effectiveness in that other section, not to the teacher's causal inference.
explanations.E: Background about unrelated courses; doesn't challenge this semester's inference.

lr.difficultyReason: 1★ analogical argument in history: a journalist generalizes from past campaigns to conclude a current one will succeed. The correct answer shows the analogy fails on the load-bearing feature. Distractors include a strengthener and irrelevancies.
lr.stimulus: Journalist: Every successful pamphlet campaign in this country's history began with a vivid, emotionally charged image on the front page. The new public-health pamphlet launched last week also features a vivid, emotionally charged image on the front page. We can therefore expect it to succeed as well.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the journalist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unlike earlier successful pamphlet campaigns, the new campaign is being distributed almost entirely through the mail rather than handed out in crowded public spaces.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The image on the new pamphlet was designed by an illustrator whose earlier work has received several awards.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Earlier successful pamphlet campaigns addressed topics such as sanitation and voting, not public health.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The public-health pamphlet is printed on heavier paper than earlier pamphlets were.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The journalist has studied pamphlet campaigns for many years.

explanations.correct: If the earlier campaigns succeeded only when handed out in crowds, and the new one lacks that distribution channel, the analogy breaks on a plausibly load-bearing feature. The prediction of similar success is no longer well-supported.
explanations.A: Correct. Breaks the analogy by showing a relevant difference.
explanations.B: Strengthens — a skilled illustrator supports the prediction.
explanations.C: Topic difference, but the journalist's generalization was about the image, not the topic.
explanations.D: Paper weight is accurate but irrelevant.
explanations.E: The journalist's expertise is irrelevant to whether the analogy holds.

lr.difficultyReason: 1★ predictive argument in policy: a city council member predicts a library-hours extension will drive a particular metric, and the correct answer offers a confounding cause for the premise. Distractors include a strengthener and a subject-shift.
lr.stimulus: Council member: Three months ago the city library extended its weekday hours until nine in the evening. Since then, recorded library attendance on weekday evenings has risen by about a quarter. If we extend the hours at the community recreation center in the same way, its evening attendance will rise as well.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the council member's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At the same time the library extended its hours, a large office building opened across the street, bringing hundreds of workers into the area each evening.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The community recreation center is already open until eight in the evening.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Library staff report that evening patrons ask for help finding books slightly more often than daytime patrons do.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A survey found that library patrons value the option of visiting in the evening.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weekday afternoon attendance at the library has remained roughly constant since the hours were extended.

explanations.correct: If a new office opened at the same time, the evening-attendance jump at the library likely reflects those new workers rather than the extended hours. Without the evidence that hours caused the jump, the prediction for the recreation center is undercut.
explanations.A: Correct. Alternative cause removes the support for the generalization.
explanations.B: Accurate but irrelevant. The argument is about extending hours, not current closing time.
explanations.C: Shift in subject — it describes staff interactions, not why attendance rose.
explanations.D: Strengthens — patrons valuing evenings supports the causal story.
explanations.E: Neutral background; doesn't threaten the evening-hours inference.

lr.difficultyReason: 1★ causal argument in the arts: a gallery director attributes a ticket-sales spike to a new lighting design. The correct answer supplies a clear confounder (a feature review of the exhibit in a widely read paper) operating over the same window. Distractors include a strengthener and two accurate-but-irrelevant details.
lr.stimulus: Gallery director: When we reinstalled our landscape exhibit last month, we replaced the overhead spotlights with softer, side-mounted lighting. In the four weeks since, ticket sales for that exhibit have climbed by nearly thirty percent compared with the previous four weeks. The new lighting must be drawing the extra visitors.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the gallery director's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A widely read weekend newspaper published a glowing feature on the landscape exhibit the same week the new lighting was installed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Visitors who returned to the exhibit after the reinstall said they noticed the different lighting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gallery's other exhibits use the same overhead spotlights that were replaced in the landscape hall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The new lighting fixtures cost slightly more to run than the fixtures they replaced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Attendance at the gallery's gift shop has risen only modestly over the same four-week period.

explanations.correct: A glowing feature in a widely read paper is a classic alternative cause of a sudden attendance spike. Once that cause is on the table, the lighting change no longer has to do the explaining.
explanations.A: Correct. Supplies an independent cause for the sales increase.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — noticing the change is consistent with its drawing visitors.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant. Lighting elsewhere doesn't bear on this exhibit.
explanations.D: Operating cost is accurate but irrelevant to attendance.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Gift-shop traffic is a neighboring measure and doesn't undercut the lighting claim.

lr.difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain in a medical context: drug lowers cholesterol, and lowered cholesterol reduces cardiac events. Weakener exposes a non-obvious alternative cause operating on the second link. Trap (B) strengthens by ruling out a different confound; trap (E) attacks a premise but not the conclusion.
lr.stimulus: A five-year clinical study found that patients who took the cholesterol-lowering drug lovastin experienced 30 percent fewer cardiac events than patients who took a placebo. Lovastin is known to reduce blood cholesterol, and elevated cholesterol is a well-established risk factor for cardiac events. The study's authors concluded that lovastin's cholesterol-lowering action is what prevented the cardiac events among patients taking the drug.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lovastin also produces a previously undocumented anti-inflammatory effect in blood vessel walls, and vascular inflammation independently contributes to cardiac events.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients in the two groups were matched for age, sex, smoking status, and family history of heart disease.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cardiac events occurred in both groups at roughly the rates researchers had projected before the study began.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lovastin is more expensive than several other cholesterol-lowering drugs currently on the market.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some patients in the lovastin group discontinued the drug before the study concluded.

explanations.correct: The authors attribute the drop in cardiac events specifically to cholesterol reduction. (A) introduces a non-obvious alternative cause — an anti-inflammatory effect that independently prevents cardiac events — so the benefit may have flowed from a mechanism other than cholesterol lowering. The second link in the causal chain is undermined.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — matching across known confounders makes the correlation more reliable.
explanations.C: Irrelevant — projection accuracy says nothing about which mechanism produced the outcome.
explanations.D: Out of scope — price has no bearing on whether the drug's effect is due to cholesterol reduction.
explanations.E: Attacks a minor feature of the trial's execution without touching the causal claim about the patients who did take the drug.

lr.difficultyReason: Predictive economic argument extrapolating from one quarter's data. Weakener denies a load-bearing background assumption about seasonality. Trap (C) strengthens; trap (D) is out-of-scope comparative.
lr.stimulus: Analyst: In the first quarter after Morven Motors redesigned its flagship sedan, sales of that model rose by 22 percent over the same quarter last year, while sales of the company's other models were flat. Morven's executives have therefore announced that the redesign will produce sustained sales growth for the sedan throughout the coming year.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the executives' prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Morven has not redesigned any of its other sedan models in the past five years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Morven historically offers its largest rebates on the flagship sedan during the first quarter, and this year's rebates were unusually generous.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Automotive reviewers gave the redesigned sedan higher marks than they gave the previous version.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A competitor of Morven's reported flat sales of its comparable sedan this quarter.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Morven spent more on its first-quarter advertising campaign than in any previous first quarter.

explanations.correct: The executives infer sustained growth from a single quarter's increase, assuming the jump reflects the redesign. (B) identifies an alternative cause peculiar to the first quarter — unusually large rebates — that will not be in place during later quarters, so the growth is unlikely to persist.
explanations.A: Irrelevant — what happened with other models doesn't speak to whether this sedan's increase will continue.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Strengthens, if anything — favorable reviews support continued demand.
explanations.D: Out of scope — a competitor's flat sales don't tell us whether Morven's jump will endure.
explanations.E: This is a confound for the first-quarter spike but weakens less than (B); heavy advertising that matches past campaigns could easily be sustained. (B) names a factor the executives cannot continue — the rebate was already described as unusually generous.

lr.difficultyReason: Analogical argument from one municipality to another. Weakener denies the background assumption that the baseline conditions in the two cities are comparable. Trap (D) strengthens via a surface-similarity cue; trap (A) attacks a subsidiary claim.
lr.stimulus: After the city of Dunsbridge installed protected bicycle lanes on its six busiest commercial streets, reported collisions involving cyclists fell by 40 percent within two years. The city council of neighboring Harrow has now approved similar protected lanes on its own busiest streets, confident that Harrow will see a comparable decline in cyclist collisions.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the council's expectation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dunsbridge's reporting of minor cycling collisions has historically been less thorough than Harrow's.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Harrow's commercial streets carry roughly the same volume of motor-vehicle traffic as Dunsbridge's did before the lanes were installed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protected bicycle lanes are more expensive to install than painted bicycle lanes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dunsbridge and Harrow have comparable proportions of experienced cyclists among their residents.

choices.label: E
choices.text: In Dunsbridge, the vast majority of cycling collisions before the lanes were installed involved cyclists being struck while turning left across oncoming traffic, a maneuver that remains legal and unaltered in Harrow.

explanations.correct: The council assumes the lanes will address the kinds of collisions Harrow faces. (E) reveals that the pre-lane collisions in Dunsbridge were dominated by a left-turn conflict unaffected by protected lanes. If the same maneuver is unaltered in Harrow, the lanes there should not produce a comparable drop — the claimed benefit depended on a cause the lanes don't actually address.
explanations.A: Attacks a subsidiary point — the reliability of the Dunsbridge count — without touching Harrow's expected outcome.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — matched traffic volume supports the analogy.
explanations.C: Out of scope — cost has no bearing on whether collisions will fall.
explanations.D: Strengthens — comparable rider experience supports the analogy.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental causal argument with an appealing mechanism. Weakener reveals reversed causation: the correlation runs the other direction. Trap (A) is an opposite answer; trap (C) attacks a minor premise.
lr.stimulus: A team of ecologists surveyed 200 streams in a large river basin and found that streams with dense populations of freshwater mussels had, on average, markedly clearer water than streams with sparse mussel populations. Because mussels filter particulates from the water as they feed, the ecologists concluded that the mussels are the primary reason the clear-water streams are clear.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the ecologists' conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In laboratory tanks, individual freshwater mussels can filter several liters of water per hour.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Freshwater mussels cannot survive in streams whose water is already murky from suspended particulates, because their gills become clogged.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some of the ecologists' survey measurements were taken during a week of unusually heavy rainfall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A different invertebrate present in many of the surveyed streams also filters particulates but on a smaller scale.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Freshwater mussel populations throughout the basin have declined over the past two decades.

explanations.correct: The ecologists infer that mussels cause the clarity. (B) reverses the causal direction: mussels can't live in already-murky water, so clear water is a precondition for dense mussel populations rather than a consequence of them. The correlation is explained in the opposite direction from the one the ecologists proposed.
explanations.A: Opposite answer — confirming filtering capacity strengthens the mussel-causes-clarity claim.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Attacks a subsidiary point about measurement conditions without directly challenging the correlation or its causal interpretation.
explanations.D: Too narrow — a smaller-scale additional filterer doesn't explain away the mussels' contribution.
explanations.E: Out of scope — basin-wide decline over two decades doesn't bear on the cross-sectional comparison among today's streams.

lr.difficultyReason: Technology causal argument with a plausible productivity story. Weakener denies a load-bearing assumption about the comparison baseline — the tasks assigned differed. Trap (E) strengthens; trap (D) is out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: Journalist: A software firm recently gave half of its junior engineers an AI coding assistant and asked the other half to continue working without one. After six months, engineers with the assistant had closed 35 percent more support tickets than engineers without it. The firm's chief technology officer has therefore concluded that the AI assistant makes junior engineers substantially more productive.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls the chief technology officer's conclusion into question?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A minority of the engineers assigned an AI assistant reported that they rarely used it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The engineers given the AI assistant were systematically routed the firm's simpler, more self-contained support tickets, while the other engineers handled tickets requiring extended investigation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At other firms that have deployed similar AI assistants, senior engineers have reported mixed opinions about their utility.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The AI assistant's annual license fee is substantial.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Independent code reviewers judged the work produced by engineers with the assistant to be of comparable quality to the work of those without it.

explanations.correct: Closed-ticket counts are only a meaningful productivity measure if the two groups handled comparable work. (B) shows the assisted group drew simpler tickets, which would inflate their count regardless of the assistant. The higher ticket-closure rate can be explained by a different, non-obvious cause: task assignment.
explanations.A: Attacks a minor execution detail; even so, most engineers in the group presumably did use the tool, and (A) doesn't explain why that group closed more tickets.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Out of scope — senior engineers at other firms are a different population with different work.
explanations.D: Irrelevant — cost has no bearing on whether productivity rose.
explanations.E: Strengthens, if anything — equal quality with higher volume supports a productivity gain.

lr.difficultyReason: Linguistic generalization from a sample. Weakener exposes a sampling flaw — the compared corpora are not contemporaneous. Trap (A) strengthens; trap (C) is out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: A recent computational study compared two corpora of English prose: one drawn from personal letters written between 1850 and 1900, the other from email and text messages written between 2010 and 2020. The study found that the average sentence in the modern corpus was 38 percent shorter than the average sentence in the nineteenth-century corpus. The linguist responsible for the study concluded that English speakers today favor dramatically shorter sentences than their nineteenth-century counterparts did.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the linguist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The nineteenth-century corpus and the modern corpus were of roughly equal total word count.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Personal letters of the nineteenth century typically used longer, more elaborated sentences than any other kind of writing produced in that period, while email and text messages today typically use shorter sentences than any other modern written form.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some of the nineteenth-century letters were originally composed in languages other than English and translated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of the modern messages in the study were composed on mobile phones.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The linguist measured sentence length by counting words between punctuation marks.

explanations.correct: The conclusion generalizes to English speakers today versus those of the nineteenth century. (B) shows the two samples were each drawn from outliers of their own era — the longest genre in 1850–1900 and the shortest genre in 2010–2020 — inflating any apparent gap. The sampling flaw undermines the generalization.
explanations.A: Strengthens, if anything — equal corpus size supports the comparability of the statistics, not their representativeness.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — a handful of translated letters wouldn't move the average enough to explain a 38 percent gap.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the composition device doesn't bear on whether the sentences represent English usage generally.
explanations.E: Attacks a methodological detail that applies equally to both corpora and so cannot account for the gap between them.

lr.difficultyReason: Historical causal argument attributing a cultural shift to a specific policy. Weakener introduces a prior alternative cause whose effects coincided with the policy. Trap (B) strengthens; trap (D) attacks a subsidiary claim.
lr.stimulus: Historian: In the Kingdom of Valoria, the rate at which commoners learned to read more than doubled in the three decades following King Edric's 1472 decree that every parish maintain a school open to all children. Edric's decree is therefore the principal cause of the dramatic rise in literacy among Valorian commoners during this period.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Edric's decree included provisions imposing modest fines on parishes that failed to maintain the required schools.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Surviving records indicate that most of the parish schools founded under Edric's decree employed clergy as teachers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Literacy rates among Valorian nobles also rose during the three decades following the decree, though less sharply.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some parishes did not comply with Edric's decree until several years after its issuance.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A process for producing inexpensive printed books arrived in Valoria in 1470, and by 1500 Valorian towns were filled with cheap printed material of the sort commoners could acquire and use to teach themselves to read.

explanations.correct: The historian credits Edric's decree with the surge in commoner literacy. (E) supplies a prior, independent cause — the arrival of cheap printed books two years before the decree — that plausibly explains the same rise. The correlation between the decree and the literacy rise is equally consistent with this competing cause, so the historian's attribution no longer follows.
explanations.A: Strengthens, if anything — an enforcement mechanism makes it more likely that the decree was implemented and thereby produced its effect.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — identifies a plausible mechanism (clergy teaching) by which the decree operated.
explanations.C: Out of scope — rising noble literacy doesn't explain away the commoners' rise.
explanations.D: Attacks a subsidiary point about compliance timing without displacing the decree as primary cause.
explanations.E: Correct.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy causal argument from aggregate data. Weakener exposes a confounder that explains the correlation. Trap (A) strengthens; trap (E) is a strengthener disguised as criticism.
lr.stimulus: Public-health official: Over the past five years, our county's 15 elementary schools have progressively adopted a new nutrition program that replaces fried side dishes with steamed vegetables in school lunches. During that same period, the proportion of elementary-school students in our county classified as overweight has fallen from 24 percent to 18 percent. The nutrition program is clearly responsible for the drop in childhood overweight in our county.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the official's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Schools that adopted the nutrition program earlier in the five-year period saw the largest drops in the proportion of students classified as overweight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: During the same five-year period, the county opened six new public parks and required each elementary school to add 90 minutes per week of physical-education activity, changes unrelated to the nutrition program.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some students in the county bring their own lunches to school rather than eating the lunches the nutrition program provides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nutrition program is more expensive per meal than the lunch program it replaced.

choices.label: E
choices.text: National surveys show that the proportion of elementary-school students classified as overweight has remained steady nationwide over the past five years.

explanations.correct: The official credits the nutrition program with the weight drop. (B) introduces a concurrent, independent cause — mandated physical-education increases and new parks — that could plausibly explain the same drop, so the correlation no longer singles out the nutrition program.
explanations.A: Strengthens — a dose-response pattern supports the causal attribution.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — some students opting out doesn't explain why the county-wide rate fell, and if anything makes the program's contribution harder, not easier, to credit.
explanations.D: Out of scope — cost has no bearing on whether the program caused the weight drop.
explanations.E: Strengthens — a stable national rate makes the county's drop harder to attribute to a general trend and thus easier to attribute to a local change like the program.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts causal argument from attendance data. Weakener reveals a sampling flaw: attendance was inflated by a short-term event. Trap (A) strengthens; trap (D) attacks a subsidiary point.
lr.stimulus: Museum director: When the Pelham Gallery reopened last year after a two-year renovation, daily attendance in its first three months was 40 percent higher than the average daily attendance in the three years before the closure. Critics doubted that the renovation, which preserved the original floor plan, would draw additional visitors. But these attendance figures show that the renovation has substantially increased the gallery's appeal to the public.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the museum director's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: During the three months following its reopening, the Pelham Gallery charged the same admission fee that it had charged before the renovation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For the three months following its reopening, the Pelham Gallery hosted a rare traveling exhibition of Renaissance drawings that attracted unusually large crowds wherever it was shown.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several other galleries in the same city undertook renovations during the Pelham's closure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Pelham Gallery's renovation cost significantly more than its director had initially projected.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some visitors to the Pelham Gallery reported that they preferred the gallery's prior appearance.

explanations.correct: The director attributes the attendance jump to the renovation's increased appeal. (B) offers a non-obvious alternative cause — a rare traveling exhibition present during exactly the measurement window — that would draw crowds regardless of the renovation. The data no longer support the renovation-as-cause claim.
explanations.A: Strengthens, if anything — an unchanged admission fee rules out price as an alternative explanation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — simultaneous renovations elsewhere don't, by themselves, explain why the Pelham's attendance rose.
explanations.D: Attacks a subsidiary point about cost, not about whether the renovation increased appeal.
explanations.E: Too narrow — a few dissenting visitors don't account for the 40 percent increase.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal analogical argument from one jurisdiction to another. Weakener denies the load-bearing assumption that the jurisdictions' enforcement regimes are comparable. Trap (B) strengthens; trap (A) attacks a subsidiary point.
lr.stimulus: Attorney: The state of Arlen enacted a law requiring all commercial truck drivers to install electronic logging devices that automatically record driving hours. Within two years, the rate of accidents involving Arlen commercial trucks had dropped by nearly a quarter. The state of Brennan has now enacted an identical logging-device requirement; Brennan should expect a similarly sharp reduction in its own rate of accidents involving commercial trucks.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the attorney's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Arlen's commercial trucking fleet is, on average, slightly older than Brennan's.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The two states have comparable highway systems and similar weather conditions throughout the year.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At the same time as it enacted the logging-device requirement, Arlen also tripled the number of state inspectors assigned to review commercial-truck records and hired a specialized prosecutorial unit to pursue hours-of-service violations; Brennan has taken no such enforcement steps.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The electronic logging devices used in Arlen were manufactured by several different companies, some of which sell their devices at a premium.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A few Arlen trucking firms complained that the logging devices were initially unreliable.

explanations.correct: The attorney infers that Brennan will see a similar drop because it enacted the same law. (C) reveals that Arlen paired the law with a major enforcement expansion — tripled inspectors and a dedicated prosecutorial unit — that Brennan has not matched. The analogy collapses once the true cause is identified as the enforcement regime, not the law alone.
explanations.A: Attacks a subsidiary point about fleet age that, if anything, predicts more accidents in Arlen and so doesn't explain away Arlen's decline.
explanations.B: Strengthens — comparable roads and weather support the analogy.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Out of scope — device pricing has no bearing on accident reduction.
explanations.E: Too narrow — complaints from a few firms about early reliability don't undermine the two-year outcome.

lr.difficultyReason: Controlled-study stimulus whose conclusion rides on an unstated methodological assumption: that the enrollment criterion did not preselect for spontaneous recovery. Correct answer reveals hidden confounding in the sample. Trap (C) strengthens by ruling out an unrelated confound; trap (D) attacks the magnitude of the result without touching causation; trap (E) is out-of-scope comparative.
lr.stimulus: Researcher: In a 12-month trial, patients with chronic lower-back pain who received biweekly acupuncture reported an average 42 percent reduction in pain, whereas a control group receiving sham needling reported only a 19 percent reduction. Because the two groups were otherwise similar in age, baseline pain, and prior treatment history, the results show that the therapeutic insertion of acupuncture needles is itself producing the additional pain reduction.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enrollment in the trial was restricted to patients whose pain had persisted for at least six months and had recently intensified — a pattern statistically associated with imminent natural remission independent of any treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The acupuncturists who administered the therapeutic needling had, on average, several more years of clinical experience than the practitioners who administered the sham procedure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither the patients nor the outcome assessors were informed of which group any given patient had been assigned to.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 42 percent reduction in self-reported pain is smaller than the reductions reported in trials of several newer pharmacological therapies for chronic lower-back pain.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sham needling has itself been shown in earlier studies to produce modest reductions in pain relative to no treatment at all.

explanations.correct: The researcher concludes that therapeutic needling itself is doing the extra work. (A) reveals a hidden selection effect: enrollment was keyed to patients poised for natural remission. If both arms improved from that baseline, the differential between arms still needs explaining — but (A) also implies that patients most prone to spontaneous improvement were precisely the kind the trial attracted, and any systematic imbalance in how fully that regression plays out across arms now confounds the comparison. More importantly, the conclusion requires that the 23-point gap reflect something therapeutic needles do; (A) undermines the assumption that the arms were comparably positioned with respect to natural recovery trajectories.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This is a live weakener candidate — experience gap is a real confound — but it is weaker than (A) because the conclusion is about whether the needles themselves did the work, and skilled handling of needles is still therapeutic needling. Reconsider against (A), which undermines the more basic assumption that the differential is not an artifact of the enrollment pool.
explanations.C: Strengthens — double-blinding protects against expectation effects.
explanations.D: Comparative magnitude vs. other treatments is out of scope; the argument is about whether needling caused the observed reduction, not whether it is the best therapy available.
explanations.E: If anything, this strengthens the study's design rationale (sham produced a real 19 percent reduction), and it does not undercut the inference that the additional reduction came from therapeutic needling.

lr.difficultyReason: Multi-step causal chain in medicine: gut-bacteria composition → inflammatory markers → depressive symptoms. Correct answer exposes a mechanism operating in the opposite direction on the first link. Trap (B) strengthens by replicating; trap (D) is a subsidiary-point attack.
lr.stimulus: Clinical researcher: Patients suffering major depressive disorder show, on average, markedly lower diversity of gut bacteria than matched healthy controls, and they also show elevated levels of circulating inflammatory cytokines. Since bacterial diversity is known to modulate cytokine production, and inflammation is increasingly implicated in depression, we conclude that the impoverished gut flora of depressed patients is a contributing cause of their depressive symptoms.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytokine levels in depressed patients vary substantially from week to week, depending on diet and sleep.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A separate study replicated the finding that bacterial diversity in depressed patients is lower than in matched controls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The loss of appetite and disturbed eating patterns that characterize major depressive disorder have been shown, in animal models, to reliably produce substantial reductions in gut bacterial diversity within weeks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cytokine levels in some patients with major depressive disorder fall within the normal range.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Certain antidepressant medications have been observed to modestly increase gut bacterial diversity over the course of treatment.

explanations.correct: The researcher infers that poor gut flora helps cause depression. (C) reveals a mechanism running the opposite direction on the first link: depression itself, via its effect on eating, reliably degrades gut diversity. The observed correlation would then be an effect of depression rather than a cause of it, undermining the causal claim.
explanations.A: Week-to-week variability doesn't touch the averaged group comparison the argument relies on.
explanations.B: Strengthens — a replicated correlation supports the premise, not the conclusion's causal direction.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Attacks a subsidiary descriptive claim (that cytokines are elevated) without challenging the core causal inference; the average can still be elevated even if some individuals are normal.
explanations.E: Consistent with either causal direction. If antidepressants work and happen to raise diversity, this says nothing about whether diversity is upstream of depression.

lr.difficultyReason: Comparative economic argument that treats two minimum-wage jurisdictions as matched. Correct answer reveals hidden confounding in the comparison baseline. Trap (A) is an opposite-answer strengthener; trap (D) is out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: Economist: Cities that raised their minimum wage above the state floor between 2018 and 2022 saw, on average, no larger increase in restaurant prices than demographically similar cities whose minimum wage remained at the state floor. Since restaurant pricing is especially sensitive to labor costs, this pattern shows that recent minimum-wage increases did not, on net, push consumer prices upward in the cities that adopted them.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Restaurants in the cities that raised their minimum wage reported, on average, the same profit margins in 2022 as they had reported in 2018.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Restaurants in many of the cities that retained the state floor operated under long-standing collective-bargaining agreements that committed them to wage increases matching or exceeding those mandated in the neighboring cities that raised their minimum wage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cities that adopted minimum-wage increases were slightly more populous, on average, than the comparison cities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nationally, restaurant prices rose more slowly between 2018 and 2022 than prices for grocery staples.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several of the cities that raised their minimum wage also simplified their restaurant licensing procedures during the same period.

explanations.correct: The argument's comparison assumes the control cities had meaningfully lower labor-cost pressure. (B) dissolves that assumption: the 'no-increase' cities were already absorbing comparable wage increases through collective bargaining. With both groups facing similar labor-cost pressure, the absence of a price differential is uninformative about what minimum-wage policy itself would do.
explanations.A: Strengthens, if anything — stable margins alongside stable prices suggest the labor cost did not force a price increase, consistent with the economist's conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Population difference is described as slight and is not shown to bear on pricing dynamics.
explanations.D: National restaurant-versus-grocery comparisons don't speak to whether minimum-wage increases pushed restaurant prices up within the studied cities.
explanations.E: Licensing simplification, if anything, might lower costs and thereby reinforce the observed pattern — but it does not undermine the causal inference about minimum-wage policy; it introduces another downward pressure without isolating the wage effect.

lr.difficultyReason: Environmental-science argument whose conclusion rests on an unstated methodological premise about sampling timing. Correct answer attacks a measurement assumption without denying any stated fact. Trap (C) attacks a premise without touching the conclusion; trap (E) is out-of-scope.
lr.stimulus: Conservation scientist: Surveys conducted over the past decade in the three largest salt marshes along the Cape Alaine coast have recorded populations of the saltmarsh sparrow that are, on average, 28 percent smaller than populations recorded a decade earlier in the same marshes. Since the marshes are otherwise undisturbed and no new predators have been documented, the sparrow's decline must be due to rising sea levels, which shorten the dry window during which the sparrows can fledge their nests.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the scientist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historically, saltmarsh sparrow populations have fluctuated more dramatically from year to year than the populations of most other marsh-nesting birds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The marshes in question were never protected as sparrow reserves, and casual recreational traffic has increased modestly over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A recent study estimates that fledging success in coastal salt marshes has declined in step with the lengthening of high-tide periods along the eastern seaboard generally.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The decade-earlier surveys were performed during the saltmarsh sparrow's peak breeding season, whereas the recent surveys were performed several weeks later, after most of the year's fledglings had dispersed to adjacent upland scrub.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conservation efforts in marshes farther south have, in some cases, stabilized local saltmarsh sparrow populations through active nest-site management.

explanations.correct: The conclusion treats the 28 percent gap as a real population decline and attributes it to sea-level rise. (D) exposes a methodological flaw: the later surveys missed dispersed fledglings that the earlier surveys would have counted, so the apparent decline may be partly or wholly an artifact of when the birds were counted. The causal claim is stranded until that confound is resolved.
explanations.A: Year-to-year fluctuation doesn't explain a sustained ten-year drop across three marshes.
explanations.B: Introduces a minor alternative cause, but the traffic is described as a modest increase — a plausible but weaker weakener than (D), which undercuts the very existence of the decline.
explanations.C: Strengthens, if anything — it supports the sea-level-rise mechanism the scientist proposes.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the argument concerns three Cape Alaine marshes, not remote management efforts.

lr.difficultyReason: Controlled-study argument about a technology intervention whose conclusion depends on the outcome metric capturing what it purports to capture. Correct answer reveals the metric is gameable in a way that breaks the inference. Trap (A) strengthens; trap (B) is an unwarranted comparison.
lr.stimulus: Technology columnist: In a controlled experiment, one group of programmers was provided with an AI coding assistant and a second, matched group was not. Over four weeks, developers using the assistant closed 35 percent more tickets from their team's issue tracker than developers in the control group. Since issue-tracker tickets are the standard unit of programmer output at this company, the experiment shows that the AI assistant makes programmers meaningfully more productive.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the columnist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Programmers in both groups reported similar levels of job satisfaction at the end of the experiment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The AI assistant was developed by a company that sells programming tools to large software firms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A substantial portion of the additional tickets closed by the AI-assisted group were later reopened by quality-assurance reviewers, who identified regressions and incomplete fixes that the control group's tickets did not exhibit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Programmers in the AI-assisted group spent roughly the same number of hours at their workstations as programmers in the control group.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Before the experiment began, both groups had been closing tickets at statistically indistinguishable rates.

explanations.correct: The conclusion depends on tickets-closed being a faithful measure of productive output. (C) shows it is not: a substantial share of the extra tickets contained regressions that had to be redone, so the raw count overstates real productivity gains. The metric the argument rests on is contaminated by work the AI group is effectively offloading onto later reviewers.
explanations.A: Irrelevant — the conclusion is about productivity, not satisfaction.
explanations.B: Attacks the source rather than the evidence; the experiment's results do not become less informative because the tool has a commercial origin.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Strengthens, if anything — equal hours with higher ticket counts sharpens the apparent productivity gain.
explanations.E: Strengthens — a matched baseline makes the post-experiment differential easier to attribute to the intervention.

lr.difficultyReason: Multi-step causal chain in linguistics: bilingual childhood → denser neural pathways → resistance to age-related cognitive decline. Correct answer attacks the unstated assumption linking the observed endpoint to the proposed mechanism, not to an unrelated factor. Trap (B) is too narrow; trap (E) strengthens.
lr.stimulus: Linguist: Adults who were raised bilingually from infancy consistently perform better on tests of executive function in late middle age than adults who were raised monolingually. Early bilingual experience is known to produce denser neural connections in brain regions responsible for switching between cognitive tasks. Since those same regions underlie executive function, we may conclude that the executive-function advantage observed in later life is itself produced by the dense neural architecture laid down during bilingual childhood.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the linguist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Longitudinal neuroimaging shows that the denser neural architecture associated with early bilingualism has, in most individuals, fully atrophied to monolingual baselines by a person's mid-thirties, whereas the adults studied were in their late fifties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The bilingual adults in the studies were, on average, no more likely than the monolingual adults to have pursued advanced degrees.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some adults who acquired a second language only in adulthood also show elevated scores on tests of executive function in late middle age.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Executive function encompasses several distinct abilities, and bilingual adults outperform monolingual adults on some of these abilities more clearly than on others.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The density of neural connections in task-switching regions correlates, in brain-imaging studies, with stronger scores on executive-function tests at every age examined.

explanations.correct: The argument attributes a late-life advantage specifically to the dense architecture laid down in childhood. (A) severs that link: by the time the advantage is measured, the architecture in question has atrophied. Whatever explains the late-life difference, it cannot be the surviving presence of childhood-built density. The proposed mechanism collapses.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Rules out one alternative explanation (education), which if anything mildly strengthens the argument.
explanations.C: Too narrow — at most this suggests there is more than one route to the executive-function advantage, not that the childhood-bilingualism route is wrong.
explanations.D: Attacks the uniformity of the advantage across subskills without touching the causal mechanism; the conclusion survives so long as the pattern holds on average.
explanations.E: Strengthens — it reinforces the density-to-executive-function link the argument relies on.

lr.difficultyReason: Policy argument from a quasi-comparison between pre- and post-intervention windows. Correct answer exposes hidden confounding from a concurrent change that the argument ignores. Trap (A) strengthens via regression-adjacent reasoning; trap (D) is an out-of-scope fact.
lr.stimulus: Policy analyst: After the city of Brenshaw adopted a mandatory counseling program for first-time nonviolent offenders four years ago, the three-year reoffense rate for participants fell from 34 percent, as measured in the four years preceding the program, to 22 percent in the years since. Opponents of the program point to various social changes over the same period, but none of those changes has been shown to affect reoffense rates in comparable cities. The drop therefore shows that the counseling program is reducing reoffense among its participants.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The three-year reoffense rate among first-time nonviolent offenders in cities that did not adopt mandatory counseling held roughly constant over the same period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Concurrent with the launch of the counseling program, Brenshaw's prosecutor's office adopted a policy of declining to charge a category of low-level offenses that had previously been prosecuted, so the post-program population of 'first-time nonviolent offenders' now excludes a group historically responsible for a disproportionate share of reoffenses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The counseling program is considerably more expensive per participant than most comparable rehabilitative interventions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In neighboring cities without mandatory counseling, reoffense rates for first-time nonviolent offenders are somewhat higher than the 22 percent now observed in Brenshaw.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A minority of offenders assigned to the program fail to complete its required sessions.

explanations.correct: The argument treats the two populations — pre- and post-program 'first-time nonviolent offenders' — as comparable, and attributes the drop in reoffense to the counseling.
