(B) dissolves that comparability: the post-program population has been quietly redefined to exclude a subgroup with especially high reoffense rates. The apparent drop could be entirely a composition effect. The counseling program's contribution is no longer supported.
explanations.A: Strengthens — comparison cities' flat trend makes the Brenshaw drop look intervention-specific.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Cost is irrelevant to whether the program works.
explanations.D: Strengthens — Brenshaw's rate is lower than neighboring rates, consistent with the program helping.
explanations.E: Non-completion doesn't undermine the claim about participants; the analyst's conclusion concerns those who participate.

lr.difficultyReason: Historiographic argument drawing a causal inference from archival evidence. Correct answer reveals a sampling bias in the surviving record that undercuts the inference. Trap (A) is out-of-scope; trap (D) strengthens a subsidiary detail.
lr.stimulus: Historian: In the merchant archives of the Hanseatic port of Vissen, letters written in the decade after the city's adoption of double-entry bookkeeping in 1472 show merchants referring to profit margins with far greater numerical specificity than letters written in the decade preceding that adoption. Since specificity about margins was a prerequisite for the kind of strategic pricing that enriched late-medieval merchants, the spread of double-entry bookkeeping in Vissen itself enabled the commercial sophistication observed after 1472.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Double-entry bookkeeping had been in use in several Italian mercantile cities for nearly two centuries before Vissen adopted it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Vissen archives preserve the correspondence of roughly the same number of merchants from the decade before 1472 as from the decade after.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A fire in 1515 destroyed the bulk of Vissen's pre-1472 merchant correspondence, and the surviving pre-1472 letters were preserved by a single guild whose members were among the city's least numerate merchants and whose letters chiefly concerned personal matters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several of the most numerically specific post-1472 letters are from merchants whose families had long been prominent in Vissen's commercial life.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Double-entry bookkeeping, as practiced in Vissen, required a formal apprenticeship of at least three years.

explanations.correct: The argument infers from a contrast in the surviving archival record that Vissen's merchants became more numerically sophisticated after 1472, and attributes that shift to the new bookkeeping. (C) exposes a crippling sampling bias: the pre-1472 record is a narrow, unrepresentative residue dominated by the city's least numerate merchants. The 'before' sample cannot be compared to the 'after' sample, so the observed contrast does not establish any change in Vissen's commercial practice.
explanations.A: Out of scope — Italian precedent does not affect what Vissen's own merchants did or why.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — comparable merchant counts in the two decades would support the comparison.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Tangential; family prominence says nothing about whether numeric specificity in the record reflects a real change.
explanations.E: Provides background on how the practice spread but does not undermine the inference from the letters.

lr.difficultyReason: Legal-reform argument with a two-step predictive chain: proposed rule will change judicial behavior, which in turn will reduce appellate reversals. Correct answer attacks the hidden assumption linking the rule to judicial behavior. Trap (B) attacks a premise without touching the conclusion; trap (D) strengthens.
lr.stimulus: Legal scholar: A proposed rule of appellate procedure would require trial judges to file, along with every contested ruling, a brief written statement summarizing the legal authorities on which the ruling rests. Judges who know that their reasoning will be laid out for inspection will take more care in forming that reasoning, and better-reasoned rulings are less likely to be overturned on appeal. If the proposed rule is adopted, therefore, the rate at which trial-court rulings are reversed on appeal will fall.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the legal scholar's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The appellate court that would review these cases already reverses trial-court rulings at a historically low rate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some of the legal authorities trial judges would cite in their written statements are difficult to locate and annotate in the course of a working day.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The written statements would be made available to appellate courts, which would use them to identify, with a precision not currently available, errors of legal reasoning in rulings whose written record is today too sparse for such errors to be confidently detected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trial judges who currently take especially detailed notes on their own reasoning are reversed on appeal at lower rates than judges who do not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proposed rule would apply only to contested rulings in civil cases, which make up the majority of the appellate court's docket.

explanations.correct: The conclusion predicts fewer reversals. The argument's two steps — better reasoning follows, reversals then fall — assume the appellate court's ability to detect reversible error remains constant. (C) undermines that hidden assumption: the same written statements that are supposed to improve reasoning also enable appellate courts to catch errors they would previously have missed. Reversals could therefore rise or remain flat even if the reasoning improves. The predictive chain is broken.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to whether the new rule will further reduce the rate; a low baseline can still fall.
explanations.B: Attacks the practicality of the rule, not the argument's conclusion about reversal rates.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Strengthens — it independently supports the link between detailed reasoning and fewer reversals.
explanations.E: Scope of application; does not undermine the mechanism.

lr.difficultyReason: Arts argument with a multi-step causal chain: funding shift → composition time → ambition of works. Correct answer attacks the crucial middle link — that the funding shift actually increased usable composition time. Trap (C) strengthens; trap (E) is an unwarranted comparison.
lr.stimulus: Music critic: When the Thaller Foundation restructured its grants to composers in 2015, it shifted from one-year fellowships to three-year fellowships of equivalent annual value. Longer fellowships insulate composers from commissioning pressures, and composers insulated from commissioning pressures produce more ambitious works. Indeed, works produced by Thaller fellows after 2015 have been reviewed as markedly more ambitious than works produced by Thaller fellows in the decade before. The restructuring, then, is what has enabled the ambition of the recent Thaller-funded output.
lr.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reviewers who assess the ambition of new compositions sometimes disagree substantially about a given work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thaller fellows typically accept the commissions offered to them, and beginning in 2014 the Thaller Foundation required its fellows to sign exclusive commissioning agreements with the foundation's own concert series — agreements that specify deadlines stricter than the deadlines associated with most outside commissions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Since 2015, Thaller fellows have reported higher satisfaction with their working conditions than fellows reported before the restructuring.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A rival foundation, which did not restructure its grants, has over the same period also seen its fellows' work reviewed as more ambitious.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some of the most ambitious works produced by Thaller fellows before 2015 remain more widely performed today than most works produced by Thaller fellows after 2015.

explanations.correct: The argument's causal chain requires that the longer fellowships actually reduce commissioning pressure on composers. (B) negates exactly that middle link: in conjunction with the restructuring, the foundation bound fellows to commissioning agreements with stricter deadlines than the outside commissions they would otherwise have faced. The increase in nominal fellowship length did not translate into insulation from commissioning pressure. The proposed mechanism for the observed ambition is cut.
explanations.A: Minor reviewer disagreement is consistent with a real average shift; it does not disturb the conclusion.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Strengthens, if anything — better working conditions align with the argument's picture of relieved composers.
explanations.D: Weakens somewhat by suggesting a period-wide rise in ambition that has nothing to do with Thaller's restructuring, but it does not foreclose that Thaller's own policy contributed. (B) more directly severs the argument's internal mechanism and is the stronger answer.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison — the durability of older works doesn't speak to whether the restructuring boosted recent ambition.

rc.passage:
Most bird species raise their young in a simple arrangement: a breeding pair attends a single brood, and older offspring disperse at the end of their first season to seek territories of their own. In a smaller but well-documented set of species, however, this pattern is replaced by what biologists call cooperative breeding. In cooperatively breeding species, some adult offspring postpone their own reproduction and remain on their parents' territory for an extended period as nonbreeding helpers, assisting in feeding nestlings, defending the territory against intruders, or standing guard against predators.

Three conditions, taken together, appear to favor the evolution of this arrangement. First, suitable territories must be scarce enough that a young adult's chance of successfully establishing a new territory in a given year is low. Second, the habitat must be stable enough from year to year that waiting on a parental territory is not simply a wasted season; if conditions shift rapidly, the value of remaining at home collapses. Third, the presence of additional helpers must measurably increase the survival of the nestlings they assist, so that a helper contributes, indirectly, to the propagation of genes it shares with its siblings.

Where all three conditions hold, cooperative breeding is observed with some regularity; where any one of them is clearly absent, the arrangement is rare or absent as well. Researchers therefore describe cooperative breeding not as a puzzle requiring a distinct explanation for each species but as a predictable response to a recurring ecological situation, one in which waiting and helping together yield more inclusive fitness than early dispersal would.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
The Florida scrub-jay, a bird confined to a narrow band of well-drained oak scrub on the Florida peninsula, provides an unusually clear illustration of cooperative breeding. Scrub-jay territories are defined by small patches of suitable scrub, and new patches rarely open up: roughly a third of adult scrub-jays spend a year or more as nonbreeders, waiting for a territory to become available through the death of a resident or the gradual expansion of their parents' range. The habitat itself is remarkably stable, with the same oak patches persisting across generations of jays and with the vegetation recovering in predictable ways after periodic fires.

During the nonbreeding period, most such birds live on their parents' territory and act as helpers. A helper's duties include feeding nestlings, escorting fledglings on their first flights, and, most notably, maintaining a sentinel position on a high perch from which approaching hawks and snakes can be spotted and announced to the group with a loud alarm call. Long-term studies at the Archbold Biological Station have shown that nests with helpers fledge measurably more young than nests without helpers, and that the helpers are almost always older offspring of the breeding pair rather than unrelated birds from neighboring territories.

The species thus displays each element one would expect to find in a cooperative breeder: a short supply of territories, a habitat that rewards waiting, and a clear fitness benefit to the helper's close relatives. For researchers, the scrub-jay has become a standard reference case against which other candidate cooperative breeders are compared.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A defends a general account that passage B shows to be mistaken in the case of one species.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A sets out a general account of cooperative breeding in birds, and passage B describes a single species that exhibits each of the features the general account identifies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A and passage B offer competing explanations for the behavior of the Florida scrub-jay.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A describes a controversy among biologists that passage B resolves in favor of one side.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A surveys a range of bird species, and passage B argues that cooperative breeding has been overreported in the literature.

explanations.correct: Passage A lays out the three conditions that favor cooperative breeding in general; passage B describes the Florida scrub-jay as a species in which each of those three conditions is satisfied. That is a generalization/instance relationship.
explanations.A: Passage B does not argue that the general account is mistaken; it presents the scrub-jay as a case that fits the account.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The two passages do not offer competing explanations; only passage B discusses the scrub-jay, and it uses the framework of passage A.
explanations.D: Passage A does not describe a controversy.
explanations.E: Passage B does not claim that cooperative breeding has been overreported; it presents the scrub-jay as a standard reference case.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cooperative breeding is a puzzle that requires a separate evolutionary explanation for each species in which it occurs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most bird species raise their young in breeding pairs rather than in cooperative groups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cooperative breeding in birds is best understood as a predictable response to three specifiable ecological conditions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Young adult birds generally benefit more from remaining on their parents' territory than from seeking territories of their own.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Helpers at the nest increase the survival of their siblings only when suitable territories are scarce.

explanations.correct: The third paragraph states the passage's main claim explicitly: cooperative breeding is not a puzzle requiring a distinct explanation for each species but a predictable response to a recurring ecological situation, namely the three conditions laid out in paragraph 2.
explanations.A: The passage's final paragraph rejects this framing.
explanations.B: This is a framing claim from paragraph 1, not the passage's thesis.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage does not claim this; helpers forgo reproduction during the waiting period.
explanations.E: The passage treats scarcity of territories and survival benefit as separate conditions, both of which must hold.

questions.questionStem: According to passage A, each of the following is a condition that favors the evolution of cooperative breeding EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: the scarcity of suitable territories for young adult birds

choices.label: B
choices.text: year-to-year stability of the relevant habitat

choices.label: C
choices.text: a measurable increase in nestling survival when helpers are present

choices.label: D
choices.text: a low average reproductive rate among the breeding pairs of the species

choices.label: E
choices.text: a genetic relationship between helpers and the nestlings they assist

explanations.correct: Passage A lists exactly three conditions: scarce territories, stable habitat, and a survival benefit from helpers that operates through shared genes. The passage does not mention low reproductive rate as a precondition.
explanations.A: This is the first condition stated.
explanations.B: This is the second condition stated.
explanations.C: This is the third condition stated.
explanations.D: Correct. The passage does not name this as a condition.
explanations.E: Passage A's third condition explicitly depends on the helper sharing genes with its siblings.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: that helpers assist in feeding nestlings

choices.label: B
choices.text: that helpers contribute indirectly to the propagation of shared genes

choices.label: C
choices.text: that helpers may take up a sentinel position from which approaching predators can be spotted

choices.label: D
choices.text: that cooperative breeding is observed in only a smaller subset of bird species

choices.label: E
choices.text: that the habitat of a cooperatively breeding species must be relatively stable from year to year

explanations.correct: Passage B states that a helper's duties include 'maintaining a sentinel position on a high perch from which approaching hawks and snakes can be spotted and announced to the group.' Passage A mentions feeding, territory defense, and guarding against predators in general terms but does not describe a sentinel perch.
explanations.A: Both passages mention feeding nestlings.
explanations.B: Passage A makes this point explicitly about shared genes; passage B mentions a fitness benefit to close relatives but does not introduce this idea for the first time.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Only passage A frames the relative frequency of the arrangement.
explanations.E: Passage A identifies habitat stability as one of the three conditions.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following features of the Florida scrub-jay, as described in passage B, most directly corresponds to the first of the three conditions identified in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: the tendency of helpers to be older offspring of the breeding pair

choices.label: B
choices.text: the fact that roughly a third of adult scrub-jays spend a year or more as nonbreeders waiting for a territory

choices.label: C
choices.text: the persistence of the same oak patches across generations of jays

choices.label: D
choices.text: the finding that nests with helpers fledge measurably more young than nests without

choices.label: E
choices.text: the use of the species as a standard reference case by researchers

explanations.correct: Passage A's first condition is that suitable territories must be scarce enough that a young adult's chance of establishing a new territory in a given year is low. Passage B's report that roughly a third of adult scrub-jays spend a year or more waiting for a territory is the direct instantiation of that scarcity.
explanations.A: This fact corresponds to the genetic-relatedness element of the third condition, not the scarcity condition.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Persistent oak patches correspond to the second condition (stable habitat), not the first.
explanations.D: This corresponds to the third condition (survival benefit from helpers).
explanations.E: This describes how other researchers use the species, not any of passage A's three conditions.

questions.questionStem: The passages most strongly support which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cooperative breeding is more common among birds than the breeding-pair arrangement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most adult Florida scrub-jays never succeed in establishing territories of their own.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A bird species whose habitat changes dramatically from year to year is unlikely to develop cooperative breeding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cooperative breeding in the Florida scrub-jay evolved independently of cooperative breeding in other species.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Helpers in cooperatively breeding species contribute more to nestling survival than the breeding pair does.

explanations.correct: Passage A identifies year-to-year habitat stability as a necessary condition; where a condition 'is clearly absent, the arrangement is rare or absent as well.' A species whose habitat changes dramatically from year to year therefore lacks that condition and is unlikely to develop cooperative breeding.
explanations.A: Passage A explicitly identifies cooperative breeding as the less common arrangement.
explanations.B: Passage B says roughly a third of adults spend a year or more waiting, not that most never establish territories.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Neither passage addresses the independent origins of cooperative breeding in different lineages.
explanations.E: Neither passage compares the contribution of helpers with that of breeding pairs.

questions.questionStem: In passage B, the reference to long-term studies at the Archbold Biological Station functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: cast doubt on the general account of cooperative breeding presented in passage A

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide evidence that helpers in the Florida scrub-jay increase the survival of nestlings to which they are closely related

choices.label: C
choices.text: identify the researchers who first proposed the three-condition framework described in passage A

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate the difficulty of observing cooperative breeding in stable habitats

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce a rival species whose behavior does not fit passage A's framework

explanations.correct: The Archbold sentence reports two findings: that nests with helpers fledge more young, and that helpers are almost always older offspring of the breeding pair. Together these support the instantiation of passage A's third condition — a fitness benefit that runs through close relatives.
explanations.A: The studies are used to support, not undermine, the general account.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Passage B does not attribute the three-condition framework to any particular researchers.
explanations.D: The studies do not illustrate any difficulty of observation.
explanations.E: No rival species is introduced; the scrub-jay is the sole focus of passage B.

rc.passage:
Historians of public health have sometimes argued that epidemics rarely introduce entirely new social trends; more often, they accelerate developments that were already under way before the outbreak began. On this view, a severe outbreak acts less as an engine of change than as a pressure that shortens the time required for existing proposals — proposals that had been circulating among reformers and officials well in advance of the crisis — to be adopted in practice.

Three features of this accelerating role tend to recur. First, the institutional proposals that an epidemic advances are typically those already in reasonably developed form when the epidemic arrives; the crisis rewards readiness rather than improvisation, and ideas that had not yet been articulated before the outbreak rarely enter the official record during it. Second, the acceleration is most pronounced in domains where the proposed changes had already begun to attract some official support, even if adoption had been delayed by competing priorities or local resistance. Third, once the emergency recedes, the newly adopted arrangements usually persist, because dismantling them would require actively reversing changes that were already on a path toward acceptance.

By treating epidemics as accelerants rather than as originators, historians can explain why outwardly similar outbreaks in different societies often produce sharply different institutional outcomes: the outcome reflects what was already available to be accelerated. This framing avoids the temptation to treat every post-epidemic reform as a direct consequence of the epidemic itself and focuses attention instead on the preexisting trajectory that the crisis intensified.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
The 1918 influenza pandemic reached the United States at a moment when American public-health administration was in an unsettled condition. For more than a decade, progressive reformers had been urging the expansion of state and municipal health departments, the systematic collection of vital statistics, and the creation of standing advisory bodies to coordinate responses across jurisdictions. These proposals had generated official interest in a number of states, and pilot arrangements existed in several cities; but full adoption had been delayed by budget disputes and by resistance from local authorities who regarded public-health administration as a local rather than a state function.

The pandemic shifted this balance within a matter of months. Several states that had been considering the expansion of their health departments enacted the relevant legislation in 1919 and 1920, drawing largely on draft statutes that had been prepared before the outbreak. The systematic reporting of communicable disease — a longstanding reformer demand — was institutionalized in many jurisdictions during the same period. Coordinating bodies that had previously been proposed and shelved were established on a standing basis.

After the pandemic subsided, these arrangements remained in place. The health departments did not shrink back to their prewar size; the reporting requirements were not repealed; the coordinating bodies continued to meet. The episode is frequently cited as a clear instance of the pattern in which a crisis rapidly advances a program of reform that was already in circulation before the crisis arrived.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A proposes a general principle about the historical role of epidemics, and passage B presents a specific episode that conforms to that principle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A describes a historical episode, and passage B draws from that episode a general principle about all crises.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A defends a principle that passage B argues is incompatible with the American historical record.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A and passage B offer competing accounts of the causes of the 1918 influenza pandemic.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A surveys reforms in several countries, and passage B narrows that survey to the United States alone.

explanations.correct: Passage A sets out the 'accelerant' principle, with three recurring features. Passage B presents the 1918 influenza pandemic as an episode that displays each of those features. That is a principle/application relationship.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The order is reversed: passage A is general, passage B is specific.
explanations.C: Passage B is presented as an instance of passage A's principle, not a counterexample.
explanations.D: Neither passage discusses the biological or epidemiological causes of the pandemic.
explanations.E: Passage A does not survey reforms in particular countries.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epidemics usually introduce entirely new social trends that would not have emerged in their absence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epidemics typically accelerate reforms that were already developing, rather than originating new ones, in ways that can be described by several recurring features.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Institutional reforms adopted during an epidemic are usually reversed once the emergency has passed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Outwardly similar epidemics in different societies generally produce similar institutional outcomes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reformers should not propose new public-health measures until an epidemic has already begun.

explanations.correct: Passage A argues that epidemics accelerate developments already under way and identifies three recurring features of this accelerating role.
explanations.A: Passage A explicitly rejects this view in its first paragraph.
explanations.C: Passage A says the opposite: the arrangements usually persist.
explanations.D: Passage A says outwardly similar outbreaks can produce sharply different outcomes.
explanations.E: Passage A makes no policy recommendation to reformers.
explanations.B: Correct.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: What role do epidemics play in shaping subsequent institutional arrangements?

choices.label: B
choices.text: What medical interventions proved most effective during the 1918 influenza pandemic?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Why did some early-twentieth-century municipalities resist state-level public-health administration?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Should reformers rely on crises to advance proposals that cannot be adopted in ordinary times?

choices.label: E
choices.text: How should historians weigh archival evidence against statistical records when studying epidemics?

explanations.correct: Passage A asks, and answers, this question in general terms (epidemics accelerate existing trends). Passage B addresses the same question in a specific case (the 1918 pandemic accelerated preexisting public-health proposals).
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Neither passage discusses medical interventions.
explanations.C: Passage B briefly notes municipal resistance but does not ask or answer this question; passage A does not touch it at all.
explanations.D: Neither passage frames the issue as a recommendation to reformers.
explanations.E: Neither passage addresses historiographical method.

questions.questionStem: According to passage B, prior to the 1918 pandemic, full adoption of the reformers' public-health proposals had been delayed primarily by

choices.label: A
choices.text: the absence of any official interest in those proposals

choices.label: B
choices.text: a lack of draft legislation suitable for enactment

choices.label: C
choices.text: budget disputes and resistance from local authorities who regarded public-health administration as a local rather than a state function

choices.label: D
choices.text: the opposition of progressive reformers to centralization

choices.label: E
choices.text: a federal statute prohibiting the states from expanding their health departments

explanations.correct: Passage B states: 'full adoption had been delayed by budget disputes and by resistance from local authorities who regarded public-health administration as a local rather than a state function.'
explanations.A: The passage says the proposals had generated official interest in a number of states.
explanations.B: The passage says states drew on draft statutes that had been prepared before the outbreak.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Progressive reformers were the ones urging the changes.
explanations.E: The passage does not mention any federal statute of this kind.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following features of the 1918 episode, as described in passage B, most directly illustrates the third of the recurring features identified in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: that reformers had been urging the expansion of state and municipal health departments for more than a decade

choices.label: B
choices.text: that pilot arrangements for the proposed reforms already existed in several cities

choices.label: C
choices.text: that states drew on draft statutes prepared before the outbreak

choices.label: D

rc.passage:
The contemporary American law of free expression is usually presented as an outgrowth of a handful of mid-twentieth-century Supreme Court decisions. That presentation obscures how recent the doctrine's current shape is. Until the First World War, the dominant judicial view held that the First Amendment prohibited only prior restraints — official attempts to block publication before it occurred — and left the government free to punish speakers after the fact for utterances deemed dangerous to public order. The modern doctrine, under which the state must ordinarily tolerate speech it finds offensive or even seditious, was assembled incrementally across the middle decades of the twentieth century.

The chief vehicle of that assembly was a series of cases involving political dissidents, labor organizers, and minority religious groups. In each, the Court gradually narrowed the categories of speech the government could punish, replacing vague standards with demanding tests: speech could be suppressed only where it posed an imminent threat of lawless action, not merely where it offended the sensibilities of the majority or the convenience of officials. That shift represents a genuine achievement, and one that the legal academy has rightly defended against recurrent pressure to reopen the categories.

It would be a mistake, however, to treat the doctrine as self-applying. The imminence test requires judges to draw lines between abstract advocacy and direct incitement, and those lines have never been drawn with perfect consistency. The doctrine's most impressive feature is less its clarity than its willingness to tolerate error on the side of the speaker — to risk permitting speech that is genuinely harmful rather than chill speech that is merely unpopular. That willingness is itself a policy choice, grounded in a judgment about the relative costs of the two kinds of mistake, and it is worth defending on those terms rather than treating it as a neutral discovery about what the Constitution requires.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
A familiar way of thinking about free speech treats the problem as essentially a matter of legal design: locate the right test, apply it consistently, and the hard cases will sort themselves out. This framing flatters the jurists who administer the doctrine, but it distorts the underlying moral question. What a society should permit its members to say is not fixed by the history of any particular legal system; it depends on an account of why speech matters in the first place, and on that question the legal tradition has been less illuminating than it pretends.

The strongest philosophical case for broad speech protections rests on a claim about the conditions of collective self-government. A community that cannot freely discuss its common affairs cannot govern itself in any meaningful sense; the capacity to hear unwelcome arguments, weigh them, and reject them on reflection is constitutive of democratic citizenship. On this view, the toleration of offensive or mistaken speech is not a regrettable cost of liberty but a component of what makes liberty valuable.

Still, the self-government argument has recognized limits. It does not straightforwardly extend to speech that operates outside the circuits of public reasoning — commercial inducements, targeted harassment, or expression whose function is to silence others rather than to contribute to debate. Serious philosophical defenders of expression have long acknowledged these limits, and so have sensible legal regimes. What both the doctrine and its critics too often obscure is that drawing the limits is itself a substantive exercise in political morality. The hard cases do not disappear once the right test is found; they reappear in the decision about what the test should be, and no formula can spare us that labor.

rc.passage:
For more than a century, educational researchers have asked whether children who grow up speaking two languages fare better or worse in school than their monolingual peers. Early studies, conducted largely in the 1920s and 1930s, reported lower verbal test scores for bilingual children and were widely cited as evidence that early exposure to a second language impaired cognitive development. Those studies, however, drew their bilingual samples almost exclusively from immigrant and working-class communities, and compared them with middle-class monolingual children tested in their stronger language. The apparent deficit was in part an artifact of that mismatch.

Later research, beginning in the 1960s, corrected the methodological imbalance. When bilingual and monolingual children were matched for socioeconomic background and each group was tested in the language it used most fluently, the earlier deficit disappeared. In several domains — particularly tasks that required the child to ignore misleading surface cues and attend to an underlying rule — bilingual children performed slightly better than monolingual controls. These findings have been replicated often enough, and across enough age groups, to warrant cautious confidence. The effect sizes are modest, but the direction of the advantage is stable.

This record supports a specific conclusion rather than a sweeping one. Growing up with two languages does not, on the evidence, impose a general cognitive penalty; in some tasks it confers a small advantage, most plausibly because the routine of managing two linguistic systems exercises the same executive processes those tasks recruit. None of this licenses the stronger claims sometimes made in the popular press — that early bilingualism raises overall intelligence or protects against cognitive decline in later life — but the more limited advantage has survived the kind of scrutiny that early bilingualism research notably lacked.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
Debates over bilingual education in the United States have generally unfolded at some distance from the research on childhood bilingualism. Advocates have defended dual-language instruction on the ground that it preserves cultural heritage and improves academic outcomes; opponents have argued that it delays acquisition of the majority language and thereby handicaps students in a labor market conducted largely in English. Both camps have routinely appealed to studies of bilingual cognition to settle the policy question, and both have misread what those studies can deliver.

The cognitive literature documents, at best, small and specific differences between bilingual and monolingual children on narrow laboratory tasks. Whatever those differences are, they are not the same thing as academic achievement, and the step from one to the other is not a short one. A child who is a few milliseconds faster at suppressing a misleading cue may or may not be better served by a dual-language classroom; that depends on how the classroom is staffed, what language the child speaks at home, how long the program runs, and what the comparison alternative actually looks like in practice.

The consequence is that the policy debate cannot be resolved by pointing at the cognitive research, however careful that research has become. A responsible argument for or against a particular bilingual program must turn on program-level evaluations — studies that track the reading, writing, and content-area performance of children in that program against children in the realistic alternatives. Such studies exist and yield mixed results, varying with program design and implementation. The cognitive literature is a genuine scientific achievement; it is simply the wrong instrument for the job that partisans on both sides have asked it to do.

rc.passage:
The question of whether the anonymous 1592 pamphlet "Greene's Groatsworth" was in fact composed by Robert Greene or by his editor Henry Chettle has divided literary scholars for more than a century. The internal evidence has always been ambiguous. The pamphlet contains turns of phrase characteristic of Greene's earlier work — certain compound epithets, a taste for rhetorical triplets, an affection for moralizing addresses to a dying author's imagined readers — but it also contains idioms, spellings, and metrical patterns uncommon in any other text Greene is known to have written.

The most persuasive case for Greene's authorship rests not on a count of features but on a reading of the pamphlet's argumentative shape. Greene's late works share a recognizable posture: the penitent speaker confessing his excesses, gesturing at the younger writers who will inherit the stage, and insisting that his own example be read as a warning. The Groatsworth adopts that posture with a fidelity no ordinary imitator is likely to have achieved. Chettle, a competent but conventional editor, had no prior history of sustaining such a voice across an entire work; Greene had produced variants of it three times before.

Nothing in the documentary record rules out Chettle's involvement in the details — the correction of copy, the insertion of a transitional phrase, the updating of a reference to a living playwright. What the internal evidence does rule out, in my view, is the stronger claim that Chettle composed the pamphlet and merely attached Greene's name. The argumentative architecture is too continuous with Greene's acknowledged work, and too foreign to Chettle's, for that hypothesis to bear the weight of the idiomatic anomalies on which it has been made to rest.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
Recent stylometric work on disputed Elizabethan pamphlets has moved the authorship question onto new ground. Where earlier investigators relied on a reader's sense of characteristic phrasing, current methods count features that authors do not consciously control — the relative frequencies of common function words, the distribution of sentence lengths, the ratio of certain contractions to their full forms — and compare these profiles against an author's undisputed corpus. Applied to "Greene's Groatsworth," the technique returns a mixed result. The pamphlet's function-word profile falls within the range established by Greene's late works, though near its margin; several of its sentence-level features fall outside that range and within the range of texts known to be by Henry Chettle.

A natural reading of this pattern is that the pamphlet is substantially Greene's but has been worked over by Chettle in ways that affect measurable surface features without disturbing the deeper frequencies. That reading is consistent with what the documentary record suggests about Chettle's editorial role. Greene died shortly before the pamphlet went to press; someone had to ready the copy, and Chettle is the likeliest candidate.

The stylometric evidence therefore does not settle the authorship question in the form it has traditionally been posed. It is compatible with Greene as sole author whose text was lightly revised, with Greene as principal author whose text was more heavily revised, and — at the outer limit of the measurements — with Chettle as author of substantial portions working from Greene's materials. What it rules out is any account that treats the pamphlet as wholly the work of either man, and any account that treats Greene's voice and Chettle's voice as so distinct that their commingling would be visible on the surface.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether a measurable difference exists between the common-function-word profiles of Robert Greene and Henry Chettle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the argumentative structure of a late Elizabethan pamphlet is a more reliable guide to authorship than its surface vocabulary

choices.label: C
choices.text: To what extent "Greene's Groatsworth" can be attributed to Robert Greene rather than to his editor Henry Chettle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether stylometric methods have generally superseded traditional literary judgments about authorship

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether Henry Chettle possessed the literary skill to sustain a penitent authorial voice across an entire pamphlet

explanations.correct: Passage A argues that the strong Chettle-sole-author hypothesis fails and Chettle's role is limited to details; passage B argues the stylometric data is compatible with a range of distributions of the pamphlet between the two. Both are working the same question: how much of the Groatsworth is Greene's.
explanations.A: Only passage B takes up function-word profiles directly; passage A does not.
explanations.B: This is a methodological question each passage implicitly engages, but neither passage poses it as its central question.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Neither passage frames its argument around the general standing of stylometric methods.
explanations.E: Passage A raises this as one consideration among several; passage B does not address Chettle's literary skill at all.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A presents a conclusion that passage B refutes using quantitative evidence unavailable to passage A.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A and passage B reach compatible but not identical conclusions about the authorship question by appealing to evidence of different kinds, each of which admits of a different sense of what it is to write in an author's style.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A argues for Greene's sole authorship on literary grounds, and passage B provides stylometric confirmation of that conclusion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A and passage B arrive at incompatible attributions of the pamphlet to its two candidate authors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage B criticizes passage A's methodology without offering an alternative account of the pamphlet's composition.

explanations.correct: A reaches a negative conclusion (the strong Chettle-sole-author hypothesis is ruled out) resting on argumentative architecture; B reaches a negative conclusion (the wholly-one-author view is ruled out) resting on frequency data. Both treat 'style' — A as argumentative posture, B as unconscious surface frequencies — and their positive conclusions are compatible rather than identical.
explanations.A: Passage B does not refute passage A; it is compatible with passage A's conclusion that Chettle did not compose the pamphlet alone.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Passage B does not confirm sole authorship; it explicitly says the data are also compatible with more extensive Chettle revision.
explanations.D: Their attributions are compatible, not incompatible.
explanations.E: Passage B offers its own positive account of what the stylometric evidence rules in and out.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over

choices.label: A
choices.text: whether Henry Chettle had some hand in readying "Greene's Groatsworth" for the press

choices.label: B
choices.text: whether the evidence concerning the pamphlet's authorship is ambiguous on its surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether the features an author does not consciously control are in principle more informative about authorship than the argumentative shape of the author's work

choices.label: D
choices.text: whether Robert Greene wrote any portion of the pamphlet

choices.label: E
choices.text: whether stylometric methods have produced reliable results on other disputed Elizabethan pamphlets

explanations.correct: Passage A rests its case on 'argumentative architecture' and treats idiomatic anomalies as weaker evidence. Passage B rests its case on features 'authors do not consciously control' and treats argumentative impressions as superseded. They tacitly disagree about which kind of feature is more probative.
explanations.A: Passage A explicitly allows Chettle's editorial involvement; passage B says the same. Agreement, not disagreement.
explanations.B: Both passages accept that the internal evidence is mixed on its surface.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Both authors accept that Greene wrote substantial portions.
explanations.E: Neither passage discusses stylometric performance on other pamphlets; there is no basis for disagreement.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is treated as evidence of authorship in passage B but not in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The use of compound epithets characteristic of Greene's earlier work

choices.label: B
choices.text: The pamphlet's affection for rhetorical triplets

choices.label: C
choices.text: The posture of a penitent speaker addressing his imagined readers

choices.label: D
choices.text: The relative frequencies of common function words across the pamphlet's text

choices.label: E
choices.text: The updating of a reference to a living playwright

explanations.correct: Function-word frequencies are a purely stylometric feature introduced by passage B as characteristic of the new methods, and are absent from passage A's catalog of evidence.
explanations.A: Compound epithets are passage A's evidence.
explanations.B: Rhetorical triplets are passage A's evidence.
explanations.C: The penitent posture is passage A's central piece of evidence.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: The updated reference to a living playwright appears in passage A as something Chettle might have inserted; passage B does not mention it.

questions.questionStem: The passages most strongly support which one of the following claims about the "idiomatic anomalies" mentioned at the end of passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage B would regard them as decisive evidence that Henry Chettle composed the pamphlet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage B would regard them as compatible with substantial Chettle revision of a text principally composed by Greene.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The author of passage A takes them to establish that Chettle corrected the copy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both authors regard them as the most probative evidence bearing on the authorship question.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The author of passage A regards them as outweighing the pamphlet's argumentative architecture.

explanations.correct: Passage B's 'natural reading' is that Chettle worked over the text 'in ways that affect measurable surface features without disturbing the deeper frequencies.' Idiomatic anomalies are exactly surface features, and B treats them as consistent with heavy revision, not as proof of sole authorship.
explanations.A: Passage B rules out the view that the pamphlet is 'wholly the work of either man,' so the anomalies cannot be decisive evidence for Chettle.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Passage A cites the anomalies as the basis of the opposing Chettle-authorship argument, not as establishing mere copy correction.
explanations.D: Neither author treats them as the most probative evidence; passage A explicitly downgrades them, and passage B treats frequency data as more informative.
explanations.E: Passage A treats the anomalies as unable to 'bear the weight' Chettle-authorship advocates place on them; architecture outweighs the anomalies in A's account, not the reverse.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the case made in passage A for attributing principal authorship to Greene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An additional undisputed late work by Greene was discovered in which the penitent speaker posture was absent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Careful analysis showed that Henry Chettle had, in two other pamphlets of the early 1590s, successfully sustained a penitent authorial voice modeled on Greene's across an entire work.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Stylometric analysis showed that the pamphlet's function-word profile fell at the center of Greene's range rather than near its margin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Documentary records showed that Chettle had edited several of Greene's earlier works without introducing stylistic changes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Literary historians agreed that the pamphlet contained a transitional phrase of the kind Chettle was known to insert into others' work.

explanations.correct: Passage A's central claim rests on the premise that 'Chettle … had no prior history of sustaining such a voice across an entire work.' (B) directly contradicts that premise, undermining A's reason for treating the penitent posture as diagnostic of Greene rather than Chettle.
explanations.A: Passage A describes the penitent posture as present in three of Greene's late works; a fourth without it would not undermine the claim that the posture is characteristic of him.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This strengthens rather than weakens Greene's attribution; it does not undermine passage A.
explanations.D: Passage A already concedes Chettle's editorial involvement without stylistic overhaul; this is neutral at worst, supportive at best.
explanations.E: Passage A already allows that Chettle may have inserted transitional phrases; acknowledging one does not undermine the stronger structural argument.

questions.questionStem: In passage B, the observation that the pamphlet's function-word profile "falls within the range established by Greene's late works, though near its margin" functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: establish that Greene was the pamphlet's sole author

choices.label: B
choices.text: reject the quantitative methods described earlier in the paragraph

choices.label: C
choices.text: set up the subsequent claim that the data are compatible with a range of distributions of the pamphlet between Greene and Chettle

choices.label: D
choices.text: dispute passage A's characterization of Greene's argumentative architecture

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that stylometric and literary methods always converge on the same answer

explanations.correct: The 'near its margin' qualifier is what licenses the paragraph's next move: that heavier Chettle revision remains consistent with the data. The sentence functions to set up the later spread of compatible scenarios.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly denies that the data establish sole authorship.
explanations.B: The passage endorses the methods it describes; it does not reject them.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Passage B does not engage passage A's argumentative-architecture claim at all.
explanations.E: The passage does not generalize about convergence of methods; the convergence here is partial.

rc.passage:
Canadian courts have held for several decades that the oral histories of Indigenous communities must be admitted as evidence in cases involving land claims and treaty interpretation. The holding addressed a genuine difficulty. The documentary record on which ordinary common-law adjudication rests was assembled by colonial officials whose interests in a dispute over land were rarely impartial, and the exclusion of oral testimony would systematically privilege the version of events favored by those officials. Admitting oral histories is therefore not a concession to cultural sensitivity but a correction of an evidentiary distortion.

The correction, however, has been implemented unevenly. Courts that admit oral histories in principle have sometimes proceeded, in practice, to discount them against any documentary source that contradicts them, on the ground that written records are more easily verified. That treatment reinstates, in the weighting of evidence, the very asymmetry that admission was supposed to remedy. The genuine achievement of the cases is threatened by this practice, and the remedy requires judges to assess each oral source on its own evidentiary merits — the continuity of its transmission, the community's procedures for verifying it, the consistency of its content across independent lines of transmission — rather than against a default preference for written sources.

None of this requires courts to treat every oral history as accurate, or to abandon the ordinary adversarial tools of cross-examination and corroboration. It requires only that the tools be applied evenhandedly, and that the criteria used to weigh an oral source be criteria appropriate to oral sources rather than those developed to assess a different kind of record.
rc.comparativeBPassage:
The Canadian jurisprudence on oral histories has been praised for its willingness to admit testimony that earlier courts would have excluded. That willingness is real, and it reflects a genuine shift in judicial attitude. The deeper question, less often addressed, is whether a court acting within the common-law adjudicative framework can do more than admit such testimony — whether it can receive it on its own terms.

An oral history transmitted within an Indigenous community typically functions not as a discrete recollection of a past event but as a structured discourse: the authority of the account depends on who is entitled to tell it, the ceremonial setting in which it is told, the relationship of the teller to the ancestors named in it, and the corrections the listening community is entitled to make. Stripped from that setting, excerpted into affidavits, and subjected to adversarial cross-examination on individual factual assertions, the testimony loses much of the structure that, within the community, gives it its standing.

A court that admits such testimony but then assesses it by criteria the testimony was not designed to satisfy has not, strictly speaking, excluded it; but it has processed it through a format that converts it into something the testifying community would not recognize as the source it provided. Genuine reception would involve a court's willingness to let the community's procedures for verifying and correcting an account enter into the court's own weighing of the testimony — a step Canadian jurisprudence has so far taken only tentatively, and without a settled account of what it would require.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately captures a point on which the authors of the two passages agree?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Canadian courts have not yet fully realized the aim behind their decision to admit Indigenous oral histories as evidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The admission of oral histories should be subject to the same rules of cross-examination that govern documentary evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adversarial cross-examination is intrinsically unsuited to the evaluation of oral testimony of any kind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Canadian courts should abandon the common-law adjudicative framework in land-claim cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The admission of oral histories has been adequately implemented in the cases decided so far.

explanations.correct: Passage A: courts 'have sometimes proceeded, in practice, to discount' oral histories, reinstating the asymmetry that admission was meant to remedy. Passage B: genuine reception 'has so far [been] taken only tentatively.' Both characterize the implementation as falling short of the announced aim.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Passage A endorses evenhanded application of cross-examination; passage B argues that cross-examination applied in the ordinary way converts the testimony into 'something the testifying community would not recognize.' Not an agreement.
explanations.C: Passage A does not reject adversarial tools in principle; it asks only that they be applied evenhandedly.
explanations.D: Passage A operates within the framework and seeks its evenhanded application; passage B raises doubts but does not call for abandonment.
explanations.E: Both passages explicitly deny this.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The passages reach the same conclusion about the shortfall in current Canadian practice, but passage A locates the shortfall in the weighing of admitted evidence while passage B locates it in the format through which the evidence is received.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A argues that Canadian jurisprudence has fully realized its aims, and passage B argues that it has not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A defends the admission of oral histories, while passage B opposes their admission on procedural grounds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A proposes reforms that passage B argues would be counterproductive.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A and passage B disagree about whether oral histories should be admitted as evidence at all.

explanations.correct: Both agree the current state of play falls short. A's diagnosis: the shortfall is in weighting — oral sources are discounted against written ones. B's diagnosis: the shortfall is upstream, in how the testimony is formatted for legal consumption. Same verdict, different explanations.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Passage A does not claim the doctrine is fully realized; it explicitly says the 'genuine achievement … is threatened' by uneven implementation.
explanations.C: Passage B does not oppose admission; it raises a subtler question about whether admission alone is sufficient.
explanations.D: Passage B does not argue A's proposed reforms (evenhanded weighting) would be counterproductive.
explanations.E: Both accept that oral histories must be admitted.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over

choices.label: A
choices.text: whether the documentary record of colonial Canada reflects partial interests

choices.label: B
choices.text: whether ordinary adversarial cross-examination, applied evenhandedly to oral histories, is sufficient for genuine reception of that testimony by a court

choices.label: C
choices.text: whether Indigenous oral histories should be admitted into evidence in land-claim cases

choices.label: D
choices.text: whether courts have historically discounted Indigenous oral histories against written records

choices.label: E
choices.text: whether common-law adjudication relies heavily on a documentary record

explanations.correct: Passage A holds that the ordinary adversarial tools are adequate if applied evenhandedly and with oral-specific criteria. Passage B holds that even evenhanded cross-examination strips the testimony of the structural features that give it its standing, so mere admission is not genuine reception. The disagreement is about the sufficiency of evenhanded adversarial handling.
explanations.A: Both accept that the colonial record reflects partial interests (A explicitly, B implicitly via the 'shift in judicial attitude' framing).
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Both accept that admission is appropriate.
explanations.D: Both accept this historical description.
explanations.E: Both accept this.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the two passages taken together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The remedy passage A proposes — the evenhanded application of adversarial tools with oral-specific criteria — would resolve all of the concerns passage B raises about genuine reception of oral histories.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage B would regard passage A's proposed remedy as an improvement over current practice but as insufficient to achieve genuine reception of oral histories by the court.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both authors believe that the community's own procedures for correcting an account should displace the court's weighing of the testimony entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A would accept passage B's description of oral histories as structured discourse whose authority depends on ceremonial setting.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage B would reject as unnecessary passage A's proposal to assess continuity of transmission and cross-line consistency.

explanations.correct: Passage A's remedy addresses the weighting step; passage B's concern is that even before weighting, the testimony is converted into affidavits and individual factual assertions stripped of ceremonial context. So passage B would regard A's remedy as improvement but insufficient for 'genuine reception,' which requires admitting the community's verifying procedures into the court's weighing.
explanations.A: Directly contradicted; passage B locates the shortfall upstream of A's remedy.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Passage B proposes that community procedures 'enter into' the court's weighing, not displace it entirely.
explanations.D: Passage A does not endorse B's specific claim about ceremonial setting; it may be neutral, not affirmative.
explanations.E: Passage B says genuine reception 'would involve' admitting community procedures — a step beyond A's criteria, not a replacement that rejects them as unnecessary.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following features of oral histories is emphasized in passage B but does not appear in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The continuity of a history's transmission across generations

choices.label: B
choices.text: The consistency of a history's content across independent lines of transmission

choices.label: C
choices.text: The community's procedures for verifying a history's content

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ceremonial setting in which a history is told and the entitlement of its teller

choices.label: E
choices.text: The susceptibility of a history to ordinary cross-examination

explanations.correct: Passage B uniquely describes oral histories as embedded in a setting where 'the ceremonial setting in which it is told' and 'who is entitled to tell it' are constitutive of the history's authority. Passage A mentions none of this.
explanations.A: Passage A explicitly cites 'the continuity of its transmission.'
explanations.B: Passage A cites 'the consistency of its content across independent lines of transmission.'
explanations.C: Passage A cites 'the community's procedures for verifying it.'
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Both passages discuss cross-examination, not unique to B.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following judicial practices would, according to passage A, most clearly exemplify the uneven implementation the passage criticizes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court admits an oral history into evidence and, finding that a colonial official's written report contradicts it, treats the report as controlling because written records are easier to verify.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court admits an oral history into evidence and, finding that it is contradicted by three independent written sources whose authors had no connection to one another, gives the written sources greater weight after considering the oral history on its own terms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court refuses to admit an oral history at all, on the ground that it cannot be tested by documentary cross-reference.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court admits an oral history and corroborates it against a community-administered record of the same tradition before assessing its weight.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court admits both a colonial official's written report and an oral history and concludes that the two sources are not in fact contradictory.

explanations.correct: Passage A specifies the flaw precisely: discounting oral histories against any contradicting documentary source on the ground that written records are more easily verified. (A) matches this description exactly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: This is the evenhanded treatment passage A endorses — weighing the oral source 'on its own terms' before reaching a conclusion.
explanations.C: This is outright exclusion, not the implementation problem passage A describes (which arises after admission).
explanations.D: This describes corroboration against community procedures, the kind of oral-source-appropriate assessment passage A endorses.
explanations.E: No contradiction arises, so no discounting takes place; passage A's criticism does not apply.

questions.questionStem: In passage B, the statement that a court which admits testimony but assesses it by unsuitable criteria "has not, strictly speaking, excluded it" functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede the technical accuracy of a characterization the author then qualifies in order to advance a stronger claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: reject as false the claim that admission and genuine reception are distinct achievements

choices.label: C
choices.text: refute passage A's description of uneven implementation in Canadian courts

choices.label: D
choices.text: propose that Canadian courts stop admitting oral histories until a new standard is settled

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide an example of ceremonial testimony processed through the adversarial format

explanations.correct: The author grants that technically the court has admitted the testimony (no formal exclusion), then pivots: 'but it has processed it through a format that converts it into something the testifying community would not recognize.' The concession sets up the stronger claim about format-driven distortion.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The statement in fact sets up that very distinction; it does not reject it.
explanations.C: Passage B does not refute passage A; the two passages are compatible.
explanations.D: Passage B does not propose halting admission.
explanations.E: The clause does not supply an example; it is a concessive move about the court's formal status.

rc.passage:
For much of the nineteenth century, the music of Johann Sebastian Bach was regarded primarily as the work of a learned craftsman rather than that of a great composer. Concertgoers who thrilled to Beethoven or wept at Schubert tended to speak of Bach with respect, but the respect was of the sort one offers to a teacher of harmony: he had, it was said, mastered the rules, but he had not, like the Romantics, expressed himself through them. This standard view persisted well into the early twentieth century, and it still echoes whenever Bach is described as a composer of the head rather than of the heart.

The view captures something real. Bach did devote unusual attention to technical problems, and many of his works were plainly written for instruction, including pieces he composed to help his own children learn the keyboard. But to leave the matter there is to mistake a composer's discipline for his final aim. A closer acquaintance with the music shows that Bach's technical ingenuity was almost always in the service of expressive ends. The unfolding of a fugue, which can look on the page like an exercise in pattern, functions in performance as a way of gradually disclosing a single musical idea from many angles, and the listener who follows its progress is led through something closer to an argument than to a puzzle.

The misreading of Bach as a pure craftsman has its roots in the changing place of instrumental music in the nineteenth century. For Beethoven's heirs, instrumental music was the privileged vehicle for the artist's inner life, and a composer who did not supply obvious emotional signals — sudden dynamic contrasts, yearning melodies, programmatic titles — was assumed to lack such a life. Bach, whose emotional signals are often embedded in the movement of inner voices rather than placed on the musical surface, did not announce himself in the expected ways, and listeners concluded that he had little to announce.

Yet a sympathetic ear, trained to follow several independent melodic lines at once, will find in Bach's cantatas and instrumental works an emotional range that compares favorably with that of any later composer. The pieces do not weep on cue, but they grieve, exult, reflect, and console, often in the space of a few minutes. What the nineteenth-century listener heard as coolness was in fact a particular kind of restraint, one that trusted the music's architecture to carry feeling without underlining it. Seen this way, Bach is not the craftsman of legend, nor a closet Romantic, but a composer whose expressive aims pass through his technical means rather than around them.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The view of Bach as a merely technical composer misses the fact that his technical devices serve expressive ends.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bach's reputation in the nineteenth century suffered because audiences of that era preferred Beethoven and Schubert.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bach should properly be regarded as an early Romantic composer whose emotional aims were simply misunderstood.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Understanding Bach's fugues requires a listener capable of following several independent melodic lines simultaneously.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Much of Bach's keyboard music was written for instructional purposes, including the training of his own children.

explanations.correct: The passage sets up the standard 'craftsman, not composer' view in paragraph 1 and devotes the remainder to showing that Bach's technical ingenuity is in the service of expressive aims. A captures both the view being corrected and the author's corrective.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Paragraph-restatement-not-main-point: captures a contextual observation, not the thesis about the relation between technique and expression.
explanations.C: Too-strong / opposite-of-author: the final paragraph explicitly denies that Bach is 'a closet Romantic.'
explanations.D: Too narrow: the ability to follow independent lines is mentioned once to support the thesis, not as the thesis.
explanations.E: Half-right / paragraph-restatement: true per paragraph 2 but leaves out the corrective move that defines the passage.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the nineteenth-century view of Bach as a craftsman rather than a composer can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: complete rejection as based on factual error

choices.label: B
choices.text: partial agreement combined with a judgment that the view is ultimately inadequate

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, qualified only by minor reservations

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference, since the view has little bearing on contemporary concerns

choices.label: E
choices.text: uncertainty about whether the view has any defensible content at all

explanations.correct: The author writes that the standard view 'captures something real' (paragraph 2) — Bach did devote unusual attention to technical problems — but argues that it 'mistakes a composer's discipline for his final aim.' That is exactly partial agreement plus a judgment of inadequacy.
explanations.A: Too-strong: the author explicitly concedes that the view captures something real.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite-tone: the author is critical of the view overall, not endorsing it.
explanations.D: The author engages with the view at length; indifference is unsupported.
explanations.E: Opposite of the text: the author clearly identifies what the view gets right.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A longstanding view is stated, partly conceded, explained historically, and then revised.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing scholarly theories are presented, and one is shown to be false.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A composer's career is traced chronologically from early instruction pieces to mature works.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An interpretive principle is introduced and then applied to a sequence of unrelated cases.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A critical consensus is described, defended against recent attacks, and reaffirmed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 states the traditional view; paragraph 2 concedes what it gets right and begins the correction; paragraph 3 explains historically why the view arose; paragraph 4 offers the author's revised reading.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Mis-sequencing: the passage is not structured as a head-to-head between two theories, and neither is shown to be 'false.'
explanations.C: No chronology of Bach's career is traced.
explanations.D: Plausible-but-unused: no single interpretive principle is applied to multiple cases.
explanations.E: Opposite-tone: the consensus is being revised, not reaffirmed.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the nineteenth-century assumption that Bach lacked an inner life rested principally on

choices.label: A
choices.text: the fact that Bach composed primarily for religious rather than concert settings

choices.label: B
choices.text: the absence in his music of the obvious emotional signals that later audiences had come to expect

choices.label: C
choices.text: the widespread belief that fugues are exercises in pattern rather than arguments

choices.label: D
choices.text: a general nineteenth-century preference for vocal music over instrumental works

choices.label: E
choices.text: a lack of documentary evidence concerning the composer's private correspondence

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that a composer who did not supply 'obvious emotional signals — sudden dynamic contrasts, yearning melodies, programmatic titles — was assumed to lack such a life,' and that Bach's signals did not announce themselves in the expected ways.
explanations.A: Plausible-world fact not stated: the passage never discusses religious versus concert settings.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Wrong sentence: the fugue-as-pattern framing appears in paragraph 2 as a misreading of the music, not as the basis for the assumption about Bach's inner life.
explanations.D: Outside scope: the passage discusses instrumental music's prestige but never a preference for vocal music.
explanations.E: Outside scope: private correspondence is never mentioned.

questions.questionStem: The author's remark in paragraph 2 that a fugue 'functions in performance as a way of gradually disclosing a single musical idea from many angles' serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate how Bach's technical devices carry out expressive aims

choices.label: B
choices.text: concede that Bach's fugues are more difficult to follow than his other works

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that fugues should be studied from the score rather than heard in performance

choices.label: D
choices.text: compare Bach's fugues unfavorably with the emotional directness of Romantic works

choices.label: E
