choices.text: suggest that Bach's fugues were composed primarily as instructional exercises

explanations.correct: The remark appears as the author's concrete example of the claim immediately above — that Bach's technical ingenuity 'was almost always in the service of expressive ends.' Its function is illustrative.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Accurate-sounding but wrong function: the passage never grades fugues by difficulty of following.
explanations.C: Opposite of the text: the remark appeals to what happens 'in performance.'
explanations.D: Wrong function / opposite-tone: the remark is used to defend Bach, not to rank him below Romantics.
explanations.E: Function from a different paragraph: instructional composition is mentioned in paragraph 2, but not as the point of this particular sentence.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A composer's emotional range cannot be judged fairly on the basis of surface features alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any composer whose music lacks programmatic titles should be classified as a formalist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bach's keyboard works are more emotionally expressive than his cantatas.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Instrumental music became the central artistic medium only after Bach's lifetime had ended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nineteenth-century listeners were incapable of recognizing musical emotion in any form.

explanations.correct: The author argues that Bach's emotional signals are embedded in inner voices rather than placed on the surface, and that listeners who judged by surface signals missed his range. That directly supports A.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too-strong: the author uses programmatic titles as an example of surface signals, not as a criterion for classifying composers.
explanations.C: Outside scope: the passage treats cantatas and instrumental works together and does not compare them.
explanations.D: Half-right: the passage discusses the rise of instrumental music in the nineteenth century but does not fix a moment relative to Bach's life.
explanations.E: Overreach: the author criticizes a misreading, not a general incapacity.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the interpretive pattern the author applies to Bach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A novelist once dismissed as merely ornamental is reappraised when readers notice that her elaborate sentences carry precise emotional content.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A painter long celebrated for technical skill falls out of fashion when a new generation prefers more austere styles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A poet's private letters are published, allowing scholars to confirm biographical speculations that had long circulated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A philosopher abandons an early technical vocabulary in favor of a plainer style accessible to general readers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A composer widely regarded as emotionally expressive is shown, on close analysis, to have relied heavily on formal conventions.

explanations.correct: The pattern is: an artist dismissed as technically accomplished but expressively empty is shown, on closer attention, to use technical devices as the very vehicle of expression. A mirrors this exactly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Surface-similarity: involves fashion and technical skill but reverses the direction — the artist falls out of favor rather than being reappraised upward.
explanations.C: Wrong mechanism: the pattern concerns the relation of technique to expression, not the emergence of new biographical evidence.
explanations.D: Wrong mechanism: the pattern does not involve a change in the artist's own style.
explanations.E: Inverts the direction: this is the opposite move — reducing an expressive artist to formalism.

rc.passage:
In the study of traditional tales, the figure known as the trickster — a clever, unruly character who outwits stronger beings by guile — has long posed a puzzle for interpreters. Anansi the spider in West African tradition, Coyote in many Native American traditions, and Hermes in early Greek mythology are all commonly grouped together under this label, and the grouping has encouraged a familiar reading: the trickster, it is said, exists to entertain, and his escapades serve chiefly as comic relief from the more solemn concerns of myth. This reading is not wrong, but it is partial, and taken alone it misses what makes the figure so persistent across cultures.

To see why, consider that the trickster's victories almost always depend on his marginal position. He is smaller than his opponents, lower in the social order, or denied access to the ordinary means of getting what he wants. His tools are speech, disguise, and an eye for rules that others follow without thinking. When Anansi secures the world's stories from the sky god, or when Coyote obtains fire from beings who hoarded it, the audience laughs, but it also absorbs a lesson about how the weak can act on a world arranged for the strong. The humor, in other words, is the vehicle of something more serious, and removing the seriousness leaves only a thin residue of jokes.

A second common reading treats the trickster as a symbol of pure disorder, a figure whose appeal lies in his willingness to break every rule. This too captures a real feature of the stories: trickster tales are full of taboo violations and reversals of expectation. But the trickster does not simply destroy the order he confronts. Often, as in the fire-theft stories, his transgressions bring a benefit that the community eventually accepts as its own. The order that results is not the order that existed before, but neither is it chaos; it is an order that has been forced to make room for something previously excluded.

Seen together, these observations suggest that the trickster's cross-cultural appeal rests on neither his comic charm nor his disruptive energy, but on the way he dramatizes a problem that every tradition faces: how to acknowledge, from within its own stories, that the settled order is not the whole of what is possible. The trickster does not merely amuse, and he does not merely rebel. He holds open a small, licensed space in which the rules can be examined from outside without being abandoned, and that, rather than his cleverness, is what keeps him at home in so many different mythologies.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The trickster figure is compelling across cultures because he gives traditions a way to reflect on their own settled order without discarding it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The trickster figure is best understood as a symbol of pure disorder whose appeal lies in his willingness to break rules.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anansi, Coyote, and Hermes should not be classified together, since each arises from a distinct cultural context.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The humor in trickster tales is the principal reason these stories have been preserved across so many traditions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Trickster tales function mainly to teach listeners specific lessons about how the weak can prevail over the strong.

explanations.correct: Paragraphs 2 and 3 qualify the 'comic relief' and 'pure disorder' readings, and paragraph 4 states the author's integrating thesis: the trickster holds open a licensed space in which a tradition examines its own rules. A captures that thesis.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Opposite-of-author: paragraph 3 explicitly rejects the 'pure disorder' reading as partial.
explanations.C: Outside scope: the passage accepts the grouping and uses it productively.
explanations.D: Paragraph-restatement-not-main-point: captures the first reading the author corrects, not the thesis.
explanations.E: Too narrow: the weak-versus-strong theme is one strand, subsumed by the larger claim about reflection on order.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the view that the trickster exists mainly to provide comic relief is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: dismissal of the view as a misreading produced by careless scholarship

choices.label: B
choices.text: acceptance of the view as capturing something real but not the whole of what matters

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement, with only a single minor qualification

choices.label: D
choices.text: suspicion that the view has no defensible content and is merely conventional

choices.label: E
choices.text: neutrality, since the author considers the question ultimately unanswerable

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 concedes that the comic-relief reading 'is not wrong, but it is partial.' That is precisely acceptance-with-qualification.
explanations.A: Too-strong: the author explicitly allows that the reading captures something real.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite-tone: the author is corrective rather than endorsing.
explanations.D: Too-strong in the other direction; the author credits the view with capturing a real feature.
explanations.E: The author is not neutral; a clear qualifying judgment is offered.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the trickster's victories almost always depend on

choices.label: A
choices.text: his unusual physical strength relative to his opponents

choices.label: B
choices.text: the direct assistance of more powerful mythological beings

choices.label: C
choices.text: his marginal position and his skill with speech, disguise, and rules

choices.label: D
choices.text: the willingness of his community to abandon its ordinary customs

choices.label: E
choices.text: the intervention of a divine authority that sanctions his rule-breaking

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that the trickster's victories 'almost always depend on his marginal position' and identifies his tools as 'speech, disguise, and an eye for rules that others follow without thinking.'
explanations.A: Altered qualifier / opposite: the passage specifies that he is smaller or lower in the social order.
explanations.B: Plausible world-fact not stated: the passage does not mention assistance from more powerful beings.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Wrong sentence: the passage says the community eventually accepts the benefit, not that it abandons its customs.
explanations.E: Outside scope: divine sanction is not mentioned.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of fire-theft stories in paragraph 3 functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: show that the trickster's transgressions can produce benefits the community comes to accept

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that Coyote tales are more sophisticated than other trickster traditions

choices.label: C
choices.text: establish the historical priority of Native American trickster tales over West African ones

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate the comic dimension of trickster tales noted in paragraph 1

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that taboo violations in trickster tales are usually punished

explanations.correct: The fire-theft example is introduced to show that the trickster's rule-breaking 'brings a benefit that the community eventually accepts as its own,' supporting the author's correction of the 'pure disorder' reading.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Outside scope: the passage does not rank traditions by sophistication.
explanations.C: Outside scope: no claim of historical priority is made.
explanations.D: Function from a different paragraph: the comic dimension is a paragraph-1 concern; in paragraph 3 the example serves the order/disorder discussion.
explanations.E: Opposite of text: the example shows benefit, not punishment.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that a story in which a trickster figure broke every rule of his society and left no lasting change behind would

choices.label: A
choices.text: confirm the author's view that the trickster represents pure disorder

choices.label: B
choices.text: fit less comfortably than usual with the author's account of trickster tales

choices.label: C
choices.text: be unintelligible to audiences outside the tradition in which it was first told

choices.label: D
choices.text: prove that the comic-relief reading of trickster tales is entirely mistaken

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that trickster tales and myths of creation share a common origin

explanations.correct: The author argues that trickster tales typically leave a changed order behind — transgression plus accepted benefit. A tale that broke every rule without lasting change would be a poor fit for that account.
explanations.A: Opposite-of-author: the author rejects the 'pure disorder' reading.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Outside scope: the passage makes no claim about cross-cultural intelligibility.
explanations.D: Too-strong: the author treats the comic-relief reading as partial, not entirely mistaken.
explanations.E: Outside scope: creation myths are not discussed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the author's position that the trickster holds open a licensed space for examining settled order?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In many traditions, trickster tales were performed during festivals in which ordinary social roles were temporarily suspended.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Trickster figures in some traditions are depicted as physically small or animal in form.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some scholars have argued that Anansi tales originated before Coyote tales.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Audiences typically laugh at the moment in a trickster tale when the trickster is first outwitted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Certain trickster tales survive only in fragments, making their endings difficult to reconstruct.

explanations.correct: If trickster tales were performed in festivals that formally suspended ordinary roles, that confirms the author's picture of a 'small, licensed space' in which the settled order can be examined from outside without being abandoned.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Off-target claim: supports the 'marginal position' observation from paragraph 2, not the licensed-space thesis of paragraph 4.
explanations.C: Outside scope: historical priority does not bear on the author's claim.
explanations.D: Wrong direction / off-target: a moment of laughter does not specifically support the licensed-examination claim.
explanations.E: Outside scope: survival of fragments does not speak to the function the author ascribes.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the role the author assigns to the trickster figure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A traditional legal system designates a ceremonial role, filled during an annual assembly, whose holder is permitted to voice complaints that other members of the community cannot.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A group of rebels overturns the government of their country and replaces its laws with entirely new ones.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historian writes a comic biography of a political leader, drawing attention to the leader's personal eccentricities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A theater troupe entertains audiences with purely slapstick performances that avoid political subjects.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A student masters the rules of a game so thoroughly that she never violates them in competition.

explanations.correct: The trickster holds open a small, licensed space in which rules can be examined from outside without being abandoned. A ceremonial role that licenses otherwise-unpermitted complaints within a standing legal order mirrors this precisely.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Inverts the direction: the trickster does not overturn the order; he opens a space within it.
explanations.C: Surface-similarity: involves humor but lacks the licensed examination of shared rules; the biography addresses one individual's eccentricities.
explanations.D: Matches only the comic-relief strand the author treats as partial; no reflection on order.
explanations.E: Opposite of the pattern: the student never steps outside the rules.

rc.passage:
Among twentieth-century movements in literary study, none exerted a more durable influence on classroom practice than the school known as the New Criticism. Its proponents, writing principally in the 1940s and 1950s, urged that a poem be treated as a self-sufficient verbal object, to be interpreted without appeal to the author's biography, the reader's reactions, or the historical moment of composition. The standard account presents the movement as an austere formalism, devoted to keeping the poem in a kind of quarantine, and it is easy to see why: Cleanth Brooks famously warned against the "heresy of paraphrase," and W. K. Wimsatt's essays on the intentional and affective fallacies seemed to seal the poem off from both its maker and its audience.

This portrait, while not inaccurate in outline, obscures a subtler commitment. For the New Critics did not actually claim that biography and history were irrelevant to a poem's meaning; they claimed, rather, that such information could not substitute for the close reading of the text itself. A critic who had exhausted the poem's internal tensions — its ironies, paradoxes, and shifts of tone — was free to consult historical context, and indeed often had to, in order to gloss an archaic word or identify an allusion that the text itself signaled. What the movement rejected was the practice, common in earlier scholarship, of treating the poem as a transparent window onto the poet's intentions or the period's concerns, with little attention paid to the pressures of the language on the page.

Seen in this light, the New Criticism was less an act of quarantine than a redistribution of interpretive labor. Its leading figures wrote extensively on Donne, Keats, and Yeats, and their readings regularly draw upon biographical and historical matter; but they insisted that such matter be earned by the text — introduced only when the text's own evidence demanded it, rather than imposed on the text from without. Later critics, working under the banners of reader-response theory and cultural studies, would charge the New Critics with naïveté about the ideological freight carried by any act of reading, and about the social forces that shape what a given community is prepared to notice in a poem. That charge has force. It is worth remembering, however, that the New Critics' close-reading discipline survived their doctrines, and continues to shape how literature is taught even in departments that officially repudiate formalism.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The New Criticism rejected biography and history as sources of poetic meaning, a position that later critics correctly repudiated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The standard view of the New Criticism as a strict formalism is oversimplified; the movement's real commitment was that extratextual information be subordinated to close reading of the text.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reader-response theory and cultural studies have exposed the ideological blindness of the New Criticism and displaced its methods from the contemporary classroom.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cleanth Brooks and W. K. Wimsatt were less doctrinaire about biography than their most famous pronouncements suggest, and their readings of Donne and Keats prove it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The enduring influence of the New Criticism on the teaching of literature owes more to its pedagogical techniques than to the philosophical doctrines that originally motivated them.

explanations.correct: The passage presents the 'austere formalism' picture as the standard account, then argues that the New Critics' real position was that extratextual material had to be earned by the text, not excluded from it. B captures both halves — the received view and the author's corrective.
explanations.A: Reverses the author's corrective: the passage denies that the New Critics rejected biography and history outright.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Paragraph-level restatement of a single point in paragraph 3; the author acknowledges the force of the charge but does not make the displacement of New Criticism his thesis.
explanations.D: Too narrow — fixates on particular critics' practice rather than the broader claim about what the movement actually held.
explanations.E: Picks up the passage's closing observation and promotes it to the thesis; the pedagogical-survival point is a coda, not the main argument.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the New Criticism can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unreserved admiration for its rigor and its rejection of historical method

choices.label: B
choices.text: qualified respect, tempered by acknowledgment of its theoretical limitations

choices.label: C
choices.text: sharp disapproval of its formalist doctrine but appreciation for the careers of its leading figures

choices.label: D
choices.text: detached neutrality toward a movement whose influence has largely ended

choices.label: E
choices.text: enthusiasm for its pedagogical legacy and indifference toward its interpretive principles

explanations.correct: The author defends the New Criticism against a simplifying portrait and credits its lasting pedagogical influence, while conceding that the charge of ideological naïveté 'has force.' That combination is qualified respect.
explanations.A: Overstated positivity; the author concedes the later critics' charge has force and never endorses rejection of historical method.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not disapprove of the doctrine — he reinterprets it more sympathetically.
explanations.D: The passage is evaluative, not neutral, and explicitly says New Critical practices 'continue to shape' teaching.
explanations.E: Mixes two attitudes in the wrong combination; the author respects both the interpretive commitment and the pedagogical legacy.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the New Critics permitted a critic to consult historical or biographical information in which of the following circumstances?

choices.label: A
choices.text: When the critic wished to recover the poet's intentions in composing the poem

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only after every trace of irony and paradox in the poem had been fully resolved

choices.label: C
choices.text: When the text's own evidence demanded it, for instance to gloss an archaic word or identify an allusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whenever such information had been authenticated by scholars in the period concerned

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only when writing for students, who could not be expected to read closely on their own

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that such material was admitted when needed 'to gloss an archaic word or identify an allusion,' and paragraph 3 generalizes this: extratextual matter was to be 'earned by the text.' C matches both formulations.
explanations.A: Reverses the New Critics' explicit position; Wimsatt's 'intentional fallacy' essay, referenced in the passage, rejects recovery of intentions as the aim.
explanations.B: Altered qualifier: the passage says a critic who had 'exhausted the poem's internal tensions' could consult such material, not that every trace had to be resolved first; 'exhausted' means 'worked through,' and no absolute threshold is described.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Plausible-world detail the passage never states.
explanations.E: Out of scope; the passage does not discuss writing for students.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to Brooks's warning against the "heresy of paraphrase" and to Wimsatt's essays on the intentional and affective fallacies (paragraph 1) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate why the standard view of the New Criticism as an austere formalism has seemed well-founded

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide textual evidence that the New Critics did in fact exclude biography and history from interpretation

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast the positions of two leading New Critics with one another

choices.label: D
choices.text: signal the author's disagreement with Brooks and Wimsatt and prepare the reader for a refutation

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that even the movement's defenders concede its philosophical naïveté

explanations.correct: These citations appear immediately after the sentence 'it is easy to see why' the standard account of the New Criticism as austere formalism arose. They are offered to motivate the received view, which the author will then complicate.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The author's whole point is that these pronouncements do not actually mean what the standard view takes them to mean.
explanations.C: No contrast between Brooks and Wimsatt is drawn; they are adduced together.
explanations.D: Too strong: the author does not refute Brooks and Wimsatt but reinterprets them sympathetically.
explanations.E: The concession of naïveté appears in paragraph 3 and is attributed to later critics, not to Brooks or Wimsatt.

questions.questionStem: The passage suggests that a scholar who treats a poem as a "transparent window onto the poet's intentions" would most likely be criticized by the author on the grounds that such a scholar

choices.label: A
choices.text: cannot explain why the New Criticism has persisted as a pedagogical influence

choices.label: B
choices.text: underestimates the ideological freight carried by any act of reading

choices.label: C
choices.text: fails to give sufficient weight to the pressures that the poem's own language exerts on its meaning

choices.label: D
choices.text: relies on biographical evidence that is often unavailable or unreliable

choices.label: E
choices.text: has confused the intentional fallacy with the affective fallacy

explanations.correct: The passage says the New Critics rejected the prior practice of reading 'with little attention paid to the pressures of the language on the page,' and the author treats that rejection sympathetically. A scholar who treats the poem as a transparent window commits exactly that error.
explanations.A: Out of scope; pedagogical persistence is not the objection raised against window-style reading.
explanations.B: That criticism is the one made of the New Critics themselves, not of their opponents.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Plausible-sounding but unsupported; the passage does not raise availability or reliability of biographical evidence.
explanations.E: The passage mentions both fallacies but does not use confusion between them as a basis for any criticism.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A movement is described; two objections to it are raised; each objection is refuted in turn.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A received view of a movement is presented; that view is qualified rather than rejected; a later criticism of the movement is acknowledged and partly conceded.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two rival schools of literary criticism are contrasted; one is shown to have survived while the other has not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A critical doctrine is endorsed; its principal advocates are named; the doctrine is applied to a representative poem.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A historical controversy is sketched; competing interpretations are evaluated; a new interpretation is proposed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 gives the standard 'austere formalism' portrait. Paragraph 2 qualifies it ('not inaccurate in outline, obscures a subtler commitment'). Paragraph 3 acknowledges the later reader-response and cultural-studies charge and concedes it has force. B matches this three-move structure.
explanations.A: The passage does not refute the later objection; it partly concedes it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No sustained contrast of two schools is developed; reader-response and cultural studies appear only briefly in paragraph 3.
explanations.D: No specific poem is analyzed.
explanations.E: No new interpretation is proposed by the author; he defends a less extreme reading of the received movement.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following interpretive practices most closely conforms to the principle the passage attributes to the New Critics?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A critic writing on a Renaissance sonnet begins by surveying the poet's letters and diaries, and uses the sonnet primarily to illustrate conclusions drawn from that archive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A critic writing on a modernist novel examines its sentence-by-sentence patterns of imagery, then consults period newspapers only to clarify a specific reference that the imagery demands.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A critic writing on a contemporary play devotes equal space to the playwright's biography, the audience's reception, and the text itself, declining to privilege any of the three.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A critic writing on an oral epic argues that its meaning is determined chiefly by the social function it served in its originating community.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A critic writing on a political poem contends that the poem's language is irrelevant to its meaning, which is fully fixed by the poet's known intentions.

explanations.correct: The passage says the New Critics required that extratextual material be 'earned by the text — introduced only when the text's own evidence demanded it.' Option B instantiates exactly that sequence: close reading first, then period research summoned only to gloss what the imagery itself requires.
explanations.A: Inverts the New Critical ordering: archive first, text second.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Treats the three sources as equal; the New Critics subordinated biography and reception to the text.
explanations.D: Treats extratextual social function as the primary determinant of meaning.
explanations.E: Endorses the very 'window' view the New Critics rejected, and in its extreme form goes further than any position described in the passage.

rc.passage:
Medieval illuminated manuscripts have long been discussed in one of two registers. Art historians of an earlier generation treated them chiefly as repositories of iconography — pictorial programs encoding theological doctrine — while bibliographers treated them as physical artifacts to be described by their bindings, quires, parchment preparation, and scripts. Both approaches produced valuable catalogues, but each tended to overlook the quality that most sharply distinguishes the illuminated page from other medieval images: its function within a reading practice.

A recent generation of scholars, led by specialists in what is sometimes called the archaeology of the book, has argued that the marginal decorations, historiated initials, and full-page miniatures of a prayerbook or psalter were not merely illustrations of the text but guides to its use. In a Book of Hours intended for private devotion, for instance, the gilded initial that opens each of the canonical hours served as a visual bookmark, allowing a reader to locate a psalm rapidly without consulting a table. The grotesques that cavort in the lower margins — hybrid beasts, acrobats, hunting scenes — have sometimes been dismissed as idle fancy, but they often mark thematic or liturgical turning points in the text and may have cued the reader to shifts in tone or intention.

This reading-centered account does not displace the older iconographic and bibliographic approaches so much as integrate them. The images still carry doctrinal meaning, and the physical features of the codex still matter; what has changed is the presumption that these dimensions can be studied in isolation from one another. The gold leaf of a historiated initial is at once theological (it figures divine radiance), material (it was beaten to a leaf one ten-thousandth of a millimeter thick and burnished with a dog's tooth), and functional (its shine catches the eye of a reader turning the page in candlelight). To pursue only one dimension is to miss how the others reinforce it. If there is a limitation to the new approach, it lies in the scarcity of direct evidence about how medieval owners actually handled their books; the reading practices reconstructed are often inferred from the books themselves rather than from external testimony such as inventories, wills, or devotional guidebooks. Still, the reconstructions are disciplined by what the page will and will not allow, and they have renewed scholarly interest in volumes that earlier generations of researchers had treated as merely decorative.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recent scholarship has shown that earlier iconographic and bibliographic studies of illuminated manuscripts were fundamentally mistaken and should be discarded.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A reading-centered approach to illuminated manuscripts, which treats their decoration as a guide to the use of the text, supplements rather than supplants earlier iconographic and bibliographic methods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The marginal grotesques of medieval prayerbooks, long dismissed as idle fancy, in fact mark turning points in the liturgical text and shape how readers moved through it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because external testimony about medieval reading practice is scarce, reconstructions of how illuminated manuscripts were used must remain largely conjectural.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Art historians and bibliographers produced valuable catalogues of illuminated manuscripts, but neither group appreciated the theological meaning of the pictorial programs they described.

explanations.correct: The thesis is set out at the start of paragraph 3: 'This reading-centered account does not displace the older iconographic and bibliographic approaches so much as integrate them.' B is a precise paraphrase.
explanations.A: Too strong and reverses the author: the passage explicitly says the older approaches are not displaced.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — fixates on a single illustrative case (grotesques) rather than the passage's broader claim.
explanations.D: Picks up a qualification from the final paragraph and promotes it to the thesis.
explanations.E: Misrepresents the older scholars; the passage says iconographers studied theological doctrine, the very thing this choice denies them.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the gilded initial that opens each of the canonical hours in a Book of Hours served which one of the following functions in addition to its decorative role?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allowed the reader to locate a particular psalm quickly without consulting a table.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It identified the manuscript's owner for purposes of later cataloguing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reproduced in miniature the theological program of the full-page miniatures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It signaled to the scribe where a new quire of the codex should begin.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It corrected errors that the reader might otherwise make in pronunciation.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states plainly: 'the gilded initial that opens each of the canonical hours served as a visual bookmark, allowing a reader to locate a psalm rapidly without consulting a table.'
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Plausible-world detail the passage never states.
explanations.C: The passage does not describe the initials as reproducing the program of the full-page miniatures.
explanations.D: Conflates scribal features (quires) with reader-oriented features (initials); the passage discusses quires only in summarizing earlier bibliographic work.
explanations.E: Out of scope; no pronunciation function is described.

questions.questionStem: The author's detailed description of gold leaf (in the third paragraph) — theological, material, and functional — most likely serves to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that the theological meaning of illumination has been overstated by earlier iconographers

choices.label: B
choices.text: illustrate the author's claim that the new approach integrates rather than replaces the older ones

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce a technical digression on medieval metallurgy

choices.label: D
choices.text: offer a counterexample to the claim that marginal decoration serves a reading-oriented function

choices.label: E
choices.text: prove that the physical features of the codex cannot be studied in isolation from its reception

explanations.correct: The sentence immediately before the gold-leaf example states the integration thesis; the three-dimension description is then given as its instance. Its function is to illustrate that thesis.
explanations.A: The description does not criticize iconographers; it credits the theological reading alongside the others.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Wrong grain: the metallurgical detail is part of a larger point, not a digression.
explanations.D: The example is not a counterexample; it supports the author's position.
explanations.E: Accurate content but wrong function: the example illustrates integration generally, not the specific sub-claim about physical features.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the reading-centered approach to illuminated manuscripts is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: wholehearted endorsement of an approach that has solved the difficulties facing earlier scholarship

choices.label: B
choices.text: approval qualified by awareness of the limitations of its evidentiary base

choices.label: C
choices.text: skepticism rooted in doubts about whether marginal decoration can be said to have any function at all

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral description of a new method, with no evaluative stance of his own

choices.label: E
choices.text: reluctant acceptance forced by the collapse of the iconographic and bibliographic traditions

explanations.correct: The author endorses the new approach ('the reconstructions are disciplined... they have renewed interest') but flags a genuine limit ('scarcity of evidence about how medieval owners actually handled their books'). That is approval with qualification.
explanations.A: Overstates: the passage explicitly notes a limitation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite tone: the author treats marginal decoration as functionally meaningful.
explanations.D: The passage is evaluative, not neutral.
explanations.E: Nothing suggests the earlier traditions have collapsed; the author says they are integrated.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests which one of the following about marginal grotesques in medieval prayerbooks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They were included chiefly to amuse wealthy patrons and had no relation to the text they accompanied.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In at least some cases, their placement correlates meaningfully with liturgical or thematic features of the text.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They were painted by a separate workshop and inserted after the main pictorial program had been completed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Earlier scholars refused to acknowledge them because they offended contemporary religious sensibilities.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Their iconography can be fully decoded once the reader identifies the associated canonical hour.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 notes that grotesques 'often mark thematic or liturgical turning points in the text' — a hedged, positive claim about correlation that B paraphrases faithfully.
explanations.A: Reverses the author's qualification: the passage denies that grotesques are 'idle fancy.'
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Plausible-world detail the passage never supplies.
explanations.D: No such motive for earlier neglect is mentioned; the passage merely says they were 'dismissed.'
explanations.E: Overreach: the author nowhere claims their iconography can be fully decoded by canonical hour.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the reading-centered approach as the author describes it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medieval scribes used different pigments for marginal decoration than for historiated initials.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several surviving Books of Hours contain no marginal grotesques at all, only full-page miniatures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Detailed diaries from medieval owners show that readers regularly skipped the illuminated pages and ignored the decorations while reciting the text.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gold leaf was also applied to liturgical objects such as chalices and altar frontals, not only to manuscript pages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some historiated initials depict scenes that do not correspond to the canonical hour they introduce.

explanations.correct: The reading-centered approach holds that illumination guided readers through the text. External testimony showing readers systematically ignored the decoration would directly undermine that functional claim — and the passage identifies scarcity of external testimony as the approach's weakest point, so this choice also targets the documented soft spot.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to whether decoration guides reading.
explanations.B: Does not undermine: a book may use initials rather than grotesques and still exhibit reading-guiding illumination.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Compatible with the passage; gold leaf's broader use does not affect its manuscript function.
explanations.E: Mild tension at most; the passage does not require a one-to-one correspondence between initial imagery and canonical hour.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Two earlier approaches are surveyed; a newer approach is presented as integrating them; the newer approach is endorsed with an acknowledged limitation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A scholarly controversy is outlined; the author sides decisively with one party; the defeated party's remaining contributions are catalogued.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A pictorial tradition is described; a chronological evolution is traced; a prediction about its future is offered.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Three methods of studying manuscripts are introduced; each is illustrated with a separate case study; the methods are ranked by explanatory power.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An approach is criticized; the criticism is answered by a new defense; the defense is shown to rest on a hidden assumption.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 surveys iconographic and bibliographic approaches. Paragraph 2 introduces the reading-centered approach. Paragraph 3 explicitly frames it as integrating the older work and endorses it while flagging a scarcity-of-evidence limit. A captures all three moves in order.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Misdescribes the author's stance: he does not treat any party as defeated.
explanations.C: No chronological evolution or future prediction is traced.
explanations.D: No separate case studies or ranking is offered.
explanations.E: The passage does not uncover a hidden assumption in the new approach.

rc.passage:
The emergence of bebop in the mid-1940s is often recounted as a revolt: a small group of musicians, chief among them Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, turned against the polished dance arrangements of the swing era and forged a harmonically dense, rhythmically unpredictable idiom playable only by virtuosos. In this telling, bebop broke with its predecessors to become the first jazz style not primarily meant for dancing, and its difficulty was understood as a badge of independence from the demands of the commercial ballroom and the bandleaders who served it. The story has the clarity of a generational break: old music for dancers, new music for listeners.

There is something to the revolt narrative, but it flattens a more interesting continuity. Many of the harmonic substitutions that became bebop's signature — tritone replacements, chromatic ii–V interpolations, the extension of chords to include the ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth — had been quietly explored by pianists and arrangers within the big bands of the late 1930s, especially in the written introductions and brief instrumental passages that sat between vocal choruses. What the beboppers did was not so much invent these devices as expose them. By thinning the ensemble to a quintet and foregrounding the soloist, they made audible the harmonic machinery that swing arrangements had kept buried under sectional voicings and dancing tempos. The rhythmic innovations, too, grew out of practices that drummers such as Jo Jones had developed while still working within the dance-band framework.

The point is not to deny bebop's distinctiveness. Its tempos were faster, its melodic lines more jagged, its expectations of the listener more demanding, and the social setting of the after-hours club did foster a kind of musicianly freedom unavailable at the Savoy Ballroom or any comparable public ballroom. But the continuities matter, because they correct a misleading picture of the swing era itself. That era is too often remembered as an age of bland commerce whose best features bebop had to rescue. In fact, the big bands were laboratories in which the material of the new music was being assembled, and the most enterprising beboppers knew it. Parker's first professional experiences were in territory bands; Gillespie arranged for Cab Calloway; the very harmonic vocabulary they are credited with inventing had been in the room, waiting to be unpacked, while they learned their craft. What looks like revolt from a distance is, up close, a studied act of foregrounding.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bebop was an entirely unprecedented musical idiom whose harmonic vocabulary bore no meaningful relation to that of the swing era it replaced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: While bebop differed from swing in important ways, its harmonic and rhythmic innovations were extensions of devices already developed within the big bands, and the revolt narrative obscures this continuity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie deserve more credit than they have traditionally received for their early apprenticeships in territory and touring dance bands.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rhythmic contributions of drummers such as Jo Jones have been undervalued by historians who treat bebop's rhythmic innovations as the work of its soloists.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The after-hours club provided a social setting for musical experimentation that the commercial ballroom could not have supported.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 opens the corrective ('flattens a more interesting continuity'), paragraph 3 concedes bebop's distinctiveness and then reasserts the continuity thesis and its implication for understanding swing. B captures both the concession and the main thesis.
explanations.A: Reverses the author: the passage affirms continuity, not unprecedentedness.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Too narrow — fixates on the careers of two musicians.
explanations.D: Too narrow — Jo Jones is mentioned only as one example.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement from paragraph 3; a concession, not the thesis.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following harmonic devices had been explored within big bands of the late 1930s before becoming a bebop signature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Modal improvisation over static harmonies sustained for many measures

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tritone substitutions and the extension of chords to include the ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth

choices.label: C
choices.text: Twelve-tone rows distributed across the soloist and rhythm section

choices.label: D
choices.text: Atonal passages in which no underlying key could be identified

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spontaneous collective improvisation in the manner of early New Orleans jazz

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 lists 'tritone replacements, chromatic ii–V interpolations, the extension of chords to include the ninth, eleventh, and thirteenth' as devices 'quietly explored by pianists and arrangers within the big bands of the late 1930s.'
explanations.A: Modal improvisation is not mentioned; it belongs to a later jazz development.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Twelve-tone writing is not mentioned.
explanations.D: The passage never describes bebop as atonal.
explanations.E: The passage does not address New Orleans collective improvisation.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the standard "revolt" narrative of bebop's origins is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: total rejection of a story with no basis in the historical record

choices.label: B
choices.text: admiration for its dramatic framing of a mid-century cultural break

choices.label: C
choices.text: partial acceptance combined with the judgment that the narrative oversimplifies bebop's relationship to swing

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference, since the revolt narrative concerns matters outside the author's subject

choices.label: E
choices.text: wholehearted endorsement, provided the narrative is supplemented with attention to the after-hours club

explanations.correct: The author writes 'there is something to the revolt narrative, but it flattens a more interesting continuity.' That is partial acceptance plus the complaint of oversimplification — exactly C.
explanations.A: Overstated negativity: the author says the narrative has 'something to' it.
explanations.B: Wrong feature: the author does not praise its dramatic framing.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Opposite tone: the author is plainly engaged with the narrative.
explanations.E: Overstated positivity: the author qualifies, not endorses.

questions.questionStem: The author mentions that "Parker's first professional experiences were in territory bands" and that "Gillespie arranged for Cab Calloway" primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: establish the personal credentials of the two musicians within the professional jazz world

choices.label: B
choices.text: support the claim that the harmonic vocabulary of bebop had been accessible inside the big bands in which its leading figures trained

choices.label: C
choices.text: contrast Parker's and Gillespie's career paths with those of later bebop musicians

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why bebop ultimately appealed more to listeners than to dancers

choices.label: E
choices.text: concede that the revolt narrative has more empirical support than the author acknowledges elsewhere

explanations.correct: The biographical items appear in the final paragraph after the claim that 'the big bands were laboratories in which the material of the new music was being assembled.' They are offered as evidence that the beboppers' own training placed them in those laboratories.
explanations.A: Accurate content, wrong function: the citations are made to support a thesis about musical continuity, not to vouch for credentials.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: No contrast with later bebop musicians is drawn.
explanations.D: The listener/dancer distinction appears in paragraph 1, not here.
explanations.E: The items are offered as evidence against the revolt narrative's sufficiency, not for it.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following statements about the swing era as commonly remembered?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It has been unfairly treated as bland commerce whose best features had to be rescued by bebop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its surviving recordings display the same tempos and melodic contours as early bebop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is universally regarded by historians as the true origin of modern jazz harmony.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its arrangements were largely written by the soloists who would later become beboppers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its commercial success has obscured the contribution of individual big-band leaders.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says the era 'is too often remembered as an age of bland commerce whose best features bebop had to rescue,' and the author treats this memory as misleading. That warrants the inference in A: the treatment has been unfair.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Contradicts paragraph 3's explicit contrast of swing and bebop tempos and melodic contours.
explanations.C: Overreach: the passage does not claim universal scholarly regard.
explanations.D: The passage mentions Gillespie arranging for Calloway but does not generalize.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the passage does not discuss the memory of individual band leaders.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations is most closely analogous to the relationship between bebop and the big bands as the passage describes it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A translator renders a foreign novel into English for the first time, giving its themes a readership they previously lacked.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A chamber ensemble performs a nineteenth-century symphony using period instruments, exposing timbres that modern orchestras tend to smooth over.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A rival political party emerges that rejects the policies of the governing party and proposes new ones built on unrelated principles.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A novelist invents a new genre by abandoning the conventions of every preceding literary tradition.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A company replaces its previous product line with goods manufactured in another country using different materials.

explanations.correct: The passage says bebop did not invent its devices but 'exposed' them — 'made audible the harmonic machinery that swing arrangements had kept buried under sectional voicings.' A chamber ensemble exposing timbres that modern orchestras smooth over instantiates the same mechanism: not invention, but foregrounding something already present.
explanations.A: Surface similarity (arts context) but wrong mechanism: translation makes material newly available, not audibly re-foregrounded from within the same tradition.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Matches the revolt narrative the author rejects: 'unrelated principles' is the wrong relation.
explanations.D: Same error as C in its extreme form: invention from nothing, the very view the passage opposes.
explanations.E: Substitution of different materials, not foregrounding of material already present.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that the author would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No musical style can ever be called genuinely innovative, since each merely foregrounds what preceded it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bebop's reduction of ensemble size played a role in making the music's harmonic content more perceptible than it had been in swing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The commercial demands of the ballroom prevented any harmonic experimentation within the big bands of the late 1930s.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historians who describe bebop as difficult have generally exaggerated the technical demands it placed on performers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The rhythmic innovations of bebop owed nothing to drummers who had worked in dance-band settings.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 says that 'by thinning the ensemble to a quintet and foregrounding the soloist,' the beboppers 'made audible the harmonic machinery that swing arrangements had kept buried.' B is a hedged paraphrase of this causal link.
explanations.A: Too strong: the passage allows that bebop was genuinely distinctive in tempo, melodic line, and social setting.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Reverses the passage's claim: the big bands were the laboratories where the experimentation took place.
explanations.D: Out of scope and contrary to the passage's own characterization of bebop as 'playable only by virtuosos.'
explanations.E: Contradicts the passage's explicit credit to Jo Jones and the dance-band drumming tradition.

rc.passage:
The eighteenth-century career of the sublime is often narrated as a tidy succession in which Edmund Burke's physiological account of terror yielded, after half a century, to Immanuel Kant's austerely cognitive one; Friedrich Schiller is then sometimes appended as a postscript who domesticated Kant's doctrine for a more recognizably moral audience. The narrative has the virtue of simplicity, but its simplicity flatters our habit of reading aesthetic history as a progression from body to mind. A closer look at the arguments themselves suggests that the three thinkers differ less over whether the sublime is bodily or cognitive than over what, in the moment of sublime apprehension, a subject has actually done.

For Burke, what the subject has done is to register, at some remove from genuine peril, the approach of an object too vast or too threatening to be possessed in perception; the tension of nerve and sinew that ensues is not incidental but constitutive, and any account that strips it away mistakes a sign for its cause. Kant's celebrated rewriting of this view appears, on first reading, to dismiss Burke's physiology outright. Yet Kant's own account turns on a parallel insufficiency, this time within the faculties themselves: imagination fails to render an overwhelming magnitude or force as a single intuition, and reason, registering that failure, seizes on it as evidence of its own supersensible vocation. The feeling of the sublime is the feeling of this two-step — defeat followed by discovery — and while it is not the tremor of a body in the presence of a threat, it is no less a report on a process the subject has undergone.

Schiller's contribution, often read as a watering-down, is in fact the most radical of the three. For Schiller the sublime is not primarily a response to an object at all but a rehearsal the subject undertakes against the conditions of its own finitude. The soul that has contemplated the storm at sea or the ruin of empires has practiced, in miniature, standing free of what would otherwise coerce it; the aesthetic feeling is prospective rather than retrospective, a preparation rather than a report. What looks like Kantian moralization is in fact a relocation of the sublime's center of gravity from event to exercise.

It would be a mistake, then, to read these three as successive refinements of a single doctrine. Each identifies a different site — the sentient body, the cognitive faculties, the ethical will in training — at which the sublime is said to occur. The question each is answering is not the same, even when the examples adduced (the storm, the mountain, the conflagration) happen to coincide. That the tradition has remembered them as a series owes more, perhaps, to the tidiness of textbooks than to the actual shape of their disagreement.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Although commonly arranged as successive refinements of one doctrine, Burke, Kant, and Schiller in fact locate the sublime in three different aspects of the subject's activity, and reading them as a sequence obscures this disagreement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kant's cognitive rewriting of Burke's physiological account of the sublime has been overstated; the two thinkers agree that the sublime is fundamentally a report on a process the subject has undergone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Schiller's treatment of the sublime, far from being a watering-down of Kant's, is the most philosophically adventurous of the three eighteenth-century treatments and ought to displace the standard narrative.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The standard textbook narrative, in which Burke's physiological sublime yields to Kant's cognitive sublime and then to Schiller's moralized version, captures the shape of an intellectual progression from body to mind.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Because Burke, Kant, and Schiller draw on the same illustrative examples — storms, mountains, and conflagrations — their theories of the sublime cannot in the end be sharply distinguished from one another.

explanations.correct: The passage opens by criticizing the 'tidy succession' narrative and closes by saying the three thinkers identify different sites (sentient body, cognitive faculties, ethical will) and are not answering the same question. A captures both halves.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Picks up a nuance (the author does say Kant's account is not straightforwardly anti-Burkean) and inflates it into the thesis; the author does not claim the two agree on a shared process.
explanations.C: Paragraph-level restatement of the passage's remark about Schiller; the main point is about all three, not the elevation of one.
explanations.D: Endorses the narrative the passage explicitly criticizes as a flattery of our reading habits.
explanations.E: Reverses the author's position: shared examples are precisely what the passage says has misled readers into treating the three as answering the same question.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the received account of the eighteenth-century sublime can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: outright repudiation of its central claims as historically false

choices.label: B
choices.text: skeptical of its tidiness but prepared to grant that it captures something genuine in the thinkers' examples

choices.label: C
choices.text: indifferent, since the author is concerned with the doctrines themselves rather than with how they have been narrated

choices.label: D
choices.text: enthusiasm for its treatment of Kant offset by reservations about its treatment of Schiller

choices.label: E
choices.text: admiration for its pedagogical economy but rejection of the progressivist metaphysics it implies

explanations.correct: The author calls the narrative tidy and traces its appeal to textbook convenience, yet concedes that the thinkers' illustrative examples 'happen to coincide' and never denies that the account captures a pattern; this is skepticism that stops short of repudiation.
explanations.A: Too strong — the author says the received account has the virtue of simplicity and criticizes only what that simplicity obscures.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage is explicitly evaluative of the received narrative, not indifferent.
explanations.D: The author criticizes the received treatment of both Kant (dismissing Burke outright) and Schiller (as a mere postscript); splitting the critique by figure misreads it.
explanations.E: Overstates the author's endorsement — 'admiration for its pedagogical economy' is not in the passage, and the critique is not merely of metaphysics.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A standard narrative is described; its appeal is acknowledged; three positions are examined in turn to show where they actually differ; the narrative's persistence is explained by a consideration other than fidelity to the arguments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A dispute among three thinkers is introduced; each thinker's position is summarized in neutral terms; a fourth position is offered as a synthesis; objections to the synthesis are canvassed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A claim is defended chronologically from its earliest statement to its most recent; objections raised at each stage are rebutted before the narrative advances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Three aesthetic positions are contrasted with a fourth, unnamed position held by the author; the author's position is then shown to reconcile the earlier three.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A historical puzzle is posed; two candidate solutions are weighed against each other; the second is endorsed; its implications for a related tradition are drawn out.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 presents the standard narrative and its appeal; paragraphs 2-3 walk through Burke, Kant, and Schiller to relocate each; paragraph 4 explains the narrative's persistence by appeal to textbook tidiness. A tracks this exactly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: No fourth synthesizing position appears; the author's move is to separate the three, not to synthesize them.
explanations.C: The passage is anti-progressivist; it does not defend a single claim across stages or canvass stage-by-stage rebuttals.
explanations.D: No unnamed fourth position is introduced, and the author does not reconcile the three.
explanations.E: There is no contest between two candidate solutions; the author rejects one narrative without offering a rival historical solution of that form.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would be likely to assent to which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A theorist who sought to combine Burke's physiological account with Schiller's ethical account would be attempting to reconcile positions that answer different questions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because imagination plays a central role in Kant's account, Kant should be read as having accepted, at a deeper level, Burke's claim that the sublime is fundamentally a bodily phenomenon.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Schiller's treatment of the sublime loses plausibility to the extent that the subject's preparatory exercise takes place in the absence of any actual storm or ruin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A satisfactory theory of the sublime must identify, within the subject, a single faculty whose activity is common to all cases in which the sublime is felt.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Burke's insistence on the constitutive role of tension of nerve and sinew is the weakest element of his theory and is better dropped.

explanations.correct: The author insists each of the three locates the sublime in a different 'site' and that they are not answering the same question. A theorist attempting to combine two such accounts would therefore be trying to reconcile answers to distinct questions — exactly what the author says has long been obscured.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reverses the author's point: Kant's imagination-failure is a 'parallel insufficiency' within the faculties, not a concealed endorsement of Burke's bodily view.
explanations.C: Schiller's whole point, as the author presents it, is that the sublime for Schiller is not primarily a response to an object; the author would not treat the absence of the object as diminishing its plausibility.
explanations.D: The passage's organizing claim is that the three theorists locate the sublime at different sites; the author gives no sign of demanding a single faculty across cases.
explanations.E: The author is explicitly sympathetic to Burke's point that the physiological element is constitutive rather than incidental.

questions.questionStem: The author's remark that Schiller's contribution is 'often read as a watering-down' (third paragraph) functions in the passage primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede a point to readers who would deny that Schiller belongs in a discussion of the sublime at all

choices.label: B
choices.text: introduce a received impression of Schiller that the author then overturns in order to show how radically Schiller relocates the sublime

choices.label: C
choices.text: identify the chief weakness of Schiller's account and explain why Kant's treatment is to be preferred

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate the 'progression from body to mind' that the author endorses as the best way of organizing the tradition

choices.label: E
choices.text: contrast Schiller's approach with Burke's in order to argue that Schiller recovers what Kant had abandoned

explanations.correct: The clause is set up in order to be reversed: the author says Schiller is 'in fact the most radical of the three,' and the sentence then explains why. Its function is to introduce a received view the author rebuts.
explanations.A: No such denial is at issue; the author treats Schiller's membership in the tradition as given.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not prefer Kant to Schiller; he argues that the two are not even answering the same question.
explanations.D: The 'progression from body to mind' is described as the flattering habit the author criticizes, not as his own organizing principle.
explanations.E: The sentence makes no contrast with Burke and advances no recovery claim; the contrast in the sentence is between the received reading of Schiller and the author's.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following scenarios most closely illustrates the account of the sublime that the passage attributes to Schiller?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hiker trembles at the sight of an approaching thunderstorm and afterward records the physiological sensations that the storm produced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A philosopher, confronted with the night sky, notes that imagination fails to represent its extent and infers from this failure the supersensible scope of reason.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A novice climber deliberately contemplates the ruin of an ancient fortress in order to strengthen, against future adversity, her capacity to remain unshaken by loss.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A historian catalogues the conflagrations of several cities and argues that their similarity shows a single underlying aesthetic principle at work.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A painter selects a mountain scene for its visual drama and paints it in a way designed to produce in the viewer a nervous apprehension of scale.

explanations.correct: Schiller's sublime, on the passage's reading, is a prospective rehearsal against finitude — the subject practices standing free of what would otherwise coerce her. The climber contemplating the ruin in order to strengthen herself against future adversity matches that mechanism exactly.
explanations.A: Reports a physiological response after the fact — this is Burke's account, not Schiller's.
explanations.B: Tracks Kant's two-step of imagination-failure and reason's self-discovery, not Schiller's prospective exercise.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Describes a historian's empirical comparison rather than an exercise undertaken by the subject against her own finitude.
explanations.E: Focuses on producing an apprehension in a viewer — again closer to Burke's physiological framing than to Schiller's preparatory exercise.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's claim that Burke, Kant, and Schiller are not answering the same question?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Schiller's lectures, now lost, reportedly acknowledged Burke's physiological description as a special case of a more general account that Schiller himself developed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kant's correspondence with colleagues shows that he was aware of Burke's treatise in its German translation and approved of its examples.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A close comparison of the three theorists' definitions reveals that each, despite differences in vocabulary, defines the sublime as a specific modification of a single faculty of the subject and addresses the identical question of what that modification is.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eighteenth-century readers typically encountered the three texts in the order in which they were written, and commentators of the period already treated them as a developmental sequence.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The examples of storms, mountains, and conflagrations that appear in all three accounts were drawn from a shared stock of illustrations circulated in contemporary rhetorical handbooks.

explanations.correct: The author's claim is that each theorist locates the sublime at a distinct site and that the question each is answering is not the same. A demonstration that all three in fact define the sublime as a modification of a single faculty and are addressing the identical question would undermine that claim directly.
explanations.A: A concession by Schiller that Burke's account is a special case of his own would support, not undermine, the author's picture of divergent questions subsuming Burke under Schiller.
explanations.B: Kant's awareness of and approval of Burke's examples is consistent with the author's view that the shared examples have misled readers about the shape of the disagreement.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author already acknowledges that the tradition has remembered the three as a series; contemporary commentators doing the same is not new evidence against his diagnosis.
explanations.E: Provides a further explanation of why the examples overlap — consistent with, not a threat to, the author's position that shared examples mask differing questions.

rc.passage:
To speak of the structuralist revolution in literary study is already to concede a framing that the movement's most careful practitioners would have resisted. Roland Barthes, in his earlier phase, is sometimes enrolled as the movement's great popularizer; Tzvetan Todorov, as its taxonomist of narrative forms; Gérard Genette, as its most austere theorist of narrative discourse. Each was, at one time or another, willing to describe his project as the extension to literature of the method Ferdinand de Saussure had proposed for language. Yet to arrange these three in a single column under the heading "structuralism" is to understate the differences in what each thought such an extension would require, and in what each believed it could deliver.

Todorov's early grammars of narrative sought what he called the "poetics" of the literary text — not a reading of any particular work but a specification of the underlying system of possibilities from which particular works are drawn. He pursued this with a confidence, later muted, that the system could in principle be fully described, and that any sufficiently careful reader could recover it from the works themselves. Genette's undertaking was more guarded. His categories of order, duration, and frequency were designed to register what a narrative does, but he treated his own apparatus as a descriptive instrument rather than as a discovery about narrative in general, and he repeatedly warned against confusing the map he was drawing with a territory that could exist independently of it. Barthes, by contrast, had by the late 1960s grown suspicious of the very project of a general poetics; his celebrated argument that the text is a "tissue of quotations" rather than the expression of a single intending author pushed against the structuralist confidence that literary works could be referred to an underlying system at all.

It is tempting to read Barthes's later turn as simply anti-structuralist and therefore as a repudiation of Todorov and Genette alike. The temptation should be resisted. Barthes continued to hold — and this is easy to miss — that literary works participate in codes, conventions, and shared stocks of meaning; his quarrel was not with the thought that such codes are at work, but with the thought that a critic's listing of them exhausts what criticism can say. Todorov's and Genette's projects, on his mature view, were not wrong so much as terminal: they described one layer of the text and then stopped where the harder work begins.

Seen this way, the standard narrative — structuralism rises with Todorov, is refined by Genette, and is dismantled by Barthes — captures the chronology but misrepresents the disagreement. All three accepted that literature operates through codes; they parted over whether recovering the codes constitutes the critic's work, supplements it, or ends only where the critic's work properly begins.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The standard narrative that structuralism rose with Todorov, was refined by Genette, and was dismantled by Barthes is chronologically accurate, and its account of the theoretical relations among the three is broadly correct as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Barthes's later work, properly understood, marks a full repudiation of the structuralist projects of Todorov and Genette, whose methods Barthes's argument for the text as a tissue of quotations makes obsolete.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Although Todorov, Genette, and Barthes are often grouped together as structuralists who broke in stages from a common project, their disagreement is better understood as concerning the status of the critic's work with respect to the codes that organize literary texts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Genette's cautious treatment of his descriptive apparatus as a map rather than a territory represents the most defensible version of the structuralist program and ought to displace the more ambitious account pursued by Todorov.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The extension of Saussure's linguistic method to literature, undertaken in different ways by Todorov, Genette, and Barthes, ultimately failed because the structuralist assumption of an underlying system of literary possibilities cannot be sustained.

explanations.correct: The passage opens by resisting a uniform 'structuralism' label, contrasts the three thinkers' positions on whether the critic's work is constituted by, supplements, or only begins after the recovery of codes, and closes by saying the standard narrative misrepresents the disagreement. C integrates all three strands.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly says the standard narrative misrepresents the disagreement, even while granting the chronology.
explanations.B: The passage warns explicitly against reading Barthes's later turn as a simple repudiation of Todorov and Genette.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Paragraph-level restatement: the passage treats Genette's caution sympathetically but does not argue he should displace Todorov.
explanations.E: Too strong — the author never claims structuralism 'failed,' and all three thinkers are credited with identifying something real about codes in literary texts.
