explanations.B: Reverses the author: he criticizes judicial declaration and treats inductive methods as the alternative whose abandonment is the problem.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too strong — the author concedes that certain prohibitions command unusual assent and does not deny a difference in degree.
explanations.E: The author's critique is structural, not a matter of better training; he says the doctrine has not supplied a stable account.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the 2011 Isuria advisory opinion in the second paragraph functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: offer an illustrative case in which the standard inductive method for identifying customary norms was properly applied

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that the tribunal's methodology collapsed into self-reference, thereby supporting the author's broader claim that peremptory norms have been charted from within the juridical order rather than discovered outside it

choices.label: C
choices.text: concede that even a flawed identification of a peremptory norm is preferable to no identification at all

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast the Isuria court's approach with the more rigorous approach of the International Law Commission's 1966 draft articles

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that the prohibition of enforced disappearance has not in fact achieved the degree of assent that genocide and slavery command

explanations.correct: The second paragraph is doing work for the metaphor introduced at the end of paragraph 1: the 'bedrock charted from above.' The thin state practice, the circular treaty-body citations, and the court's own former members as publicists together show self-reference, which is what the thesis needs to be demonstrated.
explanations.A: Reverses the function: the example is offered as a failure of inductive method, not a success.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not concede this; he denies the identification does the work claimed.
explanations.D: The ILC draft is mentioned only as the origin of the enthusiasm the author is criticizing; no rigor contrast is developed.
explanations.E: The author is silent on whether the specific prohibition has wide assent; his critique is about the method of identification, not the substantive standing of this norm.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following features of the 2011 Isuria advisory opinion's reasoning did the author identify as problematic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It relied on the writings of publicists who were not themselves former members of the tribunal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It refused to consult the pronouncements of treaty bodies on the question of enforced disappearance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It treated the opinio juris of judges as evidence of the opinio juris of states without pressing the distinction between the two.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It departed from the International Law Commission's 1966 draft articles in its definition of peremptory status.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It identified a peremptory norm without also surveying the practice of states.

explanations.correct: The author writes that 'whether that culmination reflects opinio juris in the traditional sense — a belief among states that they are legally bound — or merely the opinio juris of the judges, is a question the opinion conspicuously declines to press.' C paraphrases exactly that complaint.
explanations.A: Inverts the detail: the author complains that the publicists were predominantly the court's former members.
explanations.B: Wrong sentence: the author notes that treaty-body pronouncements were consulted but were largely circular.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author does not contrast the opinion with the 1966 draft articles on the definition of peremptory status.
explanations.E: The author says state practice was catalogued but thin, not that no survey was conducted.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the structural problem the author identifies with the current doctrine of jus cogens?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A scientific academy declares a novel result to be an established fact by surveying journal articles, most of which were authored by members of the academy and which chiefly cite one another.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A national supreme court strikes down a statute as unconstitutional by applying a long-settled textual canon of interpretation to the statute's language.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A professional association adopts a new ethical rule after a public comment period in which a majority of practitioners endorsed the rule in writing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A regulatory agency issues a guidance document interpreting a statute the agency itself administers, basing the interpretation on the statute's legislative history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A historian concludes that a disputed battle occurred on a particular date by triangulating among three independent archival sources maintained by different polities.

explanations.correct: The load-bearing structure the author identifies is self-reference masquerading as external discovery: the bedrock 'charted almost entirely from above,' with the court's own former members as publicists and treaty bodies citing one another. A reproduces that exact structure — a body declaring a truth by surveying sources that derive from itself and cite one another.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: A shares the surface feature of authoritative pronouncement but instantiates a different mechanism: application of an established canon to text, not self-referential identification of a novel norm.
explanations.C: The public-comment mechanism introduces an external constituency rather than instantiating self-reference.
explanations.D: Administrative interpretation grounded in legislative history is not self-reference in the relevant sense; the agency is interpreting an externally given text.
explanations.E: Triangulation among three independent polities is precisely the external, inductive method the author says jus cogens doctrine lacks.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's argument that the current doctrine of jus cogens fails to furnish an external check on state conduct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A comprehensive empirical study demonstrates that, in the decade following the Isuria opinion, states whose practice the tribunal had not surveyed nevertheless altered their conduct to conform with the tribunal's identification of the peremptory norm, citing the tribunal's reasoning in their own official pronouncements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several commentators have objected to the Isuria opinion on the ground that its list of publicists included members who had served on the tribunal in earlier decades.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other regional human-rights courts have issued advisory opinions identifying peremptory norms using methodologies similar to that of the Isuria tribunal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prohibitions of genocide and aggressive war were recognized as peremptory norms before the International Law Commission's 1966 draft articles.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A minority of states have rejected the Isuria opinion outright and have denied that the prohibition of enforced disappearance has peremptory status.

explanations.correct: The author's argument is that jus cogens lacks an external check because its identification is internal to the juridical order. If states not surveyed by the tribunal nevertheless conform their conduct to the tribunal's identification and cite the tribunal's reasoning as authority, then the identification does in practice operate on state conduct externally — which is the very function the author denies it performs. That most directly undermines the author's claim.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Echoes the author's own observation about the publicists rather than contradicting his structural critique.
explanations.C: Extends the pattern the author criticizes to other tribunals; it reinforces rather than undermines his diagnosis.
explanations.D: Says nothing about the method of identification or the external-check function.
explanations.E: Consistent with the author's picture: if a minority of states reject the norm outright, the supposed peremptory character does not constrain them, which cuts with rather than against the author.

rc.passage:
For nearly four decades, the administrative courts of the Republic of Caltrana have been governed by what practitioners call the Two-Step: when an agency's interpretation of a statute it administers is challenged, the court asks first whether the statute is ambiguous, and, if it is, defers to any reasonable agency reading. The doctrine was announced in a 1987 case concerning a rulemaking on flue-gas emissions and has since become a fixture of the country's public law. What has gone insufficiently noticed, however, is that the Two-Step has quietly accreted a third step — one the court has never acknowledged — that now does much of the actual work.

The accretion began, on the better reading of the cases, with a 2002 dispute over pharmaceutical labeling. The reviewing chamber purported to apply the Two-Step but prefaced its analysis with the observation that the agency's interpretation must be consistent with the statute's "animating purpose." Later opinions have elaborated this preface into a threshold inquiry: before asking whether the statute is ambiguous, the court now asks whether the agency's reading sits comfortably within what the chamber calls the statute's "ordered scheme." Only interpretations that pass this unstated step proceed to the conventional ambiguity analysis. In effect, the court has reserved to itself a prior power to pronounce on statutory coherence — a power that the original doctrine deliberately withheld from reviewing courts, precisely because coherence judgments are sensitive to the same policy considerations that the doctrine wished to leave to the agency.

Defenders of the new approach describe it as an obvious refinement: no one, they say, would wish courts to defer to readings that are in tension with the statute's evident design. The point is not without force. Yet the defense misstates what the original doctrine required. Under the 1987 formulation, a reading in tension with statutory design would ordinarily fail at step two as unreasonable; the court had no occasion to reach that question until ambiguity had been established. The effect of inserting a coherence inquiry at the threshold is not to catch interpretations the old doctrine would have missed but to permit the court to reject interpretations without undertaking the ambiguity analysis that, by its own logic, should precede any such rejection.

Whether this development represents a welcome correction or a doctrinal drift will depend, one supposes, on how much faith one has in the reviewing courts' ability to distinguish coherence from policy preference. The present author is not sanguine. The doctrine's chief virtue, when first announced, was its discipline; the accreted third step, by inviting courts to identify statutory design without the constraint of ambiguity analysis, has begun to dissolve that discipline while continuing to invoke its name.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Caltranan administrative courts have grafted an unacknowledged coherence inquiry onto the Two-Step, and the inquiry has undermined the discipline that the original doctrine was designed to supply.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Defenders of the Caltranan courts' recent approach are correct that no agency interpretation in tension with statutory design should receive deference.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 1987 Two-Step doctrine has been overtaken by more recent decisions that explicitly repudiate its premises.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reviewing courts are institutionally incapable of distinguishing judgments of statutory coherence from judgments of policy preference.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The 2002 dispute over pharmaceutical labeling should be regarded as the moment when the Two-Step doctrine ceased to be good law in Caltrana.

explanations.correct: The passage identifies a quiet accretion of a third step, traces it to the 2002 pharmaceutical case, argues that its defenders misstate the original doctrine, and closes by judging that the accretion has begun to dissolve the discipline the original doctrine was designed to supply. A captures both the descriptive and evaluative strands.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Restates the defenders' view, which the author treats as partly forceful but ultimately mistaken.
explanations.C: Too strong — the courts continue to invoke the Two-Step; the author's complaint is precisely that they do so while modifying it in substance.
explanations.D: A proposition the author's concluding skepticism is consistent with but does not establish as the main claim; the main claim is doctrinal, not epistemic-general.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement fixating on the 2002 case.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An established doctrine is described; an unacknowledged modification is identified and traced to a specific case; a defense of the modification is presented and rebutted; the author offers a skeptical concluding assessment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two rival interpretations of a statute are presented; the arguments for each are surveyed; the author concludes that the second is more faithful to the statute's design.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A doctrine is described; its historical origins are traced; an analogous doctrine in a foreign jurisdiction is introduced as a superior model; the two are compared.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A judicial decision is summarized; its reasoning is criticized as internally inconsistent; a proposed correction is offered; the correction is shown to resolve the doctrinal difficulty.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A practice is defended against a familiar objection; the objection is shown to rest on a misunderstanding; the defense is extended to a range of adjacent practices.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 describes the Two-Step and flags the accreted third step; paragraph 2 traces the accretion to the 2002 pharmaceutical case and elaborates the unstated coherence inquiry; paragraph 3 presents the defenders' view and rebuts it; paragraph 4 offers the author's skeptical concluding assessment. A maps this sequence correctly.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The passage is about a doctrine's evolution, not a choice between two statutory interpretations.
explanations.C: No foreign-jurisdiction analogue is introduced.
explanations.D: The author does not propose a correction that resolves the difficulty; he diagnoses a drift.
explanations.E: Reverses the posture: a defense is presented and rebutted, not extended.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would accept which one of the following claims about the 1987 Two-Step as originally formulated?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It permitted reviewing courts to reject an agency interpretation on the ground of statutory incoherence only after a finding that the statute was ambiguous.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It required agencies to adopt interpretations consistent with a statute's animating purpose as determined by the reviewing court in advance of any deference.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It made no provision for reviewing courts to reject unreasonable agency interpretations at any stage of the analysis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It was formulated with an implicit understanding that future courts would supplement it with a threshold coherence inquiry.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It applied only to rulemakings concerning environmental emissions and did not govern agency interpretations in other areas.

explanations.correct: The author says that under the 1987 formulation, a reading in tension with statutory design would ordinarily fail at step two as unreasonable, and that the court had no occasion to reach that question until ambiguity had been established. A restates that commitment: rejection on coherence grounds occurred only after a finding of ambiguity.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Describes the accreted third step, which the author treats as a departure from, not a feature of, the 1987 doctrine.
explanations.C: Reverses the author, who explicitly says unreasonable interpretations could be rejected at step two.
explanations.D: The author characterizes the third step as unacknowledged and as 'doctrinal drift,' not as an anticipated supplement.
explanations.E: Outside scope — the author calls the doctrine 'a fixture of the country's public law,' not confined to emissions.

questions.questionStem: The author's observation in the third paragraph that the defenders' point is "not without force" functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede the plausibility of the defense before arguing that it rests on a mischaracterization of what the original doctrine required

choices.label: B
choices.text: introduce a counterexample that the author will ultimately treat as decisive against the original doctrine

choices.label: C
choices.text: signal the author's agreement with the defenders and preface the rejection of his earlier critique of the accreted third step

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that the coherence inquiry, although unacknowledged, has been applied in a manner consistent with the 1987 formulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: indicate that the author considers the defenders' position more persuasive than his own and is preparing to abandon his earlier diagnosis

explanations.correct: The phrase is the hinge of a classic concede-then-rebut move. The author grants that no one would wish courts to defer to readings in tension with statutory design, then uses the next two sentences to argue that the original doctrine already handled such readings at step two, so the refinement is not what the defenders claim it is.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The author does not treat the defenders' point as decisive against the original doctrine; he treats it as a concession he will absorb and then turn.
explanations.C: Reverses the passage: the author does not reject his earlier critique; he reinforces it.
explanations.D: The author's rebuttal denies that the third step is consistent with the original formulation.
explanations.E: Out of register — the author's closing 'not sanguine' shows he does not abandon his diagnosis.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the reviewing courts' ability to distinguish judgments of statutory coherence from judgments of policy preference can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: confident that the courts possess the requisite capacity and exercise it reliably

choices.label: B
choices.text: guardedly doubtful, implying that the courts are not well positioned to maintain the distinction in the absence of the constraint that ambiguity analysis formerly provided

choices.label: C
choices.text: entirely agnostic, regarding the question as unanswerable on the evidence the passage supplies

choices.label: D
choices.text: dismissive, denying that the distinction itself is coherent

choices.label: E
choices.text: openly contemptuous of the courts' institutional competence in administrative matters generally

explanations.correct: The author writes 'the present author is not sanguine,' and explains that the accreted third step has begun to 'dissolve' the doctrine's discipline by inviting courts to identify statutory design 'without the constraint of ambiguity analysis.' That is guarded doubt tied to a specific structural cause — exactly B.
explanations.A: Reverses the closing sentence.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author reaches a judgment; he is not agnostic.
explanations.D: He does not deny that the distinction is coherent; he doubts that the courts will maintain it in practice.
explanations.E: Out of register — 'not sanguine' is measured, not contemptuous; the author addresses a specific doctrinal context, not the courts' general competence.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following judicial practices, if adopted in another area of law, would most closely conform to the structural development the author identifies in the Caltranan administrative courts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A court reviewing a contract dispute begins to ask, before the conventional inquiry into whether the contract language is ambiguous, whether the proposed construction is consistent with the contract's general commercial design, and rejects constructions that fail that threshold without reaching the ambiguity inquiry.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A court reviewing a criminal sentence applies a deferential standard to the trial court's findings of fact but reviews legal conclusions de novo.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A court hearing a constitutional challenge subjects the challenged statute to a higher standard of review when it implicates a fundamental right than when it does not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A court presiding over a jury trial instructs the jury to disregard evidence that the court has ruled inadmissible under established rules.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A court in a tort action declines to reach the question of damages until it has determined that the defendant is liable.

explanations.correct: The load-bearing structure is the insertion of an unacknowledged threshold inquiry into 'design' or 'scheme' before the conventional ambiguity analysis, which permits the court to reject interpretations without reaching the analysis that by its own logic should precede such rejection. A reproduces that exact structure in the contract-law setting.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Different standards for different issues is orthogonal to the threshold-inquiry mechanism the author is describing.
explanations.C: Tiered scrutiny of statutes is not a hidden threshold; it is an openly applied doctrine selecting the level of review.
explanations.D: Evidentiary rulings are not threshold interpretive inquiries of the kind at issue.
explanations.E: Surface similarity — issue-ordering — but the liability-before-damages order is the conventional sequence that has always been required, not an accreted threshold that displaces an earlier analytic step.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would regard which one of the following hypothetical judicial practices as consistent with the original 1987 doctrine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chamber finds that the statute at issue is ambiguous, considers the agency's reading, and rejects that reading as unreasonable because it cannot be squared with the statute's design.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A chamber rejects the agency's reading at the threshold on the ground that the reading does not sit comfortably within the statute's ordered scheme.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A chamber defers to the agency's reading without considering whether the statute is ambiguous, on the ground that agencies generally possess greater expertise than courts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A chamber refuses to apply the Two-Step to interpretations of statutes that were enacted before the 1987 decision.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A chamber treats its own prior characterizations of a statute's animating purpose as binding in all future cases interpreting that statute.

explanations.correct: The author writes that under the 1987 formulation, a reading in tension with statutory design would ordinarily fail at step two as unreasonable — precisely what the chamber in A does, by first finding ambiguity and then rejecting the agency's reading as unreasonable on design grounds.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Describes the accreted third step the author is criticizing, not the original doctrine.
explanations.C: Skips the ambiguity analysis altogether and so is not the original doctrine either.
explanations.D: The passage gives no indication that the 1987 doctrine was limited to post-1987 statutes.
explanations.E: The passage says nothing to support binding-precedent status for a chamber's purpose-characterizations across future cases.

rc.passage:
A moon or planet is said to be tidally locked when it rotates on its axis in exactly the time it takes to complete one orbit around its primary, with the result that it keeps the same face turned toward that body at all times. The Earth's Moon is the familiar example: the side we see from Earth is always the same side, and the so-called far side was first photographed only in 1959, by a Soviet spacecraft that passed behind it. Tidal locking is not an exotic accident; it is the predictable endpoint of a process that operates, to some degree, on every orbiting pair.

The mechanism is straightforward. Any body that is not perfectly rigid deforms slightly in response to the gravitational pull of its neighbor, bulging toward the neighbor and, by a more subtle effect, on the side facing away as well. If the deforming body rotates faster than it orbits, each bulge is carried ahead of the line connecting the two centers before the body can reshape itself, and the neighbor's gravity then pulls back on the leading bulge. This drag slowly removes rotational energy. Over time, the spin rate falls until it matches the orbital period, at which point the bulges sit on the line between the two centers and the braking torque disappears.

How long this takes depends strongly on a few variables. Smaller separations make the bulges larger and the braking more severe, so close-in bodies lock first. Bodies with less internal stiffness also lock faster, because they deform more readily and generate larger bulges in response to the same pull. For the Earth-Moon system, calculations indicate that the Moon became locked within roughly a few tens of millions of years, a brief interval on a solar-system timescale. Earth itself is being slowed by the Moon, but the process is far slower because Earth is much more massive, and full locking will not occur before the Sun's eventual expansion overtakes the system.

One implication of the mechanism is often overlooked. Because tidal locking removes rotational energy, a tidally locked body has generally lost the internal circulation that a faster spin would have driven, and its climate, if it has an atmosphere, becomes organized around a permanent day side and a permanent night side rather than around a daily cycle. Astronomers studying planets that orbit close to small, cool stars now routinely assume such planets are locked, and recent models of their atmospheres take the resulting asymmetry as a starting point rather than a complication.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tidal locking is a predictable physical process in which a rotating body's spin is gradually brought into step with its orbital period, and its effects extend to the climates of locked planets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the Moon became tidally locked to Earth within a few tens of millions of years, tidal locking must be regarded as an unusually rapid astronomical process.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Planets that orbit close to small, cool stars are almost certainly tidally locked and therefore have atmospheres organized around a permanent day side and a permanent night side.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The far side of the Moon was unknown to scientists until a Soviet spacecraft photographed it in 1959, demonstrating how little had been known about tidal locking at that time.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tidal locking results from the deformation of orbiting bodies and is impossible in any system whose members are perfectly rigid.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces locking as the endpoint of a general process; paragraphs 2 and 3 explain the mechanism and how quickly it operates; paragraph 4 extends the picture to climate on locked planets. Choice A captures both the mechanism and its broader implication.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Paragraph-restatement: captures a specific estimate from paragraph 3, not the overall thesis.
explanations.C: Too narrow: the close-in-exoplanet case is one implication in the last paragraph, not the main point.
explanations.D: Too narrow / illustrative-example: the 1959 photograph is a supporting detail in paragraph 1.
explanations.E: Too-strong: the passage says no body is perfectly rigid but does not claim locking would be impossible in a purely hypothetical rigid pair as its main thesis.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A phenomenon is defined with an example, its mechanism is explained, the variables governing its rate are identified, and a broader implication is drawn.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing accounts of a phenomenon are described, and evidence is offered that supports the second over the first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historical puzzle is introduced, an early hypothesis is rejected, and a newer hypothesis is defended.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An observation is reported, its sources of uncertainty are catalogued, and the reader is warned against overinterpreting it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A general principle is stated, illustrated with a counterexample, and then abandoned in favor of a more modest claim.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 defines tidal locking and gives the Moon as the canonical case; paragraph 2 explains the bulge-and-drag mechanism; paragraph 3 identifies the variables that control how fast locking occurs; paragraph 4 draws the climate implication.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Mis-sequencing: no competing accounts are set against one another.
explanations.C: Plausible-but-unused: no hypothesis is rejected.
explanations.D: Wrong grain / wrong tone: the passage is explanatory, not a catalogue of uncertainties.
explanations.E: Opposite: the principle is not abandoned; it is extended in the final paragraph.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the rotational braking torque responsible for tidal locking disappears when

choices.label: A
choices.text: the deforming body has become perfectly rigid and can no longer form bulges.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the two bodies have drifted far enough apart that their mutual gravitational pull is negligible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the deforming body's spin rate has fallen into step with its orbital period, so that its bulges lie on the line connecting the two centers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the orbital period of the pair has become long enough that the bulges can no longer be carried ahead of the connecting line.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the central body has itself begun to rotate at the same rate as its companion.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that as the spin rate falls to match the orbital period, 'the bulges sit on the line between the two centers and the braking torque disappears.'
explanations.A: Altered premise: the passage denies that any real body is perfectly rigid; this is not what ends the torque.
explanations.B: Outside scope: the passage does not invoke orbital separation becoming negligible.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Plausible-world fact: not stated; the relevant comparison is spin versus orbit, not orbital period in isolation.
explanations.E: The passage discusses the central body's rotation only briefly and does not tie the torque's disappearance to it.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that Earth's full tidal locking to the Moon

choices.label: A
choices.text: has effectively already occurred, though the final adjustment remains to be measured.

choices.label: B
choices.text: is proceeding, but will not be completed before the Sun's eventual expansion overtakes the system.

choices.label: C
choices.text: is prevented by Earth's internal circulation, which continually restores its rotational energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: will occur within roughly a few tens of millions of years, on the same timescale as the Moon's locking.

choices.label: E
choices.text: cannot occur because Earth is more massive than the Moon.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says Earth 'is being slowed by the Moon, but the process is far slower... and full locking will not occur before the Sun's eventual expansion overtakes the system.'
explanations.A: The passage says the process is slow, not that it has effectively occurred.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Wrong causation: internal circulation is tied to tidally locked bodies in paragraph 4, not to why Earth has not yet locked.
explanations.D: Wrong figure: the few-tens-of-millions estimate refers to the Moon's locking, not Earth's.
explanations.E: Too-strong: the passage says the process is slow because Earth is more massive, not that locking is impossible.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests which one of the following about two small moons identical in size and composition but orbiting the same planet at different distances?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The more distant moon, other things being equal, will become tidally locked sooner than the closer moon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The closer moon, other things being equal, will become tidally locked sooner than the more distant moon.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither moon will ever become tidally locked unless it has an atmosphere.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moons will become tidally locked at the same time, since composition determines the rate of locking.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tidal locking applies only to moons that are larger than their primary, and so the scenario cannot arise.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says smaller separations produce larger bulges and more severe braking, so 'close-in bodies lock first.' For two otherwise identical moons, the closer one locks sooner.
explanations.A: Direction-reversed: the passage says close-in bodies lock first.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Outside scope: atmospheres are discussed only as a consequence of locking, not as a prerequisite for it.
explanations.D: Ignores separation: composition is only one of several variables the passage identifies.
explanations.E: The passage never restricts locking to moons larger than their primary; the usual case is the reverse.

questions.questionStem: The author's mention of the 1959 Soviet photograph of the far side of the Moon functions in the passage primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate what it means for a body to keep the same face turned toward its primary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: establish that scientific understanding of tidal locking dates only to the late 1950s.

choices.label: C
choices.text: provide historical evidence that contradicts an earlier theory of the Moon's rotation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast human observation of the Moon with observation of exoplanets.

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why tidal locking is a faster process than had previously been assumed.

explanations.correct: The reference comes immediately after the sentence describing how a locked body keeps the same face toward its primary; the photograph is offered to make that abstract definition concrete.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Accurate-content-wrong-function: the passage doesn't use the date to make a claim about when tidal locking began to be understood.
explanations.C: No earlier theory of lunar rotation is under discussion.
explanations.D: Plausible-but-unused: the contrast with exoplanets appears in paragraph 4, not in connection with the 1959 photograph.
explanations.E: Unsupported: the passage does not compare prior and current estimates of locking speed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the mechanism of tidal locking described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A spinning top slows and eventually stops because friction between its tip and the floor removes rotational energy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A flexible rubber ball, repeatedly squeezed out of round as it rolls past a strong magnet, loses speed because each deformation is pulled backward by the magnet.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A ship at anchor rocks with the tide but does not drift, because its anchor chain holds it in place.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A pendulum eventually comes to rest as air resistance steadily removes energy at the bottom of each swing.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A dropped ball bounces lower each time because each collision with the floor dissipates some of its energy as heat.

explanations.correct: The passage's mechanism has three load-bearing parts: (i) a deformable body, (ii) a deformation pulled ahead of where the external pull would like it, and (iii) that external pull dragging the deformation back, which slowly removes energy. B preserves all three.
explanations.A: Surface-similarity: friction slows a rotation, but there is no deformation being pulled back by the external body.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The chain here provides a restoring force, not a braking drag from a misaligned deformation.
explanations.D: Air resistance is undirected drag; there is no deformation carried ahead of an external attractor.
explanations.E: Energy is lost to heat at each collision, but the mechanism is not the misalignment of a deformation relative to an attracting body.

rc.passage:
In many lakes at high latitudes, the sediment that settles on the bottom each year is not uniform but instead forms two thin bands of contrasting color and texture. These paired bands are called varves (a term borrowed from the Swedish word for 'turn' or 'layer'), and where conditions are right they accumulate one pair per year, much as a tree adds one ring per growing season. A careful count of varves in a suitable lake bed can therefore yield a calendar of past years, sometimes reaching back many thousands of seasons.

The formation of a varve depends on the lake's annual rhythm. During the spring melt, streams deliver a burst of suspended sediment, and the coarser particles settle first, forming a relatively pale, sandy layer on the lake bottom. As the water warms and biological activity peaks through summer, finer particles and organic matter remain in suspension. When the lake cools in autumn and, in many cases, freezes over in winter, this finer material finally settles, producing a darker, clay-rich layer above the pale one. A single pair — pale below, dark above — marks one full year.

Not all lakes preserve varves. The record depends on the absence of mixing: if currents, burrowing organisms, or seasonal overturn stir the lake bed, the delicate layers are destroyed. For that reason, well-preserved varves tend to be found in lakes that are deep, cold, and chemically stratified, so that oxygen does not reach the bottom and little lives there to disturb the sediment. A few such lakes have yielded continuous records spanning more than ten thousand years, and in some cases the individual layers can be matched across widely separated basins, suggesting that the sediment supply is responding to a regional, rather than purely local, climate.

Because each varve corresponds to a single year, thickness variations can be read with unusual directness. A thick pale band typically indicates a vigorous spring melt, and a sequence of thick pairs suggests a run of wet or warm years. Geologists combine such readings with other archives — tree rings, ice cores, and pollen records — to reconstruct past climates. Varves do not by themselves settle any large question about long-term climate change, but they offer one of the few records that is annually resolved and directly datable, and for that reason they remain a reference against which other, less precise archives are frequently checked.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Varves, annually paired sediment layers that form in certain undisturbed lakes, provide a directly datable year-by-year archive that is valuable for reconstructing past climates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because varves are disturbed by burrowing organisms and seasonal overturn in most lakes, they can rarely be used to reconstruct past climates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tree rings, ice cores, and pollen records are generally less reliable than varves and have therefore been supplanted by them in reconstructions of past climates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A thick pale band in a varve sequence invariably indicates a year of heavy spring runoff and relatively warm summer temperatures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varves demonstrate that long-term regional climate change has occurred across widely separated lake basins over the past ten thousand years.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 defines varves and their calendar-like nature; paragraphs 2 and 3 explain how they form and why some lakes preserve them; paragraph 4 describes their use in reconstructing past climates. Choice A integrates these strands.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Paragraph-restatement / opposite: paragraph 3 mentions disturbance as a limitation but emphasizes that well-preserved records do exist.
explanations.C: Too strong: the passage says varves are checked against other archives, not that they have supplanted them.
explanations.D: Too narrow / too strong: captures a detail from paragraph 4 and overstates it with 'invariably.'
explanations.E: Opposite of author's hedge: the passage explicitly says varves 'do not by themselves settle any large question about long-term climate change.'

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the use of varves in reconstructing past climates can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of varves as the single most authoritative climate archive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautious approval that acknowledges both their value and their limits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: skeptical dismissal grounded in the fragility of the sedimentary record.

choices.label: D
choices.text: impartial neutrality, neither endorsing nor criticizing their use.

choices.label: E
choices.text: anxious pessimism about the prospects for reliable reconstruction of past climates in general.

explanations.correct: The author describes varves as an unusually direct annual record that remains 'a reference against which other, less precise archives are frequently checked,' while also noting that they 'do not by themselves settle any large question' about long-term climate. That is cautious approval.
explanations.A: Too-strong: the author does not claim varves are the single most authoritative archive.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite-tone: the author treats varves as valuable.
explanations.D: The author's positive evaluation (calling them a reference standard) is explicit.
explanations.E: No anxious or pessimistic language about climate reconstruction appears.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the darker, finer-grained layer of a varve pair is deposited primarily

choices.label: A
choices.text: during the initial burst of spring runoff, when streams are carrying the greatest sediment load.

choices.label: B
choices.text: in late summer, when biological activity in the lake is at its peak.

choices.label: C
choices.text: in autumn and winter, when the lake cools and fine particles and organic matter finally settle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: only in lakes whose bottoms are regularly disturbed by burrowing organisms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: at irregular intervals that do not correspond to any particular season.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 says that when the lake cools in autumn and in many cases freezes in winter, 'this finer material finally settles, producing a darker, clay-rich layer above the pale one.'
explanations.A: Wrong sentence: spring runoff produces the pale, coarser layer.
explanations.B: Wrong sentence: during peak summer activity, the fine material remains in suspension.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Direction-reversed: burrowing organisms destroy varves rather than forming them.
explanations.E: Altered premise: the passage ties each varve to a specific annual cycle.

questions.questionStem: The passage identifies which one of the following as a feature of lakes especially likely to preserve varves?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A warm surface layer that promotes rapid biological activity year-round.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Abundant bottom-dwelling organisms whose burrows mark successive years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chemical stratification that keeps oxygen from reaching the lake bottom.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Frequent seasonal overturn that mixes deep water with surface water.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A shallow basin whose sediment is regularly resuspended by currents.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that well-preserved varves tend to occur in lakes that are 'deep, cold, and chemically stratified, so that oxygen does not reach the bottom and little lives there to disturb the sediment.'
explanations.A: Altered premise: the passage emphasizes cold, stratified lakes rather than warm surface waters.
explanations.B: Opposite: burrowing organisms are said to destroy varves, not preserve them.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Opposite: the passage lists seasonal overturn as a disturbance that destroys varves.
explanations.E: Opposite: resuspension by currents is explicitly destructive of varve layering.

questions.questionStem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that if geologists examining a well-preserved varve sequence find a run of unusually thick pale bands across several consecutive years, they would most likely conclude that during those years

choices.label: A
choices.text: the lake was repeatedly disturbed by burrowing organisms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: spring melt was especially vigorous, delivering more suspended sediment than usual.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the lake experienced exceptionally cold winters that suppressed biological activity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: organic matter made up a larger-than-usual share of the sediment reaching the lake bottom.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the lake's chemical stratification temporarily broke down.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 4 says 'a thick pale band typically indicates a vigorous spring melt, and a sequence of thick pairs suggests a run of wet or warm years.' A run of thick pale bands therefore supports the vigorous-melt inference.
explanations.A: Direction-reversed: burrowing would disturb, not thicken, the layers.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage connects thick pale bands to melt intensity, not to winter biological activity.
explanations.D: Outside scope: organic matter contributes mainly to the darker layer in the passage's model.
explanations.E: Breakdown of stratification would degrade the record, not produce thick pale bands.

questions.questionStem: The author's comparison of varves to tree rings in paragraph 1 serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: give the reader a familiar image of a yearly layered record against which the novel concept of varves can be understood.

choices.label: B
choices.text: suggest that the same biological processes responsible for tree rings also drive the formation of varves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: establish that varves are more reliable than tree rings for reconstructing past climates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: imply that tree rings are too short in record length to be useful for climate research.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that annual layered records should be preferred to any nonlayered archive.

explanations.correct: The comparison appears as varves are introduced, and functions as an orienting analogy: one pair per year, one ring per growing season. It anchors the new idea in a familiar one.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The analogy is structural, not claimed to share biological mechanism.
explanations.C: No such reliability ranking is asserted in paragraph 1; paragraph 4 treats them as complementary.
explanations.D: The passage does not say tree-ring records are too short.
explanations.E: The argumentative claim about preferring layered records is not advanced by the analogy.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the claim that a given lake's sediment record is responding to regional rather than purely local climate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lake is deeper and colder than most neighboring lakes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The thickness pattern of the lake's varves over a several-century interval closely matches the varve-thickness pattern in lakes in distant basins over the same interval.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lake is fed by a single stream whose watershed lies entirely within a few kilometers of the lake.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Individual varve pairs in the lake are unusually thick compared with those in other known varved lakes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The lake's bottom sediments contain abundant organic matter from local aquatic plants.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says that matching individual layers across widely separated basins suggests a regional rather than purely local driver. A multi-century thickness match with distant basins is exactly that kind of evidence.
explanations.A: Speaks to preservation conditions, not to whether the climate signal is regional.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: If anything, weakens: a purely local watershed favors a local explanation.
explanations.D: Thickness compared to other lakes does not show that the same climate signal is acting across them.
explanations.E: Organic content from local plants has no bearing on regional-versus-local climate inference.

rc.passage:
The Younger Dryas, a sharp return to near-glacial conditions that interrupted the warming of the North Atlantic roughly 12,900 years ago, has long puzzled paleoclimatologists. The event began abruptly—within decades, by some estimates—lasted more than a millennium, and ended with equal suddenness. Because the warming that preceded it was driven largely by orbital forcing, a slow and cumulative process, the event's speed cannot be explained by orbital changes alone. Two competing hypotheses have dominated the literature.

The more established account attributes the cooling to a shutdown of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation (the system of currents that carries warm surface water northward and returns cold, dense water south at depth). According to this hypothesis, meltwater draining from the retreating Laurentide ice sheet flooded the North Atlantic, diluting its surface salinity and preventing the sinking that drives the circulation. Deprived of northward heat transport, the high-latitude atmosphere cooled sharply. Evidence from marine sediment cores supports this mechanism: a layer of freshwater-indicating foraminifera and a distinctive shift in oxygen-isotope ratios in planktonic shells both appear at levels dated to the onset of the event.

A second hypothesis, advanced more recently, holds that an extraterrestrial impact—probably a fragmenting comet—triggered continent-scale wildfires whose smoke and ash darkened the atmosphere, while the ejecta disrupted the ice sheet and accelerated meltwater release. Proponents cite a horizon of microspherules, platinum anomalies, and elevated nanodiamond concentrations found at sites across North America and northern Europe, all within a narrow stratigraphic band consistent with the Younger Dryas boundary.

Each hypothesis faces difficulties. The meltwater account must explain why sediment evidence for a single catastrophic flood has proven elusive, and why the cooling propagated so quickly into the Southern Hemisphere, where the Atlantic's heat-transport signal should be weaker. The impact account must contend with independent dating studies that place the proposed microspherule horizon tens to hundreds of years after the cooling began, rather than coincident with it; a cause, after all, cannot postdate its effect. Advocates of the impact hypothesis have responded that existing age models for the horizon may be biased by bioturbation (the mixing of sediments by burrowing organisms), though this reply is itself contested.

What the evidence supports more clearly is that the Younger Dryas was initiated by a trigger acting on a climate system already poised for instability by orbital warming and ice-sheet retreat, rather than by a slow-building process. Whether that trigger was the release of continental meltwater, an impact-driven disturbance, or some combination that the two accounts have each captured only in part, remains an open question—one unlikely to be resolved without higher-resolution chronologies than are presently available.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Younger Dryas was caused by a shutdown of the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, a conclusion now well supported by sediment-core evidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although two competing hypotheses have been advanced to explain the abrupt onset of the Younger Dryas, each faces unresolved difficulties, and the identity of the trigger remains an open question.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because orbital forcing cannot account for the speed of the Younger Dryas, paleoclimatologists have been forced to abandon their earlier confidence in slow-acting climatic mechanisms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recent discoveries of microspherules and platinum anomalies at the Younger Dryas boundary have displaced the meltwater hypothesis as the leading explanation of the event.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Higher-resolution chronologies of the Younger Dryas boundary are needed if paleoclimatologists are to confirm that an extraterrestrial impact initiated the cooling.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces the puzzle, presents two hypotheses with their supporting evidence, catalogues the difficulties each faces, and closes by stating that the trigger remains an open question. B captures all three strands.
explanations.A: Overstates the meltwater hypothesis's status; the passage explicitly notes that evidence for a single catastrophic flood has 'proven elusive' and treats the hypothesis as unconfirmed.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Overreach. The passage says orbital forcing alone cannot explain the speed, not that slow-acting mechanisms have been abandoned; it describes the system as 'poised for instability by orbital warming.'
explanations.D: Reverses the passage's assessment. The microspherule evidence is explicitly contested on dating grounds.
explanations.E: Promotes the closing caveat about chronologies to the thesis and additionally narrows the goal to confirming the impact hypothesis, a narrowing the passage does not endorse.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A puzzle is posed; a single explanation is developed and then defended against objections; the explanation is endorsed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A puzzle is posed; two competing explanations are described with their evidence; difficulties for each are identified; the author characterizes what the evidence does and does not establish.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A long-standing consensus is reported; a new finding is shown to overturn it; the consequences of the overturning are traced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two hypotheses are compared; the author adjudicates between them on the basis of recent sediment-core evidence and concludes that one is correct.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A methodological dispute is introduced; the competing methods are applied to a single event; the superior method is identified.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 poses the puzzle; paragraphs 2 and 3 present the two hypotheses with their evidence; paragraph 4 lists difficulties for each; paragraph 5 states what the evidence does and does not show.
explanations.A: Mis-sequencing: a second explanation is introduced, not merely objections to a single account.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Neither hypothesis is said to have overturned the other; both are treated as live options.
explanations.D: The author explicitly declines to adjudicate, calling the question 'open.'
explanations.E: The dispute is substantive, not methodological; methods are discussed only incidentally.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is cited as evidence in support of the meltwater hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: elevated concentrations of nanodiamonds in stratigraphic layers across North America

choices.label: B
choices.text: a horizon of platinum anomalies at sites in northern Europe

choices.label: C
choices.text: a shift in the oxygen-isotope ratios of planktonic foraminifera in marine sediment cores

choices.label: D
choices.text: the propagation of cooling into the Southern Hemisphere within decades of the event's onset

choices.label: E
choices.text: evidence of a single catastrophic flood in sediments of the North Atlantic

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 lists two supporting findings for the meltwater account: freshwater-indicating foraminifera and 'a distinctive shift in oxygen-isotope ratios in planktonic shells.' C is a close paraphrase of the second.
explanations.A: Nanodiamonds are cited for the impact hypothesis, not meltwater.
explanations.B: Platinum anomalies are cited for the impact hypothesis.
explanations.D: The Southern Hemisphere propagation is listed as a difficulty for the meltwater account, not as evidence in its favor.
explanations.E: The passage says evidence of such a flood has 'proven elusive'; this is a trouble for the hypothesis, not support.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author regards the claim that orbital forcing alone caused the Younger Dryas as

choices.label: A
choices.text: correct, provided that ice-sheet retreat is understood as part of the orbital-forcing process

choices.label: B
choices.text: inadequate, because orbital forcing is a gradual process and cannot by itself account for the abruptness of the event

choices.label: C
choices.text: still a live option among paleoclimatologists, though less widely held than it once was

choices.label: D
choices.text: disproven by the same sediment-core evidence that supports the meltwater hypothesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: plausible with respect to the onset of the event but not its termination

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 says the warming that preceded the event was driven largely by orbital forcing, 'a slow and cumulative process,' and that the event's speed 'cannot be explained by orbital changes alone.' The conclusion supports B.
explanations.A: The passage distinguishes orbital forcing from ice-sheet retreat rather than merging them.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage does not treat orbital-forcing-alone as a current live hypothesis; the two live hypotheses are meltwater and impact.
explanations.D: The sediment-core evidence is cited as supporting meltwater, not as disproving an orbital-alone account.
explanations.E: The passage treats both onset and termination as abrupt and does not limit the orbital-alone problem to onset only.

questions.questionStem: The author's mention of bioturbation (in the fourth paragraph) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: introduce a second line of evidence that independently supports the impact hypothesis

choices.label: B
choices.text: describe a response that advocates of the impact hypothesis have offered to a challenge based on the dating of the microspherule horizon

choices.label: C
choices.text: illustrate why sediment-core evidence in general should be regarded as unreliable for paleoclimatological reconstruction

choices.label: D
choices.text: explain why the freshwater foraminifera cited in the second paragraph may not in fact date to the onset of the Younger Dryas

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide a mechanism by which a single catastrophic flood could leave no distinctive sedimentary signature

explanations.correct: The bioturbation reference appears after the author notes that dating studies place the microspherule horizon later than the cooling's onset. The sentence introduces it as the impact-hypothesis advocates' reply to that dating challenge.
explanations.A: Accurate-content-wrong-function: bioturbation is part of a defensive reply, not a new line of positive evidence.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not generalize to all sediment-core evidence; the bioturbation point is local to the impact horizon.
explanations.D: The bioturbation point is raised in connection with the impact horizon, not the foraminifera discussed in paragraph 2.
explanations.E: The flood signature is a separate difficulty from the dating of the microspherule horizon, and bioturbation is not offered as an account of it.

questions.questionStem: The passage identifies which one of the following as a difficulty facing the meltwater hypothesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The microspherule horizon has been dated to a period well before the onset of the Younger Dryas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Planktonic foraminifera in marine sediments do not reliably record changes in surface salinity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cooling propagated into the Southern Hemisphere, where the Atlantic's heat-transport signal should be weaker.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Orbital forcing was already slowing the overturning circulation before meltwater release began.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ice-sheet retreat had effectively ended by the time the Younger Dryas began.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 4 lists as a difficulty for the meltwater account that 'the cooling propagated so quickly into the Southern Hemisphere, where the Atlantic's heat-transport signal should be weaker.' C is a close paraphrase.
explanations.A: The dating complaint in the passage runs the other way—the microspherule horizon dates later than the cooling began, not earlier—and the complaint is against the impact hypothesis, not the meltwater one.
explanations.B: The passage presents foraminifera evidence approvingly; unreliability is not raised.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Plausible-world fact the passage does not state.
explanations.E: The passage describes meltwater draining 'from the retreating Laurentide ice sheet,' implying retreat was still underway.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's suggestion that the Younger Dryas was initiated by a trigger acting on an already unstable climate system?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Newly obtained ice-core records show that atmospheric methane concentrations rose, rather than fell, at the onset of the event.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The microspherule horizon has been identified at several additional sites in Asia as well as in North America and Europe.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A refined chronology of orbital parameters shows that the slow warming of the preceding millennia can by itself produce century-scale oscillations comparable to the Younger Dryas without any external trigger.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bioturbation rates in North Atlantic sediments over the past 15,000 years have been shown to be too low to shift the dated position of a stratigraphic horizon by more than a decade.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ice-sheet retreat during the late glacial period proceeded more slowly than previously estimated, though it continued throughout the warming.

explanations.correct: The author's closing claim is that a trigger was needed because orbital forcing alone could not produce the abruptness. If refined orbital chronologies could produce oscillations of the right speed and magnitude without a trigger, that claim is directly undermined.
explanations.A: A methane observation does not speak to whether a trigger was required.
explanations.B: Adds support to the impact-hypothesis evidentiary base but does not bear on whether any trigger at all was required.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Weakens one reply of the impact-hypothesis advocates, which the author treats as contested anyway; it does not undermine the author's broader claim about a trigger.
explanations.E: Adjusting the pace of ice-sheet retreat does not eliminate the need for a trigger to explain decade-scale onset.

rc.passage:
Until the mid-1990s, astronomers had confirmed the existence of planets around only one star other than our own, and the search for extrasolar planets was widely regarded as a project for the next century. Two complementary detection methods, refined over the succeeding two decades, transformed the field. Each infers a planet indirectly, from its effect on the host star's light, and each captures a different slice of the planetary population.

The first method, radial velocity, exploits the fact that a star and its planet orbit a common center of mass. As the planet moves, the star traces a small reciprocal orbit, alternately approaching and receding from a terrestrial observer. This motion produces a periodic shift in the wavelengths of absorption lines in the star's spectrum—a Doppler effect. By measuring these shifts with high-resolution spectrographs, astronomers can infer the orbital period and set a lower bound on the planet's mass. The bound is a lower bound rather than a mass proper because the radial-velocity signal depends on the angle between the planet's orbit and the observer's line of sight, an angle that the method cannot itself determine.

The second method, transit photometry, observes the star's brightness continuously and watches for the small dip that occurs when a planet passes across the stellar disk. The fractional dimming—typically less than one percent—yields the ratio of the planet's radius to the star's, and, over repeated transits, a precise orbital period. Unlike radial velocity, transit photometry responds to a planet's size rather than its mass; when the two methods can be applied to the same system, their combination yields a density, and hence a first constraint on whether the planet is predominantly rocky or gaseous.

Each method carries characteristic biases. Radial velocity favors massive planets in tight orbits, because such planets induce larger and faster stellar wobbles; small planets at long periods remain below current detection thresholds. Transit photometry favors planets whose orbits happen to be nearly edge-on as seen from Earth, a geometric condition met by only a small fraction of systems at any given orbital distance; it also favors shorter-period planets, since confirmation typically requires several transits within the monitoring interval.

These biases do not invalidate the methods, but they must be taken into account when the data are used to estimate the frequency of planets in the galaxy. The apparent prevalence of so-called hot Jupiters in early survey catalogs, for example, was a selection effect rather than a physical prevalence: both methods detect such planets easily, while smaller and more distant planets were missed. Later surveys, designed to correct for these biases, have shown that small planets at moderate distances from their stars are, if anything, the most common configuration.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Transit photometry has largely superseded radial velocity as the preferred method of detecting extrasolar planets, because it yields a planet's radius directly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two complementary methods of extrasolar-planet detection—radial velocity and transit photometry—capture different slices of the planetary population and each carries characteristic biases that must be taken into account when estimating how common planets of various kinds are.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hot Jupiters are not, as early surveys suggested, the most common kind of planet in the galaxy; small planets at moderate distances from their stars are.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because both radial velocity and transit photometry infer planets indirectly, astronomers cannot determine the true frequency of planets in the galaxy until a direct-imaging method is developed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The transformation of extrasolar-planet detection since the 1990s shows that, in astronomy, refinements in instrumentation tend to outrun advances in theory.

explanations.correct: The passage describes the two methods, their different capabilities, their biases, and the consequences of those biases for estimating planetary frequencies. B covers all of that.
explanations.A: The passage describes the two methods as complementary and nowhere asserts the superseding of one by the other.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Paragraph-level restatement of the final paragraph; the hot-Jupiter point illustrates the broader thesis rather than constituting it.
explanations.D: Overreach and outside scope; the passage does not discuss direct imaging or claim that frequencies are presently undeterminable.
explanations.E: Too broad; the passage does not make any claim about the relation between instrumentation and theory in astronomy generally.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, why does the radial-velocity method yield only a lower bound on a planet's mass?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because the precision of current spectrographs is insufficient to resolve the full Doppler shift induced by small planets

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the signal depends on the angle between the planet's orbit and the observer's line of sight, an angle the method cannot itself determine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the host star's own motion through the galaxy contributes an unknown offset that can only be partially removed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the method captures the ratio of the planet's mass to the star's, and stellar masses are themselves uncertain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Because absorption-line shifts record only approaching motion, not receding motion

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that the bound is a lower bound 'because the radial-velocity signal depends on the angle between the planet's orbit and the observer's line of sight, an angle that the method cannot itself determine.' B is a close paraphrase.
explanations.A: Spectrograph precision is not the reason the passage gives.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Galactic motion is not discussed in the passage.
explanations.D: The passage does not describe the method as yielding a mass ratio with uncertain denominator.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly says the star 'alternately approaching and receding,' so both motions are recorded.

questions.questionStem: The passage indicates that combining radial-velocity and transit-photometry observations of the same system makes it possible to

choices.label: A
choices.text: eliminate the orbital geometry as a source of uncertainty in determining the planet's orbital period

choices.label: B
choices.text: detect planets that neither method would be able to detect on its own

choices.label: C
choices.text: estimate a density for the planet and thus obtain a first constraint on whether it is predominantly rocky or gaseous

choices.label: D
choices.text: obtain an exact measurement of the host star's radius

choices.label: E
choices.text: correct the selection bias that favors hot Jupiters in single-method surveys

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that when the two methods are applied to the same system, 'their combination yields a density, and hence a first constraint on whether the planet is predominantly rocky or gaseous.' C is verbatim in spirit.
explanations.A: The passage ties the angular uncertainty to mass, not to period.
explanations.B: Plausible-world claim; the passage does not describe the combination as enabling new detections but as refining inference for already-detected planets.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Transit photometry yields the ratio of planet to star radius, not an exact stellar radius.
explanations.E: Selection bias is corrected by survey design, not by combining the two methods on a single target.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of hot Jupiters in the final paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate why both radial velocity and transit photometry remain indispensable to exoplanet astronomy

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide an example of how the biases of the two detection methods can produce a misleading picture of planetary frequencies when not corrected for

choices.label: C
choices.text: defend the catalogs produced by early surveys against the charge that they systematically misrepresented the galaxy's planetary population

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that the earliest confirmed extrasolar planets were chosen because their physical properties were the most scientifically interesting

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce a third detection method whose results conflict with those of radial velocity and transit photometry

explanations.correct: The author introduces hot Jupiters right after claiming that detection biases must be taken into account when estimating planetary frequency, and explicitly calls their apparent prevalence 'a selection effect rather than a physical prevalence.' The example supports the bias claim.
explanations.A: Accurate content, wrong function: the example concerns bias, not indispensability.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage corrects the early catalogs rather than defending them.
explanations.D: Plausible-world fact; the passage does not discuss the selection of early targets on scientific-interest grounds.
explanations.E: No third method is introduced.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that, of the following planetary configurations, the one least likely to be detected by either of the two methods the passage describes is

choices.label: A
choices.text: a massive planet in a short-period orbit whose plane is closely aligned with the observer's line of sight

choices.label: B
choices.text: a small planet in a long-period orbit whose plane is substantially inclined to the observer's line of sight

choices.label: C
choices.text: a massive planet in a long-period orbit whose plane is nearly edge-on as seen from Earth

choices.label: D
choices.text: a small planet in a short-period orbit whose plane is nearly edge-on as seen from Earth

choices.label: E
choices.text: a massive planet in a short-period orbit whose plane is nearly edge-on as seen from Earth

explanations.correct: Radial velocity favors massive short-period planets; transit photometry favors planets whose orbits are nearly edge-on and whose periods are short. The configuration most disfavored by both is a small planet in a long-period orbit whose plane is inclined.
explanations.A: Massive and short-period is favored by radial velocity, which is enough to make this configuration detectable.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Nearly edge-on gives it a transit detection opportunity, and it is massive (helping radial velocity); long period hurts both but does not exclude detection as decisively as B.
explanations.D: Short-period and edge-on both favor transit photometry; the planet's small size is the only handicap.
explanations.E: Favored by both methods; the easiest of the five to detect.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the two detection methods described in the passage is best characterized as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of their ability to yield an unbiased census of the planets in the galaxy

choices.label: B
choices.text: respect for their achievements, tempered by recognition that their characteristic biases must be corrected for in any estimate of planetary frequencies

choices.label: C
choices.text: skepticism of the inferences they support, on the grounds that both are indirect rather than direct observations of planets

choices.label: D
choices.text: indifference, since the passage treats the methods as historical curiosities now superseded by newer techniques

choices.label: E
choices.text: uneasy acceptance, because the methods' biases are said to invalidate the conclusions drawn from their data

explanations.correct: The author credits the methods with transforming the field and describes their complementary contributions in some detail, but also insists on their biases and the corrections those biases require. That is respectful endorsement with qualification.
explanations.A: Overstated positivity; the author emphasizes that the raw data are biased.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author nowhere disparages indirect inference; the indirection is described as a feature, not a ground for skepticism.
explanations.D: The passage presents the methods as central, not superseded.
explanations.E: Reverses the author's explicit statement that the biases 'do not invalidate the methods.'

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following research situations in another field most closely parallels the relationship between the biases of the two detection methods and the early catalogs' apparent prevalence of hot Jupiters, as described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chemist, using a reagent that reacts only with molecules containing a particular functional group, concludes from the presence of the reaction product that the sample contained that group, overlooking the possibility of contamination by an unrelated substance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A seismologist whose network of detectors can only record earthquakes above a given magnitude, and only within a limited range of depths, reports a catalog of events in which large shallow earthquakes are greatly overrepresented relative to their true incidence, and corrects the estimate once the network's response is modeled.

choices.label: C
