choices.text: A demographer who samples households by telephone oversamples households with landlines and therefore misestimates the average income, but the error is unrelated to any features of the sampled population other than phone ownership.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A physician who bases diagnostic decisions on the most recently published clinical trials discovers that newer trials tend to report larger treatment effects than older ones, and concludes that the treatment is becoming more effective.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A biologist studying birdsong records only in the early morning and therefore catalogs a repertoire skewed toward dawn-chorus species, a bias the biologist has no means of quantifying.

explanations.correct: The passage's case has three load-bearing features: detection methods with characterizable thresholds and selection criteria; an early catalog whose composition reflects those criteria rather than the underlying frequency; and a later correction once the biases are modeled. B reproduces all three.
explanations.A: A contamination scenario is about false positives from an unknown confound, not about a detection method that systematically favors certain kinds of targets.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The telephone-sampling case is a mismatch because the passage's biases are tied directly to properties of the detected objects (mass, size, orbital geometry), whereas the sampling bias here is 'unrelated to any features of the sampled population' — the wrong direction of causation.
explanations.D: The clinical-trials case is about temporal drift in reported effect sizes, not about detection thresholds producing a misleading catalog.
explanations.E: Shares the biased-sampling feature but omits the load-bearing correction step; the passage emphasizes that later surveys were 'designed to correct for these biases.'

rc.passage:
A long-standing account of how experiences become enduring memories, known as the standard consolidation model, holds that the hippocampus—a structure buried in the medial temporal lobe—serves as a temporary repository in which a newly formed memory is held while it is gradually transferred to distributed neocortical networks. According to this view, once consolidation is complete, the neocortical trace is self-sufficient, and the hippocampal contribution becomes dispensable. The model is motivated principally by the pattern of retrograde amnesia observed after hippocampal injury: patients typically lose memories formed in the months preceding the injury while retaining memories from years earlier, a temporal gradient that appears to suggest the hippocampus relinquishes its role over time as the neocortical representation matures.

A competing account, the multiple trace theory, accepts that memories come to depend increasingly on the neocortex but denies that the hippocampus is ever wholly bypassed. On this view, each retrieval of an episode reinstates and partially re-encodes the hippocampal trace, so that vivid, context-rich memories continue to recruit the hippocampus even decades after they were formed, with the cumulative number of traces, rather than their individual strength, securing the memory against partial injury. What appears as graded amnesia, proponents argue, is better understood as the loss of the specific, episodic features that depend on hippocampal involvement, while the gist of the same memories—preserved in more distributed neocortical networks—survives.

Evidence from high-resolution neuroimaging has complicated the older picture. Several studies, using activity-pattern analyses rather than simple measures of overall activation, have found that the hippocampus tracks the distinctive details of autobiographical memories regardless of their age, whereas neighboring medial-temporal regions show the temporally graded pattern the standard model predicts. If this distinction is real, then the apparent temporal gradient in lesion data may reflect damage extending beyond the hippocampus proper into these adjacent regions, not the completion of transfer within the hippocampus itself.

Nonetheless, the lesion literature does not fall neatly on either side. Fully developed retrograde gradients have been reported in patients whose damage imaging suggests is largely confined to the hippocampus, and rodent studies using precisely targeted lesions have sometimes reproduced the gradient and sometimes abolished it, depending on how memory is probed. What one concludes about the hippocampus's long-term role turns, accordingly, on whether one regards detail-rich recollection and schematic recall as expressions of the same underlying memory or of distinct representations supported by different substrates. The evidence at present is more consistent with the latter possibility than with the former, though a single experiment decisive between the two, one that could dissociate these two features under a hippocampus-only lesion, has not yet been reported.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recent neuroimaging studies have shown that the hippocampus, contrary to earlier assumptions, plays no specialized role in the retention of autobiographical memories.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because retrograde amnesia after hippocampal injury follows a temporal gradient, the standard consolidation model is more consistent with clinical data than its rivals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether the hippocampus remains necessary for remote memory depends on whether detail-rich recollection and schematic recall are treated as a single process, and the current evidence favors treating them as distinct.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Activity-pattern analyses of neuroimaging data should replace lesion studies as the primary basis for theories of memory consolidation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rodent studies using targeted hippocampal lesions have settled the debate over whether remote memories remain hippocampus-dependent.

explanations.correct: The passage contrasts two models, presents neuroimaging and lesion evidence that pulls in different directions, and closes by framing the choice between them as turning on whether detailed and schematic recall are one representation or two—noting that current evidence is 'more consistent with the latter possibility.' C captures both strands.
explanations.A: Overreach. The passage treats the hippocampus as plausibly retaining a role for detailed recollection; it does not deny a specialized role.
explanations.B: Reverses the author's final assessment. The author says current evidence is more consistent with multiple trace theory than with the standard model.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Methodological reform of this kind is not the passage's thesis; imaging is described as complicating the picture, not as replacing other methods.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly states rodent results cut both ways depending on how memory is probed, and that a decisive experiment 'has not yet been reported.'

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prevailing model is described together with its motivating evidence; a competing model is introduced; a body of newer evidence is shown to complicate the prevailing model; ambiguities in the older evidence are acknowledged; the author states which position the present evidence better supports.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A long-standing model is described; newer evidence is shown to refute it decisively; a replacement model is endorsed without reservation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing models are introduced; each is shown to be inadequate in light of a third alternative, which the author defends.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A methodological problem in memory research is posed; competing remedies are surveyed; the author recommends adopting high-resolution neuroimaging as the solution.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An experimental finding is reported; two interpretations of it are developed in parallel; the author concludes that the finding cannot be interpreted without further data.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1: standard model + its motivating lesion evidence. Paragraph 2: competing multiple trace theory. Paragraph 3: newer neuroimaging evidence complicating the standard model. Paragraph 4: acknowledgment that lesion data does not cleanly favor either side, followed by the author's qualified assessment.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Misstates the conclusion: the author says current evidence is 'more consistent' with the alternative, not that the standard model is decisively refuted.
explanations.C: There is no third alternative in the passage; the author's closing assessment favors one of the two introduced models.
explanations.D: Methodology is not the organizing concern; neuroimaging is one line of evidence among several.
explanations.E: The passage does not decline to interpret the evidence; it reaches a qualified conclusion.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The temporal gradient observed in retrograde amnesia may reflect injury to regions adjacent to the hippocampus rather than a completed transfer of memories out of the hippocampus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Once a memory has been consolidated in the neocortex, it cannot be further modified by subsequent retrievals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autobiographical memories lose their detailed features as soon as they are no longer dependent on hippocampal activity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The standard consolidation model's prediction about the hippocampus is better supported by rodent data than by human data.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neighboring medial-temporal regions contribute nothing distinctive to the retention of autobiographical memories.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that if activity-pattern analyses are right that the hippocampus tracks detail regardless of age, then 'the apparent temporal gradient in lesion data may reflect damage extending beyond the hippocampus proper, not the completion of transfer within it.' A is a near paraphrase.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The multiple trace theory's re-encoding claim, which the author treats sympathetically, is inconsistent with this.
explanations.C: The passage treats loss of detail as an alternative interpretation of graded amnesia, not as a general fact about autobiographical memories.
explanations.D: Rodent studies are described as cutting both ways; the author does not say rodent data favor the standard model more strongly.
explanations.E: The passage notes that neighboring regions 'show the temporally graded pattern the standard model predicts,' which implies they do contribute distinctively.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion, in the third paragraph, of activity-pattern analyses functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate a methodological advance whose results call into question an inference drawn from the older lesion evidence

choices.label: B
choices.text: concede a limitation of the multiple trace theory that its proponents have not adequately addressed

choices.label: C
choices.text: summarize a finding that both competing models have already incorporated

choices.label: D
choices.text: introduce a third hypothesis that the author will ultimately defend

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why overall measures of brain activation have historically been preferred to activity-pattern analyses

explanations.correct: The paragraph presents activity-pattern analyses as a newer method (a methodological advance) whose results—hippocampus tracking detail regardless of age—call into question the inference, drawn from the lesion gradient, that the hippocampus relinquishes its role.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Activity-pattern results are introduced on the side of the multiple trace theory, not as a concession against it.
explanations.C: The passage presents the finding as complicating the 'older picture'; it has not been absorbed by both models.
explanations.D: There is no third hypothesis.
explanations.E: The passage implies the opposite—activity-pattern analyses have revealed something overall activation did not—without asserting which was historically preferred.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from the passage that a proponent of the multiple trace theory would most likely regard a patient who retains the gist of events from a decade earlier but cannot recall their specific details as

choices.label: A
choices.text: evidence that the hippocampus transfers memories completely to the neocortex once consolidation is finished

choices.label: B
choices.text: evidence that detail-rich and schematic features of a memory depend on different substrates, only one of which has been disrupted

choices.label: C
choices.text: evidence that activity-pattern analyses overstate the hippocampus's role in remote memory

choices.label: D
choices.text: evidence that retrograde amnesia gradients are methodological artifacts of how memory is probed in rodents

choices.label: E
choices.text: evidence that neocortical networks are not themselves involved in the retention of autobiographical memories

explanations.correct: Multiple trace theory holds that detailed, context-rich recall recruits the hippocampus while gist survives in distributed neocortical networks. A patient with preserved gist but lost detail is, on that view, evidence that the two features are supported by different substrates, one of which has been disrupted.
explanations.A: That is the standard consolidation model's reading, which multiple trace theory rejects.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Activity-pattern analyses are cited in support of multiple trace theory; proponents would not use the pattern against that evidence.
explanations.D: Rodent methodology is not the multiple trace theorist's explanation of the human pattern described.
explanations.E: Both models hold that neocortex is involved; the theorist would not dispute that.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine the author's qualified assessment in the final paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A new technique demonstrates that, in patients with damage confined to the hippocampus alone, both the detail-rich and the schematic features of remote autobiographical memories are lost together in the same graded pattern.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rodent studies using targeted hippocampal lesions show that animals can still learn new spatial tasks after the lesion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A case study reports a patient whose hippocampal damage is accompanied by marked impairment in forming new memories.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Activity-pattern analyses reveal that regions outside the medial temporal lobe also track the distinctive details of autobiographical memories.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A proponent of the standard consolidation model concedes that retrieval partially reinstates the hippocampal trace.

explanations.correct: The author's assessment depends on treating detail-rich recollection and schematic recall as distinct representations supported by different substrates; a hippocampus-only lesion that abolishes both together in the same graded pattern would undercut that distinction and thus weaken the author's case for multiple trace theory.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Anterograde task learning is a different question from retrograde retention; the author's claim is about remote autobiographical memory, not new learning.
explanations.C: Impaired encoding after hippocampal damage is consistent with both models and does not bear on the author's remote-memory claim.
explanations.D: Additional regions tracking detail would not undercut the author's claim that the hippocampus also does so; it would just broaden the distributed trace.
explanations.E: A partial concession by the standard model's defenders moves in the author's direction, not against it.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following research scenarios most closely conforms to the reasoning the author employs in evaluating the two models of memory?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An ecologist observes that a predator population declines after a habitat change, concludes the change is responsible, and dismisses alternative explanations without testing them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A geneticist, confronted with two hypotheses about a trait's inheritance, notes that a pattern in pedigree data is consistent with both and proposes a cellular-level mechanism that would distinguish the two, provisionally favoring the hypothesis more compatible with recent mechanistic findings while acknowledging that a decisive test has not been run.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A chemist selects between two reaction mechanisms on the basis of computational modeling alone, ignoring the experimental yields reported in earlier studies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A physicist reports an anomaly and defers any interpretation of it until a theoretical framework addressing it has been worked out.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A clinician, finding that two treatments produce similar outcomes in a small trial, recommends whichever is less expensive and abandons further investigation of their mechanisms.

explanations.correct: The author weighs lesion data consistent with both models, introduces a newer mechanistic line of evidence (activity-pattern analyses) that distinguishes them, and provisionally favors the hypothesis better supported by that evidence while noting that no decisive experiment has been run. B mirrors each of these moves.
explanations.A: The author does not dismiss alternatives; both models are engaged with throughout.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author explicitly relies on empirical studies, not modeling alone.
explanations.D: The author reaches a qualified conclusion rather than deferring interpretation.
explanations.E: The author does not choose on extra-evidential grounds like cost, and does investigate underlying mechanisms.

rc.passage:
Hot Jupiters—gas giants orbiting their host stars at distances a small fraction of the Earth-Sun separation—are, on any reasonable accounting, losing atmosphere to space. What has remained contested is the dominant mechanism driving that loss, and the dispute bears directly on whether the planets observed today began as still larger bodies or have roughly retained their original mass.

One account, energy-limited escape, treats the process as a balance sheet: extreme ultraviolet radiation from the star deposits energy in the upper atmosphere, and some fraction of that energy is converted into the work required to lift gas out of the planet's gravitational well. Because the stellar ultraviolet flux scales with proximity and is known to decline by roughly an order of magnitude over the first billion years of a Sun-like star's life, an energy-limited calculation predicts that a hot Jupiter formed near its present orbit would have shed, at most, a few percent of its initial mass. On this view, today's population of hot Jupiters looks approximately as it has always looked.

A second account, hydrodynamic outflow driven by Roche-lobe overflow, is less forgiving. When a planet's upper atmosphere is heated enough to expand beyond the surface at which the star's gravity becomes the stronger pull (the Roche limit), gas ceases to be retained and streams away in a hydrodynamic wind whose rate is set not by radiative energy alone but by the planet's thermal structure and surface gravity. Simulations of this regime suggest that an inflated young hot Jupiter—larger and lower-density at formation than after cooling—could have lost a substantial fraction of its envelope before contracting to its present radius. If so, a meaningful share of the currently observed hot Jupiters were originally more massive objects.

The discriminating evidence ought to be a population statistic: if envelope-stripping is important, there should be a measurable deficit of hot Jupiters at the masses most vulnerable to it, a 'desert' in the mass-orbit plane around stars old enough for the process to have run to completion. Such a deficit has been reported in several surveys, though its boundaries are not sharp, and critics note that the same region is populated sparsely for reasons independent of escape, since planets of those masses are harder to detect at short periods around certain spectral types.

What can be said with some confidence is that neither mechanism alone captures the range of outcomes observed: energy-limited escape is adequate for many middle-aged systems but understates losses during the first few hundred million years, while hydrodynamic outflow is appropriate for inflated young planets but overpredicts losses once cooling and contraction have set in. A synthesis in which the dominant channel shifts with age would accommodate both the observed mass distribution and the fact that measured present-day escape rates are, in most cases, modest. Whether that synthesis will survive further data is another matter.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Recent surveys have established that most observed hot Jupiters began as substantially more massive planets that have since lost large fractions of their envelopes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the extreme ultraviolet flux of Sun-like stars declines sharply over their first billion years, hot Jupiters orbiting older stars are losing negligible amounts of mass today.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two mechanisms of atmospheric escape from hot Jupiters make sharply different predictions about their original masses, and the available evidence favors a synthesis in which the dominant mechanism depends on the planet's age.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The apparent deficit of hot Jupiters at certain masses is more plausibly explained by detection biases than by any escape mechanism.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hydrodynamic outflow models should be abandoned because they overpredict mass loss in cooled and contracted hot Jupiters.

explanations.correct: The passage presents two mechanisms with opposing implications for original mass, reviews evidence that cuts both ways, and concludes that a synthesis in which the dominant channel shifts with age fits the data best. C captures each element.
explanations.A: Overstates the survey results; the passage calls the deficit's boundaries 'not sharp' and notes alternative explanations.
explanations.B: A subsidiary claim of only one of the two models, not the passage's thesis.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage treats detection biases as one consideration among several, not as the preferred explanation.
explanations.E: The author does not reject hydrodynamic outflow; the synthesis incorporates it for young, inflated planets.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a prediction of the energy-limited escape account?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An inflated young hot Jupiter will lose gas at a rate set primarily by its thermal structure rather than by radiative input.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The dominant channel of mass loss in hot Jupiters shifts with the planet's age.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A hot Jupiter that formed near its present orbit would have lost only a small fraction of its initial mass over the first billion years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A deficit of hot Jupiters at certain masses will be observed around stars old enough for escape processes to have run to completion.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hot Jupiters initially retain their mass despite exposure to extreme ultraviolet radiation, because that radiation does no work against their gravity.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2: energy-limited calculations, given the roughly order-of-magnitude decline in stellar ultraviolet flux, predict that 'a hot Jupiter formed near its present orbit would have shed, at most, a few percent of its initial mass.' C paraphrases that prediction.
explanations.A: That is hydrodynamic outflow's account, not energy-limited escape's.
explanations.B: The age-dependent shift is the author's proposed synthesis, not a prediction of the energy-limited model alone.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The mass-deficit prediction belongs to the envelope-stripping account; energy-limited escape predicts small losses and thus no substantial deficit.
explanations.E: Reverses the model's logic: in energy-limited escape, some fraction of the ultraviolet energy is converted into the work of lifting gas out; losses are small but not zero.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to detection difficulties in the fourth paragraph serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede a consideration that weakens the inference from the observed mass deficit to the importance of envelope-stripping escape

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that the reported mass deficit is entirely an artifact of the methods used to discover short-period planets

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce a third mechanism of atmospheric escape that neither of the previous accounts has addressed

choices.label: D
choices.text: illustrate how the stellar ultraviolet flux varies with spectral type

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why hot Jupiters are more common around older stars than around younger ones

explanations.correct: Having introduced the mass deficit as potentially discriminating evidence for envelope-stripping, the author concedes that the same region is populated sparsely for reasons independent of escape, thereby weakening the inference from the deficit to envelope-stripping's importance.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The concession is qualified (the boundaries are 'not sharp,' critics 'note' an alternative); the passage does not assert the deficit is 'entirely an artifact.'
explanations.C: No third mechanism is introduced here.
explanations.D: Spectral-type variation in ultraviolet flux is not the paragraph's topic.
explanations.E: The passage does not make claims about the relative commonness of hot Jupiters by stellar age.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly supports which one of the following inferences?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Energy-limited escape predicts greater cumulative mass loss than hydrodynamic outflow does over a planet's first few hundred million years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The present-day radius of a hot Jupiter is independent of the mechanism by which it has lost mass in the past.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A hot Jupiter's susceptibility to Roche-lobe overflow is greater before it has cooled and contracted than after.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The extreme ultraviolet flux received by a planet in a fixed orbit remains approximately constant over the host star's main-sequence lifetime.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Present-day escape rates measured for hot Jupiters are generally large enough, if sustained, to remove most of a planet's envelope over a billion years.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says hydrodynamic outflow operates when the atmosphere expands beyond the Roche limit and that an 'inflated young hot Jupiter—larger and lower-density at formation than after cooling' could lose a substantial envelope; paragraph 5 says hydrodynamic outflow 'overpredicts losses once cooling and contraction have set in.' Together, these support C.
explanations.A: Reverses the relationship; the author says energy-limited escape 'understates losses' in the first few hundred million years.
explanations.B: The passage treats radius and mass-loss history as linked: inflation during early losses is precisely what drives hydrodynamic outflow.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage says ultraviolet flux declines by roughly an order of magnitude over the first billion years, contradicting constancy.
explanations.E: The final paragraph says present-day escape rates are 'in most cases, modest,' the opposite of large enough to remove most of an envelope if sustained.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the proposed synthesis described in the final paragraph is most accurately characterized as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement without reservation

choices.label: B
choices.text: qualified endorsement, with an acknowledgment that further evidence could displace it

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismissive skepticism grounded in detection biases

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral reportage without any evaluative stance

choices.label: E
choices.text: approval of the synthesis's underlying methodology combined with rejection of its specific predictions

explanations.correct: The author presents the synthesis as accommodating the data better than either mechanism alone ('would accommodate both... measured present-day escape rates are, in most cases, modest'), but closes with 'Whether that synthesis will survive further data is another matter,' a characteristic LSAT hedge.
explanations.A: The closing sentence is explicitly a reservation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The synthesis is endorsed provisionally, not dismissed.
explanations.D: The author evaluates both mechanisms and favors the synthesis; this is not neutral reportage.
explanations.E: The author approves of the synthesis's predictions for current data; nothing in the passage rejects specific predictions while approving methodology.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most support the author's claim that a synthesis in which the dominant escape channel shifts with age is preferable to either mechanism alone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A survey of young, inflated hot Jupiters finds measured escape rates substantially higher than energy-limited models predict, while a survey of older, contracted hot Jupiters finds rates close to those same models' predictions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Simulations show that hydrodynamic outflow can be driven by stellar winds rather than by radiative heating alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The extreme ultraviolet flux from Sun-like stars declines more slowly than previously estimated over their first billion years.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Detection techniques for short-period planets around certain spectral types have improved enough to remove the apparent mass deficit.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A newly discovered hot Jupiter has no detectable atmospheric escape despite orbiting a young star.

explanations.correct: The author's synthesis claims hydrodynamic outflow dominates for inflated young planets and energy-limited escape for older ones. A finding that young inflated planets show losses exceeding energy-limited predictions, while older contracted planets match those predictions, directly instantiates this age-dependent shift.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: A wind-driven variant of hydrodynamic outflow does not bear on the claim that the dominant channel shifts with age.
explanations.C: A slower UV decline affects the inputs to energy-limited escape but does not support the age-dependent shift.
explanations.D: Removing the mass deficit would undermine a separate strand of evidence for envelope-stripping, not support the synthesis.
explanations.E: A single counterexample to young-planet escape would complicate, not support, the synthesis's claim that hydrodynamic outflow dominates for inflated young planets.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the kind of reasoning by which the author evaluates the reported mass deficit as evidence for envelope-stripping?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A seismologist concludes that the scarcity of large earthquakes along a fault segment is due to the segment's low slip rate, but an interlocutor notes that few large earthquakes would be expected there anyway given the fault's short recorded history.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A botanist claims that a rare plant's distribution is explained by soil chemistry and rejects any role for climatic variables.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An economist predicts that a tax change will raise revenue and defends the prediction by citing unrelated historical cases.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An astronomer reports a new exoplanet and argues that its mere existence confirms the theory that predicted it, without considering alternative theories.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A chemist measures reaction rates under controlled conditions and concludes that the measured values apply to industrial-scale reactions.

explanations.correct: The author entertains the mass deficit as evidence for envelope-stripping but concedes that the same region is populated sparsely for independent reasons (detection difficulty), weakening the inference from the deficit to its purported cause. A mirrors this: a pattern is proposed as evidence for a mechanism, but a rival explanation (short recorded history) predicts the pattern independently.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The botanist dismisses an alternative rather than weighing it as the author does.
explanations.C: Citation of unrelated cases is not parallel to entertaining an independent explanation of the same pattern.
explanations.D: The astronomer ignores alternatives; the author explicitly raises one.
explanations.E: Extrapolation from laboratory to industrial scale does not mirror the structure of entertaining a competing explanation for the same observation.

rc.passage:
When sociologists speak of a 'profession,' they usually mean more than simply a line of work in which someone earns a living. According to the sociologist Andrew Abbott, a profession is an occupation that has secured the exclusive right to perform a particular set of tasks and that controls entry into its own ranks through training, examination, and licensure. On this definition, medicine and law are the paradigm cases, while many other lines of work — including some that pay well and require long training — fall short of full professional status.

Abbott argues that what distinguishes a profession from an ordinary occupation is the social bargain it strikes with the wider public. In return for a monopoly over certain tasks, the profession agrees to police its own members: it sets standards of competence, disciplines those who fall short, and accepts the idea that the quality of its work is something only other members can reliably judge. The public, for its part, is relieved of the burden of evaluating practitioners one by one, since the license itself is meant to serve as a guarantee.

This arrangement, however, depends on conditions that are not always met. The self-policing on which the bargain rests can weaken when the profession's internal culture discourages frank criticism, or when the cost of expelling an incompetent member is felt to fall too heavily on colleagues who must testify against him. Abbott notes that complaints about professional misconduct are, in practice, often resolved quietly, in ways that protect the profession's public standing but leave the aggrieved client without redress. When such failures accumulate, the state may step in and replace professional self-regulation with outside review — a development that Abbott treats as evidence that the original bargain has broken down.

Even where self-regulation functions tolerably well, the professional model has critics. Some sociologists argue that the monopoly granted to a profession tends, over time, to serve the interests of its members more than those of the public it nominally serves, by restricting the supply of practitioners and keeping fees high. Abbott concedes that this risk is real but contends that the alternative — a system in which clients must evaluate complex technical work without reliable credentials — would leave most of them worse off. The case for professions, on his account, is not that they are free of self-interest but that the public is better served by regulated self-interest than by no regulation at all.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: According to Abbott, a profession is best understood as a social bargain in which an occupation's monopoly over certain tasks is exchanged for self-regulation that, though imperfect, serves the public better than no regulation at all.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medicine and law are the only occupations that fully satisfy Abbott's definition of a profession, since no other line of work has secured a comparable monopoly over its tasks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Professional self-regulation has broken down so thoroughly in most fields that state review has become the standard means of disciplining incompetent practitioners.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The principal value of the professional model is that it restricts the supply of practitioners, thereby guaranteeing that those who remain are highly competent.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sociologists who study professions disagree fundamentally about whether professional licensure benefits the public or merely entrenches the interests of licensed practitioners.

explanations.correct: The passage defines professions through Abbott's bargain (paragraph 1-2), notes when the bargain breaks down (paragraph 3), addresses critics (paragraph 4), and closes with Abbott's qualified defense. A captures both the bargain and Abbott's verdict.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too narrow: medicine and law are called paradigm cases, not the only professions.
explanations.C: Overstated: state review is described as an occasional corrective, not the standard practice.
explanations.D: Confuses a criticism (restricted supply) with the author's case for professions.
explanations.E: The passage reports disagreement but its main point is Abbott's own position, not that disagreement exists.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A definition is offered; the terms of a social bargain are laid out; conditions under which the bargain can fail are described; a criticism is noted and answered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing definitions of a profession are compared; one is shown to be superior on empirical grounds; its implications for public policy are drawn out.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A puzzle about professional licensure is posed; several historical examples are surveyed; a new explanation of the puzzle is defended.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A recent criticism of the professional model is introduced; the response of its defenders is summarized; the dispute is declared unresolved.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A classification scheme is proposed; its application to medicine and law is illustrated; its application to other occupations is left for future research.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 defines; paragraph 2 lays out the bargain; paragraph 3 describes conditions under which it fails; paragraph 4 raises a criticism and gives Abbott's answer. A tracks each move.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Only one definition — Abbott's — is presented.
explanations.C: No puzzle is posed and no historical survey is offered.
explanations.D: The dispute is not declared unresolved; Abbott's qualified case closes the passage.
explanations.E: No classification scheme with multiple categories is proposed.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Abbott treats the intervention of the state to replace professional self-regulation as

choices.label: A
choices.text: the normal means by which all professions are ultimately disciplined

choices.label: B
choices.text: evidence that the bargain between the profession and the public has broken down

choices.label: C
choices.text: a development that the profession itself typically welcomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: proof that the professional model was never workable in the first place

choices.label: E
choices.text: an outcome that tends to lower standards of competence within the profession

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that outside review by the state is treated by Abbott 'as evidence that the original bargain has broken down.'
explanations.A: Altered qualifier: the passage presents state review as an occasional corrective, not the normal means.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Plausible-world fact the passage never supplies.
explanations.D: Overreach: breakdown of the bargain in some cases is not proof that the model was never workable.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the passage does not claim outside review lowers standards.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that, under the professional bargain as Abbott describes it, the public is

choices.label: A
choices.text: expected to rely on the license as a guarantee of a practitioner's competence

choices.label: B
choices.text: invited to participate directly in disciplining incompetent practitioners

choices.label: C
choices.text: guaranteed redress whenever professional misconduct occurs

choices.label: D
choices.text: charged with setting the standards of competence that the profession must meet

choices.label: E
choices.text: required to evaluate each practitioner's qualifications individually

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 says the public is relieved of evaluating practitioners one by one because 'the license itself is meant to serve as a guarantee.'
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Reverses the passage: disciplining is done by the profession, not the public.
explanations.C: Altered qualifier: paragraph 3 notes that aggrieved clients are often left without redress.
explanations.D: Reverses the passage: the profession sets standards.
explanations.E: Reverses the passage: the point of licensure is precisely to spare the public this task.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that Abbott would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A line of work that is demanding and well compensated automatically qualifies as a profession in the sociological sense.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fact that professionals sometimes act in their own interest shows that the professional model should be abandoned.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Self-regulation by a profession can be imperfect and still leave the public better off than a system in which clients must evaluate technical work on their own.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complaints of professional misconduct are generally handled in a way that fully satisfies the clients who bring them.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The monopoly granted to a profession produces no benefit for its members beyond the prestige of the title.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 4 gives Abbott's case: the professional model is not free of self-interest, but 'the public is better served by regulated self-interest than by no regulation at all.' C restates that hedged position.
explanations.A: Reverses paragraph 1: even well-paid, long-trained work may fall short of professional status.
explanations.B: Overreach: Abbott concedes self-interest is real but defends the model, not abandons it.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Reverses paragraph 3: complaints are often resolved in ways that leave aggrieved clients without redress.
explanations.E: The passage says monopoly restricts supply and keeps fees high, which is a benefit to members, not none.

questions.questionStem: The author's mention of the observation that complaints of professional misconduct are often resolved quietly serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate a way in which the conditions needed for professional self-regulation to work can fail

choices.label: B
choices.text: demonstrate that Abbott's definition of a profession is empirically inadequate

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce a new category of occupations that do not yet qualify as professions

choices.label: D
choices.text: support the claim that the state should always oversee professional discipline

choices.label: E
choices.text: establish that the public has no interest in how professions discipline their members

explanations.correct: The observation appears in paragraph 3 as an example of how the self-policing on which the bargain depends 'is not always met.' Its rhetorical function is illustrative.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Wrong function: the observation describes a failure mode, not a flaw in the definition.
explanations.C: The passage introduces no new category at this point.
explanations.D: Overstated: the passage describes state review as an occasional corrective, not something that should always occur.
explanations.E: Opposite of the passage, which treats the public as the principal beneficiary of the bargain.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Abbott's account of professions can best be described as one of

choices.label: A
choices.text: unqualified enthusiasm for its conclusions

choices.label: B
choices.text: respectful presentation of a position the author finds defensible

choices.label: C
choices.text: open hostility to its central claim

choices.label: D
choices.text: detached neutrality between Abbott and his critics

choices.label: E
choices.text: reluctant agreement with its critics despite the author's preference for Abbott

explanations.correct: The author reports Abbott's definition, gives space to its difficulties, and allows Abbott's qualified case to close the passage — the posture of respectful presentation.
explanations.A: Overstated: the author does not speak enthusiastically and notes real difficulties.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite of the text, which treats Abbott seriously.
explanations.D: Too weak: the passage is not evenhanded; it lets Abbott have the last word.
explanations.E: Reverses the passage, which gives Abbott, not the critics, the closing position.

rc.passage:
Until fairly recently, the rapid growth of cities in the nineteenth-century United States was commonly explained in simple terms: factories, it was said, drew workers from the countryside, and cities grew up around the factories. According to the urban historian Sam Bass Warner, however, this factory-first account misses much of what actually happened. Drawing on street directories, tax records, and transit maps, Warner argues that the most important engine of nineteenth-century urban growth was not the factory but the streetcar, and that the typical American city of the period expanded outward from its old commercial core in ways that had little to do with where the largest employers were located.

Warner's evidence comes chiefly from Boston, where, between roughly 1870 and 1900, the introduction of horse-drawn and then electric streetcar lines made it possible for clerks, shopkeepers, and skilled tradesmen to live several miles from the places at which they worked. As new lines pushed outward into formerly rural towns, small builders bought up inexpensive land along the route, subdivided it into narrow lots, and put up modest wooden houses for sale to families of modest means. The result was a ring of new residential neighborhoods, each one organized around a streetcar stop rather than a factory gate.

The significance of this pattern, Warner argues, is that it reshaped the social geography of the city. Under the older, walking-distance arrangement, rich and poor had lived close together, since everyone needed to be near the center. Once the streetcar made distance cheap, those who could afford the daily fare moved outward, and the inner districts were left to the poorest residents and to the workshops and warehouses that served the downtown economy. The familiar twentieth-century pattern of a poor urban core surrounded by wealthier suburbs, Warner suggests, was already visible in outline by 1900.

Warner's account has been refined by later historians, who have shown that factories did matter in some cities — Pittsburgh and Detroit among them — and that the streetcar's reach depended on local politics and the willingness of city governments to grant franchises. Still, his central insight has held up well. For a broad class of American cities, the shape of nineteenth-century urban growth is better explained by transit than by industry, and any account of the period that begins with the factory alone will miss the new suburbs that the streetcar, more than any factory whistle, called into being.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: For a broad class of American cities, the nineteenth-century expansion into new residential neighborhoods is better explained by the spread of streetcar lines than by the location of factories.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sam Bass Warner's work on Boston shows that horse-drawn and electric streetcar lines were introduced in that city between roughly 1870 and 1900.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nineteenth-century American cities grew because small builders purchased inexpensive rural land and subdivided it into narrow lots for modest wooden houses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Factories played no meaningful role in the growth of any nineteenth-century American city, despite the views of earlier historians.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The twentieth-century pattern of poor urban cores surrounded by wealthier suburbs was entirely produced by public transit decisions made before 1900.

explanations.correct: The passage presents the factory-first view, replaces it with Warner's streetcar account, draws out the social consequences, and closes with the hedged conclusion that 'for a broad class of American cities, the shape of nineteenth-century urban growth is better explained by transit than by industry.' A tracks that thesis.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too narrow: a single detail, not the passage's thesis.
explanations.C: Too narrow: a mechanism of growth, not the claim the passage is making about explanations.
explanations.D: Overstated: paragraph 4 explicitly concedes that factories did matter in Pittsburgh and Detroit.
explanations.E: Overstated: the passage says the pattern was 'already visible in outline by 1900,' not entirely produced by 1900.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, under the walking-distance arrangement that preceded the streetcar,

choices.label: A
choices.text: factories were concentrated at the edges of the city rather than in the center

choices.label: B
choices.text: rich and poor residents tended to live close to one another, since everyone needed to be near the center

choices.label: C
choices.text: most residents lived in rural towns and traveled daily into the city for work

choices.label: D
choices.text: small builders had already begun to subdivide suburban land in anticipation of transit improvements

choices.label: E
choices.text: city governments declined to grant franchises to private transportation companies

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that 'under the older, walking-distance arrangement, rich and poor had lived close together, since everyone needed to be near the center.'
explanations.A: The passage does not locate factories at the edges under the older arrangement.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Reverses the passage: the streetcar, not the walking city, enabled daily travel from outside.
explanations.D: Out of scope: builders' subdivision activity is tied to streetcar expansion, not the pre-streetcar period.
explanations.E: Out of scope: the franchise question is raised only as a later qualification of Warner's account.

questions.questionStem: The passage indicates that Warner drew his evidence chiefly from which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pittsburgh and Detroit

choices.label: B
choices.text: A comparative study of a dozen industrial cities

choices.label: C
choices.text: Boston, between roughly 1870 and 1900

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interviews with nineteenth-century streetcar operators

choices.label: E
choices.text: Records of factory employment in the northeastern United States

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that 'Warner's evidence comes chiefly from Boston, where, between roughly 1870 and 1900,' the streetcar network was built out.
explanations.A: Pittsburgh and Detroit are mentioned as counterexamples by later historians, not as Warner's evidence.
explanations.B: The passage does not describe Warner's work as a comparative study of many cities.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Plausible-world fact the passage never supplies; Warner's sources are given as directories, tax records, and transit maps.
explanations.E: Factory-employment records are not among the sources the passage credits to Warner.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to Pittsburgh and Detroit serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the typical pattern of streetcar-driven residential growth

choices.label: B
choices.text: qualify Warner's account by acknowledging cities in which factories did matter

choices.label: C
choices.text: identify the cities from which Warner drew his principal evidence

choices.label: D
choices.text: argue that later historians have generally failed to improve on Warner's account

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that the factory-first explanation has no empirical basis anywhere

explanations.correct: The reference appears in paragraph 4, where later historians 'have shown that factories did matter in some cities — Pittsburgh and Detroit among them.' Its function is to qualify, not to overturn, Warner's account.
explanations.A: Wrong function: these cities are cited as exceptions to Warner's pattern, not illustrations of it.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Confuses Warner's evidence (Boston) with the later qualifying examples.
explanations.D: Opposite of the passage, which says Warner's central insight has held up well.
explanations.E: Overstated: the reference shows the factory-first view has some application, not that it is wholly baseless.

questions.questionStem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that Warner would agree with which one of the following statements about nineteenth-century American cities?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A city's pattern of residential growth in this period cannot be understood without some attention to how its inhabitants moved around.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factories played no role in shaping the neighborhoods of any American city in this period.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The social segregation of rich and poor that appears in twentieth-century cities is unrelated to nineteenth-century transit decisions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Street directories and tax records are not reliable sources for urban historians working on the period.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The development of suburban neighborhoods in this period was essentially the work of city governments rather than private builders.

explanations.correct: Warner's whole case — drawn from transit maps and neighborhood growth — rests on the importance of how people moved through the city. A is a hedged statement he would plainly accept.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Overreach: Warner's qualifier about Pittsburgh and Detroit shows he would not deny factories any role.
explanations.C: Contradicts paragraph 3, which ties twentieth-century segregation directly to nineteenth-century transit.
explanations.D: Reverses the passage: these are the sources on which Warner himself relies.
explanations.E: Reverses paragraph 2: small private builders, not city governments, developed the new neighborhoods.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Warner's account can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: broadly approving, while acknowledging that later historians have refined it

choices.label: B
choices.text: dismissive, on the grounds that it ignores the role of factories

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic, without reservation of any kind

choices.label: D
choices.text: skeptical, because the evidence is drawn from a single city

choices.label: E
choices.text: neutral, since the author takes no position between Warner and his critics

explanations.correct: The author presents Warner's case at length, notes that later historians have added qualifications, and concludes that Warner's 'central insight has held up well.' A captures the mixed-but-positive posture.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Opposite of the passage, which endorses Warner's insight.
explanations.C: Overstated: the author explicitly records the qualifications of later historians.
explanations.D: Wrong direction: the author accepts Warner despite the Boston focus.
explanations.E: Too weak: the final paragraph's closing sentence is clearly on Warner's side.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most support Warner's claim that streetcar expansion, rather than factory location, drove the residential growth of typical nineteenth-century American cities?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In several cities other than Boston, new residential neighborhoods formed in the late nineteenth century were consistently organized around streetcar stops rather than around industrial sites.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In Pittsburgh and Detroit, factory employment grew substantially between 1870 and 1900.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Street directories from nineteenth-century Boston are the most detailed records of their kind to survive from the period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The electric streetcar replaced the horse-drawn streetcar in most American cities during the 1890s.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some nineteenth-century city governments granted streetcar franchises only after long political disputes.

explanations.correct: Warner's claim is general: transit, not industry, shaped the typical residential pattern. Direct evidence from other cities showing the same transit-centered pattern most strongly supports that generalization.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Off-target: growth of factory employment in the atypical cities the passage already concedes does not support Warner's generalization.
explanations.C: Concerns the quality of one source, not whether the claim generalizes beyond Boston.
explanations.D: A technological detail that does not speak to the causal claim the question targets.
explanations.E: Concerns political conditions for streetcar franchises, not whether they, rather than factories, drove residential growth.

rc.passage:
For much of the twentieth century, historians of the French Revolution worked under the long shadow of the thesis associated with Georges Lefebvre. According to Lefebvre's classic account, the Revolution is best understood as a bourgeois revolution: an ascendant commercial and professional class, frustrated by a political order that still privileged the nobility, moved decisively in 1789 to sweep away feudal constraints and install a regime congenial to its economic interests. The narrative had the virtue of coherence — it explained why the Revolution happened when it did, who its principal beneficiaries were, and why it took the legal forms it took — and for two generations textbooks echoed it with minor variations.

That consensus began to erode in the 1960s, when the historian Alfred Cobban argued that Lefebvre's bourgeoisie was a category with little empirical content. Examining the occupations of the deputies elected to the Estates-General in 1789, Cobban found that the Third Estate's representatives were, for the most part, not capitalist merchants or industrialists but office-holders, lawyers, and professionals — a group whose wealth was drawn from venal offices and landed rents rather than from trade or manufacture. If these men were the revolutionaries, Cobban contended, then the Revolution could not be explained as the political triumph of a rising commercial class; it had to be explained in other terms, perhaps as a conflict internal to the propertied elite over access to the state.

Cobban's challenge has not gone unanswered, and the picture that has emerged over the last several decades is less tidy than either his account or Lefebvre's. Subsequent social historians, working with parish registers, notarial archives, and tax rolls, have shown that the boundary between commercial and office-holding wealth in eighteenth-century France was more porous than Cobban's prosopography suggested: a successful merchant often bought offices for his sons, and an office-holding family often maintained an interest in trade. What has fallen away, however, is any confident identification of the Revolution with the interests of a single coherent class. In its place stands a more cautious formulation: that the Revolution emerged from a shifting coalition of groups whose members shared grievances against the old regime without sharing a unified economic program. This reformulation preserves what was durable in Lefebvre's attention to social structure while accepting the force of Cobban's evidence that the social structure in question was not simply bourgeois. The cost of the reformulation is a loss of narrative drive. What it offers in return is a version of the Revolution that the sources will actually support.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Georges Lefebvre's bourgeois-revolution thesis, long accepted as the definitive account of the French Revolution, has been conclusively refuted by later social historians.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alfred Cobban's demonstration that the deputies of the Third Estate were not capitalists showed that class analysis has no role to play in the history of the French Revolution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cobban's empirical challenge to Lefebvre has led not to outright rejection of Lefebvre's attention to social structure but to a more cautious account of the Revolution as emerging from a coalition of groups without a unified economic program.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recent work in parish registers, notarial archives, and tax rolls has shown that the boundary between commercial and office-holding wealth in eighteenth-century France was more porous than earlier historians supposed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Narrative coherence, rather than empirical support, is the principal virtue that has recommended Lefebvre's interpretation of the French Revolution to generations of textbook writers.

explanations.correct: The passage sets up Lefebvre (paragraph 1), presents Cobban's challenge (paragraph 2), and settles on a synthesis (paragraph 3) that 'preserves what was durable in Lefebvre's attention to social structure while accepting the force of Cobban's evidence.' C captures both halves.
explanations.A: Overstated: the passage says Lefebvre's attention to social structure is preserved, not refuted.
explanations.B: Reverses the passage: class analysis survives in a revised form.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too narrow — the archival detail is one piece of evidence for a broader reformulation.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement that promotes a coda about narrative drive to the thesis.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historical thesis is introduced; an empirical challenge to it is presented; a qualified synthesis is endorsed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two historians' views are summarized; a third view is shown to be superior to both; the limitations of the third view are catalogued.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A methodological dispute is sketched; the contending parties are named; the dispute is declared insoluble on present evidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A long-standing consensus is defended against a recent challenge, which is shown to rest on a misreading of its principal sources.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A class analysis is applied to one historical event, then extended to two additional events, and finally generalized into a theory of revolution.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 presents Lefebvre's thesis; paragraph 2 presents Cobban's empirical challenge; paragraph 3 endorses a qualified synthesis. A matches each move in order.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Mis-sequences: the synthesis is not a third view superior to both; it integrates elements of each.
explanations.C: The passage treats the dispute as productive, not insoluble.
explanations.D: Reverses the author's direction: Cobban's challenge is granted force, not rebutted.
explanations.E: Only one event (the French Revolution) is considered.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Cobban's examination of the deputies elected to the Estates-General in 1789 revealed that the representatives of the Third Estate were

choices.label: A
choices.text: chiefly capitalist merchants and industrialists whose interests lay in overseas trade

choices.label: B
choices.text: for the most part office-holders, lawyers, and professionals whose wealth came from venal offices and landed rents

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawn almost equally from the commercial bourgeoisie and the remnants of the feudal nobility

choices.label: D
choices.text: primarily tenant farmers with grievances against the seigneurial system

choices.label: E
choices.text: a mixture of urban artisans and rural clergy who shared a common hostility to the monarchy

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that Cobban found the Third Estate's representatives 'were, for the most part, not capitalist merchants or industrialists but office-holders, lawyers, and professionals — a group whose wealth was drawn from venal offices and landed rents.'
explanations.A: Reverses what Cobban found; this is the Lefebvrian picture he challenged.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Plausible-world detail the passage never supplies.
explanations.D: Out of scope; the passage does not discuss tenant farmers.
explanations.E: Out of scope; urban artisans and rural clergy are not mentioned.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the reformulation described in the final paragraph is best characterized as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of an account that has resolved the disputes among earlier historians

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautious approval, tempered by recognition that the new account sacrifices narrative drive

choices.label: C
choices.text: skepticism about a compromise position that evades the choice between Lefebvre and Cobban

choices.label: D
choices.text: detached neutrality toward a reformulation whose acceptance remains in dispute

choices.label: E
choices.text: frustration that the reformulation has failed to satisfy readers who prefer Lefebvre's clarity

explanations.correct: The author credits the reformulation with preserving what was durable in Lefebvre and accepting what was forceful in Cobban, and closes by saying it offers 'a version of the Revolution that the sources will actually support' — clear approval. The passage also flags the 'cost' of lost narrative drive. Cautious approval, tempered by that acknowledgment, is exactly B.
explanations.A: Overstates: the passage explicitly notes a cost.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite direction: the author treats the compromise as disciplined by evidence, not as evasion.
explanations.D: The final paragraph takes a clear evaluative position.
explanations.E: Frustration is not the tone; the author accepts the loss of drive as the price of fidelity to sources.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of parish registers, notarial archives, and tax rolls in the final paragraph functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the kinds of sources that have enabled historians to complicate Cobban's prosopographic picture of eighteenth-century French wealth

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that Cobban's reliance on occupational data alone has been decisively repudiated by specialists in archival research

choices.label: C
choices.text: introduce a methodological digression on the documentary resources available for the study of eighteenth-century France

choices.label: D
choices.text: provide evidence that the French Revolution was indeed the political triumph of a rising commercial class, contrary to Cobban

choices.label: E
choices.text: demonstrate that later social historians have relied on a wider range of sources than Lefebvre or Cobban did

explanations.correct: The archival sources appear in the sentence that says the boundary between commercial and office-holding wealth 'was more porous than Cobban's prosopography suggested.' Their function is to illustrate the evidence that has blurred that boundary.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Too strong: the passage says the picture has been complicated, not that Cobban has been 'decisively repudiated' — and the final paragraph preserves the force of his evidence.
explanations.C: Wrong grain: the mention is not a digression but a compressed evidentiary citation.
explanations.D: Reverses the passage: the new evidence does not restore the Lefebvrian thesis.
explanations.E: Accurate content, wrong function: the point is not a source comparison but a correction to Cobban's specific claim.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about Lefebvre's account of the French Revolution?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It should be dismissed as an artifact of the ideological commitments of an earlier generation of historians.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its attention to the social composition of the revolutionary movement remains valuable, even though its identification of that composition as straightforwardly bourgeois has not held up.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its principal weakness was a failure to consult the notarial and parish records that later historians would exploit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It correctly identified the Third Estate's deputies as representatives of a rising commercial class.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its coherence as a narrative outweighs any empirical difficulties that have been raised against it.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says the reformulation 'preserves what was durable in Lefebvre's attention to social structure while accepting the force of Cobban's evidence that the social structure in question was not simply bourgeois.' B is a precise paraphrase of that endorsement-with-qualification.
explanations.A: Too strong: the passage preserves something of Lefebvre, not dismisses him.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage does not blame Lefebvre for not using sources that became central in later work.
explanations.D: Reverses the passage: the Third Estate deputies were not, on Cobban's evidence, a rising commercial class.
explanations.E: Inverts the author's priorities: the passage accepts loss of narrative drive as the cost of empirical fidelity.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the reformulated account of the French Revolution described in the final paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A newly discovered set of merchant ledgers shows that commercial profits in eighteenth-century France were larger than previously estimated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A systematic study of the cahiers de doléances reveals that grievances against the old regime were voiced with equal intensity by office-holders, merchants, and professionals but diverged sharply when remedies were proposed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Parish registers demonstrate that population growth in French cities outpaced that in the countryside during the decades preceding 1789.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A monograph on a single province shows that its Third Estate delegation consisted almost entirely of capitalist merchants.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Contemporary pamphleteers used the word 'bourgeois' in a sense broad enough to include office-holders and professionals.

explanations.correct: The reformulated account holds that the Revolution emerged from 'a shifting coalition of groups whose members shared grievances against the old regime without sharing a unified economic program.' Evidence that grievances were shared across occupational categories but that proposed remedies diverged is precisely the pattern that coalition-without-unified-program predicts.
explanations.A: Off-target: larger commercial profits would tend to revive a Lefebvrian reading, not support the coalition account.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Demographic trends do not speak to the coalition claim.
explanations.D: Would support Lefebvre, not the reformulated account.
explanations.E: Addresses vocabulary, not whether the coalition shared an economic program.

rc.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, sociologists who studied the professions treated them as an unambiguous good. On the influential account developed by Talcott Parsons in the 1940s and refined by his students, an occupation such as medicine or law earned the title of profession by virtue of a trio of features: a body of esoteric knowledge acquired through long training, a set of ethical standards that bound practitioners to serve clients' interests rather than their own, and a system of collegial self-regulation that prevented abuse of the specialized authority clients had to grant. On this reading, professional autonomy was the price society paid, and should pay willingly, for competent and disinterested service.

That picture was challenged in the 1970s by a group of sociologists — Eliot Freidson, Magali Larson, and Andrew Abbott among the most prominent — who argued that Parsons had mistaken the professions' self-description for their sociological reality. On this revisionist view, professions are better understood as occupational groups that have successfully organized to secure control over a segment of the labor market. The esoteric knowledge is real, but it also serves as an entry barrier; the ethical code is real, but it also legitimates the group's claim to exclude outsiders; and self-regulation, whatever its protections, also insulates members from the kinds of accountability imposed on ordinary workers. Where Parsons saw a functional exchange, the revisionists saw an exercise of power, achieved through what Larson called a 'professional project' of market closure.

Recent scholarship has tried to hold both accounts in view. The revisionists were surely right that Parsons understated the interests served by professional organization, and case studies of medicine, law, and accountancy in the twentieth century repeatedly find episodes in which professional bodies acted to exclude competitors or to shield members from outside scrutiny. But a purely market-closure account has trouble explaining why clients, regulators, and the wider public continue to treat professional claims seriously, and why the most egregious failures of self-regulation — when they are exposed — generate the kind of scandal that treats betrayal, rather than mere self-interest, as the appropriate category. That reaction makes sense only if the service-oriented commitments Parsons described are still, to some degree, believed. The professions, on the current reading, are neither the selfless institutions of functionalist description nor the naked cartels of the revisionist counter-picture; they are hybrid arrangements whose legitimacy depends on a plausible performance of disinterest even when the incentives for self-dealing are strong.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Talcott Parsons's functionalist account of the professions has been conclusively refuted by the market-closure analyses of Freidson, Larson, and Abbott.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because self-regulation has so often failed in medicine, law, and accountancy, professions should be subjected to the same accountability mechanisms as ordinary occupations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sociology of the professions has moved from a functionalist picture of disinterested service, through a revisionist picture of market closure, toward a hybrid account on which legitimacy depends on a plausible performance of disinterest.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Magali Larson's concept of the 'professional project' has become the dominant analytic framework for understanding the development of the modern professions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Scandals involving failures of professional self-regulation demonstrate that the public's faith in the professions' ethical commitments has been systematically misplaced.

explanations.correct: The passage traces three views in order — Parsons's functionalism (paragraph 1), the revisionist market-closure account (paragraph 2), and a hybrid synthesis (paragraph 3) on which professional legitimacy depends on a 'plausible performance of disinterest.' C captures all three moves.
explanations.A: Overstated: the passage says the revisionists were 'surely right' on one point, not that Parsons has been refuted.
explanations.B: Too strong and outside scope: the author does not recommend accountability reforms.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Too narrow: Larson's term is one element in a broader analytic development.
explanations.E: Paragraph-level restatement that misreads the author, who treats public reaction to scandals as evidence that the service-oriented commitments are still believed.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Parsons's account identified which one of the following as among the defining features of a profession?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Credentialing examinations administered by the state rather than by the professional body itself

choices.label: B
choices.text: A body of esoteric knowledge acquired through long training

choices.label: C
choices.text: An openness to competitive entry from adjacent occupations

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fees calibrated to the market rate of comparable unskilled labor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Public oversight of individual disciplinary proceedings

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 lists the trio of features Parsons identified: 'a body of esoteric knowledge acquired through long training,' 'a set of ethical standards,' and 'a system of collegial self-regulation.'
explanations.A: Reverses Parsons's picture: self-regulation, not state credentialing, is the feature he named.
explanations.B: Correct.
