explanations.C: Contradicts Parsons: his picture emphasized controlled entry, not openness.
explanations.D: Out of scope; fees are not discussed.
explanations.E: Contradicts Parsons: self-regulation excluded external oversight of discipline.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the revisionist account developed by Freidson, Larson, and Abbott is best described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unreserved endorsement of an account that has definitively replaced Parsons's functionalism

choices.label: B
choices.text: respect for its corrective insight, tempered by judgment that on its own it cannot explain the public's sustained reaction to professional scandals

choices.label: C
choices.text: dismissal of a polemical critique whose conclusions have not survived subsequent case-study work

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutrality toward a view whose prospects the author declines to evaluate

choices.label: E
choices.text: sharp disagreement rooted in a preference for Parsons's earlier formulation

explanations.correct: The author says the revisionists 'were surely right' that Parsons understated interests, but argues that a 'purely market-closure account has trouble explaining' the public's scandal reaction. That is respect plus a limitation — exactly B.
explanations.A: Overstates: the passage denies that the revisionist view alone suffices.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Opposite valence: the author credits the revisionists.
explanations.D: The final paragraph takes a clear evaluative stance.
explanations.E: The author also credits the revisionists against Parsons; no preference for Parsons is expressed.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of public reaction to 'the most egregious failures of self-regulation' (in paragraph 3) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: concede that professional self-regulation has failed so often that the functionalist picture can no longer be defended

choices.label: B
choices.text: supply evidence that the service-oriented commitments Parsons described are, to some degree, still believed and therefore not reducible to market closure

choices.label: C
choices.text: illustrate the political difficulties that professional bodies face when their internal disputes become public

choices.label: D
choices.text: distinguish the accountancy profession, which has experienced more public scandal, from medicine and law

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that scandal, rather than routine regulation, is the most effective mechanism for disciplining the professions

explanations.correct: The author says the scandal reaction 'makes sense only if the service-oriented commitments Parsons described are still, to some degree, believed.' The reference is offered as evidence that the revisionist market-closure account is incomplete.
explanations.A: Reverses the author's conclusion: the scandal reaction is taken to show Parsons's picture is still partly operative.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Wrong grain: the passage is interested in public reaction, not in professional bodies' political difficulties.
explanations.D: No distinction among medicine, law, and accountancy is drawn in the passage.
explanations.E: Outside scope; the passage does not recommend scandal as a disciplinary mechanism.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that, on the author's current reading, a profession could lose its claim to legitimacy if

choices.label: A
choices.text: its members were required, for the first time, to acquire their knowledge through long formal training

choices.label: B
choices.text: competing occupations were permitted to perform tasks previously reserved to it

choices.label: C
choices.text: the service-oriented performance on which its authority rests ceased to be plausible to clients, regulators, and the wider public

choices.label: D
choices.text: sociologists convinced the public that the revisionist account was entirely correct and Parsons's account entirely wrong

choices.label: E
choices.text: the profession's ethical code were codified in state statute rather than in the profession's own charter

explanations.correct: The final paragraph says professions are 'hybrid arrangements whose legitimacy depends on a plausible performance of disinterest.' If that performance ceased to be plausible to the relevant audiences, legitimacy would, on the author's account, fail. C is a hedged paraphrase.
explanations.A: Out of scope; the passage does not treat the introduction of formal training as a legitimacy threshold.
explanations.B: Off-target: market-closure competition is one pressure but not what the author identifies as the condition of legitimacy.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage concerns sociological analysis, not whether public opinion about sociology affects legitimacy.
explanations.E: Out of scope; statutory codification is not addressed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations is most closely analogous to the 'hybrid arrangement' the author attributes to the professions in the final paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A charitable foundation that raises funds solely to deliver services to those in need, and that discloses all expenditures in an audited annual report.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A cartel of manufacturers that fixes prices through secret agreements, deriving its profits entirely from the elimination of competition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A judicial body whose authority over the parties before it depends on their continued belief in its impartiality, and whose exclusive jurisdiction also shields its members from outside review.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A publicly traded corporation whose directors are elected by shareholders and whose financial performance is monitored by regulators.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A labor union whose members negotiate wages collectively and whose internal discipline is enforced by elected officers.

explanations.correct: The author's principle is that legitimacy depends on a plausible performance of disinterest even when the insider group also enjoys the advantages of market closure. A judicial body whose authority rests on perceived impartiality while its exclusive jurisdiction insulates its members is a close instance of that dual structure.
explanations.A: Matches only the service-oriented half; no closure-like insulation is described.
explanations.B: Matches only the closure half, with no service-oriented performance that could fail or succeed.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Corporate governance involves shareholder monitoring and external regulation — accountability mechanisms the passage explicitly contrasts with professional self-regulation.
explanations.E: A union bargains on behalf of its own members; no claim of disinterested service to clients or the public is in play.

questions.questionStem: The phrase 'professional project' as used in the passage most nearly refers to

choices.label: A
choices.text: a coordinated program of research in which members of a profession define their field's central problems

choices.label: B
choices.text: an organized effort by an occupational group to secure control over a segment of the labor market

choices.label: C
choices.text: the long course of formal training that produces a profession's esoteric knowledge

choices.label: D
choices.text: an individual practitioner's career plan for moving from apprentice to senior status

choices.label: E
choices.text: a government initiative aimed at bringing new occupations under professional regulation

explanations.correct: The term is introduced in paragraph 2 alongside 'market closure': 'an exercise of power, achieved through what Larson called a professional project of market closure.' The contextual sense is the organized effort to secure labor-market control.
explanations.A: Common-meaning trap: in ordinary usage 'project' can mean a research program, but the passage uses the term in Larson's narrower sense.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Conflates 'professional project' with one of the features (training) rather than the market-closure effort.
explanations.D: Wrong grain: the term names a collective phenomenon, not an individual career plan.
explanations.E: Reverses agency: in the passage, the project is the occupational group's own, not a government initiative.

rc.difficultyReason: Three competing historiographical positions (James, Trouillot, Dubois) with nested comparisons across methodological commitments. The author's stance is only inferable from a pattern of qualified concessions: the author grants James his revisionist achievement, treats Trouillot's silence thesis as the most penetrating diagnostic, yet quietly withholds endorsement of Trouillot's strongest form — a reservation visible only through the asymmetric reporting verbs in paragraph 4.
rc.passage:
For most of the twentieth century, Western historians treated the Haitian Revolution — the 1791–1804 uprising that ended French colonial slavery and produced the first Black republic in the Americas — as a peripheral episode in the larger drama of the French Revolution. C.L.R. James broke decisively with that framing in 1938, arguing in The Black Jacobins that the enslaved laborers of Saint-Domingue were not passive beneficiaries of Parisian ideals but political actors whose demands reshaped metropolitan debate. James's account, written partly as an intervention in mid-century anticolonial politics, restored the revolution to the center of Atlantic history and remains the starting point for nearly all subsequent work.

But later scholars have argued that James, for all his innovations, inherited a problem he did not fully see. Michel-Rolph Trouillot, writing in the 1990s, contends that the real difficulty is not one of emphasis but of archive — that the revolution was, for its European contemporaries, literally unthinkable, and that this unthinkability produced systematic silences in the documents James necessarily drew upon. The planter correspondence, the diplomatic cables, even the abolitionist pamphlets, Trouillot argues, were structured by categories that rendered slave self-emancipation a conceptual impossibility; a historian who corrects the interpretation without interrogating the evidentiary frame merely reproduces the silence at a higher level.

Laurent Dubois, by contrast, accepts much of Trouillot's diagnosis but resists its most sweeping form. Dubois maintains that archival silences are uneven rather than uniform: revolutionary administrators in the French Caribbean left quite detailed records of their deliberations with formerly enslaved soldiers, and regimental rolls, petitions, and judicial testimony can be read — carefully, against the grain — to recover political thought that colonial observers failed to transcribe. Where Trouillot emphasizes what cannot be known, Dubois emphasizes what has not yet been read.

The disagreement is more than methodological. James, Trouillot, and Dubois all reject the older peripheral framing, but they rank the remaining tasks differently: James sought to restore a suppressed narrative; Trouillot sought to expose the epistemology that suppressed it; Dubois seeks to extend the archive by redirecting attention within it. Trouillot's position is the most searching of the three, and the one historians now most often cite — partly because it seems to offer an immunizing metacritique of any reconstruction that proceeds without it. Yet immunity has its costs. If every new source is, by stipulation, already distorted by the categories that produced it, the resources for correction grow scarce, and the field risks settling into a cycle of diagnosis rather than discovery.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Trouillot's critique of colonial archives offers a more penetrating account of the historiography of the Haitian Revolution than either James's or Dubois's, and should be adopted without the reservations Dubois proposes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although three successive scholars have reframed the historiography of the Haitian Revolution in valuable ways, the dominance of Trouillot's archival critique carries interpretive costs that its adherents have been slow to acknowledge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: James's restoration of the Haitian Revolution to the center of Atlantic history has been superseded by later scholarship that treats his account as naively narrative.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The historiography of the Haitian Revolution is best understood as a sequence of corrections in which each scholar repairs a specific blind spot left by a predecessor.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Dubois's archival practice demonstrates that the silences Trouillot identified in colonial records are less severe than Trouillot supposed.

explanations.correct: The passage surveys three reframings (James, Trouillot, Dubois), grants that each is valuable, singles out Trouillot's as the most influential and searching, and then — in the final two sentences — quietly registers the cost of that dominance. B captures both the survey and the concluding qualification.
explanations.A: Overshoots the author's stance: the passage does not call for adopting Trouillot without reservation; the final paragraph is precisely a reservation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The passage says James 'remains the starting point for nearly all subsequent work,' not that he has been superseded.
explanations.D: A plausible-sounding structural claim, but the author's final point is not 'each corrects a predecessor' — it is that the newest framework has immunizing costs.
explanations.E: Attributes to the author a ranking Dubois makes, not one the passage endorses; the author is careful not to claim Trouillot's thesis is empirically overstated.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Trouillot's position can most accurately be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: unreserved endorsement of its diagnostic reach

choices.label: B
choices.text: appreciation for its analytical power combined with wariness of its self-sealing tendency

choices.label: C
choices.text: skepticism that silences in the colonial archive are as systematic as Trouillot claims

choices.label: D
choices.text: resigned acceptance of a framework the author regards as flawed but unavoidable

choices.label: E
choices.text: enthusiasm tempered by concern that Trouillot unfairly marginalizes James

explanations.correct: The author calls Trouillot's position 'the most searching of the three' (appreciation) and then warns that its immunizing metacritique may produce 'a cycle of diagnosis rather than discovery' (wariness of a self-sealing tendency). B captures both strands at the right intensity.
explanations.A: 'Unreserved' conflicts with the final paragraph's reservation.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The author does not dispute the empirical reach of the silences; the concern is methodological self-sealing, not factual overstatement.
explanations.D: Too negative — the author calls Trouillot's position the most searching, not merely unavoidable.
explanations.E: The passage says Trouillot builds on James, not that he marginalizes him; this is the wrong feature to target.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A founding account is presented; two successive critiques of that account are summarized; the author evaluates the relative standing of the three positions and notes a drawback of the most influential one.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A historical event is described; three scholars offer competing factual reconstructions; the author adjudicates among them in favor of the earliest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A methodological dispute is introduced; each of three scholars proposes a different solution; the author endorses a synthesis none of them proposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A conventional view is stated and rejected; a replacement view is defended; two minor refinements to the replacement view are considered and dismissed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A sequence of interpretive frameworks is listed in chronological order, and the author concludes that the most recent framework is empirically flawed.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces James's founding account; paragraphs 2 and 3 present Trouillot's and Dubois's critiques; paragraph 4 ranks the three and flags the cost of Trouillot's dominance. A tracks all four paragraphs accurately.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The scholars are not offering competing factual reconstructions of the revolution itself; they disagree about historiographical method.
explanations.C: The author does not propose a synthesis; the final paragraph registers a concern, not a fourth position.
explanations.D: Dubois's view is not 'dismissed'; the author treats it as a reasonable moderation of Trouillot.
explanations.E: The author's concern with Trouillot is methodological (self-sealing), not empirical; describing Trouillot as 'empirically flawed' misstates the critique.

questions.questionStem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that the author would agree with which one of the following statements about Dubois's approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It represents a return to the pre-Jamesian framing of the Haitian Revolution as peripheral to European events.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It rejects the premise that colonial archives contain systematic silences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It preserves the critical insight of Trouillot's position while leaving more room for new historical findings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has displaced Trouillot's framework as the dominant approach in the field.

choices.label: E
choices.text: It treats regimental rolls and judicial testimony as unmediated records of the political thought of formerly enslaved people.

explanations.correct: The author says Dubois 'accepts much of Trouillot's diagnosis but resists its most sweeping form' and reads sources 'against the grain.' Combined with the final paragraph's worry about a cycle of diagnosis, Dubois's moderated position is precisely the kind of approach that keeps room for discovery while preserving the critical insight. C is hedged in the right way.
explanations.A: Contradicts the passage — Dubois joins James and Trouillot in rejecting the peripheral framing.
explanations.B: Too strong — Dubois accepts Trouillot's diagnosis in large part; he denies only its most sweeping form.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly says historians 'now most often cite' Trouillot, not Dubois.
explanations.E: Dubois reads sources 'against the grain,' which implies mediated reading, not unmediated transcription.

questions.questionStem: The author's reference to regimental rolls, petitions, and judicial testimony (third paragraph) functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate the specific kinds of evidence Dubois believes can still be recovered despite the silences Trouillot identifies

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide examples of the sources James relied on in The Black Jacobins

choices.label: C
choices.text: suggest that Trouillot overlooked straightforward empirical resources available in the archive

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that colonial record-keeping was more extensive than either James or Trouillot acknowledged

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce a fourth interpretive position distinct from those of James, Trouillot, and Dubois

explanations.correct: The list is introduced as part of Dubois's argument that 'archival silences are uneven rather than uniform' and that specific source types 'can be read — carefully, against the grain' to recover political thought. Its rhetorical function is to make Dubois's moderation concrete.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: James is not the referent of the third paragraph; the list is attached to Dubois's methodological claim.
explanations.C: The author does not endorse the view that Trouillot overlooked these sources; Dubois's point is about unevenness of silence, not Trouillot's blindness. This is a wrong-function trap: accurate content but incorrect purpose.
explanations.D: No claim is made about colonial record-keeping being more extensive than acknowledged — the claim is about uneven silence.
explanations.E: Dubois's own position uses these sources; they do not introduce a fourth view.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following scenarios most closely parallels the concern the author raises in the final paragraph about Trouillot's position?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An economist revises a model to accommodate new data, then publishes a corrected prediction the following year.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A literary critic argues that every literary judgment is shaped by unacknowledged class position — a claim that, if accepted, discredits any rival reading in advance without requiring the critic to engage its details.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A biologist discovers that a long-used laboratory technique introduces a previously unnoticed artifact into results and retracts several earlier papers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A policy analyst synthesizes two rival schools of thought into a single framework that each school partially endorses.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A geologist refuses to accept a new dating technique until multiple laboratories have independently confirmed its accuracy.

explanations.correct: The author's worry is that Trouillot's metacritique is self-sealing: any new source is 'by stipulation, already distorted,' so rivals are discredited in advance. B instantiates exactly this load-bearing feature — a claim that wins against rivals without having to engage their specifics.
explanations.A: Model revision in light of data is the opposite of the author's concern; it is responsive, not self-sealing.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Retraction based on discovered artifact is ordinary error-correction, not immunizing metacritique.
explanations.D: Synthesis is a cooperative move; the author's concern is about a move that forecloses engagement.
explanations.E: Demanding independent confirmation is a standard epistemic check, not a self-sealing discrediting of rivals.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, which one of the following is a claim that James, Trouillot, and Dubois all share?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The colonial archive's silences are uniform across document types.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Haitian Revolution should not be treated as peripheral to the French Revolution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Historians cannot recover the political thought of formerly enslaved soldiers from existing records.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mid-century anticolonial politics distorted earlier accounts of the revolution.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The categories used by European contemporaries rendered slave self-emancipation unthinkable.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 4 states: 'James, Trouillot, and Dubois all reject the older peripheral framing.' That is the one claim the passage explicitly attributes to all three.
explanations.A: Uniformity of silence is Trouillot's strong form; Dubois resists it. Not shared.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: This is closer to the strongest form of Trouillot's view; Dubois explicitly resists it.
explanations.D: The passage notes James wrote partly as an intervention in mid-century anticolonial politics but does not say the other two share a view about distortion from that.
explanations.E: This is Trouillot's specific claim about unthinkability; the passage does not attribute it to James or Dubois.

rc.difficultyReason: Three sociological accounts of the emergence of the modern accounting profession (Larson's market-closure thesis, Abbott's jurisdictional-competition thesis, and MacDonald's cultural-authority thesis), with nested comparisons across mechanisms (credentialing, inter-professional conflict, symbolic legitimacy). The author's stance is subtly skeptical of pure market-closure accounts and sympathetic to Abbott without fully endorsing him — visible only through the distribution of reporting verbs ('argues' vs. 'establishes') and the asymmetric objections noted in paragraph 3.
rc.passage:
The modern accounting profession emerged in Britain between roughly 1850 and 1900, consolidating through a series of chartered institutes whose members could audit the books of limited-liability firms. Sociologists have offered sharply different explanations for why this consolidation succeeded when earlier attempts had not. According to Magali Sarfatti Larson, the chartered institutes were primarily engines of market closure: by binding a credential to a legally protected title, accountants converted an ordinary service into a scarce commodity and secured rents that non-chartered bookkeepers could not. Larson's account is elegant and has been widely imitated in studies of other occupations.

Andrew Abbott acknowledges the importance of credentialing but argues that market closure alone cannot explain why the accounting institutes prevailed against rival occupations also seeking professional status. On Abbott's view, professions develop within a system of jurisdictional competition — ongoing contests in which one occupation attempts to claim exclusive authority over a particular kind of work, often at the expense of neighbors. Chartered accountants, Abbott contends, won their jurisdiction not by inventing a credential but by out-competing solicitors and actuaries for the specific task of audit once corporate statutes made audit legally mandatory. Credentialing, in this telling, follows jurisdictional success rather than producing it.

A third line, associated with Keith MacDonald, allows for both mechanisms but insists they depend on a prior resource neither Larson nor Abbott fully explains: cultural authority, the tacit trust that certain kinds of numbers, produced by certain kinds of people, deserve to be treated as facts. Without this prior trust, MacDonald maintains, a credentialed monopoly would be an empty title and a jurisdictional victory a hollow one. Clients, courts, and regulators had to come to regard the chartered accountant's signature as presumptively authoritative, and this cultural shift cannot be reduced to the institute's lobbying or its jurisdictional maneuvers.

The dispute is not symmetrical. Larson's thesis, though influential, struggles to account for occupations that achieved legal credentials but failed commercially, as several nineteenth-century surveying institutes did. Abbott's jurisdictional model absorbs this anomaly comfortably, since jurisdiction must be won against rivals and sometimes is not. MacDonald's challenge is harder to dismiss in principle, but it is also harder to operationalize: it is not clear what evidence, short of the outcome it is meant to explain, would establish that cultural authority had shifted prior to the institutes' success. Until that evidentiary question is settled, MacDonald's contribution is best understood as a standing caution rather than a rival account — a reminder that credentialing and jurisdiction do not suspend themselves in a vacuum.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Three competing explanations of the rise of the modern accounting profession are available, and only MacDonald's account of cultural authority is supported by the historical record.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Market-closure, jurisdictional-competition, and cultural-authority accounts of the accounting profession each capture something real, but on present evidence the jurisdictional account is the strongest, while the cultural-authority account functions best as a caution rather than a rival.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Larson's market-closure thesis has been decisively refuted by the historical record of nineteenth-century British professions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The emergence of the modern accounting profession cannot be explained by any single sociological mechanism and requires a fully integrated framework.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Credentialing, jurisdictional competition, and cultural authority are three stages through which every professionalizing occupation must pass.

explanations.correct: The passage surveys three accounts, notes the specific weakness of Larson's thesis (surveying institutes that got credentials but failed), credits Abbott with 'absorbing' that anomaly, and characterizes MacDonald's contribution as a 'standing caution rather than a rival account.' B captures all three assessments at the right intensity.
explanations.A: The passage does not claim MacDonald alone is supported; it specifically notes MacDonald's evidentiary problem.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: 'Decisively refuted' overstates; the passage says Larson 'struggles to account for' certain cases, not that the thesis has been refuted.
explanations.D: The passage does not call for an integrated framework; it ranks the three unequally.
explanations.E: No claim is made about a universal sequence of stages.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following best describes the author's attitude toward MacDonald's cultural-authority thesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dismissive, on the ground that the thesis is circular

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enthusiastic, because it supplies what Larson and Abbott omit

choices.label: C
choices.text: Respectful in principle but unconvinced that the thesis has yet been given independent evidential support

choices.label: D
choices.text: Indifferent, since the thesis is outside the scope of the passage's inquiry

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hostile, because the thesis cannot be reconciled with Abbott's jurisdictional model

explanations.correct: The author says MacDonald's challenge 'is harder to dismiss in principle' (respect) but that it 'is not clear what evidence, short of the outcome it is meant to explain, would establish' the claim (unconvinced about independent support). C captures both the valence and the intensity.
explanations.A: 'Dismissive' is too strong; the author says the thesis is 'harder to dismiss in principle.' The author's worry is operationalization, not circularity per se.
explanations.B: 'Enthusiastic' is overstated; the author declines to treat MacDonald as a rival account.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: The author engages with the thesis at length — not indifferent.
explanations.E: The author does not portray MacDonald as incompatible with Abbott; MacDonald 'allows for both' mechanisms.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any sociological account of professionalization that fails to explain commercial failure as well as success is at that point inadequate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jurisdictional competition is a sufficient condition for an occupation to achieve professional status.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cultural authority plays no role in the success of professional institutes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Market-closure mechanisms are irrelevant to the study of modern professions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: MacDonald's thesis should be accepted whenever Larson's thesis fails to fit the evidence.

explanations.correct: The author's specific complaint against Larson is that the market-closure thesis 'struggles to account for' institutes that 'achieved legal credentials but failed commercially,' and explicitly credits Abbott for 'absorbing this anomaly.' The general principle underwriting that complaint is A — explaining both success and failure matters. The inference is hedged appropriately.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: The author treats jurisdictional competition as the strongest account but never claims it is sufficient; MacDonald's caution is taken seriously.
explanations.C: Reverses the author's position: the author says MacDonald is 'harder to dismiss in principle.'
explanations.D: Too strong; the author says Larson's account has been 'widely imitated' and never claims market closure is irrelevant.
explanations.E: The author explicitly declines to treat MacDonald as a rival account; a fallback-to-MacDonald rule is not endorsed.

questions.questionStem: The reference to nineteenth-century surveying institutes in the final paragraph functions primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: provide an example of an occupation that succeeded through cultural authority rather than credentialing

choices.label: B
choices.text: identify a counterexample to Larson's market-closure thesis that Abbott's model accommodates but Larson's does not

choices.label: C
choices.text: illustrate the kind of evidence that would be needed to confirm MacDonald's thesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: suggest that the chartered accountants' institute modeled itself on earlier surveying institutes

choices.label: E
choices.text: show that legal credentialing was rarely granted to nineteenth-century British occupations

explanations.correct: The surveying institutes are cited as cases of 'occupations that achieved legal credentials but failed commercially' — precisely the pattern Larson's thesis struggles with and Abbott's absorbs. Their function is comparative adjudication between Larson and Abbott.
explanations.A: MacDonald is not connected to the surveying institutes in the passage.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: The reference is used against Larson and for Abbott; it is not offered as the evidence MacDonald needs.
explanations.D: No institutional-modeling claim is made.
explanations.E: The passage implies the opposite — that legal credentialing was granted to institutes that nonetheless failed; frequency is not claimed to be low.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations is most closely analogous to the mechanism Abbott identifies as explaining the chartered accountants' success?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A guild of metalworkers petitions the legislature for a protected title, then uses that title to restrict entry into the trade.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A newly trained group of paramedics expands its scope of practice at the expense of nurses once emergency-response legislation specifies tasks only paramedics may perform, after which paramedic certification becomes mandatory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A regional dialect becomes prestigious because speakers of that dialect come to be regarded by the broader public as cultivated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A university redesigns its curriculum to match the entry requirements of a competitive job market.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A firm buys out its competitors and then raises prices for its services.

explanations.correct: Abbott's mechanism has three load-bearing features: (1) jurisdictional competition against rival occupations, (2) a legal change that creates a specific task, and (3) credentialing that follows the jurisdictional win rather than producing it. B instantiates all three: paramedics win a task from nurses when legislation creates it, and certification becomes mandatory afterward.
explanations.A: Matches Larson's market-closure mechanism (title-then-restriction), not Abbott's (jurisdictional contest).
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Matches MacDonald's cultural-authority mechanism, not Abbott's.
explanations.D: No inter-occupational competition; curriculum redesign lacks the jurisdictional-contest feature.
explanations.E: Ordinary monopoly consolidation — missing the inter-professional contest and the law-driven task creation.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken Larson's account of the accounting profession's consolidation as the author presents it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several occupations in nineteenth-century Britain that did not obtain legally protected titles nevertheless achieved durable commercial dominance in their fields.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The chartered accounting institutes spent large sums on parliamentary lobbying before their credentials were recognized.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Most chartered accountants in 1880 came from commercial rather than aristocratic backgrounds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Corporate statutes in the 1860s increased the demand for audit services faster than the supply of chartered accountants grew.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Non-chartered bookkeepers were able to serve small firms profitably throughout the late nineteenth century.

explanations.correct: Larson's thesis claims the legal credential is the engine of commercial success. Cases in which occupations achieved durable commercial dominance without legal credentials directly undermine that claim — the credential would not be necessary for the outcome it is said to produce. A targets the exact load-bearing feature the author's critique already flags.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Lobbying expenditure is consistent with — indeed supports — Larson's view that legal title matters.
explanations.C: Background of entrants doesn't affect the claim that credentials produce closure.
explanations.D: Excess demand is compatible with the credential creating scarce supply — a strengthener, not a weakener.
explanations.E: Small-firm bookkeeping outside chartered territory doesn't challenge Larson's claim about the chartered audit market; it is off-target.
explanations.other_notes: The trap to avoid is 'overreach' answers (B, D) that affect neighboring claims; the stem asks specifically about Larson's account of consolidation.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Abbott's account differs from Larson's in which one of the following ways?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abbott denies that credentialing plays any role in professionalization, whereas Larson treats credentialing as central.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Abbott treats credentialing as a consequence of a prior jurisdictional contest, whereas Larson treats it as the mechanism producing the profession's market position.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Abbott focuses on the cultural authority of numerical facts, whereas Larson focuses on rents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Abbott restricts his account to twentieth-century occupations, whereas Larson addresses the nineteenth century.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Abbott rejects the evidentiary record on which Larson relies.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that, on Abbott's view, 'Credentialing ... follows jurisdictional success rather than producing it,' while Larson is described in paragraph 1 as holding that binding a credential to a legally protected title is what produces the rents. B captures the ordering contrast exactly.
explanations.A: Abbott 'acknowledges the importance of credentialing'; he does not deny it plays a role.
explanations.B: Correct.
explanations.C: Cultural authority is MacDonald's theme, not Abbott's.
explanations.D: No such temporal restriction is mentioned.
explanations.E: No evidentiary-record dispute between the two is described.

lg.scenario: Exactly five university lectures — Ames, Boyd, Chen, Diaz, and Elkin — will be delivered one after another in five consecutive time slots numbered first through fifth. Each lecture is given in either the morning session or the afternoon session. The first three slots are in the morning; the last two slots are in the afternoon. The schedule must satisfy the following constraints. The Boyd lecture is given before the Chen lecture. The Diaz lecture and the Elkin lecture are given in immediately consecutive slots. The Ames lecture is not the fifth lecture.

rules.description: The first three slots are in the morning.
The last two slots are in the afternoon.

choices.text: 1(Ames, afternoon), 2(Boyd, morning), 3(Chen, morning), 4(Diaz, afternoon), 5(Elkin, afternoon)

explanations.correct: Boyd(2) is before Chen(3); Diaz(4) and Elkin(5) are in immediately consecutive slots; Ames(1) is not fifth; slots 1-3 are labeled morning and slots 4-5 are labeled afternoon. All constraints are satisfied.
explanations.A: Correct. Every constraint holds.
explanations.B: Boyd is in slot 3 and Chen is in slot 2, so Boyd is not before Chen.
explanations.C: Ames is in slot 5, violating the rule that Ames is not the fifth lecture.
explanations.D: Diaz is in slot 1 and Elkin is in slot 4; they are not in immediately consecutive slots.
explanations.E: Slot 1 is labeled afternoon, but the first three slots must be in the morning.

explanations.A: Correct. Chen occupies slot 2, 3, or 5 in every verified world.
explanations.B: Boyd can be in slot 4 (afternoon) in some worlds, so Boyd is not forced into the morning.
explanations.C: Ames appears in slots 1, 2, 3, or 4 across the verified worlds; not forced to 1.
explanations.D: Diaz can be in slot 4 or 5 in some worlds, so Diaz is not forced into the morning.
explanations.E: Elkin appears in slots 1-5 across verified worlds; not forced to slot 5.

explanations.A: Correct. In every Chen-at-3 world Boyd occupies slot 1 or 2.
explanations.B: Ames is at slot 1 in 2 of the 4 Chen-at-3 worlds and at slot 2 in the other 2; not forced.
explanations.C: Diaz is at slot 4 in 2 of the 4 Chen-at-3 worlds and at slot 5 in the other 2; not forced.
explanations.D: Elkin is at slot 4 or 5 with equal frequency; not forced to 5.

explanations.B: Ames is at slot 3 in one Elkin-at-1 world and at slot 4 in the other; not forced.
explanations.C: Boyd is at slot 3 (morning) in one world and slot 4 (afternoon) in the other; not forced.
explanations.D: Chen is at slot 5 in both Elkin-at-1 worlds, so Chen at slot 3 is false — this is not forced-true.

explanations.correct: Boyd must be given before Chen, so Chen cannot be first. Chen never appears in slot 1 in any verified world.
explanations.A: Boyd is at slot 3 in 2 verified worlds (e.g., Ames=4 afternoon, Boyd=3 morning, Chen=5, Diaz=2, Elkin=1).
explanations.B: Correct. Chen is never first because Boyd must precede Chen.
explanations.C: Diaz is at slot 3 in 4 verified worlds (e.g., Ames=1, Boyd=2, Chen=5, Diaz=3, Elkin=4).
explanations.D: Ames is at slot 4 in 4 verified worlds (e.g., Ames=4, Boyd=1, Chen=5, Diaz=2, Elkin=3).
explanations.E: Elkin is at slot 5 in 3 verified worlds (e.g., Ames=1, Boyd=2, Chen=3, Diaz=4, Elkin=5).

Quan does not sit in chair 1. Rios sits in a chair immediately adjacent to Sato's chair.

Chairs 2 and 4 are blue.

explanations.B: Park is in chair 5 and Sato is in chair 4, so Park is not before Sato.
explanations.C: Quan is in chair 1, violating the rule that Quan does not sit in chair 1.
explanations.D: Rios is in chair 2 and Sato is in chair 4, so Rios is not immediately adjacent to Sato.

explanations.C: Toma is in chair 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 across the worlds; not forced to 5.
explanations.D: Quan sits in chair 2 or 4 (blue) in some worlds, so Quan is not forced to red.

explanations.C: Rios appears in chairs 3, 4, or 5 when Toma=1; not forced to 4.

explanations.A: Park is at chair 2 in 4 worlds (e.g., Toma=1, Park=2, Quan=3, Rios=4, Sato=5).
explanations.B: Toma is at chair 1 in 6 worlds (e.g., Toma=1, Park=2, Quan=3, Rios=4, Sato=5).

explanations.E: Sato is at chair 2 in 2 worlds (e.g., Park=1, Sato=2, Rios=3, Quan=4, Toma=5).

lg.scenario: A bicycle courier will make exactly five deliveries — to Harris, Ingram, Jolen, Kato, and Lund — one after another, in order from first through fifth. The route zigzags between the north side of the street and the south side of the street: the first, third, and fifth stops are on the north side, and the second and fourth stops are on the south side. The route must satisfy the following constraints. The Harris delivery is made before the Ingram delivery. The Jolen delivery and the Kato delivery are made at immediately consecutive stops. The Lund delivery is not the first stop.

rules.description: Stops 1, 3, and 5 are on the north side.
Stops 2 and 4 are on the south side.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the complete delivery route, listed as stop(recipient, side) from first to fifth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1(Harris, north), 2(Ingram, south), 3(Jolen, north), 4(Kato, south), 5(Lund, north)

explanations.correct: Harris(1) is before Ingram(2); Jolen(3) and Kato(4) are at immediately consecutive stops; Lund(5) is not the first stop; stops 1, 3, 5 are north and stops 2, 4 are south. All constraints hold.
explanations.A: Correct. Every constraint holds.
explanations.B: Harris is at stop 2 and Ingram is at stop 1, so Harris is not before Ingram.
explanations.C: Jolen is at stop 1 and Kato is at stop 3; they are not at immediately consecutive stops.
explanations.D: Lund is at the first stop, violating the rule that Lund is not the first stop.
explanations.E: Stop 1 is labeled south, but the first stop must be on the north side.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.text: The Ingram delivery is at stop 5.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Lund delivery is at stop 5.

choices.label: D

explanations.correct: Harris must precede Ingram, so Harris cannot be at stop 5. Moreover, Harris cannot be at stop 2 (which would block adjacency for Jolen/Kato given Lund ≠ 1). Across all 18 verified worlds Harris appears only at stop 1, stop 3, or stop 4.
explanations.A: Correct. Harris occupies stop 1, 3, or 4 in every verified world.
explanations.B: Ingram appears at stops 2, 3, 4, or 5; not forced to 5.
explanations.C: Lund appears at stops 2, 3, 4, or 5; not forced to 5.
explanations.D: Jolen sits on the south side (stop 2 or 4) in several worlds; not forced to north.
explanations.E: Kato appears at stops 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5; not forced to 2.

questions.questionStem: If the Lund delivery is the fifth stop, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.text: The Harris delivery is at stop 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Jolen delivery is on the north side.

choices.label: E

explanations.A: Correct. Harris appears only at stop 1 or stop 3 when Lund is at stop 5.
explanations.B: Harris is at stop 1 in 4 of the 6 Lund-at-5 worlds and at stop 3 in the other 2; not forced.
explanations.C: Ingram is at stop 2, 3, or 4 when Lund=5; not forced to 2.
explanations.D: Jolen is on the south side in some Lund-at-5 worlds (e.g., Jolen=2); not forced to north.
explanations.E: Kato is at stop 2, 3, or 4 when Lund=5; not forced to 3.

questions.questionStem: If the Harris delivery is the fourth stop, then which one of the following must be true?

explanations.B: Lund is at stop 3 (north) in every Harris-at-4 world; Lund is not on the south side.
explanations.C: Jolen is at stop 1 or stop 2 when Harris=4; not forced to 2.
explanations.D: Kato is at stop 1 or stop 2 when Harris=4; not forced to 1.

explanations.A: Kato is at stop 4 in 4 verified worlds (e.g., Harris=1, Ingram=2, Jolen=3, Kato=4, Lund=5).
explanations.B: Ingram is at stop 2 in 4 verified worlds (e.g., Harris=1, Ingram=2, Jolen=3, Kato=4, Lund=5).
explanations.C: Correct. Lund cannot be the first stop by the explicit rule.
explanations.D: Lund is at stop 2 in 4 verified worlds (e.g., Harris=1, Ingram=3, Jolen=4, Kato=5, Lund=2).
explanations.E: Jolen is at stop 5 in 2 verified worlds (e.g., Harris=1, Ingram=2, Jolen=5, Kato=4, Lund=3).

lg.scenario: Exactly six talks — Alder, Banik, Cho, Dorsey, Epps, and Finch — will be scheduled at a one-day conference in six consecutive slots numbered first through sixth. Each talk is assigned to either the A-track or the B-track, with exactly three talks on each track. The schedule must satisfy the following constraints. The Alder talk is scheduled before the Dorsey talk. The Banik talk is scheduled immediately before or immediately after the Cho talk. The Epps talk is not the first talk. The Finch talk is scheduled before the Epps talk. The Alder talk and the Finch talk are not scheduled in immediately consecutive slots. The Dorsey talk is not the first talk. The Banik talk is scheduled before the Epps talk. The Alder talk is scheduled before the Epps talk. The Alder talk and the Dorsey talk are assigned to the same track. The Banik talk and the Cho talk are assigned to different tracks. The Epps talk and the Finch talk are assigned to the same track. The Alder talk and the Finch talk are assigned to different tracks. The talk in slot 3 is on the A-track. The talk in slot 6 is on the B-track.

rules.description: The talk in slot 3 is on the A-track.
The talk in slot 6 is on the B-track.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the complete assignment of talks to slots and tracks, listed as slot(talk, track) from first to sixth?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

Track counts: A = {Alder, Cho, Dorsey} and B = {Banik, Finch, Epps}, each 3.
explanations.A: Correct. Every ordinal and track rule is satisfied.
explanations.B: Dorsey is in slot 1, violating the rule that Dorsey is not the first talk.
explanations.C: Alder(1) and Finch(2) are in immediately consecutive slots, violating the not-adjacent rule.
explanations.D: Cho is on the B-track while assigned to slot 3, but the talk in slot 3 must be on the A-track.
explanations.E: Epps is assigned to the A-track, but Epps and Finch must be on the same track and Finch is on B; also violates the slot-6 = B rule.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Alder talk is on the A-track.

choices.label: E

explanations.correct: Epps is never first (given), Finch precedes Epps, Alder precedes Epps, and Banik precedes Epps, so at least three talks precede Epps. Since Dorsey also cannot precede Alder (Alder precedes Dorsey) but Dorsey may or may not precede Epps, Epps is forced into slot 5 or 6 across all 16 verified worlds.
explanations.A: Cho occupies slot 1, 2, 3, or 4 across the 16 worlds, so it is not forced into 3.
explanations.B: Alder is on the A-track in 12/16 worlds and on the B-track in 4/16 worlds. Not forced.
explanations.C: Correct. In all 16 verified worlds Epps is in slot 5 or slot 6.
explanations.D: Dorsey appears in slot 2, 4, 5, or 6 — not forced to 4.
explanations.E: Banik is on the A-track in 8/16 worlds and on the B-track in 8/16 worlds. Not forced.

questions.questionStem: If the Finch talk is in slot 1, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Alder talk is in slot 3.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Alder talk is in slot 4.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Dorsey talk is in slot 5.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Banik talk is in slot 2.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Cho talk is in slot 3.

explanations.correct: If Finch is at 1, then Alder cannot be at 2 (not adjacent to Finch), cannot be at 5 or 6 (before Epps, and Epps is at 5 or 6), and cannot be at 3 (the talk at 3 is on the A-track while Alder and Finch are on different tracks; also there is no valid Alder-at-3 world with Finch-at-1). Enumerating the four worlds with Finch=1 shows Alder is always in slot 4.
explanations.A: No world with Finch=1 has Alder=3.
explanations.B: Correct. All four Finch-at-1 worlds place Alder at slot 4.
explanations.C: Dorsey is at 5 or 6 in the Finch=1 worlds, so not forced to 5.
explanations.D: Banik is at 2 or 3 in the Finch=1 worlds, not forced.
explanations.E: Cho is at 2 or 3 in the Finch=1 worlds, not forced.

questions.questionStem: If the Epps talk is in slot 5, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Dorsey talk is in slot 6.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Alder talk is on the A-track.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Banik talk is in slot 3.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Cho talk is on the B-track.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Finch talk is in slot 4.

explanations.correct: Epps at 5 means slot 6 must be filled by someone after Epps in the ordering. Finch, Alder, and Banik all precede Epps and so cannot occupy slot 6. Slot 6 is also on the B-track. Cho is same-track as the slot-3 talk (A) only when Banik is at 3; otherwise Cho is at 3 and Banik is adjacent. Enumeration of the 4 Epps-at-5 worlds shows Dorsey is always the slot-6 talk.
explanations.A: Correct. All four Epps-at-5 worlds place Dorsey at slot 6.
explanations.B: When Epps is at 5, Alder is on the B-track in all four Epps-at-5 worlds (Alder is same-track as Dorsey, who is on B when at slot 6). So Alder is on B, not A — this choice is false, not forced-true.
explanations.C: Banik appears at slot 2 or 3 when Epps is at 5; not forced to 3.
explanations.D: Cho is on the A-track in all four Epps-at-5 worlds (because Cho is different-track from Banik, and Banik settles to A or B depending on slot). Not forced to B — in fact, Cho is always A here.
explanations.E: Finch is at slot 1 in two Epps-at-5 worlds and at slot 4 in two. Not forced to any single slot.

questions.questionStem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Banik talk is in slot 1.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Cho talk is in slot 4.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Alder talk is in slot 5.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Dorsey talk is in slot 2.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Finch talk is in slot 1.

explanations.correct: Alder must come before Dorsey and before Epps. Since Dorsey cannot be first, Alder occupies slot 1, 3, or 4 in every verified world. Alder is never in slot 5 — if Alder were at 5, Dorsey (after Alder) would have to be at 6 and Epps (after Alder) would also have to be after 5, but Epps can only be at 5 or 6, leaving no room.
explanations.A: Banik is in slot 1 in some worlds (e.g., Alder=3, Banik=1, Cho=2, Dorsey=4, Epps=6, Finch=5).
explanations.B: Cho is in slot 4 in some worlds (e.g., Alder=1, Banik=3, Cho=4, Dorsey=2, Epps=6, Finch=5).
explanations.C: Correct. Alder is in slot 1, 3, or 4 in every verified world; Alder is never in slot 5.
explanations.D: Dorsey is in slot 2 in some worlds (e.g., Alder=1, Banik=3, Cho=4, Dorsey=2, Epps=6, Finch=5).
explanations.E: Finch is in slot 1 in some worlds (e.g., Alder=4, Banik=2, Cho=3, Dorsey=5, Epps=6, Finch=1).

lg.scenario: At a small gallery opening, exactly five patrons — Perez, Quinn, Ruiz, Soto, and Tang — will occupy five seats arranged in a row and numbered first through fifth. Each patron wears either a crimson jacket or a navy jacket, and exactly three wear crimson and exactly two wear navy. The seating and jackets must satisfy the following. Perez does not sit in the first seat. Perez does not sit in the fifth seat. Quinn sits in some seat before Ruiz. Soto and Tang sit in immediately consecutive seats. Tang sits in some seat before Perez. Soto and Tang wear jackets of different colors. Quinn and Ruiz wear jackets of the same color. The patron in the second seat wears a navy jacket.

rules.description: The patron in the second seat wears a navy jacket.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the complete seating and jacket assignment, listed as seat(patron, jacket) from first to fifth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1(Soto, crimson), 2(Tang, navy), 3(Perez, navy), 4(Quinn, crimson), 5(Ruiz, crimson)

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1(Soto, crimson), 2(Tang, crimson), 3(Perez, navy), 4(Quinn, crimson), 5(Ruiz, navy)

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1(Quinn, crimson), 2(Perez, navy), 3(Soto, crimson), 4(Tang, navy), 5(Ruiz, crimson)

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1(Tang, crimson), 2(Perez, navy), 3(Soto, navy), 4(Quinn, crimson), 5(Ruiz, crimson)

choices.label: E
choices.text: 1(Soto, navy), 2(Tang, crimson), 3(Perez, navy), 4(Quinn, crimson), 5(Ruiz, crimson)

explanations.correct: Perez(3) is not at 1 or 5; Quinn(4) before Ruiz(5); Soto(1) and Tang(2) adjacent; Tang(2) before Perez(3); Soto(crimson) and Tang(navy) different colors; Quinn(crimson) and Ruiz(crimson) same color; jacket counts crimson=3, navy=2; the patron in seat 2 (Tang) wears navy.
explanations.A: Correct. All rules hold.
explanations.B: Soto(crimson) and Tang(crimson) are the same color, violating the different-colors rule.
explanations.C: Tang is seated fourth and Perez is seated second, so Tang is not before Perez.
explanations.D: Soto and Tang are not seated in immediately consecutive positions (Soto is at 3 and Tang is at 1).
explanations.E: The patron in seat 2 (Tang) wears crimson, violating the cross-dimensional rule that seat 2 is navy.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perez sits in the third seat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tang wears a navy jacket.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ruiz sits in the fifth seat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Soto sits in the first seat.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quinn wears a navy jacket.

explanations.correct: Ruiz must follow Quinn, and no other patron has a forced position after Ruiz; enumerating all 6 verified worlds shows Ruiz is always in seat 5.
explanations.A: Perez is at seat 3 or 4 — not forced to 3.
explanations.B: Tang is navy in 3 worlds and crimson in 3 worlds. Not forced.
explanations.C: Correct. Ruiz is at seat 5 in all 6 verified worlds.
explanations.D: Soto is at seat 1, 2, or 3 — not forced to 1.
explanations.E: Quinn wears crimson in all 6 worlds (not navy). The statement that Quinn wears navy is actually false in every world.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tang wears a navy jacket.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perez wears a crimson jacket.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Quinn wears a navy jacket.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ruiz sits in the fourth seat.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Soto sits in the fourth seat.

explanations.correct: Tang wears a navy jacket in 3 of the 6 verified worlds (the worlds where Tang is seated second or where Soto is crimson and Tang is navy).
explanations.A: Correct. Tang wears navy in 3/6 worlds (e.g., Soto=1 crimson, Tang=2 navy, Perez=3 navy, Quinn=4 crimson, Ruiz=5 crimson).
explanations.B: Perez wears navy in every verified world (Perez is at seat 3 or 4 and wears navy in all 6). Perez never wears crimson.
explanations.C: Quinn wears crimson in every verified world (forced because Quinn/Ruiz are the same color and Ruiz is at seat 5, which is crimson in every world). Quinn never wears navy.
explanations.D: Ruiz is at seat 5 in every verified world. Ruiz is never at seat 4.
explanations.E: Soto is at seat 1, 2, or 3 in every verified world. Soto is never at seat 4.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true about the jacket colors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Soto wears a crimson jacket.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tang wears a navy jacket.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perez wears a navy jacket.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Soto and Quinn wear jackets of the same color.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tang and Quinn wear jackets of different colors.

explanations.correct: Perez is at seat 3 or 4 in every world, and Perez is navy in every verified world. This follows because Quinn and Ruiz must be same color (and they fill the two highest seats available together with seat 5), Soto/Tang must be different, and seat 2 is navy. Enumerating the worlds shows Perez wears navy in all 6.
explanations.A: Soto is crimson in 3 worlds and navy in 3 worlds. Not forced.
explanations.B: Tang is navy in 3 worlds and crimson in 3 worlds. Not forced.
explanations.C: Correct. Perez wears a navy jacket in all 6 verified worlds.
explanations.D: Soto and Quinn are both crimson in some worlds but different colors in others. Not forced.
explanations.E: Tang and Quinn have the same color in some worlds (both crimson) and different in others. Not forced.

questions.questionStem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Quinn sits in the first seat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Soto sits in the first seat.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tang sits in the second seat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perez sits in the second seat.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Quinn sits in the third seat.

explanations.correct: Perez is never in the first seat (rule) and is at seat 3 or 4 in every verified world. More specifically, seat 2 wears navy and Perez could wear navy, but Tang must precede Perez, so Perez cannot be at seat 2.
explanations.A: Quinn is at seat 1 in some verified worlds (e.g., Quinn=1, Soto=2, Tang=3, Perez=4, Ruiz=5).
explanations.B: Soto is at seat 1 in some verified worlds (e.g., Soto=1, Tang=2, Perez=3, Quinn=4, Ruiz=5).
explanations.C: Tang is at seat 2 in some verified worlds (e.g., Soto=1, Tang=2, Perez=3, Quinn=4, Ruiz=5).
explanations.D: Correct. Tang must precede Perez, and Tang must be in one of seats 1-4; if Perez were at seat 2, Tang would need to be at seat 1 — but then Soto/Tang adjacency would put Soto at seat 2, not Perez. So Perez is never at seat 2.
explanations.E: Quinn is at seat 3 in some verified worlds (e.g., Soto=1, Tang=2, Quinn=3, Perez=4, Ruiz=5).

lg.scenario: A courier will make deliveries at exactly six stops — Harlan, Ives, Juno, Keele, Lowen, and Marsh — one after another, in order from first through sixth. Each delivery occurs either in the morning or in the afternoon, and exactly three deliveries occur in each half of the day. The route must satisfy the following constraints. The Harlan delivery is made at some point before the Marsh delivery. The Juno delivery is made at some point before the Keele delivery. The Ives delivery and the Lowen delivery are made at immediately consecutive stops. The Harlan delivery is not the sixth stop. The Juno delivery and the Marsh delivery are not made at immediately consecutive stops. The Marsh delivery is made at some point after the Keele delivery. The Ives delivery is not the first stop. The Keele delivery is not the second stop. The Harlan and Juno deliveries occur in the same half of the day. The Keele and Marsh deliveries occur in different halves of the day. The Ives and Lowen deliveries occur in the same half of the day. The first stop is in the morning. The sixth stop is in the afternoon.

rules.description: The first stop is in the morning.
The sixth stop is in the afternoon.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the complete delivery route, listed as stop(name, half-of-day) from first to sixth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1(Harlan, morning), 2(Ives, afternoon), 3(Lowen, afternoon), 4(Juno, morning), 5(Keele, morning), 6(Marsh, afternoon)

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1(Harlan, morning), 2(Keele, morning), 3(Juno, morning), 4(Ives, afternoon), 5(Lowen, afternoon), 6(Marsh, afternoon)

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1(Harlan, morning), 2(Juno, morning), 3(Marsh, afternoon), 4(Ives, afternoon), 5(Lowen, afternoon), 6(Keele, morning)

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1(Juno, morning), 2(Harlan, morning), 3(Marsh, afternoon), 4(Ives, afternoon), 5(Lowen, afternoon), 6(Keele, afternoon)

choices.label: E
choices.text: 1(Harlan, afternoon), 2(Juno, morning), 3(Ives, afternoon), 4(Lowen, afternoon), 5(Keele, morning), 6(Marsh, afternoon)

explanations.correct: Harlan(1) before Marsh(6); Juno(4) before Keele(5); Ives(2) and Lowen(3) adjacent; Harlan(1) not at 6; Juno(4) and Marsh(6) not adjacent; Marsh(6) after Keele(5); Ives not at 1; Keele(5) not at 2; Harlan(morning) and Juno(morning) same half; Keele(morning) and Marsh(afternoon) different halves; Ives(afternoon) and Lowen(afternoon) same half; stop 1 = morning; stop 6 = afternoon. Morning counts: {Harlan, Juno, Keele} = 3; afternoon: {Ives, Lowen, Marsh} = 3.
explanations.A: Correct. All ordinal and attribute rules hold.
explanations.B: Keele is at stop 2, violating the rule that Keele is not the second stop.
explanations.C: Marsh is before Keele here (Marsh=3, Keele=6), violating the Marsh-after-Keele rule; also stop 6 must be afternoon.
explanations.D: Keele is at stop 6 wearing afternoon, but Marsh must come after Keele — Marsh is at stop 3, so Marsh is not after Keele.
explanations.E: Stop 1 (Harlan) is afternoon, violating the cross-dimensional rule that the first stop is morning.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Marsh delivery is the sixth stop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Keele delivery is in the morning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Marsh delivery is at stop 4 or stop 6.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Juno delivery is in the morning.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Harlan delivery is the first stop.

explanations.correct: Marsh must come after Keele and after Harlan, and Marsh cannot be adjacent to Juno. Across all 25 verified worlds Marsh occupies either stop 4 or stop 6.
explanations.A: Marsh is at stop 4 in several worlds (e.g., Harlan=1, Ives=6, Juno=2, Keele=3, Lowen=5, Marsh=4). Not forced to 6.
explanations.B: Keele is morning in 21/25 worlds and afternoon in 4/25. Not forced to morning.
explanations.C: Correct. Marsh appears only at stop 4 or stop 6 across all 25 verified worlds.
explanations.D: Juno is morning in 22/25 worlds and afternoon in 3/25. Not forced.
explanations.E: Harlan is at stops 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 across the verified worlds. Not forced to 1.

questions.questionStem: If the Marsh delivery is the fourth stop, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Juno delivery is the first stop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Ives delivery is the sixth stop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Keele delivery is the third stop.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Harlan delivery is the first stop.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Lowen delivery is the fifth stop.

explanations.correct: If Marsh is at stop 4, Keele precedes Marsh but is not at stop 2 and is not at stop 4 (that is Marsh). Juno precedes Keele. Juno and Marsh are not adjacent, so Juno is not at stop 3 or stop 5. Harlan precedes Marsh and is not at stop 6. Working through, Keele must be at stop 3 in every Marsh-at-4 world.
explanations.A: Juno is at stop 1 or stop 2 when Marsh is at 4 — not forced to 1.
explanations.B: Ives is at stop 5, 6, or elsewhere — not forced to 6.
explanations.C: Correct. Keele must be at stop 3 whenever Marsh is at stop 4.
explanations.D: Harlan is at stop 1 or stop 2 when Marsh is at 4 — not forced to 1.
explanations.E: Lowen is at stop 5 or 6 when Marsh is at 4 — not forced to 5.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Keele delivery is at stop 2.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Harlan delivery is at stop 6.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Juno delivery is in the afternoon.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Marsh delivery is at stop 2.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Ives delivery is at stop 1.

explanations.correct: Juno is in the afternoon in 3 of the 25 verified worlds (those where Harlan is also in the afternoon, since Harlan and Juno share a half-of-day).
explanations.A: The rules explicitly forbid Keele from being at stop 2.
explanations.B: The rules explicitly forbid Harlan from being at stop 6.
explanations.C: Correct. Juno is in the afternoon in 3/25 worlds (e.g., Lowen=1 morning, Ives=2 morning, Juno=3 afternoon, Harlan=4 afternoon, Keele=5 morning, Marsh=6 afternoon).
explanations.D: Marsh must come after Keele and after Harlan, and Marsh is never at stop 2 in any verified world.
explanations.E: The rules explicitly forbid Ives from being at stop 1.

questions.questionStem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Harlan delivery is at stop 4.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Ives delivery is at stop 6.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Keele delivery is at stop 2.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Juno delivery is at stop 4.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Lowen delivery is at stop 6.

explanations.correct: The rules explicitly forbid Keele from being at stop 2.
explanations.A: Harlan is at stop 4 in some verified worlds (e.g., Harlan=4, Juno=1, Lowen=3, Ives=2, Keele=5, Marsh=6).
explanations.B: Ives is at stop 6 in some verified worlds (e.g., Harlan=1, Juno=2, Keele=3, Marsh=4, Lowen=5, Ives=6).
explanations.C: Correct. Keele at stop 2 violates the explicit 'Keele is not the second stop' rule.
explanations.D: Juno is at stop 4 in some verified worlds (e.g., Harlan=1, Juno=4, Keele=5, Lowen=3, Ives=2, Marsh=6).
explanations.E: Lowen is at stop 6 in some verified worlds (e.g., Harlan=1, Juno=2, Keele=3, Ives=5, Lowen=6, Marsh=4).

lg.scenario: A bakery produces exactly six specialty pastries — Almond, Brioche, Cruller, Danish, Eclair, and Florentine — one at a time, in six consecutive slots numbered first through sixth. Each pastry is baked in either the deck oven or the convection oven, with exactly three pastries baked in each oven. The schedule must satisfy the following constraints. The Almond is baked at some point before the Florentine. The Brioche is baked at some point before the Danish. The Cruller and the Eclair are baked in immediately consecutive slots. The Almond is not in slot 1. The Florentine is not in slot 6. The Almond and the Brioche are baked in the same oven. The Cruller and the Eclair are baked in different ovens. The pastry in slot 1 is baked in the deck oven. The Danish is baked in the convection oven. If the Almond is in slot 2, then the Florentine is baked in the deck oven. If the Cruller is baked in the deck oven, then the Brioche is in slot 3.

rules.description: The pastry in slot 1 is baked in the deck oven.
The Danish is baked in the convection oven.
If the Almond is in slot 2, then the Florentine is baked in the deck oven.
If the Cruller is baked in the deck oven, then the Brioche is in slot 3.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be a complete and accurate assignment of pastries to slots and ovens, listed as slot(pastry, oven) from first to sixth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1(Brioche, deck), 2(Eclair, deck), 3(Cruller, convection), 4(Almond, deck), 5(Florentine, convection), 6(Danish, convection)

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1(Almond, deck), 2(Brioche, deck), 3(Cruller, deck), 4(Eclair, convection), 5(Florentine, convection), 6(Danish, convection)

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1(Brioche, deck), 2(Danish, convection), 3(Almond, deck), 4(Cruller, convection), 5(Eclair, deck), 6(Florentine, convection)

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1(Brioche, convection), 2(Danish, convection), 3(Almond, deck), 4(Florentine, convection), 5(Cruller, convection), 6(Eclair, deck)

choices.label: E
choices.text: 1(Eclair, deck), 2(Cruller, convection), 3(Almond, deck), 4(Danish, convection), 5(Brioche, deck), 6(Florentine, convection)

explanations.correct: Brioche(1, deck): slot 1 is deck ✓; Almond and Brioche same oven (both deck) ✓. Cruller(3, convection) and Eclair(2, deck): adjacent ✓, different ovens ✓. Almond(4, deck), Florentine(5, convection), Danish(6, convection). Almond before Florentine ✓; Brioche before Danish ✓; Almond not at 1 ✓; Florentine not at 6 ✓; Danish convection ✓. Almond not at 2 so that conditional is vacuously satisfied; Cruller is convection so the Cruller-deck conditional is vacuously satisfied.
explanations.A: Correct. Every ordinal, attribute, and cross-dimensional rule is satisfied.
explanations.B: Almond is in slot 1, violating the rule that Almond is not in slot 1.
explanations.C: Florentine is in slot 6, violating the rule that Florentine is not in slot 6.
explanations.D: Almond and Brioche must be in the same oven (Brioche is convection, Almond is deck), and the slot-1 pastry (Brioche) must be deck, not convection.
explanations.E: Brioche is before Danish is required; here Brioche is in slot 5 and Danish is in slot 4, so Brioche is after Danish — violation.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Almond is in slot 3.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Florentine is baked in the convection oven.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Brioche is in slot 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Danish is in slot 6.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Eclair is baked in the deck oven.

explanations.correct: Florentine is convection in every verified world. Since Almond and Brioche share an oven and Almond is always deck, the three deck slots are {Almond, Brioche, one of Cruller/Eclair}. That forces Danish and Florentine (plus the other of Cruller/Eclair) into convection.
explanations.A: Almond can be at slot 3 or slot 4 across the verified worlds; not forced to slot 3.
explanations.B: Correct. Florentine is baked in the convection oven in all 8 verified worlds.
explanations.C: Brioche can be at slots 1, 3, 4, or 5 across verified worlds; not forced to slot 1.
explanations.D: Danish is at slot 2 in some verified worlds and slot 6 in others; not forced.
explanations.E: Eclair is deck in some worlds and convection in others; not forced.

questions.questionStem: If the Cruller is baked in the deck oven, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Brioche is in slot 3.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Almond is in slot 3.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Eclair is in slot 1.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Florentine is baked in the deck oven.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Danish is in slot 2.

explanations.correct: If Cruller is baked in the deck oven, the conditional "If Cruller is deck, then Brioche is in slot 3" fires. In the resulting world Cruller=1 deck, Eclair=2 convection, Brioche=3 deck, Almond=4 deck, Florentine=5 convection, Danish=6 convection. So Brioche is in slot 3.
explanations.A: Correct. The chained conditional forces Brioche into slot 3.
explanations.B: Almond is in slot 4 when Cruller is deck; not slot 3.
explanations.C: Eclair is in slot 2 when Cruller is deck; not slot 1.
explanations.D: Florentine is always baked in the convection oven; it is never deck.
explanations.E: Danish is in slot 6 when Cruller is deck; not slot 2.

questions.questionStem: If the Danish is in slot 2, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Cruller is in slot 5.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Eclair is in slot 5.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Cruller is baked in the deck oven.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Brioche is in slot 1.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Florentine is in slot 5.

explanations.correct: If Danish is in slot 2, Brioche must be in slot 1 (Brioche precedes Danish). In both verified Danish=2 worlds, Brioche is in slot 1, Almond is in slot 3, Florentine is in slot 4, and the Cruller/Eclair pair occupies slots 5 and 6 in some order.
explanations.A: Cruller occupies slot 5 in one Danish=2 world and slot 6 in the other. Not forced to 5.
explanations.B: Eclair occupies slot 5 in one Danish=2 world and slot 6 in the other. Not forced to 5.
explanations.C: Cruller is convection in both Danish=2 worlds; never deck in this case.
explanations.D: Correct. Brioche must precede Danish, and slot 2 is Danish, so Brioche is in slot 1.
explanations.E: Florentine is in slot 4 in both Danish=2 worlds, not slot 5.

Enumeration confirms Brioche is never at slot 2.
explanations.A: Almond is at slot 4 in several verified worlds (e.g., W5: 1Brioche-d, 2Cruller-c, 3Eclair-d, 4Almond-d, 5Florentine-c, 6Danish-c).
explanations.B: Danish is at slot 2 in some verified worlds (e.g., W1: 1Brioche-d, 2Danish-c, 3Almond-d, 4Florentine-c, 5Cruller-c, 6Eclair-d).

lg.scenario: A museum will present exactly seven lectures — by Aquino, Bosch, Cayetano, Delgado, Espino, Faure, and Gallego — in seven consecutive slots numbered first through seventh. Each lecture is delivered either upstairs or downstairs, with exactly four upstairs and exactly three downstairs. The schedule must satisfy the following constraints. Aquino lectures at some point before Espino. Bosch lectures at some point before Faure, and Faure lectures at some point before Gallego. Cayetano lectures at some point before Delgado. Delgado and Espino lecture in immediately consecutive slots. Aquino and Bosch do not lecture in immediately consecutive slots. Cayetano is not in slot 7. Aquino is not in slot 7. Aquino and Bosch lecture on different floors. Delgado and Espino lecture on different floors. Faure and Gallego lecture on different floors. The lecture in slot 1 is upstairs. The lecture in slot 3 is downstairs. The lecture in slot 7 is upstairs. Gallego lectures downstairs. If Cayetano is in slot 4, then Faure lectures upstairs. If Bosch lectures downstairs, then Aquino is in slot 1 or slot 2.

rules.description: Exactly four lectures are delivered upstairs and exactly three are delivered downstairs.
The lecture in slot 1 is delivered upstairs.
The lecture in slot 3 is delivered downstairs.
The lecture in slot 7 is delivered upstairs.
Gallego lectures downstairs.
If Cayetano is in slot 4, then Faure lectures upstairs.
If Bosch lectures downstairs, then Aquino is in slot 1 or slot 2.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the complete schedule of lectures, listed as slot(lecturer, floor) from first to seventh?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1(Aquino, upstairs), 2(Cayetano, upstairs), 3(Bosch, downstairs), 4(Faure, upstairs), 5(Gallego, downstairs), 6(Delgado, downstairs), 7(Espino, upstairs)
