choices.text: 1(Bosch, upstairs), 2(Aquino, upstairs), 3(Gallego, downstairs), 4(Cayetano, upstairs), 5(Faure, upstairs), 6(Espino, downstairs), 7(Delgado, upstairs)

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1(Aquino, upstairs), 2(Faure, upstairs), 3(Bosch, downstairs), 4(Cayetano, upstairs), 5(Gallego, downstairs), 6(Delgado, downstairs), 7(Espino, upstairs)

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1(Bosch, upstairs), 2(Cayetano, upstairs), 3(Aquino, downstairs), 4(Faure, upstairs), 5(Gallego, downstairs), 6(Delgado, downstairs), 7(Espino, downstairs)

choices.label: E
choices.text: 1(Aquino, upstairs), 2(Cayetano, upstairs), 3(Gallego, downstairs), 4(Faure, upstairs), 5(Bosch, upstairs), 6(Delgado, downstairs), 7(Espino, upstairs)

explanations.correct: Checking (A) against every rule: Aquino(1) before Espino(7) ✓; Bosch(3) before Faure(4) before Gallego(5) ✓; Cayetano(2) before Delgado(6) ✓; Delgado(6) and Espino(7) adjacent ✓; Aquino(1) and Bosch(3) not adjacent ✓; Cayetano not at 7 ✓; Aquino not at 7 ✓; Aquino and Bosch on different floors (up vs. down) ✓; Delgado and Espino different (dn vs. up) ✓; Faure and Gallego different (up vs. dn) ✓; 4 upstairs {Aquino, Cayetano, Faure, Espino} and 3 downstairs {Bosch, Gallego, Delgado} ✓; slot-1 upstairs ✓; slot-3 downstairs ✓; slot-7 upstairs ✓; Gallego downstairs ✓.
explanations.A: Correct. All rules hold.
explanations.B: Aquino(2) and Bosch(1) are in immediately consecutive slots, violating the not-adjacent rule for Aquino and Bosch. Also slot 3 (Gallego) is downstairs (OK) but this places Gallego before Faure, and there is no Faure-before-Gallego violation check needed; however the Aquino-Bosch adjacency alone kills this choice.
explanations.C: Bosch is in slot 3, but Faure is in slot 2 and the rule requires Bosch before Faure — violated.
explanations.D: Slot 7 (Espino) is marked downstairs, but the rule requires slot 7 to be upstairs.
explanations.E: Bosch is in slot 5 and Faure is in slot 4, violating the rule that Bosch is before Faure.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bosch is in slot 1.

explanations.correct: Faure is always upstairs. Faure and Gallego are on different floors, and Gallego is always downstairs, so Faure must be upstairs in every verified world.
explanations.A: Cayetano is at slot 2, 4, or 5 across the verified worlds; not forced to 2.
explanations.B: Bosch is at slot 1 in some worlds and slot 3 in others; not forced.
explanations.C: Espino is at slot 6 or 7; when at slot 7, Espino is upstairs. So Espino is not always downstairs.
explanations.D: Correct. Faure is always upstairs because Faure and Gallego differ on floor and Gallego is always downstairs.
explanations.E: Aquino is at slots 1, 3, 4, or 5 across verified worlds; not forced.

questions.questionStem: If Bosch is in slot 1, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: E

explanations.correct: Bosch at slot 1 means Bosch is upstairs (slot-1 rule). Aquino and Bosch are on different floors, so Aquino lectures downstairs.
explanations.A: Correct. Aquino and Bosch differ on floor; slot-1 (Bosch) is upstairs, so Aquino is downstairs.
explanations.B: When Bosch=1, Cayetano can be at slot 2 or slot 4 across verified worlds; not forced.
explanations.C: Gallego can be at slot 3 or slot 5 in Bosch=1 worlds; not forced.
explanations.D: Espino can be at slot 6 or slot 7 in Bosch=1 worlds; not forced.
explanations.E: Delgado can be at slot 6 or slot 7 in Bosch=1 worlds; not forced.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be true?

choices.text: Aquino is in slot 7.

explanations.correct: Gallego can be in slot 3 when Bosch and Aquino occupy slots 1 and 2 in some order. Several verified worlds place Gallego at slot 3 (e.g., W9: 1Bosch-up, 2Faure-up, 3Gallego-dn, 4Aquino-dn, 5Cayetano-up, 6Delgado-dn, 7Espino-up).
explanations.A: Cayetano is always upstairs in every verified world, so this cannot be true.
explanations.B: Correct. Gallego is in slot 3 in several verified worlds.
explanations.C: Cayetano is in slots 2, 4, or 5 — never in slot 7 (and explicit rule forbids 7).
explanations.D: Faure is in slots 2 or 4 — never in slot 6.
explanations.E: Aquino is never in slot 7 (explicit rule).

explanations.A: Aquino is in slot 1 in some verified worlds (e.g., 1Aquino, 2Cayetano, 3Bosch ...).
explanations.B: Delgado is in slot 6 in several verified worlds.
explanations.C: Espino is in slot 6 in several verified worlds.
explanations.D: Correct. Slot 3 must be downstairs and Faure must be upstairs — contradiction.
explanations.E: Gallego is in slot 5 in several verified worlds.

lg.scenario: A symposium features exactly six talks — by Hadley, Ichiro, Jurek, Kaplan, Leung, and Moreno — scheduled in six consecutive slots numbered first through sixth. Each talk is held in either the red room or the blue room, with exactly three talks in each room. The schedule must satisfy the following constraints. Hadley speaks at some point before Moreno. Jurek speaks at some point before Leung. Ichiro and Kaplan speak in immediately consecutive slots. Hadley is not in slot 6. Leung is not in slot 1. Moreno is not in slot 1. Hadley and Jurek speak in the same room. Ichiro and Kaplan speak in different rooms. Leung and Moreno speak in the same room. The talk in slot 1 is held in the red room. The talk in slot 6 is held in the blue room. If Kaplan is in slot 3, then Moreno speaks in the red room. If Leung speaks in the blue room, then Hadley is in slot 2.

rules.description: The talk in slot 1 is held in the red room.
The talk in slot 6 is held in the blue room.
If Kaplan is in slot 3, then Moreno speaks in the red room.
If Leung speaks in the blue room, then Hadley is in slot 2.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the complete schedule of talks, listed as slot(speaker, room) from first to sixth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1(Jurek, red), 2(Hadley, red), 3(Ichiro, red), 4(Kaplan, blue), 5(Leung, blue), 6(Moreno, blue)

choices.label: B
choices.text: 1(Hadley, red), 2(Jurek, red), 3(Leung, blue), 4(Ichiro, red), 5(Kaplan, blue), 6(Moreno, blue)

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1(Jurek, red), 2(Hadley, red), 3(Moreno, blue), 4(Ichiro, red), 5(Kaplan, blue), 6(Leung, red)

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1(Jurek, red), 2(Hadley, blue), 3(Leung, blue), 4(Ichiro, red), 5(Kaplan, blue), 6(Moreno, blue)

choices.label: E
choices.text: 1(Jurek, red), 2(Hadley, red), 3(Ichiro, red), 4(Leung, blue), 5(Kaplan, red), 6(Moreno, blue)

explanations.correct: Jurek(1, red): slot 1 red ✓. Hadley(2, red): Hadley-Jurek same room ✓. Ichiro(3, red) and Kaplan(4, blue): adjacent ✓, different rooms ✓. Leung(5, blue), Moreno(6, blue): Leung-Moreno same ✓, Jurek before Leung ✓, Hadley before Moreno ✓, slot 6 blue ✓, room counts red={Jurek, Hadley, Ichiro}=3 and blue={Kaplan, Leung, Moreno}=3. The conditional "If Leung is blue, Hadley is at slot 2": Leung is blue and Hadley is at slot 2 ✓. The conditional "If Kaplan is at slot 3, then Moreno is red" is vacuously satisfied (Kaplan is not at slot 3).
explanations.A: Correct. All ordinal, attribute, and cross-dimensional rules are satisfied.
explanations.B: Ichiro(4) and Kaplan(5) adjacent ✓, but Leung is in slot 3 and Jurek is in slot 2 — so Jurek is before Leung ✓. However Hadley is in slot 1 and the cross-dim rule "If Leung is blue, then Hadley is at slot 2" fires (Leung is blue in this choice) and requires Hadley at slot 2 — violated.
explanations.C: Slot 6 is Leung in the red room, violating the rule that slot 6 is blue.
explanations.D: Hadley and Jurek must be in the same room. Jurek is red (slot 1) but Hadley is blue — violation.
explanations.E: Ichiro(3) and Kaplan(5) are not adjacent — violated. Also Kaplan is red in slot 5 but Leung/Moreno occupy remaining positions; red count would exceed 3.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hadley speaks in the red room.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ichiro is in slot 3.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kaplan speaks in the blue room.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Moreno is in slot 6.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Leung is in slot 3.

explanations.correct: Hadley is in the red room in every verified world. Since Leung is always blue (same room as Moreno, who is always blue via the slot-6 forcing chain), the Leung-blue conditional fires and forces Hadley=2. Hadley/Jurek same room and Jurek=1 (red) forces Hadley=red.
explanations.A: Correct. Hadley speaks in the red room in all 16 verified worlds.
explanations.B: Ichiro can be in slot 3, 4, 5, or 6 across verified worlds; not forced.
explanations.C: Kaplan speaks in blue in some worlds and red in others; not forced.
explanations.D: Moreno is in slot 3, 4, 5, or 6 across verified worlds; not forced to 6.
explanations.E: Leung is in slot 3, 4, 5, or 6 across verified worlds; not forced to 3.

questions.questionStem: If Ichiro is in slot 3, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kaplan speaks in the blue room.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ichiro speaks in the red room.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leung is in slot 5.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Moreno is in slot 6.

explanations.correct: If Ichiro is in slot 3, Kaplan must be adjacent to Ichiro. Slots 1 and 2 are occupied by Jurek and Hadley, so Kaplan must be in slot 4.
explanations.A: Correct. Kaplan must be adjacent to Ichiro; slots 1 and 2 are taken, so Kaplan is in slot 4.
explanations.B: Kaplan can be blue or red in Ichiro=3 worlds (Ichiro and Kaplan differ, and Ichiro can be red or blue).
explanations.C: Ichiro can be red (slot 3 is red in some worlds) or blue (in others); not forced.
explanations.D: Leung can be in slot 5 or slot 6 in Ichiro=3 worlds; not forced.
explanations.E: Moreno can be in slot 5 or slot 6 in Ichiro=3 worlds; not forced.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be true?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Leung speaks in the red room.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jurek speaks in the blue room.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hadley is in slot 3.

explanations.correct: Moreno can be in slot 3 — for example when Ichiro and Kaplan fill slots 4 and 5, Leung occupies slot 6, and Moreno takes slot 3. Several verified worlds place Moreno at slot 3 (e.g., W7: 1Jurek-r, 2Hadley-r, 3Moreno-b, 4Ichiro-r, 5Kaplan-b, 6Leung-b).
explanations.A: Correct. Moreno is in slot 3 in multiple verified worlds.
explanations.B: Kaplan is always in slot 4, 5, or 6; never in slot 3 (Ichiro-Kaplan adjacency plus slots 1,2 being occupied keeps the pair later).
explanations.C: Leung is blue in every verified world (same room as Moreno, who is always blue in every world).
explanations.D: Jurek speaks in the red room in every verified world (slot 1 is always red, and Jurek is always slot 1).
explanations.E: Hadley is always in slot 2, never slot 3.

questions.questionStem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ichiro is in slot 6.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leung is in slot 3.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kaplan speaks in the red room.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Moreno speaks in the red room.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Leung is in slot 5.

explanations.correct: Moreno is blue in every verified world. Slot 6 is blue; Leung-Moreno same room; and across the base rules and cross-dim constraints, Moreno is forced blue.
explanations.A: Ichiro is in slot 6 in some verified worlds (e.g., W15-16 where Kaplan is in slot 5 or 6).
explanations.B: Leung is in slot 3 in multiple verified worlds.
explanations.C: Kaplan speaks in red in some worlds (when Ichiro is blue, Kaplan is red).
explanations.D: Correct. Moreno is always blue — slot 6 is blue and Moreno is in the blue group with Leung; the chained conditional "If Leung blue, Hadley=2" is always satisfied because Leung is always blue.
explanations.E: Leung is in slot 5 in several verified worlds.

lg.scenario: Exactly five speakers — Farrell, Gupta, Huang, Ibanez, and Jain — will each deliver one keynote on one of five consecutive days, Monday through Friday. Each speaker delivers exactly one keynote, and each day is assigned exactly one speaker. The schedule conforms to the following constraints. Farrell speaks on Monday. Huang speaks on some day before Ibanez. Gupta and Jain speak on consecutive days.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the order in which the speakers deliver their keynotes, from Monday through Friday?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Farrell, Huang, Jain, Gupta, Ibanez

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gupta, Huang, Jain, Farrell, Ibanez

choices.label: C
choices.text: Farrell, Ibanez, Gupta, Jain, Huang

choices.label: D
choices.text: Farrell, Huang, Gupta, Ibanez, Jain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Farrell, Jain, Huang, Gupta, Ibanez

explanations.correct: Farrell is on Monday (position 1); Huang (Tuesday, 2) is before Ibanez (Friday, 5); Gupta (Thursday, 4) and Jain (Wednesday, 3) are on consecutive days. All three rules are satisfied.
explanations.A: Correct. Farrell first, Huang before Ibanez, Gupta and Jain consecutive.
explanations.B: Gupta is on Monday rather than Farrell, violating the rule that Farrell speaks on Monday.
explanations.C: Ibanez (Tuesday) speaks before Huang (Friday), violating the rule that Huang speaks before Ibanez.
explanations.D: Gupta is on Wednesday and Jain is on Friday, so they are not on consecutive days. Violates the Gupta-Jain adjacency rule.
explanations.E: Jain is on Tuesday and Gupta is on Thursday, so they are not on consecutive days. Violates the Gupta-Jain adjacency rule.

questions.questionStem: If Ibanez speaks on Wednesday, then which one of the following could be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gupta speaks on Friday.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jain speaks on Wednesday.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Huang speaks on Thursday.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gupta speaks on Tuesday.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ibanez speaks on Friday.

explanations.correct: With Farrell on Monday and Ibanez on Wednesday, Huang must be on Tuesday (the only earlier open slot). Gupta and Jain fill Thursday and Friday in either order, so Gupta on Friday is one admissible outcome.
explanations.A: Correct. Farrell(1), Huang(2), Ibanez(3), Jain(4), Gupta(5) is valid.
explanations.B: Ibanez already occupies Wednesday, so Jain cannot also be on Wednesday.
explanations.C: Huang must be before Ibanez (Wednesday), and Monday is taken by Farrell, so Huang must be on Tuesday — not Thursday.
explanations.D: Huang must be on Tuesday (the only slot before Ibanez), so Gupta cannot be on Tuesday.
explanations.E: Ibanez is on Wednesday by hypothesis, not Friday.

questions.questionStem: If Huang speaks on Thursday, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ibanez speaks on Friday.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gupta speaks on Tuesday.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jain speaks on Wednesday.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ibanez speaks on Wednesday.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gupta speaks on Thursday.

explanations.correct: Huang on Thursday forces Ibanez into Friday, since Ibanez must come after Huang and no later day is available. Gupta and Jain then take Tuesday and Wednesday (in either order) to satisfy their adjacency.
explanations.A: Correct. Friday is the only day available that satisfies Huang-before-Ibanez.
explanations.B: Gupta could be on Tuesday or Wednesday; not forced.
explanations.C: Jain could be on Tuesday or Wednesday; not forced.
explanations.D: Ibanez must come after Huang (Thursday), so Ibanez cannot be on Wednesday.
explanations.E: Huang is on Thursday by hypothesis, so Gupta cannot also be on Thursday.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Huang does not speak on Friday.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ibanez speaks on Friday.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gupta speaks on Tuesday.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jain speaks on Monday.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ibanez speaks on Wednesday.

explanations.correct: Ibanez must speak on some day after Huang. If Huang were on Friday, no day would remain for Ibanez. Therefore Huang cannot be on Friday.
explanations.A: Correct. Huang must leave at least one later day for Ibanez.
explanations.B: Ibanez could be on Wednesday, Thursday, or Friday depending on the arrangement; not forced.
explanations.C: Gupta can occupy Tuesday through Friday in various valid worlds; not forced.
explanations.D: Farrell is on Monday, so Jain cannot be on Monday.
explanations.E: Ibanez can be on Wednesday or Friday in various valid worlds; not forced.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ibanez speaks on Tuesday.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gupta speaks on Wednesday.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Huang speaks on Tuesday.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jain speaks on Thursday.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ibanez speaks on Friday.

explanations.correct: Farrell is on Monday, so Huang (who must come before Ibanez) would have to be on Monday to put Ibanez on Tuesday — but Monday is already taken. No valid schedule has Ibanez on Tuesday.
explanations.A: Correct. Huang has no earlier day available if Ibanez is on Tuesday.
explanations.B: Gupta on Wednesday is realized (e.g., Farrell, Huang, Gupta, Jain, Ibanez).
explanations.C: Huang on Tuesday is realized (e.g., Farrell, Huang, Gupta, Jain, Ibanez).
explanations.D: Jain on Thursday is realized (e.g., Farrell, Huang, Gupta, Jain, Ibanez).
explanations.E: Ibanez on Friday is realized (e.g., Farrell, Huang, Gupta, Jain, Ibanez).

lg.scenario: A museum docent will guide visitors past exactly six exhibits — coins, drums, etchings, fossils, gowns, and helmets — one exhibit at a time, in an order numbered first through sixth. Each exhibit is visited exactly once. The tour conforms to the following constraints. The coins exhibit is visited at some point before the drums exhibit. The etchings exhibit and the fossils exhibit are visited in immediately consecutive positions. The gowns exhibit is visited third. The helmets exhibit is not visited first.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the order of exhibits the docent visits, from first to sixth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: coins, drums, gowns, etchings, fossils, helmets

choices.label: B
choices.text: drums, coins, gowns, etchings, fossils, helmets

choices.label: C
choices.text: coins, drums, helmets, etchings, fossils, gowns

choices.label: D
choices.text: coins, etchings, gowns, drums, fossils, helmets

choices.label: E
choices.text: helmets, coins, gowns, drums, etchings, fossils

explanations.correct: Coins (1) precedes drums (2); etchings (4) and fossils (5) are in consecutive positions; gowns is third; helmets (6) is not first. Every rule holds.
explanations.A: Correct. All four constraints are satisfied.
explanations.B: Drums is first and coins is second, so coins does not precede drums. Violates the coins-before-drums rule.
explanations.C: Gowns is sixth rather than third. Violates the rule that gowns is third.
explanations.D: Etchings is second and fossils is fifth, so they are not in consecutive positions. Violates the etchings-fossils adjacency rule.
explanations.E: Helmets is first. Violates the rule that helmets is not first.

questions.questionStem: If coins is the fourth exhibit visited, then which one of the following could be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Helmets is the sixth exhibit visited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drums is the second exhibit visited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gowns is the fourth exhibit visited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coins is the first exhibit visited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drums is the third exhibit visited.

explanations.correct: With coins at 4 and gowns at 3, drums must be at 5 or 6, and etchings/fossils occupy the remaining adjacent pair from {1,2}. Helmets then fills whichever of {5, 6} is left. Helmets sixth is realized, for example, by etchings(1), fossils(2), gowns(3), coins(4), drums(5), helmets(6).
explanations.A: Correct. Etchings(1), fossils(2), gowns(3), coins(4), drums(5), helmets(6) satisfies every rule.
explanations.B: Drums must come after coins (position 4), so drums cannot be at 2.
explanations.C: Gowns is fixed at position 3 by rule, so it cannot be at 4.
explanations.D: Coins is at 4 by hypothesis, not 1.
explanations.E: Gowns is at 3 by rule, so drums cannot be at 3.

questions.questionStem: If etchings is the first exhibit visited, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fossils is the second exhibit visited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drums is the fifth exhibit visited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helmets is the fourth exhibit visited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coins is the fourth exhibit visited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Drums is the sixth exhibit visited.

explanations.correct: Etchings and fossils must be adjacent. With etchings at 1, fossils must be at 2 — no other adjacent position is available.
explanations.A: Correct. Position 2 is the only position adjacent to position 1.
explanations.B: Drums can be at 5 or 6 depending on the arrangement; not forced.
explanations.C: Helmets can be at 4, 5, or 6 in these worlds; not forced to 4.
explanations.D: Coins can be at 4 or 5; not forced to 4.
explanations.E: Drums can be at 5 or 6; not forced to 6.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Coins is not the sixth exhibit visited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Drums is the sixth exhibit visited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helmets is the sixth exhibit visited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Coins is the first exhibit visited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Etchings is the fourth exhibit visited.

explanations.correct: Drums must come after coins, so coins must leave at least one later position for drums. Therefore coins cannot occupy the final position.
explanations.A: Correct. Coins must have drums somewhere later, so coins is never sixth.
explanations.B: Drums can be at 2, 4, 5, or 6 in various valid tours; not forced.
explanations.C: Helmets can be at 2, 4, 5, or 6; not forced to 6.
explanations.D: Coins can be at 1, 4, or 5; not forced to 1.
explanations.E: Etchings can be at 1, 2, 4, 5, or 6; not forced to 4.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Drums is the first exhibit visited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helmets is the second exhibit visited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Coins is the fifth exhibit visited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fossils is the sixth exhibit visited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Etchings is the second exhibit visited.

explanations.correct: Coins must precede drums. If drums were first, no position would remain before it for coins. So drums cannot be first.
explanations.A: Correct. Coins would have nowhere earlier to go if drums were first.
explanations.B: Helmets second is realized (e.g., coins, helmets, gowns, drums, etchings, fossils).
explanations.C: Coins fifth is realized (e.g., etchings, fossils, gowns, helmets, coins, drums).
explanations.D: Fossils sixth is realized (e.g., coins, drums, gowns, helmets, etchings, fossils).
explanations.E: Etchings second is realized (e.g., fossils, etchings, gowns, coins, drums, helmets).

lg.scenario: Exactly five runners — Ortiz, Perez, Quinn, Reyes, and Singh — finish a marathon, each in a different finishing position from first through fifth. There are no ties. The finishing order conforms to the following constraints. Ortiz finishes at some point before Perez. Quinn does not finish first. Reyes and Singh finish in consecutive positions. Singh does not finish fifth.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the order in which the runners finish, from first to fifth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ortiz, Perez, Quinn, Singh, Reyes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perez, Ortiz, Quinn, Singh, Reyes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Quinn, Ortiz, Perez, Singh, Reyes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ortiz, Singh, Perez, Reyes, Quinn

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ortiz, Perez, Quinn, Reyes, Singh

explanations.correct: Ortiz (1) finishes before Perez (2); Quinn (3) is not first; Reyes (5) and Singh (4) are in consecutive positions; Singh (4) is not fifth. All rules hold.
explanations.A: Correct. Every constraint is satisfied.
explanations.B: Perez is first and Ortiz is second, so Ortiz does not finish before Perez. Violates the Ortiz-before-Perez rule.
explanations.C: Quinn is first. Violates the rule that Quinn does not finish first.
explanations.D: Singh is second and Reyes is fourth, so they are not in consecutive positions. Violates the Reyes-Singh adjacency rule.
explanations.E: Singh is fifth. Violates the rule that Singh does not finish fifth.

questions.questionStem: If Quinn finishes second, then which one of the following could be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perez finishes fifth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Singh finishes fifth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ortiz finishes second.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Quinn finishes first.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reyes finishes second.

explanations.correct: With Quinn at 2, Ortiz must be first (since Ortiz precedes Perez and Quinn occupies 2). Reyes and Singh take an adjacent pair from the remaining positions 3, 4 (since Singh cannot be 5), leaving Perez at either 3 or 5. Perez fifth is realized, for example, by Ortiz(1), Quinn(2), Reyes(3), Singh(4), Perez(5).
explanations.A: Correct. Ortiz(1), Quinn(2), Reyes(3), Singh(4), Perez(5) satisfies every rule.
explanations.B: Singh cannot be fifth by rule.
explanations.C: Quinn is at 2 by hypothesis, so Ortiz cannot also be at 2.
explanations.D: Quinn is at 2 by hypothesis, not 1.
explanations.E: Quinn is at 2 by hypothesis, so Reyes cannot also be at 2.

questions.questionStem: If Ortiz finishes third, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reyes does not finish third.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Quinn finishes fourth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perez finishes fourth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Singh finishes second.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reyes finishes first.

explanations.correct: With Ortiz at 3, position 3 is occupied, so no one else can be at 3; in particular Reyes is not at 3. (In every such arrangement, Reyes and Singh fill positions 1 and 2 as an adjacent pair, while Perez and Quinn fill positions 4 and 5.)
explanations.A: Correct. Position 3 is taken by Ortiz.
explanations.B: Quinn is at 4 or 5; not forced to 4.
explanations.C: Perez is at 4 or 5 (since Perez follows Ortiz at 3); not forced to 4.
explanations.D: Singh is at 1 or 2; not forced to 2.
explanations.E: Reyes is at 1 or 2; not forced to 1.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perez does not finish first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ortiz finishes first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Quinn finishes fifth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reyes finishes third.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Singh finishes second.

explanations.correct: Ortiz finishes before Perez, so at least one earlier position must exist for Ortiz. Therefore Perez cannot finish first.
explanations.A: Correct. Ortiz must finish earlier than Perez.
explanations.B: Ortiz can finish first, third, or fourth in various valid orders; not forced to first.
explanations.C: Quinn can finish second, third, fourth, or fifth; not forced to fifth.
explanations.D: Reyes can finish at 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 depending on the arrangement; not forced to 3.
explanations.E: Singh can finish at 1, 2, 3, or 4; not forced to 2.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ortiz finishes fifth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perez finishes fifth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Quinn finishes third.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reyes finishes fifth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Singh finishes third.

explanations.correct: Ortiz must finish before Perez, so Ortiz cannot take the last position — there would be no later position available for Perez.
explanations.A: Correct. Perez must finish after Ortiz, so Ortiz cannot be fifth.
explanations.B: Perez fifth is realized (e.g., Ortiz, Quinn, Reyes, Singh, Perez).
explanations.C: Quinn third is realized (e.g., Ortiz, Perez, Quinn, Singh, Reyes).
explanations.D: Reyes fifth is realized (e.g., Ortiz, Perez, Quinn, Singh, Reyes).
explanations.E: Singh third is realized (e.g., Ortiz, Reyes, Singh, Quinn, Perez).

lg.scenario: A delivery truck must make exactly one stop in each of six towns — Ashford, Bellbrook, Carver, Denton, Easton, and Franklin — in some order, first through sixth. The route is constrained as follows. The stop at Ashford occurs at some point before the stop at Denton. The stop at Bellbrook occurs either immediately before or immediately after the stop at Carver. Easton is neither the first stop nor the sixth stop. The stop at Franklin occurs at some point before the stop at Easton. Ashford and Franklin are not stopped at consecutively. If Franklin is the second stop, then Ashford is the first stop.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the order in which the truck stops at the towns, from first to sixth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ashford, Bellbrook, Carver, Franklin, Easton, Denton

choices.label: B
choices.text: Denton, Bellbrook, Carver, Franklin, Easton, Ashford

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bellbrook, Ashford, Carver, Franklin, Easton, Denton

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ashford, Bellbrook, Carver, Franklin, Denton, Easton

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ashford, Franklin, Bellbrook, Carver, Easton, Denton

explanations.correct: Ashford(1) is before Denton(6); Bellbrook(2) and Carver(3) are consecutive; Easton(5) is neither first nor sixth; Franklin(4) is before Easton(5); Ashford(1) and Franklin(4) are not consecutive; Franklin is not at position 2 so the conditional is vacuously satisfied. All rules hold.
explanations.A: Correct. Every rule is satisfied.
explanations.B: Denton is first and Ashford is sixth, so Ashford is not before Denton. Violates the Ashford-before-Denton rule.
explanations.C: Bellbrook is first and Carver is third, so Bellbrook and Carver are not in consecutive positions. Violates the Bellbrook-Carver adjacency rule.
explanations.D: Easton is sixth, which the rules forbid.
explanations.E: Ashford is first and Franklin is second, putting them in consecutive positions. Violates the rule that Ashford and Franklin are not stopped at consecutively.

questions.questionStem: If Franklin is the third stop, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ashford is the first stop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ashford is the fifth stop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Denton is the sixth stop.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Easton is the fourth stop.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bellbrook is the fifth stop.

explanations.correct: With Franklin at 3, the not-adjacent rule forces Ashford into 1 or 5. Franklin(3) must come before Easton, and Easton cannot be at 1 or 6, so Easton is at 4, 5, or 6. Positions 5 and 6 must be populated without violating any rule; enumerating shows Easton is pinned at 4 in every admissible assignment.
explanations.A: Ashford can be at either 1 or 5; it is not forced to position 1.
explanations.B: Ashford can be at either 1 or 5; it is not forced to position 5.
explanations.C: Denton can be at 6 (when Ashford is at 1 or 5) but also at 2 in the Ashford-at-1 worlds, so it is not forced.
explanations.D: Correct. Every arrangement with Franklin at 3 places Easton at 4.
explanations.E: Bellbrook can occupy several positions (including 1, 2, 5, or 6) given the Bellbrook-Carver block; it is not forced to 5.

questions.questionStem: If Easton is the second stop, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ashford is the third stop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Franklin is the first stop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Denton is the sixth stop.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Bellbrook is the fifth stop.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Carver is the fourth stop.

explanations.correct: Franklin must come before Easton, so Franklin is at 1. (Franklin cannot be at 2 since Easton is at 2.) The contrapositive of the conditional matters as well: Franklin being at 2 would require Ashford at 1, but Franklin is not at 2 here, leaving Franklin forced into position 1.
explanations.A: Ashford can be at 3 or 5; not forced.
explanations.B: Correct. Franklin must precede Easton, and only position 1 remains available.
explanations.C: Denton can be at 4 or 6; not forced.
explanations.D: Bellbrook has several possible positions (3, 4, 5, or 6); not forced.
explanations.E: Carver has several possible positions and is not forced to 4.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Denton is the sixth stop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Franklin is not the second stop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Easton is the fifth stop.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ashford is the first stop.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Bellbrook is the third stop.

explanations.correct: Suppose Franklin were at 2. The conditional rule would force Ashford to position 1. But then Ashford and Franklin would be at 1 and 2 — consecutive positions — violating the not-adjacent rule. Therefore Franklin cannot be at 2.
explanations.A: Denton could be at 6 (most arrangements) but can also be at 2 or 4; not forced.
explanations.B: Correct. Franklin at 2 triggers Ashford to 1, which contradicts the not-adjacent rule.
explanations.C: Easton can be at 2, 4, or 5; not forced to 5.
explanations.D: Ashford can be at 3, 4, or 5 as well; not forced to 1.
explanations.E: Bellbrook can occupy many positions; not forced to 3.

questions.questionStem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bellbrook is the second stop.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Carver is the sixth stop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Easton is the fourth stop.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Denton is the second stop.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ashford is the second stop.

explanations.correct: If Ashford were at 2, Franklin would have to lie elsewhere and still precede Easton while not being adjacent to Ashford. That forces Franklin to position 4, 5, or 6, but Franklin must also come before Easton and Easton cannot be at 1 or 6. Testing all possibilities shows no valid arrangement places Ashford at 2.
explanations.A: Bellbrook at 2 with Carver at 3 is realized (e.g., Ashford(1), Bellbrook(2), Carver(3), Franklin(4), Easton(5), Denton(6)).
explanations.B: Carver at 6 with Bellbrook at 5 is realized (e.g., Ashford(1), Denton(2), Franklin(3), Easton(4), Bellbrook(5), Carver(6)).
explanations.C: Easton at 4 is realized in several arrangements (e.g., Ashford(5), Bellbrook(1), Carver(2), Franklin(3), Easton(4), Denton(6)).
explanations.D: Denton at 2 is realized when Ashford is at 1 (e.g., Ashford(1), Denton(2), Franklin(3), Easton(4), Bellbrook(5), Carver(6)).
explanations.E: Correct. No assignment satisfies all rules with Ashford at 2.

lg.scenario: A museum docent will lead visitors past exactly seven exhibits — glass, helmets, icons, jade, kites, lanterns, and masks — one at a time, in an order numbered first through seventh. The order must conform to the following constraints. The glass exhibit is visited at some point before the masks exhibit. The helmets exhibit and the icons exhibit are visited in immediately consecutive positions. The jade exhibit is not the fourth exhibit visited. The lanterns exhibit is visited at some point after the kites exhibit. The jade exhibit is visited at some point before the kites exhibit. The glass and jade exhibits are not visited in immediately consecutive positions. The helmets exhibit is visited at some point before the lanterns exhibit. The kites exhibit is not the second exhibit visited. If the kites exhibit is the third exhibit visited, then the masks exhibit is the seventh.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the order in which the exhibits are visited, from first to seventh?

choices.label: A
choices.text: glass, helmets, icons, masks, jade, kites, lanterns

choices.label: B
choices.text: masks, helmets, icons, glass, jade, kites, lanterns

choices.label: C
choices.text: glass, helmets, jade, icons, masks, kites, lanterns

choices.label: D
choices.text: glass, helmets, icons, jade, masks, kites, lanterns

choices.label: E
choices.text: glass, helmets, icons, masks, jade, lanterns, kites

explanations.correct: glass(1) is before masks(4); helmets(2) and icons(3) are consecutive; jade is at 5, not 4; lanterns(7) is after kites(6); jade(5) is before kites(6); glass(1) and jade(5) are not consecutive; helmets(2) is before lanterns(7); kites is at 6, not 2; kites is not at 3 so the conditional is vacuous.
explanations.A: Correct. All rules are satisfied.
explanations.B: masks is first and glass is fourth, so glass is not before masks. Violates the glass-before-masks rule.
explanations.C: helmets is at 2 and icons is at 4, so they are not in consecutive positions. Violates the helmets-icons adjacency rule.
explanations.D: jade is the fourth exhibit, which the rules forbid.
explanations.E: lanterns is at 6 and kites is at 7, so lanterns is not after kites. Violates the lanterns-after-kites rule.

questions.questionStem: If glass is the third exhibit visited, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: masks is the second exhibit visited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: jade is the first exhibit visited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: lanterns is the seventh exhibit visited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: kites is the fourth exhibit visited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: helmets is the fourth exhibit visited.

explanations.correct: Glass at 3 makes jade unable to sit at 2 or 4 (jade cannot be adjacent to glass, and jade cannot be at 4). Jade must precede kites, and the remaining slots force jade to 5, kites to 6, lanterns to 7, and masks to 4. Helmets and icons share positions 1 and 2 in either order.
explanations.A: Masks lands at 4, not 2.
explanations.B: Jade lands at 5, not 1.
explanations.C: Correct. With glass at 3, every valid arrangement places lanterns at 7.
explanations.D: Kites lands at 6, not 4.
explanations.E: Helmets lands at 1 or 2, not 4.

questions.questionStem: If jade is the first exhibit visited, then which one of the following could be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: glass is the third exhibit visited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: kites is the fourth exhibit visited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: helmets is the first exhibit visited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: lanterns is the fourth exhibit visited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: masks is the third exhibit visited.

explanations.correct: With jade at 1, glass cannot be at 2 (glass-jade not adjacent). The helmets-icons block plus jade-before-kites and helmets-before-lanterns admit arrangements in which kites sits at 4, 5, or 6. At least one admissible arrangement places kites at 4 (e.g., jade 1, helmets 2, icons 3, kites 4, glass 5, lanterns 6, masks 7).
explanations.A: Glass cannot be at 3 while jade is at 1, because jade-kites ordering together with the remaining constraints leave glass at 4, 5, or 6.
explanations.B: Correct. Kites at 4 is realized (e.g., jade 1, helmets 2, icons 3, kites 4, glass 5, lanterns 6, masks 7).
explanations.C: With jade at 1, helmets cannot occupy position 1.
explanations.D: Lanterns must come after kites and after helmets, and is always at position 5, 6, or 7 when jade is at 1; it never lands at 4.
explanations.E: Masks cannot be at 3 while jade is at 1; glass must precede masks and the remaining slots leave masks at 5 or later.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: kites is the sixth exhibit visited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: glass is the first exhibit visited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: jade is visited at some point before lanterns.

choices.label: D
choices.text: masks is the seventh exhibit visited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: jade is the fifth exhibit visited.

explanations.correct: Jade must precede kites (given), and lanterns must be after kites (given). By transitivity, jade is before kites is before lanterns, so jade precedes lanterns in every valid arrangement.
explanations.A: Kites can sit at 4, 5, or 6, not only 6.
explanations.B: Glass can sit at 1, 3, 4, 5, or 6; not forced to 1.
explanations.C: Correct. Derived from jade-before-kites and kites-before-lanterns.
explanations.D: Masks can sit at several positions including 2, 4, 5, 6, or 7; not forced to 7.
explanations.E: Jade can sit at 1, 3, or 5; not forced to 5.

questions.questionStem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: kites is the fourth exhibit visited.

choices.label: B
choices.text: glass is the third exhibit visited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: helmets is the first exhibit visited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: masks is the fifth exhibit visited.

choices.label: E
choices.text: kites is the third exhibit visited.

explanations.correct: If kites were third, the conditional rule would force masks to 7. But jade must precede kites, so jade sits at 1 or 2. Jade at 2 makes jade adjacent to glass (glass would be at 1), violating the glass-jade non-adjacency rule; jade at 1 leaves positions 2 available only for helmets or icons, and then the helmets-before-lanterns and glass-before-masks constraints leave no valid seat for glass without creating another violation. No arrangement places kites at 3.
explanations.A: Kites at 4 is realized (e.g., glass 5, helmets 2, icons 3, jade 1, kites 4, lanterns 6, masks 7).
explanations.B: Glass at 3 is realized (e.g., glass 3, helmets 1, icons 2, jade 5, kites 6, lanterns 7, masks 4).
explanations.C: Helmets at 1 is realized (e.g., helmets 1, icons 2, jade 3, kites 4, glass 5, lanterns 6, masks 7).
explanations.D: Masks at 5 is realized (e.g., jade 1, helmets 3, icons 2, glass 4, kites 6, lanterns 7, masks 5).
explanations.E: Correct. No assignment satisfies all rules with kites at 3.

lg.scenario: Six runners — Patel, Quinn, Reyes, Sato, Tran, and Uman — will finish a relay training course in some order, first through sixth, with no two runners finishing in the same position. The finishing order conforms to the following conditions. Patel finishes at some point before Quinn. Reyes finishes at some point before Sato. Tran and Uman finish in immediately consecutive positions. Patel does not finish first. Quinn does not finish sixth. If Tran finishes third, then Reyes finishes first.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the finishing order of the runners, from first to sixth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reyes, Patel, Quinn, Sato, Tran, Uman

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reyes, Quinn, Patel, Sato, Tran, Uman

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sato, Patel, Quinn, Reyes, Tran, Uman

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reyes, Tran, Patel, Quinn, Uman, Sato

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reyes, Patel, Sato, Tran, Uman, Quinn

explanations.correct: Patel(2) is before Quinn(3); Reyes(1) is before Sato(4); Tran(5) and Uman(6) are consecutive; Patel is not first; Quinn is not sixth; Tran is not at 3 so the conditional is vacuous. All rules hold.
explanations.A: Correct. Every rule is satisfied.
explanations.B: Quinn is second and Patel is third, so Patel is not before Quinn. Violates the Patel-before-Quinn rule.
explanations.C: Sato is first and Reyes is fourth, so Reyes is not before Sato. Violates the Reyes-before-Sato rule.
explanations.D: Tran is second and Uman is fifth, so they are not in consecutive positions. Violates the Tran-Uman adjacency rule.
explanations.E: Quinn is sixth, which the rules forbid.

questions.questionStem: If Tran finishes first, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patel finishes second.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reyes finishes first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sato finishes sixth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Quinn finishes fourth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uman finishes third.

explanations.correct: If Tran is first, Uman is second (Tran-Uman adjacency). The remaining runners — Patel, Quinn, Reyes, Sato — fill positions 3–6. Patel cannot be first (already taken) and must precede Quinn, and Reyes must precede Sato. Every admissible filling of 3–6 places Sato at position 6.
explanations.A: Patel can finish at 3 or 4; not forced.
explanations.B: Tran is first, so Reyes is not first.
explanations.C: Correct. Every arrangement with Tran first places Sato at 6.
explanations.D: Quinn can finish at 4 or 5; not forced to 4.
explanations.E: Uman is at 2, not 3.

questions.questionStem: If Quinn finishes third, then which one of the following could be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sato finishes fourth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tran finishes first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patel finishes third.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Uman finishes first.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reyes finishes fourth.

explanations.correct: With Quinn at 3 and Patel before Quinn, Patel is at 2 (Patel is not at 1). Reyes then takes 1 (so Reyes precedes Sato), and Sato, Tran, and Uman occupy 4, 5, 6 with Tran-Uman consecutive. Sato at 4 is realized (e.g., Reyes 1, Patel 2, Quinn 3, Sato 4, Tran 5, Uman 6).
explanations.A: Correct. Sato at 4 is realized (e.g., Reyes 1, Patel 2, Quinn 3, Sato 4, Tran 5, Uman 6).
explanations.B: With Reyes forced to 1, Tran cannot finish first.
explanations.C: Patel is forced to 2 (Patel not at 1, Patel before Quinn at 3), so Patel is not at 3.
explanations.D: With Reyes forced to 1, Uman cannot finish first.
explanations.E: Reyes is forced to 1, not 4.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reyes finishes first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Uman finishes second.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tran finishes before Patel.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sato finishes sixth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reyes does not finish sixth.

explanations.correct: Reyes must finish before Sato, so Reyes cannot be last. Therefore Reyes never finishes sixth.
explanations.A: Reyes can finish at 1, 3, 4, or 5; not forced to 1.
explanations.B: Uman can finish at several positions (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 depending on Tran); not forced.
explanations.C: Tran can finish before or after Patel; not forced.
explanations.D: Sato often finishes sixth but can also finish at 2, 3, or 4; not forced.
explanations.E: Correct. Reyes must precede Sato, so Reyes cannot be at 6.

questions.questionStem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patel finishes fourth.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

choices.label: E

explanations.correct: If Reyes finished second, then either Patel takes 1 (forbidden) or someone else takes 1 while Patel is at 3, 4, or 5 — but Reyes must precede Sato, and with Patel blocked from 1 and Reyes at 2, Tran/Uman would need to span position 1 (Tran-Uman adjacent), leaving Sato, Quinn, and Patel for the remaining slots. Testing all such fillings shows every candidate violates either the Patel-before-Quinn rule, the Quinn-not-at-6 rule, or the Tran-at-3 conditional. No valid arrangement places Reyes at 2.
explanations.A: Patel at 4 is realized (e.g., Reyes 1, Tran 2, Uman 3, Patel 4, Quinn 5, Sato 6).
explanations.B: Uman at 1 is realized (e.g., Uman 1, Tran 2, Patel 3, Quinn 4, Reyes 5, Sato 6).
explanations.C: Tran at 3 is realized when Reyes is at 1 (e.g., Reyes 1, Patel 2, Tran 3, Uman 4, Quinn 5, Sato 6).
explanations.D: Sato at 2 is realized (e.g., Reyes 1, Sato 2, Patel 3, Quinn 4, Tran 5, Uman 6).
explanations.E: Correct. No assignment satisfies all rules with Reyes at 2.

lg.scenario: Seven runners — Ortiz, Park, Quinn, Rao, Santos, Tyler, and Unger — finish a marathon in positions first through seventh, with exactly one runner in each position. The finishing order is constrained as follows. Park finishes immediately before Quinn. Rao and Santos finish in consecutive positions, in either order. Tyler finishes before Park. Ortiz finishes after Quinn. Unger does not finish fourth. Tyler and Unger do not finish in consecutive positions. If Park finishes third, then Rao finishes sixth. If Rao finishes before Tyler, then Ortiz finishes seventh.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the order in which the runners finish, from first to seventh?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tyler, Park, Quinn, Ortiz, Rao, Santos, Unger

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tyler, Park, Rao, Santos, Quinn, Ortiz, Unger

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tyler, Park, Quinn, Rao, Unger, Santos, Ortiz

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tyler, Park, Quinn, Unger, Rao, Santos, Ortiz

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unger, Tyler, Rao, Santos, Park, Quinn, Ortiz

explanations.correct: Tyler,Park,Quinn,Ortiz,Rao,Santos,Unger satisfies every rule: Park@2 immediately before Quinn@3; Rao@5 and Santos@6 are consecutive; Tyler@1 is before Park@2; Ortiz@4 is after Quinn@3; Unger@7 is not fourth; Tyler@1 and Unger@7 are not consecutive; Park is not third so the first conditional is vacuous; Rao@5 is after Tyler@1 so the second conditional is vacuous.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Quinn is fifth and Park is second, so they are not in consecutive positions. Violates Park-immediately-before-Quinn.
explanations.C: Rao is fourth and Santos is sixth, so they are not consecutive. Violates the Rao-Santos adjacency rule.
explanations.D: Unger is fourth, which the rules forbid.
explanations.E: Tyler is second and Unger is first, so they are in consecutive positions. Violates the Tyler-Unger not-consecutive rule.

questions.questionStem: If Ortiz finishes fourth, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tyler finishes first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rao finishes fifth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Unger finishes seventh.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Santos finishes sixth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unger finishes fifth.

explanations.correct: With Ortiz fourth, Park and Quinn (a consecutive block) must occur before Ortiz, and Tyler precedes Park. The only way to fit the Tyler-then-Park-then-Quinn chain in positions 1, 2, and 3 is Tyler first, Park second, Quinn third. The Rao-Santos block and Unger fill positions 5-7 in various orders consistent with the Tyler-Unger non-adjacency, but Tyler is always first.
explanations.A: Correct. Tyler must be first.
explanations.B: Rao can be fifth, sixth, or seventh; not forced.
explanations.C: Unger can be fifth or seventh; not forced.
explanations.D: Santos can occupy fifth, sixth, or seventh; not forced.
explanations.E: Unger can be fifth or seventh; not forced.

questions.questionStem: If Unger finishes first, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rao finishes second.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Santos finishes second.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ortiz finishes seventh.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tyler finishes third.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Park finishes fourth.

explanations.correct: If Unger is first, Tyler cannot be second (Tyler-Unger non-adjacent). Tyler must still be before Park, so the Rao-Santos block must occupy two of positions 2 and 3 (they are consecutive). That forces Tyler into position 4, Park into 5, Quinn into 6, and Ortiz into 7. The second conditional (Rao before Tyler triggers Ortiz seventh) is also triggered here.
explanations.A: Rao can be at position 2 or 3 (Rao-Santos block in either order).
explanations.B: Santos can be at position 2 or 3.
explanations.C: Correct. Ortiz must finish seventh.
explanations.D: Tyler must be fourth, not third.
explanations.E: Park must be fifth, not fourth.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Santos finishes first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rao finishes third.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tyler finishes second.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Quinn finishes fifth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unger finishes seventh.

explanations.correct: Tyler must precede Park, and Park is immediately before Quinn. If Tyler were second, Park would need to be at least third and Quinn at least fourth; moreover, position 1 would have to hold an entity other than Tyler, Park, or Quinn, and the Rao-Santos block could not begin at position 1 without being split. Enumerating shows no admissible arrangement places Tyler second.
explanations.A: Santos can finish first (e.g., Santos, Rao, Tyler, Park, Quinn, Unger, Ortiz).
explanations.B: Rao can finish third (e.g., Tyler, Santos, Rao, Park, Quinn, Ortiz, Unger).
explanations.C: Correct. Tyler cannot be second.
explanations.D: Quinn can finish fifth when Park is fourth (e.g., Tyler, Rao, Santos, Park, Quinn, Ortiz, Unger).
explanations.E: Unger can finish seventh (e.g., Tyler, Park, Quinn, Ortiz, Rao, Santos, Unger).

questions.questionStem: If Tyler finishes third, then each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rao finishes first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Santos finishes second.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Park finishes fourth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ortiz finishes sixth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Santos finishes first.

explanations.correct: If Tyler is third, the Rao-Santos block must occupy positions 1 and 2 (the only remaining consecutive pair before Tyler that avoids violating Tyler-Unger non-adjacency). That forces Park@4, Quinn@5, Unger@6, Ortiz@7. Hence Ortiz finishes seventh, never sixth.
explanations.A: Rao can finish first (Rao, Santos, Tyler, Park, Quinn, Unger, Ortiz).
explanations.B: Santos can finish second (Rao, Santos, Tyler, Park, Quinn, Unger, Ortiz).
explanations.C: Park must finish fourth (it is in fact forced), so this could be true.
explanations.D: Correct. Ortiz is forced to seventh when Tyler is third; Ortiz cannot be sixth.
explanations.E: Santos can finish first (Santos, Rao, Tyler, Park, Quinn, Unger, Ortiz).

lg.scenario: A museum audio tour visits exactly eight exhibits — Baroque, Cubism, Dada, Expressionism, Futurism, Gothic, Impressionism, and Japonisme — one exhibit at a time, in positions first through eighth. The sequence is constrained as follows. Cubism is visited immediately before Dada. Gothic is visited immediately before Baroque. Futurism is neither first nor eighth. Impressionism is visited at some point after Dada. Japonisme and Expressionism are not visited in consecutive positions. Gothic is visited before Futurism. Cubism is visited before Futurism. Japonisme is not visited first. Expressionism is not visited eighth. If Cubism is second, then Baroque is sixth. If Expressionism is visited before Gothic, then Impressionism is visited before Baroque.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the order in which the exhibits are visited, from first to eighth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gothic, Baroque, Cubism, Dada, Expressionism, Futurism, Impressionism, Japonisme

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cubism, Dada, Gothic, Expressionism, Baroque, Futurism, Impressionism, Japonisme

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gothic, Baroque, Cubism, Dada, Expressionism, Impressionism, Japonisme, Futurism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gothic, Baroque, Dada, Cubism, Expressionism, Futurism, Impressionism, Japonisme

choices.label: E
choices.text: Gothic, Baroque, Cubism, Dada, Japonisme, Expressionism, Futurism, Impressionism

explanations.correct: Gothic@1 immediately before Baroque@2; Cubism@3 immediately before Dada@4; Futurism@6 is neither first nor eighth; Impressionism@7 is after Dada@4; Japonisme@8 and Expressionism@5 are not adjacent; Gothic and Cubism both precede Futurism; Japonisme is not first; Expressionism is not eighth. Neither conditional is triggered.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Gothic is third and Baroque is fifth, so Gothic is not immediately before Baroque.
explanations.C: Futurism is eighth, which the rules forbid.
explanations.D: Dada is third and Cubism is fourth, so Cubism is not before Dada.
explanations.E: Japonisme is fifth and Expressionism is sixth, so they are visited in consecutive positions.

questions.questionStem: If Cubism is visited first, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dada is visited second.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Baroque is visited fourth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Futurism is visited sixth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Impressionism is visited eighth.

explanations.correct: Since Cubism is immediately before Dada, placing Cubism at 1 forces Dada into position 2.
explanations.A: Correct. Dada must be second.
explanations.B: Gothic can be at 3, 4, or 5 depending on where the Gothic-Baroque block fits.
explanations.C: Baroque can be fourth, fifth, or sixth.
explanations.D: Futurism is in {5, 6, 7}; it is not forced to 6.
explanations.E: Impressionism can be anywhere after Dada; it is not forced to 8.

questions.questionStem: If Expressionism is visited first, then which one of the following must be true?

explanations.correct: Expressionism first triggers the second conditional: Expressionism before Gothic implies Impressionism before Baroque. With Expressionism at 1, the Cubism-Dada block and the Gothic-Baroque block each occupy two consecutive slots; pinning Impressionism before Baroque forces the unique arrangement Expressionism, Cubism, Dada, Impressionism, Gothic, Baroque, Futurism, Japonisme.
explanations.A: Correct. Cubism must be second.
explanations.B: Gothic is fifth in the forced arrangement, not third.
explanations.C: Impressionism is fourth in the forced arrangement, not fifth.
explanations.D: Futurism is seventh in the forced arrangement, not sixth.
explanations.E: Japonisme is eighth in the forced arrangement, not seventh.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Japonisme is visited sixth.

explanations.correct: Futurism must come after both Cubism and Gothic, each of which heads a two-exhibit block. The earliest that Futurism can appear, once both blocks precede it, is position 5. Thus Futurism cannot be at position 4.
explanations.A: Baroque can be second (Gothic first, Baroque second).
explanations.B: Gothic can be fifth when it heads the Gothic-Baroque block in positions 5-6.
explanations.C: Correct. Futurism cannot be fourth.
explanations.D: Expressionism can be third (e.g., Gothic, Baroque, Expressionism, Cubism, Dada, Futurism, Impressionism, Japonisme).
explanations.E: Japonisme can be sixth in multiple arrangements.

questions.questionStem: If Gothic is visited third, then which one of the following must be true?

explanations.B: Expressionism can be at 5, 6, or 7.
explanations.C: Futurism can be 5, 6, or 7.
explanations.D: Impressionism can be anywhere from 5 through 8.
explanations.E: Japonisme can be 5, 7, or 8.

lg.scenario: Exactly seven floats — Lions, Mariners, Nomads, Oaks, Phoenix, Raptors, and Sentinels — pass a reviewing stand in positions first through seventh, with exactly one float in each position. The order is constrained as follows. Nomads passes immediately before Oaks. Lions passes at some point before Mariners. Lions passes at some point before Nomads. Oaks passes at some point before Mariners. Phoenix is neither third nor fifth. Raptors and Sentinels do not pass in consecutive positions. If Lions is first, then Sentinels is fourth. If Phoenix passes before Lions, then Raptors is seventh.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be the order in which the floats pass the reviewing stand, from first to seventh?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lions, Nomads, Oaks, Sentinels, Mariners, Phoenix, Raptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sentinels, Raptors, Lions, Nomads, Oaks, Mariners, Phoenix

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sentinels, Lions, Mariners, Nomads, Oaks, Phoenix, Raptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Raptors, Lions, Phoenix, Nomads, Oaks, Mariners, Sentinels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lions, Nomads, Oaks, Phoenix, Sentinels, Mariners, Raptors

explanations.correct: Nomads@2 immediately before Oaks@3; Lions@1 precedes Mariners@5, Nomads@2, and (via Oaks) the rest; Oaks@3 precedes Mariners@5; Phoenix@6 is neither third nor fifth; Raptors@7 and Sentinels@4 are not consecutive; Lions@1 triggers cond1 which forces Sentinels@4, satisfied.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Raptors is second and Sentinels is first, so they pass in consecutive positions.
explanations.C: Oaks is fifth and Mariners is third, so Oaks is not before Mariners.
explanations.D: Phoenix is third, which the rules forbid.
explanations.E: Lions is first but Sentinels is fifth, not fourth, violating the Lions-first conditional.

questions.questionStem: If Phoenix passes first, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lions passes second.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Raptors passes seventh.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oaks passes fourth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nomads passes third.

explanations.correct: Phoenix first means Phoenix is before Lions, triggering the second conditional: Raptors must be seventh.
explanations.A: Lions can be second or third.
explanations.B: Correct. Raptors must be seventh.
explanations.C: Sentinels can be second, third, or fifth.
explanations.D: Oaks can be fourth or fifth.
explanations.E: Nomads can be third or fourth.

questions.questionStem: If Raptors passes first, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lions passes second.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nomads passes third.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phoenix passes sixth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sentinels passes third.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mariners passes fifth.

explanations.correct: Raptors first forces Lions into position 2: Lions must precede Nomads and Mariners, so Lions is in {1,2,3}; but Raptors@1 blocks position 1, and Lions cannot be at 3 (which would require Nomads@4 and leave no valid non-adjacent place for Sentinels given the other constraints). Enumerating the solutions confirms Lions is always second.
explanations.A: Correct. Lions must pass second.
explanations.B: Nomads can be third, fourth, or fifth.
explanations.C: Phoenix can be at 4, 6, or 7.
explanations.D: Sentinels can be at 3, 4, 5, or 6.
explanations.E: Mariners can be fifth, sixth, or seventh.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following CANNOT be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sentinels passes first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Raptors passes third.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lions passes fourth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oaks passes fifth.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phoenix passes seventh.

explanations.correct: Lions must precede Nomads, Oaks, and Mariners, pinning Lions into one of the first three positions. Lions at 4 would leave only three later slots for Nomads, Oaks, and Mariners; but Nomads-Oaks is a block and must itself precede Mariners, which is impossible in three slots when Lions also sits at 4. So Lions at 4 is unreachable.
explanations.A: Sentinels can be first.
explanations.B: Raptors can be third.
explanations.C: Correct. Lions cannot pass fourth.
explanations.D: Oaks can be fifth.
explanations.E: Phoenix can be seventh.

questions.questionStem: If Nomads passes fifth, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lions passes first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Raptors passes first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mariners passes seventh.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sentinels passes third.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Phoenix passes sixth.

explanations.correct: Nomads@5 forces Oaks@6 (adjacency) and Mariners@7 (since Oaks precedes Mariners and only position 7 remains after 5-6 are taken). Lions@2 also follows because Lions must precede Nomads and Phoenix is not first (Phoenix first would trigger cond2 and place Raptors@7, conflict); but Mariners@7 is the one forced across all worlds.
explanations.A: Lions is second in both arrangements where Nomads is fifth, not first.
explanations.B: Raptors can be first or third depending on Sentinels placement.
explanations.C: Correct. Mariners must pass seventh.
explanations.D: Sentinels can be first or third.
explanations.E: Phoenix is fourth when Nomads is fifth, not sixth.

lg.scenario: Exactly six chefs — Alvarez, Bello, Chen, Dufresne, Engel, and Fiori — will each be assigned to exactly one of two shifts at a restaurant: Brunch and Dinner. Each shift is assigned exactly three chefs. The assignment must satisfy the following conditions. Alvarez is assigned to the Brunch shift. Bello and Chen are assigned to different shifts.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be a complete and accurate assignment of chefs to shifts?

choices.label: E

explanations.correct: Alvarez is assigned to Brunch. Bello (Brunch) and Chen (Dinner) are assigned to different shifts. Each shift has exactly three chefs.

explanations.B: Alvarez is assigned to Dinner, violating the rule that Alvarez is assigned to Brunch.
explanations.C: Bello and Chen are both assigned to Brunch, violating the rule that they are assigned to different shifts.

questions.questionStem: If Fiori is assigned to the Brunch shift, then which one of the following must be true?

explanations.B: Chen could be assigned to Brunch or Dinner.

explanations.D: Engel must be assigned to Dinner.

explanations.B: Bello and Chen must be assigned to different shifts.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Bello and Chen must be assigned to different shifts.

lg.scenario: Exactly six students — Park, Qiu, Reyes, Sousa, Tran, and Udo — will each be placed in exactly one of two sections of a chemistry course: Lab and Seminar. Each section contains exactly three students. The placement must satisfy the following conditions. Park is placed in the Lab section. Qiu and Reyes are placed in different sections. If Sousa is placed in the Seminar section, then Tran is placed in the Lab section.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be a complete and accurate placement of students in sections?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lab: Qiu, Reyes, Sousa; Seminar: Park, Tran, Udo

choices.text: Lab: Park, Qiu, Reyes; Seminar: Sousa, Tran, Udo

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lab: Park, Qiu, Sousa, Tran; Seminar: Reyes, Udo

explanations.correct: Park is in Lab. Qiu (Lab) and Reyes (Seminar) are in different sections. Sousa is in Lab, so the conditional's antecedent is false and the conditional is vacuously satisfied. Each section contains exactly three students.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Park is placed in Seminar, violating the rule that Park is placed in Lab.
explanations.C: Qiu and Reyes are both placed in Lab, violating the rule that they are placed in different sections.
explanations.D: Sousa is placed in Seminar but Tran is also placed in Seminar, violating the rule that if Sousa is in Seminar then Tran is in Lab.
explanations.E: Lab contains four students and Seminar contains two, violating the requirement that each section contains exactly three students.

explanations.B: Reyes could be in either section.

That accounts for two of Lab's three slots; the third Lab slot is filled by Sousa or Tran, whichever is forced in by the conditional. In every valid placement, Udo ends up in Seminar because Lab's three slots are always taken by Park, one of {Qiu, Reyes}, and one of {Sousa, Tran}.
explanations.A: Qiu could be in either section.
explanations.B: Reyes could be in either section.
explanations.C: Sousa could be in either section.
explanations.D: Tran could be in either section.

So the last Lab slot holds Sousa xor Tran — the two cannot share a section. If Sousa is in Seminar, the conditional forces Tran to Lab; if Sousa is in Lab, then Lab is full and Tran goes to Seminar. lg.scenario: Exactly six volunteers — Ames, Barr, Cho, Doyle, Ek, and Flores — will be assigned to exactly one of two neighborhood cleanup crews: Harbor and Maple. Each crew is assigned exactly three volunteers. The assignment must satisfy the following conditions. Barr and Cho are assigned to different crews. If Flores is assigned to the Harbor crew, then Cho is assigned to the Maple crew. If Ames is assigned to the Maple crew, then Doyle is also assigned to the Maple crew.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be a complete and accurate assignment of volunteers to crews?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Harbor: Ames, Barr, Doyle; Maple: Cho, Ek, Flores

choices.label: B
choices.text: Harbor: Ames, Barr, Cho; Maple: Doyle, Ek, Flores

choices.label: C
choices.text: Harbor: Barr, Doyle, Ek; Maple: Ames, Cho, Flores

choices.label: D
choices.text: Harbor: Cho, Ek, Flores; Maple: Ames, Barr, Doyle

choices.label: E
choices.text: Harbor: Ames, Barr, Doyle, Ek; Maple: Cho, Flores

explanations.correct: Barr (Harbor) and Cho (Maple) are in different crews. Flores is in Maple, so the Flores-Harbor conditional is vacuously satisfied. Ames is in Harbor, so the Ames-Maple conditional is vacuously satisfied. Each crew has exactly three volunteers.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Barr and Cho are both in Harbor. Violates the rule that Barr and Cho are in different crews.
explanations.C: Ames is in Maple but Doyle is in Harbor. Violates the rule that if Ames is in Maple then Doyle is in Maple.
explanations.D: Flores is in Harbor but Cho is also in Harbor. Violates the rule that if Flores is in Harbor then Cho is in Maple.
explanations.E: Harbor has four volunteers. Violates the requirement that each crew has exactly three volunteers.

questions.questionStem: If Ames is assigned to the Maple crew, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Barr is assigned to the Maple crew.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cho is assigned to the Harbor crew.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Flores is assigned to the Harbor crew.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Doyle is assigned to the Harbor crew.

explanations.correct: If Ames is in Maple, Doyle must also be in Maple. Since Maple already has Ames and Doyle, Cho must take the third Maple slot (Barr and Cho are in different crews and only one Harbor slot remains after Barr fills one of Barr/Cho). Working it out: Maple contains Ames, Doyle, and Cho; Harbor must therefore contain Barr, Ek, and Flores. So Flores is in Harbor.
explanations.A: Barr must be in Harbor, not Maple (Barr and Cho differ, and Cho is in Maple).
explanations.B: Cho must be in Maple to fill the third Maple slot.
explanations.C: Ek must be in Harbor to fill out that crew.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Doyle must be in Maple because of the Ames-Maple conditional.

questions.questionStem: If Flores is assigned to the Harbor crew, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ames is assigned to the Harbor crew.

choices.text: Barr is assigned to the Maple crew.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Doyle is assigned to the Maple crew.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cho is assigned to the Harbor crew.

explanations.correct: If Flores is in Harbor, the first conditional forces Cho into Maple. Barr (who must be in a different crew from Cho) is therefore in Harbor. Harbor now holds Flores and Barr plus one more; Maple holds Cho plus two more. Whichever of Ames and Ek takes the last Harbor slot, the other goes to Maple along with Doyle — and in every case Doyle ends up in Maple (if Ames took Maple, the second conditional forces Doyle to Maple; if Ames took Harbor, Maple still needs Doyle alongside Cho and Ek).
explanations.A: Ames could be in Harbor or Maple.
explanations.B: Barr must be in Harbor because Cho is in Maple.
explanations.C: Ek could be in Harbor (with Ames in Maple) or Maple.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Cho must be in Maple because Flores is in Harbor.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Barr and Cho are both assigned to the Harbor crew.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Flores is assigned to the Harbor crew and Cho is assigned to the Harbor crew.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ames is assigned to the Maple crew and Doyle is assigned to the Harbor crew.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ek is assigned to the Harbor crew.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Barr, Cho, and Ek are all assigned to the Harbor crew.

explanations.correct: For example, the assignment Harbor: Ames, Barr, Ek; Maple: Cho, Doyle, Flores satisfies every rule: Barr and Cho are in different crews, Flores is in Maple (so the Flores conditional is vacuous), Ames is in Harbor (so the Ames conditional is vacuous), and each crew has three members.
explanations.A: Barr and Cho must be in different crews.
explanations.B: If Flores is in Harbor, Cho must be in Maple; this combination is forbidden.
explanations.C: If Ames is in Maple, Doyle must also be in Maple.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Barr and Cho must be in different crews, so they cannot both be in Harbor.

questions.questionStem: Each of the following could be true EXCEPT:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ames is assigned to the Maple crew.

choices.text: Barr is assigned to the Maple crew.

choices.text: Cho is assigned to the Harbor crew.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ek is assigned to the Harbor crew.

explanations.correct: If Flores is in Harbor, then Cho must be in Maple. Barr must then be in Harbor (different from Cho). Harbor thus contains Flores and Barr and needs one more slot; Maple contains Cho and needs two more. If Doyle were also in Harbor, Harbor would have Flores, Barr, Doyle — full — and Maple would need Ames and Ek to join Cho. But then Ames is in Maple, which forces Doyle into Maple, contradicting Doyle in Harbor. So Doyle cannot be in Harbor when Flores is in Harbor.
explanations.A: Possible — e.g., Harbor: Barr, Ek, Flores; Maple: Ames, Cho, Doyle.
explanations.B: Possible — e.g., Harbor: Ames, Cho, Doyle; Maple: Barr, Ek, Flores.
explanations.C: Possible — e.g., Harbor: Ames, Cho, Doyle; Maple: Barr, Ek, Flores.
explanations.D: Correct — this combination cannot occur.
explanations.E: Possible — e.g., Harbor: Ames, Barr, Ek; Maple: Cho, Doyle, Flores.

explanations.B: Reyes could enroll in either Biology or Civics.

lg.scenario: Exactly eight jurors — Ito, Jain, Klein, Lam, Mori, Nash, Ota, and Park — will be assigned to exactly one of two trial pools: North and South. Each pool is assigned exactly four jurors. The assignment must satisfy the following conditions. Ito is assigned to the North pool. Jain and Klein are assigned to different pools. Lam and Mori are assigned to the same pool. Exactly two of Nash, Ota, and Park are assigned to the North pool. If Jain is assigned to the North pool, then Lam is assigned to the South pool.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following could be a complete and accurate assignment of jurors to pools?

choices.label: A
choices.text: North: Ito, Jain, Nash, Ota; South: Klein, Lam, Mori, Park

choices.label: B
choices.text: North: Jain, Klein, Lam, Mori; South: Ito, Nash, Ota, Park

choices.label: C
choices.text: North: Ito, Jain, Klein, Nash; South: Lam, Mori, Ota, Park

choices.label: D
choices.text: North: Ito, Klein, Lam, Nash; South: Jain, Mori, Ota, Park

choices.label: E
choices.text: North: Ito, Klein, Lam, Mori; South: Jain, Nash, Ota, Park

explanations.correct: Ito is in North. Jain (North) and Klein (South) are in different pools. Lam and Mori are both in South. Exactly two of Nash, Ota, and Park (Nash and Ota) are in North. Jain is in North, so by the conditional Lam must be in South — and Lam is in South. Each pool has four jurors.
explanations.A: Correct.
explanations.B: Ito is in South, violating the rule that Ito is in North.
explanations.C: Jain and Klein are both in North, violating the rule that they are in different pools.
explanations.D: Lam is in North and Mori is in South, violating the rule that they are assigned to the same pool.
explanations.E: None of Nash, Ota, and Park are in North, violating the rule that exactly two of them are in the North pool.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mori is assigned to the South pool.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Klein is assigned to the North pool.

explanations.correct: If Jain is in North, then Lam is in South (by the conditional), and Mori is in the same pool as Lam, so Mori is in South.
explanations.A: Nash could be in North or South (two of Nash, Ota, Park are in North).
explanations.B: Ota could be in North or South.
explanations.C: Park could be in North or South.
explanations.D: Correct.
explanations.E: Klein is in the opposite pool from Jain; since Jain is in North, Klein is in South.

questions.questionStem: If Park is assigned to the South pool, then which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jain is assigned to the North pool.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Klein is assigned to the South pool.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nash is assigned to the North pool.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lam is assigned to the North pool.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ota is assigned to the South pool.

explanations.correct: Exactly two of Nash, Ota, and Park are in the North pool. If Park is in South, then both Nash and Ota must be in North.
explanations.A: Jain could be in either pool.
explanations.B: Klein could be in either pool.
explanations.C: Correct.
explanations.D: Lam is always in the same pool as Mori, and because Ito is in North, the distribution constraints leave Lam and Mori together in South in every valid scenario.
explanations.E: Ota must be in North when Park is in South.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following must be true?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jain is assigned to the South pool.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Klein is assigned to the North pool.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lam is assigned to the South pool.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nash is assigned to the North pool.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ota is assigned to the South pool.

explanations.correct: Ito is in North. Exactly two of Nash, Ota, and Park are in North, so one of them is in South. That means North contains Ito plus two of {Nash, Ota, Park} plus one of {Jain, Klein} — four total. The remaining four go to South: the third of {Nash, Ota, Park}, the other of {Jain, Klein}, and both Lam and Mori (who must be together). lg.scenario: Exactly nine interns — Asano, Bello, Choi, Diaz, Ellis, Fadel, Gur, Huang, and Imura — will be assigned to exactly one of three hospital departments: Cardiology, Dermatology, and ER. Diaz and Ellis are assigned to the same department. Choi is not assigned to ER. Fadel is not assigned to ER. If Fadel is assigned to Cardiology, then Gur is assigned to ER. If Gur is assigned to Dermatology, then Huang is assigned to Cardiology. If Imura is assigned to Cardiology, then Diaz is assigned to ER.
